The dataset has a known, small number of clusters already established by prior supervised annotation — a direct classifier comparison suffices rather than recursive subtype re-discovery. Input is single-cell data requiring batch integration at scale (millions of cells); the article notes integration with scanorama and geometric sketching was only proposed, not demonstrated. Computational time is severely constrained — the article lists RCC's computational time (tied to consensus clustering with k-means) as a limitation. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 A validation workflow for reproducing published RCC (Recursive Consensus Clustering) subtype discoveries on bulk transcriptomic datasets (Ivy GAP, GTEx, TCGA pan-cancer) by re-running RCC_clus and its companion functions and checking recovered cluster counts and subtype compositions against the reported structures. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-67016-3
skills.summary: A validation workflow for reproducing published RCC (Recursive Consensus Clustering) subtype discoveries on bulk transcriptomic datasets (Ivy GAP, GTEx, TCGA pan-cancer) by re-running RCC_clus and its companion functions and checking recovered cluster counts and subtype compositions against the reported structures.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has a known, small number of clusters already established by prior supervised annotation — a direct classifier comparison suffices rather than recursive subtype re-discovery. Input is single-cell data requiring batch integration at scale (millions of cells); the article notes integration with scanorama and geometric sketching was only proposed, not demonstrated. Computational time is severely constrained — the article lists RCC's computational time (tied to consensus clustering with k-means) as a limitation.

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how sensitive a scRNA-seq clustering method is to cell subsampling: run each method on 10 random 95%-cell subsets, compute ARI/NMI per repeat against ground truth, and compare per-method medians.
skills.name: clustering-robustness-subset-resampling
skills.search_text: clustering-robustness-subset-resampling Use when you need to quantify how sensitive a scRNA-seq clustering method is to cell subsampling: run each method on 10 random 95%-cell subsets, compute ARI/NMI per repeat against ground truth, and compare per-method medians. The input is not labeled single-cell expression data (no ground-truth cell-type labels), since ARI/NMI against ground truth cannot be computed The goal is a single clustering run on the full dataset rather than a subsampling-based robustness comparison across multiple methods http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Evaluates scRNA-seq clustering robustness by repeatedly clustering randomly sampled 95% cell subsets (10 repeats) and comparing median ARI/NMI across methods. In the scAce paper this demonstrated scAce attains the highest median ARI and NMI among ten clustering methods on simulated data. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad546
skills.summary: Evaluates scRNA-seq clustering robustness by repeatedly clustering randomly sampled 95% cell subsets (10 repeats) and comparing median ARI/NMI across methods. In the scAce paper this demonstrated scAce attains the highest median ARI and NMI among ten clustering methods on simulated data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not labeled single-cell expression data (no ground-truth cell-type labels), since ARI/NMI against ground truth cannot be computed The goal is a single clustering run on the full dataset rather than a subsampling-based robustness comparison across multiple methods

skills.description: Use when clustering single-cell (e.g., PBMC scRNA-seq) data on a KNN/adaptive-kernel affinity matrix and a deterministic, assumption-light label-propagation procedure is needed that guarantees every vertex receives exactly one cluster label without a predefined cluster count.
skills.name: clustering-seed-selection-strategy
skills.search_text: clustering-seed-selection-strategy Use when clustering single-cell (e.g., PBMC scRNA-seq) data on a KNN/adaptive-kernel affinity matrix and a deterministic, assumption-light label-propagation procedure is needed that guarantees every vertex receives exactly one cluster label without a predefined cluster count. When the data has only one cluster in it — Monte Carlo internal validation cannot accurately estimate uncertainty since every data point can only receive one type of label When distances are dominated by high dimensionality — the method is sensitive to high dimensionality because it mimics a low-dimensional fire propagation process, and the curse of dimensionality degrades clustering as distances become more uniform When a fixed, reproducible number of validation trials is required — the number of Monte Carlo trials varies with the number of clusters in the data Deterministic seed-selection strategy from Forest Fire Clustering (Chen et al., Nature Communications 2022): labels are iteratively cast on a seed vertex and propagated through an affinity graph until equilibrium, and each subsequent seed is chosen as the data point that experienced the lowest heat from the previous cluster, repeating until every vertex is labeled. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-31107-8
skills.summary: Deterministic seed-selection strategy from Forest Fire Clustering (Chen et al., Nature Communications 2022): labels are iteratively cast on a seed vertex and propagated through an affinity graph until equilibrium, and each subsequent seed is chosen as the data point that experienced the lowest heat from the previous cluster, repeating until every vertex is labeled.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the data has only one cluster in it — Monte Carlo internal validation cannot accurately estimate uncertainty since every data point can only receive one type of label When distances are dominated by high dimensionality — the method is sensitive to high dimensionality because it mimics a low-dimensional fire propagation process, and the curse of dimensionality degrades clustering as distances become more uniform When a fixed, reproducible number of validation trials is required — the number of Monte Carlo trials varies with the number of clusters in the data

skills.description: Use when many candidate clusterings of a trajectory-containing single-cell dataset must be ranked and compared by selection criteria (connectivity+VRC, ASW, VRC, random) to pick clusterings for MST-based trajectory inference.
skills.name: clustering-selection-criteria-ranking
skills.search_text: clustering-selection-criteria-ranking Use when many candidate clusterings of a trajectory-containing single-cell dataset must be ranked and compared by selection criteria (connectivity+VRC, ASW, VRC, random) to pick clusterings for MST-based trajectory inference. The dataset contains extremely rare and extremely prevalent cell types simultaneously, where k-medoids may not work properly and manual cluster merging is needed The trajectory of interest is disconnected, contains cycles, or requires correct pseudotime for a multi-root (converging) trajectory, which Totem/dynplot cannot handle Only a single pre-existing clustering is available and no ranking over many clusterings is intended — use direct Slingshot MST construction instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Ranks many k-medoids (CLARA) clusterings of single-cell data by alternative criteria — Totem cell connectivity combined with the Calinski-Harabasz (VRC) score, average silhouette width (ASW), VRC alone, and a random baseline — to select clusterings for trajectory construction and compare which criterion yields the best-performing inferred trajectories. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad515
skills.summary: Ranks many k-medoids (CLARA) clusterings of single-cell data by alternative criteria — Totem cell connectivity combined with the Calinski-Harabasz (VRC) score, average silhouette width (ASW), VRC alone, and a random baseline — to select clusterings for trajectory construction and compare which criterion yields the best-performing inferred trajectories.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset contains extremely rare and extremely prevalent cell types simultaneously, where k-medoids may not work properly and manual cluster merging is needed The trajectory of interest is disconnected, contains cycles, or requires correct pseudotime for a multi-root (converging) trajectory, which Totem/dynplot cannot handle Only a single pre-existing clustering is available and no ranking over many clusterings is intended — use direct Slingshot MST construction instead

skills.description: Use when a Totem-style trajectory pipeline has produced thousands of candidate clusterings and you must automatically pick which clustering(s) to feed into Slingshot MST construction, rather than hand-picking a biologically sensible model.
skills.name: clustering-selection-for-trajectory-inference
skills.search_text: clustering-selection-for-trajectory-inference Use when a Totem-style trajectory pipeline has produced thousands of candidate clusterings and you must automatically pick which clustering(s) to feed into Slingshot MST construction, rather than hand-picking a biologically sensible model. The input is a raw single-cell expression matrix or low-dimensional embedding without prior clustering generation — clustering selection presupposes a pool of candidate clusterings and a computed cell-connectivity vector. The data contain a disconnected trajectory or trajectories with cycles, which Totem cannot generate. The dataset mixes extremely rare and extremely prevalent cell types, where k-medoids fails and the connectivity-based ranking would be unreliable. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Ranks a large pool of candidate CLARA k-medoids clusterings using the Calinski-Harabasz variance ratio criterion computed on the one-dimensional cell-connectivity vector, then selects the top-ranked clustering(s) whose cells have similar connectivity for constructing the MST of a tree-shaped trajectory in Totem. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad515
skills.summary: Ranks a large pool of candidate CLARA k-medoids clusterings using the Calinski-Harabasz variance ratio criterion computed on the one-dimensional cell-connectivity vector, then selects the top-ranked clustering(s) whose cells have similar connectivity for constructing the MST of a tree-shaped trajectory in Totem.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a raw single-cell expression matrix or low-dimensional embedding without prior clustering generation — clustering selection presupposes a pool of candidate clusterings and a computed cell-connectivity vector. The data contain a disconnected trajectory or trajectories with cycles, which Totem cannot generate. The dataset mixes extremely rare and extremely prevalent cell types, where k-medoids fails and the connectivity-based ranking would be unreliable.

skills.description: Use when integration quality of uniPort-embedded scATAC/scRNA (or other single-cell) datasets must be quantified by Silhouette plus ARI, NMI and F1 to compare modality-linking or cell-type-removal scenarios.
skills.name: clustering-silhouette-assessment
skills.search_text: clustering-silhouette-assessment Use when integration quality of uniPort-embedded scATAC/scRNA (or other single-cell) datasets must be quantified by Silhouette plus ARI, NMI and F1 to compare modality-linking or cell-type-removal scenarios. When cells are paired across modalities and you need vertical integration (mode='v') with matched-cell evaluation rather than label-transfer-free clustering metrics When only the global OT plan is needed (save_OT=True) and no cell-type/clustering assessment is required http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3934 Evaluates uniPort multi-omics integration quality by computing the Silhouette coefficient on the shared latent-space embeddings and combining it with ARI+NMI+F1 from kNN label transfer, e.g. reaching 0.676/0.688 Silhouette on UBM-ATAC/UBM-RNA mouse spleen scATAC-scRNA integrations. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-35094-8
skills.summary: Evaluates uniPort multi-omics integration quality by computing the Silhouette coefficient on the shared latent-space embeddings and combining it with ARI+NMI+F1 from kNN label transfer, e.g. reaching 0.676/0.688 Silhouette on UBM-ATAC/UBM-RNA mouse spleen scATAC-scRNA integrations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When cells are paired across modalities and you need vertical integration (mode='v') with matched-cell evaluation rather than label-transfer-free clustering metrics When only the global OT plan is needed (save_OT=True) and no cell-type/clustering assessment is required

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a dimensionality reduction or clustering variant on scRNA-seq embeddings and you need quantitative agreement scores (ECS, kNN-overlap) against ground-truth labels or a reference method's embedding.
skills.name: clustering-similarity-metric-computation
skills.search_text: clustering-similarity-metric-computation Use when benchmarking a dimensionality reduction or clustering variant on scRNA-seq embeddings and you need quantitative agreement scores (ECS, kNN-overlap) against ground-truth labels or a reference method's embedding. Input is raw count data that has not yet been preprocessed and embedded — QC via scLENS.preprocess and the scLENS/scLENS-med runs must precede metric computation No ground-truth labels and no reference embedding exist, since both ECS and kNN-overlap are defined relative to a ground truth or a reference method http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Computes embedding-quality metrics — element-centric similarity (ECS) against ground-truth labels and average kNN-overlap across k from 5 to 50 — to quantify whether a modified scLENS variant (e.g., median scaling) preserves dimensionality reduction performance. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-47884-3
skills.summary: Computes embedding-quality metrics — element-centric similarity (ECS) against ground-truth labels and average kNN-overlap across k from 5 to 50 — to quantify whether a modified scLENS variant (e.g., median scaling) preserves dimensionality reduction performance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw count data that has not yet been preprocessed and embedded — QC via scLENS.preprocess and the scLENS/scLENS-med runs must precede metric computation No ground-truth labels and no reference embedding exist, since both ECS and kNN-overlap are defined relative to a ground truth or a reference method

skills.description: Use when comparing unsupervised clustering methods on droplet-based scRNA-seq data and you need perturbation-based stability (APN) and tightness (silhouette width) metrics, as in BAMM-SC benchmarking on human PBMC, mouse lung, and human skin datasets.
skills.name: clustering-stability-assessment
skills.search_text: clustering-stability-assessment Use when comparing unsupervised clustering methods on droplet-based scRNA-seq data and you need perturbation-based stability (APN) and tightness (silhouette width) metrics, as in BAMM-SC benchmarking on human PBMC, mouse lung, and human skin datasets. You have ground-truth cell labels — use clustering accuracy metrics such as adjustedRandIndex instead of perturbation-based APN/silhouette stability Your goal is rare cell type identification — the gene filtering step (removing genes with excessive zeros and dropping 100 HVGs) may be problematic for rare cell types Input is already a stability/tightness metrics table rather than raw UMI count matrices requiring clustering http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Quantifies cluster stability via average proportion of nonoverlap (APN) and cluster tightness via silhouette width by rerunning a clustering method (e.g., BAMM-SC) on perturbed gene sets and comparing memberships to a reference run. This reproduces the benchmarking logic of Supplementary Tables 7-8 comparing BAMM-SC against nine competing methods. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-09639-3
skills.summary: Quantifies cluster stability via average proportion of nonoverlap (APN) and cluster tightness via silhouette width by rerunning a clustering method (e.g., BAMM-SC) on perturbed gene sets and comparing memberships to a reference run. This reproduces the benchmarking logic of Supplementary Tables 7-8 comparing BAMM-SC against nine competing methods.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have ground-truth cell labels — use clustering accuracy metrics such as adjustedRandIndex instead of perturbation-based APN/silhouette stability Your goal is rare cell type identification — the gene filtering step (removing genes with excessive zeros and dropping 100 HVGs) may be problematic for rare cell types Input is already a stability/tightness metrics table rather than raw UMI count matrices requiring clustering

skills.description: Use when genotype data may have been binarized with the wrong encoding and you must decide whether HOGImine's additive-encoding mode better recovers the planted phenotype association than binary-encoding mode.
skills.name: cmh-pvalue-comparison-across-encodings
skills.search_text: cmh-pvalue-comparison-across-encodings Use when genotype data may have been binarized with the wrong encoding and you must decide whether HOGImine's additive-encoding mode better recovers the planted phenotype association than binary-encoding mode. The correct binarization is already known and matches the phenotype's encoding mechanism — just run the matching binary-encoding mode directly. Markers are natively additive-encoded (0/1/2 allele counts) with no binarization ambiguity — the additive-mode run alone is sufficient; no cross-encoding comparison is needed. The goal is significant-interval discovery with covariate conditioning in FastCMH's CMH framework on purely binary features rather than encoding-mode comparison in HOGImine. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 A benchmarking skill for HOGImine that quantifies the loss of statistical power caused by applying the wrong binary encoding (e.g., dominant) to data whose phenotype signal follows another encoding (e.g., recessive), by comparing significant-pattern counts and smallest CMH p-values between binary-encoding and additive-encoding runs at k=1,2. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad273
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill for HOGImine that quantifies the loss of statistical power caused by applying the wrong binary encoding (e.g., dominant) to data whose phenotype signal follows another encoding (e.g., recessive), by comparing significant-pattern counts and smallest CMH p-values between binary-encoding and additive-encoding runs at k=1,2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The correct binarization is already known and matches the phenotype's encoding mechanism — just run the matching binary-encoding mode directly. Markers are natively additive-encoded (0/1/2 allele counts) with no binarization ambiguity — the additive-mode run alone is sufficient; no cross-encoding comparison is needed. The goal is significant-interval discovery with covariate conditioning in FastCMH's CMH framework on purely binary features rather than encoding-mode comparison in HOGImine.

skills.description: Use when comparing the statistical power of significant-pattern mining methods (e.g. HOGImine vs SiNIMin vs FastCMH) on synthetic binary genotype data, where the goal is to count significant patterns or extract minimum CMH p-values per method under a fixed FWER such as 0.05.
skills.name: cmh-pvalue-significance-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cmh-pvalue-significance-benchmarking Use when comparing the statistical power of significant-pattern mining methods (e.g. HOGImine vs SiNIMin vs FastCMH) on synthetic binary genotype data, where the goal is to count significant patterns or extract minimum CMH p-values per method under a fixed FWER such as 0.05. The goal is discovering associations in real biological datasets with known covariate structure (e.g. FastCMH's categorical covariate conditioning) rather than benchmarking statistical power on synthetic data. The markers are additive-encoded rather than binary, and the question is not a power comparison of binary-encoded synthetic benchmarks. Only a single method needs to be run for discovery, with no comparison against SiNIMin or FastCMH baselines required. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmarks statistical power of genetic meta-marker discovery tools (HOGImine, SiNIMin, FastCMH) by counting significant patterns under FWER control at alpha=0.05 on synthetic binary-encoded genotype/label datasets, comparing how higher-order gene interactions (k>=2) yield more discoveries than pairwise-baseline miners. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad273
skills.summary: Benchmarks statistical power of genetic meta-marker discovery tools (HOGImine, SiNIMin, FastCMH) by counting significant patterns under FWER control at alpha=0.05 on synthetic binary-encoded genotype/label datasets, comparing how higher-order gene interactions (k>=2) yield more discoveries than pairwise-baseline miners.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is discovering associations in real biological datasets with known covariate structure (e.g. FastCMH's categorical covariate conditioning) rather than benchmarking statistical power on synthetic data. The markers are additive-encoded rather than binary, and the question is not a power comparison of binary-encoded synthetic benchmarks. Only a single method needs to be run for discovery, with no comparison against SiNIMin or FastCMH baselines required.

skills.description: Use when comparing significant meta-marker/interval outputs from CMH-based miners (HOGImine, SiNIMin, FastCMH) on the same binary-encoded biobank, or benchmarking their runtimes across sample counts n and SNPs-per-gene l.
skills.name: cmh-significance-interpretation
skills.search_text: cmh-significance-interpretation Use when comparing significant meta-marker/interval outputs from CMH-based miners (HOGImine, SiNIMin, FastCMH) on the same binary-encoded biobank, or benchmarking their runtimes across sample counts n and SNPs-per-gene l. The goal is additive-encoded or permutation-tested (SiNIMin-WY / p > 0) results rather than binary-encoding runtime and pattern-set comparison The analysis requires conditioning on a categorical covariate beyond what CMH handles, or FastCMH's synthetic-data generation (makefastcmhdata only supports K=2 covariate classes) You need to interpret FastCMH's significance intervals in isolation without a comparable HOGImine/SiNIMin run, since the skill centers on cross-tool pattern-set equivalence http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Interprets and cross-validates CMH-based significant-interval / genetic meta-marker outputs from HOGImine, SiNIMin, and FastCMH, including verifying that HOGImine k=2 and SiNIMin return identical pattern sets and quantifying HOGImine's one-to-two order-of-magnitude runtime speedup. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad273
skills.summary: Interprets and cross-validates CMH-based significant-interval / genetic meta-marker outputs from HOGImine, SiNIMin, and FastCMH, including verifying that HOGImine k=2 and SiNIMin return identical pattern sets and quantifying HOGImine's one-to-two order-of-magnitude runtime speedup.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is additive-encoded or permutation-tested (SiNIMin-WY / p > 0) results rather than binary-encoding runtime and pattern-set comparison The analysis requires conditioning on a categorical covariate beyond what CMH handles, or FastCMH's synthetic-data generation (makefastcmhdata only supports K=2 covariate classes) You need to interpret FastCMH's significance intervals in isolation without a comparable HOGImine/SiNIMin run, since the skill centers on cross-tool pattern-set equivalence

skills.description: Use when samples carry a categorical covariate (e.g. country of origin) and you must test SNP-interval patterns for binary phenotype association while controlling FWER via Tarone's method, as in HOGImine/FastCMH-style mining.
skills.name: cmh-test-conditional-association-scoring
skills.search_text: cmh-test-conditional-association-scoring Use when samples carry a categorical covariate (e.g. country of origin) and you must test SNP-interval patterns for binary phenotype association while controlling FWER via Tarone's method, as in HOGImine/FastCMH-style mining. The goal is a plain association scan without covariate conditioning or network priors — a simple univariate test or FastCMH single-interval search (data.txt, label.txt, cov.txt) is the simpler fit. The phenotype is not binary or the features are not SNP markers ordered by genomic position — the CMH/Tarone machinery assumes binary labels and naturally ordered features. You need calibrated permutation p-values by default — permutation testing is off unless -p > 0 is explicitly set. http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Scores candidate genetic meta-markers (combinations of SNP intervals spanning interacting genes) with the Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel statistic conditioned on covariate classes, integrated with Tarone's testability pruning so that only patterns testable at the target FWER are enumerated and reported. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad273
skills.summary: Scores candidate genetic meta-markers (combinations of SNP intervals spanning interacting genes) with the Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel statistic conditioned on covariate classes, integrated with Tarone's testability pruning so that only patterns testable at the target FWER are enumerated and reported.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a plain association scan without covariate conditioning or network priors — a simple univariate test or FastCMH single-interval search (data.txt, label.txt, cov.txt) is the simpler fit. The phenotype is not binary or the features are not SNP markers ordered by genomic position — the CMH/Tarone machinery assumes binary labels and naturally ordered features. You need calibrated permutation p-values by default — permutation testing is off unless -p > 0 is explicitly set.

skills.description: Use when discovering combinations of genetic markers (meta-markers) associated with a binary phenotype and the number of tested patterns is large enough that raw CMH p-values would inflate family-wise error; supports conditioning on covariate classes.
skills.name: cmh-test-family-wise-error-control
skills.search_text: cmh-test-family-wise-error-control Use when discovering combinations of genetic markers (meta-markers) associated with a binary phenotype and the number of tested patterns is large enough that raw CMH p-values would inflate family-wise error; supports conditioning on covariate classes. When testing a single, pre-specified SNP association with no multiple-testing burden — a plain CMH test without permutation FWER control suffices When the phenotype is not binary (HOGImine's labels file must be a binary matrix of cases/controls) When no biological prior on gene interactions (PPI network, pathways, protein complexes) is available and the unrestricted search is infeasible for the target k http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Assess statistical significance of genetic meta-markers using CMH (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel) p-values with family-wise error rate (FWER) control at 0.05 via a Westfall-Young permutation procedure, as implemented in HOGImine for higher-order gene interaction discovery. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad273
skills.summary: Assess statistical significance of genetic meta-markers using CMH (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel) p-values with family-wise error rate (FWER) control at 0.05 via a Westfall-Young permutation procedure, as implemented in HOGImine for higher-order gene interaction discovery.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When testing a single, pre-specified SNP association with no multiple-testing burden — a plain CMH test without permutation FWER control suffices When the phenotype is not binary (HOGImine's labels file must be a binary matrix of cases/controls) When no biological prior on gene interactions (PPI network, pathways, protein complexes) is available and the unrestricted search is infeasible for the target k

skills.description: Use when comparing a trained CMS/DeepCC classifier against baseline machine-learning classifiers on independent CRC expression validation sets, or when reporting per-dataset sensitivity/specificity/accuracy with paired significance tests.
skills.name: cms-classifier-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cms-classifier-benchmark-comparison Use when comparing a trained CMS/DeepCC classifier against baseline machine-learning classifiers on independent CRC expression validation sets, or when reporting per-dataset sensitivity/specificity/accuracy with paired significance tests. The goal is unsupervised grouping of cancer patients — DeepCC is built for classification, not clustering of cancer patients Samples cannot be represented as gene expression profiles with Entrez-identifier columns, or no trained model/baseline signatures exist for the cancer type You need to detect novel subtypes rather than assign samples to the four established CMS classes http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 Benchmark a DeepCC deep-learning subtype classifier against widely used signature gene-based baselines (RF, SVM, GBM, multinomial logistic regression) on independent colorectal cancer validation sets, using sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and McNemar's test to quantify significance. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41389-019-0157-8
skills.summary: Benchmark a DeepCC deep-learning subtype classifier against widely used signature gene-based baselines (RF, SVM, GBM, multinomial logistic regression) on independent colorectal cancer validation sets, using sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and McNemar's test to quantify significance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is unsupervised grouping of cancer patients — DeepCC is built for classification, not clustering of cancer patients Samples cannot be represented as gene expression profiles with Entrez-identifier columns, or no trained model/baseline signatures exist for the cancer type You need to detect novel subtypes rather than assign samples to the four established CMS classes

skills.description: Use when CMS-classifying pre-clinical CRC expression data (PDX, cell lines, organoids) and you need to derive NTP templates or assess how robust CMScaller assignments are to template-derivation thresholds and marker-selection choices.
skills.name: cms-prediction-template-generation
skills.search_text: cms-prediction-template-generation Use when CMS-classifying pre-clinical CRC expression data (PDX, cell lines, organoids) and you need to derive NTP templates or assess how robust CMScaller assignments are to template-derivation thresholds and marker-selection choices. Classifying samples with a human stromal component different from primary CRCs, e.g. patient biopsies of metastatic CRC — the article states CMScaller is not recommended for such samples Single-cell RNA-sequencing data, which is exceedingly noisy and for which CMScaller is not optimized Datasets with fewer than approximately forty samples — centering and scaling input expression data inescapably introduces prediction uncertainty for small datasets http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Generate and stress-test CMScaller nearest-template prediction (NTP) templates for consensus molecular subtyping (CMS) of colorectal cancer pre-clinical models by building a reference template plus 1+4 alternative templates, each varying one derivation parameter (adjusted p-value cutoff 1e-4, alternative cell line panel, LFC threshold of 1, removal of genes lost between the Isella et al. panel and the primary template). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-017-16747-x
skills.summary: Generate and stress-test CMScaller nearest-template prediction (NTP) templates for consensus molecular subtyping (CMS) of colorectal cancer pre-clinical models by building a reference template plus 1+4 alternative templates, each varying one derivation parameter (adjusted p-value cutoff 1e-4, alternative cell line panel, LFC threshold of 1, removal of genes lost between the Isella et al. panel and the primary template).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Classifying samples with a human stromal component different from primary CRCs, e.g. patient biopsies of metastatic CRC — the article states CMScaller is not recommended for such samples Single-cell RNA-sequencing data, which is exceedingly noisy and for which CMScaller is not optimized Datasets with fewer than approximately forty samples — centering and scaling input expression data inescapably introduces prediction uncertainty for small datasets

skills.description: Use when cell line, PDX, or organoid models already have CMScaller CMS labels and per-model drug response values (e.g. 5-FU IC50), and you want to test whether subtype predicts drug sensitivity independently of MSI status.

skills.search_text: cms-subtype-drug-association-testing Use when cell line, PDX, or organoid models already have CMScaller CMS labels and per-model drug response values (e.g. 5-FU IC50), and you want to test whether subtype predicts drug sensitivity independently of MSI status. skills.name: cna-based-aml-cell-classification
skills.search_text: cna-based-aml-cell-classification Use when a scRNA-seq sample has known eWGS-discovered CNA events (e.g. 1p/7q losses in AML) and you need per-cell tumor/normal labels from copy number, or want to validate SNV-based cell calls against a CNA-based ground truth. The tumor sample has no detectable copy-number alterations — the article notes 'CNAs are rare in some tumor types, such as AML', so CNA-based classification cannot serve as a benchmark in CNA-silent cases like normal-karyotype AML. No eWGS-discovered CNA event regions are available to restrict the expression matrix, so clustering would be driven by expression rather than tumor-specific copy number. The goal is de novo CNA calling from bulk sequencing rather than per-cell classification — use copyCat on paired tumor/normal BAMs instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Classify individual AML cells as tumor vs. normal using single-cell copy-number alteration (CNA) profiles inferred from scRNA-seq expression data with CONICSmat, then benchmark those calls against an independent SNV/expression-based classification of the same cells. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-11591-1

No single-cell DNA copy-number ground truth is available for the clone of interest — ROC-AUC scoring cannot be performed and only qualitative concordance checks apply. The analysis goal is detecting copy-neutral LOH with InferCNV or CopyKAT, which do not consider allelic information and hence cannot detect copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (LOH). The dataset is bulk DNA-seq or already-phased single-cell DNA data, where direct copy-number calling from DNA makes scRNA-seq-based CNA inference unnecessary. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Benchmarks single-cell RNA-seq CNA-detection methods (XClone, CaSpER, Numbat, InferCNV, CopyKAT) by computing ROC curves and ROC-AUC for per-cell copy-gain and copy-loss calls against single-cell DNA-seq (scOne-seq) copy-number profiles used as ground truth. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-51026-0
skills.summary: Benchmarks single-cell RNA-seq CNA-detection methods (XClone, CaSpER, Numbat, InferCNV, CopyKAT) by computing ROC curves and ROC-AUC for per-cell copy-gain and copy-loss calls against single-cell DNA-seq (scOne-seq) copy-number profiles used as ground truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No single-cell DNA copy-number ground truth is available for the clone of interest — ROC-AUC scoring cannot be performed and only qualitative concordance checks apply. skills.name: cnv-based-malignancy-calling-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cnv-based-malignancy-calling-benchmarking Use when a scRNA-seq dataset requires distinguishing malignant from non-malignant cells and you must decide between marker-based aberrant annotation and CNV-based callers (SCEVAN, CopyKAT), or quantify their accuracy and runtime trade-offs. The task is general healthy-tissue cell-type annotation rather than malignant vs non-malignant cell discrimination — the CNV-based callers and the disease benchmark are specific to aberrant/malignant populations Only a small tumor cohort or no ground-truth malignant annotations exist — the article notes the benchmark is limited to two liquid and two solid tumors and that limited availability of high-quality ground-truth datasets constrains expansion A direct comparison with non-marker-based annotation tools is required — the authors state such a comparison was not conducted in this study http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark of marker-based aberrant cell identification (Cell Marker Accordion accordion_disease) against CNV-calling malignant cell tools SCEVAN and CopyKAT on glioblastoma and lung adenocarcinoma scRNA-seq, using F1 score, percentage of recovered malignant cells, and wall-clock runtime. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-60900-4
skills.summary: Benchmark of marker-based aberrant cell identification (Cell Marker Accordion accordion_disease) against CNV-calling malignant cell tools SCEVAN and CopyKAT on glioblastoma and lung adenocarcinoma scRNA-seq, using F1 score, percentage of recovered malignant cells, and wall-clock runtime.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is general healthy-tissue cell-type annotation rather than malignant vs non-malignant cell discrimination — the CNV-based callers and the disease benchmark are specific to aberrant/malignant populations Only a small tumor cohort or no ground-truth malignant annotations exist — the article notes the benchmark is limited to two liquid and two solid tumors and that limited availability of high-quality ground-truth datasets constrains expansion A direct comparison with non-marker-based annotation tools is required — the authors state such a comparison was not conducted in this study

skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq data (e.g., the 430-cell single-cell GBM dataset) require reconstruction of a CNV-based clonal tree and testing of mutually exclusive vs co-occurring subclone CNV events across cells.
skills.name: cnv-based-phylogenetic-clustering
skills.search_text: cnv-based-phylogenetic-clustering Use when scRNA-seq data (e.g., the 430-cell single-cell GBM dataset) require reconstruction of a CNV-based clonal tree and testing of mutually exclusive vs co-occurring subclone CNV events across cells. Bulk RNA-seq cohorts (e.g., yale_meningioma, TCGA-GBM/BRCA demos) — the CNV-based clonal evolution tree and single-cell mutual exclusivity analysis require per-cell CNV profiles, not bulk samples. 3′-only sequencing (e.g., DropSeq-style) single-cell data where the BAF shift signal is degraded because shifts are measured only for variants near gene 3′ ends, weakening the allelic component that supports CNV calls. http://edamontology.org/topic_0084 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Infers CNV-based clonal evolution from single-cell RNA-seq using CaSpER: the per-cell gene-level CNV matrix from multiscale HMM segmentation (integrated with BAF allele-shift signal) is converted into a clonal phylogenetic tree, and subclonal CNV architecture is tested for mutual exclusivity/co-occurrence with Fisher's exact test. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-13779-x
skills.summary: Infers CNV-based clonal evolution from single-cell RNA-seq using CaSpER: the per-cell gene-level CNV matrix from multiscale HMM segmentation (integrated with BAF allele-shift signal) is converted into a clonal phylogenetic tree, and subclonal CNV architecture is tested for mutual exclusivity/co-occurrence with Fisher's exact test.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Bulk RNA-seq cohorts (e.g., yale_meningioma, TCGA-GBM/BRCA demos) — the CNV-based clonal evolution tree and single-cell mutual exclusivity analysis require per-cell CNV profiles, not bulk samples. 3′-only sequencing (e.g., DropSeq-style) single-cell data where the BAF shift signal is degraded because shifts are measured only for variants near gene 3′ ends, weakening the allelic component that supports CNV calls.

skills.description: Use when normalized bulk RNA-seq expression matrices (with optional BAF shift files) must be mined for chromosome-arm, segment, and gene-level CNV events, or when RNA-derived CNV calls need TPR/FPR benchmarking against genotyping-array calls.
skills.name: cnv-calling-from-bulk-rna-seq
skills.search_text: cnv-calling-from-bulk-rna-seq Use when normalized bulk RNA-seq expression matrices (with optional BAF shift files) must be mined for chromosome-arm, segment, and gene-level CNV events, or when RNA-derived CNV calls need TPR/FPR benchmarking against genotyping-array calls. 3′-only sequencing data (e.g., DropSeq): BAF shift will be measured only for variants near gene 3′ ends, degrading the BAF-shift signal CaSpER relies on The input is single-cell RNA-seq (use the single-cell variant of this workflow with sequencing.type='single-cell'); bulk and single-cell parameterizations differ Only raw FASTQ without aligned BAMs is available, since BAFExtract requires mapped reads for pileup/BAF generation http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Multiscale HMM-based CNV calling from bulk RNA-seq using CaSpER, which integrates smoothed genome-wide expression signal with BAF allelic-shift (LOH) signal to detect large-scale, segment-level, and gene-level amplifications/deletions, benchmarked against genotyping-array gold standards. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-13779-x
skills.summary: Multiscale HMM-based CNV calling from bulk RNA-seq using CaSpER, which integrates smoothed genome-wide expression signal with BAF allelic-shift (LOH) signal to detect large-scale, segment-level, and gene-level amplifications/deletions, benchmarked against genotyping-array gold standards.
skills.when_to_use_negative: 3′-only sequencing data (e.g., DropSeq): BAF shift will be measured only for variants near gene 3′ ends, degrading the BAF-shift signal CaSpER relies on The input is single-cell RNA-seq (use the single-cell variant of this workflow with sequencing.type='single-cell'); bulk and single-cell parameterizations differ Only raw FASTQ without aligned BAMs is available, since BAFExtract requires mapped reads for pileup/BAF generation

skills.description: Use when you have a cell-annotated cancer scRNA-seq object (e.g., Seurat object from scWizard annotation) and need to identify malignant cells by copy-number alteration and display them in a clustered inferCNV heatmap.
skills.name: cnv-clustered-heatmap-visualization
skills.search_text: cnv-clustered-heatmap-visualization Use when you have a cell-annotated cancer scRNA-seq object (e.g., Seurat object from scWizard annotation) and need to identify malignant cells by copy-number alteration and display them in a clustered inferCNV heatmap. Input is a raw unannotated counts matrix without cell-type labels, since no reference (non-malignant) or observation (malignant) cell sets can yet be designated Analysis goal is pathway scoring or transcription-factor regulation rather than chromosome copy-number alterations — use scWizard's 'GSVA' or 'TF-SCENIC' functions instead Tissue-specific or non-cancer cell types dominate and scWizard's annotation model labels them 'Unknown' (e.g., alveolar cells in lung cancers), leaving no reliable non-malignant reference set http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Runs inferCNV through scWizard's 'inferCNV' function to estimate large-scale chromosome copy-number alterations (CNA) from annotated cancer scRNA-seq data, using non-malignant cells as reference, and visualizes the result as a clustered CNA heatmap separating malignant epithelial cells from non-malignant populations. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.08.028
skills.summary: Runs inferCNV through scWizard's 'inferCNV' function to estimate large-scale chromosome copy-number alterations (CNA) from annotated cancer scRNA-seq data, using non-malignant cells as reference, and visualizes the result as a clustered CNA heatmap separating malignant epithelial cells from non-malignant populations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw unannotated counts matrix without cell-type labels, since no reference (non-malignant) or observation (malignant) cell sets can yet be designated Analysis goal is pathway scoring or transcription-factor regulation rather than chromosome copy-number alterations — use scWizard's 'GSVA' or 'TF-SCENIC' functions instead Tissue-specific or non-cancer cell types dominate and scWizard's annotation model labels them 'Unknown' (e.g., alveolar cells in lung cancers), leaving no reliable non-malignant reference set

skills.description: Use when SSrGE eeSNV/gene rankings from scRNA-seq (e.g., Patel, Ting, Kim, Miyamoto cancer datasets) need a sensitivity check against copy-number variation as an additional predictor.
skills.name: cnv-covariate-sensitivity-check
skills.search_text: cnv-covariate-sensitivity-check Use when SSrGE eeSNV/gene rankings from scRNA-seq (e.g., Patel, Ting, Kim, Miyamoto cancer datasets) need a sensitivity check against copy-number variation as an additional predictor. No CNV data are available for the same cells (the fit call requires a n_cells x n_genes CNV matrix matching the expression matrix) The goal is subgroup-specific feature ranking (rank_features_for_a_subgroup) rather than global ranking stability http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Refit SSrGE LASSO models with a copy-number-variation (CNV) matrix passed as a covariate to the fit call, then compare eeSNV/gene rankings with the SNV-only models (Kendall-Tau close to 1) to test whether CNVs alter the genotype-phenotype linkage rankings. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-07170-5
skills.summary: Refit SSrGE LASSO models with a copy-number-variation (CNV) matrix passed as a covariate to the fit call, then compare eeSNV/gene rankings with the SNV-only models (Kendall-Tau close to 1) to test whether CNVs alter the genotype-phenotype linkage rankings.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No CNV data are available for the same cells (the fit call requires a n_cells x n_genes CNV matrix matching the expression matrix) The goal is subgroup-specific feature ranking (rank_features_for_a_subgroup) rather than global ranking stability

skills.description: Use when SCEVAN (pipelineCNA with SUBCLONES=TRUE) has produced heatmap/clone-tree/OncoPrint outputs for a scRNA-seq tumor sample and you must interpret truncal vs. shared vs. subclone-specific CNAs and verify them against published profiles.
skills.name: cnv-heatmap-and-oncoprint-interpretation
skills.search_text: cnv-heatmap-and-oncoprint-interpretation Use when SCEVAN (pipelineCNA with SUBCLONES=TRUE) has produced heatmap/clone-tree/OncoPrint outputs for a scRNA-seq tumor sample and you must interpret truncal vs. shared vs. subclone-specific CNAs and verify them against published profiles. The tumor has minimal genomic alterations (e.g., leukemia, pediatric cancers, ependymomas) where the aneuploidy-based heatmap/OncoPrint view is uninformative per the article's limitation statement Only malignant vs. non-malignant classification is needed, with no interest in clonal structure — run pipelineCNA with SUBCLONES = FALSE instead of interpreting subclone plots The input is bulk WES/WGS segmentation data rather than a scRNA-seq count matrix; use bulk tools (CNVkit, DNAcopy) instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Reading and validating the visualization outputs of SCEVAN's clonal copy-number pipeline — CNA heatmaps, subclone heatmaps, phylogenetic clone trees, consensus plots, and OncoHeat2/OncoPrint-style figures — to confirm truncal vs. subclonal alterations and link alteration regions to differential gene expression (e.g., UBE2T up-regulation). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-36790-9
skills.summary: Reading and validating the visualization outputs of SCEVAN's clonal copy-number pipeline — CNA heatmaps, subclone heatmaps, phylogenetic clone trees, consensus plots, and OncoHeat2/OncoPrint-style figures — to confirm truncal vs. subclonal alterations and link alteration regions to differential gene expression (e.g., UBE2T up-regulation).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The tumor has minimal genomic alterations (e.g., leukemia, pediatric cancers, ependymomas) where the aneuploidy-based heatmap/OncoPrint view is uninformative per the article's limitation statement Only malignant vs. non-malignant classification is needed, with no interest in clonal structure — run pipelineCNA with SUBCLONES = FALSE instead of interpreting subclone plots The input is bulk WES/WGS segmentation data rather than a scRNA-seq count matrix; use bulk tools (CNVkit, DNAcopy) instead

skills.description: Use when single-cell data have both mtDNA-variant clone labels (e.g., from vireoSNP on MQuad SNPs) and CNV-based clone labels (e.g., CellRanger/VireoSNP BAF clustering) and you need to quantify concordance or finer subclonal resolution.
skills.name: cnv-mtdna-clone-confusion-analysis
skills.search_text: cnv-mtdna-clone-confusion-analysis Use when single-cell data have both mtDNA-variant clone labels (e.g., from vireoSNP on MQuad SNPs) and CNV-based clone labels (e.g., CellRanger/VireoSNP BAF clustering) and you need to quantify concordance or finer subclonal resolution. The dataset has no independent CNV or nuclear clone labels to compare against mtDNA clones, so a confusion matrix would be uninformative CNV subclones are expected to be the target resolution themselves — coverage-inferred CNV subclones may be less dynamic than subclones shown by propagation of true point mutations, so mtDNA clones should not be forced to match CNV clones Only a handful of cells carry both label types, making cross-tabulation counts too sparse to interpret http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Cross-modality validation of mtDNA-inferred clones against nuclear copy-number-variation clones by building a confusion matrix and checking overlap (e.g., CNV clone 1 with mitochondrial clone 0 in MKN-45), demonstrating that mtDNA variants complement CNV-based clonal structure. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-28845-0
skills.summary: Cross-modality validation of mtDNA-inferred clones against nuclear copy-number-variation clones by building a confusion matrix and checking overlap (e.g., CNV clone 1 with mitochondrial clone 0 in MKN-45), demonstrating that mtDNA variants complement CNV-based clonal structure.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has no independent CNV or nuclear clone labels to compare against mtDNA clones, so a confusion matrix would be uninformative CNV subclones are expected to be the target resolution themselves — coverage-inferred CNV subclones may be less dynamic than subclones shown by propagation of true point mutations, so mtDNA clones should not be forced to match CNV clones Only a handful of cells carry both label types, making cross-tabulation counts too sparse to interpret

skills.description: Use when building a fixed transcriptional module repertoire from multiple gene expression cohorts, by quantifying cross-dataset co-clustering of transcripts over shared profiles.
skills.name: co-clustering-frequency-tabulation
skills.search_text: co-clustering-frequency-tabulation Use when building a fixed transcriptional module repertoire from multiple gene expression cohorts, by quantifying cross-dataset co-clustering of transcripts over shared profiles. Analyses of tissues other than human blood, or other species — the BloodGen3 repertoire is specifically designed for human blood transcriptome profiling data The goal is downstream group comparison or fingerprinting of samples against an existing repertoire (use the BloodGen3Module Groupcomparison/Individualcomparison functions instead) A framework capturing specificities of a narrowly defined system outside blood is needed — co-clustering across diverse immunological/physiological states may miss such specificity http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 Tabulates how frequently gene pairs (transcripts on Illumina HT-12 v3 BeadArrays) co-cluster across multiple blood transcriptome datasets and converts those frequencies into a weighted co-expression graph, which is iteratively mined to define a fixed module repertoire such as the 382-module BloodGen3 repertoire. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-24584-w
skills.summary: Tabulates how frequently gene pairs (transcripts on Illumina HT-12 v3 BeadArrays) co-cluster across multiple blood transcriptome datasets and converts those frequencies into a weighted co-expression graph, which is iteratively mined to define a fixed module repertoire such as the 382-module BloodGen3 repertoire.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Analyses of tissues other than human blood, or other species — the BloodGen3 repertoire is specifically designed for human blood transcriptome profiling data The goal is downstream group comparison or fingerprinting of samples against an existing repertoire (use the BloodGen3Module Groupcomparison/Individualcomparison functions instead) A framework capturing specificities of a narrowly defined system outside blood is needed — co-clustering across diverse immunological/physiological states may miss such specificity

skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq cluster markers must be cluster-specific (binary) DEGs — e.g. to detect genes exclusive to one sub_cluster population — or when comparing CDI against standard DE methods like Wilcoxon on DEG counts and specificity.
skills.name: co-dependency-index-differential-expression
skills.search_text: co-dependency-index-differential-expression Use when scRNA-seq cluster markers must be cluster-specific (binary) DEGs — e.g. to detect genes exclusive to one sub_cluster population — or when comparing CDI against standard DE methods like Wilcoxon on DEG counts and specificity. The analysis goal is detecting graded/continuous DEGs across populations rather than binary, cluster-exclusive (bDEG) markers — CDI is designed specifically for cluster-specific binary DEGs The dataset contains multiple biological replicates whose variation must be modeled — the CDI approach does not account for variation in biological replicates The full feature space must be scanned without preprocessing — CDI is computationally intensive, so unfiltered feature spaces (without getExpressedGenes() restriction) are impractical http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Applies the co-dependency index (CDI), implemented in scMiko's findCDIMarkers(), as a differential expression method for identifying binary differentially-expressed genes (bDEGs) — genes exclusively expressed in one cell population — within scRNA-seq data, scoring gene-cluster pairs by binomial co-occurrence enrichment. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-022-04093-2
skills.summary: Applies the co-dependency index (CDI), implemented in scMiko's findCDIMarkers(), as a differential expression method for identifying binary differentially-expressed genes (bDEGs) — genes exclusively expressed in one cell population — within scRNA-seq data, scoring gene-cluster pairs by binomial co-occurrence enrichment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is detecting graded/continuous DEGs across populations rather than binary, cluster-exclusive (bDEG) markers — CDI is designed specifically for cluster-specific binary DEGs The dataset contains multiple biological replicates whose variation must be modeled — the CDI approach does not account for variation in biological replicates The full feature space must be scanned without preprocessing — CDI is computationally intensive, so unfiltered feature spaces (without getExpressedGenes() restriction) are impractical

skills.description: Use when clustering scRNA-seq data (normalized, log-transformed expression matrix of genes x cells) and you want biologically meaningful co-expression-derived features (e.g. attractor gene sets seeded by markers like AIF1) to feed clustering rather than raw or PCA-only features.
skills.name: co-expression-attractor-feature-selection
skills.search_text: co-expression-attractor-feature-selection Use when clustering scRNA-seq data (normalized, log-transformed expression matrix of genes x cells) and you want biologically meaningful co-expression-derived features (e.g. attractor gene sets seeded by markers like AIF1) to feed clustering rather than raw or PCA-only features. Input data is raw counts or otherwise not normalized/log-transformed — CASCC.featureSelection expects 'well-normalized' input Input is already a reduced feature/embedding table (e.g. PCA or CCA components) rather than a gene x cell expression matrix You need a quick numeric-only clustering with no biological feature interpretation — generic k-means on PCA features suffices http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Selects gene co-expression features for single-cell RNA-seq clustering using the CASCC adaptive attractor algorithm, replacing generic feature spaces with biologically interpretable co-expression modules before clustering. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae283
skills.summary: Selects gene co-expression features for single-cell RNA-seq clustering using the CASCC adaptive attractor algorithm, replacing generic feature spaces with biologically interpretable co-expression modules before clustering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data is raw counts or otherwise not normalized/log-transformed — CASCC.featureSelection expects 'well-normalized' input Input is already a reduced feature/embedding table (e.g. PCA or CCA components) rather than a gene x cell expression matrix You need a quick numeric-only clustering with no biological feature interpretation — generic k-means on PCA features suffices

skills.description: Use when benchmarking co-expression estimators on permuted null UMI count data (z_i ~ F_p(mu, Sigma), x_ij | z_ij ~ Poisson(s_i * z_ij)) to visualize depth-induced bias, e.g. mean-expression vs. average estimated co-expression curves.
skills.name: co-expression-estimation-bias-curve-generation
skills.search_text: co-expression-estimation-bias-curve-generation Use when benchmarking co-expression estimators on permuted null UMI count data (z_i ~ F_p(mu, Sigma), x_ij | z_ij ~ Poisson(s_i * z_ij)) to visualize depth-induced bias, e.g. mean-expression vs. average estimated co-expression curves. Data contain true co-expression signal (non-null data) — the curve's deviation from zero is only interpretable as bias when no gene pairs are truly co-expressed Input is normalized or transformed expression rather than raw UMI counts — several methods in the benchmark require raw counts and normalization can itself induce the depth bias being tested Goal is testing type-I error calibration via p-value Q-Q plots rather than estimation bias — use the Q-Q / BH-correction workflow (Fig. 1b) instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Generates sequencing-depth bias curves (Fig. 1a of Su et al. 2023, Nature Communications) by averaging a method's co-expression estimates over gene pairs binned by mean expression on permuted null scRNA-seq data, revealing whether estimates drift away from zero as sequencing depth varies. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-40503-7
skills.summary: Generates sequencing-depth bias curves (Fig. 1a of Su et al. 2023, Nature Communications) by averaging a method's co-expression estimates over gene pairs binned by mean expression on permuted null scRNA-seq data, revealing whether estimates drift away from zero as sequencing depth varies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data contain true co-expression signal (non-null data) — the curve's deviation from zero is only interpretable as bias when no gene pairs are truly co-expressed Input is normalized or transformed expression rather than raw UMI counts — several methods in the benchmark require raw counts and normalization can itself induce the depth bias being tested Goal is testing type-I error calibration via p-value Q-Q plots rather than estimation bias — use the Q-Q / BH-correction workflow (Fig. 1b) instead

skills.description: Use when evaluating or benchmarking scRNA-seq co-expression detection methods that output gene-pair p-values, by simulating UMI counts from a ground-truth sparse co-expression network and scoring precision-recall and runtime.
skills.name: co-expression-hypothesis-testing-benchmark
skills.search_text: co-expression-hypothesis-testing-benchmark Use when evaluating or benchmarking scRNA-seq co-expression detection methods that output gene-pair p-values, by simulating UMI counts from a ground-truth sparse co-expression network and scoring precision-recall and runtime. The task is co-expression estimation accuracy or module/GO analysis rather than benchmarking detection accuracy and runtime of p-value-based methods The comparison involves methods without hypothesis tests (e.g. plain network-module tools), since this benchmark's PR analysis requires per-gene-pair p-values Input is real data with no ground-truth co-expression network, so precision-recall cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Benchmark protocol comparing CS-CORE against co-expression methods with hypothesis tests (Pearson, Spearman, locCSN, normalisr, NoiseRegularization) on simulated UMI counts, using precision-recall detection accuracy and wall-clock running time as the evaluation axes (Fig. 3b,c of the CS-CORE paper). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-40503-7
skills.summary: Benchmark protocol comparing CS-CORE against co-expression methods with hypothesis tests (Pearson, Spearman, locCSN, normalisr, NoiseRegularization) on simulated UMI counts, using precision-recall detection accuracy and wall-clock running time as the evaluation axes (Fig. 3b,c of the CS-CORE paper).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is co-expression estimation accuracy or module/GO analysis rather than benchmarking detection accuracy and runtime of p-value-based methods The comparison involves methods without hypothesis tests (e.g. plain network-module tools), since this benchmark's PR analysis requires per-gene-pair p-values Input is real data with no ground-truth co-expression network, so precision-recall cannot be computed

skills.description: Use when validating a set of predicted RBP candidates by asking whether they are co-expressed with known (gold-standard) circRNA regulators, using the Harmonizome MSigDB Cancer Gene Co-expression Modules resource and permutation-based enrichment testing.
skills.name: co-expression-module-enrichment-analysis
skills.search_text: co-expression-module-enrichment-analysis Use when validating a set of predicted RBP candidates by asking whether they are co-expressed with known (gold-standard) circRNA regulators, using the Harmonizome MSigDB Cancer Gene Co-expression Modules resource and permutation-based enrichment testing. The validation question concerns physical protein-protein interactions or shared transcription factor (TRANSFAC) modulation instead of co-expression — these are separate Harmonizome-based analyses with their own backgrounds and expected results. The candidate list did not come from CRIT's NMF clustering (e.g., an arbitrary RBP set), so the candidate–background design and the 57/73 or 5-candidate expectations no longer apply. The study system is not human cancer samples with Harmonizome coverage — the MSigDB Cancer Gene Co-expression Modules are cancer-focused and human-specific. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Tests whether CRIT-predicted candidate circRNA regulators are co-expressed with gold-standard circRNA regulators using the Harmonizome MSigDB Cancer Gene Co-expression Modules dataset, with significance assessed by 10,000 random-sampling permutations against both gene and RBP backgrounds. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.omtn.2022.10.015
skills.summary: Tests whether CRIT-predicted candidate circRNA regulators are co-expressed with gold-standard circRNA regulators using the Harmonizome MSigDB Cancer Gene Co-expression Modules dataset, with significance assessed by 10,000 random-sampling permutations against both gene and RBP backgrounds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The validation question concerns physical protein-protein interactions or shared transcription factor (TRANSFAC) modulation instead of co-expression — these are separate Harmonizome-based analyses with their own backgrounds and expected results. The candidate list did not come from CRIT's NMF clustering (e.g., an arbitrary RBP set), so the candidate–background design and the 57/73 or 5-candidate expectations no longer apply. The study system is not human cancer samples with Harmonizome coverage — the MSigDB Cancer Gene Co-expression Modules are cancer-focused and human-specific.

skills.description: Use when given a gene-by-sample bulk RNA-seq expression matrix (e.g. 100-sample ENCODE or MODEL-AD brain data) and the goal is to find co-expressed gene modules, relate them to traits like genotype or time point, and run GO/KEGG/REACTOME enrichment.
skills.name: co-expression-module-identification
skills.search_text: co-expression-module-identification Use when given a gene-by-sample bulk RNA-seq expression matrix (e.g. 100-sample ENCODE or MODEL-AD brain data) and the goal is to find co-expressed gene modules, relate them to traits like genotype or time point, and run GO/KEGG/REACTOME enrichment. The input is single-cell data or already a feature/summary table rather than a raw gene-by-sample expression matrix needing data cleaning and pre-processing The analysis requires differential expression or pathway testing on individual genes rather than co-expression module-level structure The dataset is small enough that runtime/memory are non-issues and an existing R WGCNA workflow is already in place http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Identifies clusters (modules) of highly correlated genes from bulk RNA-seq expression matrices using PyWGCNA's weighted correlation network analysis, then summarizes each module via its eigengene. Enables downstream module-trait correlation and functional enrichment on large datasets where the R WGCNA implementation is slower or exhausts memory. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad415
skills.summary: Identifies clusters (modules) of highly correlated genes from bulk RNA-seq expression matrices using PyWGCNA's weighted correlation network analysis, then summarizes each module via its eigengene. Enables downstream module-trait correlation and functional enrichment on large datasets where the R WGCNA implementation is slower or exhausts memory.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is single-cell data or already a feature/summary table rather than a raw gene-by-sample expression matrix needing data cleaning and pre-processing The analysis requires differential expression or pathway testing on individual genes rather than co-expression module-level structure The dataset is small enough that runtime/memory are non-issues and an existing R WGCNA workflow is already in place

skills.description: Use when a scRNA-seq dataset has been decomposed into co-expression gene modules (e.g. WGCNA-style modules like M4 or M11) and the goal is to prioritize hub genes inside a disease/trait-associated module as drug targets.
skills.name: co-expression-network-hub-targeting
skills.search_text: co-expression-network-hub-targeting Use when a scRNA-seq dataset has been decomposed into co-expression gene modules (e.g. WGCNA-style modules like M4 or M11) and the goal is to prioritize hub genes inside a disease/trait-associated module as drug targets. The question is differential expression or cell-type annotation, not network-level target prioritization — SCANet's drug repurposing step operates on GCN/GRN modules, not gene lists alone You need causal regulatory evidence: GCNs rely on correlation, not causation, so hub status alone does not establish a causal driver Reproducibility across time is critical and the exact Drugst.One database version cannot be fixed, since gene–drug databases update weekly http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Identifies hub genes (top 10% most connected) within trait/cell-type-specific co-expression modules inferred from scRNA-seq data, then maps those hubs to pharmacological targets for mechanistic drug repurposing via SCANet's Drugst.One/NeDRex integration. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad644
skills.summary: Identifies hub genes (top 10% most connected) within trait/cell-type-specific co-expression modules inferred from scRNA-seq data, then maps those hubs to pharmacological targets for mechanistic drug repurposing via SCANet's Drugst.One/NeDRex integration.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The question is differential expression or cell-type annotation, not network-level target prioritization — SCANet's drug repurposing step operates on GCN/GRN modules, not gene lists alone You need causal regulatory evidence: GCNs rely on correlation, not causation, so hub status alone does not establish a causal driver Reproducibility across time is critical and the exact Drugst.One database version cannot be fixed, since gene–drug databases update weekly

skills.description: Use when a CODEX spatial proteomics dataset (per-cell protein expression plus spatial coordinates, e.g. AnnData with 46,840 cells) needs unsupervised clustering and spatial projection to reveal B/T-cell tissue organization without prior normalization.
skills.name: codex-protein-clustering
skills.search_text: codex-protein-clustering Use when a CODEX spatial proteomics dataset (per-cell protein expression plus spatial coordinates, e.g. AnnData with 46,840 cells) needs unsupervised clustering and spatial projection to reveal B/T-cell tissue organization without prior normalization. The input is scRNA-seq or another modality that requires preprocessing (e.g. CPM total-count normalization to 1e5, log1p-transform, scaling to unit variance/zero-mean) — the CODEX workflow in Cellar explicitly runs without normalization. The goal is reference-based cell-type assignment or supervised label transfer (e.g. scanpy Ingest between HBMP2-spleen-2 and HBMP3-spleen-CC3) rather than unsupervised spatial clustering. No spatial coordinates are available, so clusters cannot be projected back onto the CODEX image tile. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Unsupervised Leiden clustering of CODEX spatial-proteomics protein expression (via a 10-dim UMAP embedding and a faiss 15-neighbor graph at resolution 0.1) with the cluster assignments projected back onto the spatial CODEX image to reveal tissue-level organization such as B-cell follicles surrounded by T cells. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-29744-0
skills.summary: Unsupervised Leiden clustering of CODEX spatial-proteomics protein expression (via a 10-dim UMAP embedding and a faiss 15-neighbor graph at resolution 0.1) with the cluster assignments projected back onto the spatial CODEX image to reveal tissue-level organization such as B-cell follicles surrounded by T cells.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is scRNA-seq or another modality that requires preprocessing (e.g. CPM total-count normalization to 1e5, log1p-transform, scaling to unit variance/zero-mean) — the CODEX workflow in Cellar explicitly runs without normalization. skills.description: Use when evaluating whether an imputation method reduces gene-expression variability across cells of the same type — i.e., you have unimputed and imputed count/log matrices plus cell-type annotations and need a variance-stabilization comparison.
skills.name: coefficient-of-variation-variance-stabilization-analysis
skills.search_text: coefficient-of-variation-variance-stabilization-analysis Use when evaluating whether an imputation method reduces gene-expression variability across cells of the same type — i.e., you have unimputed and imputed count/log matrices plus cell-type annotations and need a variance-stabilization comparison. The analysis goal is expression recovery from subsampled (masked-matrix) data or clustering accuracy — those require different evaluations (e.g., AutoImpute's --masked_matrix_test masked-matrix recovery test), not intra-subpopulation CV. You want to assess cell-type separability across subpopulations rather than variance within a single randomly picked subpopulation; CV-based stabilization is a within-type metric. Only one imputation method or no unimputed baseline is available, making a per-method CV comparison impossible. http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Compares how well scRNA-seq imputation methods (AutoImpute, scImpute, MAGIC, drImpute) stabilize intra-subpopulation gene-expression variance by computing per-gene coefficients of variation (CV = SD/mean) within a randomly chosen cell-type subpopulation, log-transforming the CVs, and visualizing them as grouped boxplots (Fig. 4 style). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-018-34688-x
skills.summary: Compares how well scRNA-seq imputation methods (AutoImpute, scImpute, MAGIC, drImpute) stabilize intra-subpopulation gene-expression variance by computing per-gene coefficients of variation (CV = SD/mean) within a randomly chosen cell-type subpopulation, log-transforming the CVs, and visualizing them as grouped boxplots (Fig. 4 style).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is expression recovery from subsampled (masked-matrix) data or clustering accuracy — those require different evaluations (e.g., AutoImpute's --masked_matrix_test masked-matrix recovery test), not intra-subpopulation CV. You want to assess cell-type separability across subpopulations rather than variance within a single randomly picked subpopulation; CV-based stabilization is a within-type metric.
