skills.search_text: crispr-barcode-mutation-dropout-modeling Use when you need simulated ground-truth cell division trees with paired barcode/expression data under varying mutation rates, dropout conditions, and cell counts (e.g., 1024–4096 cells) to benchmark lineage tree inference methods. Analyzing real lineage-barcode data with no ground-truth division tree — RF distance and CID against truth cannot be computed; use Nye similarity among methods or biological validation instead The biological system has reversible cell state transitions — LinRace assumes irreversible state transitions, so simulated asymmetric-division benchmarks would not represent that regime Ancestral/intermediate cell states are fast-changing and absent from current-day scRNA-seq — the state-label reconstruction step will be misspecified http://edamontology.org/topic_3293 Simulates paired CRISPR lineage-barcode and scRNA-seq datasets with TedSim under controlled mutation rates (e.g., mu = 0.025–0.075, 16 barcode characters, Sigma = 0.5), with and without dropout events, to benchmark lineage reconstruction methods like LinRace against Cassiopeia, DCLEAR, Startle, and LinTIMaT using RF distance, Nye similarity, and CID. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-44173-3
skills.summary: Simulates paired CRISPR lineage-barcode and scRNA-seq datasets with TedSim under controlled mutation rates (e.g., mu = 0.025–0.075, 16 barcode characters, Sigma = 0.5), with and without dropout events, to benchmark lineage reconstruction methods like LinRace against Cassiopeia, DCLEAR, Startle, and LinTIMaT using RF distance, Nye similarity, and CID.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Analyzing real lineage-barcode data with no ground-truth division tree — RF distance and CID against truth cannot be computed; use Nye similarity among methods or biological validation instead The biological system has reversible cell state transitions — LinRace assumes irreversible state transitions, so simulated asymmetric-division benchmarks would not represent that regime Ancestral/intermediate cell states are fast-changing and absent from current-day scRNA-seq — the state-label reconstruction step will be misspecified

skills.description: Use when a lineage-reconstruction benchmark needs paired barcode-and-expression data with a known true tree, e.g., sweeping mutation rates on the C. elegans L1 tree or TedSim-simulated phyla.
skills.name: crispr-barcode-simulation
skills.search_text: crispr-barcode-simulation Use when a lineage-reconstruction benchmark needs paired barcode-and-expression data with a known true tree, e.g., sweeping mutation rates on the C. elegans L1 tree or TedSim-simulated phyla. You have real, experimentally acquired lineage barcode data with a validated tree — simulation is only a benchmark surrogate The system has reversible cell-state transitions or synchronous differentiation, which LinRace/TedSim-based asymmetric-division assumptions do not model You need barcode technology realism beyond TedSim's CRISPR mutation/dropout model (e.g., high-diversity recording outcomes not parameterized by mu and N_char) http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Simulate CRISPR lineage barcodes on a known ground-truth lineage tree with TedSim's SimulateCIFs, optionally with dropouts, to create paired barcode/expression benchmarks for evaluating lineage-reconstruction methods such as LinRace. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-44173-3
skills.summary: Simulate CRISPR lineage barcodes on a known ground-truth lineage tree with TedSim's SimulateCIFs, optionally with dropouts, to create paired barcode/expression benchmarks for evaluating lineage-reconstruction methods such as LinRace.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have real, experimentally acquired lineage barcode data with a validated tree — simulation is only a benchmark surrogate The system has reversible cell-state transitions or synchronous differentiation, which LinRace/TedSim-based asymmetric-division assumptions do not model You need barcode technology realism beyond TedSim's CRISPR mutation/dropout model (e.g., high-diversity recording outcomes not parameterized by mu and N_char)

skills.description: Use when you need to verify that a differential-expression pipeline (e.g., Normalisr on a Perturb-seq/CRISPR screen dataset) produces uniformly distributed null P values across gene expression levels before trusting its significance calls.
skills.name: crispr-screen-null-calibration
skills.search_text: crispr-screen-null-calibration Use when you need to verify that a differential-expression pipeline (e.g., Normalisr on a Perturb-seq/CRISPR screen dataset) produces uniformly distributed null P values across gene expression levels before trusting its significance calls. The goal is inference of actual guide (gRNA) trans-effects or CRISPR screen hits — this skill uses only gRNA-free cells and provides no guide-effect sensitivity estimates The dataset is full-length (non-UMI) scRNA-seq — the article only focused on UMI-based datasets and nonlinear covariates may need revalidation on full-length platforms You need hypothesis testing of arbitrary nonlinear associations — Normalisr is explicitly not designed for that A null-calibration procedure that validates unbiased P-value estimation of Normalisr differential expression by repeatedly running null DE between random two-group partitions of gRNA-free cells and testing uniformity of the resulting P values across ten expression bins with Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-26682-1
skills.summary: A null-calibration procedure that validates unbiased P-value estimation of Normalisr differential expression by repeatedly running null DE between random two-group partitions of gRNA-free cells and testing uniformity of the resulting P values across ten expression bins with Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is inference of actual guide (gRNA) trans-effects or CRISPR screen hits — this skill uses only gRNA-free cells and provides no guide-effect sensitivity estimates The dataset is full-length (non-UMI) scRNA-seq — the article only focused on UMI-based datasets and nonlinear covariates may need revalidation on full-length platforms You need hypothesis testing of arbitrary nonlinear associations — Normalisr is explicitly not designed for that

skills.description: Use when you have gRNA assignment and UMI count matrices from a high-MOI CRISPRi screen (e.g., GSE120861 K562) and want to infer causal trans-gene regulations from TSS-targeting gRNAs.
skills.name: crispr-screen-trans-regulatory-inference
skills.search_text: crispr-screen-trans-regulatory-inference Use when you have gRNA assignment and UMI count matrices from a high-MOI CRISPRi screen (e.g., GSE120861 K562) and want to infer causal trans-gene regulations from TSS-targeting gRNAs. You need arbitrary nonlinear association testing — Normalisr is not designed for hypothesis testing of nonlinear associations You need causal inference via v-structures, regularized regression, or Granger causality with longitudinal data — explicitly out of scope Data are non-UMI full-length platforms or multi-dataset integrations needing batch-effect correction — only UMI-based datasets were validated http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Reconstruct a putative gene regulatory network from high-MOI single-cell CRISPRi (CROP-seq) screens by chaining TSS-repression gRNA→targeted-gene links with trans-associations through Normalisr's causal inference framework, yielding 833 high-confidence regulations (all four Q ≤ 0.2). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-26682-1
skills.summary: Reconstruct a putative gene regulatory network from high-MOI single-cell CRISPRi (CROP-seq) screens by chaining TSS-repression gRNA→targeted-gene links with trans-associations through Normalisr's causal inference framework, yielding 833 high-confidence regulations (all four Q ≤ 0.2).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need arbitrary nonlinear association testing — Normalisr is not designed for hypothesis testing of nonlinear associations You need causal inference via v-structures, regularized regression, or Granger causality with longitudinal data — explicitly out of scope Data are non-UMI full-length platforms or multi-dataset integrations needing batch-effect correction — only UMI-based datasets were validated

skills.description: Use when analyzing time-course scRNA-seq data (e.g. zebrafish embryogenesis Drop-seq with 38,731 cells x 11,588 genes) to discover genes that dynamically regulate cells into mature cell types via gene-gene network edges.
skills.name: critical-gene-identification
skills.search_text: critical-gene-identification Use when analyzing time-course scRNA-seq data (e.g. zebrafish embryogenesis Drop-seq with 38,731 cells x 11,588 genes) to discover genes that dynamically regulate cells into mature cell types via gene-gene network edges. Data are single-time-point scRNA-seq with no cell-to-cell correspondence between time points, since the functional concurrent models require trajectories across adjacent time points The goal is a bulk population pseudotime trajectory rather than individual cell fate trajectories and gene-gene dynamic relationships http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Identifies critical genes regulating cell differentiation by constructing dynamic gene networks from individual cell fate trajectories produced by CellST, using functional concurrent linear models with Bayesian confidence intervals on time-course scRNA-seq data (e.g. zebrafish embryogenesis Drop-seq). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.ailsci.2023.100068
skills.summary: Identifies critical genes regulating cell differentiation by constructing dynamic gene networks from individual cell fate trajectories produced by CellST, using functional concurrent linear models with Bayesian confidence intervals on time-course scRNA-seq data (e.g. zebrafish embryogenesis Drop-seq).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are single-time-point scRNA-seq with no cell-to-cell correspondence between time points, since the functional concurrent models require trajectories across adjacent time points The goal is a bulk population pseudotime trajectory rather than individual cell fate trajectories and gene-gene dynamic relationships

skills.description: Use when a trained deep drug-response predictor must be interpreted — i.e., you need ranked lists of genes contributing to sensitivity vs resistance predictions and want to measure bulk-vs-single-cell overlap (reported ~46% / 53%).
skills.name: critical-gene-identification-from-trained-networks
skills.search_text: critical-gene-identification-from-trained-networks Use when a trained deep drug-response predictor must be interpreted — i.e., you need ranked lists of genes contributing to sensitivity vs resistance predictions and want to measure bulk-vs-single-cell overlap (reported ~46% / 53%). The model has not yet been trained — IG attribution requires a converged bulk and single-cell checkpoint with matching encoder/predictor dimensions You only need drug-response labels per cell rather than gene-level mechanistic interpretation (run scmodel.py with --printgene "F" instead) Input scRNA-seq lacks homologous gene mapping to the human bulk training space (e.g. non-human species without homolog filtering) http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Extract critical genes driving drug-response predictions from trained scDEAL networks using integrated-gradient (IG) feature attribution at both the bulk (GDSC/CCLE-trained bulkmodel) and single-cell (scmodel) levels, then compare the top-contributing sensitivity/resistance gene sets across the two levels. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-34277-7
skills.summary: Extract critical genes driving drug-response predictions from trained scDEAL networks using integrated-gradient (IG) feature attribution at both the bulk (GDSC/CCLE-trained bulkmodel) and single-cell (scmodel) levels, then compare the top-contributing sensitivity/resistance gene sets across the two levels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The model has not yet been trained — IG attribution requires a converged bulk and single-cell checkpoint with matching encoder/predictor dimensions You only need drug-response labels per cell rather than gene-level mechanistic interpretation (run scmodel.py with --printgene "F" instead) Input scRNA-seq lacks homologous gene mapping to the human bulk training space (e.g. non-human species without homolog filtering)

skills.description: Use when evaluating supervised cell-type label transfer across developmental ages or samples in scRNA-seq, e.g. testing whether a classifier trained on one age generalizes to another.
skills.name: cross-age-label-transfer-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-age-label-transfer-evaluation Use when evaluating supervised cell-type label transfer across developmental ages or samples in scRNA-seq, e.g. testing whether a classifier trained on one age generalizes to another. When the query tissue is from a different species than the training annotations — the authors limited SIMS to within-species transfer because neuronal subtypes diverge significantly between species When no pre-existing expert annotations are available for training, since SIMS is fully supervised and relies on prior normalization, clustering, and differential-expression-derived labels http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmark SIMS (TabNet-based single-cell classifier) label transfer on the Di Bella developing mouse cortex dataset, evaluating an E18+P1 combined-age split (84.2% accuracy / 0.791 Macro F1 over 17 cell types) versus a cross-age P1-to-E18 transfer (73.6% accuracy / 0.674 Macro F1). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.xgen.2024.100581
skills.summary: Benchmark SIMS (TabNet-based single-cell classifier) label transfer on the Di Bella developing mouse cortex dataset, evaluating an E18+P1 combined-age split (84.2% accuracy / 0.791 Macro F1 over 17 cell types) versus a cross-age P1-to-E18 transfer (73.6% accuracy / 0.674 Macro F1).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the query tissue is from a different species than the training annotations — the authors limited SIMS to within-species transfer because neuronal subtypes diverge significantly between species When no pre-existing expert annotations are available for training, since SIMS is fully supervised and relies on prior normalization, clustering, and differential-expression-derived labels

skills.description: Use when a downstream transformation or trajectory conclusion must be shown to be robust to the choice of pseudotime algorithm, e.g. MAPiT-transformed Ki-67, RNA or p27 spatial profiles derived from Wanderlust vs DPT orderings.
skills.name: cross-algorithm-consistency-comparison-with-confidence-intervals
skills.search_text: cross-algorithm-consistency-comparison-with-confidence-intervals Use when a downstream transformation or trajectory conclusion must be shown to be robust to the choice of pseudotime algorithm, e.g. MAPiT-transformed Ki-67, RNA or p27 spatial profiles derived from Wanderlust vs DPT orderings. Only one pseudotime ordering is available, so no cross-algorithm comparison can be made No prior knowledge of the true-scale cell density distribution exists (MAPiT's transformation itself is then undefined) The goal is to compare algorithms at the pseudotime level rather than on the transformed real scale — MAPiT is reliant on the correctness of the provided cell order and does not fix a wrong ordering http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 A validation strategy that runs two independent pseudotime algorithms (Wanderlust and Diffusion Maps/DPT) on the same single-cell dataset, MAPiT-transforms each ordering to the true spatial or temporal scale, and checks whether marker profiles with 50% confidence bands overlap — demonstrating the result is not an artifact of the trajectory-inference algorithm. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-60400-z
skills.summary: A validation strategy that runs two independent pseudotime algorithms (Wanderlust and Diffusion Maps/DPT) on the same single-cell dataset, MAPiT-transforms each ordering to the true spatial or temporal scale, and checks whether marker profiles with 50% confidence bands overlap — demonstrating the result is not an artifact of the trajectory-inference algorithm.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one pseudotime ordering is available, so no cross-algorithm comparison can be made No prior knowledge of the true-scale cell density distribution exists (MAPiT's transformation itself is then undefined) The goal is to compare algorithms at the pseudotime level rather than on the transformed real scale — MAPiT is reliant on the correctness of the provided cell order and does not fix a wrong ordering

skills.description: Use when you need to quantitatively compare signature-detection performance of multiple fitting algorithms against ground-truth contributions, e.g., validating a new error-suppression rule (bootstrap 95% CI) against fixed contribution thresholds.
skills.name: cross-algorithm-detection-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-algorithm-detection-benchmarking Use when you need to quantitatively compare signature-detection performance of multiple fitting algorithms against ground-truth contributions, e.g., validating a new error-suppression rule (bootstrap 95% CI) against fixed contribution thresholds. Catalogs with fewer than ~500 mutations (e.g., targeted capture panels covering a few megabases), where mutational burdens are too low for meaningful individual-patient signature fitting and benchmark conclusions do not transfer Whole-exome data where the expected signature profile in coding versus non-coding regions differs substantially, complicating ground-truth comparisons De novo signature discovery from large cohorts — this skill benchmarks fitting against known reference signatures, not extraction http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 Benchmarking the detection sensitivity and specificity of mutational signature fitting algorithms (mmsig, deconstructSigs, MutationalPatterns) on simulated dilution catalogs with known signature contributions, to compare a dynamic error-suppression approach against hard threshold-based calling. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-021-01938-0
skills.summary: Benchmarking the detection sensitivity and specificity of mutational signature fitting algorithms (mmsig, deconstructSigs, MutationalPatterns) on simulated dilution catalogs with known signature contributions, to compare a dynamic error-suppression approach against hard threshold-based calling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Catalogs with fewer than ~500 mutations (e.g., targeted capture panels covering a few megabases), where mutational burdens are too low for meaningful individual-patient signature fitting and benchmark conclusions do not transfer Whole-exome data where the expected signature profile in coding versus non-coding regions differs substantially, complicating ground-truth comparisons De novo signature discovery from large cohorts — this skill benchmarks fitting against known reference signatures, not extraction

skills.description: Use when two trajectory-inference algorithms (e.g., CellRouter flow networks vs Monocle 2 DDRTree) must be compared on the same count matrix to test whether underrepresented or rare lineage bifurcations are resolved or collapsed.
skills.name: cross-algorithm-lineage-comparison-visualization
skills.search_text: cross-algorithm-lineage-comparison-visualization Use when two trajectory-inference algorithms (e.g., CellRouter flow networks vs Monocle 2 DDRTree) must be compared on the same count matrix to test whether underrepresented or rare lineage bifurcations are resolved or collapsed. You need a trajectory between two chosen cell states, including transitions to or from rare cell types — Monocle 2's DDRTree is explicitly not designed for this; use CellRouter alone. The input is not a single-cell count matrix with cell annotations but a pseudotime vector, feature table, or already-completed trajectory object — a re-run comparison cannot be performed. A priori knowledge of the number of branches is required by the downstream analysis — CellRouter requires no a priori knowledge of trajectory structure, so forced branch counts defeat the comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 A side-by-side lineage resolution comparison between CellRouter's subpopulation-aware flow-network trajectories and Monocle 2's default DDRTree branching, applied to the same single-cell RNA-seq matrix, with a comparison table and two-panel figure. It exposes when one algorithm resolves an underrepresented bifurcation (e.g., megakaryocyte/erythrocyte in Olsson GSE70245) that the other collapses onto a single branch. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-03214-y
skills.summary: A side-by-side lineage resolution comparison between CellRouter's subpopulation-aware flow-network trajectories and Monocle 2's default DDRTree branching, applied to the same single-cell RNA-seq matrix, with a comparison table and two-panel figure. It exposes when one algorithm resolves an underrepresented bifurcation (e.g., megakaryocyte/erythrocyte in Olsson GSE70245) that the other collapses onto a single branch.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a trajectory between two chosen cell states, including transitions to or from rare cell types — Monocle 2's DDRTree is explicitly not designed for this; use CellRouter alone. The input is not a single-cell count matrix with cell annotations but a pseudotime vector, feature table, or already-completed trajectory object — a re-run comparison cannot be performed. A priori knowledge of the number of branches is required by the downstream analysis — CellRouter requires no a priori knowledge of trajectory structure, so forced branch counts defeat the comparison.

skills.description: Use when you have pseudotime orderings from two or more trajectory-inference algorithms run on the same single-cell RNA-seq dataset and need a quantitative smoothness benchmark (correlated-gene counts and lag-1 autocorrelation of lineage markers) to compare them.
skills.name: cross-algorithm-pseudotime-comparison-table-construction
skills.search_text: cross-algorithm-pseudotime-comparison-table-construction Use when you have pseudotime orderings from two or more trajectory-inference algorithms run on the same single-cell RNA-seq dataset and need a quantitative smoothness benchmark (correlated-gene counts and lag-1 autocorrelation of lineage markers) to compare them. The dataset contains only a single algorithm's pseudotime ordering — with no competing trajectories there is nothing to tabulate against. The question is about CellRouter's own trajectory reconstruction or regulatory-network analysis rather than benchmarking it against Monocle 2, DPT, Wishbone, or Waterfall smoothness. The input data lacks lineage-specific branch markers (e.g., Klf1/Car2/Cited4 or Mpo/Prtn3/Ctsg orthologs), since lag-1 autocorrelation of these markers is a core metric. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmark CellRouter's subpopulation-aware trajectories against competing trajectory-inference algorithms (Monocle 2, DPT, Wishbone, Waterfall) on the same scRNA-seq dataset (Paul et al. GSE72857 myeloid progenitors) by computing, per algorithm, the number of genes significantly correlated with pseudotime and the lag-1 autocorrelation of branch markers, then assembling a single comparison table (algorithm_comparison.csv). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-03214-y
skills.summary: Benchmark CellRouter's subpopulation-aware trajectories against competing trajectory-inference algorithms (Monocle 2, DPT, Wishbone, Waterfall) on the same scRNA-seq dataset (Paul et al. GSE72857 myeloid progenitors) by computing, per algorithm, the number of genes significantly correlated with pseudotime and the lag-1 autocorrelation of branch markers, then assembling a single comparison table (algorithm_comparison.csv).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset contains only a single algorithm's pseudotime ordering — with no competing trajectories there is nothing to tabulate against. The question is about CellRouter's own trajectory reconstruction or regulatory-network analysis rather than benchmarking it against Monocle 2, DPT, Wishbone, or Waterfall smoothness. The input data lacks lineage-specific branch markers (e.g., Klf1/Car2/Cited4 or Mpo/Prtn3/Ctsg orthologs), since lag-1 autocorrelation of these markers is a core metric.

skills.description: Use when you need to test whether a UMI-read mapping-shift pattern is specific to one alignment algorithm by re-aligning the same quality-filtered, UMI-clipped FASTQ reads with STAR, GSNAP and HISAT2 and overlaying the resulting shift-distance density curves.
skills.name: cross-aligner-density-plot-visualization
skills.search_text: cross-aligner-density-plot-visualization Use when you need to test whether a UMI-read mapping-shift pattern is specific to one alignment algorithm by re-aligning the same quality-filtered, UMI-clipped FASTQ reads with STAR, GSNAP and HISAT2 and overlaying the resulting shift-distance density curves. Input reads have not been quality-filtered and UMI-clipped (fastq_qual_filter / fastq_umi_clipper run first), since umi_counterizer.pl assumes the UMI is in the FASTQ/SAM header Paired-end sequencing data — the ncgr/UMI-analysis pipeline's use case 'only involves single ended sequencing at this stage' You want to quantify gene-level expression rather than characterize the shift artefact; use the gene_umi_counter.pl / read-count branch of the pipeline instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Reproduce the UMI-read mapping-shift distributions under three independent aligners (STAR, GSNAP, HISAT2) and plot them as overlapping density curves, demonstrating (as in Fig. 5 of Sena et al. 2018) that the mapping-shift artefact is aligner-independent rather than an artefact of one algorithm. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-018-31064-7
skills.summary: Reproduce the UMI-read mapping-shift distributions under three independent aligners (STAR, GSNAP, HISAT2) and plot them as overlapping density curves, demonstrating (as in Fig. 5 of Sena et al. 2018) that the mapping-shift artefact is aligner-independent rather than an artefact of one algorithm.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads have not been quality-filtered and UMI-clipped (fastq_qual_filter / fastq_umi_clipper run first), since umi_counterizer.pl assumes the UMI is in the FASTQ/SAM header Paired-end sequencing data — the ncgr/UMI-analysis pipeline's use case 'only involves single ended sequencing at this stage' You want to quantify gene-level expression rather than characterize the shift artefact; use the gene_umi_counter.pl / read-count branch of the pipeline instead

skills.description: Use when you need to predict gene-expression count matrices for unseen condition/batch combinations (e.g., ctrl/healthy vs stim/severe) from multi-batch, multi-condition scRNA-seq data, including out-of-sample held-out cell subsets.
skills.name: cross-batch-condition-effect-prediction
skills.search_text: cross-batch-condition-effect-prediction Use when you need to predict gene-expression count matrices for unseen condition/batch combinations (e.g., ctrl/healthy vs stim/severe) from multi-batch, multi-condition scRNA-seq data, including out-of-sample held-out cell subsets. Each batch is measured under only one condition — there is not enough information to fully disentangle batch and condition effects Condition types are strongly correlated/correlated with batch effects, since scDisInFact assumes condition types are mutually independent and condition effect independent of batch effect The task is single-task batch effect removal or key gene detection only, where task-specific methods may suffice and the multi-condition latent structure is unnecessary http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Perturbation prediction across conditions and batches in multi-batch multi-condition scRNA-seq data using scDisInFact's disentangled latent factors, benchmarked against scGen and scPreGAN with cell-type-specific MSE, Pearson correlation, and R2. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-45227-w
skills.summary: Perturbation prediction across conditions and batches in multi-batch multi-condition scRNA-seq data using scDisInFact's disentangled latent factors, benchmarked against scGen and scPreGAN with cell-type-specific MSE, Pearson correlation, and R2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Each batch is measured under only one condition — there is not enough information to fully disentangle batch and condition effects Condition types are strongly correlated/correlated with batch effects, since scDisInFact assumes condition types are mutually independent and condition effect independent of batch effect The task is single-task batch effect removal or key gene detection only, where task-specific methods may suffice and the multi-condition latent structure is unnecessary

skills.description: Use when a low-dimensional embedding claimed to remove batch effects must be validated: compute pseudotime or another per-cell quantity per batch and test cross-batch consistency via regional KL divergence of batch mixing.
skills.name: cross-batch-consistency-validation
skills.search_text: cross-batch-consistency-validation Use when a low-dimensional embedding claimed to remove batch effects must be validated: compute pseudotime or another per-cell quantity per batch and test cross-batch consistency via regional KL divergence of batch mixing. Technical differences across batches exceed true biological variations — DESC's batch removal and hence this validation rely on the assumption that technical differences are smaller than biological ones The dataset has only one processing batch, so no cross-batch KL divergence or consistency check is possible The input is raw count data not yet normalized (UMI normalization to 10,000 and log transform, gene standardization, and highly variable gene selection via filter_genes_dispersion should precede embedding) http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Validates batch effect removal in an embedding (e.g., the DESC X_Embeded_z representation) by checking that downstream quantities such as Monocle3 pseudotime have consistent distributions across processing batches, quantified with regional batch-mixing KL divergence. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-15851-3
skills.summary: Validates batch effect removal in an embedding (e.g., the DESC X_Embeded_z representation) by checking that downstream quantities such as Monocle3 pseudotime have consistent distributions across processing batches, quantified with regional batch-mixing KL divergence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Technical differences across batches exceed true biological variations — DESC's batch removal and hence this validation rely on the assumption that technical differences are smaller than biological ones The dataset has only one processing batch, so no cross-batch KL divergence or consistency check is possible The input is raw count data not yet normalized (UMI normalization to 10,000 and log transform, gene standardization, and highly variable gene selection via filter_genes_dispersion should precede embedding)

skills.description: Use when integrating scRNA-seq count tables from multiple platforms/batches whose gene sets differ, and a shared gene universe must be established before multi-table CA (corralm) or before comparing against PCA/Harmony baselines.
skills.name: cross-batch-gene-feature-intersection
skills.search_text: cross-batch-gene-feature-intersection Use when integrating scRNA-seq count tables from multiple platforms/batches whose gene sets differ, and a shared gene universe must be established before multi-table CA (corralm) or before comparing against PCA/Harmony baselines. Analyzing a single table — use single-table corral for dimensionality reduction instead of intersecting features for multi-table CA Batches assayed such divergent gene sets that the intersection is too small to be a meaningful feature space Inputs are already batch-corrected embeddings rather than raw count matrices — feature intersection at the count level is no longer applicable http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Restricts multiple scRNA-seq batches (e.g., 10X, Celseq2, Dropseq in SCMixology) to their intersecting set of genes so all tables share a common feature space, a prerequisite for multi-table correspondence analysis with corralm. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-022-26434-1
skills.summary: Restricts multiple scRNA-seq batches (e.g., 10X, Celseq2, Dropseq in SCMixology) to their intersecting set of genes so all tables share a common feature space, a prerequisite for multi-table correspondence analysis with corralm.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Analyzing a single table — use single-table corral for dimensionality reduction instead of intersecting features for multi-table CA Batches assayed such divergent gene sets that the intersection is too small to be a meaningful feature space Inputs are already batch-corrected embeddings rather than raw count matrices — feature intersection at the count level is no longer applicable

skills.description: Use when integrating multiple independently preprocessed single-sample scRNA-seq batches in the scdrake integration pipeline and a joint HVG set is needed before running batch integration methods.
skills.name: cross-batch-highly-variable-gene-selection
skills.search_text: cross-batch-highly-variable-gene-selection Use when integrating multiple independently preprocessed single-sample scRNA-seq batches in the scdrake integration pipeline and a joint HVG set is needed before running batch integration methods. Running the single-sample pipeline on one dataset — no cross-batch HVG selection is needed or available there Batches were not preprocessed by the single-sample pipeline (e.g. raw Cell Ranger output without prior QC/normalization) Only one batch is supplied — integration HVG selection has nothing to reconcile across samples http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Selects highly variable genes jointly across multiple single-sample scRNA-seq batches (e.g. PBMC 1k and PBMC 3k) as the HVG step of the scdrake 01_integration stage, so that batch integration methods can compute corrected reduced dimensions on a shared gene space. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad089
skills.summary: Selects highly variable genes jointly across multiple single-sample scRNA-seq batches (e.g. PBMC 1k and PBMC 3k) as the HVG step of the scdrake 01_integration stage, so that batch integration methods can compute corrected reduced dimensions on a shared gene space.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Running the single-sample pipeline on one dataset — no cross-batch HVG selection is needed or available there Batches were not preprocessed by the single-sample pipeline (e.g. raw Cell Ranger output without prior QC/normalization) Only one batch is supplied — integration HVG selection has nothing to reconcile across samples

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a model can predict single-cell expression toward an unseen condition-batch combination (e.g., <moderate, 40-65> in batch Lee_2020) and comparing it against baselines across multiple prediction scenarios.

skills.search_text: cross-batch-prediction-scenario-benchmarking Use when evaluating whether a model can predict single-cell expression toward an unseen condition-batch combination (e.g., <moderate, 40-65> in batch Lee_2020) and comparing it against baselines across multiple prediction scenarios. Each batch in the dataset was measured under only one condition, so there is insufficient information to fully disentangle batch and condition effects The condition types are strongly correlated and cannot be assumed mutually independent (consider a combined condition type instead) The goal is batch effect removal or key gene detection only, without perturbation prediction toward a held-out condition http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Benchmarks perturbation prediction toward a held-out condition-batch combination across within-batch and cross-batch scenarios, comparing a multi-condition model (scDisInFact) against baselines (scGen, scPreGAN) using cell-type-specific MSE, R2, and Pearson correlation under both in-sample and out-of-sample settings. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-45227-w
skills.summary: Benchmarks perturbation prediction toward a held-out condition-batch combination across within-batch and cross-batch scenarios, comparing a multi-condition model (scDisInFact) against baselines (scGen, scPreGAN) using cell-type-specific MSE, R2, and Pearson correlation under both in-sample and out-of-sample settings.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Each batch in the dataset was measured under only one condition, so there is insufficient information to fully disentangle batch and condition effects The condition types are strongly correlated and cannot be assumed mutually independent (consider a combined condition type instead) The goal is batch effect removal or key gene detection only, without perturbation prediction toward a held-out condition

skills.search_text: cross-benchmark-method-ranking-comparison Use when ranking GRN inference algorithms against a known ground-truth GRN on simulated scRNA-seq data (BoneMarrow, PBMC) and checking whether the resulting method ordering reproduces BEELINE's experimental-benchmark results. Benchmarking on the multi-cell-type PBMC-All dataset, where the paper states the benchmarking results are not conclusive and follow-up studies are required Comprehensively evaluating cell-specific GRN inference methods such as CeSpGRN — the paper explicitly notes no comprehensive study of this method class has been performed Judging simulated-data quality rather than GRN inference performance — use GRouNdGAN's --evaluate command instead of --benchmark_grn http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmarks eight GRN inference methods (GRNBoost2, GENIE3, PIDC, PPCOR, LEAP, SCODE, SINCERITIES, CeSpGRN) on GRouNdGAN-simulated BoneMarrow and PBMC data and aggregates precision-at-k and AUPRC into a single ranking table that is validated against BEELINE's curated-benchmark method ordering. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-48516-6
skills.summary: Benchmarks eight GRN inference methods (GRNBoost2, GENIE3, PIDC, PPCOR, LEAP, SCODE, SINCERITIES, CeSpGRN) on GRouNdGAN-simulated BoneMarrow and PBMC data and aggregates precision-at-k and AUPRC into a single ranking table that is validated against BEELINE's curated-benchmark method ordering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Benchmarking on the multi-cell-type PBMC-All dataset, where the paper states the benchmarking results are not conclusive and follow-up studies are required Comprehensively evaluating cell-specific GRN inference methods such as CeSpGRN — the paper explicitly notes no comprehensive study of this method class has been performed Judging simulated-data quality rather than GRN inference performance — use GRouNdGAN's --evaluate command instead of --benchmark_grn

skills.description: Use when comparing a new or existing single-cell CNA caller against HiScanner, Ginkgo, CHISEL, SCYN, and SCOPE on high-coverage (≥20x) PTA-amplified scWGS with simulated ground-truth CNAs or a known aneuploid single cell.
skills.name: cross-caller-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-caller-benchmark-comparison Use when comparing a new or existing single-cell CNA caller against HiScanner, Ginkgo, CHISEL, SCYN, and SCOPE on high-coverage (≥20x) PTA-amplified scWGS with simulated ground-truth CNAs or a known aneuploid single cell. Input is low-coverage (<0.05x per cell) scWGS from DLP+ or 10x Genomics CNV assays — CHISEL/Alleloscope are designed for that regime, and HiScanner's ADO-based bin-size selection assumes high-coverage PTA data Goal is germline or clonal variant genotyping rather than somatic CNA benchmarking — SCAN2 excludes candidates with any read support in matched bulk Only a single caller's output exists with no matched bulk, ground-truth simulations, or comparator calls — precision/sensitivity and cross-caller concordance cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Benchmarks HiScanner against four single-cell CNA callers (Ginkgo, CHISEL, SCYN, SCOPE) on simulated SDX data and a single 29x PTA-amplified aneuploid neuron (5823PFC-B), quantifying precision, sensitivity, and breakpoint density per caller across CNA types and sizes (200 kb–5 Mb). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-60446-5
skills.summary: Benchmarks HiScanner against four single-cell CNA callers (Ginkgo, CHISEL, SCYN, SCOPE) on simulated SDX data and a single 29x PTA-amplified aneuploid neuron (5823PFC-B), quantifying precision, sensitivity, and breakpoint density per caller across CNA types and sizes (200 kb–5 Mb).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is low-coverage (<0.05x per cell) scWGS from DLP+ or 10x Genomics CNV assays — CHISEL/Alleloscope are designed for that regime, and HiScanner's ADO-based bin-size selection assumes high-coverage PTA data Goal is germline or clonal variant genotyping rather than somatic CNA benchmarking — SCAN2 excludes candidates with any read support in matched bulk Only a single caller's output exists with no matched bulk, ground-truth simulations, or comparator calls — precision/sensitivity and cross-caller concordance cannot be computed

skills.description: Use when a query single-cell RNA-seq dataset (e.g., six-cancer-type myeloid cells) needs cell-type labels transferred from a differently sourced reference (e.g., KIDNEY/UCEC/ESCA pan-cancer myeloid), especially across batches or cancer types where annotation consistency and interpretability matter.
skills.name: cross-cancer-label-transfer
skills.search_text: cross-cancer-label-transfer Use when a query single-cell RNA-seq dataset (e.g., six-cancer-type myeloid cells) needs cell-type labels transferred from a differently sourced reference (e.g., KIDNEY/UCEC/ESCA pan-cancer myeloid), especially across batches or cancer types where annotation consistency and interpretability matter. The reference and query AnnData cannot be reconciled to identical, same-ordered var_names (genes), which TOSICA explicitly warns against. You need unsupervised discovery of novel cell types rather than transferring existing reference labels to a query dataset. The task requires a method applicable to a very large number of batches where Seurat-based integration approaches are being compared — note some competitors become inapplicable above ~85 batches, so benchmark scope must be checked per method. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Transfer cell-type labels across cancers by training a TOSICA Transformer model with a pathway-masked attention layer on a reference scRNA-seq dataset and predicting labels on a query dataset, using scanpy AnnData objects and pre-prepared gmt masks such as reactome.gmt. The pathway masking makes the model batch-insensitive while retaining interpretable, traceable attention over original input genes. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-35923-4
skills.summary: Transfer cell-type labels across cancers by training a TOSICA Transformer model with a pathway-masked attention layer on a reference scRNA-seq dataset and predicting labels on a query dataset, using scanpy AnnData objects and pre-prepared gmt masks such as reactome.gmt. The pathway masking makes the model batch-insensitive while retaining interpretable, traceable attention over original input genes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reference and query AnnData cannot be reconciled to identical, same-ordered var_names (genes), which TOSICA explicitly warns against. You need unsupervised discovery of novel cell types rather than transferring existing reference labels to a query dataset. The task requires a method applicable to a very large number of batches where Seurat-based integration approaches are being compared — note some competitors become inapplicable above ~85 batches, so benchmark scope must be checked per method.

skills.description: Use when building or auditing a pan-cancer malignant-vs-normal single-cell classifier from unioned cross-dataset DEG features, and you need to quantify whether cross-cancer-type common DEGs (≥2 cancer types) drive performance versus cancer-type-unique DEGs.
skills.name: cross-cancer-type-deg-classification
skills.search_text: cross-cancer-type-deg-classification Use when building or auditing a pan-cancer malignant-vs-normal single-cell classifier from unioned cross-dataset DEG features, and you need to quantify whether cross-cancer-type common DEGs (≥2 cancer types) drive performance versus cancer-type-unique DEGs. The goal is to annotate malignant cells in tissues of unknown or controversial origin (e.g. synovial sarcoma, certain brain tumors) — the paper states these capabilities require further testing. Input data are not single-cell/spatial transcriptomics of cancerous lineages with prerequisite basic cell-type identification; scMalignantFinder is designed for malignant cells within cancerous lineages only. The analysis goal is CNV-based malignancy inference (e.g. CopyKAT/inferCNV-style) rather than supervised DEG-feature classification. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Trains logistic-regression malignant-cell classifiers on the 2707-DEG feature set from multiple cancer types (scMalignantFinder) and tests whether DEGs common to ≥2 cancer types — rather than cancer-type-unique DEGs — carry the classification performance, using per-gene logistic-regression coefficients as importance. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-025-07942-y
skills.summary: Trains logistic-regression malignant-cell classifiers on the 2707-DEG feature set from multiple cancer types (scMalignantFinder) and tests whether DEGs common to ≥2 cancer types — rather than cancer-type-unique DEGs — carry the classification performance, using per-gene logistic-regression coefficients as importance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to annotate malignant cells in tissues of unknown or controversial origin (e.g. synovial sarcoma, certain brain tumors) — the paper states these capabilities require further testing. Input data are not single-cell/spatial transcriptomics of cancerous lineages with prerequisite basic cell-type identification; scMalignantFinder is designed for malignant cells within cancerous lineages only. The analysis goal is CNV-based malignancy inference (e.g. CopyKAT/inferCNV-style) rather than supervised DEG-feature classification.

skills.description: Use when you have normalized scRNA-seq expression matrices from cancer types disjoint from the training data (e.g., P1_BC through P11_Melanoma) and need to reproduce or extend reported malignant vs non-malignant prediction performance metrics.
skills.name: cross-cancer-validation-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-cancer-validation-benchmarking Use when you have normalized scRNA-seq expression matrices from cancer types disjoint from the training data (e.g., P1_BC through P11_Melanoma) and need to reproduce or extend reported malignant vs non-malignant prediction performance metrics. The goal is annotating non-cancer cell subpopulations (immune, stromal, epithelial) — the article explicitly states the algorithm 'is not designed for identifying subpopulations of non-cancer cells' The test data overlap the training sets used for feature selection, which would overestimate performance ('the reported predictive performance in the training set could be overestimated due to the predicted sets being involved in feature selection') The input is raw (unnormalized) counts — PreCanCell_data() requires a normalized expression matrix with rownames being genes and colnames being cells http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Benchmark the PreCanCell ensemble k-NN classifier on independent single-cell transcriptome test sets spanning multiple cancer types, computing accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, and AUROC against published cell annotations. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.07.009
skills.summary: Benchmark the PreCanCell ensemble k-NN classifier on independent single-cell transcriptome test sets spanning multiple cancer types, computing accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, and AUROC against published cell annotations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is annotating non-cancer cell subpopulations (immune, stromal, epithelial) — the article explicitly states the algorithm 'is not designed for identifying subpopulations of non-cancer cells' The test data overlap the training sets used for feature selection, which would overestimate performance ('the reported predictive performance in the training set could be overestimated due to the predicted sets being involved in feature selection') The input is raw (unnormalized) counts — PreCanCell_data() requires a normalized expression matrix with rownames being genes and colnames being cells

skills.description: Use when multiple GRN inference methods must be compared on identical single-cell datasets and the goal is to rank them by biological validity, e.g. disease subnetwork modeling accuracy across tissues or cell types.
skills.name: cross-cell-type-benchmarking-of-grn-methods
skills.search_text: cross-cell-type-benchmarking-of-grn-methods Use when multiple GRN inference methods must be compared on identical single-cell datasets and the goal is to rank them by biological validity, e.g. disease subnetwork modeling accuracy across tissues or cell types. When the goal is perturbation-target prediction accuracy — use the Perturb-seq benchmark instead of disease subnetwork modeling When comparing methods on datasets without disease gene set overlap — degree-preserved nulls and DisGeNET random walks require gene-set membership in the GRN http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_3407 Benchmarks SCING against GRNBOOST2, ppcor, and PIDC by building GRNs on the same scRNA-seq cells and scoring each network's ability to model DisGeNET disease subnetworks (Immune, Metabolic, Neuronal) via the Huang et al. random walk framework, reporting performance gain over degree-preserved random GRNs across mouse cell atlas tissues and cell types. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2023.107124
skills.summary: Benchmarks SCING against GRNBOOST2, ppcor, and PIDC by building GRNs on the same scRNA-seq cells and scoring each network's ability to model DisGeNET disease subnetworks (Immune, Metabolic, Neuronal) via the Huang et al. random walk framework, reporting performance gain over degree-preserved random GRNs across mouse cell atlas tissues and cell types.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is perturbation-target prediction accuracy — use the Perturb-seq benchmark instead of disease subnetwork modeling When comparing methods on datasets without disease gene set overlap — degree-preserved nulls and DisGeNET random walks require gene-set membership in the GRN

skills.description: Use when you have DH profiles (predicted or imputed) for the same set of cell types from two methods and need genome-wide cross-locus and cross-cell-type agreement metrics, plus differential-DH comparison for similar cell type pairs.
skills.name: cross-cell-type-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-cell-type-correlation-analysis Use when you have DH profiles (predicted or imputed) for the same set of cell types from two methods and need genome-wide cross-locus and cross-cell-type agreement metrics, plus differential-DH comparison for similar cell type pairs. You only have DH profiles from a single method and no second method or ground truth to compare against Cell types have no shared genomic loci or are on incompatible genome builds without coordinate alignment You need to discover new DHS locations — BIRD prediction will not identify new DH sites and this comparison framework evaluates agreement only at fixed loci http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Compares predicted/imputed DNase I hypersensitivity (DH) profiles across multiple cell types by computing genome-wide cross-locus and cross-cell-type agreement (e.g., correlation) between methods such as BIRD (gene expression only) and ChromImpute (multiple functional genomic data types), plus differential-DH comparison for highly similar cell type pairs. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-017-01188-x
skills.summary: Compares predicted/imputed DNase I hypersensitivity (DH) profiles across multiple cell types by computing genome-wide cross-locus and cross-cell-type agreement (e.g., correlation) between methods such as BIRD (gene expression only) and ChromImpute (multiple functional genomic data types), plus differential-DH comparison for highly similar cell type pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have DH profiles from a single method and no second method or ground truth to compare against Cell types have no shared genomic loci or are on incompatible genome builds without coordinate alignment You need to discover new DHS locations — BIRD prediction will not identify new DH sites and this comparison framework evaluates agreement only at fixed loci

skills.description: Use when single-cell RNAseq data from multiple cell types is sampled across circadian time points and the goal is to test whether circadian phase heterogeneity (not just mean phase) differs between cell types.
skills.name: cross-cell-type-phase-heterogeneity-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-cell-type-phase-heterogeneity-analysis Use when single-cell RNAseq data from multiple cell types is sampled across circadian time points and the goal is to test whether circadian phase heterogeneity (not just mean phase) differs between cell types. When tauFisher's performance is already subpar for the dataset type (e.g., human blood samples) — dispersion comparisons inherit prediction noise When the goal is mean circadian phase estimation of bulk samples rather than comparing within-cell-type phase dispersion When single-cell data lacks multiple ZT time points — bootstrapping at each ZT requires a sampled time series to compare per time point http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Quantifies whether circadian phases are more heterogeneous in one cell type than another by bootstrapping pseudobulk replicates from single-cell data, predicting circadian time per replicate with tauFisher, and comparing prediction dispersion (SD) and circular distributions across cell types at each ZT time point. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-48041-6
skills.summary: Quantifies whether circadian phases are more heterogeneous in one cell type than another by bootstrapping pseudobulk replicates from single-cell data, predicting circadian time per replicate with tauFisher, and comparing prediction dispersion (SD) and circular distributions across cell types at each ZT time point.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When tauFisher's performance is already subpar for the dataset type (e.g., human blood samples) — dispersion comparisons inherit prediction noise When the goal is mean circadian phase estimation of bulk samples rather than comparing within-cell-type phase dispersion When single-cell data lacks multiple ZT time points — bootstrapping at each ZT requires a sampled time series to compare per time point

skills.description: Use when comparing circadian rhythmicity between annotated cell types in single-cell RNAseq time-course data, e.g., counting rhythmic genes per cell type and their shared overlap.
skills.name: cross-cell-type-rhythmic-gene-overlap
skills.search_text: cross-cell-type-rhythmic-gene-overlap Use when comparing circadian rhythmicity between annotated cell types in single-cell RNAseq time-course data, e.g., counting rhythmic genes per cell type and their shared overlap. You need circadian phase/timestamp prediction for individual samples rather than rhythmic-gene detection per cell type — use tauFisher's train/test functions instead Input is raw single-cell expression without aggregation — JTK_Cycle cannot handle single-cell dropout; pseudobulk aggregation per cell type and time point is required The data lack circadian time-point structure (no ordered time series per cell type), since meta2d requires columns ordered by circadian time http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Detect cell-type-specific circadian rhythmic genes by running JTK_Cycle (via MetaCycle meta2d through tauFisher) on normalized per-cell-type pseudobulk scRNAseq time series, then intersecting the rhythmic gene lists across cell types. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-48041-6
skills.summary: Detect cell-type-specific circadian rhythmic genes by running JTK_Cycle (via MetaCycle meta2d through tauFisher) on normalized per-cell-type pseudobulk scRNAseq time series, then intersecting the rhythmic gene lists across cell types.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need circadian phase/timestamp prediction for individual samples rather than rhythmic-gene detection per cell type — use tauFisher's train/test functions instead Input is raw single-cell expression without aggregation — JTK_Cycle cannot handle single-cell dropout; pseudobulk aggregation per cell type and time point is required The data lack circadian time-point structure (no ordered time series per cell type), since meta2d requires columns ordered by circadian time

skills.description: Use when evaluating which classifier variant better rejects cells from unseen cell populations: you have a labeled hierarchical dataset, can hold out one population (e.g. Group 3 / four AMB nodes), and need per-variant rejection rates.
skills.name: cross-classifier-rejection-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-classifier-rejection-comparison Use when evaluating which classifier variant better rejects cells from unseen cell populations: you have a labeled hierarchical dataset, can hold out one population (e.g. Group 3 / four AMB nodes), and need per-variant rejection rates. Your goal is accurate classification of known populations rather than rejection of unseen ones — the linear SVM had accuracy equal to or higher than the one-class SVM on all datasets, and the one-class SVM degrades more on small populations The datasets are not yet aligned — scHPL is not a batch correction tool, so alignment (scVI or scArches) must be done before matching cell populations http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 A benchmarking procedure that trains the same hierarchical classification tree with two scHPL classifier variants (linear SVM vs one-class SVM) and compares their ability to reject cells from unseen populations, e.g. the simulated dataset with 'Group 3' held out. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-23196-8
skills.summary: A benchmarking procedure that trains the same hierarchical classification tree with two scHPL classifier variants (linear SVM vs one-class SVM) and compares their ability to reject cells from unseen populations, e.g. the simulated dataset with 'Group 3' held out.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is accurate classification of known populations rather than rejection of unseen ones — the linear SVM had accuracy equal to or higher than the one-class SVM on all datasets, and the one-class SVM degrades more on small populations The datasets are not yet aligned — scHPL is not a batch correction tool, so alignment (scVI or scArches) must be done before matching cell populations

skills.description: Use when a query scRNA-seq dataset has been clustered and per-cluster marker gene expression must be put on a comparable, standardized scale (z-scores) before correlating against deCS reference panels or before ranking cell-type-specific genes.
skills.name: cross-cluster-zscore-normalization
skills.search_text: cross-cluster-zscore-normalization Use when a query scRNA-seq dataset has been clustered and per-cluster marker gene expression must be put on a comparable, standardized scale (z-scores) before correlating against deCS reference panels or before ranking cell-type-specific genes. The reference or query panel is derived from bulk RNA-seq data — deCS uses regression t-statistics (t-score) for bulk references, not z-scores The input is already a scaled/normalized z-score matrix (double-scaling would distort the cross-cluster contrast) The goal is cluster-level annotation at the single-cell level rather than the cluster level — deCS defines cell types at the cell cluster level http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Row-wise z-score transformation via t(scale(t(...))) of averaged gene expression per cell cluster, used in deCS both to build scRNA-seq reference panels (HCL, HCAF) and to scale query cluster-level expression before correlation-based annotation. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2022.04.001
skills.summary: Row-wise z-score transformation via t(scale(t(...))) of averaged gene expression per cell cluster, used in deCS both to build scRNA-seq reference panels (HCL, HCAF) and to scale query cluster-level expression before correlation-based annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reference or query panel is derived from bulk RNA-seq data — deCS uses regression t-statistics (t-score) for bulk references, not z-scores The input is already a scaled/normalized z-score matrix (double-scaling would distort the cross-cluster contrast) The goal is cluster-level annotation at the single-cell level rather than the cluster level — deCS defines cell types at the cell cluster level

skills.description: Use when a component model (e.g., 86 MeCs learned by ICA from integrated TME scRNA-seq) must be shown to be reproducible rather than an artifact of any single training dataset, by testing exclusion of each cohort in turn.
skills.name: cross-cohort-component-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-cohort-component-correlation-analysis Use when a component model (e.g., 86 MeCs learned by ICA from integrated TME scRNA-seq) must be shown to be reproducible rather than an artifact of any single training dataset, by testing exclusion of each cohort in turn. The learned components are being generated for the first time with no full-data reference set available to correlate against. The task is per-dataset integration/batch correction of cell representations (e.g., Harmony/scVI/scArches joint embeddings) rather than testing component-set robustness under cohort exclusion. Input is a single cohort with no multi-dataset structure, since leave-one-out across cohorts is undefined. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Assess whether data-learned transcriptional components (e.g., MetaTiME MeCs) are robust to cohort composition by re-learning components under leave-one-out cohort removal and correlating each perturbed component set against the full-data reference set. This quantifies reproducibility of latent gene-expression programs learned from integrated single-cell data. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-38333-8
skills.summary: Assess whether data-learned transcriptional components (e.g., MetaTiME MeCs) are robust to cohort composition by re-learning components under leave-one-out cohort removal and correlating each perturbed component set against the full-data reference set. This quantifies reproducibility of latent gene-expression programs learned from integrated single-cell data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The learned components are being generated for the first time with no full-data reference set available to correlate against. The task is per-dataset integration/batch correction of cell representations (e.g., Harmony/scVI/scArches joint embeddings) rather than testing component-set robustness under cohort exclusion. Input is a single cohort with no multi-dataset structure, since leave-one-out across cohorts is undefined.

skills.description: Use when an scRNA-seq dataset exceeds available RAM (e.g. >0.6M cells on a 128GB machine, or ~11.5M-cell cross-cohort data) and you must run or benchmark annotation pipelines like scaLR, scBalance, scvi, devCellPy, or CellPLM under that limit.
skills.name: cross-cohort-dataset-scaling
skills.search_text: cross-cohort-dataset-scaling Use when an scRNA-seq dataset exceeds available RAM (e.g. >0.6M cells on a 128GB machine, or ~11.5M-cell cross-cohort data) and you must run or benchmark annotation pipelines like scaLR, scBalance, scvi, devCellPy, or CellPLM under that limit. Dataset fits comfortably in RAM (e.g. small PBMCs-BS-style studies well under the 128GB ceiling) — a standard annotation tool without batch partitioning is simpler and likely faster Input data is not in .h5ad/anndata format or adata.X lacks log1p-normalized values in the 0-10 range — scaLR performance varies with input format and requires prior preprocessing The goal is biomarker/feature ranking from comparison tools (scBalance, scvi, devCellPy, CellPLM), since top features cannot be extracted from those models http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmarking and executing cell type annotation pipelines on multi-million-cell, cross-cohort scRNA-seq datasets (sourced from Cellxgene and the Broad Single Cell Portal) under a fixed memory ceiling, using scaLR's batch partitioning and backed-mode loading to stay within ~128GB RAM. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbaf243
skills.summary: Benchmarking and executing cell type annotation pipelines on multi-million-cell, cross-cohort scRNA-seq datasets (sourced from Cellxgene and the Broad Single Cell Portal) under a fixed memory ceiling, using scaLR's batch partitioning and backed-mode loading to stay within ~128GB RAM.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Dataset fits comfortably in RAM (e.g. small PBMCs-BS-style studies well under the 128GB ceiling) — a standard annotation tool without batch partitioning is simpler and likely faster Input data is not in .h5ad/anndata format or adata.X lacks log1p-normalized values in the 0-10 range — scaLR performance varies with input format and requires prior preprocessing The goal is biomarker/feature ranking from comparison tools (scBalance, scvi, devCellPy, CellPLM), since top features cannot be extracted from those models

skills.description: Use when a derived gene read-count or DE table from one RNA-seq cohort must be validated against a second public cohort (e.g. dbGap vs TCGA) before downstream pathway interpretation.
skills.name: cross-cohort-expression-consistency-check
skills.search_text: cross-cohort-expression-consistency-check Use when a derived gene read-count or DE table from one RNA-seq cohort must be validated against a second public cohort (e.g. dbGap vs TCGA) before downstream pathway interpretation. Only one cohort is available, so no independent replication dataset exists to correlate against The cohorts used different aligners or gene definitions that were not harmonized, making direct read-count correlation invalid The goal is pathway visualization itself rather than validation of expression measurements http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 A validation step for the FunHoP prostate cancer workflow that checks whether independently processed RNA-seq cohorts (Prensner dbGap phs000443.v1.p1 and TCGA) yield broadly consistent gene expression measurements before cohort-specific results are trusted for pathway analysis. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2021.03.003
skills.summary: A validation step for the FunHoP prostate cancer workflow that checks whether independently processed RNA-seq cohorts (Prensner dbGap phs000443.v1.p1 and TCGA) yield broadly consistent gene expression measurements before cohort-specific results are trusted for pathway analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one cohort is available, so no independent replication dataset exists to correlate against The cohorts used different aligners or gene definitions that were not harmonized, making direct read-count correlation invalid The goal is pathway visualization itself rather than validation of expression measurements

skills.description: Use when the same RNA-seq pipeline has been run on two independent patient cohorts and you must quantify whether node-level (FunHoP-aggregated) pathway results — dominant genes and read-count ratios — are consistent across cohorts.
skills.name: cross-cohort-gene-expression-correlation
skills.search_text: cross-cohort-gene-expression-correlation Use when the same RNA-seq pipeline has been run on two independent patient cohorts and you must quantify whether node-level (FunHoP-aggregated) pathway results — dominant genes and read-count ratios — are consistent across cohorts. Pathways are from KEGG category 1.7 'Glycan biosynthesis and metabolism' — these use 'links' instead of nodes and cannot be expanded or coloured by FunHoP Data are already gene-length corrected, so the gene-length adjustment step (correct=True in load_countdata) would double-correct the counts The goal is pathway analysis of non-metabolic processes; the current FunHoP version only supports human metabolic pathways from KEGG (excluding glycan pathways) http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Validates reproducibility of FunHoP node-level pathway analyses by correlating log2 RNA-seq read counts and per-gene abundance ratios between two independent prostate cancer cohorts (TCGA and Prensner), and checking that dominant genes in multi-gene KEGG nodes correspond across cohorts. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2021.03.003
skills.summary: Validates reproducibility of FunHoP node-level pathway analyses by correlating log2 RNA-seq read counts and per-gene abundance ratios between two independent prostate cancer cohorts (TCGA and Prensner), and checking that dominant genes in multi-gene KEGG nodes correspond across cohorts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Pathways are from KEGG category 1.7 'Glycan biosynthesis and metabolism' — these use 'links' instead of nodes and cannot be expanded or coloured by FunHoP Data are already gene-length corrected, so the gene-length adjustment step (correct=True in load_countdata) would double-correct the counts The goal is pathway analysis of non-metabolic processes; the current FunHoP version only supports human metabolic pathways from KEGG (excluding glycan pathways)

skills.description: Use when a pan-cancer single-cell integration stage has produced per-cohort ICA z-weight matrices and you must derive cohort-shared transcriptional meta-components instead of dataset-specific components.
skills.name: cross-cohort-single-cell-integration
skills.search_text: cross-cohort-single-cell-integration Use when a pan-cancer single-cell integration stage has produced per-cohort ICA z-weight matrices and you must derive cohort-shared transcriptional meta-components instead of dataset-specific components. The goal is annotating cells in a new TME scRNA-seq dataset with pretrained components — use the MetaTiME-Annotator projection workflow instead of re-deriving MeCs. The analysis needs a joint low-dimensional embedding of cells across cohorts (e.g. Harmony/scVI-style integration) rather than interpretable gene-program components. Input is a single cohort's scRNA data with no multi-cohort ICA z-weight matrix, so reproducibility across ≥3 datasets cannot be assessed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 Reproducibility-filter independent components (ICs) learned by ICA across multiple tumor scRNA-seq cohorts, cluster them into consensus meta-components (MeCs) via Louvain community detection, and average gene z-weights per cluster to define a shared, interpretable MeC space rather than cohort-specific programs. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-38333-8
skills.summary: Reproducibility-filter independent components (ICs) learned by ICA across multiple tumor scRNA-seq cohorts, cluster them into consensus meta-components (MeCs) via Louvain community detection, and average gene z-weights per cluster to define a shared, interpretable MeC space rather than cohort-specific programs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is annotating cells in a new TME scRNA-seq dataset with pretrained components — use the MetaTiME-Annotator projection workflow instead of re-deriving MeCs. The analysis needs a joint low-dimensional embedding of cells across cohorts (e.g. Harmony/scVI-style integration) rather than interpretable gene-program components. Input is a single cohort's scRNA data with no multi-cohort ICA z-weight matrix, so reproducibility across ≥3 datasets cannot be assessed.

skills.description: Use when several scRNA-seq cohorts with responder-status annotations must be jointly scanned for perturbed cell populations, and naive per-cell-type testing would be confounded by individual-to-individual and cohort-to-cohort variability.
skills.name: cross-cohort-single-cell-integration
skills.search_text: cross-cohort-single-cell-integration Use when several scRNA-seq cohorts with responder-status annotations must be jointly scanned for perturbed cell populations, and naive per-cell-type testing would be confounded by individual-to-individual and cohort-to-cohort variability. The goal is differential abundance (changing cell proportions), not transcriptomic state — use DA-seq, Milo, or Meld instead Only raw counts are available without normalization — scDist cannot currently be applied directly to raw counts The data are heavily over-clustered — over-clustering drives estimated distances toward 0 and produces false negatives http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Jointly test multiple single-cell immunotherapy scRNA cohorts for cell-type-specific transcriptomic differences between responders and non-responders using scDist's mixed-effects model, which separates responder signal from patient-to-patient and cohort-to-cohort variability. This surfaced the FCER1G+ NK-cell compartment that the authors validated in bulk transcriptomes from 789 patients. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-51649-3
skills.summary: Jointly test multiple single-cell immunotherapy scRNA cohorts for cell-type-specific transcriptomic differences between responders and non-responders using scDist's mixed-effects model, which separates responder signal from patient-to-patient and cohort-to-cohort variability. This surfaced the FCER1G+ NK-cell compartment that the authors validated in bulk transcriptomes from 789 patients.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is differential abundance (changing cell proportions), not transcriptomic state — use DA-seq, Milo, or Meld instead Only raw counts are available without normalization — scDist cannot currently be applied directly to raw counts The data are heavily over-clustered — over-clustering drives estimated distances toward 0 and produces false negatives

skills.description: Use when a published finding links a categorical subtype/label (e.g., CMS2 from CMScaller) to a binary drug-response outcome across multiple independent cohorts and the target is to reproduce the reported p-values and odds ratios per cohort.
skills.name: cross-cohort-statistical-reproducibility
skills.search_text: cross-cohort-statistical-reproducibility Use when a published finding links a categorical subtype/label (e.g., CMS2 from CMScaller) to a binary drug-response outcome across multiple independent cohorts and the target is to reproduce the reported p-values and odds ratios per cohort. The subtype labels are not cancer-cell-intrinsic classifications (CMScaller was designed for pre-clinical models and is not recommended for metastatic CRC biopsies with different human stromal content) The outcome variable is continuous or multi-class rather than a binary responder/non-responder grouping suitable for a 2x2 Fisher's exact test Any single cohort contains fewer than approximately forty samples, where CMScaller's centered/scaled input introduces prediction uncertainty http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Reproduces a reported biology-association finding (e.g., CMS2 classification predicting cetuximab response) by rebuilding cohort-specific contingency tables and applying per-cohort Fisher's exact tests, then verifying p-values and odds ratios against published values across PDX and cell line datasets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-017-16747-x
skills.summary: Reproduces a reported biology-association finding (e.g., CMS2 classification predicting cetuximab response) by rebuilding cohort-specific contingency tables and applying per-cohort Fisher's exact tests, then verifying p-values and odds ratios against published values across PDX and cell line datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The subtype labels are not cancer-cell-intrinsic classifications (CMScaller was designed for pre-clinical models and is not recommended for metastatic CRC biopsies with different human stromal content) The outcome variable is continuous or multi-class rather than a binary responder/non-responder grouping suitable for a 2x2 Fisher's exact test Any single cohort contains fewer than approximately forty samples, where CMScaller's centered/scaled input introduces prediction uncertainty

skills.description: Use when independent breast cancer RNA-seq cohorts (e.g., GSE96058, PanCA, GSE81538, TCGA) must be assigned PAM50 intrinsic subtypes using a reference computed on a different cohort, and subtype-call concordance must be quantified.
skills.name: cross-cohort-subtype-classification
skills.search_text: cross-cohort-subtype-classification Use when independent breast cancer RNA-seq cohorts (e.g., GSE96058, PanCA, GSE81538, TCGA) must be assigned PAM50 intrinsic subtypes using a reference computed on a different cohort, and subtype-call concordance must be quantified. Input is microarray data (e.g., GSE4922, GSE1456 Affymetrix) rather than RNA-seq; use the AWCA-based classification route validated on Affymetrix log2-transformed data instead of the RNA-seq cross-cohort porting scheme Only PAM50 gene-panel data (e.g., Nanostring nCounter/Prosigna) is available rather than global RNA-seq expression; use the platform-native assay A reference-free single-sample caller is preferred and no pre-defined external reference exists; consider the regularized multiclass logistic regression (mLR) models, which reached 90% concordance with PAM50 calls without need of a reference sample http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Port AWCA-PAM50 breast cancer intrinsic subtyping references built on one RNA-seq cohort to classify independent cohorts (e.g., TCGA RSEM reference to PanCA; GSE96058 FPKM reference to GSE81538), validating against internal-reference calls with concordance thresholds of ~95% internal and >96% external. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-70832-2
skills.summary: Port AWCA-PAM50 breast cancer intrinsic subtyping references built on one RNA-seq cohort to classify independent cohorts (e.g., TCGA RSEM reference to PanCA; GSE96058 FPKM reference to GSE81538), validating against internal-reference calls with concordance thresholds of ~95% internal and >96% external.
