skills.description: Use when you have several bulk transcriptomic cohorts with matched survival data (e.g., metastatic melanoma datasets like TCGA SKCM06) and need to test whether inferred cell-cell interaction networks are reproducible across cohorts and across different cell-type marker annotations.
skills.name: cross-dataset-network-consistency-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-network-consistency-analysis Use when you have several bulk transcriptomic cohorts with matched survival data (e.g., metastatic melanoma datasets like TCGA SKCM06) and need to test whether inferred cell-cell interaction networks are reproducible across cohorts and across different cell-type marker annotations. Datasets lack matched survival information — TimiGP requires a large gene expression dataset with matched survival information to identify prognostic gene pairs The goal is immunotherapy response rather than prognosis — use the TimiGP-Response module with therapy response info (e.g., TNBCaPD1info) instead of the survival-based workflow Cell types of interest have very few marker genes — enrichment-based identification is underpowered for marker-sparse cell types http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Repeat the full TimiGP pipeline (TimiCheckEvent → TimiPrePropress → TimiGenePair → TimiCOX → TimiBG/TimiCellPair → TimiEnrich → TimiPermFDR → TimiCellNetwork → TimiFS) across multiple independent cohorts and alternative cell-type marker sets, then compare the resulting directed cell-cell interaction networks and favorability rankings to demonstrate robustness of inferred TIME interactions. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.xcrm.2023.101121
skills.summary: Repeat the full TimiGP pipeline (TimiCheckEvent → TimiPrePropress → TimiGenePair → TimiCOX → TimiBG/TimiCellPair → TimiEnrich → TimiPermFDR → TimiCellNetwork → TimiFS) across multiple independent cohorts and alternative cell-type marker sets, then compare the resulting directed cell-cell interaction networks and favorability rankings to demonstrate robustness of inferred TIME interactions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Datasets lack matched survival information — TimiGP requires a large gene expression dataset with matched survival information to identify prognostic gene pairs The goal is immunotherapy response rather than prognosis — use the TimiGP-Response module with therapy response info (e.g., TNBCaPD1info) instead of the survival-based workflow Cell types of interest have very few marker genes — enrichment-based identification is underpowered for marker-sparse cell types

skills.search_text: cross-dataset-node-importance-comparison Use when you have scBONITA rule-inference node importance scores for KEGG pathway networks from one or more scRNA-seq datasets and need to check whether importance scores carry context-dependent signaling information beyond topology alone. When the goal is to rank genes for experimental prioritization rather than to validate that importance scores encode context-dependent signaling information. skills.summary: Validate scBONITA node importance scores by testing whether they are decoupled from network topology (Spearman correlations against six centrality measures) and reproducible across datasets (Pearson correlations of importance scores over shared KEGG networks between comparable cell subpopulations).

When networks are not available as KEGG or GRAPHML topologies from which centrality measures can be computed.

skills.description: Use when a reference dataset (e.g. annotated HuBMAP data such as HBMP3-spleen-CC3) is being used to transfer labels to a query dataset (e.g. HBMP2-spleen-2) whose AnnData object has a different gene set, or when comparing clusterings across the two objects.
skills.name: cross-dataset-overlapping-gene-selection
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-overlapping-gene-selection Use when a reference dataset (e.g. annotated HuBMAP data such as HBMP3-spleen-CC3) is being used to transfer labels to a query dataset (e.g. HBMP2-spleen-2) whose AnnData object has a different gene set, or when comparing clusterings across the two objects. Reference and query come from the same experiment or were processed together, so their gene sets already match and intersection only removes useful features. The datasets have minimal shared gene space (e.g. cross-species or scATAC gene-activity vs scRNA-seq matrices), where the intersection is too small to support a stable reference PCA space. The analysis goal is not reference-based label transfer or cross-dataset clustering comparison (e.g. single-dataset differential expression with diffxpy), where subsetting to an external dataset's genes would bias results. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Restricts a reference and a query dataset loaded as AnnData objects to the genes they share, so that label transfer or clustering comparison operates on a common feature space. In the Cellar HBMP2-spleen-2 vs HBMP3-spleen-CC3 analysis, this intersection was the prerequisite for Ingest-based label transfer in the 40-component PCA space. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-29744-0

skills.when_to_use_negative: Reference and query come from the same experiment or were processed together, so their gene sets already match and intersection only removes useful features. skills.description: Use when two or more transcription start site (TSS) datasets for the same organism must be benchmarked against each other, and a motif-positioning-based quality comparison of nascent vs. annotated TSSs is desired.

skills.description: Use when you have scRNA-seq h5ad files annotated with adata.obs['cell_cycle_theta'] from a DeepCycle run and need to verify cell cycle annotation or the RNA-doubling prior by quantifying UMI-vs-phase fold change across multiple cell systems.
skills.name: cross-dataset-reproducibility-analysis

skills.name: cross-dataset-subpopulation-separation-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-subpopulation-separation-analysis Use when comparing dimension-reduction/visualization methods for temporal scRNA-seq data on their ability to resolve subpopulations within the final time point, using dip-test multimodality scores across multiple datasets. The scRNA-seq data lack a complete time index, or the time index is not correlated with the underlying dynamic expression pattern (TCM's stated requirement) The goal is immediate biological interpretation of cell clusters rather than quantitative separation benchmarking — the article notes further pathway analysis is needed for cluster meaning Data are not temporal (no time-course structure); the last-time-point subpopulation separation metric is undefined without developmental stages/time points http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A benchmarking protocol that quantifies how well latent-space embeddings (TCM, t-SNE, diffusion map, diffusion pseudotime, Wishbone, Monocle, TSCAN) separate subpopulations of cells from the last time point across 11 temporal single-cell expression datasets, using Hartigan's dip statistics of the cells' distribution on the latent space. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-05112-9
skills.summary: A benchmarking protocol that quantifies how well latent-space embeddings (TCM, t-SNE, diffusion map, diffusion pseudotime, Wishbone, Monocle, TSCAN) separate subpopulations of cells from the last time point across 11 temporal single-cell expression datasets, using Hartigan's dip statistics of the cells' distribution on the latent space.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The scRNA-seq data lack a complete time index, or the time index is not correlated with the underlying dynamic expression pattern (TCM's stated requirement) The goal is immediate biological interpretation of cell clusters rather than quantitative separation benchmarking — the article notes further pathway analysis is needed for cluster meaning Data are not temporal (no time-course structure); the last-time-point subpopulation separation metric is undefined without developmental stages/time points

skills.description: Use when you need to compare/relate cell subtype label schemes across published TME scRNA-seq references, or to cross-validate a subtype annotation model and report fold-wise accuracy and kappa within each dataset.
skills.name: cross-dataset-subtype-similarity-mapping
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-subtype-similarity-mapping Use when you need to compare/relate cell subtype label schemes across published TME scRNA-seq references, or to cross-validate a subtype annotation model and report fold-wise accuracy and kappa within each dataset. You need to identify malignant cells when no internal reference cells exist — scCancer2 handles that with a separate XGBoost-style classifier trained on TCGA bulk + scRNA-seq data (threshold 0.5), not the subtype classifiers Input is bulk RNA-seq (e.g. TCGA samples) — the subtype annotation/similarity framework operates on single-cell RNA assay data Your cell types fall outside the five TME compartments (T.cells, Myeloid.cells, B.cells, Fibroblast, Endothelial), since the annotation is restricted to that intersection http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Train lightweight multinomial subtype classifiers for the five TME compartments (T.cells, Myeloid.cells, B.cells, Fibroblast, Endothelial) on published scRNA-seq references, then use those trained classifiers to quantitatively score similarity between cell subtype labels defined in different reference datasets. Evaluation is via 5-fold cross-validated accuracy and Cohen's kappa across all 15 datasets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae028
skills.summary: Train lightweight multinomial subtype classifiers for the five TME compartments (T.cells, Myeloid.cells, B.cells, Fibroblast, Endothelial) on published scRNA-seq references, then use those trained classifiers to quantitatively score similarity between cell subtype labels defined in different reference datasets. Evaluation is via 5-fold cross-validated accuracy and Cohen's kappa across all 15 datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to identify malignant cells when no internal reference cells exist — scCancer2 handles that with a separate XGBoost-style classifier trained on TCGA bulk + scRNA-seq data (threshold 0.5), not the subtype classifiers Input is bulk RNA-seq (e.g. TCGA samples) — the subtype annotation/similarity framework operates on single-cell RNA assay data Your cell types fall outside the five TME compartments (T.cells, Myeloid.cells, B.cells, Fibroblast, Endothelial), since the annotation is restricted to that intersection

skills.description: Use when two FateCompass differential motif activity results exist for orthologous cell fates (e.g., beta cells) in distinct species or systems, and you need to compute the intersection fraction and label species-specific TF groupings.
skills.name: cross-dataset-tf-set-intersection-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-tf-set-intersection-analysis Use when two FateCompass differential motif activity results exist for orthologous cell fates (e.g., beta cells) in distinct species or systems, and you need to compute the intersection fraction and label species-specific TF groupings. Only one dataset is available, or the two systems are not orthologous at the fate level (e.g., alpha vs beta comparison), making a cross-species beta-TF intersection meaningless. Differential motif activity analysis has not yet been run (bootstrapping.m and differential_motif_activity_analysis.m outputs are missing), so no differentially active TF sets exist to intersect. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Quantifies the overlap between differentially active beta-specific transcription factor sets inferred by FateCompass for two independent systems (mouse E15.5 in vivo pancreatic development vs human in vitro beta-cell differentiation), classifying shared vs species-specific factors. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2023.100512
skills.summary: Quantifies the overlap between differentially active beta-specific transcription factor sets inferred by FateCompass for two independent systems (mouse E15.5 in vivo pancreatic development vs human in vitro beta-cell differentiation), classifying shared vs species-specific factors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one dataset is available, or the two systems are not orthologous at the fate level (e.g., alpha vs beta comparison), making a cross-species beta-TF intersection meaningless. Differential motif activity analysis has not yet been run (bootstrapping.m and differential_motif_activity_analysis.m outputs are missing), so no differentially active TF sets exist to intersect.

skills.description: Decision support for choosing between raw-CT optimization and external-dataset (e.g. TCGA) weight optimization when only ~20–30 qPCR samples and a few internal controls are available.
skills.name: cross-dataset-weight-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-weight-comparison Decision support for choosing between raw-CT optimization and external-dataset (e.g. TCGA) weight optimization when only ~20–30 qPCR samples and a few internal controls are available. When a sufficiently large qPCR cohort is available, raw CT optimization on the full sample set is preferable — external-dataset weights were only on par at 30 samples When the external dataset is not biologically compatible with the qPCR experiment (the paper explicitly required a compatible external dataset, e.g. matched tissue type/cancer) When aggregating more than 5 reference genes — geom(sd) weighting 'does not have the expected benefits compared to the regular geometric mean' http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0204 Compares virtual reference gene aggregation weights (geom(sd)/geom(sd+)) computed from raw CT values of a small qPCR sample subset against weights computed from a normalized external high-throughput dataset (TCGA BRCA miRNA-seq), assembling weights and stability measures (SD, CV) into one comparison table. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2023.107945
skills.summary: Compares virtual reference gene aggregation weights (geom(sd)/geom(sd+)) computed from raw CT values of a small qPCR sample subset against weights computed from a normalized external high-throughput dataset (TCGA BRCA miRNA-seq), assembling weights and stability measures (SD, CV) into one comparison table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a sufficiently large qPCR cohort is available, raw CT optimization on the full sample set is preferable — external-dataset weights were only on par at 30 samples When the external dataset is not biologically compatible with the qPCR experiment (the paper explicitly required a compatible external dataset, e.g. matched tissue type/cancer) When aggregating more than 5 reference genes — geom(sd) weighting 'does not have the expected benefits compared to the regular geometric mean'

skills.description: Use when two phase I/II dose-finding designs (e.g., TSNP vs U-BOIN) must be compared on the same simulated scenarios: generate correlated outcomes with Gumbel() in R, run both designs with matched seeds, and tabulate OBD selection and patient-allocation percentages.
skills.name: cross-design-operating-characteristics-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-design-operating-characteristics-comparison Use when two phase I/II dose-finding designs (e.g., TSNP vs U-BOIN) must be compared on the same simulated scenarios: generate correlated outcomes with Gumbel() in R, run both designs with matched seeds, and tabulate OBD selection and patient-allocation percentages. The response outcome is binary but requires long follow-up to assess; TSNP is only appropriate for responses observable shortly after treatment initiation The goal is a drug-combination phase I/II trial — the TSNP design does not yet handle dose-combination optimization (future work) The comparison targets a Bayesian parametric design benchmark rather than U-BOIN — that is a different comparison workflow than this TSNP-vs-U-BOIN skill Head-to-head simulation comparison of the TSNP two-stage nonparametric phase I/II design against U-BOIN under identical correlated toxicity-efficacy scenarios (Gumbel copula, association parameter 0.2), benchmarking OBD selection percentages and per-dose patient-assignment operating characteristics. transcriptomics/v2 10.1002/pst.2075
skills.summary: Head-to-head simulation comparison of the TSNP two-stage nonparametric phase I/II design against U-BOIN under identical correlated toxicity-efficacy scenarios (Gumbel copula, association parameter 0.2), benchmarking OBD selection percentages and per-dose patient-assignment operating characteristics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The response outcome is binary but requires long follow-up to assess; TSNP is only appropriate for responses observable shortly after treatment initiation The goal is a drug-combination phase I/II trial — the TSNP design does not yet handle dose-combination optimization (future work) The comparison targets a Bayesian parametric design benchmark rather than U-BOIN — that is a different comparison workflow than this TSNP-vs-U-BOIN skill

skills.name: cross-disease-cohort-generalisation-testing
skills.search_text: cross-disease-cohort-generalisation-testing Use when a severity biomarker score built from one disease's transcriptomic cohorts must be validated for discriminative power (severe vs mild) in independent cohorts of other pathogens, treating AUC~0.5 as no discrimination. The goal is identifying differentially regulated genes within COVID-19 cohorts rather than testing a fixed two-gene score in external-pathogen cohorts Cohorts lack severe/mild phenotype labels, so a positive class cannot be defined for ROC analysis The biomarkers of interest are proteins or clinical measurements rather than transcriptomic MCEMP1/HLA-DRA expression http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Tests whether a gene-expression severity score derived in COVID-19 cohorts (combined MCEMP1/HLA-DRA Z-score) generalises to independent cohorts of other viral infections (influenza, RSV, dengue) by recomputing ROC/AUC per cohort. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.ebiom.2023.104472
skills.summary: Tests whether a gene-expression severity score derived in COVID-19 cohorts (combined MCEMP1/HLA-DRA Z-score) generalises to independent cohorts of other viral infections (influenza, RSV, dengue) by recomputing ROC/AUC per cohort.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is identifying differentially regulated genes within COVID-19 cohorts rather than testing a fixed two-gene score in external-pathogen cohorts Cohorts lack severe/mild phenotype labels, so a positive class cannot be defined for ROC analysis The biomarkers of interest are proteins or clinical measurements rather than transcriptomic MCEMP1/HLA-DRA expression

skills.description: Use when a candidate isoform switch (e.g. HSPH1-001↔HSPH1-002, SLC25A25-005) found in one CanIsoNet disease dataset must be checked for absence in the OIH, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Behcet's Disease datasets to claim disease specificity.
skills.name: cross-disease-isoform-specificity-check
skills.search_text: cross-disease-isoform-specificity-check Use when a candidate isoform switch (e.g. HSPH1-001↔HSPH1-002, SLC25A25-005) found in one CanIsoNet disease dataset must be checked for absence in the OIH, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and Behcet's Disease datasets to claim disease specificity. The input is raw RNA-Seq reads or an unquantified transcript abundance matrix — CanIsoNet serves precomputed isoform switching events, not primary quantification The isoform of interest falls in one of the 27 PCAWG cancer types only, where the cross-disease panel should instead compare against other PCAWG disease types rather than the four non-cancer RNA-Seq datasets The question is functional/pathogenic impact of a switch (STRING network disruption, ClinVar annotation) rather than its sample-level frequency and cross-disease specificity http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Verifies that an isoform switching event observed in one disease dataset in CanIsoNet is specific to that disease by recomputing per-sample frequencies across the other disease datasets (OIH, Parkinson's Disease, Behcet's Disease) hosted in the same database. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad050
skills.summary: Verifies that an isoform switching event observed in one disease dataset in CanIsoNet is specific to that disease by recomputing per-sample frequencies across the other disease datasets (OIH, Parkinson's Disease, Behcet's Disease) hosted in the same database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw RNA-Seq reads or an unquantified transcript abundance matrix — CanIsoNet serves precomputed isoform switching events, not primary quantification The isoform of interest falls in one of the 27 PCAWG cancer types only, where the cross-disease panel should instead compare against other PCAWG disease types rather than the four non-cancer RNA-Seq datasets The question is functional/pathogenic impact of a switch (STRING network disruption, ClinVar annotation) rather than its sample-level frequency and cross-disease specificity

skills.description: Use when two or more disease gene lists have each been run through E.PAGE enrichment and you need the set of significantly enriched environmental gene modules common to all queries.
skills.name: cross-disease-module-intersection-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-disease-module-intersection-analysis Use when two or more disease gene lists have each been run through E.PAGE enrichment and you need the set of significantly enriched environmental gene modules common to all queries. You have only one query signature and need enrichment itself, not a cross-disease intersection — use E.PAGE's compute() directly. The enrichment results are not significance-filtered and you want to intersect raw ranked module lists without an FDR decision point. The queries target different module databases or annotation versions, making module names non-comparable across diseases. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Identifies gene modules enriched in common across two disease query signatures by intersecting the statistically significant (FDR-adjusted) E.PAGE enrichment results for each disease, e.g. the infection-associated modules shared by T1D and RA DE gene lists. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-022-21988-6
skills.summary: Identifies gene modules enriched in common across two disease query signatures by intersecting the statistically significant (FDR-adjusted) E.PAGE enrichment results for each disease, e.g. the infection-associated modules shared by T1D and RA DE gene lists.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have only one query signature and need enrichment itself, not a cross-disease intersection — use E.PAGE's compute() directly. The enrichment results are not significance-filtered and you want to intersect raw ranked module lists without an FDR decision point. The queries target different module databases or annotation versions, making module names non-comparable across diseases.

skills.description: Use when two or more dimensionality-reduction algorithms (e.g. t-SNE vs UMAP) have been run on the same dataset and you need a statistical, per-cell measure of which embedding and which hyperparameter setting better preserves high-dimensional neighborhoods.
skills.name: cross-embedding-dr-quality-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-embedding-dr-quality-comparison Use when two or more dimensionality-reduction algorithms (e.g. t-SNE vs UMAP) have been run on the same dataset and you need a statistical, per-cell measure of which embedding and which hyperparameter setting better preserves high-dimensional neighborhoods. The goal is a single global embedding-quality score rather than local, per-cell p-values against an empirical null — EMBEDR's value is per-sample statistical comparison, not a global metric. The dataset has not been normalized/processed consistently with EMBEDR's marginal-resampling null generation, which has not been extended to non-normalized datasets. Only one DR algorithm at one hyperparameter setting is of interest with no comparison planned — running the full sweep and null machinery is unnecessary overhead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Compares the neighborhood-structure quality of t-SNE and UMAP embeddings of the same scRNA-seq data at default versus EMBEDR-optimized hyperparameters, using per-cell EMBEDR p-values as the comparison metric. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2022.100443
skills.summary: Compares the neighborhood-structure quality of t-SNE and UMAP embeddings of the same scRNA-seq data at default versus EMBEDR-optimized hyperparameters, using per-cell EMBEDR p-values as the comparison metric.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a single global embedding-quality score rather than local, per-cell p-values against an empirical null — EMBEDR's value is per-sample statistical comparison, not a global metric. The dataset has not been normalized/processed consistently with EMBEDR's marginal-resampling null generation, which has not been extended to non-normalized datasets. Only one DR algorithm at one hyperparameter setting is of interest with no comparison planned — running the full sweep and null machinery is unnecessary overhead.

When the trajectory inference method does not rely on a two-dimensional representation — Escort only considers trajectory inference approaches that use two-dimensional representations When Escort's evaluation yields no candidate embedding with a total score > 0, since Escort is not guaranteed to identify a recommended embedding among the choices evaluated When the dataset contains disconnected cell clusters or homogeneous cells lacking trajectory signal, so that fitting a trajectory at all is inappropriate http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A method for comparing trajectory/lineage structures fitted on different embeddings of the same scRNA-seq dataset: run Escort's three-step evaluation over candidate embeddings, then fit Slingshot + scLANE on the Escort-recommended vs the original (e.g., Monocle3-default) embedding to show which recovers more biologically faithful lineages. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbae216

skills.description: Use when training or evaluating cross-tissue cell type classifiers (scTab/TabNet) on the CELLxGENE Merlin store and you need the cross-entropy loss and macro F1-score on unseen-donor test data, e.g. to compare training-dataset-size scaling regimes.
skills.name: cross-entropy-loss-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-entropy-loss-evaluation Use when training or evaluating cross-tissue cell type classifiers (scTab/TabNet) on the CELLxGENE Merlin store and you need the cross-entropy loss and macro F1-score on unseen-donor test data, e.g. to compare training-dataset-size scaling regimes. Evaluating linear reference baselines for comparisons where the expected scTab-over-linear gap (0.0447 ± 0.0008 macro F1 at full data) is the validation target — the gap definition requires the nonlinear scTab model specifically Datasets whose cell types fail the corpus filters (e.g. fewer than 5000 cells per cell type, fewer than 30 donors per cell type, or labels not subtypes of 'native cell'), where the observed loss may be confounded by coarse or missing Cell Ontology annotations http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Quantify cell-type classification quality of scTab/TabNet models by cross-entropy loss (paired with macro F1-score) on donor-held-out test splits, enabling comparison of scaling regimes and model checkpoints in the scTab CELLxGENE corpus. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-51059-5

skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating linear reference baselines for comparisons where the expected scTab-over-linear gap (0.0447 ± 0.0008 macro F1 at full data) is the validation target — the gap definition requires the nonlinear scTab model specifically Datasets whose cell types fail the corpus filters (e.g. fewer than 5000 cells per cell type, fewer than 30 donors per cell type, or labels not subtypes of 'native cell'), where the observed loss may be confounded by coarse or missing Cell Ontology annotations

skills.name: cross-entropy-loss-negative-sampling
skills.search_text: cross-entropy-loss-negative-sampling Use when a similarity matrix (e.g. EDGE's ensemble similarity matrix S) has been built and the initial spectral embedding must be refined so rare and common cell groups separate in the low-dimensional plot. The similarity matrix or k-NNG graph has not yet been constructed — the embedding optimization stage requires the weighted adjacency matrix S from the weak-learner ensemble. The goal is feature gene identification rather than embedding refinement; EDGE's gene-selection cutoff (mu - 1.5 x sigma of averaged entropy values) is a separate stage. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Optimize the low-dimensional cell embedding produced by EDGE's spectral embedding stage by minimizing a cross-entropy loss via two-stage stochastic gradient descent with decreasing step size, drawing negative samples randomly from a uniform distribution. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-19465-7
skills.summary: Optimize the low-dimensional cell embedding produced by EDGE's spectral embedding stage by minimizing a cross-entropy loss via two-stage stochastic gradient descent with decreasing step size, drawing negative samples randomly from a uniform distribution.

The goal is feature gene identification rather than embedding refinement; EDGE's gene-selection cutoff (mu - 1.5 x sigma of averaged entropy values) is a separate stage.

skills.description: Use when you have a phenotype x feature score matrix M from scRNA-seq data (e.g., IPF, mouse cortex, or human cell atlas datasets) and need a discriminative marker set covering all phenotype pairs at a fixed coverage, especially when comparing against or substituting for the greedy G-PC solution.
skills.name: cross-entropy-method-feature-selection
skills.search_text: cross-entropy-method-feature-selection Use when you have a phenotype x feature score matrix M from scRNA-seq data (e.g., IPF, mouse cortex, or human cell atlas datasets) and need a discriminative marker set covering all phenotype pairs at a fixed coverage, especially when comparing against or substituting for the greedy G-PC solution. When only a small number of distinct groups with non-overlapping DE genes exist — standard per-group differential expression marker selection suffices When an exact optimal marker set is required — G-PC and CEM-PC are polynomial-time approximations to the NP-complete multiset multicover problem and do not provide an optimal solution When raw untransformed counts are passed directly — the README notes X may need log-transformation before fitting http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Applies CEM-PC, the cross-entropy-method approximation to the phenotype cover (PC) problem, to select a global marker set from a phenotype x feature score matrix so that every phenotype pair is covered by discriminative features. skills.summary: Applies CEM-PC, the cross-entropy-method approximation to the phenotype cover (PC) problem, to select a global marker set from a phenotype x feature score matrix so that every phenotype pair is covered by discriminative features. It is the sampling-based alternative to the greedy G-PC solver shipped in the phenotype-cover package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only a small number of distinct groups with non-overlapping DE genes exist — standard per-group differential expression marker selection suffices When an exact optimal marker set is required — G-PC and CEM-PC are polynomial-time approximations to the NP-complete multiset multicover problem and do not provide an optimal solution When raw untransformed counts are passed directly — the README notes X may need log-transformation before fitting

skills.description: Use when you need a small global biomarker set that distinguishes between all pairs of phenotypes (e.g., cell type × tissue combinations in scRNA-seq) from a phenotype-feature score matrix, and a greedy approximation (G-PC) is insufficient.
skills.name: cross-entropy-method-optimization
skills.search_text: cross-entropy-method-optimization Use when you need a small global biomarker set that distinguishes between all pairs of phenotypes (e.g., cell type × tissue combinations in scRNA-seq) from a phenotype-feature score matrix, and a greedy approximation (G-PC) is insufficient. You only need per-phenotype differentially-expressed markers rather than a global set discriminating every phenotype pair You require an optimal solution — G-PC and CEM-PC are polynomial-time approximations and do not guarantee optimality You are doing minimal-optimal (mRMR-style) feature selection for a single ML target instead of covering all phenotype pairs http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Application of the cross-entropy-method variant of phenotype cover (CEM-PC) to solve the multiset multicover marker-selection problem, selecting a global gene set that discriminates every phenotype pair from a phenotype × gene score matrix, with final markers extracted where probability scores exceed 0.98. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2022.100332
skills.summary: Application of the cross-entropy-method variant of phenotype cover (CEM-PC) to solve the multiset multicover marker-selection problem, selecting a global gene set that discriminates every phenotype pair from a phenotype × gene score matrix, with final markers extracted where probability scores exceed 0.98.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need per-phenotype differentially-expressed markers rather than a global set discriminating every phenotype pair You require an optimal solution — G-PC and CEM-PC are polynomial-time approximations and do not guarantee optimality You are doing minimal-optimal (mRMR-style) feature selection for a single ML target instead of covering all phenotype pairs

skills.search_text: cross-experiment-standardized-metric-interpretation Use when a DemuxmixResult (fitted HTO mixture model) is available and you need a per-HTO data quality metric of droplet separability that can be compared across experiments or used for QC filtering. skills.name: cross-feature-benchmark-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-feature-benchmark-analysis Use when you have cell coordinates in a common low-dimensional embedding (e.g., 2D UMAP) from multiple feature spaces for the same cells, plus reference cell-type labels, and need to score how well each feature space reproduces the reference structure. Cells from different feature spaces do not correspond 1:1 (no shared cell set), so silhouette scores are not computed against a common reference structure Only one feature space is available — there is nothing to benchmark against, use a standard single-space clustering evaluation instead You have raw expression/count matrices rather than a common low-dimensional embedding; the paper's protocol scores silhouette on the 2D UMAP coordinates, not on high-dimensional feature matrices http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Quantitative benchmark that compares clustering/structure quality across different feature spaces (annotated genes, aTARs, uTARs) by computing silhouette coefficients on a shared 2D UMAP embedding, as done in the TAR-scRNA-seq paper's Fig. 2b to show uTAR reads separate cell types comparably to gene expression. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-22496-3
skills.summary: Quantitative benchmark that compares clustering/structure quality across different feature spaces (annotated genes, aTARs, uTARs) by computing silhouette coefficients on a shared 2D UMAP embedding, as done in the TAR-scRNA-seq paper's Fig. 2b to show uTAR reads separate cell types comparably to gene expression.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Cells from different feature spaces do not correspond 1:1 (no shared cell set), so silhouette scores are not computed against a common reference structure Only one feature space is available — there is nothing to benchmark against, use a standard single-space clustering evaluation instead You have raw expression/count matrices rather than a common low-dimensional embedding; the paper's protocol scores silhouette on the 2D UMAP coordinates, not on high-dimensional feature matrices

skills.description: Use when a gene expression dataset (.csv or .xlsx) opened in Excel contains date-like terms or outdated gene symbols in the first column that fail pathway-database lookups (Enrichr, GSEA, Ingenuity) and need mapping to HGNC-approved names.
skills.name: cross-file-gene-identifier-reconciliation
skills.search_text: cross-file-gene-identifier-reconciliation Use when a gene expression dataset (.csv or .xlsx) opened in Excel contains date-like terms or outdated gene symbols in the first column that fail pathway-database lookups (Enrichr, GSEA, Ingenuity) and need mapping to HGNC-approved names. The gene list already uses current HGNC-approved symbols and contains no date-converted terms — reconciliation is unnecessary The input is not gene nomenclature data (e.g. protein IDs, Ensembl accessions) not covered by the hgnc-symbol-check2.csv previous-name mapping Ambiguous Mar-01/Mar-02 terms cannot be resolved because neither a gene description column nor the raw dataset is available to distinguish MTARC1/MARCHF1 or MTARC2/MARCHF2 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Reconciles gene identifiers across files by converting Excel date-corrupted terms (Dec-01, Mar-01..Mar-11, Sep-01..Sep-15) and old gene names into current HGNC-approved symbols, using the Gene Updater tool's mapping built from hgnc-symbol-check2.csv. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-022-17104-3
skills.summary: Reconciles gene identifiers across files by converting Excel date-corrupted terms (Dec-01, Mar-01..Mar-11, Sep-01..Sep-15) and old gene names into current HGNC-approved symbols, using the Gene Updater tool's mapping built from hgnc-symbol-check2.csv.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The gene list already uses current HGNC-approved symbols and contains no date-converted terms — reconciliation is unnecessary The input is not gene nomenclature data (e.g. protein IDs, Ensembl accessions) not covered by the hgnc-symbol-check2.csv previous-name mapping Ambiguous Mar-01/Mar-02 terms cannot be resolved because neither a gene description column nor the raw dataset is available to distinguish MTARC1/MARCHF1 or MTARC2/MARCHF2

skills.description: Use when comparing how two TE-expression quantification tools (e.g., SoloTE vs scTE) recover known cell populations across two genome builds (hg38, mm10) using Seurat clustering and UMAP on simulated or ground-truth matrices.
skills.name: cross-genome-scrna-seq-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-genome-scrna-seq-comparison Use when comparing how two TE-expression quantification tools (e.g., SoloTE vs scTE) recover known cell populations across two genome builds (hg38, mm10) using Seurat clustering and UMAP on simulated or ground-truth matrices. Input is already a clustered result or dimensionality-reduced embedding rather than a gene/TE cell expression matrix requiring Seurat preprocessing. The goal is locus-specific TE quantification from raw scRNA-Seq alignments (BAM) — that is SoloTE's own pipeline role, not this downstream cross-tool clustering comparison. Analysis targets bulk RNA-Seq or other TEs than those classifiable as young/old by consensus divergence ≤10%/ >10%. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmark workflow that processes ground-truth, SoloTE, and scTE gene/TE cell expression matrices from simulated hg38 and mm10 scRNA-Seq experiments through Seurat's standard preprocessing, PCA, UMAP, and graph-based clustering, then judges tool performance by how many of the four expected cell clusters are recovered, stratified by TE age (young: divergence from consensus ≤10%; old: >10%). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-022-04020-5
skills.summary: Benchmark workflow that processes ground-truth, SoloTE, and scTE gene/TE cell expression matrices from simulated hg38 and mm10 scRNA-Seq experiments through Seurat's standard preprocessing, PCA, UMAP, and graph-based clustering, then judges tool performance by how many of the four expected cell clusters are recovered, stratified by TE age (young: divergence from consensus ≤10%; old: >10%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a clustered result or dimensionality-reduced embedding rather than a gene/TE cell expression matrix requiring Seurat preprocessing. The goal is locus-specific TE quantification from raw scRNA-Seq alignments (BAM) — that is SoloTE's own pipeline role, not this downstream cross-tool clustering comparison. Analysis targets bulk RNA-Seq or other TEs than those classifiable as young/old by consensus divergence ≤10%/ >10%.

skills.description: Use when a reimplemented ligand-receptor communication probability model (Hill/mass-action form) must be checked against CellChat's computeCommunProb reference outputs to confirm numerical and statistical agreement.
skills.name: cross-implementation-communication-probability-verification
skills.search_text: cross-implementation-communication-probability-verification Use when a reimplemented ligand-receptor communication probability model (Hill/mass-action form) must be checked against CellChat's computeCommunProb reference outputs to confirm numerical and statistical agreement. The goal is primary cell-cell communication inference on a new dataset rather than validating a reimplementation — use CellChat's own pipeline directly. Input lacks pre-computed cell group labels; CellChat analysis requires clustering as a pre-requisite. Cross-method comparison against non-CellChat tools, since different ligand-receptor databases confound the comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Validates an independent reimplementation of CellChat's law-of-mass-action ligand-receptor communication probability model and permutation significance test by numerically comparing inferred probabilities against CellChat's computeCommunProb outputs on the same scRNA-seq dataset. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9
skills.summary: Validates an independent reimplementation of CellChat's law-of-mass-action ligand-receptor communication probability model and permutation significance test by numerically comparing inferred probabilities against CellChat's computeCommunProb outputs on the same scRNA-seq dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is primary cell-cell communication inference on a new dataset rather than validating a reimplementation — use CellChat's own pipeline directly. Input lacks pre-computed cell group labels; CellChat analysis requires clustering as a pre-requisite. Cross-method comparison against non-CellChat tools, since different ligand-receptor databases confound the comparison.

skills.description: Use when the same segmentation pipeline exists in two implementations (e.g. Matlab vs Python) and you need to demonstrate the outputs are largely similar before distributing or adopting either version on multiplexed image data.
skills.name: cross-implementation-segmentation-agreement-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-implementation-segmentation-agreement-analysis Use when the same segmentation pipeline exists in two implementations (e.g. Matlab vs Python) and you need to demonstrate the outputs are largely similar before distributing or adopting either version on multiplexed image data. Comparing two different segmentation algorithms (e.g. MIRIAM vs Mesmer vs Voronoi) against manual annotation — that is a benchmarking task with different metrics and reference ground truth, not cross-implementation agreement of the same pipeline Input data is not image segmentation masks from the same pipeline run on identical stacks (e.g. raw mzML, FASTQ, or single-cell feature tables) — mask-overlap metrics like DSC/JSC do not apply Only one implementation is available, so no pairwise mask comparison can be made http://edamontology.org/topic_3382 http://edamontology.org/topic_3384 Quantifies whether two independent implementations of the same segmentation pipeline (here MIRIAM's Matlab R2018b and Python 3.7 versions) produce concordant cell/membrane segmentation masks on identical multiplexed immunofluorescence TMA core images, using image-correlation, Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), and Jaccard similarity coefficient (JSC). transcriptomics/v2 10.1002/cyto.a.24541
skills.summary: Quantifies whether two independent implementations of the same segmentation pipeline (here MIRIAM's Matlab R2018b and Python 3.7 versions) produce concordant cell/membrane segmentation masks on identical multiplexed immunofluorescence TMA core images, using image-correlation, Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), and Jaccard similarity coefficient (JSC).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Comparing two different segmentation algorithms (e.g. MIRIAM vs Mesmer vs Voronoi) against manual annotation — that is a benchmarking task with different metrics and reference ground truth, not cross-implementation agreement of the same pipeline Input data is not image segmentation masks from the same pipeline run on identical stacks (e.g. raw mzML, FASTQ, or single-cell feature tables) — mask-overlap metrics like DSC/JSC do not apply Only one implementation is available, so no pairwise mask comparison can be made

skills.description: Use when an analysis requires tools from both ecosystems — e.g. simulating scRNA-seq data with splatter in R and scoring cells with the FiRE Python module — and the intermediate expression matrix must be exchanged between languages.
skills.name: cross-language-python-r-pipeline-execution
skills.search_text: cross-language-python-r-pipeline-execution Use when an analysis requires tools from both ecosystems — e.g. simulating scRNA-seq data with splatter in R and scoring cells with the FiRE Python module — and the intermediate expression matrix must be exchanged between languages. The entire pipeline can run in one language — e.g. FiRE's R package (install.packages('FiRE') or './INSTALL --R') suffices if R scoring is acceptable, avoiding a file handoff The input is a single static dataset rather than a simulated-data loop, where language choice can follow the primary toolchain without R/Python interop overhead http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Orchestrates a single analysis pipeline that spans R and Python: R (e.g. the splatter package) generates simulated scRNA-seq data while the Python FiRE module (built via './INSTALL --py') assigns rareness scores, joining the two halves through flat data files such as CSV. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-07234-6
skills.summary: Orchestrates a single analysis pipeline that spans R and Python: R (e.g. the splatter package) generates simulated scRNA-seq data while the Python FiRE module (built via './INSTALL --py') assigns rareness scores, joining the two halves through flat data files such as CSV.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The entire pipeline can run in one language — e.g. FiRE's R package (install.packages('FiRE') or './INSTALL --R') suffices if R scoring is acceptable, avoiding a file handoff The input is a single static dataset rather than a simulated-data loop, where language choice can follow the primary toolchain without R/Python interop overhead

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a Python reimplementation is faster or more memory-robust than its R reference: you have matched expression datasets, both packages installed, and need replicate-timed scaling runs across feature-count subsets.
skills.name: cross-language-runtime-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-language-runtime-benchmarking Use when evaluating whether a Python reimplementation is faster or more memory-robust than its R reference: you have matched expression datasets, both packages installed, and need replicate-timed scaling runs across feature-count subsets. The analysis goal is biological (e.g. identifying co-expression modules or functional enrichment) rather than measuring implementation performance Only one implementation of the algorithm is available or only one language runtime is installed, so no cross-language comparison is possible Datasets are small enough that runtime differences are dominated by I/O overhead rather than the co-expression network computation http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 A benchmarking protocol for comparing the wall-clock runtime of two implementations of the same algorithm in different languages (Python vs R), exemplified by PyWGCNA vs R WGCNA co-expression module detection on ENCODE expression matrices with increasing feature counts. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad415
skills.summary: A benchmarking protocol for comparing the wall-clock runtime of two implementations of the same algorithm in different languages (Python vs R), exemplified by PyWGCNA vs R WGCNA co-expression module detection on ENCODE expression matrices with increasing feature counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is biological (e.g. identifying co-expression modules or functional enrichment) rather than measuring implementation performance Only one implementation of the algorithm is available or only one language runtime is installed, so no cross-language comparison is possible Datasets are small enough that runtime differences are dominated by I/O overhead rather than the co-expression network computation

skills.description: Use when the same analysis toolkit exists in both an R/Bioconductor and a Python implementation and you need to quantify how execution time scales with dataset size, expressed per sample and regulator.
skills.name: cross-language-runtime-comparison-r-python
skills.search_text: cross-language-runtime-comparison-r-python Use when the same analysis toolkit exists in both an R/Bioconductor and a Python implementation and you need to quantify how execution time scales with dataset size, expressed per sample and regulator. You are benchmarking predictive performance (AUROC/AUPRC on perturbation experiments) rather than execution time — that is decoupleRBench's job, not this runtime skill. You only need to profile a single implementation's internals; this skill is specifically a cross-language comparison on matched simulated matrices. You need to infer biological activities from real omics data — use decoupleR/decoupler directly, not the manuscript's scalability scripts. Benchmarks the execution-speed scalability of dual-language implementations of the same method suite — decoupleR in R (Bioconductor) vs decoupler-py — by timing each method on simulated omics matrices and reporting median ms per sample and regulator per language. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac016
skills.summary: Benchmarks the execution-speed scalability of dual-language implementations of the same method suite — decoupleR in R (Bioconductor) vs decoupler-py — by timing each method on simulated omics matrices and reporting median ms per sample and regulator per language.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are benchmarking predictive performance (AUROC/AUPRC on perturbation experiments) rather than execution time — that is decoupleRBench's job, not this runtime skill. You only need to profile a single implementation's internals; this skill is specifically a cross-language comparison on matched simulated matrices. You need to infer biological activities from real omics data — use decoupleR/decoupler directly, not the manuscript's scalability scripts.

skills.description: Use when CEFCON has been run independently per lineage on scRNA-seq trajectory data and you need to determine which driver regulators (e.g., top-20 per lineage) are common versus lineage-specific, and how overlapping sets affect control metrics.
skills.name: cross-lineage-driver-regulator-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-lineage-driver-regulator-overlap-analysis Use when CEFCON has been run independently per lineage on scRNA-seq trajectory data and you need to determine which driver regulators (e.g., top-20 per lineage) are common versus lineage-specific, and how overlapping sets affect control metrics. When only a single cell fate trajectory is available — CEFCON can only handle one cell lineage at a time and the cross-lineage overlap is undefined without at least two independently inferred driver sets When cell fate trajectories bifurcate within one dataset and must be processed simultaneously, since CEFCON cannot process multiple fate trajectories with bifurcations at once and each lineage must be analyzed separately first http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Compares the top-N driver regulator sets identified by CEFCON across separate cell fate trajectories (erythroid, granulocyte-monocyte, lymphoid in mouse hematopoietic stem cell differentiation) to find shared and lineage-specific regulators, quantified via controllability score, Jaccard index, and coverage metrics (Fig. 6c-i). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-44103-3
skills.summary: Compares the top-N driver regulator sets identified by CEFCON across separate cell fate trajectories (erythroid, granulocyte-monocyte, lymphoid in mouse hematopoietic stem cell differentiation) to find shared and lineage-specific regulators, quantified via controllability score, Jaccard index, and coverage metrics (Fig. 6c-i).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only a single cell fate trajectory is available — CEFCON can only handle one cell lineage at a time and the cross-lineage overlap is undefined without at least two independently inferred driver sets When cell fate trajectories bifurcate within one dataset and must be processed simultaneously, since CEFCON cannot process multiple fate trajectories with bifurcations at once and each lineage must be analyzed separately first

skills.description: Use when evaluating a scRNA-seq cell-type annotation method head-to-head with published baselines under multiple label-overlap settings, and accuracy values must be matched against a reference table.
skills.name: cross-method-accuracy-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-method-accuracy-benchmarking Use when evaluating a scRNA-seq cell-type annotation method head-to-head with published baselines under multiple label-overlap settings, and accuracy values must be matched against a reference table. When raw source data are available and explicit source-target feature alignment is intended — scEMAIL is designed for the source-free regime where raw source data are unavailable When the goal is annotating data types outside the validated scope (e.g., non-single-cell bulk data); the paper only demonstrates scRNA-seq, CITE-seq, and scATAC-seq When novel cell types are known a priori and a manual threshold suffices — the skill's adaptive E-score/bimodality pipeline is meant to replace manually defined thresholds http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Reproduce and compare cell-type annotation accuracy of scEMAIL against competing methods (scmap, Seurat v3, ItClust, scSemiCluster, scArches, source-only) across the four label-overlap settings (closed, partial, open, open-partial) on real scRNA-seq dataset pairs, using annotation accuracy as the metric. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2022.12.008
skills.summary: Reproduce and compare cell-type annotation accuracy of scEMAIL against competing methods (scmap, Seurat v3, ItClust, scSemiCluster, scArches, source-only) across the four label-overlap settings (closed, partial, open, open-partial) on real scRNA-seq dataset pairs, using annotation accuracy as the metric.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When raw source data are available and explicit source-target feature alignment is intended — scEMAIL is designed for the source-free regime where raw source data are unavailable When the goal is annotating data types outside the validated scope (e.g., non-single-cell bulk data); the paper only demonstrates scRNA-seq, CITE-seq, and scATAC-seq When novel cell types are known a priori and a manual threshold suffices — the skill's adaptive E-score/bimodality pipeline is meant to replace manually defined thresholds

skills.description: Use when a new method claims improved accuracy on a task (e.g., circadian phase inference from scRNA-seq) and you must quantify how close its errors are to a theoretical optimum versus baseline methods on simulated data with ground truth.
skills.name: cross-method-accuracy-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-accuracy-comparison Use when a new method claims improved accuracy on a task (e.g., circadian phase inference from scRNA-seq) and you must quantify how close its errors are to a theoretical optimum versus baseline methods on simulated data with ground truth. The task is real (non-simulated) data with no ground-truth phases, since this skill's validation relies on comparing to simulated ground truth rather than reporter-based validation The method under test does not produce per-cell point estimates comparable to the baselines' outputs (e.g., only uncertainty summaries without phase estimates) Goal is uncertainty calibration assessment rather than point-estimate accuracy — Tempo's separate calibration property would need a different evaluation design http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Benchmark a new computational method (Tempo) against competing baselines (Cyclops, Cyclum, PCA) on simulated datasets with known ground truth, comparing phase point-estimate error distributions (eCDFs) and median errors. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-34185-w
skills.summary: Benchmark a new computational method (Tempo) against competing baselines (Cyclops, Cyclum, PCA) on simulated datasets with known ground truth, comparing phase point-estimate error distributions (eCDFs) and median errors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is real (non-simulated) data with no ground-truth phases, since this skill's validation relies on comparing to simulated ground truth rather than reporter-based validation The method under test does not produce per-cell point estimates comparable to the baselines' outputs (e.g., only uncertainty summaries without phase estimates) Goal is uncertainty calibration assessment rather than point-estimate accuracy — Tempo's separate calibration property would need a different evaluation design

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify whether a supervised annotator (NeuCA) outperforms existing clustering/annotation methods across training-size and testing-size regimes on scRNA-seq data with known labels.
skills.name: cross-method-accuracy-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-accuracy-comparison Use when you need to quantify whether a supervised annotator (NeuCA) outperforms existing clustering/annotation methods across training-size and testing-size regimes on scRNA-seq data with known labels. No training data with known labels exist for the tissue of interest — supervised annotation is not viable and unsupervised methods are the only option The new sample is expected to contain cell types absent from the reference/training data — NeuCA is designed only for settings where all cell types already exist in the reference The goal is detecting novel or rare/unknown cell types rather than exhaustive label assignment among known types http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmarks NeuCA against unsupervised baselines (Seurat, SC3) on simulated PBMC cell-annotation tasks, varying training proportion (10/20/50/80%) and testing size (800/1600/4000 cells) and scoring accuracy (accurately assigned rate) and ARI. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-04473-4
skills.summary: Benchmarks NeuCA against unsupervised baselines (Seurat, SC3) on simulated PBMC cell-annotation tasks, varying training proportion (10/20/50/80%) and testing size (800/1600/4000 cells) and scoring accuracy (accurately assigned rate) and ARI.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No training data with known labels exist for the tissue of interest — supervised annotation is not viable and unsupervised methods are the only option The new sample is expected to contain cell types absent from the reference/training data — NeuCA is designed only for settings where all cell types already exist in the reference The goal is detecting novel or rare/unknown cell types rather than exhaustive label assignment among known types

skills.description: Use when comparing source-free scRNA-seq annotation methods on target datasets containing target-private (novel) cell types, to test whether adaptive unknown-cell detection outperforms user-defined thresholds.
skills.name: cross-method-annotation-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-method-annotation-benchmark-comparison Use when comparing source-free scRNA-seq annotation methods on target datasets containing target-private (novel) cell types, to test whether adaptive unknown-cell detection outperforms user-defined thresholds. Target data contain no novel cell types (closed/partial settings without target-private types) — the bimodality tests and known/unknown partitioning are not triggered and threshold comparison is not informative Raw source data are available and explicit source-target feature alignment is possible — a non-source-free benchmark framing is more appropriate You need only overall annotation accuracy (e.g., accuracy/H-score) without evaluating novel-cell detection outcomes Benchmarks scEMAIL's novel cell-type perception module (E-score, bimodality tests, adaptive manifold-mixup threshold) against manually thresholded annotation competitors (scmap, ItClust, scSemiCluster) on open and open-partial scRNA-seq settings, quantifying unknown-cell detection rather than only classification accuracy. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2022.12.008
skills.summary: Benchmarks scEMAIL's novel cell-type perception module (E-score, bimodality tests, adaptive manifold-mixup threshold) against manually thresholded annotation competitors (scmap, ItClust, scSemiCluster) on open and open-partial scRNA-seq settings, quantifying unknown-cell detection rather than only classification accuracy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Target data contain no novel cell types (closed/partial settings without target-private types) — the bimodality tests and known/unknown partitioning are not triggered and threshold comparison is not informative Raw source data are available and explicit source-target feature alignment is possible — a non-source-free benchmark framing is more appropriate You need only overall annotation accuracy (e.g., accuracy/H-score) without evaluating novel-cell detection outcomes

skills.description: Use when a labeled scRNA-seq dataset with author/expert-provided cell-type annotations is available and you need to compare the prediction quality and speed of several automated annotation methods on identical inputs.
skills.name: cross-method-annotation-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-method-annotation-benchmarking Use when a labeled scRNA-seq dataset with author/expert-provided cell-type annotations is available and you need to compare the prediction quality and speed of several automated annotation methods on identical inputs. The dataset has no reference/author cell-type annotations, so F1, balanced accuracy, and label similarity cannot be computed against ground truth. skills.summary: Benchmark multiple automated scRNA-seq cell-type annotators (Census, scType, scATOMIC, scibet, scCATCH) on the same dataset by comparing each method's predicted labels against author-provided annotations using F1, balanced accuracy, label similarity, total accuracy, and runtime.

You only need a single method's annotations rather than a head-to-head comparison of multiple annotators. The tissue of interest is not covered by the available pretrained models (Census supports 24 organs and cancer models for Kidney, Large_Intestine, Liver, Lung, Mammary, Pancreas only).
