skills.name: cross-platform-transcriptome-model-training
skills.search_text: cross-platform-transcriptome-model-training Use when a training set from one transcriptomic platform (e.g., RNA-seq GSE151189 .csv with sample names in the first column and labels in the last) must yield a model that predicts clinical outcomes on samples from a different platform (e.g., GSE59098 microarray). The training and validation datasets share no common genes — Ciclops fails silently, producing ./training/ csv splits with only sample-name and label columns and no gene expression columns The goal is SHAP-based biomarker analysis with a regression model (gpr or lr) — SHAP is implemented only for LightGBM, XGBoost, and Random Forest The datasets were already jointly normalized during preprocessing, in which case quantile normalization should be skipped via --no_quantile http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Train and transfer clinical outcome prediction models across transcriptomic platforms using Ciclops, which preprocesses a training .csv, runs 10-fold cross-validation, and applies the fitted model to an external validation dataset (e.g., GSE151189 RNA-seq training transferred to the GSE59098 microarray validation set). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.xpro.2022.101583
skills.summary: Train and transfer clinical outcome prediction models across transcriptomic platforms using Ciclops, which preprocesses a training .csv, runs 10-fold cross-validation, and applies the fitted model to an external validation dataset (e.g., GSE151189 RNA-seq training transferred to the GSE59098 microarray validation set).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The training and validation datasets share no common genes — Ciclops fails silently, producing ./training/ csv splits with only sample-name and label columns and no gene expression columns The goal is SHAP-based biomarker analysis with a regression model (gpr or lr) — SHAP is implemented only for LightGBM, XGBoost, and Random Forest The datasets were already jointly normalized during preprocessing, in which case quantile normalization should be skipped via --no_quantile

skills.description: Use when RNA-seq-derived variant calls (multi-sample VCF from GATK) must be quality-checked against an independent genotyping platform (e.g., Axiom array VCF) to confirm sample identity and call accuracy.
skills.name: cross-platform-variant-concordance-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-platform-variant-concordance-comparison Use when RNA-seq-derived variant calls (multi-sample VCF from GATK) must be quality-checked against an independent genotyping platform (e.g., Axiom array VCF) to confirm sample identity and call accuracy. VADT is the wrong tool here — use Compare_VCF_Files instead when the goal is genotype concordance between platforms, not allele-specific expression detection The two VCFs share no overlapping samples or the genotyping panel has negligible SNP overlap with the RNA-seq call set (the paper notes low overlap due to commercial panel limitations) Variant calls come from a caller other than GATK HaplotypeCaller in a non-standard VCF format, which the README warns could trigger parsing bugs http://edamontology.org/topic_3516 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Validates RNA-seq variant calls against orthogonal genotyping array data by filtering both VCFs, matching samples and overlapping SNPs with Compare_VCF_Files, and computing per-sample genotype concordance (99.46% self-by-self vs 54.30% randomly-paired baseline in the broiler chicken ASE study). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-83459-8
skills.summary: Validates RNA-seq variant calls against orthogonal genotyping array data by filtering both VCFs, matching samples and overlapping SNPs with Compare_VCF_Files, and computing per-sample genotype concordance (99.46% self-by-self vs 54.30% randomly-paired baseline in the broiler chicken ASE study).
skills.when_to_use_negative: VADT is the wrong tool here — use Compare_VCF_Files instead when the goal is genotype concordance between platforms, not allele-specific expression detection The two VCFs share no overlapping samples or the genotyping panel has negligible SNP overlap with the RNA-seq call set (the paper notes low overlap due to commercial panel limitations) Variant calls come from a caller other than GATK HaplotypeCaller in a non-standard VCF format, which the README warns could trigger parsing bugs

skills.description: Use when comparing the state/progression of an unseen cell population against a labeled reference population along shared axes — e.g., asking whether CD57high senescent T cells overlap CD57low cells at days 2–3 of TCR stimulation on LD axes.
skills.name: cross-population-trajectory-mapping
skills.search_text: cross-population-trajectory-mapping Use when comparing the state/progression of an unseen cell population against a labeled reference population along shared axes — e.g., asking whether CD57high senescent T cells overlap CD57low cells at days 2–3 of TCR stimulation on LD axes. Class labels are unknown or an unbiased view of the data is preferable — the supervised approach is inappropriate in these situations per the article's discussion. More than ~100 features must be considered, since HSS feature selection is not feasible at that dimensionality (plain LDA without HSS may still be used). The target population requires preserving local data structure or capturing non-linear relationships — LDA maximizes class separability at the expense of local structure and does not capture non-linear relationships. http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Projects an unseen cell population onto linear discriminant (LD) axes trained on a reference population, so that two biological trajectories (e.g., senescent CD57high vs non-senescent CD57low T cells over TCR stimulation days 0–5) can be compared on a shared manifold. Grounded in the HSS-LDA makeAxes workflow of Amouzgar et al. 2022 (Patterns). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2022.100536
skills.summary: Projects an unseen cell population onto linear discriminant (LD) axes trained on a reference population, so that two biological trajectories (e.g., senescent CD57high vs non-senescent CD57low T cells over TCR stimulation days 0–5) can be compared on a shared manifold. Grounded in the HSS-LDA makeAxes workflow of Amouzgar et al. 2022 (Patterns).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Class labels are unknown or an unbiased view of the data is preferable — the supervised approach is inappropriate in these situations per the article's discussion. More than ~100 features must be considered, since HSS feature selection is not feasible at that dimensionality (plain LDA without HSS may still be used). The target population requires preserving local data structure or capturing non-linear relationships — LDA maximizes class separability at the expense of local structure and does not capture non-linear relationships.

skills.description: Use when comparing Staem5's m5C prediction performance against SVM/RF-based baselines on the same A. thaliana and M. musculus training and independent test datasets to reproduce Tables 3 and 4.
skills.name: cross-predictor-performance-comparison-across-species
skills.search_text: cross-predictor-performance-comparison-across-species Use when comparing Staem5's m5C prediction performance against SVM/RF-based baselines on the same A. thaliana and M. musculus training and independent test datasets to reproduce Tables 3 and 4. Input is already a metric/feature table rather than raw m5C sequence datasets that need prediction runs The goal is developing or tuning a new m5C predictor (base-classifier selection, Bayesian optimization, F score feature selection) rather than comparing existing trained predictors Prediction is needed for species other than A. thaliana or M. musculus, since Staem5 only accepts 'Arabidopsis' or 'Mouse' and species-specific models are required http://edamontology.org/topic_3307 Benchmarking skill for evaluating the Staem5 stacked m5C predictor against state-of-the-art predictors (iRNA-m5C, m5CPred-SVM, iRNA-m5C_SVM) on identical A. thaliana and M. musculus training and independent test datasets, computing Sn, Sp, Acc, MCC, and AUC from confusion-matrix counts. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.omtn.2021.10.012
skills.summary: Benchmarking skill for evaluating the Staem5 stacked m5C predictor against state-of-the-art predictors (iRNA-m5C, m5CPred-SVM, iRNA-m5C_SVM) on identical A. thaliana and M. musculus training and independent test datasets, computing Sn, Sp, Acc, MCC, and AUC from confusion-matrix counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a metric/feature table rather than raw m5C sequence datasets that need prediction runs The goal is developing or tuning a new m5C predictor (base-classifier selection, Bayesian optimization, F score feature selection) rather than comparing existing trained predictors Prediction is needed for species other than A. thaliana or M. musculus, since Staem5 only accepts 'Arabidopsis' or 'Mouse' and species-specific models are required

skills.description: Use when testing transfer of a trained protein-imputation model to data whose cell types are not perfectly aligned with training, or generated by a different antibody-tagging protocol (CITE-seq vs REAP-seq).
skills.name: cross-protocol-protein-prediction-validation
skills.search_text: cross-protocol-protein-prediction-validation Use when testing transfer of a trained protein-imputation model to data whose cell types are not perfectly aligned with training, or generated by a different antibody-tagging protocol (CITE-seq vs REAP-seq). Input expression is TPM/RPKM or otherwise not UMI-based count data — cTP-net can only apply to count-based expression input (UMI-based), and CITE-seq data with TPM/RPKM metrics were not available for testing Target cells are outside the hematopoietic lineage — the article states imputation of these immune-related markers has not been tried on non-hematopoietic cells Evaluating same-population within-sample accuracy rather than cross-tissue/cross-protocol transfer — in that case the same-population trained model is the proper comparison, and it is slightly more accurate than cross-tissue imputation http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 http://edamontology.org/topic_3516 Benchmark whether a cTP-net model trained on one tissue or assay protocol (e.g., CITE-CBMC or CITE-seq) generalizes to imputing surface protein abundances on a different tissue (PBMC) or protocol (REAP-seq), by comparing cross-cell Pearson correlations of imputed proteins against SAVER-X-denoised RNA baselines. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-14391-0
skills.summary: Benchmark whether a cTP-net model trained on one tissue or assay protocol (e.g., CITE-CBMC or CITE-seq) generalizes to imputing surface protein abundances on a different tissue (PBMC) or protocol (REAP-seq), by comparing cross-cell Pearson correlations of imputed proteins against SAVER-X-denoised RNA baselines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input expression is TPM/RPKM or otherwise not UMI-based count data — cTP-net can only apply to count-based expression input (UMI-based), and CITE-seq data with TPM/RPKM metrics were not available for testing Target cells are outside the hematopoietic lineage — the article states imputation of these immune-related markers has not been tried on non-hematopoietic cells Evaluating same-population within-sample accuracy rather than cross-tissue/cross-protocol transfer — in that case the same-population trained model is the proper comparison, and it is slightly more accurate than cross-tissue imputation

skills.description: Use when clustering scRNA-seq data generated by multiple scRNA-seq protocols where batch effects confound cell-type separation, and you need batch-corrected embeddings plus cluster assignments evaluated with silhouette metrics.
skills.name: cross-protocol-scrnaseq-integration
skills.search_text: cross-protocol-scrnaseq-integration Use when clustering scRNA-seq data generated by multiple scRNA-seq protocols where batch effects confound cell-type separation, and you need batch-corrected embeddings plus cluster assignments evaluated with silhouette metrics. Single-protocol scRNA-seq data with no batch structure — the clustering-only scMGCA workflow suffices and no batch-merging evaluation is meaningful Bulk RNA-seq or non-single-cell expression matrices — the cell graph / PPMI construction and dropout modeling are specific to scRNA-seq sparsity Datasets where batch labels and cell-type identity are confounded (e.g. each protocol captured a different tissue), where ASW-based batch mixing cannot be interpreted http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Removes batch effects from multi-protocol scRNA-seq data (e.g. human pancreas profiled by CEL-seq, CEL-seq2, Fluidigm C1 and Smart-seq2) by running scMGCA's graph-embedding autoencoder to produce batch-merged cell clusters, benchmarked against DESC and related integration methods. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-36134-7
skills.summary: Removes batch effects from multi-protocol scRNA-seq data (e.g. human pancreas profiled by CEL-seq, CEL-seq2, Fluidigm C1 and Smart-seq2) by running scMGCA's graph-embedding autoencoder to produce batch-merged cell clusters, benchmarked against DESC and related integration methods.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Single-protocol scRNA-seq data with no batch structure — the clustering-only scMGCA workflow suffices and no batch-merging evaluation is meaningful Bulk RNA-seq or non-single-cell expression matrices — the cell graph / PPMI construction and dropout modeling are specific to scRNA-seq sparsity Datasets where batch labels and cell-type identity are confounded (e.g. each protocol captured a different tissue), where ASW-based batch mixing cannot be interpreted

skills.description: Use when fitting mutational signatures to a mutation catalog and you need to assess sensitivity of per-sample signature exposures to the reference signature set version (e.g. COSMIC v2 vs v3.1), or to justify which reference version's cleaner signature definitions to report.
skills.name: cross-reference-version-signature-exposure-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-reference-version-signature-exposure-comparison Use when fitting mutational signatures to a mutation catalog and you need to assess sensitivity of per-sample signature exposures to the reference signature set version (e.g. COSMIC v2 vs v3.1), or to justify which reference version's cleaner signature definitions to report. Targeted capture panels covering only a few megabases, where mutational burdens are too low for meaningful individual-patient signature fitting Mutation catalogs with fewer than ~500 mutations, where signature fitting accuracy is not optimal De novo signature extraction tasks — this skill assumes reference-based fitting against fixed COSMIC signature sets http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Quantifies how the choice of COSMIC mutational signature reference version (v2 vs v3.1) changes fitted signature exposures and reconstruction accuracy, by re-running the same fitting workflow (e.g. mmsig on multiple myeloma samples) against both references and comparing per-sample estimates. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-021-01938-0
skills.summary: Quantifies how the choice of COSMIC mutational signature reference version (v2 vs v3.1) changes fitted signature exposures and reconstruction accuracy, by re-running the same fitting workflow (e.g. mmsig on multiple myeloma samples) against both references and comparing per-sample estimates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Targeted capture panels covering only a few megabases, where mutational burdens are too low for meaningful individual-patient signature fitting Mutation catalogs with fewer than ~500 mutations, where signature fitting accuracy is not optimal De novo signature extraction tasks — this skill assumes reference-based fitting against fixed COSMIC signature sets

skills.description: Use when two or more replicate sections from the same platform (e.g., Xenium-BreastCancer1 and Xenium-BreastCancer2) have been segmented with BIDCell and you need to quantify whether cell segmentation and cell-type annotation results are concordant across replicates.
skills.name: cross-replicate-agreement-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-replicate-agreement-analysis Use when two or more replicate sections from the same platform (e.g., Xenium-BreastCancer1 and Xenium-BreastCancer2) have been segmented with BIDCell and you need to quantify whether cell segmentation and cell-type annotation results are concordant across replicates. You are comparing segmentation methods on a single section (use the full CellSPA method-comparison framework instead of cross-replicate agreement) Only one replicate section exists, so no cross-replicate concordance can be computed Input data is not subcellular spatial transcriptomics (e.g., bulk or single-cell-only data), since segmentation replicability is not defined http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Assesses whether BIDCell's subcellular segmentation of spatial transcriptomics data is replicable across replicate tissue sections by running the full BIDCell pipeline on each replicate and comparing agreement metrics following the CellSPA evaluation framework (e.g., Fig. 3i-j and Supplementary Fig. 16 of the BIDCell paper). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-44560-w
skills.summary: Assesses whether BIDCell's subcellular segmentation of spatial transcriptomics data is replicable across replicate tissue sections by running the full BIDCell pipeline on each replicate and comparing agreement metrics following the CellSPA evaluation framework (e.g., Fig. 3i-j and Supplementary Fig. 16 of the BIDCell paper).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are comparing segmentation methods on a single section (use the full CellSPA method-comparison framework instead of cross-replicate agreement) Only one replicate section exists, so no cross-replicate concordance can be computed Input data is not subcellular spatial transcriptomics (e.g., bulk or single-cell-only data), since segmentation replicability is not defined

skills.description: Use when you have spatially barcoded ST poly(A) site data for multiple tissue-section replicates (e.g., ST-MOB Replicates 5, 11, 12) and need to test whether spatial APA patterns and gene-level DEAPA calls reproduce across sections.
skills.name: cross-replicate-apa-profile-correlation
skills.search_text: cross-replicate-apa-profile-correlation Use when you have spatially barcoded ST poly(A) site data for multiple tissue-section replicates (e.g., ST-MOB Replicates 5, 11, 12) and need to test whether spatial APA patterns and gene-level DEAPA calls reproduce across sections. Input is single-cell or imaging-based spatial data (MERFISH/seqFISH) — the article states APA sites can only be identified from spatially barcoded ST data using tools like scAPAtrap or Sierra You only have one ST tissue section and no replicate APA profile to correlate against — the skill's acceptance criteria depend on cross-replicate comparison The goal is gene-level spatial expression variability rather than APA usage — use gene-expression spatial tools (SPARK, SpatialDE, Trendsceek) on the count matrix instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 A robustness-analysis skill for spatial APA studies: rerun the stAPAminer pipeline (RUD quantification, KNN imputation, spot clustering, DEAPA calling) on independent adjacent-tissue-section replicates and quantify reproducibility by Pearson correlation of APA profiles against a reference replicate (e.g., ST-MOB Replicates 5 and 12 vs Replicate 11). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2023.01.003
skills.summary: A robustness-analysis skill for spatial APA studies: rerun the stAPAminer pipeline (RUD quantification, KNN imputation, spot clustering, DEAPA calling) on independent adjacent-tissue-section replicates and quantify reproducibility by Pearson correlation of APA profiles against a reference replicate (e.g., ST-MOB Replicates 5 and 12 vs Replicate 11).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is single-cell or imaging-based spatial data (MERFISH/seqFISH) — the article states APA sites can only be identified from spatially barcoded ST data using tools like scAPAtrap or Sierra You only have one ST tissue section and no replicate APA profile to correlate against — the skill's acceptance criteria depend on cross-replicate comparison The goal is gene-level spatial expression variability rather than APA usage — use gene-expression spatial tools (SPARK, SpatialDE, Trendsceek) on the count matrix instead

skills.description: Use when benchmarking 2D location or spatial domain recovery on ST data with replicate sections, and you need training scenarios ranging from same-section splits to cross-replicate transfer with merged training sets.
skills.name: cross-replicate-st-training-scenario-design
skills.search_text: cross-replicate-st-training-scenario-design Use when benchmarking 2D location or spatial domain recovery on ST data with replicate sections, and you need training scenarios ranging from same-section splits to cross-replicate transfer with merged training sets. Only a single non-replicate ST section is available, making cross-replicate or merged-training scenarios impossible The goal is spatial domain (categorical) recovery, which requires differentially expressed genes via Scanpy's rank_genes_groups rather than spatially variable gene selection http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 Designs intra- and cross-replicate training/testing splits of spatial transcriptomics reference sections (e.g., Vizgen MERSCOPE mouse brain S1R1/S1R2) to benchmark spatial location recovery methods under progressively harder generalization scenarios. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-39895-3
skills.summary: Designs intra- and cross-replicate training/testing splits of spatial transcriptomics reference sections (e.g., Vizgen MERSCOPE mouse brain S1R1/S1R2) to benchmark spatial location recovery methods under progressively harder generalization scenarios.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single non-replicate ST section is available, making cross-replicate or merged-training scenarios impossible The goal is spatial domain (categorical) recovery, which requires differentially expressed genes via Scanpy's rank_genes_groups rather than spatially variable gene selection

skills.description: Use when scRNAseq cells have been clustered by Sparsely-Connected Autoencoder (SCA) across repeated runs and you must quantify cluster reconstruction reproducibility (QCC/QCM >= 0.5) or validate the autoencoder's clustering stability.
skills.name: cross-run-clustering-consistency-measurement
skills.search_text: cross-run-clustering-consistency-measurement Use when scRNAseq cells have been clustered by Sparsely-Connected Autoencoder (SCA) across repeated runs and you must quantify cluster reconstruction reproducibility (QCC/QCM >= 0.5) or validate the autoencoder's clustering stability. Only a single clustering result exists (no repeated SCA runs) — QCC and QCM are cross-run metrics and cannot be computed without multiple run labelings The goal is functional annotation of clusters (TF/miRNA/kinase mining from the SCA encoded space) rather than evaluating the robustness/reproducibility of the clustering itself Clusters were produced by a non-SCA method — the 0.5 explainability threshold was calibrated for SCA's selective cluster reconstruction and does not transfer automatically http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Implements the SCA paper's QCC (Quality Control of Cluster) and QCM (Quality Control of Model) metrics, which quantify how consistently cell clusters are reconstructed across multiple SCA clustering runs, using QCC/QCM >= 0.5 to declare a cluster 'explainable' by SCA analysis. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41540-020-00162-6
skills.summary: Implements the SCA paper's QCC (Quality Control of Cluster) and QCM (Quality Control of Model) metrics, which quantify how consistently cell clusters are reconstructed across multiple SCA clustering runs, using QCC/QCM >= 0.5 to declare a cluster 'explainable' by SCA analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single clustering result exists (no repeated SCA runs) — QCC and QCM are cross-run metrics and cannot be computed without multiple run labelings The goal is functional annotation of clusters (TF/miRNA/kinase mining from the SCA encoded space) rather than evaluating the robustness/reproducibility of the clustering itself Clusters were produced by a non-SCA method — the 0.5 explainability threshold was calibrated for SCA's selective cluster reconstruction and does not transfer automatically

skills.description: Use when repeating a marker-selection procedure (e.g., phenotype-cover G-PC/CEM-PC) over multiple resampled runs and you need a stability index showing how much of the feature set is retained across runs.
skills.name: cross-run-feature-set-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-run-feature-set-comparison Use when repeating a marker-selection procedure (e.g., phenotype-cover G-PC/CEM-PC) over multiple resampled runs and you need a stability index showing how much of the feature set is retained across runs. When the goal is classification accuracy or deconvolution performance rather than reproducibility of the selected marker set When only a single deterministic selection run is planned — stability metrics require multiple resampled runs When the data are not split into resamples with a shared phenotype/label structure, so feature sets across runs are not comparable http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies the stability of marker/feature sets selected by G-PC (GreedyPC), CEM-PC (CEMPC), and competing methods (e.g., ReliefF, F values, mRMR) by repeating selection over 5 runs on randomly sampled halves of scRNA-seq data and computing pairwise overlap statistics across runs. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2022.100332
skills.summary: Quantifies the stability of marker/feature sets selected by G-PC (GreedyPC), CEM-PC (CEMPC), and competing methods (e.g., ReliefF, F values, mRMR) by repeating selection over 5 runs on randomly sampled halves of scRNA-seq data and computing pairwise overlap statistics across runs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is classification accuracy or deconvolution performance rather than reproducibility of the selected marker set When only a single deterministic selection run is planned — stability metrics require multiple resampled runs When the data are not split into resamples with a shared phenotype/label structure, so feature sets across runs are not comparable

skills.description: Use when pseudotime/trajectory output from RNA velocity-based methods must be validated: repeated runs of a stochastic method (e.g., 10 Cytopath initialisations) need robustness checks and known cell type orderings are available for correlation.
skills.name: cross-run-pseudotime-robustness-assessment
skills.search_text: cross-run-pseudotime-robustness-assessment Use when pseudotime/trajectory output from RNA velocity-based methods must be validated: repeated runs of a stochastic method (e.g., 10 Cytopath initialisations) need robustness checks and known cell type orderings are available for correlation. When the underlying RNA velocity estimation itself is faulty — the authors state trajectory inference with Cytopath is not meaningful in that case (e.g., the erythroid gastrulation dataset with spurious root/terminal states). When root and terminal cell states are not clearly identifiable — the authors do not recommend performing trajectory inference with Cytopath in this situation. When there is no known cell type ordering or equivalent ground truth available to define the Spearman correlation target. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Assess whether trajectory-inference pseudotime (e.g., Cytopath on RNA velocity fields) is biologically consistent and stable across independent initialisations by computing per-run, per-lineage Spearman correlations against known cell type ordering and benchmarking against baseline methods. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2022.100359
skills.summary: Assess whether trajectory-inference pseudotime (e.g., Cytopath on RNA velocity fields) is biologically consistent and stable across independent initialisations by computing per-run, per-lineage Spearman correlations against known cell type ordering and benchmarking against baseline methods.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the underlying RNA velocity estimation itself is faulty — the authors state trajectory inference with Cytopath is not meaningful in that case (e.g., the erythroid gastrulation dataset with spurious root/terminal states). When root and terminal cell states are not clearly identifiable — the authors do not recommend performing trajectory inference with Cytopath in this situation. When there is no known cell type ordering or equivalent ground truth available to define the Spearman correlation target.

skills.description: Use when multiplexed 10x Genomics droplet data sequenced on a patterned flow-cell instrument (HiSeq 4000/X/NovaSeq) needs per-sample assessment of how many cell calls are artefactual after swapped-molecule removal.
skills.name: cross-sample-cell-library-loss-quantification
skills.search_text: cross-sample-cell-library-loss-quantification Use when multiplexed 10x Genomics droplet data sequenced on a patterned flow-cell instrument (HiSeq 4000/X/NovaSeq) needs per-sample assessment of how many cell calls are artefactual after swapped-molecule removal. Data are plate-based scRNA-seq where molecule exclusion is not applicable — use the per-plate linear model / cell exclusion approaches instead Libraries were sequenced on non-patterned flow-cell instruments (e.g. HiSeq 2500), where swapping is negligible and cell-call loss after molecule exclusion would reflect noise rather than artefactual libraries http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Quantifies how many called cells each multiplexed sample loses after removal of barcode-swapped molecules, exposing samples that consist almost entirely of artefactual swapped libraries (e.g. samples B1/B2 of the mouse epithelial HiSeq 4000 dataset). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-05083-x
skills.summary: Quantifies how many called cells each multiplexed sample loses after removal of barcode-swapped molecules, exposing samples that consist almost entirely of artefactual swapped libraries (e.g. samples B1/B2 of the mouse epithelial HiSeq 4000 dataset).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are plate-based scRNA-seq where molecule exclusion is not applicable — use the per-plate linear model / cell exclusion approaches instead Libraries were sequenced on non-patterned flow-cell instruments (e.g. HiSeq 2500), where swapping is negligible and cell-call loss after molecule exclusion would reflect noise rather than artefactual libraries

skills.description: Use when you have an annotated single-cell/nuclei RNA-seq dataset (e.g., .h5ad with 'class_label' in AnnData.obs) and need to predict cell-type labels on cells from a different donor or sample using SIMS label transfer.
skills.name: cross-sample-label-transfer
skills.search_text: cross-sample-label-transfer Use when you have an annotated single-cell/nuclei RNA-seq dataset (e.g., .h5ad with 'class_label' in AnnData.obs) and need to predict cell-type labels on cells from a different donor or sample using SIMS label transfer. Cells come from a different species than the training data — the authors explicitly limited validation to samples within the same species because 'neuronal subtypes diverge significantly between species' The training data lacks expert annotations ('class_label') — SIMS is fully supervised and cannot bootstrap labels from scratch Input matrices are gene x cell rather than cell x gene — SIMS assumes transcriptomes of individual cells as training samples http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Train a SIMS (TabNet-based) single-cell RNA-seq classifier on an annotated donor/sample and transfer cell-type labels to held-out samples, validated on the Allen human adult cerebral cortex single-nuclei dataset (49,495 nuclei from donors H200.1023, H200.1025, H200.1030) where trans-sample accuracy falls in the 93.1%–95.8% range. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.xgen.2024.100581
skills.summary: Train a SIMS (TabNet-based) single-cell RNA-seq classifier on an annotated donor/sample and transfer cell-type labels to held-out samples, validated on the Allen human adult cerebral cortex single-nuclei dataset (49,495 nuclei from donors H200.1023, H200.1025, H200.1030) where trans-sample accuracy falls in the 93.1%–95.8% range.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Cells come from a different species than the training data — the authors explicitly limited validation to samples within the same species because 'neuronal subtypes diverge significantly between species' The training data lacks expert annotations ('class_label') — SIMS is fully supervised and cannot bootstrap labels from scratch Input matrices are gene x cell rather than cell x gene — SIMS assumes transcriptomes of individual cells as training samples

skills.description: Use when you already hold two denoised scGRNs (sparse dgCMatrix X and Y over the same gene set) and need commensurable per-gene coordinates to detect differential regulation between conditions.
skills.name: cross-sample-network-coordinate-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-sample-network-coordinate-comparison Use when you already hold two denoised scGRNs (sparse dgCMatrix X and Y over the same gene set) and need commensurable per-gene coordinates to detect differential regulation between conditions. The two samples are highly dissimilar (e.g., different cell types) rather than two populations of the same cell type — the article states scTenifoldNet is more suitable for comparing highly similar samples Input is still raw count data or un-denoised PC-regression networks — manifold alignment must be applied after tensorDecomposition You only need a ranked gene list without network-structure comparison — the upstream dRegulation output alone would not exist without this step, but a simpler differential-expression analysis would not require network alignment http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Non-linear manifold alignment (scTenifoldNet's `manifoldAlignment` step) that projects two denoised single-cell gene regulatory networks onto a shared low-dimensional manifold via a joint-Laplacian eigenvalue problem, so each gene's regulatory position can be compared across samples. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2020.100139
skills.summary: Non-linear manifold alignment (scTenifoldNet's `manifoldAlignment` step) that projects two denoised single-cell gene regulatory networks onto a shared low-dimensional manifold via a joint-Laplacian eigenvalue problem, so each gene's regulatory position can be compared across samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The two samples are highly dissimilar (e.g., different cell types) rather than two populations of the same cell type — the article states scTenifoldNet is more suitable for comparing highly similar samples Input is still raw count data or un-denoised PC-regression networks — manifold alignment must be applied after tensorDecomposition You only need a ranked gene list without network-structure comparison — the upstream dRegulation output alone would not exist without this step, but a simpler differential-expression analysis would not require network alignment

skills.description: Use when comparing pseudotemporal gene expression dynamics across two or more conditions where each condition has multiple biological sample replicates, and cell-level methods would inflate false discoveries.
skills.name: cross-sample-variability-adjustment
skills.search_text: cross-sample-variability-adjustment Use when comparing pseudotemporal gene expression dynamics across two or more conditions where each condition has multiple biological sample replicates, and cell-level methods would inflate false discoveries. Data are single-sample trajectories with no biological replicates per condition — condiments-style assumptions or single-trajectory methods apply instead The goal is cell-level abundance or topology change detection rather than cross-condition gene expression dynamics (use Lamian's cell density / topology modules instead) Data have already been collapsed to a per-sample feature table where cell-level variability is no longer distinguishable http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A skill for testing differential gene expression along pseudotime in multi-sample scRNA-seq data while explicitly modeling biological sample-to-sample variability, so that significance calls generalize to new samples and FDR is appropriately controlled. The paper's null-dataset benchmark on 8 HCA bone-marrow donors shows this eliminates the thousands of false positives produced by methods that ignore sample variability. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-42841-y
skills.summary: A skill for testing differential gene expression along pseudotime in multi-sample scRNA-seq data while explicitly modeling biological sample-to-sample variability, so that significance calls generalize to new samples and FDR is appropriately controlled. The paper's null-dataset benchmark on 8 HCA bone-marrow donors shows this eliminates the thousands of false positives produced by methods that ignore sample variability.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are single-sample trajectories with no biological replicates per condition — condiments-style assumptions or single-trajectory methods apply instead The goal is cell-level abundance or topology change detection rather than cross-condition gene expression dynamics (use Lamian's cell density / topology modules instead) Data have already been collapsed to a per-sample feature table where cell-level variability is no longer distinguishable

skills.description: Use when a sub-micrometer-resolution ST dataset (e.g. Seq-Scope, >1M spatial barcodes per mm2) has too few UMIs per spatial barcode for direct clustering, and cell-type labels from coarse bins must be transferred to finer overlapping sliding-window bins.
skills.name: cross-scale-cell-type-label-transfer
skills.search_text: cross-scale-cell-type-label-transfer Use when a sub-micrometer-resolution ST dataset (e.g. Seq-Scope, >1M spatial barcodes per mm2) has too few UMIs per spatial barcode for direct clustering, and cell-type labels from coarse bins must be transferred to finer overlapping sliding-window bins. Attempting subcellular-resolution label transfer: each spatial segment must be larger than subcellular compartments (~10 um), so subcellular analysis with MSSW is not feasible The dataset already has sufficient UMIs per spatial barcode (e.g. VISIUM 100 um spots), so simple square-grid clustering without sliding-window transfer is adequate Only a single spatial aggregation scale exists — the method requires paired Step C1 simple grids and Step C2 sliding-window grids as query and reference http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Assign cell types at subcellular/super-cellular resolution by clustering STtools' multiscale sliding-window (MSSW) bins against labels learned on simple square-grid bins, using Seurat reference mapping. This overcomes the low UMI counts per barcode at sub-micrometer Seq-Scope resolution by transferring labels from coarser aggregation to finer overlapping grids. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac061
skills.summary: Assign cell types at subcellular/super-cellular resolution by clustering STtools' multiscale sliding-window (MSSW) bins against labels learned on simple square-grid bins, using Seurat reference mapping. This overcomes the low UMI counts per barcode at sub-micrometer Seq-Scope resolution by transferring labels from coarser aggregation to finer overlapping grids.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Attempting subcellular-resolution label transfer: each spatial segment must be larger than subcellular compartments (~10 um), so subcellular analysis with MSSW is not feasible The dataset already has sufficient UMIs per spatial barcode (e.g. VISIUM 100 um spots), so simple square-grid clustering without sliding-window transfer is adequate Only a single spatial aggregation scale exists — the method requires paired Step C1 simple grids and Step C2 sliding-window grids as query and reference

skills.description: Use when reconstructing a causal gene regulatory network from gRNA-to-gene perturbation data where multiple gRNAs per regulator and replicate screens are available, and only regulations surviving all four Q ≤ 0.2 tests should be kept.
skills.name: cross-screen-reproducibility-filtering
skills.search_text: cross-screen-reproducibility-filtering Use when reconstructing a causal gene regulatory network from gRNA-to-gene perturbation data where multiple gRNAs per regulator and replicate screens are available, and only regulations surviving all four Q ≤ 0.2 tests should be kept. The goal is testing arbitrary nonlinear associations or reconstructing causal networks via v-structures, regularized regression, or Granger causality — Normalisr explicitly does not support these The study spans multiple datasets requiring batch-effect correction, which Normalisr's framework does not address The data are from full-length (non-UMI) scRNA-seq platforms, for which Normalisr's nonlinear covariates were not validated http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 A causal-filtering procedure that compiles high-confidence putative gene regulatory networks (833 regulations) from high-MOI CRISPRi screens by intersecting Normalisr's TSS-repression and trans-association calls across gRNAs and across the full-scale and small-scale CROP-seq screens. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-26682-1
skills.summary: A causal-filtering procedure that compiles high-confidence putative gene regulatory networks (833 regulations) from high-MOI CRISPRi screens by intersecting Normalisr's TSS-repression and trans-association calls across gRNAs and across the full-scale and small-scale CROP-seq screens.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is testing arbitrary nonlinear associations or reconstructing causal networks via v-structures, regularized regression, or Granger causality — Normalisr explicitly does not support these The study spans multiple datasets requiring batch-effect correction, which Normalisr's framework does not address The data are from full-length (non-UMI) scRNA-seq platforms, for which Normalisr's nonlinear covariates were not validated

skills.description: Use when integrating multiple spatial transcriptomics slices (e.g., 11 human breast cancer 10X Visium slices) whose batch effects would confound slice-by-slice domain identification, and uniform cross-slice domains are required.
skills.name: cross-slice-batch-effect-mitigation
skills.search_text: cross-slice-batch-effect-mitigation Use when integrating multiple spatial transcriptomics slices (e.g., 11 human breast cancer 10X Visium slices) whose batch effects would confound slice-by-slice domain identification, and uniform cross-slice domains are required. Slices with substantial defects (e.g., partial overlap, crop ratios >= 0.25) requiring nonlinear alignment — the current version of Scube/Splane pipeline does not support nonlinear alignment A new slice is added to an existing large-scale analysis — the entire deep learning model needs retraining from scratch, limiting computational efficiency Single-slice analysis with no cross-slice integration need — batch effect mitigation across slices is unnecessary http://edamontology.org/topic_3473 Mitigates batch effects when identifying spatial domains across multiple ST slices by using Spoint-derived cell type composition (rather than raw gene expression) as input to Splane's graph convolutional network with adversarial learning, producing domains (D1–D9) that are uniform across slices. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-43220-3
skills.summary: Mitigates batch effects when identifying spatial domains across multiple ST slices by using Spoint-derived cell type composition (rather than raw gene expression) as input to Splane's graph convolutional network with adversarial learning, producing domains (D1–D9) that are uniform across slices.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Slices with substantial defects (e.g., partial overlap, crop ratios >= 0.25) requiring nonlinear alignment — the current version of Scube/Splane pipeline does not support nonlinear alignment A new slice is added to an existing large-scale analysis — the entire deep learning model needs retraining from scratch, limiting computational efficiency Single-slice analysis with no cross-slice integration need — batch effect mitigation across slices is unnecessary

skills.description: Use when building or extending a ligand-receptor reference database from multiple prior L-R resources and you must reconcile, deduplicate, and verify literature support per pair before publishing the merged set.
skills.name: cross-source-pair-merge-deduplication
skills.search_text: cross-source-pair-merge-deduplication Use when building or extending a ligand-receptor reference database from multiple prior L-R resources and you must reconcile, deduplicate, and verify literature support per pair before publishing the merged set. You need to model heteromeric complexes — CellPhoneDB complex members were excluded and 'we do not model them in NATMI' Your input is already a single clean pair list — this skill is for reconciling conflicting multi-source resources, not consuming a finished database You need predicted or inferred interactions — this merge only admits pairs with primary literature support Assembles a curated ligand-receptor database (connectomeDB2020) by merging pair lists from prior resources (CellPhoneDB v2.0, RNA-Magnet, SingleCellSignalR/LRdb, ICELLNET, the authors' 2015 resource) with new manual curation, deduplicating and verifying literature support to yield 2293 literature-supported human pairs. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-18873-z
skills.summary: Assembles a curated ligand-receptor database (connectomeDB2020) by merging pair lists from prior resources (CellPhoneDB v2.0, RNA-Magnet, SingleCellSignalR/LRdb, ICELLNET, the authors' 2015 resource) with new manual curation, deduplicating and verifying literature support to yield 2293 literature-supported human pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to model heteromeric complexes — CellPhoneDB complex members were excluded and 'we do not model them in NATMI' Your input is already a single clean pair list — this skill is for reconciling conflicting multi-source resources, not consuming a finished database You need predicted or inferred interactions — this merge only admits pairs with primary literature support

skills.description: Use when you need to reproduce or extend cell-type-by-age analyses of cellular senescence in single-cell atlases spanning multiple ages/species, e.g. scoring cells with SenePy signatures and comparing old vs young marker-positive proportions per cell type.
skills.name: cross-species-aging-atlas-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-species-aging-atlas-analysis Use when you need to reproduce or extend cell-type-by-age analyses of cellular senescence in single-cell atlases spanning multiple ages/species, e.g. scoring cells with SenePy signatures and comparing old vs young marker-positive proportions per cell type. The input is already a scored/feature table of senescence positivity rather than raw or normalized single-cell counts in AnnData — re-scoring would be redundant. The data are scaled (z-scored) — score_hub explicitly requires non-scaled data for correct binarized scoring. The goal is differential aging expression rather than senescence-marker proportion dynamics; SenePy signatures discount genes overlapping the general transcriptional shift of aging and do not capture downregulated genes. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Quantifies how the proportion of senescence-positive cells changes with age across cell types in the Tabula Muris Senis mouse atlas (328K cells, 19 tissues, 1–30 months) and a human single-cell aging atlas, using SenePy cell-type-specific senescence hub signatures scored per cell and aggregated into old/young positive-cell ratios. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-57047-7
skills.summary: Quantifies how the proportion of senescence-positive cells changes with age across cell types in the Tabula Muris Senis mouse atlas (328K cells, 19 tissues, 1–30 months) and a human single-cell aging atlas, using SenePy cell-type-specific senescence hub signatures scored per cell and aggregated into old/young positive-cell ratios.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a scored/feature table of senescence positivity rather than raw or normalized single-cell counts in AnnData — re-scoring would be redundant. The data are scaled (z-scored) — score_hub explicitly requires non-scaled data for correct binarized scoring. The goal is differential aging expression rather than senescence-marker proportion dynamics; SenePy signatures discount genes overlapping the general transcriptional shift of aging and do not capture downregulated genes.

skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq FASTQs from multiple organisms must be assessed for how much transcriptional signal falls outside current genome annotations, or when reproducing reported uTAR read fractions (e.g., hg38 2%, lemur 7.1%, mole rat 4.2%, sea urchin 10.7%).
skills.name: cross-species-benchmark-reproduction
skills.search_text: cross-species-benchmark-reproduction Use when scRNA-seq FASTQs from multiple organisms must be assessed for how much transcriptional signal falls outside current genome annotations, or when reproducing reported uTAR read fractions (e.g., hg38 2%, lemur 7.1%, mole rat 4.2%, sea urchin 10.7%). Reads are already aligned with cellranger count against a fixed annotation — use the from_cellranger workflow variant instead of from_fastqs, since the benchmark requires annotation-independent alignment. The goal is differential-expression or cell-clustering analysis on an existing expression matrix rather than quantifying reads outside gene annotations. Only a single organism is of interest and no cross-species comparison of annotation completeness is intended; the per-organism fraction aggregation and tolerance-band validation would be unnecessary overhead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Reproduces the TAR-scRNA-seq annotation-gap benchmark: quantifying the fraction of unique scRNA-seq reads that align outside gene annotations (assigned to uTARs) per organism, from raw FASTQs through groHMM TAR calling to a per-dataset fraction summary table. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-22496-3
skills.summary: Reproduces the TAR-scRNA-seq annotation-gap benchmark: quantifying the fraction of unique scRNA-seq reads that align outside gene annotations (assigned to uTARs) per organism, from raw FASTQs through groHMM TAR calling to a per-dataset fraction summary table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads are already aligned with cellranger count against a fixed annotation — use the from_cellranger workflow variant instead of from_fastqs, since the benchmark requires annotation-independent alignment. The goal is differential-expression or cell-clustering analysis on an existing expression matrix rather than quantifying reads outside gene annotations. Only a single organism is of interest and no cross-species comparison of annotation completeness is intended; the per-organism fraction aggregation and tolerance-band validation would be unnecessary overhead.

skills.description: Use when a query scRNA-seq dataset from one species must receive continuous cell fate (differentiation potential) annotations from a curated reference dataset in another species, requiring cross-batch and cross-species distribution alignment.
skills.name: cross-species-cell-fate-annotation-transfer
skills.search_text: cross-species-cell-fate-annotation-transfer Use when a query scRNA-seq dataset from one species must receive continuous cell fate (differentiation potential) annotations from a curated reference dataset in another species, requiring cross-batch and cross-species distribution alignment. Reference and query datasets are from the same species with only batch effects to correct — a standard within-species cell-type query suffices Datasets contain fewer than ~1000 cells, where Cell BLAST's over-parameterized neural network model may suffer under-training issues The goal is assigning discrete Cell Ontology terms via the ACA/BLAST2CO curation pipeline rather than continuous fate probabilities http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Transfers continuous cell fate annotations across species by training Cell BLAST's DIRECTi deep generative model on a reference dataset (e.g. mouse Tusi hematopoietic progenitors) with adversarial batch alignment-based online tuning, then querying an independent cross-species dataset (e.g. human Velten) via posterior-distribution cell-to-cell similarity. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-17281-7
skills.summary: Transfers continuous cell fate annotations across species by training Cell BLAST's DIRECTi deep generative model on a reference dataset (e.g. mouse Tusi hematopoietic progenitors) with adversarial batch alignment-based online tuning, then querying an independent cross-species dataset (e.g. human Velten) via posterior-distribution cell-to-cell similarity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reference and query datasets are from the same species with only batch effects to correct — a standard within-species cell-type query suffices Datasets contain fewer than ~1000 cells, where Cell BLAST's over-parameterized neural network model may suffer under-training issues The goal is assigning discrete Cell Ontology terms via the ACA/BLAST2CO curation pipeline rather than continuous fate probabilities

skills.description: Use when training labels exist only in one species (e.g., mouse Tabula Muris) and you must annotate scRNA-seq cells from another species (e.g., human pancreas) using a shared one-to-one orthologue gene space.
skills.name: cross-species-cell-type-annotation
skills.search_text: cross-species-cell-type-annotation Use when training labels exist only in one species (e.g., mouse Tabula Muris) and you must annotate scRNA-seq cells from another species (e.g., human pancreas) using a shared one-to-one orthologue gene space. Query cells are of types not represented in the reference — the null-dataset/conf_score machinery, not the plain Bet classifier, is needed to control false positives Data are not UMI counts or full-length read counts with the paper's normalization (TPM + log or size-factor 10,000 + add-one + log), since SciBet is technology-dependent on matched preprocessing http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Cross-species cell type annotation trains a SciBet multinomial classifier on annotated mouse scRNA-seq data (Tabula Muris) restricted to one-to-one human-mouse orthologues from HomoloGene Build 68, then predicts human cell types via maximum likelihood estimation. It demonstrates that a supervised classifier transfers across species when the gene space is orthologue-restricted. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-15523-2
skills.summary: Cross-species cell type annotation trains a SciBet multinomial classifier on annotated mouse scRNA-seq data (Tabula Muris) restricted to one-to-one human-mouse orthologues from HomoloGene Build 68, then predicts human cell types via maximum likelihood estimation. It demonstrates that a supervised classifier transfers across species when the gene space is orthologue-restricted.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Query cells are of types not represented in the reference — the null-dataset/conf_score machinery, not the plain Bet classifier, is needed to control false positives Data are not UMI counts or full-length read counts with the paper's normalization (TPM + log or size-factor 10,000 + add-one + log), since SciBet is technology-dependent on matched preprocessing

skills.description: Use when matching/aligning cell types between two species from scRNA-seq count data (e.g., human–mouse, human–marmoset, mouse–marmoset cortex), especially when homologous gene lists are incomplete and protein-sequence-based gene similarity is needed.
skills.name: cross-species-cell-type-matching
skills.search_text: cross-species-cell-type-matching Use when matching/aligning cell types between two species from scRNA-seq count data (e.g., human–mouse, human–marmoset, mouse–marmoset cortex), especially when homologous gene lists are incomplete and protein-sequence-based gene similarity is needed. The goal is single-cell (per-cell) species integration rather than cell-type-level matching — TACTiCS embeddings do not mix individual cells of the two species well; alignment is at the cell-type level Only a standard ortholog table (BLAST one-to-one matches) is desired as the gene-matching basis — the paper shows ProtBERT-based gene matching yields better cell type matches than BLAST within TACTiCS Datasets are small or heavily unbalanced — on equal-sized 50k subsets TACTiCS performance drops relative to the full datasets http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 TACTiCS matches cell types across species (human, mouse, marmoset primary motor cortex) by combining ProtBERT-based protein-sequence gene matching, neural-network cell-type classification within a species, and transfer-learning label propagation between species. It outperforms Seurat and SAMap on these datasets and avoids reliance on one-to-one ortholog tables such as BLAST. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad248
skills.summary: TACTiCS matches cell types across species (human, mouse, marmoset primary motor cortex) by combining ProtBERT-based protein-sequence gene matching, neural-network cell-type classification within a species, and transfer-learning label propagation between species. It outperforms Seurat and SAMap on these datasets and avoids reliance on one-to-one ortholog tables such as BLAST.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is single-cell (per-cell) species integration rather than cell-type-level matching — TACTiCS embeddings do not mix individual cells of the two species well; alignment is at the cell-type level Only a standard ortholog table (BLAST one-to-one matches) is desired as the gene-matching basis — the paper shows ProtBERT-based gene matching yields better cell type matches than BLAST within TACTiCS Datasets are small or heavily unbalanced — on equal-sized 50k subsets TACTiCS performance drops relative to the full datasets

skills.description: Use when you have predicted core promoter element records (position, score, TSS) for multiple species and want to test whether element positioning — e.g. TATA, dInr, PB relative to CAGE-annotated TSSs — is conserved across metazoans.
skills.name: cross-species-conservation-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-species-conservation-comparison Use when you have predicted core promoter element records (position, score, TSS) for multiple species and want to test whether element positioning — e.g. TATA, dInr, PB relative to CAGE-annotated TSSs — is conserved across metazoans. Input sequences have not yet been scanned with ElemeNT — run ElemeNT 2023 (web or command line) first to generate predicted element records before comparing species Goal is de novo motif discovery rather than comparing positions/scores of already-predicted core promoter elements across species Only one species is available — the skill's value is the cross-species comparison (worm to human), which requires multi-species CORE database records http://edamontology.org/topic_0749 http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 Reproduces the ElemeNT 2023 cross-species analysis (Supplementary Fig. S3) in which per-species position and score distributions of predicted core promoter elements from the 10-species CORE database are compared relative to EPDnew CAGE-annotated TSSs to assess evolutionary conservation of TATA, dInr and PB positioning. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae110
skills.summary: Reproduces the ElemeNT 2023 cross-species analysis (Supplementary Fig. S3) in which per-species position and score distributions of predicted core promoter elements from the 10-species CORE database are compared relative to EPDnew CAGE-annotated TSSs to assess evolutionary conservation of TATA, dInr and PB positioning.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences have not yet been scanned with ElemeNT — run ElemeNT 2023 (web or command line) first to generate predicted element records before comparing species Goal is de novo motif discovery rather than comparing positions/scores of already-predicted core promoter elements across species Only one species is available — the skill's value is the cross-species comparison (worm to human), which requires multi-species CORE database records

skills.description: Use when a tissue-specific RNA modification predictor (e.g., im6A-TS-CNN on 41-nt m6A segments) must be shown to generalize across species-tissue combinations before deployment or comparison.
skills.name: cross-species-cross-tissue-model-validation
skills.search_text: cross-species-cross-tissue-model-validation Use when a tissue-specific RNA modification predictor (e.g., im6A-TS-CNN on 41-nt m6A segments) must be shown to generalize across species-tissue combinations before deployment or comparison. The goal is comparison against another predictor rather than assessing cross-species/cross-tissue transfer — use the dedicated iRNA-m6A comparison workflow instead Input sequences are not 41-nt m6A benchmark segments from human, mouse, or rat brain/liver/kidney/heart/testis tissues Only a single species-tissue dataset is available, so no cross-species or cross-tissue transfer assessment is possible http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Validates that the im6A-TS-CNN m6A-site predictor trained on one species-tissue benchmark transfers effectively to other species (human, mouse, rat) and tissues (brain, liver, kidney, heart, testis), demonstrating method universality. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.omtn.2020.07.034
skills.summary: Validates that the im6A-TS-CNN m6A-site predictor trained on one species-tissue benchmark transfers effectively to other species (human, mouse, rat) and tissues (brain, liver, kidney, heart, testis), demonstrating method universality.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is comparison against another predictor rather than assessing cross-species/cross-tissue transfer — use the dedicated iRNA-m6A comparison workflow instead Input sequences are not 41-nt m6A benchmark segments from human, mouse, or rat brain/liver/kidney/heart/testis tissues Only a single species-tissue dataset is available, so no cross-species or cross-tissue transfer assessment is possible

skills.description: Use when trained cross-species cell embeddings exist and you need to judge cell-type-level alignment across species, e.g. homologous types (Vip, Sncg) mixing while species-specific types (Meis2, pericytes, SMC) stay separated.
skills.name: cross-species-embedding-integration-interpretation
skills.search_text: cross-species-embedding-integration-interpretation Use when trained cross-species cell embeddings exist and you need to judge cell-type-level alignment across species, e.g. homologous types (Vip, Sncg) mixing while species-specific types (Meis2, pericytes, SMC) stay separated. You need cell-type matches with confidence scores rather than qualitative visual alignment — use TACTiCS label transfer/evaluation instead of UMAP interpretation. The embeddings have not been trained yet: TACTiCS first requires protein-sequence-based gene matching (`embed_proteins`, `calc_dist`) and transfer learning before embeddings exist to visualize. Data are raw/unprocessed counts — use the preprocessed 50k subsets from Zenodo rather than integrating raw matrices directly. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 Visualize and interpret cross-species cell embeddings (e.g. TACTiCS-trained embeddings of human, mouse, and marmoset motor cortex scRNA-seq cells) in 2D with UMAP to assess whether homologous cell types align and species-specific types separate. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad248
skills.summary: Visualize and interpret cross-species cell embeddings (e.g. TACTiCS-trained embeddings of human, mouse, and marmoset motor cortex scRNA-seq cells) in 2D with UMAP to assess whether homologous cell types align and species-specific types separate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need cell-type matches with confidence scores rather than qualitative visual alignment — use TACTiCS label transfer/evaluation instead of UMAP interpretation. The embeddings have not been trained yet: TACTiCS first requires protein-sequence-based gene matching (`embed_proteins`, `calc_dist`) and transfer learning before embeddings exist to visualize. Data are raw/unprocessed counts — use the preprocessed 50k subsets from Zenodo rather than integrating raw matrices directly.

skills.description: Use when interpreting differential expression results from ExpressAnalyst across taxonomically diverse species lacking reference transcriptomes, where KO-based mapping could double-count homologous genes as separate DE ortholog groups.
skills.name: cross-species-expression-pattern-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-species-expression-pattern-comparison Use when interpreting differential expression results from ExpressAnalyst across taxonomically diverse species lacking reference transcriptomes, where KO-based mapping could double-count homologous genes as separate DE ortholog groups. The analysis is within a single species with a reference genome, so gene IDs are directly comparable and ortholog duplication cannot inflate DEG counts Input is functional enrichment (pathway) results rather than a per-ortholog DE table with per-species FDR values The comparison uses different tissues, treatments, or timepoints within one species rather than the same gene compared across species via ortholog mapping http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Quantifies how much of the significant differential expression count in a multi-species analysis is inflated by reads from the same gene mapping to similar but distinct ortholog IDs in different species. In the ExpressAnalyst salamander case study this duplication was rare (~3% of significant results), validating the KO/EcoOmicsDB ortholog-level quantification strategy. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-38785-y
skills.summary: Quantifies how much of the significant differential expression count in a multi-species analysis is inflated by reads from the same gene mapping to similar but distinct ortholog IDs in different species. In the ExpressAnalyst salamander case study this duplication was rare (~3% of significant results), validating the KO/EcoOmicsDB ortholog-level quantification strategy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis is within a single species with a reference genome, so gene IDs are directly comparable and ortholog duplication cannot inflate DEG counts Input is functional enrichment (pathway) results rather than a per-ortholog DE table with per-species FDR values The comparison uses different tissues, treatments, or timepoints within one species rather than the same gene compared across species via ortholog mapping

skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq gene identifiers come from a species (e.g., mouse) whose names must be mapped to homologs (e.g., human) before matching against a default L-R pair database such as dsCellNet's 5,744-pair list.
skills.name: cross-species-gene-homolog-mapping
skills.search_text: cross-species-gene-homolog-mapping Use when scRNA-seq gene identifiers come from a species (e.g., mouse) whose names must be mapped to homologs (e.g., human) before matching against a default L-R pair database such as dsCellNet's 5,744-pair list. When the expression matrix and the L-R pair database already share the same species namespace — mapping adds noise or drops genes with ambiguous one-to-many homologs. When the study needs interactions involving ligands or receptors absent from the default L-R gene list; the paper notes this size limitation can cause missing interactions (e.g., MG–Neurons) and recommends supplying supplementary L-R genes instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Maps ligand and receptor gene identifiers to a consistent species namespace using the homologene human/mouse homolog database so that dsCellNet can classify L-R pairs into membrane-ligand, secreted-ligand, and membrane-receptor classes before network inference. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.07.047
skills.summary: Maps ligand and receptor gene identifiers to a consistent species namespace using the homologene human/mouse homolog database so that dsCellNet can classify L-R pairs into membrane-ligand, secreted-ligand, and membrane-receptor classes before network inference.

skills.description: Use when training data and query data come from different species (e.g. mouse reference, human query) and cell type labels must be transferred across species via orthologous genes.
skills.name: cross-species-gene-ortholog-mapping
skills.search_text: cross-species-gene-ortholog-mapping Use when training data and query data come from different species (e.g. mouse reference, human query) and cell type labels must be transferred across species via orthologous genes. Training and query data are from the same species and share a gene namespace — direct gene-space intersection suffices without HomoloGene conversion Genes lack reliable one-to-one orthology (e.g. many-to-many paralogue families), since the method retains only one-to-one orthologue pairs http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0621 Restrict a single-cell classifier's feature space to one-to-one human-mouse orthologues via the NCBI HomoloGene Build 68 lookup table, so a model trained on mouse Tabula Muris data can be applied directly to human scRNA-seq queries (achieving ~92% correct mapping of human pancreas cells). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-15523-2
skills.summary: Restrict a single-cell classifier's feature space to one-to-one human-mouse orthologues via the NCBI HomoloGene Build 68 lookup table, so a model trained on mouse Tabula Muris data can be applied directly to human scRNA-seq queries (achieving ~92% correct mapping of human pancreas cells).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Training and query data are from the same species and share a gene namespace — direct gene-space intersection suffices without HomoloGene conversion Genes lack reliable one-to-one orthology (e.g. many-to-many paralogue families), since the method retains only one-to-one orthologue pairs

skills.description: Use when bulk RNA-seq samples from one species (e.g., rat micro-dissected renal tubule segments, GSE56743) must be deconvolved with a single-cell reference from another species (e.g., mouse kidney scRNA-seq, GSE107585), which first requires homologous-gene mapping.
skills.name: cross-species-gene-orthology-mapping
skills.search_text: cross-species-gene-orthology-mapping Use when bulk RNA-seq samples from one species (e.g., rat micro-dissected renal tubule segments, GSE56743) must be deconvolved with a single-cell reference from another species (e.g., mouse kidney scRNA-seq, GSE107585), which first requires homologous-gene mapping. Bulk and single-cell reference are from the same species with matching gene identifiers — no orthology mapping is needed, proceed directly to MuSiC Input expression values are TPM or other normalized units — cell type proportions cannot be estimated with TPM as the input; RPKM is only usable if cell type-specific total RNA abundance estimates are provided Ortholog coverage is too sparse or no one-to-one orthologs exist, leaving too small a shared gene set to support reliable W-NNLS estimation http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Enables MuSiC deconvolution of bulk RNA-seq from one species against a scRNA-seq reference from another by mapping genes to one-to-one orthologs and intersecting both datasets on the shared homologous gene set while preserving raw read counts. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-08023-x
skills.summary: Enables MuSiC deconvolution of bulk RNA-seq from one species against a scRNA-seq reference from another by mapping genes to one-to-one orthologs and intersecting both datasets on the shared homologous gene set while preserving raw read counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Bulk and single-cell reference are from the same species with matching gene identifiers — no orthology mapping is needed, proceed directly to MuSiC Input expression values are TPM or other normalized units — cell type proportions cannot be estimated with TPM as the input; RPKM is only usable if cell type-specific total RNA abundance estimates are provided Ortholog coverage is too sparse or no one-to-one orthologs exist, leaving too small a shared gene set to support reliable W-NNLS estimation

skills.description: Use when building training data for RNA modification site prediction from RMBase v2.0 BED/GTF annotations across multiple species, requiring genome-coordinate extraction of flanking sequence windows.
