skills.description: Use when you have per-tissue ASE SNP call sets (e.g. VADT sig_meta_analysis_variants.txt files) mapped to gene IDs and need to test whether the same genes show ASE across multiple tissues and what pathways they share.
skills.name: cross-tissue-gene-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-tissue-gene-overlap-analysis Use when you have per-tissue ASE SNP call sets (e.g. VADT sig_meta_analysis_variants.txt files) mapped to gene IDs and need to test whether the same genes show ASE across multiple tissues and what pathways they share. Input is still at the ASE SNP level — SNP overlap across tissues was only 3.7% in this study; aggregation to the gene level is required before comparing tissues The variant call sets are not filtered by VADT criteria (quality score >= 20, SNP read count threshold of 20, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR cutoff 0.05), so the informative-SNP denominators for ASE scores are invalid http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Compares ASE gene sets (genes containing ASE SNPs) across three broiler chicken tissues (breast muscle, abdominal fat, liver) to quantify conserved cis-regulatory overlap, then characterizes the shared gene set via protein-protein interaction and KEGG pathway enrichment in STRING. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-83459-8
skills.summary: Compares ASE gene sets (genes containing ASE SNPs) across three broiler chicken tissues (breast muscle, abdominal fat, liver) to quantify conserved cis-regulatory overlap, then characterizes the shared gene set via protein-protein interaction and KEGG pathway enrichment in STRING.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still at the ASE SNP level — SNP overlap across tissues was only 3.7% in this study; aggregation to the gene level is required before comparing tissues The variant call sets are not filtered by VADT criteria (quality score >= 20, SNP read count threshold of 20, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR cutoff 0.05), so the informative-SNP denominators for ASE scores are invalid

skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq profiles lack miRNA measurements (poly(A) capture precludes mature miRNAs) and paired bulk mRNA-miRNA training cohorts exist for the tissue(s) of interest, so miRNA expression can be predicted from mRNA profiles.
skills.name: cross-tissue-mirna-activity-inference
skills.search_text: cross-tissue-mirna-activity-inference Use when scRNA-seq profiles lack miRNA measurements (poly(A) capture precludes mature miRNAs) and paired bulk mRNA-miRNA training cohorts exist for the tissue(s) of interest, so miRNA expression can be predicted from mRNA profiles. The goal is to infer miRNA activity from putative targets alone without a large cohort of paired miRNA-mRNA training data — miRSCAPE explicitly requires such training, unlike target-set enrichment approaches (e.g., miReact-style) The training tissue/context differs substantially from the application context — a substantive performance loss is expected (quantified in Figure S9) A pre-trained model is being applied to scRNA-seq with high dropout where most model genes are undetected — retraining on only reasonably detected genes may be required instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 Train miRSCAPE XGBoost regression models on paired bulk mRNA-miRNA cohorts (e.g., TCGA brain and kidney) and apply them to pooled scRNA-seq pseudo-bulk profiles to infer cell type-specific miRNA expression, validated by correlating predicted vs observed inter-cell-type fold-differences. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2022.104962
skills.summary: Train miRSCAPE XGBoost regression models on paired bulk mRNA-miRNA cohorts (e.g., TCGA brain and kidney) and apply them to pooled scRNA-seq pseudo-bulk profiles to infer cell type-specific miRNA expression, validated by correlating predicted vs observed inter-cell-type fold-differences.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to infer miRNA activity from putative targets alone without a large cohort of paired miRNA-mRNA training data — miRSCAPE explicitly requires such training, unlike target-set enrichment approaches (e.g., miReact-style) The training tissue/context differs substantially from the application context — a substantive performance loss is expected (quantified in Figure S9) A pre-trained model is being applied to scRNA-seq with high dropout where most model genes are undetected — retraining on only reasonably detected genes may be required instead

skills.description: Use when you need to chart miRNA activity across many cell types in a scRNA-seq atlas using a model trained on diverse bulk paired miRNA-mRNA cohorts, rather than tissue-matched training.
skills.name: cross-tissue-model-transfer-to-single-cell-data
skills.search_text: cross-tissue-model-transfer-to-single-cell-data Use when you need to chart miRNA activity across many cell types in a scRNA-seq atlas using a model trained on diverse bulk paired miRNA-mRNA cohorts, rather than tissue-matched training. When the application sample's cellular/tissue context matches a specific training cohort — a context-matched (non-global) model is expected to be more accurate When the scRNA-seq data has very high dropout such that a pre-trained model fails — miRSCAPE should instead be retrained using only genes detected at a reasonable level When the goal is inferring miRNA activity from putative target expression alone (e.g., target-set enrichment approaches) rather than a trained paired miRNA-mRNA model http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Train a single global miRSCAPE XGBoost model on a multi-tissue compendium of paired bulk miRNA-mRNA profiles (~10,000 TCGA/GTEx/CCLE samples across 10 tissues) and transfer it to bootstrapped, cell-type-pooled scRNA-seq profiles (e.g., the 56 cell types of the Human Cell Landscape) to predict 523 miRNA activities per cell type. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2022.104962
skills.summary: Train a single global miRSCAPE XGBoost model on a multi-tissue compendium of paired bulk miRNA-mRNA profiles (~10,000 TCGA/GTEx/CCLE samples across 10 tissues) and transfer it to bootstrapped, cell-type-pooled scRNA-seq profiles (e.g., the 56 cell types of the Human Cell Landscape) to predict 523 miRNA activities per cell type.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the application sample's cellular/tissue context matches a specific training cohort — a context-matched (non-global) model is expected to be more accurate When the scRNA-seq data has very high dropout such that a pre-trained model fails — miRSCAPE should instead be retrained using only genes detected at a reasonable level When the goal is inferring miRNA activity from putative target expression alone (e.g., target-set enrichment approaches) rather than a trained paired miRNA-mRNA model

skills.description: Use when cell types in training and test single-cell multi-omic data are not perfectly aligned and you need to test whether a trained protein-imputation model generalizes across tissues or across CITE-seq/REAP-seq protocols.
skills.name: cross-tissue-protein-imputation-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-tissue-protein-imputation-benchmarking Use when cell types in training and test single-cell multi-omic data are not perfectly aligned and you need to test whether a trained protein-imputation model generalizes across tissues or across CITE-seq/REAP-seq protocols. Input expression data is not UMI-based counts (e.g., TPM or RPKM) — the article states prediction accuracy for such metrics is unknown and cTP-net 'can only apply to count-based expression input (UMI-based)' Cells are outside the hematopoietic lineage — cross-tissue/protocol generalization was only benchmarked on immune (PBMC/CBMC/BMMC) cells, so results there are unsupported Training and test data are from the same population and same protocol — a same-tissue model comparison, not a generalization benchmark, is what is being run http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 Benchmark cTP-net's ability to impute surface protein abundances when the test tissue (e.g., CITE-PBMC vs CITE-CBMC) or protocol (CITE-seq vs REAP-seq) differs from the training data, comparing per-protein Pearson correlations of imputed values against denoised RNA baselines. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-14391-0
skills.summary: Benchmark cTP-net's ability to impute surface protein abundances when the test tissue (e.g., CITE-PBMC vs CITE-CBMC) or protocol (CITE-seq vs REAP-seq) differs from the training data, comparing per-protein Pearson correlations of imputed values against denoised RNA baselines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input expression data is not UMI-based counts (e.g., TPM or RPKM) — the article states prediction accuracy for such metrics is unknown and cTP-net 'can only apply to count-based expression input (UMI-based)' Cells are outside the hematopoietic lineage — cross-tissue/protocol generalization was only benchmarked on immune (PBMC/CBMC/BMMC) cells, so results there are unsupported Training and test data are from the same population and same protocol — a same-tissue model comparison, not a generalization benchmark, is what is being run

skills.description: Use when you have a multi-tissue single-cell atlas (e.g. blood, bone marrow, lymph node, lung) with a shared cell-type annotation and want to find pathway-level features unique to one tissue site rather than testing tissue pairs in isolation.
skills.name: cross-tissue-qval-variance-ranking
skills.search_text: cross-tissue-qval-variance-ranking Use when you have a multi-tissue single-cell atlas (e.g. blood, bone marrow, lymph node, lung) with a shared cell-type annotation and want to find pathway-level features unique to one tissue site rather than testing tissue pairs in isolation. Your dataset contains only one tissue site, so variance across tissue-vs-blood comparisons is undefined — use a two-population compare_pathways analysis instead. You need per-gene differential expression rather than pathway-level distribution changes; use DE tools rather than qval ranking. Your object is not a Seurat/SCE single-cell object with metadata you can split by tissue (e.g. it is already an aggregated feature table) — seurat_extract cannot subset it. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 A systematic SCPA-based workflow that ranks pathway perturbations (qvals) by their variance across many tissue-vs-blood comparisons to expose tissue-specific pathway features, e.g. alpha-defensin expression in bone-marrow T cells. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.celrep.2022.111697
skills.summary: A systematic SCPA-based workflow that ranks pathway perturbations (qvals) by their variance across many tissue-vs-blood comparisons to expose tissue-specific pathway features, e.g. alpha-defensin expression in bone-marrow T cells.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your dataset contains only one tissue site, so variance across tissue-vs-blood comparisons is undefined — use a two-population compare_pathways analysis instead. You need per-gene differential expression rather than pathway-level distribution changes; use DE tools rather than qval ranking. Your object is not a Seurat/SCE single-cell object with metadata you can split by tissue (e.g. it is already an aggregated feature table) — seurat_extract cannot subset it.

skills.description: Use when you have per-tissue significant sQTL results (e.g. GTEx sqtls-*fdr.nominal.tsv tables) and need to quantify, cluster, or visualize cross-tissue sQTL sharing, especially to test whether brain tissues share sQTLs differently from non-brain tissues.
skills.name: cross-tissue-sqtl-effect-size-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-tissue-sqtl-effect-size-correlation-analysis Use when you have per-tissue significant sQTL results (e.g. GTEx sqtls-*fdr.nominal.tsv tables) and need to quantify, cluster, or visualize cross-tissue sQTL sharing, especially to test whether brain tissues share sQTLs differently from non-brain tissues. You only have eQTL (expression) results rather than splicing QTL results with MD effect sizes — this skill's correlations are defined over splicing effect sizes You need causal colocalization between paired sQTL/eQTL effects — the paper notes same-variant vs LD-different-variant cases cannot be distinguished here Your sQTL tables have not been filtered to a common significance level in both tissues of each pair (default FDR 0.05), since correlations over non-shared pairs are not comparable http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Quantifies splicing QTL sharing across GTEx tissues by correlating MD (maximum difference) effect sizes of variant-gene pairs significant in both tissues of each pair, then applies hierarchical clustering to the tissue-by-tissue correlation matrix. It reproduces the paper's finding that brain subregions form a distinct sQTL sharing cluster (Fig. 2d). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-20578-2
skills.summary: Quantifies splicing QTL sharing across GTEx tissues by correlating MD (maximum difference) effect sizes of variant-gene pairs significant in both tissues of each pair, then applies hierarchical clustering to the tissue-by-tissue correlation matrix. It reproduces the paper's finding that brain subregions form a distinct sQTL sharing cluster (Fig. 2d).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have eQTL (expression) results rather than splicing QTL results with MD effect sizes — this skill's correlations are defined over splicing effect sizes You need causal colocalization between paired sQTL/eQTL effects — the paper notes same-variant vs LD-different-variant cases cannot be distinguished here Your sQTL tables have not been filtered to a common significance level in both tissues of each pair (default FDR 0.05), since correlations over non-shared pairs are not comparable

skills.description: Use when a 10x scRNA-seq sample has been analyzed for pathogen reads by more than one alignment strategy and you need to verify that EGFP+/pathogen+ cell calls and per-cell UMI counts are consistent across methods.
skills.name: cross-tool-alignment-consistency-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-alignment-consistency-comparison Use when a 10x scRNA-seq sample has been analyzed for pathogen reads by more than one alignment strategy and you need to verify that EGFP+/pathogen+ cell calls and per-cell UMI counts are consistent across methods. Input is a single-method analysis with no alternative alignment strategy available — no cross-method comparison can be computed Data are not 10x single-cell outputs (e.g. bulk RNA-seq or non-UMI data), since CellRanger barcodes/UMIs and pathogen_al_counts.csv per-cell counts are the comparison units The goal is absolute quantification benchmarking against other packages (ViralTrack, Venus, PathogenTrack) rather than internal consistency of CellRanger vs. scPathoQuant aligners http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Validates pathogen detection robustness in 10x scRNA-seq by running the same sample through multiple alignment strategies (CellRanger with an integrated pathogen genome vs. scPathoQuant with bbmap vs. scPathoQuant with bowtie2) and quantifying agreement in per-cell pathogen-positive calls and UMI counts. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae145
skills.summary: Validates pathogen detection robustness in 10x scRNA-seq by running the same sample through multiple alignment strategies (CellRanger with an integrated pathogen genome vs. scPathoQuant with bbmap vs. scPathoQuant with bowtie2) and quantifying agreement in per-cell pathogen-positive calls and UMI counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single-method analysis with no alternative alignment strategy available — no cross-method comparison can be computed Data are not 10x single-cell outputs (e.g. bulk RNA-seq or non-UMI data), since CellRanger barcodes/UMIs and pathogen_al_counts.csv per-cell counts are the comparison units The goal is absolute quantification benchmarking against other packages (ViralTrack, Venus, PathogenTrack) rather than internal consistency of CellRanger vs. scPathoQuant aligners

skills.description: Use when you have 3' UTR predictions from multiple annotation tools plus a trusted canonical annotation (e.g. WormBase chrI GFF) and need to quantify which tool agrees with the reference.
skills.name: cross-tool-annotation-agreement-quantification
skills.search_text: cross-tool-annotation-agreement-quantification Use when you have 3' UTR predictions from multiple annotation tools plus a trusted canonical annotation (e.g. WormBase chrI GFF) and need to quantify which tool agrees with the reference. There is no trusted canonical annotation to compare against, so agreement fractions cannot be computed Only one tool's predictions are available, making cross-tool agreement and shared-UTR counting impossible http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark a 3' UTR annotation tool (peaks2utr) against competing tools (GETUTR, UTRme) by comparing each tool's predicted UTRs to a canonical reference annotation within a fixed end-position tolerance, and quantify per-tool agreement fractions and shared predictions. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad112
skills.summary: Benchmark a 3' UTR annotation tool (peaks2utr) against competing tools (GETUTR, UTRme) by comparing each tool's predicted UTRs to a canonical reference annotation within a fixed end-position tolerance, and quantify per-tool agreement fractions and shared predictions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: There is no trusted canonical annotation to compare against, so agreement fractions cannot be computed Only one tool's predictions are available, making cross-tool agreement and shared-UTR counting impossible

skills.description: Use when you need to compare annotation pipelines head-to-head on million-cell datasets (>1 million cells) and quantify accuracy together with resource metrics (training time, peak memory, GPU requirement) to derive cost-efficiency conclusions.
skills.name: cross-tool-annotation-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-tool-annotation-benchmarking Use when you need to compare annotation pipelines head-to-head on million-cell datasets (>1 million cells) and quantify accuracy together with resource metrics (training time, peak memory, GPU requirement) to derive cost-efficiency conclusions. Your goal is only to annotate one dataset accurately — use a single pipeline rather than a full cross-tool benchmark with resource profiling. Datasets are small enough to fit in memory on a workstation; the backed-mode/batch-wise resource comparison is designed for datasets over 1 million cells. You need to compare biomarker/feature rankings across tools — feature importances cannot be extracted from several comparison tools (scBalance, scvi, devCellPy, CellPLM), limiting comparability. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark cell-type annotation tools (scaLR vs scvi-tools and CellTypist) on the same large scRNA-seq datasets, comparing classification accuracy, runtime, memory consumption, and derived analysis cost on equivalent hardware. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbaf243
skills.summary: Benchmark cell-type annotation tools (scaLR vs scvi-tools and CellTypist) on the same large scRNA-seq datasets, comparing classification accuracy, runtime, memory consumption, and derived analysis cost on equivalent hardware.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is only to annotate one dataset accurately — use a single pipeline rather than a full cross-tool benchmark with resource profiling. Datasets are small enough to fit in memory on a workstation; the backed-mode/batch-wise resource comparison is designed for datasets over 1 million cells. You need to compare biomarker/feature rankings across tools — feature importances cannot be extracted from several comparison tools (scBalance, scvi, devCellPy, CellPLM), limiting comparability.

skills.description: Use when you have barcode count tables produced by two or more pre-processing tools on the same FASTQ dataset and need to benchmark their detection concordance, quantify three-tool overlaps, and compare runtime/memory.
skills.name: cross-tool-barcode-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-tool-barcode-overlap-analysis Use when you have barcode count tables produced by two or more pre-processing tools on the same FASTQ dataset and need to benchmark their detection concordance, quantify three-tool overlaps, and compare runtime/memory. Your dataset has a gold-standard truth set with known barcode abundances — direct accuracy benchmarking on simulated or spike-in data is preferable (the article notes such simulation benchmarking was not performed and would give further insight into accuracy and optimal parameter selection) The tools being compared operate on different inputs or parameter spaces that cannot be harmonized — the article notes differing parameter flexibility between tools made benchmarking difficult Evolving (editing-prone) barcode methods are the target — the article states these are not officially supported http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Quantify agreement between barcode pre-processing tools (BARtab, pycashier, Rewind/TimeMachine) by combining their per-sample barcode count tables and computing set overlaps and count correlations with bartools in R, as done for the 22-sample Goyal population-level barcoding dataset. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2024.100763
skills.summary: Quantify agreement between barcode pre-processing tools (BARtab, pycashier, Rewind/TimeMachine) by combining their per-sample barcode count tables and computing set overlaps and count correlations with bartools in R, as done for the 22-sample Goyal population-level barcoding dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your dataset has a gold-standard truth set with known barcode abundances — direct accuracy benchmarking on simulated or spike-in data is preferable (the article notes such simulation benchmarking was not performed and would give further insight into accuracy and optimal parameter selection) The tools being compared operate on different inputs or parameter spaces that cannot be harmonized — the article notes differing parameter flexibility between tools made benchmarking difficult Evolving (editing-prone) barcode methods are the target — the article states these are not officially supported

skills.description: Use when selecting among gene-name/date correction tools: you need an apples-to-apples capability matrix covering multi-file processing, dd/mm/yy vs mixed date formats, and HGNC name updating.
skills.name: cross-tool-capability-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-tool-capability-benchmarking Use when selecting among gene-name/date correction tools: you need an apples-to-apples capability matrix covering multi-file processing, dd/mm/yy vs mixed date formats, and HGNC name updating. skills.summary: Benchmarking method for comparing gene-name/date correction tools (e.g., Gene Updater, Oct4th, Truke) on an identical corpus of Excel-corrupted .csv/.xlsx files, scoring multi-file support, mixed date-format handling, and conversion to updated HGNC names.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input gene lists contain no Excel date auto-conversions or outdated aliases, so tool selection is moot — any tool would be a no-op pass-through. You only need to run Gene Updater itself to correct files, not to choose among competing tools — use the correction workflow directly instead of benchmarking.

skills.description: Use when validating a new pathogen-detection tool for 10x scRNAseq against established tools by measuring concordance of infected-cell calls and correlating per-cell pathogen read/UMI counts.
skills.name: cross-tool-cell-call-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-tool-cell-call-overlap-analysis Use when validating a new pathogen-detection tool for 10x scRNAseq against established tools by measuring concordance of infected-cell calls and correlating per-cell pathogen read/UMI counts. Input scRNAseq data has not yet been processed by cellranger count, so no unaligned reads or 10x output folders exist for pathogen mapping. The goal is detection of a pathogen with a complicated fasta header and no gtf, without simplifying the header — total read quantification relies on the fasta header name. Comparing against tools not benchmarked here or data types outside 10x single-cell output, where the four-tool overlap design does not apply. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0781 Benchmark scPathoQuant (SPQ) HIV-infected cell calls against ViralTrack, PathogenTrack, and Venus by building a four-tool overlap table of per-cell HIV+ calls and computing HIV read-abundance correlations between SPQ and each comparator tool. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae145
skills.summary: Benchmark scPathoQuant (SPQ) HIV-infected cell calls against ViralTrack, PathogenTrack, and Venus by building a four-tool overlap table of per-cell HIV+ calls and computing HIV read-abundance correlations between SPQ and each comparator tool.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input scRNAseq data has not yet been processed by cellranger count, so no unaligned reads or 10x output folders exist for pathogen mapping. The goal is detection of a pathogen with a complicated fasta header and no gtf, without simplifying the header — total read quantification relies on the fasta header name. Comparing against tools not benchmarked here or data types outside 10x single-cell output, where the four-tool overlap design does not apply.

skills.description: Use when comparing alternative circRNA quantification tools on the same ribo− RNA-seq data to decide whether a CIRCscore-style normalized ratio is more accurate than CLR-style back-splice counting, e.g. for loci with RT-qPCR validation values.
skills.name: cross-tool-circrna-quantification-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-circrna-quantification-comparison Use when comparing alternative circRNA quantification tools on the same ribo− RNA-seq data to decide whether a CIRCscore-style normalized ratio is more accurate than CLR-style back-splice counting, e.g. for loci with RT-qPCR validation values. Input is poly(A)−/ribo− or RNase R-treated RNA-seq: linear RNAs are largely depleted, so FPBlinear/CIRCscore evaluation is unsuitable per the article's limitation. Goal is de novo circRNA discovery/annotation rather than comparing quantification accuracy between CLEAR and DCC/circtools. Only one quantification tool's output is available; a cross-tool comparison requires both CIRCexplorer2/CLEAR and DCC results on the same mapped BAM. http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 Benchmark circRNA quantification accuracy across CLEAR (CIRCscore from FPBcirc/FPBlinear) and circtools/DCC (CLR from DCC-called BSJ fragment counts) on ribo− RNA-seq, validating CIRCscore against RT-qPCR for loci such as circCAMSAP1-1. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2019.11.004
skills.summary: Benchmark circRNA quantification accuracy across CLEAR (CIRCscore from FPBcirc/FPBlinear) and circtools/DCC (CLR from DCC-called BSJ fragment counts) on ribo− RNA-seq, validating CIRCscore against RT-qPCR for loci such as circCAMSAP1-1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is poly(A)−/ribo− or RNase R-treated RNA-seq: linear RNAs are largely depleted, so FPBlinear/CIRCscore evaluation is unsuitable per the article's limitation. Goal is de novo circRNA discovery/annotation rather than comparing quantification accuracy between CLEAR and DCC/circtools. Only one quantification tool's output is available; a cross-tool comparison requires both CIRCexplorer2/CLEAR and DCC results on the same mapped BAM.

skills.description: Use when evaluating a malignant cell annotation method against published baselines on shared gold/silver standard scRNA-seq datasets, or when benchmarking inference runtime and memory scaling with dataset size.

skills.search_text: cross-tool-comparison-evaluation Use when evaluating a malignant cell annotation method against published baselines on shared gold/silver standard scRNA-seq datasets, or when benchmarking inference runtime and memory scaling with dataset size. skills.summary: Benchmark protocol comparing Cancer-Finder against SCEVAN, CopyKAT, CaSee, and ikarus on gold/silver standard scRNA-seq datasets for malignant cell annotation accuracy and on subsampled cell counts (100 to 1,000,000 cells) for inference speed and memory, reproducing the Fig. 3 accuracy and runtime comparisons.

skills.description: Use when comparing multiple driver-gene prediction tools' gene lists against known driver sets (e.g. CGC 616 genes, NCG 711 genes, PMH 501 genes) over matched datasets, and recall-weighted performance must be quantified and ranked.
skills.name: cross-tool-driver-prediction-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-driver-prediction-comparison Use when comparing multiple driver-gene prediction tools' gene lists against known driver sets (e.g. CGC 616 genes, NCG 711 genes, PMH 501 genes) over matched datasets, and recall-weighted performance must be quantified and ranked. When the goal is to discover driver genes de novo rather than to score and rank already-produced prediction lists against a benchmark When precision should be weighted more heavily than recall — the beta^2 = 0.2 setting deliberately weights recall five times more; use balanced F1 or another beta if the goal does not prioritize recall When no trusted curated gene set (CGC/NCG/PMH-like) is available to serve as ground truth for TP/FP/FN counting Benchmark driver-gene prediction tool outputs against curated gene sets (CGC, NCG, PMH) by computing precision, recall and the recall-weighted F0.2-measure per cancer type, then ranking all tools by F0.2 score. This reproduces the WMDS.net evaluation scheme, which weights recall far more heavily than precision. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad071
skills.summary: Benchmark driver-gene prediction tool outputs against curated gene sets (CGC, NCG, PMH) by computing precision, recall and the recall-weighted F0.2-measure per cancer type, then ranking all tools by F0.2 score. This reproduces the WMDS.net evaluation scheme, which weights recall far more heavily than precision.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to discover driver genes de novo rather than to score and rank already-produced prediction lists against a benchmark When precision should be weighted more heavily than recall — the beta^2 = 0.2 setting deliberately weights recall five times more; use balanced F1 or another beta if the goal does not prioritize recall When no trusted curated gene set (CGC/NCG/PMH-like) is available to serve as ground truth for TP/FP/FN counting

skills.description: Use when comparing computational efficiency (CPU time and wall-clock time) of multiple pathogen-quantification pipelines for scRNAseq data, and a measured ranking must be reproduced on an identical input sample.
skills.name: cross-tool-execution-time-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-execution-time-comparison Use when comparing computational efficiency (CPU time and wall-clock time) of multiple pathogen-quantification pipelines for scRNAseq data, and a measured ranking must be reproduced on an identical input sample. The goal is accuracy or sensitivity comparison of pathogen read detection rather than runtime cost The tools cannot be run on the same input sample with identical thread allocation, so measured runtimes would not be comparable Input is a single tool's run and no cross-tool benchmark is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Benchmark the CPU-time cost of scPathoQuant's quantification step against ViralTrack, PathogenTrack, and Venus by wrapping each tool in the Linux `time` command on the same 10x scRNAseq sample and ranking fastest-to-slowest. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae145
skills.summary: Benchmark the CPU-time cost of scPathoQuant's quantification step against ViralTrack, PathogenTrack, and Venus by wrapping each tool in the Linux `time` command on the same 10x scRNAseq sample and ranking fastest-to-slowest.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is accuracy or sensitivity comparison of pathogen read detection rather than runtime cost The tools cannot be run on the same input sample with identical thread allocation, so measured runtimes would not be comparable Input is a single tool's run and no cross-tool benchmark is needed

skills.description: Use when several cell-cell communication scoring methods (e.g., CellChat, CellPhoneDB, NATMI, SingleCellSignalR, rank-based cell2cell scores) have been applied to the same multi-sample dataset and you need to assess whether Tensor-cell2cell decompositions agree across tools.
skills.name: cross-tool-factor-similarity-correlation-index
skills.search_text: cross-tool-factor-similarity-correlation-index Use when several cell-cell communication scoring methods (e.g., CellChat, CellPhoneDB, NATMI, SingleCellSignalR, rank-based cell2cell scores) have been applied to the same multi-sample dataset and you need to assess whether Tensor-cell2cell decompositions agree across tools. You have only one communication scoring method or a single context/sample — there are no multiple factorizations to cross-compare Tensors contain many LR pairs or cell types missing in some contexts, since the algorithm is not optimized for missing values and shared-members filtering is required The goal is tool accuracy benchmarking against ground truth rather than cross-tool consistency — the article notes benchmarking CCC prediction tools is challenging due to the lack of a ground truth http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Quantify whether tensor decompositions of cell-cell communication are consistent across different LR-scoring tools by computing pairwise 1-CorrIndex similarities between the factorizations of multiple 4D communication tensors. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-31369-2
skills.summary: Quantify whether tensor decompositions of cell-cell communication are consistent across different LR-scoring tools by computing pairwise 1-CorrIndex similarities between the factorizations of multiple 4D communication tensors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have only one communication scoring method or a single context/sample — there are no multiple factorizations to cross-compare Tensors contain many LR pairs or cell types missing in some contexts, since the algorithm is not optimized for missing values and shared-members filtering is required The goal is tool accuracy benchmarking against ground truth rather than cross-tool consistency — the article notes benchmarking CCC prediction tools is challenging due to the lack of a ground truth

skills.description: Use when a single-locus long-read splicing assay (e.g. a minigene) has been aligned once and you need to compare how two isoform callers (VIsoQLR vs StringTie2) disagree on isoform counts, abundances, and isoform lengths.
skills.name: cross-tool-isoform-abundance-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-isoform-abundance-comparison Use when a single-locus long-read splicing assay (e.g. a minigene) has been aligned once and you need to compare how two isoform callers (VIsoQLR vs StringTie2) disagree on isoform counts, abundances, and isoform lengths. The goal is whole-transcriptome discovery across many samples — VIsoQLR is tailored to low-throughput, one-gene-at-a-time splicing assays, not genome-scale transcriptome profiling The BAM alignment has not yet been produced — first build the GMAP reference index and align the FASTQ reads (workflow step, not a comparison step) A known reference annotation should guide quantification — VIsoQLR is designed to work without prior knowledge of splice sites, so an annotation-guided workflow is a different skill http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3320 Side-by-side comparison of isoform detection and abundance rankings produced by VIsoQLR and StringTie2 on the same long-read BAM alignment (e.g. the PAX6 minigene splicing assay), to quantify tool-specific differences in isoform counts, abundances, and lengths. transcriptomics/v2 10.1007/s00439-023-02539-z
skills.summary: Side-by-side comparison of isoform detection and abundance rankings produced by VIsoQLR and StringTie2 on the same long-read BAM alignment (e.g. the PAX6 minigene splicing assay), to quantify tool-specific differences in isoform counts, abundances, and lengths.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is whole-transcriptome discovery across many samples — VIsoQLR is tailored to low-throughput, one-gene-at-a-time splicing assays, not genome-scale transcriptome profiling The BAM alignment has not yet been produced — first build the GMAP reference index and align the FASTQ reads (workflow step, not a comparison step) A known reference annotation should guide quantification — VIsoQLR is designed to work without prior knowledge of splice sites, so an annotation-guided workflow is a different skill

skills.search_text: cross-tool-performance-comparison Use when comparing the runtime and RAM footprint of ORIGINS, LandSCENT, and CytoTRACE on the same GEO scRNA-seq count matrices to reproduce or extend the paper's Table 1 performance benchmark. skills.summary: Benchmark the computational efficiency (elapsed runtime) and extra RAM usage of ORIGINS activity scoring against LandSCENT (SR) and CytoTRACE across the four healthy human scRNA-seq datasets (breast, colon, hematopoietic, lung), reproducing the Table 1 runtime/memory comparison that motivated ORIGINS as a lightweight pluripotency tool.

skills.description: Use when you hold a labeled RNA transcript FASTA test set (e.g., H-Test mRNAs vs lncRNAs) and need to verify or replicate reported accuracy differences across multiple lncRNA-coding-potential predictors rather than run just one tool.
skills.name: cross-tool-prediction-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-prediction-comparison Use when you hold a labeled RNA transcript FASTA test set (e.g., H-Test mRNAs vs lncRNAs) and need to verify or replicate reported accuracy differences across multiple lncRNA-coding-potential predictors rather than run just one tool. Your goal is to discover novel lncRNAs from RNA-Seq samples (e.g., the 180 TARGET osteosarcoma samples) rather than to compare classifiers on a labeled benchmark set. The input sequences are genomic contigs or proteins rather than transcript FASTA sequences — LncDC and the six competitors are trained on RNA transcripts. Transcripts lack known mRNA/lncRNA labels, so classification accuracy against ground truth cannot be computed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 Reproduces a head-to-head accuracy benchmark of a new lncRNA identification tool (LncDC) against six state-of-the-art classifiers — CPAT, PLEK, CPC2, CPPred, LncFinder, and COME — on a common labeled human transcript test set (H-Test). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-022-22082-7
skills.summary: Reproduces a head-to-head accuracy benchmark of a new lncRNA identification tool (LncDC) against six state-of-the-art classifiers — CPAT, PLEK, CPC2, CPPred, LncFinder, and COME — on a common labeled human transcript test set (H-Test).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is to discover novel lncRNAs from RNA-Seq samples (e.g., the 180 TARGET osteosarcoma samples) rather than to compare classifiers on a labeled benchmark set. The input sequences are genomic contigs or proteins rather than transcript FASTA sequences — LncDC and the six competitors are trained on RNA transcripts. Transcripts lack known mRNA/lncRNA labels, so classification accuracy against ground truth cannot be computed.

skills.description: Use when a task requires benchmarking phasiRNA prediction tools by comparing the number and overlap of predicted 21-PHAS genes from multiple tools on the same small RNA-seq dataset with a shared reference sequence.
skills.name: cross-tool-prediction-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-tool-prediction-overlap-analysis Use when a task requires benchmarking phasiRNA prediction tools by comparing the number and overlap of predicted 21-PHAS genes from multiple tools on the same small RNA-seq dataset with a shared reference sequence. The goal is to benchmark tools on the genome reference rather than the transcriptome — this skill's workflow fixes the transcriptome as the reference sequence. The dataset is not a plant small RNA-seq library or the tools under comparison do not predict 21-PHAS loci (e.g., comparing 24-nt phasiRNA pipelines). skills.summary: Reproduce the benchmark in which PhasiHunter is run against unitas, PhaseTank, and PhasiRNAnalyzer on a maize small RNA-seq test dataset using the transcriptome as reference, counting 21-PHAS gene predictions per tool and computing cross-tool overlap fractions (e.g., 175/181 = 96.7% for PhasiHunter and 168/178 = 94.4% for PhasiRNAnalyzer).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to benchmark tools on the genome reference rather than the transcriptome — this skill's workflow fixes the transcriptome as the reference sequence. The dataset is not a plant small RNA-seq library or the tools under comparison do not predict 21-PHAS loci (e.g., comparing 24-nt phasiRNA pipelines). Only one prediction tool is being run and no cross-tool overlap comparison is requested.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking two or more RNA editing detection tools on a shared bona fide site set and you need per-site predictions aligned by genomic position to compute head-to-head ROC curves, AUC, or FNR.
skills.name: cross-tool-probability-collection
skills.search_text: cross-tool-probability-collection Use when benchmarking two or more RNA editing detection tools on a shared bona fide site set and you need per-site predictions aligned by genomic position to compute head-to-head ROC curves, AUC, or FNR. skills.summary: Collect per-tool predicted editing probabilities from multiple RNA editing classifiers (REDInet, EditPredict, RED-ML, RDDpred) run on the identical site set, join them with ground-truth positive/negative labels by genomic position, and compute comparative metrics such as ROC-AUC and false negative rate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single tool's raw output with no ground truth labels — probability collection only supports comparison once positive/negative labels exist at matched genomic positions Tools were run on different site sets or with incompatible site definitions — joining by position would compare unlike inputs; the article explicitly required 'the same set of bona fide sites ... according the guidelines of each specific program' A tool does not output per-site probabilities or decisions (only aggregate statistics), making per-site ROC-AUC/FNR computation impossible

skills.name: cross-tool-pseudotime-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-tool-pseudotime-correlation-analysis Use when you need to benchmark or validate trajectory-inference consistency across multiple pseudotime tools on a preprocessed plant scRNA-seq Seurat object with known root-state cell types (e.g., meristem). skills.summary: Reproduce and compare developmental pseudotime trajectories on the Arabidopsis root scRNA-seq atlas (Zhang et al., 2019, PRJNA517021) using scPlant's four trajectory-inference wrappers (CytoTRACE, Slingshot, Monocle2, Monocle3), then verify that the predicted pseudotimes show the overall positive correlation reported in Figure 4E-4F despite differing cell orderings.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a raw count matrix with no preprocessed Seurat object or cell-type annotations to root the trajectory at meristem cells The goal is a single-tool trajectory analysis rather than cross-tool consistency benchmarking of pseudotime predictions The dataset is bulk transcriptomic data rather than single-cell data, since trajectory inference in scPlant operates on single-cell objects

skills.search_text: cross-validated-auc-evaluation Use when you have a binary gene cluster absence/presence matrix with literature-assigned lifestyle labels and need to quantify how predictable each lifestyle is via cross-validated AUC. Input is already a per-lifestyle AUC table or the prediction model has already been evaluated — no retraining needed The goal is experimental validation of individual lifestyle-associated genes (use site-directed mutagenesis and plant bioassays instead) Genomes lack literature-based lifestyle labels, so no supervised target exists for training the binary classifiers http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains binary random forest classifiers (n_estimators=50) on chi2-selected gene cluster absence/presence features to predict bacterial lifestyles, and reports mean AUC over 5-fold cross-validation per lifestyle and genus, as in the bacLIFE paper. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-46302-y
skills.summary: Trains binary random forest classifiers (n_estimators=50) on chi2-selected gene cluster absence/presence features to predict bacterial lifestyles, and reports mean AUC over 5-fold cross-validation per lifestyle and genus, as in the bacLIFE paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a per-lifestyle AUC table or the prediction model has already been evaluated — no retraining needed The goal is experimental validation of individual lifestyle-associated genes (use site-directed mutagenesis and plant bioassays instead) Genomes lack literature-based lifestyle labels, so no supervised target exists for training the binary classifiers

skills.description: Use when a fitted penalized regression model on high-dimensional genomic covariates with a binary outcome (e.g., NMIBC vs MIBC invasion subtype) needs an unbiased estimate of prediction performance.
skills.name: cross-validated-binary-classifier-performance-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-validated-binary-classifier-performance-evaluation Use when a fitted penalized regression model on high-dimensional genomic covariates with a binary outcome (e.g., NMIBC vs MIBC invasion subtype) needs an unbiased estimate of prediction performance. The outcome is survival time (use the Cox ridge/Lasso/adaptive Lasso variants instead of logistic regression) Cross validation is not desired — in HDMAC, choosing fold number 1 disables cross validation entirely The variable count is at the magnitude of a hundred thousand, where penalized regression models fall short and FDR screening is recommended before model fitting http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 Estimates the prediction power of penalized logistic regression models (ridge, Lasso, adaptive Lasso) fitted to high-dimensional TCGA molecular data by k-fold cross validation, reporting sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and AUC as in the HDMAC bladder cancer mRNA illustration. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-60791-z
skills.summary: Estimates the prediction power of penalized logistic regression models (ridge, Lasso, adaptive Lasso) fitted to high-dimensional TCGA molecular data by k-fold cross validation, reporting sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and AUC as in the HDMAC bladder cancer mRNA illustration.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The outcome is survival time (use the Cox ridge/Lasso/adaptive Lasso variants instead of logistic regression) Cross validation is not desired — in HDMAC, choosing fold number 1 disables cross validation entirely The variable count is at the magnitude of a hundred thousand, where penalized regression models fall short and FDR screening is recommended before model fitting

skills.description: Use when a trained LDA or HSS-LDA model with a priori labels (e.g., cell-cycle phase, day, cell type) must be validated by cross-validated classification accuracy and analysis of which classes are confused.
skills.name: cross-validated-classification-accuracy-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-validated-classification-accuracy-evaluation Use when a trained LDA or HSS-LDA model with a priori labels (e.g., cell-cycle phase, day, cell type) must be validated by cross-validated classification accuracy and analysis of which classes are confused. Class labels are unknown or an unbiased view of the data is preferable — the article states this supervised approach is inappropriate in those situations The goal is to preserve local data structure in the embedding rather than maximize class separability, since LDA maximizes class separability at the expense of local structure The dataset has a large number of populations or high heterogeneity within a class (e.g., PBMCs labeled by time point), where LDA performance suffers http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Quantifies how well an LDA/HSS-LDA supervised embedding separates a priori class labels by performing cross-validated classification of cells and reporting overall accuracy plus the adjacency structure of misclassifications. This turns the linear discriminant axes from a visualization into a verifiable metric of class separation. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2022.100536
skills.summary: Quantifies how well an LDA/HSS-LDA supervised embedding separates a priori class labels by performing cross-validated classification of cells and reporting overall accuracy plus the adjacency structure of misclassifications. This turns the linear discriminant axes from a visualization into a verifiable metric of class separation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Class labels are unknown or an unbiased view of the data is preferable — the article states this supervised approach is inappropriate in those situations The goal is to preserve local data structure in the embedding rather than maximize class separability, since LDA maximizes class separability at the expense of local structure The dataset has a large number of populations or high heterogeneity within a class (e.g., PBMCs labeled by time point), where LDA performance suffers

skills.description: Use when evaluating the predictive performance of penalized Cox regression (Ridge, Lasso, adaptive Lasso) fitted to high-dimensional genomic covariates (e.g., 9,548 mRNA entries or 670 mutated genes vs. 316 patients' survival times) with a 5-fold cross-validated concordance index.
skills.name: cross-validated-concordance-index-estimation
skills.search_text: cross-validated-concordance-index-estimation Use when evaluating the predictive performance of penalized Cox regression (Ridge, Lasso, adaptive Lasso) fitted to high-dimensional genomic covariates (e.g., 9,548 mRNA entries or 670 mutated genes vs. 316 patients' survival times) with a 5-fold cross-validated concordance index. Outcome is binary rather than time-to-event: HDMAC pairs the same penalized regression framework with logistic regression, where a survival C-index is not the correct metric Covariate dimension is around a hundred thousand variables: penalized regression models fall short, and HDMAC itself recommends including FDR screening first Low-dimensional data with few covariates, where a standard (unpenalized) Cox model does not require cross-validated tuning or this evaluation scheme http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 HDMAC's method for estimating the prediction power of penalized Cox regression models (Ridge, Lasso, adaptive Lasso) by computing the concordance index (C-index) via cross-validation on high-dimensional TCGA survival data, optionally after a first-step FDR screening. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-60791-z
skills.summary: HDMAC's method for estimating the prediction power of penalized Cox regression models (Ridge, Lasso, adaptive Lasso) by computing the concordance index (C-index) via cross-validation on high-dimensional TCGA survival data, optionally after a first-step FDR screening.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Outcome is binary rather than time-to-event: HDMAC pairs the same penalized regression framework with logistic regression, where a survival C-index is not the correct metric Covariate dimension is around a hundred thousand variables: penalized regression models fall short, and HDMAC itself recommends including FDR screening first Low-dimensional data with few covariates, where a standard (unpenalized) Cox model does not require cross-validated tuning or this evaluation scheme

skills.description: Use when a multivariate logistic or Cox model has been built from genes selected by first-step screening (e.g., adaptive Lasso with FDR) and you need an unbiased estimate of prediction power via cross validation.
skills.name: cross-validated-prediction-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-validated-prediction-evaluation Use when a multivariate logistic or Cox model has been built from genes selected by first-step screening (e.g., adaptive Lasso with FDR) and you need an unbiased estimate of prediction power via cross validation. Only a single candidate variable or a low-dimensional model is being evaluated — cross-validated high-dimensional penalized regression is unnecessary The user is still at the first-step screening stage (FDR/mutation/expression frequency filtering) and has not yet fitted a multivariate regression model to screen output Fold number 1 is chosen — the article states cross validation will not be performed, so no prediction-power estimate is produced http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Estimates the predictive performance (e.g., cross-validated AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy) of a multivariate regression model built from high-dimensionally screened genes using HDMAC's built-in cross validation, so that penalized-regression-selected models can be assessed rather than just reported. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-60791-z
skills.summary: Estimates the predictive performance (e.g., cross-validated AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy) of a multivariate regression model built from high-dimensionally screened genes using HDMAC's built-in cross validation, so that penalized-regression-selected models can be assessed rather than just reported.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single candidate variable or a low-dimensional model is being evaluated — cross-validated high-dimensional penalized regression is unnecessary The user is still at the first-step screening stage (FDR/mutation/expression frequency filtering) and has not yet fitted a multivariate regression model to screen output Fold number 1 is chosen — the article states cross validation will not be performed, so no prediction-power estimate is produced

skills.description: Use when training a penalized multinomial classifier (e.g. glmnet) on per-cell signature-score features and the regularization strength must be tuned by k-fold cross-validation rather than fixed a priori.
skills.name: cross-validated-regularization-tuning
skills.search_text: cross-validated-regularization-tuning Use when training a penalized multinomial classifier (e.g. glmnet) on per-cell signature-score features and the regularization strength must be tuned by k-fold cross-validation rather than fixed a priori. Input is raw scRNA-seq counts rather than per-cell signature scores — the pairwise DEG signatures and AUCell scoring steps must be run first to build the feature matrix. Classifying non-CD8 T cells (Treg, CD4T, NKT): TILPRED routes these to curated signature-based classification, not the cross-validated glmnet CD8-state model. A maintained alternative is needed — the TILPRED README states it is no longer maintained and recommends ProjecTILs instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Train a glmnet multinomial logistic regression with lasso (alpha=1) regularization on AUCell-derived feature matrices, selecting the penalty (lambda) by 10-fold cross-validation on a 70% training subset — the approach used to fit the TILPRED CD8 TIL state classifier from 12 pairwise MAST DEG signature scores. transcriptomics/v2 10.1080/2162402x.2020.1737369
skills.summary: Train a glmnet multinomial logistic regression with lasso (alpha=1) regularization on AUCell-derived feature matrices, selecting the penalty (lambda) by 10-fold cross-validation on a 70% training subset — the approach used to fit the TILPRED CD8 TIL state classifier from 12 pairwise MAST DEG signature scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw scRNA-seq counts rather than per-cell signature scores — the pairwise DEG signatures and AUCell scoring steps must be run first to build the feature matrix. Classifying non-CD8 T cells (Treg, CD4T, NKT): TILPRED routes these to curated signature-based classification, not the cross-validated glmnet CD8-state model. A maintained alternative is needed — the TILPRED README states it is no longer maintained and recommends ProjecTILs instead.

skills.description: Use when fitting suffPCR (row-sparse PCA + OLS/logistic) on high-dimensional, correlated omics data like the DLBCL expression set and the penalty lambda / subspace dimension d must be chosen by 5-fold cross-validation before extracting sparse loadings.
skills.name: cross-validated-regularization-tuning
skills.search_text: cross-validated-regularization-tuning Use when fitting suffPCR (row-sparse PCA + OLS/logistic) on high-dimensional, correlated omics data like the DLBCL expression set and the penalty lambda / subspace dimension d must be chosen by 5-fold cross-validation before extracting sparse loadings. Features are low-dimensional and only weakly correlated, so plain OLS or logistic regression without a sparse PCA step is adequate — SuffPCR's advantage targets omics data with correlated features You need only class labels or predictions from an already-fitted model and have no need to tune lambda or select features The response cannot be plausibly modeled as a linear (or logistic) function of a low-dimensional sparse principal component subspace — the paper notes near-optimality holds only 'when the model assumptions are satisfied' http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Selects the sparsity penalty (lambda) and subspace dimension d for sufficient principal component regression (SuffPCR) by running 5-fold cross-validation over the lambda grid (lambda_max, lambda_min, lambda_seq), then refitting the model on all samples at the best lambda so that downstream feature selection is reproducible. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac033
skills.summary: Selects the sparsity penalty (lambda) and subspace dimension d for sufficient principal component regression (SuffPCR) by running 5-fold cross-validation over the lambda grid (lambda_max, lambda_min, lambda_seq), then refitting the model on all samples at the best lambda so that downstream feature selection is reproducible.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Features are low-dimensional and only weakly correlated, so plain OLS or logistic regression without a sparse PCA step is adequate — SuffPCR's advantage targets omics data with correlated features You need only class labels or predictions from an already-fitted model and have no need to tune lambda or select features The response cannot be plausibly modeled as a linear (or logistic) function of a low-dimensional sparse principal component subspace — the paper notes near-optimality holds only 'when the model assumptions are satisfied'

skills.description: Use when predicting labels for an unlabeled scRNA-seq dataset against a trained hierarchical classifier and you need a data-driven cutoff to reject cells that belong to no known population.
skills.name: cross-validated-threshold-estimation
skills.search_text: cross-validated-threshold-estimation Use when predicting labels for an unlabeled scRNA-seq dataset against a trained hierarchical classifier and you need a data-driven cutoff to reject cells that belong to no known population. Datasets are not yet aligned/batch-corrected — scHPL requires alignment beforehand (e.g. with scVI or scArches) and is not itself a batch correction tool The goal is to assign labels within known populations rather than detect unseen populations; use the trained classification tree prediction alone http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 Estimates a per-dataset rejection threshold from cross-validated reconstruction-error percentiles so that scHPL-style classifiers can flag cells from unseen cell populations instead of forcing a known label. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-23196-8
skills.summary: Estimates a per-dataset rejection threshold from cross-validated reconstruction-error percentiles so that scHPL-style classifiers can flag cells from unseen cell populations instead of forcing a known label.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Datasets are not yet aligned/batch-corrected — scHPL requires alignment beforehand (e.g. with scVI or scArches) and is not itself a batch correction tool The goal is to assign labels within known populations rather than detect unseen populations; use the trained classification tree prediction alone

skills.description: Use when evaluating how training-cohort composition (tissue-specific vs pooled multi-cancer cohorts) changes the cross-validation accuracy of a trained miRNA-inference model such as miRSCAPE.
skills.name: cross-validation-accuracy-assessment
skills.search_text: cross-validation-accuracy-assessment Use when evaluating how training-cohort composition (tissue-specific vs pooled multi-cancer cohorts) changes the cross-validation accuracy of a trained miRNA-inference model such as miRSCAPE. The goal is miRNA prediction on new scRNA-seq clusters (use the miRSCAPE prediction workflow with modifySeuratObject/bulkTransform/miRSCAPE, not the accuracy-benchmarking setup) No paired miRNA-mRNA bulk training cohort is available — miRSCAPE must be trained on a large paired cohort, so accuracy assessment is not applicable The application sample's cellular/tissue context differs from the training cohort, where the paper expects reduced accuracy that this pooled-cohort benchmark does not model http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Benchmark the miRSCAPE XGBoost model's cross-validation accuracy across tissue-specific, tissue-vs-normal, and pooled multi-cohort configurations (TCGA and GTEx bulk miRNA-mRNA profiles) to quantify how sample heterogeneity affects miRNA-inference accuracy. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2022.104962
skills.summary: Benchmark the miRSCAPE XGBoost model's cross-validation accuracy across tissue-specific, tissue-vs-normal, and pooled multi-cohort configurations (TCGA and GTEx bulk miRNA-mRNA profiles) to quantify how sample heterogeneity affects miRNA-inference accuracy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is miRNA prediction on new scRNA-seq clusters (use the miRSCAPE prediction workflow with modifySeuratObject/bulkTransform/miRSCAPE, not the accuracy-benchmarking setup) No paired miRNA-mRNA bulk training cohort is available — miRSCAPE must be trained on a large paired cohort, so accuracy assessment is not applicable The application sample's cellular/tissue context differs from the training cohort, where the paper expects reduced accuracy that this pooled-cohort benchmark does not model

skills.description: Use when a new sequence-based predictor (e.g., a stacked ensemble for m5C sites in A. thaliana or M. musculus) must be benchmarked against tools on identical training and independent test datasets.
skills.name: cross-validation-and-independent-test-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-validation-and-independent-test-evaluation Use when a new sequence-based predictor (e.g., a stacked ensemble for m5C sites in A. thaliana or M. musculus) must be benchmarked against tools on identical training and independent test datasets. The goal is feature encoding or model training/parameter tuning (e.g., F-score feature selection or Bayesian optimization) rather than benchmark comparison of a trained predictor The datasets differ from the published benchmark sets (different species, sizes, or construction), so metrics would not be comparable to Table 3/Table 4 values Only cross-validation is needed and no independent test or comparison against iRNA-m5C, m5CPred-SVM, or iRNA-m5C_SVM is required http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 Evaluates an m5C site predictor such as Staem5 by 10-fold cross-validation on training sets and prediction on species-specific independent test sets, computing Sn, Sp, Acc, MCC, and AUC from confusion-matrix counts (TP, TN, FP, FN) to enable side-by-side comparison with existing predictors. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.omtn.2021.10.012
skills.summary: Evaluates an m5C site predictor such as Staem5 by 10-fold cross-validation on training sets and prediction on species-specific independent test sets, computing Sn, Sp, Acc, MCC, and AUC from confusion-matrix counts (TP, TN, FP, FN) to enable side-by-side comparison with existing predictors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is feature encoding or model training/parameter tuning (e.g., F-score feature selection or Bayesian optimization) rather than benchmark comparison of a trained predictor The datasets differ from the published benchmark sets (different species, sizes, or construction), so metrics would not be comparable to Table 3/Table 4 values Only cross-validation is needed and no independent test or comparison against iRNA-m5C, m5CPred-SVM, or iRNA-m5C_SVM is required

skills.description: Use when benchmarking cell-type classifiers on scRNA-seq data with predefined hierarchical trees, requiring k-fold cross-validated HF1-scores, rejection rates of unseen populations, and comparison to published baselines.
skills.name: cross-validation-benchmark-evaluation-scrnaseq
skills.search_text: cross-validation-benchmark-evaluation-scrnaseq Use when benchmarking cell-type classifiers on scRNA-seq data with predefined hierarchical trees, requiring k-fold cross-validated HF1-scores, rejection rates of unseen populations, and comparison to published baselines. Datasets are not yet aligned (batch-corrected) — scHPL requires datasets to be aligned before matching cell populations and is not a batch correction tool The goal is de novo tree construction rather than evaluating performance of a predefined tree with known folds Cell population labels are missing or at inconsistent resolutions without a defined hierarchical structure to train against http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Reproduce cross-validated benchmarking of scHPL's linear SVM versus one-class SVM classifiers across simulated, PBMC-FACS, and AMB datasets by computing median hierarchical F1 (HF1) scores and rejection percentages, and comparing against CHETAH and SVMrejection baselines. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-23196-8
skills.summary: Reproduce cross-validated benchmarking of scHPL's linear SVM versus one-class SVM classifiers across simulated, PBMC-FACS, and AMB datasets by computing median hierarchical F1 (HF1) scores and rejection percentages, and comparing against CHETAH and SVMrejection baselines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Datasets are not yet aligned (batch-corrected) — scHPL requires datasets to be aligned before matching cell populations and is not a batch correction tool The goal is de novo tree construction rather than evaluating performance of a predefined tree with known folds Cell population labels are missing or at inconsistent resolutions without a defined hierarchical structure to train against

skills.description: Use when benchmarking automated single-cell cell-type classifiers (e.g., SIMS vs scANVI, Seurat, Scnym, SingleR, SciBet) on pre-annotated datasets to quantify accuracy and Macro F1 under cross-validation.
skills.name: cross-validation-benchmark-of-cell-classifiers
skills.search_text: cross-validation-benchmark-of-cell-classifiers Use when benchmarking automated single-cell cell-type classifiers (e.g., SIMS vs scANVI, Seurat, Scnym, SingleR, SciBet) on pre-annotated datasets to quantify accuracy and Macro F1 under cross-validation. Data are unlabeled with no trusted class_label annotations, since SIMS is a supervised method requiring pre-existing expert annotations Goal is trans-species label transfer — the article limits evaluation to samples within the same species The input needs the fastest possible classifier — SIMS 'is not the fastest of the methods we benchmarked' http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 A 5-fold cross-validation benchmarking protocol comparing the SIMS TabNet-based single-cell label transfer tool against scANVI, Seurat, Scnym, SingleR, and SciBet on accuracy and Macro F1 across five diverse scRNA-seq datasets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.xgen.2024.100581
skills.summary: A 5-fold cross-validation benchmarking protocol comparing the SIMS TabNet-based single-cell label transfer tool against scANVI, Seurat, Scnym, SingleR, and SciBet on accuracy and Macro F1 across five diverse scRNA-seq datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are unlabeled with no trusted class_label annotations, since SIMS is a supervised method requiring pre-existing expert annotations Goal is trans-species label transfer — the article limits evaluation to samples within the same species The input needs the fastest possible classifier — SIMS 'is not the fastest of the methods we benchmarked'

skills.description: Use when classifying unlabelled genes as TSGs or OGs from a gene-by-feature mutation matrix (e.g. 37 ratio-metric/entropy features) where a single model would risk overfitting the small CGC-labelled training set.
skills.name: cross-validation-fold-model-consensus
skills.search_text: cross-validation-fold-model-consensus Use when classifying unlabelled genes as TSGs or OGs from a gene-by-feature mutation matrix (e.g. 37 ratio-metric/entropy features) where a single model would risk overfitting the small CGC-labelled training set. Input genes already have trusted TSG/OG labels (they are the training set, not prediction targets) The goal is a mutation-rate/background-model-based driver prediction (e.g. MutSigCV-style) rather than a feature-based TSG/OG classifier — cTaG deliberately avoids background mutation rate modelling Only one trained model or fold is available, since the consensus rule (>4 of 5 models plus top 5 percentile) cannot be applied http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Train a random forest model per cross-validation fold (on a subset of 136 TSGs and 76 OGs labelled from Cancer Gene Census) and consolidate the per-fold TSG/OG predictions on unlabelled genes into a single consensus driver-gene call, avoiding bias towards highly mutated genes. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-04015-y
skills.summary: Train a random forest model per cross-validation fold (on a subset of 136 TSGs and 76 OGs labelled from Cancer Gene Census) and consolidate the per-fold TSG/OG predictions on unlabelled genes into a single consensus driver-gene call, avoiding bias towards highly mutated genes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input genes already have trusted TSG/OG labels (they are the training set, not prediction targets) The goal is a mutation-rate/background-model-based driver prediction (e.g. MutSigCV-style) rather than a feature-based TSG/OG classifier — cTaG deliberately avoids background mutation rate modelling Only one trained model or fold is available, since the consensus rule (>4 of 5 models plus top 5 percentile) cannot be applied

skills.description: Use when choosing among several candidate classifiers on a high-dimensional expression matrix (e.g. 19,737-gene TCGA RNA-seq with subtype labels) and you need unbiased per-model hyperparameter selection plus held-out generalization estimates.
skills.name: cross-validation-grid-search-hyperparameter-tuning
skills.search_text: cross-validation-grid-search-hyperparameter-tuning Use when choosing among several candidate classifiers on a high-dimensional expression matrix (e.g. 19,737-gene TCGA RNA-seq with subtype labels) and you need unbiased per-model hyperparameter selection plus held-out generalization estimates. The labels themselves were produced by the same assay you are tuning against (e.g. PAM50-derived calls on the same gene panel), which the article notes biases accuracy estimates You need a single-sample classifier applied with a predefined external reference (AWCA-PAM50 or trained mLR models from the repo) rather than model selection among learners The dataset lacks matched subtype training labels or is not five-class intrinsic subtyping of breast cancer http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmarks multiple supervised learners (regularized multiclass logistic regression, Decision Forest, Decision Jungle, FFNN, SVM) on high-dimensional RNA-seq data by coupling each to a scikit-learn Pipeline hyperparameter grid and selecting best settings with tenfold stratified GridSearchCV, then comparing held-out test accuracy to pick the strongest classifier. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-70832-2
skills.summary: Benchmarks multiple supervised learners (regularized multiclass logistic regression, Decision Forest, Decision Jungle, FFNN, SVM) on high-dimensional RNA-seq data by coupling each to a scikit-learn Pipeline hyperparameter grid and selecting best settings with tenfold stratified GridSearchCV, then comparing held-out test accuracy to pick the strongest classifier.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The labels themselves were produced by the same assay you are tuning against (e.g. PAM50-derived calls on the same gene panel), which the article notes biases accuracy estimates You need a single-sample classifier applied with a predefined external reference (AWCA-PAM50 or trained mLR models from the repo) rather than model selection among learners The dataset lacks matched subtype training labels or is not five-class intrinsic subtyping of breast cancer

skills.description: Use when training a classifier on a small labelled gene set (e.g. 136 TSGs and 76 OGs from CGC) where overfitting risk is high and hyper-parameters must be estimated stably before predictions are trusted.
