Input is already a quality-filtered matrix produced by Cell Ranger or another tool rather than raw spliced/unspliced scKB matrices The user has a trusted externally computed doublet rate and only needs rate estimation toggled off via doublet.rate=NULL semantics unrelated to this step Running cell type/developmental stage annotation on non-Arabidopsis data, since COPILOT annotation only supports Arabidopsis thaliana root http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Estimates the expected doublet rate from the 10X Genomics loading estimation and removes heterotypic/homotypic doublets from gene-by-cell UMI matrices during COPILOT quality filtering, using DoubletFinder downstream of the noise-model-based cell filtering. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.xpro.2022.101729
skills.summary: Estimates the expected doublet rate from the 10X Genomics loading estimation and removes heterotypic/homotypic doublets from gene-by-cell UMI matrices during COPILOT quality filtering, using DoubletFinder downstream of the noise-model-based cell filtering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a quality-filtered matrix produced by Cell Ranger or another tool rather than raw spliced/unspliced scKB matrices The user has a trusted externally computed doublet rate and only needs rate estimation toggled off via doublet.rate=NULL semantics unrelated to this step Running cell type/developmental stage annotation on non-Arabidopsis data, since COPILOT annotation only supports Arabidopsis thaliana root

skills.description: Use when running Chord (or any simulated-doublet method) on droplet scRNA-seq data without experimental doublet labels (no demuxlet/cell hashing) and you must supply an expected doubletrate before calling doublets.
skills.name: doublet-rate-estimation-per-cell-count
skills.search_text: doublet-rate-estimation-per-cell-count Use when running Chord (or any simulated-doublet method) on droplet scRNA-seq data without experimental doublet labels (no demuxlet/cell hashing) and you must supply an expected doubletrate before calling doublets. Experimental doublet labels already exist (e.g., demuxlet called doublets from natural genetic variation, or cell hashing/MULTI-seq was performed) — use those directly instead of an estimated rate The dataset is not droplet-based microfluidic scRNA-seq, where the doublet-counted-as-one-cell artefact and the 10X rate rule do not apply The sample is a merged multi-sample object whose cell-type proportions are not representative of any single sample (cf. Scrublet best practice to run per sample) http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Estimates the expected doublet rate for a droplet scRNA-seq sample from its cell count using the 10X rule of thumb (~0.9% per 1,000 cells), supplying the doubletrate parameter that Chord, its overkill filtering stage, and simulated-doublet generation all depend on. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-022-03476-9
skills.summary: Estimates the expected doublet rate for a droplet scRNA-seq sample from its cell count using the 10X rule of thumb (~0.9% per 1,000 cells), supplying the doubletrate parameter that Chord, its overkill filtering stage, and simulated-doublet generation all depend on.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Experimental doublet labels already exist (e.g., demuxlet called doublets from natural genetic variation, or cell hashing/MULTI-seq was performed) — use those directly instead of an estimated rate The dataset is not droplet-based microfluidic scRNA-seq, where the doublet-counted-as-one-cell artefact and the 10X rate rule do not apply The sample is a merged multi-sample object whose cell-type proportions are not representative of any single sample (cf. Scrublet best practice to run per sample)

skills.description: Use when you need to benchmark doublet detection methods by their downstream effect on developmental trajectory inference, especially on synthetic data with known doublet labels and a bifurcating trajectory.
skills.name: doublet-removal-effect-on-trajectory-branching-comparison
skills.search_text: doublet-removal-effect-on-trajectory-branching-comparison Use when you need to benchmark doublet detection methods by their downstream effect on developmental trajectory inference, especially on synthetic data with known doublet labels and a bifurcating trajectory. You lack a reference trajectory (clean data or known ground truth) against which to compare branch structure — the evaluation depends on it The dataset has no doublet contamination or the doublet proportion is unknown, so the fixed top-20% removal fraction cannot be justified Your analysis goal is doublet classification accuracy (precision/recall vs labels), not downstream trajectory robustness A benchmarking procedure that scores cells for doublets with multiple detection methods (Chord, Scrublet, bcds, cxds, doubletCells), removes the top-scoring fraction matching the known doublet rate, and tests whether Slingshot/monocle trajectory re-inference reproduces the clean-data branch structure or introduces spurious branches. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-022-03476-9
skills.summary: A benchmarking procedure that scores cells for doublets with multiple detection methods (Chord, Scrublet, bcds, cxds, doubletCells), removes the top-scoring fraction matching the known doublet rate, and tests whether Slingshot/monocle trajectory re-inference reproduces the clean-data branch structure or introduces spurious branches.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You lack a reference trajectory (clean data or known ground truth) against which to compare branch structure — the evaluation depends on it The dataset has no doublet contamination or the doublet proportion is unknown, so the fixed top-20% removal fraction cannot be justified Your analysis goal is doublet classification accuracy (precision/recall vs labels), not downstream trajectory robustness

skills.description: Use when a Seurat/SCE dataset has already been run once through chord() and you want to boost the ensemble with additional doublet detectors' per-cell score columns.
skills.name: doublet-score-integration-across-methods
skills.search_text: doublet-score-integration-across-methods Use when a Seurat/SCE dataset has already been run once through chord() and you want to boost the ensemble with additional doublet detectors' per-cell score columns. No prior chord() run exists — the .robj exported objects and overkill/simulated-data score files are prerequisites for the addmethods1/addmethods2 port The goal is a single-method doublet call rather than an ensemble — running one external detector directly is faster, and Chord is known to be suboptimal in runtime because it integrates multiple methods Data comes from multiple samples merged into one matrix — Scrublet should be run per sample separately, and merged datasets with unrepresentative cell-type proportions degrade performance http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Extends the Chord ensemble doublet detector beyond its three built-in methods by scoring real and simulated datasets with external tools (e.g., Scrublet, DoubletDetection) and re-fitting the GBM over the union of built-in plus appended per-cell scores. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-022-03476-9
skills.summary: Extends the Chord ensemble doublet detector beyond its three built-in methods by scoring real and simulated datasets with external tools (e.g., Scrublet, DoubletDetection) and re-fitting the GBM over the union of built-in plus appended per-cell scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No prior chord() run exists — the .robj exported objects and overkill/simulated-data score files are prerequisites for the addmethods1/addmethods2 port The goal is a single-method doublet call rather than an ensemble — running one external detector directly is faster, and Chord is known to be suboptimal in runtime because it integrates multiple methods Data comes from multiple samples merged into one matrix — Scrublet should be run per sample separately, and merged datasets with unrepresentative cell-type proportions degrade performance

skills.description: Use when a droplet-based scRNA-seq dataset has an estimated doublet proportion and doublet scores from one or more tools (Chord, Scrublet, bcds, cxds, doubletCells), and you need to remove doublets by score cutoff and assess the effect on trajectory/branch inference.
skills.name: doublet-score-rank-filtering
skills.search_text: doublet-score-rank-filtering Use when a droplet-based scRNA-seq dataset has an estimated doublet proportion and doublet scores from one or more tools (Chord, Scrublet, bcds, cxds, doubletCells), and you need to remove doublets by score cutoff and assess the effect on trajectory/branch inference. The data already carry experimental doublet labels (cell hashing, MULTI-seq, demuxlet) that only mark cross-sample doublets and cannot annotate within-sample ones — score-rank filtering is still needed, but do not treat demuxlet labels as the score being filtered The dataset is a merged multi-sample collection where cell-type proportions are not representative of any single sample — Scrublet's README warns it 'may perform poorly on merged datasets' and should be run per sample Rank cells by a per-method doublet score and remove the top-scoring fraction (matched to the expected doublet rate, e.g. the top 20% when 20% of cells are labelled doublets) so all detection methods can be compared at equal stringency, then verify the filtering by re-inferring downstream trajectories (Slingshot/monocle) against clean-data branch structure. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-022-03476-9
skills.summary: Rank cells by a per-method doublet score and remove the top-scoring fraction (matched to the expected doublet rate, e.g. the top 20% when 20% of cells are labelled doublets) so all detection methods can be compared at equal stringency, then verify the filtering by re-inferring downstream trajectories (Slingshot/monocle) against clean-data branch structure.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data already carry experimental doublet labels (cell hashing, MULTI-seq, demuxlet) that only mark cross-sample doublets and cannot annotate within-sample ones — score-rank filtering is still needed, but do not treat demuxlet labels as the score being filtered The dataset is a merged multi-sample collection where cell-type proportions are not representative of any single sample — Scrublet's README warns it 'may perform poorly on merged datasets' and should be run per sample

skills.description: Use when constructing controlled doublet-detection benchmarks: you have the 68k PBMC dataset with NK, B and CD14+ monocyte labels and need synthetic doublets at known abundance gradients (e.g. 2 monocytes at 0.08%-5%) to evaluate F1 of rare-cell detectors.
skills.name: doublet-simulation-from-pbmc-data
skills.search_text: doublet-simulation-from-pbmc-data Use when constructing controlled doublet-detection benchmarks: you have the 68k PBMC dataset with NK, B and CD14+ monocyte labels and need synthetic doublets at known abundance gradients (e.g. 2 monocytes at 0.08%-5%) to evaluate F1 of rare-cell detectors. The goal is to detect naturally occurring rare cells in a real dataset rather than to benchmark detectors against synthetic planted doublets The input dataset lacks cell-type labels (e.g. NK, B, CD14+ monocytes) needed to construct homogeneous subsamples and ground truth Only rare-cell (single-population) benchmarks are needed — the 99 rare-cell datasets with 2-100 planted monocytes are the appropriate construction instead http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 A benchmark-construction skill that builds 140 doublet detection datasets by embedding 2 monocytes into subsampled 68k PBMC data at mixing proportions from 0.08% to 5%, so that rare-cell/doublet methods like GapClust, RaceID, GiniClust, CellSIUS and FiRE can be scored by precision, recall and F1 against known ground truth. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-24489-8
skills.summary: A benchmark-construction skill that builds 140 doublet detection datasets by embedding 2 monocytes into subsampled 68k PBMC data at mixing proportions from 0.08% to 5%, so that rare-cell/doublet methods like GapClust, RaceID, GiniClust, CellSIUS and FiRE can be scored by precision, recall and F1 against known ground truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to detect naturally occurring rare cells in a real dataset rather than to benchmark detectors against synthetic planted doublets The input dataset lacks cell-type labels (e.g. NK, B, CD14+ monocytes) needed to construct homogeneous subsamples and ground truth Only rare-cell (single-population) benchmarks are needed — the 99 rare-cell datasets with 2-100 planted monocytes are the appropriate construction instead

skills.description: Use when a droplet-based scRNA-seq Seurat/SingleCellExperiment object needs DoubletFinder pANN doublet scores — either to prefilter likely doublets before Chord simulates its artificial-doublet training set, or as one of three predictors (with cxds and bcds) for the GBM ensemble.
skills.name: doubletfinder-artificial-nearest-neighbor-scoring
skills.search_text: doubletfinder-artificial-nearest-neighbor-scoring Use when a droplet-based scRNA-seq Seurat/SingleCellExperiment object needs DoubletFinder pANN doublet scores — either to prefilter likely doublets before Chord simulates its artificial-doublet training set, or as one of three predictors (with cxds and bcds) for the GBM ensemble. Input is not droplet-based scRNA-seq in a Seurat/SingleCellExperiment object, or the goal is experimental doublet labeling across samples (cell hashing, MULTI-seq, demuxlet are used instead) A single gold-standard doublet method is already known to work well for the dataset — Chord's rationale is that individual methods vary greatly in performance and no method is a gold standard for each scenario Runtime is the binding constraint — Chord integrates multiple methods' scores (including DoubletFinder's), so it is not optimal in terms of time efficiency http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Run DoubletFinder's pANN-based artificial-nearest-neighbor scoring to assign per-cell doublet scores in the Chord ensemble, both on the merged real-artificial data during the overkill prefilter and as a predictor feature for the GBM training model. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-022-03476-9
skills.summary: Run DoubletFinder's pANN-based artificial-nearest-neighbor scoring to assign per-cell doublet scores in the Chord ensemble, both on the merged real-artificial data during the overkill prefilter and as a predictor feature for the GBM training model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not droplet-based scRNA-seq in a Seurat/SingleCellExperiment object, or the goal is experimental doublet labeling across samples (cell hashing, MULTI-seq, demuxlet are used instead) A single gold-standard doublet method is already known to work well for the dataset — Chord's rationale is that individual methods vary greatly in performance and no method is a gold standard for each scenario Runtime is the binding constraint — Chord integrates multiple methods' scores (including DoubletFinder's), so it is not optimal in terms of time efficiency

skills.description: Use when running Chord's chord() call (or simulating artificial doublets generally) on 10X-style droplet scRNA-seq data and an input 'doubletrate' must be supplied before doublet detection can proceed.
skills.name: doubletrate-estimation-for-droplet-scrnaseq
skills.search_text: doubletrate-estimation-for-droplet-scrnaseq Use when running Chord's chord() call (or simulating artificial doublets generally) on 10X-style droplet scRNA-seq data and an input 'doubletrate' must be supplied before doublet detection can proceed. Input is plate-based scRNA-seq or an already doublet-filtered dataset where no new artificial doublets need to be simulated The rate should not be copied across samples: it depends on the number of cells in the sample, so recompute it per sample rather than reusing a previous value Estimates the expected doublet rate for a droplet-based scRNA-seq sample from its cell count and passes it to ensemble doublet callers like Chord, which uses the rate to control how many artificial doublets are simulated for training the GBM/AdaBoost classifier. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-022-03476-9
skills.summary: Estimates the expected doublet rate for a droplet-based scRNA-seq sample from its cell count and passes it to ensemble doublet callers like Chord, which uses the rate to control how many artificial doublets are simulated for training the GBM/AdaBoost classifier.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is plate-based scRNA-seq or an already doublet-filtered dataset where no new artificial doublets need to be simulated The rate should not be copied across samples: it depends on the number of cells in the sample, so recompute it per sample rather than reusing a previous value

skills.description: Use when validating that a cluster-significance/merging method retains test performance (AUROC) and acceptable runtime at reduced cell counts, e.g. reproducing Cytocipher's Tabula Sapiens 483152-cell benchmark and its 7385-cell downsample.
skills.name: downsampled-dataset-reproducibility
skills.search_text: downsampled-dataset-reproducibility Use when validating that a cluster-significance/merging method retains test performance (AUROC) and acceptable runtime at reduced cell counts, e.g. reproducing Cytocipher's Tabula Sapiens 483152-cell benchmark and its 7385-cell downsample. The dataset lacks known cell-type labels, so AUROC of merged clusters against ground truth cannot be computed and the benchmark cannot be validated. The analysis goal is novel biological discovery (e.g. identifying new subpopulations) rather than benchmarking scalability/reproducibility of a published result. Cluster labels come from low Leiden resolution with no deliberate over-clustering, leaving nothing for Cytocipher to merge and making the AUROC benchmark ill-posed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Reproduces the Cytocipher Tabula Sapiens scalability benchmark by running cluster merging (code-scoring and coexpr-scoring) on the 483152-cell artificial over-cluster AnnData and on a 7385-cell downsample, computing AUROCs of merged clusters against known cell-type labels, and timing Sc-SHC versus Cytocipher on a 500-cell 12-cell-type subset. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad435
skills.summary: Reproduces the Cytocipher Tabula Sapiens scalability benchmark by running cluster merging (code-scoring and coexpr-scoring) on the 483152-cell artificial over-cluster AnnData and on a 7385-cell downsample, computing AUROCs of merged clusters against known cell-type labels, and timing Sc-SHC versus Cytocipher on a 500-cell 12-cell-type subset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset lacks known cell-type labels, so AUROC of merged clusters against ground truth cannot be computed and the benchmark cannot be validated. The analysis goal is novel biological discovery (e.g. identifying new subpopulations) rather than benchmarking scalability/reproducibility of a published result. Cluster labels come from low Leiden resolution with no deliberate over-clustering, leaving nothing for Cytocipher to merge and making the AUROC benchmark ill-posed.

skills.description: Use when comparing normalized scRNA-seq matrices across downsampling or imputation conditions and you need a rotation-invariant measure (subspace angle of signal PCs) of whether multivariate structure is preserved.
skills.name: downsampled-matrix-comparison
skills.search_text: downsampled-matrix-comparison Use when comparing normalized scRNA-seq matrices across downsampling or imputation conditions and you need a rotation-invariant measure (subspace angle of signal PCs) of whether multivariate structure is preserved. The goal is entry-level matrix comparison (e.g., RMSE or correlation of imputed values) rather than preservation of low-rank subspace structure The data has not been normalized (ALRA expects library- and log-normalized input with cells as rows and genes as columns), so PCA/jackstraw-based comparison would be confounded by library size No matched original/downsampled pair exists — subspace angles require the same gene space and a common reference PC basis http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Quantifies whether ALRA preserves biological signal in downsampled scRNA-seq data by computing the subspace angle between the top-k principal components (k chosen via Seurat jackstraw, p ≤ 1e-5) of original vs. downsampled matrices, before and after ALRA imputation. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-27729-z
skills.summary: Quantifies whether ALRA preserves biological signal in downsampled scRNA-seq data by computing the subspace angle between the top-k principal components (k chosen via Seurat jackstraw, p ≤ 1e-5) of original vs. downsampled matrices, before and after ALRA imputation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is entry-level matrix comparison (e.g., RMSE or correlation of imputed values) rather than preservation of low-rank subspace structure The data has not been normalized (ALRA expects library- and log-normalized input with cells as rows and genes as columns), so PCA/jackstraw-based comparison would be confounded by library size No matched original/downsampled pair exists — subspace angles require the same gene space and a common reference PC basis

skills.description: Use when you need to compare zero-preserving imputation methods on scRNA-seq count matrices by quantifying whether imputation improves cell-type separability via out-of-bag classification error.
skills.name: downsampled-scrnaseq-matrix-handling
skills.search_text: downsampled-scrnaseq-matrix-handling Use when you need to compare zero-preserving imputation methods on scRNA-seq count matrices by quantifying whether imputation improves cell-type separability via out-of-bag classification error. Datasets exceeding 100,000 cells where SAVER and scImpute become extremely slow — use scalable methods instead Tasks where the goal is to preserve true biological zeros at zero (MAGIC and DCA output a matrix in which every gene is expressed in every cell) Already-normalized or already-imputed matrices — this skill expects raw downsampled count matrices plus labels http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Protocol for loading and benchmarking imputation methods (ALRA, MAGIC, SAVER, DCA, scImpute) on downsampled scRNA-seq expression matrices (Zeisel, Baron, Chen, La Manno) using random-forest out-of-bag classification error as the evaluation metric. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-27729-z
skills.summary: Protocol for loading and benchmarking imputation methods (ALRA, MAGIC, SAVER, DCA, scImpute) on downsampled scRNA-seq expression matrices (Zeisel, Baron, Chen, La Manno) using random-forest out-of-bag classification error as the evaluation metric.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Datasets exceeding 100,000 cells where SAVER and scImpute become extremely slow — use scalable methods instead Tasks where the goal is to preserve true biological zeros at zero (MAGIC and DCA output a matrix in which every gene is expressed in every cell) Already-normalized or already-imputed matrices — this skill expects raw downsampled count matrices plus labels

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a tool that downsamples cells per condition (e.g. SCPA's default 500 cells) loses information or gains speed relative to a full-dataset method on million-cell-scale scRNA-seq data with >1000 pathways.
skills.name: downsampling-based-method-benchmarking
skills.search_text: downsampling-based-method-benchmarking Use when evaluating whether a tool that downsamples cells per condition (e.g. SCPA's default 500 cells) loses information or gains speed relative to a full-dataset method on million-cell-scale scRNA-seq data with >1000 pathways. Datasets with fewer than ~15 samples: scPAFA's MOFA-based multicellular module identification requires at least 15 samples (not cells), so the module-agreement validation step is not applicable to small studies Analyses where the target method is not downsampling-based and consumes all cells anyway — the 500/1000/2000-cell budget sweep only characterizes information loss from downsampling strategies Pathway sets that are redundant or biologically misaligned with the context — the article notes redundant pathway sets increase result complexity and misaligned sets cause information loss, confounding the differential-pathway comparison Benchmarking protocol for comparing a full-data method (scPAFA's fast_Ucell PAS computation) against a downsampling-based competitor (SCPA) across 500/1000/2000-cell budgets per condition, measuring wall-clock runtime, peak memory, and differential-pathway agreement on CRC and lupus scRNA-seq subsets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-024-07238-7
skills.summary: Benchmarking protocol for comparing a full-data method (scPAFA's fast_Ucell PAS computation) against a downsampling-based competitor (SCPA) across 500/1000/2000-cell budgets per condition, measuring wall-clock runtime, peak memory, and differential-pathway agreement on CRC and lupus scRNA-seq subsets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Datasets with fewer than ~15 samples: scPAFA's MOFA-based multicellular module identification requires at least 15 samples (not cells), so the module-agreement validation step is not applicable to small studies Analyses where the target method is not downsampling-based and consumes all cells anyway — the 500/1000/2000-cell budget sweep only characterizes information loss from downsampling strategies Pathway sets that are redundant or biologically misaligned with the context — the article notes redundant pathway sets increase result complexity and misaligned sets cause information loss, confounding the differential-pathway comparison

skills.description: Use when validating that a cluster-purity metric or entropy-fit parameter (e.g. S in ROGUE) remains stable under varying cell numbers or sequencing-depth differences (2- to 100-fold) between replicates.
skills.name: downsampling-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: downsampling-correlation-analysis Use when validating that a cluster-purity metric or entropy-fit parameter (e.g. S in ROGUE) remains stable under varying cell numbers or sequencing-depth differences (2- to 100-fold) between replicates. Input is real (non-simulated) integrated data from different protocols/platforms — the article notes ROGUE does not yet assess purity of such integrated populations Low-quality or continuous data where the recommended 0.9 purity threshold must instead be determined from global ROGUE values rather than the default validation criteria http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 A robustness-testing procedure that down-samples the number of cells (or varies sequencing depth) in single-cell populations, recomputes the ROGUE entropy-fit parameter S at each level, and quantifies Pearson correlations of S across down-sampling levels to demonstrate metric stability. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-16904-3
skills.summary: A robustness-testing procedure that down-samples the number of cells (or varies sequencing depth) in single-cell populations, recomputes the ROGUE entropy-fit parameter S at each level, and quantifies Pearson correlations of S across down-sampling levels to demonstrate metric stability.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real (non-simulated) integrated data from different protocols/platforms — the article notes ROGUE does not yet assess purity of such integrated populations Low-quality or continuous data where the recommended 0.9 purity threshold must instead be determined from global ROGUE values rather than the default validation criteria

skills.description: Use when benchmarking runtime scaling of supervised dimensionality reduction (HSS-LDA) vs unsupervised methods across increasing single-cell counts (up to ~50,000-200,000 cells), or when deciding whether to keep the runHSS downsample=TRUE default.
skills.name: downsampling-heuristic-evaluation
skills.search_text: downsampling-heuristic-evaluation Use when benchmarking runtime scaling of supervised dimensionality reduction (HSS-LDA) vs unsupervised methods across increasing single-cell counts (up to ~50,000-200,000 cells), or when deciding whether to keep the runHSS downsample=TRUE default. When labels are unknown or an unbiased view of the data is preferable — the supervised LDA approach is inappropriate in these situations When the dataset exceeds 100 dimensions — HSS feature selection is not feasible in that regime When preserving local data structure or capturing non-linear relationships is the primary goal, since LDA maximizes class separability at the expense of local structure http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 A skill for benchmarking the runtime scaling of the hsslda downsample heuristic (a Boolean defaulting to TRUE that subsets cells to improve runtime) against competing dimensionality-reduction methods (PCA, UMAP, PHATE) as single-cell dataset size grows, using silhouette and pixel class entropy (PCE) scores to confirm embedding quality is preserved. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2022.100536
skills.summary: A skill for benchmarking the runtime scaling of the hsslda downsample heuristic (a Boolean defaulting to TRUE that subsets cells to improve runtime) against competing dimensionality-reduction methods (PCA, UMAP, PHATE) as single-cell dataset size grows, using silhouette and pixel class entropy (PCE) scores to confirm embedding quality is preserved.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When labels are unknown or an unbiased view of the data is preferable — the supervised LDA approach is inappropriate in these situations When the dataset exceeds 100 dimensions — HSS feature selection is not feasible in that regime When preserving local data structure or capturing non-linear relationships is the primary goal, since LDA maximizes class separability at the expense of local structure

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a pooling or counting strategy improves single-cell allelic proportion estimates from sparsely sequenced scRNA-Seq data, using down-sampled reads and MSE against full-data estimates as the accuracy metric.
skills.name: downsampling-mse-benchmarking
skills.search_text: downsampling-mse-benchmarking Use when evaluating whether a pooling or counting strategy improves single-cell allelic proportion estimates from sparsely sequenced scRNA-Seq data, using down-sampled reads and MSE against full-data estimates as the accuracy metric. The data are UMI-based counts without allelic multi-read ambiguity (e.g. the Larsson et al. 224-cell UMI data), where multi-read allocation and pooling gains of this kind do not apply as designed. The goal is inference of transcriptional burst kinetics parameters (k_on, k_off, k_syn) rather than allelic proportion estimation accuracy — use txburst instead. Full-depth data are unavailable, so no reference allelic proportions exist against which down-sampled MSE can be computed. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Benchmark estimation precision of allelic proportion methods by randomly down-sampling reads (1% in 122 blastocyst cells), re-estimating proportions under alternative read-counting schemes, and comparing per-gene mean squared error (MSE) against full-data estimates. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-13099-0
skills.summary: Benchmark estimation precision of allelic proportion methods by randomly down-sampling reads (1% in 122 blastocyst cells), re-estimating proportions under alternative read-counting schemes, and comparing per-gene mean squared error (MSE) against full-data estimates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are UMI-based counts without allelic multi-read ambiguity (e.g. the Larsson et al. 224-cell UMI data), where multi-read allocation and pooling gains of this kind do not apply as designed. The goal is inference of transcriptional burst kinetics parameters (k_on, k_off, k_syn) rather than allelic proportion estimation accuracy — use txburst instead. Full-depth data are unavailable, so no reference allelic proportions exist against which down-sampled MSE can be computed.

skills.description: Use when classifying target scRNA-seq cells against reference clusters with scID and you need to select c+/c- training cells and estimate gene signature weights, especially when data have batch effect.
skills.name: dpr-training-cell-selection
skills.search_text: dpr-training-cell-selection Use when classifying target scRNA-seq cells against reference clusters with scID and you need to select c+/c- training cells and estimate gene signature weights, especially when data have batch effect. The reference and target data lack good clustering and well-defined gene signatures — the article states scID 'is not a recommended approach' in that case Input gene expression matrices are log-transformed — scID requires library-depth (TPM/CPM) normalized data, 'but not log-transformed data' The goal is cell-type discovery without a labeled reference; scID/DPR training-cell selection presupposes reference clusters with known labels http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Stage-2 of the scID pipeline: identify putative positive (c+) and negative (c-) training cells via differential precision-recall (DPR) and fit discriminative Fisher's Linear Discriminant Analysis-like gene signature weights from them. This bridges reference-cluster gene signatures and target-cell scoring in scID. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2020.100914
skills.summary: Stage-2 of the scID pipeline: identify putative positive (c+) and negative (c-) training cells via differential precision-recall (DPR) and fit discriminative Fisher's Linear Discriminant Analysis-like gene signature weights from them. This bridges reference-cluster gene signatures and target-cell scoring in scID.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reference and target data lack good clustering and well-defined gene signatures — the article states scID 'is not a recommended approach' in that case Input gene expression matrices are log-transformed — scID requires library-depth (TPM/CPM) normalized data, 'but not log-transformed data' The goal is cell-type discovery without a labeled reference; scID/DPR training-cell selection presupposes reference clusters with known labels

skills.description: Use when one or more predicted driver gene lists (from WMDS.net, unweighted MDS, or degree-only ranking) must be scored against a curated cancer gene benchmark to compare precision/recall trade-offs.

skills.search_text: driver-gene-benchmark-evaluation Use when one or more predicted driver gene lists (from WMDS.net, unweighted MDS, or degree-only ranking) must be scored against a curated cancer gene benchmark to compare precision/recall trade-offs. The compared gene lists come from networks of different sizes or different node sets, making equal-size baseline comparisons invalid. You only need raw differential co-expression network construction — this skill evaluates downstream driver predictions, not the ΔZ Fisher-Z network itself. http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmarks predicted cancer driver gene lists against the 616-gene CGC benchmark using precision, recall, and the Fβ-measure with β² = 0.2, in order to verify that biologically weighted network-control methods (e.g. WMDS.net) beat unweighted MDS and degree-only baselines. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad071
skills.summary: Benchmarks predicted cancer driver gene lists against the 616-gene CGC benchmark using precision, recall, and the Fβ-measure with β² = 0.2, in order to verify that biologically weighted network-control methods (e.g. WMDS.net) beat unweighted MDS and degree-only baselines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The prediction target is not cancer driver genes and no curated benchmark gene set (like the CGC 616-gene set) is available for validation. skills.description: Use when you have per-patient personalized driver gene lists from sample-specific networks (e.g., WMDS.netP on TCGA RNA-seq) and need to tabulate how often each driver gene recurs across patients by cancer type.
skills.name: driver-gene-frequency-stratification
skills.search_text: driver-gene-frequency-stratification Use when you have per-patient personalized driver gene lists from sample-specific networks (e.g., WMDS.netP on TCGA RNA-seq) and need to tabulate how often each driver gene recurs across patients by cancer type. Your driver calls come from a global (pan-cohort) method like WMDS.net rather than per-patient WMDS.netP lists — recurrence stratification requires patient-level driver sets, and the global list has no per-patient frequency (e.g., CDKN2A is in the LUAD WMDS.netP list but absent from the global WMDS.net list) You only have a single cohort without per-patient sample-specific networks — with no per-patient driver sets there is no recurrence frequency to bin http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Stratify personalized driver genes predicted per-patient by WMDS.net (WMDS.netP) into high (>=0.6), medium (0.3-0.6), and low (<0.3) recurrence-frequency classes per cancer type, in order to quantify within-cancer-type tumor heterogeneity. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad071
skills.summary: Stratify personalized driver genes predicted per-patient by WMDS.net (WMDS.netP) into high (>=0.6), medium (0.3-0.6), and low (<0.3) recurrence-frequency classes per cancer type, in order to quantify within-cancer-type tumor heterogeneity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your driver calls come from a global (pan-cohort) method like WMDS.net rather than per-patient WMDS.netP lists — recurrence stratification requires patient-level driver sets, and the global list has no per-patient frequency (e.g., CDKN2A is in the LUAD WMDS.netP list but absent from the global WMDS.net list) You only have a single cohort without per-patient sample-specific networks — with no per-patient driver sets there is no recurrence frequency to bin

skills.description: Use when you have a differential co-expression network with per-edge differential co-expression P-values p_ij and need node weights for a weighted minimum dominating set formulation of driver-node selection.
skills.name: driver-node-weight-computation
skills.search_text: driver-node-weight-computation Use when you have a differential co-expression network with per-edge differential co-expression P-values p_ij and need node weights for a weighted minimum dominating set formulation of driver-node selection. The network is a plain gene interaction/hub network without per-edge differential co-expression P-values, so −log p_ij sums cannot be computed (e.g. the DawnRank-derived Gene_Net used only as the hub backbone). The goal is driver-node selection by methods other than weighted minimum dominating set, such as ranking-based or per-sample approaches like DawnRank. Only a single physiological state is available, so differential co-expression significance between two states cannot be assessed. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3366 Computes per-node weights w_i = (Σ_{j∈∂i} −log p_ij)^(−γ), with γ = 0.01, from a differential gene co-expression network so that driver-node selection via weighted minimum dominating set (WMDS) integrates node degree and the significance of co-expression difference between two physiological states. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad071
skills.summary: Computes per-node weights w_i = (Σ_{j∈∂i} −log p_ij)^(−γ), with γ = 0.01, from a differential gene co-expression network so that driver-node selection via weighted minimum dominating set (WMDS) integrates node degree and the significance of co-expression difference between two physiological states.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The network is a plain gene interaction/hub network without per-edge differential co-expression P-values, so −log p_ij sums cannot be computed (e.g. the DawnRank-derived Gene_Net used only as the hub backbone). skills.search_text: drop-one-out-cluster-perturbation-analysis Use when you have per-patient ASGARD drug scores across annotated cell clusters and want to quantify how sensitive those scores are to each cell type by excluding one cluster at a time. skills.description: Use when raw 10X droplet count matrices (CellRanger raw_feature_bc_matrix or 10X feature-barcode output) show extranuclear RNA contamination (elevated MT%/MALAT1%) or spurious cell types after hard-count-cutoff filtering of snRNA-seq data.
skills.name: droplet-based-scrnaseq-preprocessing
skills.search_text: droplet-based-scrnaseq-preprocessing Use when raw 10X droplet count matrices (CellRanger raw_feature_bc_matrix or 10X feature-barcode output) show extranuclear RNA contamination (elevated MT%/MALAT1%) or spurious cell types after hard-count-cutoff filtering of snRNA-seq data. skills.name: dropout-non-detection-probability-estimation
skills.search_text: dropout-non-detection-probability-estimation Use when computing gene-gene co-expression correlations from sparse, zero-inflated single-cell RNA-seq count matrices (e.g. ~70% zeros) where naive Pearson/Spearman correlations are distorted by dropout zeros. Input data are bulk RNA-seq or otherwise not zero-inflated single-cell counts — the dropout-mixture filtering adds no benefit and discards information The goal is a sparse network of direct gene associations rather than pairwise co-expression; use scLink's sclink_net (penalized Gaussian graphical model) instead of correlation-only output Data have already been imputed (e.g. with scImpute) — the article notes imputed data may still be much sparser than bulk data and imputation can be time-consuming, so the estimator's confidence filtering is intended for the observed count matrix http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Reconstructs scLink's robust co-expression estimator, which fits a per-gene Gamma-Normal mixture model by EM to estimate each cell's non-detection (dropout) probability d_ij, then computes pairwise-complete Pearson correlations using only confidently measured cells (d_ij < 0.5). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2020.11.006
skills.summary: Reconstructs scLink's robust co-expression estimator, which fits a per-gene Gamma-Normal mixture model by EM to estimate each cell's non-detection (dropout) probability d_ij, then computes pairwise-complete Pearson correlations using only confidently measured cells (d_ij < 0.5).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data are bulk RNA-seq or otherwise not zero-inflated single-cell counts — the dropout-mixture filtering adds no benefit and discards information The goal is a sparse network of direct gene associations rather than pairwise co-expression; use scLink's sclink_net (penalized Gaussian graphical model) instead of correlation-only output Data have already been imputed (e.g. with scImpute) — the article notes imputed data may still be much sparser than bulk data and imputation can be time-consuming, so the estimator's confidence filtering is intended for the observed count matrix

skills.description: Use when you must quantify how robust a cell-type annotation method is to dropout by sweeping Splatter's dropout.shape/dropout.mid parameters over simulated datasets with known ground-truth labels.
skills.name: dropout-parameter-sweep-design
skills.search_text: dropout-parameter-sweep-design Use when you must quantify how robust a cell-type annotation method is to dropout by sweeping Splatter's dropout.shape/dropout.mid parameters over simulated datasets with known ground-truth labels. Your input is real experimental scRNA-seq data without ground-truth labels — this skill requires simulated datasets with known cell-type labels for accuracy scoring The comparator method cannot accept custom marker sets (e.g. scCATCH was excluded because 'its implementation does not allow for the use custom markers') Your goal is dropout correction/imputation of data rather than benchmarking annotation robustness — the article notes dropout correction (e.g. scDoc) is planned but not part of the current ScType pipeline Design a Splatter-based simulation parameter sweep that generates scRNA-seq datasets across controlled dropout levels (~50%, ~65%, ~80%) to benchmark the robustness of ScType's marker-based cell-type annotation against comparators such as scSorter and SCINA. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-28803-w
skills.summary: Design a Splatter-based simulation parameter sweep that generates scRNA-seq datasets across controlled dropout levels (~50%, ~65%, ~80%) to benchmark the robustness of ScType's marker-based cell-type annotation against comparators such as scSorter and SCINA.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your input is real experimental scRNA-seq data without ground-truth labels — this skill requires simulated datasets with known cell-type labels for accuracy scoring The comparator method cannot accept custom marker sets (e.g. scCATCH was excluded because 'its implementation does not allow for the use custom markers') Your goal is dropout correction/imputation of data rather than benchmarking annotation robustness — the article notes dropout correction (e.g. scDoc) is planned but not part of the current ScType pipeline

skills.description: Use when simulating CRISPR lineage barcodes (e.g., TedSim SimulateCIFs) and you need to measure how dropout events degrade barcode quality — via Qr/Qh — or how they change relative performance of reconstruction methods like LinRace, DCLEAR, or Cassiopeia.
skills.name: dropout-perturbation-analysis
skills.search_text: dropout-perturbation-analysis Use when simulating CRISPR lineage barcodes (e.g., TedSim SimulateCIFs) and you need to measure how dropout events degrade barcode quality — via Qr/Qh — or how they change relative performance of reconstruction methods like LinRace, DCLEAR, or Cassiopeia. Barcode data contains no simulated or known ground-truth lineage tree, so Qr/Qh and RF/Nye/CID evaluation against truth cannot be computed The expression data are being analyzed for cell-state dynamics rather than barcode data-quality benchmarking — this skill is a perturbation/benchmark workflow, not a biological discovery analysis Dropout is negligible (p_d=0 and empirically absent) and the question is only about absolute mutation-rate effects without a paired no-dropout control http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 A benchmark-design skill for quantifying how lineage barcode dropout events perturb data quality and lineage-reconstruction accuracy, by sweeping dropout probability (p_d) alongside mutation rate in TedSim simulations and tracking both downstream method performance (RF distance, Nye similarity, CID) and barcode-quality metrics (reconstruction potential Qr, homoplasy edge ratio Qh). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-44173-3
skills.summary: A benchmark-design skill for quantifying how lineage barcode dropout events perturb data quality and lineage-reconstruction accuracy, by sweeping dropout probability (p_d) alongside mutation rate in TedSim simulations and tracking both downstream method performance (RF distance, Nye similarity, CID) and barcode-quality metrics (reconstruction potential Qr, homoplasy edge ratio Qh).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Barcode data contains no simulated or known ground-truth lineage tree, so Qr/Qh and RF/Nye/CID evaluation against truth cannot be computed The expression data are being analyzed for cell-state dynamics rather than barcode data-quality benchmarking — this skill is a perturbation/benchmark workflow, not a biological discovery analysis Dropout is negligible (p_d=0 and empirically absent) and the question is only about absolute mutation-rate effects without a paired no-dropout control

skills.description: Use when you must test whether a denoising method preserves or recovers biological structure (celltypes) in scRNA-seq data corrupted by dropout, using simulated ground truth rather than real data.
skills.name: dropout-perturbation-benchmarking
skills.search_text: dropout-perturbation-benchmarking Use when you must test whether a denoising method preserves or recovers biological structure (celltypes) in scRNA-seq data corrupted by dropout, using simulated ground truth rather than real data. Real scRNA-seq data with no reliable ground truth — the article notes evaluation of denoising is difficult because defining a ground truth for real data is challenging Questions about differential expression or trajectory accuracy rather than celltype structure recovery — this benchmark only assesses celltype separation metrics Datasets without dropout perturbation (no-dropout ground-truth simulations) — the contrast being tested requires the noisy vs. clean pair http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Benchmark scRNA-seq denoising methods under controlled dropout perturbation by simulating count data (e.g., with Splatter), applying methods such as DCA with a ZINB count loss versus a plain MSE autoencoder, and comparing celltype recovery against the no-dropout ground truth. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-07931-2
skills.summary: Benchmark scRNA-seq denoising methods under controlled dropout perturbation by simulating count data (e.g., with Splatter), applying methods such as DCA with a ZINB count loss versus a plain MSE autoencoder, and comparing celltype recovery against the no-dropout ground truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Real scRNA-seq data with no reliable ground truth — the article notes evaluation of denoising is difficult because defining a ground truth for real data is challenging Questions about differential expression or trajectory accuracy rather than celltype structure recovery — this benchmark only assesses celltype separation metrics Datasets without dropout perturbation (no-dropout ground-truth simulations) — the contrast being tested requires the noisy vs. clean pair

skills.description: Use when you have imputed single-cell expression matrices (hd5, log10(count+1) scale) plus a ground truth, and need to verify that dropout imputation recovers nonlinear gene-gene patterns rather than blurring them.
skills.name: dropout-recovery-assessment
skills.search_text: dropout-recovery-assessment Use when you have imputed single-cell expression matrices (hd5, log10(count+1) scale) plus a ground truth, and need to verify that dropout imputation recovers nonlinear gene-gene patterns rather than blurring them. No ground-truth (or reference) matrix exists for the dataset — the paper sets ground truth equal to the input in that case, so the recovery assessment is uninformative The imputed matrices are on a different scale than log10(count+1) or lack shared gene/cell identifiers with the input — panels would be incomparable until harmonized The goal is quantitative imputation accuracy (e.g. mean squared error comparison) rather than visual assessment of recovered nonlinear gene-gene relationships http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Assesses whether imputation methods (LATE, TRANSLATE) recover nonlinear gene-gene relationships masked by scRNA-seq dropouts, by drawing scatterplots of gene-pair expression from imputed matrices (LATE, TRANSLATE, MAGIC, SAVER, ALRA, scImpute, DCA, scVI) against the ground truth on datasets such as MAGIC_mouse, GTEx_4tissues, and PBMC_G949. transcriptomics/v2 10.1007/s40484-019-0192-7
skills.summary: Assesses whether imputation methods (LATE, TRANSLATE) recover nonlinear gene-gene relationships masked by scRNA-seq dropouts, by drawing scatterplots of gene-pair expression from imputed matrices (LATE, TRANSLATE, MAGIC, SAVER, ALRA, scImpute, DCA, scVI) against the ground truth on datasets such as MAGIC_mouse, GTEx_4tissues, and PBMC_G949.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No ground-truth (or reference) matrix exists for the dataset — the paper sets ground truth equal to the input in that case, so the recovery assessment is uninformative The imputed matrices are on a different scale than log10(count+1) or lack shared gene/cell identifiers with the input — panels would be incomparable until harmonized The goal is quantitative imputation accuracy (e.g. mean squared error comparison) rather than visual assessment of recovered nonlinear gene-gene relationships

skills.description: Use when a heterogeneous single-cell RNA-seq matrix shows high noise/dropout and you need to identify the genes that explain differences across inferred sample populations, downstream of SIMLR similarity learning.
skills.name: dropout-robust-gene-expression-analysis
skills.search_text: dropout-robust-gene-expression-analysis Use when a heterogeneous single-cell RNA-seq matrix shows high noise/dropout and you need to identify the genes that explain differences across inferred sample populations, downstream of SIMLR similarity learning. The analysis goal requires supervised feature selection against a known functional gene subset — SIMLR is unsupervised and allows only de novo discovery from the data Input is a large-scale dataset where the standard implementation is too slow — use SIMLR_Large_Scale for the clustering step instead (feature ranking operates on the learned similarities) Data are bulk RNA-seq or non-single-cell expression profiles for which the noise/dropout model of SIMLR was not designed http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Rank genes by their concordance with the sample-to-sample similarities learned by SIMLR's multi-kernel framework, using graph diffusion to correct weak similarities caused by noise and dropout events in single-cell RNA-seq data. This makes feature prioritization de novo and dropout-robust rather than dependent on pre-selected gene subsets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1002/pmic.201700232
skills.summary: Rank genes by their concordance with the sample-to-sample similarities learned by SIMLR's multi-kernel framework, using graph diffusion to correct weak similarities caused by noise and dropout events in single-cell RNA-seq data. This makes feature prioritization de novo and dropout-robust rather than dependent on pre-selected gene subsets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal requires supervised feature selection against a known functional gene subset — SIMLR is unsupervised and allows only de novo discovery from the data Input is a large-scale dataset where the standard implementation is too slow — use SIMLR_Large_Scale for the clustering step instead (feature ranking operates on the learned similarities) Data are bulk RNA-seq or non-single-cell expression profiles for which the noise/dropout model of SIMLR was not designed

skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq data contain high noise and dropout events that weaken cell-to-cell similarity measures, and an unsupervised distance metric is needed for clustering heterogeneous populations (e.g., PBMC subpopulations).
skills.name: dropout-robust-graph-diffusion
skills.search_text: dropout-robust-graph-diffusion Use when scRNA-seq data contain high noise and dropout events that weaken cell-to-cell similarity measures, and an unsupervised distance metric is needed for clustering heterogeneous populations (e.g., PBMC subpopulations). The analysis requires pre-selected gene subsets of known function — SIMLR is explicitly unsupervised, allowing de novo discovery from the data. The data are not single-cell expression measurements with noise/dropout-driven weak similarities; the multi-kernel and graph-diffusion machinery targets scRNA-seq statistical characteristics. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A similarity-learning approach from SIMLR that combines multiple kernels and applies graph diffusion to strengthen cell-to-cell similarities weakened by noise and dropout events in single-cell RNA-seq data, supporting unsupervised dimension reduction, clustering, and visualization. transcriptomics/v2 10.1002/pmic.201700232
skills.summary: A similarity-learning approach from SIMLR that combines multiple kernels and applies graph diffusion to strengthen cell-to-cell similarities weakened by noise and dropout events in single-cell RNA-seq data, supporting unsupervised dimension reduction, clustering, and visualization.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis requires pre-selected gene subsets of known function — SIMLR is explicitly unsupervised, allowing de novo discovery from the data. The data are not single-cell expression measurements with noise/dropout-driven weak similarities; the multi-kernel and graph-diffusion machinery targets scRNA-seq statistical characteristics.

skills.description: Use when stress-testing a cross-omics integration/label-transfer method against simulated dropout noise in scRNA-seq data, or when reporting stability of scBridge under count down-sampling regimes.
skills.name: dropout-robustness-benchmarking
skills.search_text: dropout-robustness-benchmarking Use when stress-testing a cross-omics integration/label-transfer method against simulated dropout noise in scRNA-seq data, or when reporting stability of scBridge under count down-sampling regimes. The goal is to evaluate robustness to batch effects, normalization differences, or paired multi-omics differences rather than simulated dropout noise Input data are protein (CITE-seq/ASAP-seq) measurements, since this benchmark's down-sampling targets the scRNA-seq count matrix The method under test cannot accept the scuttle downsampleMatrix-generated corrupted source matrices in h5ad format http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark robustness of scBridge's scRNA-seq to scATAC-seq integration and label transfer by down-sampling source counts at 25%, 50%, and 75% dropout and comparing label transfer accuracy and silhouette score against the uncorrupted baseline. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-41795-5
skills.summary: Benchmark robustness of scBridge's scRNA-seq to scATAC-seq integration and label transfer by down-sampling source counts at 25%, 50%, and 75% dropout and comparing label transfer accuracy and silhouette score against the uncorrupted baseline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to evaluate robustness to batch effects, normalization differences, or paired multi-omics differences rather than simulated dropout noise Input data are protein (CITE-seq/ASAP-seq) measurements, since this benchmark's down-sampling targets the scRNA-seq count matrix The method under test cannot accept the scuttle downsampleMatrix-generated corrupted source matrices in h5ad format

skills.description: Use when a scRNA-seq clustering/dimensionality-reduction method's robustness to dropout (zero-inflation) must be quantified, i.e. simulated count matrices at multiple dropout rates with ground-truth cell labels are available and NMI versus true labels is the target metric.
skills.name: dropout-robustness-evaluation-across-simulated-scenarios
skills.search_text: dropout-robustness-evaluation-across-simulated-scenarios Use when a scRNA-seq clustering/dimensionality-reduction method's robustness to dropout (zero-inflation) must be quantified, i.e. simulated count matrices at multiple dropout rates with ground-truth cell labels are available and NMI versus true labels is the target metric. Input is a single empirical dataset without ground-truth labels or controlled dropout levels — NMI versus true labels cannot be computed and dropout robustness cannot be swept Goal is 2D visualization rather than robustness quantification — the paper notes the graph autoencoder cannot directly embed into 2D and requires an intermediate dimension plus tSNE, a different workflow The competing method is scGNN-style trajectory inference — the evaluation target here is clustering NMI, where the paper reports scGAE, not trajectory reconstruction, as the differentiator http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Quantifies how robust a scRNA-seq dimensionality-reduction-and-clustering pipeline is to zero-inflation by recomputing clustering NMI across simulated scenario4 datasets spanning four dropout rates (12%, 17%, 23%, 30%) and showing the metric stays near-constant (0.61–0.65 for scGAE). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-99003-7
skills.summary: Quantifies how robust a scRNA-seq dimensionality-reduction-and-clustering pipeline is to zero-inflation by recomputing clustering NMI across simulated scenario4 datasets spanning four dropout rates (12%, 17%, 23%, 30%) and showing the metric stays near-constant (0.61–0.65 for scGAE).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single empirical dataset without ground-truth labels or controlled dropout levels — NMI versus true labels cannot be computed and dropout robustness cannot be swept Goal is 2D visualization rather than robustness quantification — the paper notes the graph autoencoder cannot directly embed into 2D and requires an intermediate dimension plus tSNE, a different workflow The competing method is scGNN-style trajectory inference — the evaluation target here is clustering NMI, where the paper reports scGAE, not trajectory reconstruction, as the differentiator

skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq count data are sparse with high dropout rates and a robust binary low-dimensional cell representation is needed before clustering, e.g. SMARTer or CEL-Seq2 data such as Xin GSE81608.
skills.name: dropout-tolerant-consensus-landmark-computation
skills.search_text: dropout-tolerant-consensus-landmark-computation Use when scRNA-seq count data are sparse with high dropout rates and a robust binary low-dimensional cell representation is needed before clustering, e.g. SMARTer or CEL-Seq2 data such as Xin GSE81608. The input is already a binary or feature-reduced landmark table — LC1 expects raw/log-normalized continuous expression values to binarize The analysis goal is quantitative trend-preserved gene clustering — that is the separate scQA LC2 module, not LC1 Preserving per-gene expression magnitude is required, since binarization discards expression levels entirely http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Implements scQA's qualitative landmark constructor (LC1), which binarizes dropout-prone scRNA-seq expression and amalgamates genes sharing analogous binary expression patterns into consensus binary landmarks, yielding a low-dimensional qualitative representation of cells. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.12.021
skills.summary: Implements scQA's qualitative landmark constructor (LC1), which binarizes dropout-prone scRNA-seq expression and amalgamates genes sharing analogous binary expression patterns into consensus binary landmarks, yielding a low-dimensional qualitative representation of cells.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a binary or feature-reduced landmark table — LC1 expects raw/log-normalized continuous expression values to binarize The analysis goal is quantitative trend-preserved gene clustering — that is the separate scQA LC2 module, not LC1 Preserving per-gene expression magnitude is required, since binarization discards expression levels entirely

skills.description: Use when benchmarking network inference methods on synthetic scRNA-seq data where excess zero counts (dropout) must be introduced at controlled rates, or when ground-truth power-law/hub network topologies are needed for AUPRC/AUROC evaluation.
skills.name: dropout-zero-count-simulation
skills.search_text: dropout-zero-count-simulation Use when benchmarking network inference methods on synthetic scRNA-seq data where excess zero counts (dropout) must be introduced at controlled rates, or when ground-truth power-law/hub network topologies are needed for AUPRC/AUROC evaluation. Analyzing a real single-cell dataset without known ground-truth network topology — simulated AUPRC/AUROC validation does not apply The input is already a sparse count matrix and the goal is network inference itself (e.g., running sclink_net) rather than benchmarking method accuracy under dropout Evaluating methods that require direction-aware (regulatory) networks, since scLink edges are based on statistical dependencies and do not have directions http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3523 Simulates single-cell expression data with controlled dropout (extra zero counts) to benchmark gene co-expression network inference methods like scLink against correlation- and model-based baselines under known ground-truth topologies. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2020.11.006
skills.summary: Simulates single-cell expression data with controlled dropout (extra zero counts) to benchmark gene co-expression network inference methods like scLink against correlation- and model-based baselines under known ground-truth topologies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Analyzing a real single-cell dataset without known ground-truth network topology — simulated AUPRC/AUROC validation does not apply The input is already a sparse count matrix and the goal is network inference itself (e.g., running sclink_net) rather than benchmarking method accuracy under dropout Evaluating methods that require direction-aware (regulatory) networks, since scLink edges are based on statistical dependencies and do not have directions

skills.description: Use when building a benchmark simulation for confounder-removal or normalization methods in scRNA-seq: you need count matrices with known latent factors, a group signature of 200 DE genes, and controlled zero inflation via dropout.
skills.name: dropout-zero-inflation-simulation
skills.search_text: dropout-zero-inflation-simulation Use when building a benchmark simulation for confounder-removal or normalization methods in scRNA-seq: you need count matrices with known latent factors, a group signature of 200 DE genes, and controlled zero inflation via dropout. Applying the simulated-data rationale directly to real scRNAseq studies: scPLS's framework itself does not model count data, and extending it to modeling count data is explicitly left as future work Using the simulation to recover biological factors u_i themselves — the associated method can only infer biological effects (Lambda_u u_i), not the factors, because of model identifiability Evaluating downstream analyses other than clustering (e.g. differential expression, lineage reconstruction), which the source study declares beyond its scope http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Generates synthetic scRNA-seq count matrices with latent confounding (kz=2) and biological (ku=5) factors over 200 cells and 1,050 genes (50 control + 1,000 target), converting continuous expression to UMI-like counts via Poisson sampling and optionally applying a dropout procedure to mimic zero inflation, for benchmarking scPLS against other confounding-effect removal methods. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-017-13665-w
skills.summary: Generates synthetic scRNA-seq count matrices with latent confounding (kz=2) and biological (ku=5) factors over 200 cells and 1,050 genes (50 control + 1,000 target), converting continuous expression to UMI-like counts via Poisson sampling and optionally applying a dropout procedure to mimic zero inflation, for benchmarking scPLS against other confounding-effect removal methods.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Applying the simulated-data rationale directly to real scRNAseq studies: scPLS's framework itself does not model count data, and extending it to modeling count data is explicitly left as future work Using the simulation to recover biological factors u_i themselves — the associated method can only infer biological effects (Lambda_u u_i), not the factors, because of model identifiability Evaluating downstream analyses other than clustering (e.g. differential expression, lineage reconstruction), which the source study declares beyond its scope

skills.description: Use when validating that a Bayesian scRNA-seq model's dropout (zero-inflation) component captures observed zero-count rates, or when quantifying how much model misfit a negative-binomial-only model incurs under non-UMI protocols.
skills.name: dropout-zero-rate-estimation-scrna-seq
skills.search_text: dropout-zero-rate-estimation-scrna-seq Use when validating that a Bayesian scRNA-seq model's dropout (zero-inflation) component captures observed zero-count rates, or when quantifying how much model misfit a negative-binomial-only model incurs under non-UMI protocols. The input is UMI count data where zero rates are driven by sequencing depth rather than protocol-level dropout, so the non-UMI misfit signal (SMART-seq2-type batches) will not be diagnostic The goal is batch effects correction or cell-type clustering itself rather than model-fit validation of the zero-inflation component A completely confounded experimental design applies (batch 1 measures cell types 1 and 2, batch 2 measures cell types 3 and 4), for which no method including BUSseq is applicable http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Reproduce a posterior predictive check of per-batch zero rates by fitting the full zero-inflated BUSseq model and the reduced BUSseq-nzf model (dropout coefficient fixed at zero) to real scRNA-seq read counts, then comparing posterior-mean zero rates from simulated replicates against the observed zero rates (Table 1). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-16905-2
skills.summary: Reproduce a posterior predictive check of per-batch zero rates by fitting the full zero-inflated BUSseq model and the reduced BUSseq-nzf model (dropout coefficient fixed at zero) to real scRNA-seq read counts, then comparing posterior-mean zero rates from simulated replicates against the observed zero rates (Table 1).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is UMI count data where zero rates are driven by sequencing depth rather than protocol-level dropout, so the non-UMI misfit signal (SMART-seq2-type batches) will not be diagnostic The goal is batch effects correction or cell-type clustering itself rather than model-fit validation of the zero-inflation component A completely confounded experimental design applies (batch 1 measures cell types 1 and 2, batch 2 measures cell types 3 and 4), for which no method including BUSseq is applicable

skills.description: Use when a simulated scRNA-Seq dataset was generated by applying dropout noise to a known true count matrix (e.g., a Splatter simulation) and you need a scalar measure of imputation recovery at dropout positions.
skills.name: dropout-zero-recovery-quantification
skills.search_text: dropout-zero-recovery-quantification Use when a simulated scRNA-Seq dataset was generated by applying dropout noise to a known true count matrix (e.g., a Splatter simulation) and you need a scalar measure of imputation recovery at dropout positions. The dataset is real experimental scRNA-Seq data with no known true counts, so the set of dropout zero positions cannot be defined against ground truth The noise in the simulated data is not dropout (e.g., uniform, Gaussian, Gamma, Poisson, or negative binomial noise); use MSE between true and imputed values instead, as done for Datasets 3-7 You only need cell-type structure recovery rather than value-level recovery at zeroed positions; average silhouette width (ASW) on the t-SNE embedding is the appropriate metric http://edamontology.org/topic_3524 Quantifies how well an imputation/denoising method restores expression values at positions where simulated dropout noise zeroed out true counts, by comparing average recovered values against average true values at exactly those dropout zero positions. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-29576-y
skills.summary: Quantifies how well an imputation/denoising method restores expression values at positions where simulated dropout noise zeroed out true counts, by comparing average recovered values against average true values at exactly those dropout zero positions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is real experimental scRNA-Seq data with no known true counts, so the set of dropout zero positions cannot be defined against ground truth The noise in the simulated data is not dropout (e.g., uniform, Gaussian, Gamma, Poisson, or negative binomial noise); use MSE between true and imputed values instead, as done for Datasets 3-7 You only need cell-type structure recovery rather than value-level recovery at zeroed positions; average silhouette width (ASW) on the t-SNE embedding is the appropriate metric

skills.description: Use when analyzing Drosophila embryo scRNA-seq (Synapse syn15665609) with a SpaOTsc-derived cell–cell distance matrix and the goal is to infer which gene in one cell regulates a gene in a neighbor cell across spatial distances.
skills.name: drosophila-embryo-gene-expression-analysis
skills.search_text: drosophila-embryo-gene-expression-analysis Use when analyzing Drosophila embryo scRNA-seq (Synapse syn15665609) with a SpaOTsc-derived cell–cell distance matrix and the goal is to infer which gene in one cell regulates a gene in a neighbor cell across spatial distances. No spatial measurements or SpaOTsc-derived cell–cell distance matrix is available — PID neighborhoods cannot be constructed without a spatial metric for individual cells The dataset is excessively large — the article notes 'the computation can become intractable when the dataset is excessively large' for optimal-transport-based distance inference over all cell pairs The goal is signaling between known ligand–receptor pairs with effect ranges (e.g. Wnt5–fz at 10/50/100 µm) rather than genome-wide information flow — use spsc.infer_signal_range_ml or spsc.spatial_signaling_ot instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Infers intercellular gene–gene regulatory information flow in the Drosophila embryo by computing partial information decomposition (PID) over spatially arranged scRNA-seq neighborhoods derived from SpaOTsc cell–cell distances, e.g. detecting the Twist→Snail link peaking at ~25 µm. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-15968-5
skills.summary: Infers intercellular gene–gene regulatory information flow in the Drosophila embryo by computing partial information decomposition (PID) over spatially arranged scRNA-seq neighborhoods derived from SpaOTsc cell–cell distances, e.g. detecting the Twist→Snail link peaking at ~25 µm.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No spatial measurements or SpaOTsc-derived cell–cell distance matrix is available — PID neighborhoods cannot be constructed without a spatial metric for individual cells The dataset is excessively large — the article notes 'the computation can become intractable when the dataset is excessively large' for optimal-transport-based distance inference over all cell pairs The goal is signaling between known ligand–receptor pairs with effect ranges (e.g. Wnt5–fz at 10/50/100 µm) rather than genome-wide information flow — use spsc.infer_signal_range_ml or spsc.spatial_signaling_ot instead

skills.description: Use when mapping scRNA-seq cells to spatial positions of the Drosophila embryo (bdtnp.txt, geometry.txt, dge_normalized.txt) and you need the dissimilarity/distance matrices for an unbalanced structured optimal transport plan.
skills.name: drosophila-embryo-spatial-coordinate-processing
skills.search_text: drosophila-embryo-spatial-coordinate-processing Use when mapping scRNA-seq cells to spatial positions of the Drosophila embryo (bdtnp.txt, geometry.txt, dge_normalized.txt) and you need the dissimilarity/distance matrices for an unbalanced structured optimal transport plan.
