skills.description: Use when assembling viral contigs from unmapped RNAseq FASTQ reads without an aligner, using model-predicted viral reads as seeds and exact k-mer overlap extension to grow contigs.
skills.name: exact-kmer-overlap-extension
skills.search_text: exact-kmer-overlap-extension Use when assembling viral contigs from unmapped RNAseq FASTQ reads without an aligner, using model-predicted viral reads as seeds and exact k-mer overlap extension to grow contigs. Reads are already aligned to the human genome (hg19) or to phiX phage — viRNAtrap is applied only to unaligned reads to reduce running time. The analysis requires full-fledged genome assembly with mismatch/gap tolerance — this greedy method only extends through exact 24bp k-mer overlaps. An output file for the same input already exists — virnatrap-predict will not overwrite existing output files and must have them removed first. http://edamontology.org/topic_0781 http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Alignment-free greedy contig assembly used in viRNAtrap: seed on deep-learning-scored viral 48bp reads, then iteratively extend left and right by finding reads sharing an exact 24bp k-mer with the current contig end, guided by model scores. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-36336-z
skills.summary: Alignment-free greedy contig assembly used in viRNAtrap: seed on deep-learning-scored viral 48bp reads, then iteratively extend left and right by finding reads sharing an exact 24bp k-mer with the current contig end, guided by model scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads are already aligned to the human genome (hg19) or to phiX phage — viRNAtrap is applied only to unaligned reads to reduce running time. The analysis requires full-fledged genome assembly with mismatch/gap tolerance — this greedy method only extends through exact 24bp k-mer overlaps. An output file for the same input already exists — virnatrap-predict will not overwrite existing output files and must have them removed first.

skills.name: excel-date-conversion-gene-list-recovery
skills.search_text: excel-date-conversion-gene-list-recovery Use when a .csv or .xlsx gene expression list opened in Excel contains gene symbols auto-converted to dates (e.g. Mar-01, Mar-02) or outdated gene names that pathway enrichment tools like Enrichr or GSEA cannot recognize. The gene list already contains valid, current HGNC symbols and never passed through Excel — no date conversion or name update is needed You need to run pathway enrichment on an already-corrected gene list — use pathway enrichment tools (e.g. Enrichr against GO Biological Processes) instead of the date-recovery workflow The 'date-like' entries are legitimate date values in a non-gene column — converting them would corrupt real data http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 Recover gene lists corrupted by Excel's automatic conversion of gene symbols to dates (e.g. SEPT1, MARC1 becoming 1-Sep, 1-Mar) using the Gene Updater Streamlit web tool, and convert old gene names back to HGNC-recommended symbols so pathway databases can recognize them. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-022-17104-3
skills.summary: Recover gene lists corrupted by Excel's automatic conversion of gene symbols to dates (e.g. SEPT1, MARC1 becoming 1-Sep, 1-Mar) using the Gene Updater Streamlit web tool, and convert old gene names back to HGNC-recommended symbols so pathway databases can recognize them.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The gene list already contains valid, current HGNC symbols and never passed through Excel — no date conversion or name update is needed You need to run pathway enrichment on an already-corrected gene list — use pathway enrichment tools (e.g. Enrichr against GO Biological Processes) instead of the date-recovery workflow The 'date-like' entries are legitimate date values in a non-gene column — converting them would corrupt real data

skills.description: Use when scaling claims about a feature selection or clustering method must be quantified: run the method on downsamplings (10k, 100k cells) and the full dataset (1M+ cells) and record per-method runtime and peak memory.
skills.name: execution-time-memory-profiling
skills.search_text: execution-time-memory-profiling Use when scaling claims about a feature selection or clustering method must be quantified: run the method on downsamplings (10k, 100k cells) and the full dataset (1M+ cells) and record per-method runtime and peak memory. The goal is clustering accuracy comparison (silhouette index, number of feature genes) rather than computational scalability profiling The input dataset is small enough that runtime and memory differences between methods are not informative The method under test is a correlation-free baseline whose memory behavior is already established and does not need re-benchmarking http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Benchmark wall-clock runtime and peak memory consumption of scRNA-seq feature selection methods (DUBStepR, HVGDisp, HVGVST, trendVar, devianceFS, M3DropDANB, GiniClust, HLG) across dataset scales on the mouse organogenesis scRNA-seq data, to quantify scalability claims such as DUBStepR's 6.4x memory increase from 100k to 1M cells. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-26085-2
skills.summary: Benchmark wall-clock runtime and peak memory consumption of scRNA-seq feature selection methods (DUBStepR, HVGDisp, HVGVST, trendVar, devianceFS, M3DropDANB, GiniClust, HLG) across dataset scales on the mouse organogenesis scRNA-seq data, to quantify scalability claims such as DUBStepR's 6.4x memory increase from 100k to 1M cells.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is clustering accuracy comparison (silhouette index, number of feature genes) rather than computational scalability profiling The input dataset is small enough that runtime and memory differences between methods are not informative The method under test is a correlation-free baseline whose memory behavior is already established and does not need re-benchmarking

When the goal is predictive performance alone (sensitivity/specificity/accuracy) and runtime is irrelevant to the comparison When tools are run on different hardware or with non-default parameters, making runtime comparisons unfair and non-reproducible http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Profiles wall-clock execution time of GRN inference tools (Augusta with/without refinement, GENIE3, TDAracne, KBoost) on the same dataset and hardware, including per-step timing for Augusta's MI inference, TFBM discovery, and database-search refinement, to build a fair runtime benchmark table. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2024.01.013

skills.description: Use when comparing the consistency (not just the speed) of execution times between two methods or implementations across repeated benchmark runs, e.g. GPU-accelerated vs CPU-based pipelines on the same workstation.
skills.name: execution-time-variability-analysis
skills.search_text: execution-time-variability-analysis Use when comparing the consistency (not just the speed) of execution times between two methods or implementations across repeated benchmark runs, e.g. GPU-accelerated vs CPU-based pipelines on the same workstation. The goal is to compare mean/absolute runtime speed of the methods rather than run-to-run consistency — a simple mean execution-time comparison suffices and CoV adds no information. Only a single execution per condition is available, making the standard deviation (and hence CoV) undefined or unstable. The inputs are modelling outputs (3D structures) or biological results rather than benchmark timing logs — timing variability analysis does not apply. http://edamontology.org/topic_3315 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Quantifies run-time stability of cudaMMC versus 3D-GNOME by computing the coefficient of variation (CoV = std/mean × 100) of execution times over 10 repeated modelling runs per chromosome (chr1, chr14, chr21) from benchmark timing logs. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad588
skills.summary: Quantifies run-time stability of cudaMMC versus 3D-GNOME by computing the coefficient of variation (CoV = std/mean × 100) of execution times over 10 repeated modelling runs per chromosome (chr1, chr14, chr21) from benchmark timing logs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to compare mean/absolute runtime speed of the methods rather than run-to-run consistency — a simple mean execution-time comparison suffices and CoV adds no information. Only a single execution per condition is available, making the standard deviation (and hence CoV) undefined or unstable. The inputs are modelling outputs (3D structures) or biological results rather than benchmark timing logs — timing variability analysis does not apply.

skills.description: Use when re-implementing scBASE's seven-region gene classification on the Deng et al. CAST×B6 F1 pre-implantation data and you need to validate your mixture-weight thresholds and P/B/M posterior assignments against the paper's exemplar gene calls.
skills.name: exemplar-gene-call-reconciliation
skills.search_text: exemplar-gene-call-reconciliation Use when re-implementing scBASE's seven-region gene classification on the Deng et al. CAST×B6 F1 pre-implantation data and you need to validate your mixture-weight thresholds and P/B/M posterior assignments against the paper's exemplar gene calls. Input is raw FASTQ or unaligned reads — this skill operates on already-classified per-cell P/B/M posteriors, not on alignment or read counting (use EMASE weighted allocation first). Data are not from a CAST×B6 (or reciprocal) F1 hybrid with a phase-known diploid transcriptome — the P/B/M state labels and exemplar calls are allele-parent specific. The goal is burst-kinetics inference (k_on, k_off, k_syn) rather than descriptive ASE class assignment — txburst, not scBASE class thresholds, is the appropriate tool. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Reconciles gene-level ASE class assignments (P, B, M, PB, BM, MP, PBM) produced from scBASE posterior state probabilities against the exemplar gene calls reported in Choi et al. 2019 (Nature Communications), verifying that Pacs2, Mtdh, Timm23, Tulp3, and Akr1b3 fall in the same classes and that the blastocyst PBM-region fraction matches the reported 56.9%. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-13099-0
skills.summary: Reconciles gene-level ASE class assignments (P, B, M, PB, BM, MP, PBM) produced from scBASE posterior state probabilities against the exemplar gene calls reported in Choi et al. 2019 (Nature Communications), verifying that Pacs2, Mtdh, Timm23, Tulp3, and Akr1b3 fall in the same classes and that the blastocyst PBM-region fraction matches the reported 56.9%.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTQ or unaligned reads — this skill operates on already-classified per-cell P/B/M posteriors, not on alignment or read counting (use EMASE weighted allocation first). Data are not from a CAST×B6 (or reciprocal) F1 hybrid with a phase-known diploid transcriptome — the P/B/M state labels and exemplar calls are allele-parent specific. The goal is burst-kinetics inference (k_on, k_off, k_syn) rather than descriptive ASE class assignment — txburst, not scBASE class thresholds, is the appropriate tool.

skills.description: Use when you need a classical, deterministic single--split classification tree (e.g. on anorexia weight-change data with treatment/coding/interacting variable types) rather than the DIPM random-forest-based node fitting.
skills.name: exhaustive-split-search-tree-construction
skills.search_text: exhaustive-split-search-tree-construction Use when you need a classical, deterministic single--split classification tree (e.g. on anorexia weight-change data with treatment/coding/interacting variable types) rather than the DIPM random-forest-based node fitting. When you want the DIPM method itself, which fits a random forest at each node—use dipm(formula, data, types, nmin, nmin2, ntree, mtry, maxdepth, maxdepth2, ncores, print, dataframe, prune) instead When you need forest-based tuning parameters such as ntree, mtry, or ncores—spmtree does not fit a random forest and exposes only nmin and maxdepth http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Fits a subgroup-identification classification tree with the dipm package's spmtree function, which—unlike the DIPM forest-based node fitting—exhaustively evaluates every possible split of every candidate split variable at each node and keeps the single split with the highest split-criteria score. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac041
skills.summary: Fits a subgroup-identification classification tree with the dipm package's spmtree function, which—unlike the DIPM forest-based node fitting—exhaustively evaluates every possible split of every candidate split variable at each node and keeps the single split with the highest split-criteria score.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you want the DIPM method itself, which fits a random forest at each node—use dipm(formula, data, types, nmin, nmin2, ntree, mtry, maxdepth, maxdepth2, ncores, print, dataframe, prune) instead When you need forest-based tuning parameters such as ntree, mtry, or ncores—spmtree does not fit a random forest and exposes only nmin and maxdepth

skills.description: Use when RNA-seq alignments are available and the goal is to capture neoantigen sources beyond SNVs/indels, specifically exitron-splicing events that most neoantigen-prediction tools overlook.
skills.name: exitron-splicing-event-detection
skills.search_text: exitron-splicing-event-detection Use when RNA-seq alignments are available and the goal is to capture neoantigen sources beyond SNVs/indels, specifically exitron-splicing events that most neoantigen-prediction tools overlook. The variant of interest is a long indel or gene fusion — use the transIndel or Arriba modules instead, not the exitron module Only DNA-seq data is available with no RNA-seq alignment, since exitron splicing is called exclusively from RNA-seq The goal is canonical alternative splicing (exon skipping etc.) rather than exitrons — the SplAdder module covers that source http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Detects exitron-splicing events from RNA-seq alignments using ScanExitron within ScanNeo2's variant-calling stage, converting exitron calls into VCF records annotated with GRP and SRC=exitron INFO keys for downstream neoantigen extraction. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad659
skills.summary: Detects exitron-splicing events from RNA-seq alignments using ScanExitron within ScanNeo2's variant-calling stage, converting exitron calls into VCF records annotated with GRP and SRC=exitron INFO keys for downstream neoantigen extraction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The variant of interest is a long indel or gene fusion — use the transIndel or Arriba modules instead, not the exitron module Only DNA-seq data is available with no RNA-seq alignment, since exitron splicing is called exclusively from RNA-seq The goal is canonical alternative splicing (exon skipping etc.) rather than exitrons — the SplAdder module covers that source

skills.description: Use when you have per-event inclusion (IJC) and skipping (SJC) junction counts for reference and alternative alleles plus effective isoform lengths, and need length-normalized exon inclusion levels for ASAS testing.
skills.name: exon-inclusion-count-length-normalization
skills.search_text: exon-inclusion-count-length-normalization Use when you have per-event inclusion (IJC) and skipping (SJC) junction counts for reference and alternative alleles plus effective isoform lengths, and need length-normalized exon inclusion levels for ASAS testing. Input lacks effective isoform lengths (incLen/skpLen) — raw IJC/SJC counts alone cannot be length-normalized correctly The goal is within-condition quantification of PSI where the two isoforms have comparable effective lengths and the analysis is not differential (length correction is still advisable but this pipeline's IncLevel1/2 schema is allele-pair specific) Reads are not haplotype-assigned counts per allele (e.g., bulk gene-level counts from a standard quantifier), since IJC/SJC_REF vs IJC/SJC_ALT partitioning is required http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Normalizes splicing junction counts by effective isoform lengths to estimate percent-spliced-in (PSI) levels per allele, the quantity PAIRADISE models statistically. Effective lengths (incLen, skpLen) correct inclusion and skipping counts so length-dependent count biases do not masquerade as allelic splicing differences. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.ajhg.2020.07.005
skills.summary: Normalizes splicing junction counts by effective isoform lengths to estimate percent-spliced-in (PSI) levels per allele, the quantity PAIRADISE models statistically. Effective lengths (incLen, skpLen) correct inclusion and skipping counts so length-dependent count biases do not masquerade as allelic splicing differences.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input lacks effective isoform lengths (incLen/skpLen) — raw IJC/SJC counts alone cannot be length-normalized correctly The goal is within-condition quantification of PSI where the two isoforms have comparable effective lengths and the analysis is not differential (length correction is still advisable but this pipeline's IncLevel1/2 schema is allele-pair specific) Reads are not haplotype-assigned counts per allele (e.g., bulk gene-level counts from a standard quantifier), since IJC/SJC_REF vs IJC/SJC_ALT partitioning is required

skills.name: exon-skipping-event-count-filtering
skills.search_text: exon-skipping-event-count-filtering Use when preparing exon inclusion/exclusion count matrices (e.g., from a SingleCellExperiment with raw_M1 and raw_M2 assays) for GEDI splicing-mode integration, to drop low-sequencing-depth cells and low-coverage events before model fitting. Input is gene-level single-cell expression data rather than paired exon inclusion/exclusion read counts — the cell/event thresholds are splicing-specific Data is already normalized PSI estimates rather than raw inclusion/exclusion counts — the method models the paired counts' log-ratio directly and a naïve PSI estimate performs worse Applying to spliced/unspliced stability data — analogous but distinct filtering would be needed for that modality http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Pre-GEDI quality filtering of paired exon inclusion (M1) and exclusion (M2) count matrices from Quantas-processed single-cell splicing data, removing low-content cells and poorly covered cassette-exon events so the paired binomial log-ratio model is fit on reliable counts. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-50963-0
skills.summary: Pre-GEDI quality filtering of paired exon inclusion (M1) and exclusion (M2) count matrices from Quantas-processed single-cell splicing data, removing low-content cells and poorly covered cassette-exon events so the paired binomial log-ratio model is fit on reliable counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is gene-level single-cell expression data rather than paired exon inclusion/exclusion read counts — the cell/event thresholds are splicing-specific Data is already normalized PSI estimates rather than raw inclusion/exclusion counts — the method models the paired counts' log-ratio directly and a naïve PSI estimate performs worse Applying to spliced/unspliced stability data — analogous but distinct filtering would be needed for that modality

skills.description: Use when you need simulated circRNA isoform panels with known full-length sequences and expression levels — e.g. benchmarking assembly or quantification tools like CircAST across depth, read-length, or multi-condition series.
skills.name: exon-skipping-variation-modeling
skills.search_text: exon-skipping-variation-modeling Use when you need simulated circRNA isoform panels with known full-length sequences and expression levels — e.g. benchmarking assembly or quantification tools like CircAST across depth, read-length, or multi-condition series. The goal is to detect or quantify circRNAs from real RNA-seq data rather than to build simulated ground truth for benchmarking The circRNAs of interest are intronic or intergenic — the CircAST pipeline assembles and quantifies only exon-annotated circular transcripts Samples are not RNase R-treated, since CircAST can be applied only to RNase R-treated samples in which remnant linear mRNA may still affect assembly http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Model exon-skipping variation in circular transcripts by building circular transcript structures on a UCSC hg19 GTF annotation and randomly skipping exons to generate isoform variants, then assigning theoretical abundances so that CircAST's assembly and relative quantification (correlation 0.85-0.99) can be evaluated against known ground truth. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2019.03.004
skills.summary: Model exon-skipping variation in circular transcripts by building circular transcript structures on a UCSC hg19 GTF annotation and randomly skipping exons to generate isoform variants, then assigning theoretical abundances so that CircAST's assembly and relative quantification (correlation 0.85-0.99) can be evaluated against known ground truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to detect or quantify circRNAs from real RNA-seq data rather than to build simulated ground truth for benchmarking The circRNAs of interest are intronic or intergenic — the CircAST pipeline assembles and quantifies only exon-annotated circular transcripts Samples are not RNase R-treated, since CircAST can be applied only to RNase R-treated samples in which remnant linear mRNA may still affect assembly

skills.description: Use when smoothed per-cell segment-level expression means from scRNA-seq data must be discretized into a fixed set of copy number states via unsupervised mixture-model fitting with EM.
skills.name: expectation-maximization-parameter-estimation
skills.search_text: expectation-maximization-parameter-estimation Use when smoothed per-cell segment-level expression means from scRNA-seq data must be discretized into a fixed set of copy number states via unsupervised mixture-model fitting with EM. The tumor has minimal genomic alterations (e.g. leukemia, pediatric cancers, Ependymomas) so aneuploidy-based state discretization is unsuitable You need continuous copy number ratios rather than discretized states — use the CNA_mtx_relat ratios directly Segments have not yet been defined — EM requires the post-segmentation per-cell segment means, not raw gene-level counts http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Per-cell genomic segment mean expression values are modeled as a mixture of five truncated normal distributions whose parameters are estimated by EM starting from empirically chosen fixed initial parameters; the resulting per-cell states are aggregated by majority vote across cells to assign each segment one of five copy number states (deletion, loss, neutral, gain, amplification). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-36790-9
skills.summary: Per-cell genomic segment mean expression values are modeled as a mixture of five truncated normal distributions whose parameters are estimated by EM starting from empirically chosen fixed initial parameters; the resulting per-cell states are aggregated by majority vote across cells to assign each segment one of five copy number states (deletion, loss, neutral, gain, amplification).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The tumor has minimal genomic alterations (e.g. leukemia, pediatric cancers, Ependymomas) so aneuploidy-based state discretization is unsuitable You need continuous copy number ratios rather than discretized states — use the CNA_mtx_relat ratios directly Segments have not yet been defined — EM requires the post-segmentation per-cell segment means, not raw gene-level counts

skills.description: Use when you have a name-sorted paired-end SAM from TopHat2, a UCSC-format GTF, and a back-spliced junction list from CIRCexplorer2/CIRI2/UROBORUS, and you need full-length circRNA isoform sequences plus isoform-level expression (FPKM/TPM).
skills.name: expectation-maximization-read-assignment-quantification
skills.search_text: expectation-maximization-read-assignment-quantification Use when you have a name-sorted paired-end SAM from TopHat2, a UCSC-format GTF, and a back-spliced junction list from CIRCexplorer2/CIRI2/UROBORUS, and you need full-length circRNA isoform sequences plus isoform-level expression (FPKM/TPM). The sample was not RNase R-treated — CircAST can be applied only to RNase R-treated samples, and remnant linear mRNA can degrade assembly and generate false transcripts You need intronic or intergenic circular transcripts — the pipeline assembles only exon-annotated circular transcripts The input junction list comes from a tool whose output format has not been converted to CircAST input format http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 CircAST reconstructs full-length circRNA isoforms with multiple splice graphs and the EMPC algorithm, then quantifies isoform expression by allocating reads to isoforms with an expectation-maximization / maximum likelihood estimation procedure. This yields FPKM/TPM and read counts per circular transcript. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2019.03.004
skills.summary: CircAST reconstructs full-length circRNA isoforms with multiple splice graphs and the EMPC algorithm, then quantifies isoform expression by allocating reads to isoforms with an expectation-maximization / maximum likelihood estimation procedure. This yields FPKM/TPM and read counts per circular transcript.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample was not RNase R-treated — CircAST can be applied only to RNase R-treated samples, and remnant linear mRNA can degrade assembly and generate false transcripts You need intronic or intergenic circular transcripts — the pipeline assembles only exon-annotated circular transcripts The input junction list comes from a tool whose output format has not been converted to CircAST input format

skills.description: Use when demultiplexing HTO-labeled scRNA-seq droplets with demuxmix and both a naive NB mixture and a genes-detected regression mixture have been fit per HTO, so the model with the lower expected classification error must be chosen for classification.
skills.name: expected-classification-error-model-selection
skills.search_text: expected-classification-error-model-selection Use when demultiplexing HTO-labeled scRNA-seq droplets with demuxmix and both a naive NB mixture and a genes-detected regression mixture have been fit per HTO, so the model with the lower expected classification error must be chosen for classification. skills.summary: Selects between demuxmix's two negative binomial mixture models per HTO — the naive model and the regression model using genes-detected-per-droplet as covariate — by minimizing the expected classification error, before using the winning model's posteriors to demultiplex droplets.

Droplets are being demultiplexed by sample genotype or SNP data rather than oligonucleotide barcodes.

skills.description: Use when fitting a deep Boltzmann machine (scDBM) to raw scRNA-seq UMI count matrices (e.g., PBMC4k, 4182 cells × 1000 highly variable genes) and per-gene negative-binomial inverse dispersion parameters must be estimated during training.
skills.name: exponential-family-harmonium-parametrization
skills.search_text: exponential-family-harmonium-parametrization Use when fitting a deep Boltzmann machine (scDBM) to raw scRNA-seq UMI count matrices (e.g., PBMC4k, 4182 cells × 1000 highly variable genes) and per-gene negative-binomial inverse dispersion parameters must be estimated during training. Input is already normalized/log-transformed or batch-corrected expression rather than raw UMI counts — the negative-binomial likelihood and Fisher scoring assume integer counts The goal is batch-effect correction: the paper states explicitly that 'Currently, batch effects cannot be learned with scDBMs' and all models were examined without batch-correction capabilities A separate quantitative benchmark of the dispersion estimator is required — the paper describes the mechanism but does not separately benchmark it http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Adapts deep Boltzmann machines (harmonium-style exponential-family parametrization) to scRNA-seq UMI counts by modeling each gene with a negative-binomial likelihood and estimating the per-gene inverse dispersion θ via a regularized Fisher scoring algorithm, integrated into the scDBM training loop as described by Treppner et al. (2021). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-88875-4
skills.summary: Adapts deep Boltzmann machines (harmonium-style exponential-family parametrization) to scRNA-seq UMI counts by modeling each gene with a negative-binomial likelihood and estimating the per-gene inverse dispersion θ via a regularized Fisher scoring algorithm, integrated into the scDBM training loop as described by Treppner et al. (2021).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already normalized/log-transformed or batch-corrected expression rather than raw UMI counts — the negative-binomial likelihood and Fisher scoring assume integer counts The goal is batch-effect correction: the paper states explicitly that 'Currently, batch effects cannot be learned with scDBMs' and all models were examined without batch-correction capabilities A separate quantitative benchmark of the dispersion estimator is required — the paper describes the mechanism but does not separately benchmark it

skills.search_text: exponential-trend-fitting Use when h5ad cells carry a continuous cell-cycle angle (cell_cycle_theta) and you must verify whether total UMI counts per cell double (fold change ~2.0-2.1) across the transcriptional phase before mitosis. The anndata lacks obs['cell_cycle_theta'] (DeepCycle was never run); fit the phase first rather than substituting gene-marker-based phases, which the paper notes lack generalizability No cycling genes were detected (per the README, 'If you do not find any cycling genes the results will not be reliable') — sequencing depth must first be increased The question concerns per-gene expression waves (e.g. G1 transcription waves), not global per-cell RNA content doubling Quantify pre-mitotic doubling of cellular RNA content by fitting an exponential trend to binned UMI counts along the DeepCycle transcriptional phase (adata.obs['cell_cycle_theta']) and computing the fold change across the doubling segment. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-30545-8
skills.summary: Quantify pre-mitotic doubling of cellular RNA content by fitting an exponential trend to binned UMI counts along the DeepCycle transcriptional phase (adata.obs['cell_cycle_theta']) and computing the fold change across the doubling segment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The anndata lacks obs['cell_cycle_theta'] (DeepCycle was never run); fit the phase first rather than substituting gene-marker-based phases, which the paper notes lack generalizability No cycling genes were detected (per the README, 'If you do not find any cycling genes the results will not be reliable') — sequencing depth must first be increased The question concerns per-gene expression waves (e.g. G1 transcription waves), not global per-cell RNA content doubling

skills.search_text: expression-based-regulome-prediction Use when you have RNA-seq (FPKM matrix) or exon array gene expression for a sample and need genome-scale chromatin accessibility predictions, e.g., to pseudo-replicate DNase-seq or convert GEO expression samples into regulomes. You need to discover new DHS locations not represented in the model's ~1M pre-specified loci — BIRD will not discover new locations of DHSs Input is raw reads rather than gene expression (process with Tophat/Cufflinks or HISAT2/StringTie first to obtain FPKM) Data are from non-human species or platforms lacking a prebuilt BIRD model http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Predict genome-wide DNase I hypersensitivity (chromatin accessibility) across ~1M genomic loci from a biological sample's transcriptome using BIRD, a big data regression model trained on ENCODE data, enabling regulome mapping for samples with only gene expression data. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-017-01188-x
skills.summary: Predict genome-wide DNase I hypersensitivity (chromatin accessibility) across ~1M genomic loci from a biological sample's transcriptome using BIRD, a big data regression model trained on ENCODE data, enabling regulome mapping for samples with only gene expression data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to discover new DHS locations not represented in the model's ~1M pre-specified loci — BIRD will not discover new locations of DHSs Input is raw reads rather than gene expression (process with Tophat/Cufflinks or HISAT2/StringTie first to obtain FPKM) Data are from non-human species or platforms lacking a prebuilt BIRD model

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how accurately normalization/DE methods estimate effect sizes (logFC) on simulated single-cell data with known ground truth, especially to detect expression-level-dependent bias.
skills.name: expression-bin-stratified-logfc-regression
skills.search_text: expression-bin-stratified-logfc-regression Use when you need to quantify how accurately normalization/DE methods estimate effect sizes (logFC) on simulated single-cell data with known ground truth, especially to detect expression-level-dependent bias. You lack ground-truth effect sizes — the regression against truth requires simulated data with known per-gene logFC, not real datasets. Evaluating p-value calibration or FDR sensitivity/specificity rather than effect-size (logFC) accuracy — this skill targets bias and variance of logFC, not significance calling. Data are full-length (non-UMI) scRNA-seq — the authors only focused on UMI-based datasets and note count distributions may differ on full-length platforms. http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Benchmark accuracy of differential-expression effect-size estimation by binning genes by expression level and regressing each method's estimated logFC against simulation ground-truth logFC, recording regression coefficient (bias) and R2 (variance). Used to show Normalisr obtains among the lowest logFC bias and variance across expression levels versus edgeR and single-cell alternatives. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-26682-1
skills.summary: Benchmark accuracy of differential-expression effect-size estimation by binning genes by expression level and regressing each method's estimated logFC against simulation ground-truth logFC, recording regression coefficient (bias) and R2 (variance). Used to show Normalisr obtains among the lowest logFC bias and variance across expression levels versus edgeR and single-cell alternatives.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You lack ground-truth effect sizes — the regression against truth requires simulated data with known per-gene logFC, not real datasets. Evaluating p-value calibration or FDR sensitivity/specificity rather than effect-size (logFC) accuracy — this skill targets bias and variance of logFC, not significance calling. Data are full-length (non-UMI) scRNA-seq — the authors only focused on UMI-based datasets and note count distributions may differ on full-length platforms.

skills.description: Use when selecting well-correlated candidate feature genes from a log-normalized scRNA-seq matrix, and gene-level correlation statistics must be normalized against expression-level confounding by binning genes by mean expression.
skills.name: expression-binned-zscore-normalization
skills.search_text: expression-binned-zscore-normalization Use when selecting well-correlated candidate feature genes from a log-normalized scRNA-seq matrix, and gene-level correlation statistics must be normalized against expression-level confounding by binning genes by mean expression. Input is already a ranked feature set or a cell-cluster assignment — this skill only selects the initial candidate feature genes The expression matrix has not been filtered/normalized (raw counts with mitochondrial, ribosomal, spike-in, and pseudogenes still present), since the GGC and range scores would be dominated by technical genes You need the final minimally redundant feature set — that requires the subsequent DUBStepR stepwise regression and guilt-by-association expansion steps http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 DUBStepR's initial candidate feature selection step: after removing mitochondrial, ribosomal, spike-in, and pseudogenes, it builds a gene-gene correlation (GGC) matrix, computes each gene's correlation range score c_i = max3(G_i) - 0.75*min(G_i), bins genes by mean expression, converts range scores to z-scores within bins, and retains genes with z-score > 0.7. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-26085-2
skills.summary: DUBStepR's initial candidate feature selection step: after removing mitochondrial, ribosomal, spike-in, and pseudogenes, it builds a gene-gene correlation (GGC) matrix, computes each gene's correlation range score c_i = max3(G_i) - 0.75*min(G_i), bins genes by mean expression, converts range scores to z-scores within bins, and retains genes with z-score > 0.7.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a ranked feature set or a cell-cluster assignment — this skill only selects the initial candidate feature genes The expression matrix has not been filtered/normalized (raw counts with mitochondrial, ribosomal, spike-in, and pseudogenes still present), since the GGC and range scores would be dominated by technical genes You need the final minimally redundant feature set — that requires the subsequent DUBStepR stepwise regression and guilt-by-association expansion steps

skills.search_text: expression-data-adjustment-preprocessing Use when filtered RNA-seq expression matrices from multiple infection-condition samples must be distribution-adjusted (quantile normalization) before computing gene-gene correlations or building coexpression modules. The expression data are already quantile-normalized and adjusted, so re-running normalization would distort distributions A signed network is required where positive and negative correlations must be distinguished rather than collapsed via absolute correlation values The goal is candidate-gene prioritization from GWAS resistance alleles without any expression preprocessing step upstream http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Preprocesses filtered soybean RNA-seq expression data from five fungal-pathogen stress conditions using BioNERO's expression preprocessing (quantile normalization and adjustment) so that sample-level distributions are comparable before coexpression network construction. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-03864-x
skills.summary: Preprocesses filtered soybean RNA-seq expression data from five fungal-pathogen stress conditions using BioNERO's expression preprocessing (quantile normalization and adjustment) so that sample-level distributions are comparable before coexpression network construction.

skills.description: Use when starting from an RNA-Seq time-series count table (e.g., C. beijerinckii 5442 genes × 6 time points) and you need an initial genome-wide GRN via mutual information between gene pairs.
skills.name: expression-data-binning-entropy-estimation
skills.search_text: expression-data-binning-entropy-estimation Use when starting from an RNA-Seq time-series count table (e.g., C. beijerinckii 5442 genes × 6 time points) and you need an initial genome-wide GRN via mutual information between gene pairs. The data are single-cell RNA-Seq — the article notes alternative tools (Inferelator 3.0, GRNBoost2, Arboreto) are designed for scRNA-Seq, whereas Augusta targets bulk whole-genome time-series data A refined, directional network with activation/repression signs is already required as the immediate output — MI binning only yields the initial undirected estimation before MSD time-lag typing and TFBM refinement Only a Boolean model is needed from an existing GRN — use Augusta.GRN_to_BN instead of re-inferring from expression data http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Discretize continuous RNA-Seq expression values into bins and compute pairwise mutual information (MI) between all gene pairs to infer an initial gene regulatory network, as implemented in the Augusta package. This information-theory step converts high-throughput time-series expression data into undirected TF–TG associations prior to edge-direction assignment. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2024.01.013
skills.summary: Discretize continuous RNA-Seq expression values into bins and compute pairwise mutual information (MI) between all gene pairs to infer an initial gene regulatory network, as implemented in the Augusta package. This information-theory step converts high-throughput time-series expression data into undirected TF–TG associations prior to edge-direction assignment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are single-cell RNA-Seq — the article notes alternative tools (Inferelator 3.0, GRNBoost2, Arboreto) are designed for scRNA-Seq, whereas Augusta targets bulk whole-genome time-series data A refined, directional network with activation/repression signs is already required as the immediate output — MI binning only yields the initial undirected estimation before MSD time-lag typing and TFBM refinement Only a Boolean model is needed from an existing GRN — use Augusta.GRN_to_BN instead of re-inferring from expression data

skills.search_text: expression-feature-extraction-from-simulated-data Use when OU-simulated deletion-event expression data (or empirical data in the same format) must be transformed into the p=3m feature file that CLOUDeClassifyNN/XGB/RF/SVM and CLOUDePredict* require. Expression data is not in the two-species derived/survived/lost deletion-event layout (3m columns with log10(x+1) values) — the CLOUDe feature schema does not apply A testing feature file already exists on the same standardized scale — re-extraction is unnecessary and only CLOUDeClassify*/CLOUDePredict* should be run The goal is hyperparameter tuning or final classification (ClassifierCVnn, CLOUDeClassifyNN), which consume these features rather than produce them http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Feature-extraction step of the CLOUDe pipeline: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck-simulated expression data for derived, survived, and lost genes is converted into a p=3m standardized feature matrix (plus one-hot class labels and parameter responses) that the CLOUDe classifiers and predictors consume. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbae002

skills.description: Use when a barcode-annotated (lineage-labeled) scRNA-seq matrix must be screened for genes with unusually stable expression across related cells, and each hit classified as quantitative or qualitative memory.
skills.name: expression-skewness-gene-classification
skills.search_text: expression-skewness-gene-classification Use when a barcode-annotated (lineage-labeled) scRNA-seq matrix must be screened for genes with unusually stable expression across related cells, and each hit classified as quantitative or qualitative memory. The scRNA-seq dataset has no lineage annotations (barcodes or otherwise) — lineage-mean CV2 cannot be computed against a lineage-level null without them The population contains only distantly related cells, where GEMLI's gene-expression-memory approach performs less robustly The goal is long-term lineage tracing over weeks or months — expression-memory signals cover roughly 1–5 cell divisions http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Identifies 'memory genes' whose expression is stably maintained across cell divisions in lineage-annotated scRNA-seq, by comparing per-gene lineage-mean CV2 against a lineage-size-matched null, then splits them into quantitative (skewness < 3) and qualitative (skewness ≥ 3) memory classes. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-47158-y
skills.summary: Identifies 'memory genes' whose expression is stably maintained across cell divisions in lineage-annotated scRNA-seq, by comparing per-gene lineage-mean CV2 against a lineage-size-matched null, then splits them into quantitative (skewness < 3) and qualitative (skewness ≥ 3) memory classes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The scRNA-seq dataset has no lineage annotations (barcodes or otherwise) — lineage-mean CV2 cannot be computed against a lineage-level null without them The population contains only distantly related cells, where GEMLI's gene-expression-memory approach performs less robustly The goal is long-term lineage tracing over weeks or months — expression-memory signals cover roughly 1–5 cell divisions

skills.description: Use when building a subtype/classification gene template from bulk tumor data that must generalize to cell lines, organoids or PDXs lacking human stromal/immune compartments.
skills.name: expression-variation-filtering-in-cell-lines
skills.search_text: expression-variation-filtering-in-cell-lines Use when building a subtype/classification gene template from bulk tumor data that must generalize to cell lines, organoids or PDXs lacking human stromal/immune compartments. The target samples have a human stromal component different from primary CRCs, e.g. patient biopsies of metastatic CRC — CMScaller is explicitly not recommended there Input is single-cell RNA-sequencing data, which the authors call exceedingly noisy and for which a dedicated classifier is needed You only need to classify already-subtyped bulk primary tumors with full stromal content — the original CMS classifier applies http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A marker-gene filtering strategy from CMScaller (Eide 2017) that restricts the CMS subtype template to cancer cell-intrinsic genes by successively applying primary-CRC differential-expression, cell-line expression-variation (top 25% inter-percentile range, expressed in ≥3 lines), and pCRC-vs-PDX xenotransplantation (LFC < 2) filters. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-017-16747-x
skills.summary: A marker-gene filtering strategy from CMScaller (Eide 2017) that restricts the CMS subtype template to cancer cell-intrinsic genes by successively applying primary-CRC differential-expression, cell-line expression-variation (top 25% inter-percentile range, expressed in ≥3 lines), and pCRC-vs-PDX xenotransplantation (LFC < 2) filters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target samples have a human stromal component different from primary CRCs, e.g. patient biopsies of metastatic CRC — CMScaller is explicitly not recommended there Input is single-cell RNA-sequencing data, which the authors call exceedingly noisy and for which a dedicated classifier is needed You only need to classify already-subtyped bulk primary tumors with full stromal content — the original CMS classifier applies
