The expression matrix was generated with a different platform or normalization than the training cohort (e.g. Affymetrix microarray log2 data) — performance is not guaranteed by the article's external-testing setup The goal is to train or re-fit classifiers rather than score an unseen cohort with existing frozen models Reference labels are unavailable and no AWCA-PAM50 calls can be generated, leaving no ground truth for accuracy/concordance computation http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 Applies pre-trained mLR intrinsic subtype classifiers (PAM50, limma50, limma50_BWE feature sets) trained on TCGA (RSEM) and GSE96058 (FPKM) to wholly unseen external RNA-seq cohorts (PanCA, GSE81538) to measure generalization accuracy against published PAM50 reference labels and AWCA-PAM50 concordance. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-70832-2
skills.summary: Applies pre-trained mLR intrinsic subtype classifiers (PAM50, limma50, limma50_BWE feature sets) trained on TCGA (RSEM) and GSE96058 (FPKM) to wholly unseen external RNA-seq cohorts (PanCA, GSE81538) to measure generalization accuracy against published PAM50 reference labels and AWCA-PAM50 concordance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The expression matrix was generated with a different platform or normalization than the training cohort (e.g. Affymetrix microarray log2 data) — performance is not guaranteed by the article's external-testing setup The goal is to train or re-fit classifiers rather than score an unseen cohort with existing frozen models Reference labels are unavailable and no AWCA-PAM50 calls can be generated, leaving no ground truth for accuracy/concordance computation

skills.description: Use when Chord's built-in tools (DoubletFinder, scds) are insufficient and you want to boost the GBM ensemble with an additional detector such as Scrublet or solo via the addmethods1/addmethods2 port.
skills.name: external-doublet-detector-scoring
skills.search_text: external-doublet-detector-scoring Use when Chord's built-in tools (DoubletFinder, scds) are insufficient and you want to boost the GBM ensemble with an additional detector such as Scrublet or solo via the addmethods1/addmethods2 port. When Chord has not been run previously — the score CSVs and 'seu.robj'/'sce.robj'/'overkilled.robj' objects must already exist in the working directory. When you have not yet estimated a doublet rate for the dataset — the re-run requires doubletrate (10X: ~0.9% per 1,000 cells). When only experimental labeling (cell hashing, MULTI-seq, demuxlet) is needed, since those approaches require special operations and additional costs and serve a different purpose than computational score boosting. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Scores a scRNA-seq dataset with an external Python doublet detector (e.g., Scrublet) and appends the per-cell scores to Chord's 'real_data.scores.csv' and 'simulated_data.scores.csv' so the GBM ensemble can be refit over built-in plus external methods, producing an enhanced 'Chord Plus' (ChordP) model. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-022-03476-9
skills.summary: Scores a scRNA-seq dataset with an external Python doublet detector (e.g., Scrublet) and appends the per-cell scores to Chord's 'real_data.scores.csv' and 'simulated_data.scores.csv' so the GBM ensemble can be refit over built-in plus external methods, producing an enhanced 'Chord Plus' (ChordP) model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When Chord has not been run previously — the score CSVs and 'seu.robj'/'sce.robj'/'overkilled.robj' objects must already exist in the working directory. When you have not yet estimated a doublet rate for the dataset — the re-run requires doubletrate (10X: ~0.9% per 1,000 cells). When only experimental labeling (cell hashing, MULTI-seq, demuxlet) is needed, since those approaches require special operations and additional costs and serve a different purpose than computational score boosting.

skills.description: Use when you have computed performance metrics for your method on a shared benchmark dataset and need to integrate them with previously published scores of competing algorithms so all methods can be compared on identical data and metrics.
skills.name: external-reference-score-integration
skills.search_text: external-reference-score-integration Use when you have computed performance metrics for your method on a shared benchmark dataset and need to integrate them with previously published scores of competing algorithms so all methods can be compared on identical data and metrics. The reference study used different dataset versions or preprocessing than yours — merged scores would not be comparable You need to re-evaluate the reference algorithms themselves (e.g. with new parameters) rather than integrate their published scores http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Merge newly computed benchmark scores (accuracy, NMI, ARI) for a method such as KMD clustering with published reference scores from prior benchmark studies (Liu et al. scores for Xshift, DEPECHE, Accense, FlowSOM, kmeans, PhenoGraph) into a single comparison table. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-023-05480-z
skills.summary: Merge newly computed benchmark scores (accuracy, NMI, ARI) for a method such as KMD clustering with published reference scores from prior benchmark studies (Liu et al. scores for Xshift, DEPECHE, Accense, FlowSOM, kmeans, PhenoGraph) into a single comparison table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reference study used different dataset versions or preprocessing than yours — merged scores would not be comparable You need to re-evaluate the reference algorithms themselves (e.g. with new parameters) rather than integrate their published scores

skills.description: Use when training a multi-domain deep-learning model (e.g. Cancer-Finder on 13 TISCH tissue domains) and you need to choose the saved checkpoint by generalization to an unseen domain rather than internal-validation loss.
skills.name: extra-domain-validation-checkpoint-selection
skills.search_text: extra-domain-validation-checkpoint-selection Use when training a multi-domain deep-learning model (e.g. Cancer-Finder on 13 TISCH tissue domains) and you need to choose the saved checkpoint by generalization to an unseen domain rather than internal-validation loss. Input is hematologic tumor data — the article explicitly does not recommend Cancer-Finder for hematologic tumor data The target domain is included in the training tissues, in which case internal-validation accuracy alone suffices and extra-domain checkpoint selection is redundant Training spatial transcriptomics spot models where spatial relationships among spots matter — Cancer-Finder overlooks these http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 A model-selection strategy from Cancer-Finder training in which, after each epoch of domain-generalization risk-extrapolation optimization, the model is additionally evaluated on normalized breast cancer data from the original CopyKAT study (a tissue not in the 13-tissue training set), and only the checkpoint whose extra-domain accuracy is maximal is retained. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-46413-6
skills.summary: A model-selection strategy from Cancer-Finder training in which, after each epoch of domain-generalization risk-extrapolation optimization, the model is additionally evaluated on normalized breast cancer data from the original CopyKAT study (a tissue not in the 13-tissue training set), and only the checkpoint whose extra-domain accuracy is maximal is retained.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is hematologic tumor data — the article explicitly does not recommend Cancer-Finder for hematologic tumor data The target domain is included in the training tissues, in which case internal-validation accuracy alone suffices and extra-domain checkpoint selection is redundant Training spatial transcriptomics spot models where spatial relationships among spots matter — Cancer-Finder overlooks these

skills.description: Use when functional enrichment results from a DEG list (e.g. PMM2-CDG DEGs selected by a minimum vote threshold of three) must be filtered and interpreted for basement membrane, extracellular matrix, or collagen-related biological process terms.
skills.name: extracellular-matrix-term-interpretation
skills.search_text: extracellular-matrix-term-interpretation Use when functional enrichment results from a DEG list (e.g. PMM2-CDG DEGs selected by a minimum vote threshold of three) must be filtered and interpreted for basement membrane, extracellular matrix, or collagen-related biological process terms. The input is raw RNA-seq data or count tables rather than an already-computed DEG results table — use the upstream DEgenes Hunter differential expression pipeline instead The biological question concerns co-expression modules or DEG method consensus voting rather than interpreting overrepresented biological process terms The organism is non-model and requires orthologous translation before functional annotation is meaningful for ECM/basement membrane terms http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Interprets functional enrichment results from the ExpHunterSuite functional Hunter module applied to prevalent PMM2-CDG differentially expressed genes, filtering for basement membrane and extracellular matrix (ECM)/collagen terms to support the finding that basement membrane formation and composition are altered in PMM2-CDG. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-94343-w
skills.summary: Interprets functional enrichment results from the ExpHunterSuite functional Hunter module applied to prevalent PMM2-CDG differentially expressed genes, filtering for basement membrane and extracellular matrix (ECM)/collagen terms to support the finding that basement membrane formation and composition are altered in PMM2-CDG.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw RNA-seq data or count tables rather than an already-computed DEG results table — use the upstream DEgenes Hunter differential expression pipeline instead The biological question concerns co-expression modules or DEG method consensus voting rather than interpreting overrepresented biological process terms The organism is non-model and requires orthologous translation before functional annotation is meaningful for ECM/basement membrane terms

skills.description: Use when evaluating a DEG-calling method or combined classifier (e.g. Naïve Bayes over multi-method p-value vectors) against a spike-in dataset with known DEG/non-DEG truth labels, to quantify performance as an F-measure.
skills.name: f-measure-classification-metric-computation
skills.search_text: f-measure-classification-metric-computation Use when evaluating a DEG-calling method or combined classifier (e.g. Naïve Bayes over multi-method p-value vectors) against a spike-in dataset with known DEG/non-DEG truth labels, to quantify performance as an F-measure. The dataset has no known DEG/non-DEG ground truth (e.g. the Lafora disease or PMM2-CDG model datasets), so an F-measure cannot be computed — use consensus/vote-threshold heuristics instead The goal is choosing a single DEG detection method for a new dataset rather than quantifying classification performance of a trained combiner Evaluating ranking-based or continuous score outputs without thresholding to binary DEG calls, since F-measure requires discrete class predictions http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Computes the F-measure of DEG-calling methods or combined classifiers (e.g. the ExpHunter Suite Naïve Bayes model trained on simulated p-value vectors) against spike-in data with known DEG/non-DEG ground truth, enabling comparison against single methods like DESeq2 and vote-threshold combinations. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-94343-w
skills.summary: Computes the F-measure of DEG-calling methods or combined classifiers (e.g. the ExpHunter Suite Naïve Bayes model trained on simulated p-value vectors) against spike-in data with known DEG/non-DEG ground truth, enabling comparison against single methods like DESeq2 and vote-threshold combinations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has no known DEG/non-DEG ground truth (e.g. the Lafora disease or PMM2-CDG model datasets), so an F-measure cannot be computed — use consensus/vote-threshold heuristics instead The goal is choosing a single DEG detection method for a new dataset rather than quantifying classification performance of a trained combiner Evaluating ranking-based or continuous score outputs without thresholding to binary DEG calls, since F-measure requires discrete class predictions

skills.description: Use when ranking gene-prediction tools by F0.2-measure against curated driver gene lists (CGC 616 genes, NCG 711 genes, PMH 501 genes) over multiple TCGA cancer-type prediction sets.
skills.name: f-measure-precision-recall-computation
skills.search_text: f-measure-precision-recall-computation Use when ranking gene-prediction tools by F0.2-measure against curated driver gene lists (CGC 616 genes, NCG 711 genes, PMH 501 genes) over multiple TCGA cancer-type prediction sets. When the analysis goal favors recall over precision (e.g. discovering novel candidate drivers), since the beta^2 = 0.2 setting deliberately underweights recall When the candidate predictions are continuous confidence scores rather than gene sets — precision/recall as defined here requires binary gene lists and does not use thresholds or AUC-style ranking http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Compute precision, recall, and the F_beta-measure (with beta^2 = 0.2, plus an F1 robustness check) to score cancer driver gene predictions against the CGC, NCG and PMH benchmark gene lists across 14 TCGA datasets, as used to benchmark WMDS.net/WMDS.netP against 11 competitor tools. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad071
skills.summary: Compute precision, recall, and the F_beta-measure (with beta^2 = 0.2, plus an F1 robustness check) to score cancer driver gene predictions against the CGC, NCG and PMH benchmark gene lists across 14 TCGA datasets, as used to benchmark WMDS.net/WMDS.netP against 11 competitor tools.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the analysis goal favors recall over precision (e.g. discovering novel candidate drivers), since the beta^2 = 0.2 setting deliberately underweights recall When the candidate predictions are continuous confidence scores rather than gene sets — precision/recall as defined here requires binary gene lists and does not use thresholds or AUC-style ranking

skills.description: Use when a fused high-dimensional sequence-encoding feature matrix (e.g., PCPseDNC + PSP + k-mer + PseEIIP) must be reduced before training classifiers and you need a fast filter-type ranking such as the F score used by Staem5.
skills.name: f-score-feature-selection
skills.search_text: f-score-feature-selection Use when a fused high-dimensional sequence-encoding feature matrix (e.g., PCPseDNC + PSP + k-mer + PseEIIP) must be reduced before training classifiers and you need a fast filter-type ranking such as the F score used by Staem5. Input is still raw FASTA RNA sequences — encode them first with PCPseDNC/PSP/k-mer/PseEIIP, since the F score operates on numeric feature vectors, not sequence strings The goal is a general cross-species m5C predictor — the paper states it is necessary to set up species-specific models, so a subset selected on M. musculus should not be assumed to transfer to A. thaliana Feature dimensionality and computing time are not constraints and you want joint-subset (wrapper/embedded) selection — Staem5's scope is filter ranking, with MRMD and PCC evaluated as the alternatives (Tables S5–S7) http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Applies the F score as a filter-type ranking to progressively trim the fused PCPseDNC, PSP, k-mer (k=1,2,3), and PseEIIP encoding matrix, retaining the subset (185 features for M. musculus) that maximizes stacked-model accuracy while cutting computing time. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.omtn.2021.10.012
skills.summary: Applies the F score as a filter-type ranking to progressively trim the fused PCPseDNC, PSP, k-mer (k=1,2,3), and PseEIIP encoding matrix, retaining the subset (185 features for M. musculus) that maximizes stacked-model accuracy while cutting computing time.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still raw FASTA RNA sequences — encode them first with PCPseDNC/PSP/k-mer/PseEIIP, since the F score operates on numeric feature vectors, not sequence strings The goal is a general cross-species m5C predictor — the paper states it is necessary to set up species-specific models, so a subset selected on M. musculus should not be assumed to transfer to A. thaliana Feature dimensionality and computing time are not constraints and you want joint-subset (wrapper/embedded) selection — Staem5's scope is filter ranking, with MRMD and PCC evaluated as the alternatives (Tables S5–S7)

skills.description: Use when comparing cell type annotation classifiers on single-cell expression data with ground-truth labels, especially to measure whether adding confidently self-labeled (pseudo-labeled) cells improves held-out F1 relative to ground-truth-only training.
skills.name: f1-benchmark-comparison-across-annotation-methods
skills.search_text: f1-benchmark-comparison-across-annotation-methods Use when comparing cell type annotation classifiers on single-cell expression data with ground-truth labels, especially to measure whether adding confidently self-labeled (pseudo-labeled) cells improves held-out F1 relative to ground-truth-only training. The dataset has no held-out test set or ground-truth labels, so F1 cannot be computed against reference annotations The goal is unsupervised clustering or marker discovery rather than supervised classification performance benchmarking There is no unlabeled cell pool for pseudo-labeling, so self-training comparison reduces to a plain baseline benchmark http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmark single-cell type annotation methods (SingleR, scmap, SingleCellNet, logistic regression, random forest) by F1-score on a stratified held-out test set, including retraining on ground-truth plus pseudo-labeled cells to quantify self-training F1 gains as in Geuenich et al. 2024 (Nature Communications). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-45198-y
skills.summary: Benchmark single-cell type annotation methods (SingleR, scmap, SingleCellNet, logistic regression, random forest) by F1-score on a stratified held-out test set, including retraining on ground-truth plus pseudo-labeled cells to quantify self-training F1 gains as in Geuenich et al. 2024 (Nature Communications).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has no held-out test set or ground-truth labels, so F1 cannot be computed against reference annotations The goal is unsupervised clustering or marker discovery rather than supervised classification performance benchmarking There is no unlabeled cell pool for pseudo-labeling, so self-training comparison reduces to a plain baseline benchmark

skills.description: Use when a detector's calls (e.g. ecDNA callers on ATAC-Seq data) must be validated against known ground truth, especially to characterize performance sensitivity to local sequencing depth (e.g. 10x–30x+) and read length (e.g. 35–150 bp).
skills.name: f1-benchmark-evaluation-across-sequencing-conditions
skills.search_text: f1-benchmark-evaluation-across-sequencing-conditions Use when a detector's calls (e.g. ecDNA callers on ATAC-Seq data) must be validated against known ground truth, especially to characterize performance sensitivity to local sequencing depth (e.g. 10x–30x+) and read length (e.g. 35–150 bp). Input is real tumor data without ground-truth ecDNA coordinates — accuracy cannot be scored, only discovery performed Target detector is meant for WGS-based focal amplification detection — the article's benchmarking strategy is ATAC-Seq-specific and cannot guarantee accuracy for all types of focal amplifications Libraries have local depth below 10x — the benchmark itself shows circlehunter does not outperform Circle_finder in this regime http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Benchmark ecDNA detection accuracy by sequencing ecDNA calls from competing tools (circlehunter vs Circle_finder) against simulated ground truth, computing precision, recall, and F1 across varying local depth and read-length conditions. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41389-023-00476-0
skills.summary: Benchmark ecDNA detection accuracy by sequencing ecDNA calls from competing tools (circlehunter vs Circle_finder) against simulated ground truth, computing precision, recall, and F1 across varying local depth and read-length conditions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real tumor data without ground-truth ecDNA coordinates — accuracy cannot be scored, only discovery performed Target detector is meant for WGS-based focal amplification detection — the article's benchmarking strategy is ATAC-Seq-specific and cannot guarantee accuracy for all types of focal amplifications Libraries have local depth below 10x — the benchmark itself shows circlehunter does not outperform Circle_finder in this regime

skills.description: Use when comparing malignant-vs-non-malignant cell classifiers on scRNA-seq count matrices with bulk WES/WGS-derived copy number ground truth, and you need per-sample F1 aggregation across cancer types and platforms.
skills.name: f1-classification-performance-comparison
skills.search_text: f1-classification-performance-comparison Use when comparing malignant-vs-non-malignant cell classifiers on scRNA-seq count matrices with bulk WES/WGS-derived copy number ground truth, and you need per-sample F1 aggregation across cancer types and platforms. The sample is believed to be pure tumor with minimal genomic alterations (e.g. leukemia, pediatric cancers, Ependymomas) — aneuploidy-based classifiers and their benchmarks are unsuitable there You only have synthetic/simulated data or no bulk-derived copy number reference — the F1 comparison requires reference ground truth from bulk tumor profiling Your goal is clonal substructure or phylogeny rather than pure malignant/non-malignant classification (use SUBCLONES = TRUE workflows instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark protocol for comparing automatic malignant/non-malignant cell classification of scRNA-seq methods (SCEVAN vs CopyKAT) by computing per-sample F1 scores against bulk-derived copy number ground truth across 106 real tumor samples. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-36790-9
skills.summary: Benchmark protocol for comparing automatic malignant/non-malignant cell classification of scRNA-seq methods (SCEVAN vs CopyKAT) by computing per-sample F1 scores against bulk-derived copy number ground truth across 106 real tumor samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample is believed to be pure tumor with minimal genomic alterations (e.g. leukemia, pediatric cancers, Ependymomas) — aneuploidy-based classifiers and their benchmarks are unsuitable there You only have synthetic/simulated data or no bulk-derived copy number reference — the F1 comparison requires reference ground truth from bulk tumor profiling Your goal is clonal substructure or phylogeny rather than pure malignant/non-malignant classification (use SUBCLONES = TRUE workflows instead)

skills.description: Use when processing scRNA-Seq reads from a CAST×B6 F1 cross where reads must be assigned to maternal vs. paternal transcript copies, e.g., before EMASE-based multi-read allocation or unique-read allele counting.
skills.name: f1-cross-parental-origin-read-tagging
skills.search_text: f1-cross-parental-origin-read-tagging Use when processing scRNA-Seq reads from a CAST×B6 F1 cross where reads must be assigned to maternal vs. paternal transcript copies, e.g., before EMASE-based multi-read allocation or unique-read allele counting. Input reads are from a non-F1 or non-mouse strain cross where CAST/B6-specific variants (Sanger REL-1505) and a two-parent transcriptome are not applicable Data are UMI counts already assigned per allele (e.g., Larsson et al. 224-cell fibroblast UMI counts) — alignment/tagging has already been done upstream The downstream analysis only needs unique-read counts and discarding multi-reads is acceptable — though the article warns this raises variability and sampling zeros http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Constructs a diploid (CAST/B6) transcriptome so that single-cell RNA-Seq reads can be aligned to parental-origin-specific sequences and emitted as allele-specific alignments tagged by maternal/paternal copy, enabling ASE analysis in F1 hybrid single cells. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-13099-0
skills.summary: Constructs a diploid (CAST/B6) transcriptome so that single-cell RNA-Seq reads can be aligned to parental-origin-specific sequences and emitted as allele-specific alignments tagged by maternal/paternal copy, enabling ASE analysis in F1 hybrid single cells.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are from a non-F1 or non-mouse strain cross where CAST/B6-specific variants (Sanger REL-1505) and a two-parent transcriptome are not applicable Data are UMI counts already assigned per allele (e.g., Larsson et al. 224-cell fibroblast UMI counts) — alignment/tagging has already been done upstream The downstream analysis only needs unique-read counts and discarding multi-reads is acceptable — though the article warns this raises variability and sampling zeros

skills.description: Use when two active learning classifiers (e.g., random forest vs logistic regression) have been evaluated with F1 across multiple train/test splits and you must aggregate into a single relative improvement metric per search/threshold combination.
skills.name: f1-improvement-aggregation-across-splits
skills.search_text: f1-improvement-aggregation-across-splits Use when two active learning classifiers (e.g., random forest vs logistic regression) have been evaluated with F1 across multiple train/test splits and you must aggregate into a single relative improvement metric per search/threshold combination. When comparing a classifier other than random forest vs logistic regression, the standardization by the LR F1 baseline is not meaningful When the initial training set is not randomly selected (e.g., marker-informed selection via leader adaptive reweighting), the RF-over-LR improvement finding this aggregation tests does not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Aggregates per-iteration F1 scores from active learning runs into a relative improvement score — (RF F1 minus LR F1) standardized by the LR F1 — averaged over ten 50:50 stratified train/test splits and annotation methods, to compare random forest vs logistic regression active learning performance. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-45198-y
skills.summary: Aggregates per-iteration F1 scores from active learning runs into a relative improvement score — (RF F1 minus LR F1) standardized by the LR F1 — averaged over ten 50:50 stratified train/test splits and annotation methods, to compare random forest vs logistic regression active learning performance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When comparing a classifier other than random forest vs logistic regression, the standardization by the LR F1 baseline is not meaningful When the initial training set is not randomly selected (e.g., marker-informed selection via leader adaptive reweighting), the RF-over-LR improvement finding this aggregation tests does not apply

skills.description: Use when a classifier's predicted cell labels must be scored against held-out true labels, e.g. comparing Symphony-based predictions to benchmarked classifiers via per-cell-type F1 and median F1 across train-test experiments.
skills.name: f1-metric-benchmark-evaluation
skills.search_text: f1-metric-benchmark-evaluation Use when a classifier's predicted cell labels must be scored against held-out true labels, e.g. comparing Symphony-based predictions to benchmarked classifiers via per-cell-type F1 and median F1 across train-test experiments. No held-out true labels exist for the query cells, so F1 against ground truth cannot be computed The goal is novel cell type discovery in the query — Symphony does not replace de novo analyses and unmapped populations would make label-based F1 misleading Evaluating mapping/conservation quality (e.g., LISI or embedding geometry) rather than supervised classification accuracy http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmark-evaluation skill that scores predicted single-cell type annotations against true labels using per-cell-type F1-scores, taking the median F1 across cell types per train-test experiment and averaging across experiments. It is the evaluation utility used by the Abdelaal et al. classifier benchmark and reused to quantify Symphony-based classification on PbmcBench. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-25957-x
skills.summary: Benchmark-evaluation skill that scores predicted single-cell type annotations against true labels using per-cell-type F1-scores, taking the median F1 across cell types per train-test experiment and averaging across experiments. It is the evaluation utility used by the Abdelaal et al. classifier benchmark and reused to quantify Symphony-based classification on PbmcBench.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No held-out true labels exist for the query cells, so F1 against ground truth cannot be computed The goal is novel cell type discovery in the query — Symphony does not replace de novo analyses and unmapped populations would make label-based F1 misleading Evaluating mapping/conservation quality (e.g., LISI or embedding geometry) rather than supervised classification accuracy

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a cell type annotation method against baselines and you need per-class F1/precision distributions that are fair across methods with different reference sets.
skills.name: f1-precision-metric-computation
skills.search_text: f1-precision-metric-computation Use when benchmarking a cell type annotation method against baselines and you need per-class F1/precision distributions that are fair across methods with different reference sets. If the question is aggregate detection-quality rather than per-cell-type classification, average precision is preferred — the paper itself notes F1-score performance lags average precision and 'better calibration needed for binary yes-no decisions' When the goal is annotating a new dataset rather than benchmarking classifiers against a labeled test set with ontology-grounded ground truth Do not compare methods on all Cell Ontology terms — comparing a method on cell types absent from its own training set produces unfair metrics http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Compute per-cell-type F1-score and precision for hierarchical cell type classifiers (CellO, scMatch, SingleR) over a common single-cell test set, restricting evaluation to cell types present in each method's own prepackaged reference set. This reproduces the Figure 5B benchmark methodology from the CellO paper. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2020.101913
skills.summary: Compute per-cell-type F1-score and precision for hierarchical cell type classifiers (CellO, scMatch, SingleR) over a common single-cell test set, restricting evaluation to cell types present in each method's own prepackaged reference set. This reproduces the Figure 5B benchmark methodology from the CellO paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If the question is aggregate detection-quality rather than per-cell-type classification, average precision is preferred — the paper itself notes F1-score performance lags average precision and 'better calibration needed for binary yes-no decisions' When the goal is annotating a new dataset rather than benchmarking classifiers against a labeled test set with ontology-grounded ground truth Do not compare methods on all Cell Ontology terms — comparing a method on cell types absent from its own training set produces unfair metrics

skills.description: Use when comparing a generalized model trained on merged multi-dataset training data against disease-specific counterparts on each cancer type's validation set, using macro-averaged F1 deltas.
skills.name: f1-score-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: f1-score-benchmark-comparison Use when comparing a generalized model trained on merged multi-dataset training data against disease-specific counterparts on each cancer type's validation set, using macro-averaged F1 deltas. Evaluating a single disease-specific model in isolation with no generalized counterpart to compare against — there is no delta to compute Inputs are already aggregated F1 score tables rather than per-cell predictions — you would only compute the subtraction, not the full training/prediction pipeline Classifying normal (non-cancer) tissue data — the benchmarking workflow removes normal epithelial cells and validates on diseased-held-out sets http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmarking workflow for quantifying how well a generalized pan-cancer Pollock model performs relative to disease-specific modules, by computing macro-averaged F1 scores per cancer type on held-out validation data and subtracting disease-specific F1 to obtain per-cancer-type deltas. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac028
skills.summary: Benchmarking workflow for quantifying how well a generalized pan-cancer Pollock model performs relative to disease-specific modules, by computing macro-averaged F1 scores per cancer type on held-out validation data and subtracting disease-specific F1 to obtain per-cancer-type deltas.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating a single disease-specific model in isolation with no generalized counterpart to compare against — there is no delta to compute Inputs are already aggregated F1 score tables rather than per-cell predictions — you would only compute the subtraction, not the full training/prediction pipeline Classifying normal (non-cancer) tissue data — the benchmarking workflow removes normal epithelial cells and validates on diseased-held-out sets

skills.search_text: fairness-constrained-cell-sketching Use when a large single-cell expression matrix must be subsampled for trajectory or clustering analysis while preserving a minimum number of cells per collection time point or class label, e.g. to remove outlier cells whose transcriptomic state disagrees with their time point. The downstream task needs no per-class guarantees — use Sphetcher's plain three-argument mode (sphetcher expression_matrix.csv sketch_size sketch_indicator_output.csv) instead of the fairness-constrained mode. The goal is uniform random subsampling rather than transcriptomic-space coverage; uniform subsampling ignores similarity between expression patterns and risks overlooking rare cell states, which Sphetcher is designed to avoid. Your goal is the biological result itself (which cell types shift in proportion) rather than characterizing the statistical method's error behavior — run scanpro directly instead of a simulation sweep The dataset contains rare cell types supported by less than 2% of all cells, where benchmarking showed unstable results and limited bootstrapping benefit The input is already replicated per condition — with a real samples column, bootstrapping and pseudo-replicate tuning are unnecessary http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark-style estimation of false-positive rates (and sensitivity/auROC) for Scanpro proportion analysis by simulating replicate datasets with sim_scanpro and scoring statistical calls (ANOVA/t-test) against a known simulated ground truth. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-024-66381-7
skills.summary: Benchmark-style estimation of false-positive rates (and sensitivity/auROC) for Scanpro proportion analysis by simulating replicate datasets with sim_scanpro and scoring statistical calls (ANOVA/t-test) against a known simulated ground truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is the biological result itself (which cell types shift in proportion) rather than characterizing the statistical method's error behavior — run scanpro directly instead of a simulation sweep The dataset contains rare cell types supported by less than 2% of all cells, where benchmarking showed unstable results and limited bootstrapping benefit The input is already replicated per condition — with a real samples column, bootstrapping and pseudo-replicate tuning are unnecessary

skills.description: Use when validating a scRNA-seq mutation-calling pipeline: apply it to cells known to lack the somatic variants (e.g., 8057 bone marrow cells from four healthy donors) to measure per-site false-positive rates and confirm no spurious calls in wild-type cells.
skills.name: false-positive-rate-estimation-in-healthy-controls
skills.search_text: false-positive-rate-estimation-in-healthy-controls Use when validating a scRNA-seq mutation-calling pipeline: apply it to cells known to lack the somatic variants (e.g., 8057 bone marrow cells from four healthy donors) to measure per-site false-positive rates and confirm no spurious calls in wild-type cells. You are genotyping cells that may genuinely harbor the somatic mutations (e.g., AML tumor samples) — this skill estimates the null FPR in mutation-negative cells only. The BAM data are not from a 10x Chromium pipeline with CB/UB molecular barcodes, since cb_sniffer and UB-tag duplicate collapse depend on cellranger tag conventions. No independently discovered variant set (e.g., eWGS from paired tumor/normal) is available — scRNA-seq-derived variant calls have a high noise-driven false-positive rate and cannot serve as the trusted query set. http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Estimates the site-specific false-positive rate of scRNA-seq somatic SNV calling by applying the same variant-detection approach (cb_sniffer on 10x Chromium BAMs with UB-tag duplicate collapse) to healthy donor cells that should not carry the tested variants, providing a null/control benchmark for the mutation-calling method. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-11591-1
skills.summary: Estimates the site-specific false-positive rate of scRNA-seq somatic SNV calling by applying the same variant-detection approach (cb_sniffer on 10x Chromium BAMs with UB-tag duplicate collapse) to healthy donor cells that should not carry the tested variants, providing a null/control benchmark for the mutation-calling method.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are genotyping cells that may genuinely harbor the somatic mutations (e.g., AML tumor samples) — this skill estimates the null FPR in mutation-negative cells only. The BAM data are not from a 10x Chromium pipeline with CB/UB molecular barcodes, since cb_sniffer and UB-tag duplicate collapse depend on cellranger tag conventions. No independently discovered variant set (e.g., eWGS from paired tumor/normal) is available — scRNA-seq-derived variant calls have a high noise-driven false-positive rate and cannot serve as the trusted query set.

skills.description: Use when replicating or auditing how suffPCR turns a sparse PCA (FPS) solution into a row-sparse loading matrix V̂d — i.e., Fantope projection via truncated eigendecomposition, ADMM soft-thresholding, and Algorithm 2 elbow threshold selection.
skills.name: fantope-projection-eigendecomposition
skills.search_text: fantope-projection-eigendecomposition Use when replicating or auditing how suffPCR turns a sparse PCA (FPS) solution into a row-sparse loading matrix V̂d — i.e., Fantope projection via truncated eigendecomposition, ADMM soft-thresholding, and Algorithm 2 elbow threshold selection. When the analysis goal is standard (dense) PCA rather than row-sparse PCA with a downstream regression — the hard-thresholding of small-ℓ2-norm rows is specific to SuffPCR's goal of feature-sparse subspaces When features are known in advance and no sparse subspace recovery is needed, e.g., if the phenotype already depends on an explicit, verified gene list rather than an unknown feature grouping Reconstructs the SuffPCR estimation pipeline: an ADMM solver whose Fantope projection step is approximated by a truncated eigendecomposition with elementwise soft-thresholding (Algorithm 1), followed by elbow-based hard-thresholding of row norms (Algorithm 2) to obtain row-sparse principal components before regressing the phenotype on the recovered subspace. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac033
skills.summary: Reconstructs the SuffPCR estimation pipeline: an ADMM solver whose Fantope projection step is approximated by a truncated eigendecomposition with elementwise soft-thresholding (Algorithm 1), followed by elbow-based hard-thresholding of row norms (Algorithm 2) to obtain row-sparse principal components before regressing the phenotype on the recovered subspace.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the analysis goal is standard (dense) PCA rather than row-sparse PCA with a downstream regression — the hard-thresholding of small-ℓ2-norm rows is specific to SuffPCR's goal of feature-sparse subspaces When features are known in advance and no sparse subspace recovery is needed, e.g., if the phenotype already depends on an explicit, verified gene list rather than an unknown feature grouping

skills.description: Use when raw demultiplexed small RNA-seq FASTQ reads must be reduced to unique sequences with embedded counts (FASTX-Toolkit-style headers) before alignment and counting, e.g. preparing collapsed.fa for tinyRNA.
skills.name: fasta-identifier-count-embedding
skills.search_text: fasta-identifier-count-embedding Use when raw demultiplexed small RNA-seq FASTQ reads must be reduced to unique sequences with embedded counts (FASTX-Toolkit-style headers) before alignment and counting, e.g. preparing collapsed.fa for tinyRNA. Input is already a collapsed FASTA with count-embedded identifiers (re-collapsing would discard the count information embedded in headers) Input is a feature count table or alignment output rather than raw sequencing reads Input FASTQ files are not demultiplexed, which the tinyRNA workflow requires of sequencing data http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Collapse unique small RNA sequencing reads into a FASTA file in which each record's identifier embeds the per-sequence read count using the FASTX-Toolkit collapse convention, as done by the tiny-collapse step of the tinyRNA workflow. This reduces redundant sequences before downstream genomic alignment and feature counting with tiny-count. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad065
skills.summary: Collapse unique small RNA sequencing reads into a FASTA file in which each record's identifier embeds the per-sequence read count using the FASTX-Toolkit collapse convention, as done by the tiny-collapse step of the tinyRNA workflow. This reduces redundant sequences before downstream genomic alignment and feature counting with tiny-count.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a collapsed FASTA with count-embedded identifiers (re-collapsing would discard the count information embedded in headers) Input is a feature count table or alignment output rather than raw sequencing reads Input FASTQ files are not demultiplexed, which the tinyRNA workflow requires of sequencing data

skills.description: Use when assembling tissue-specific m6A benchmark FASTA datasets — 41-nt RNA segments from human/mouse/rat brain, liver, kidney, heart, or testis — need redundancy removal (CD-HIT <80%) and balanced train/test splits before model training.
skills.name: fasta-sequence-file-curation
skills.search_text: fasta-sequence-file-curation Use when assembling tissue-specific m6A benchmark FASTA datasets — 41-nt RNA segments from human/mouse/rat brain, liver, kidney, heart, or testis — need redundancy removal (CD-HIT <80%) and balanced train/test splits before model training. The input FASTA is already a deduplicated benchmark matching the Table 3 counts — re-running CD-HIT could discard valid sequences without benefit. The goal is m6A prediction on new sequences rather than benchmark construction — invoke im6A-TS-CNN directly with its -s/-t/-ts options instead. Segments are not 41-nt windows centered on candidate sites, or come from species/tissues outside the human/mouse/rat brain, liver, kidney, heart, and testis scope of the source m6A data. http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Curation of tissue-specific m6A benchmark FASTA collections: extracting 41-nt RNA segments centered on candidate sites from human, mouse, and rat tissues, labeling site-containing segments as positive, and removing redundancy with CD-HIT at <80% sequence similarity before CNN training. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.omtn.2020.07.034
skills.summary: Curation of tissue-specific m6A benchmark FASTA collections: extracting 41-nt RNA segments centered on candidate sites from human, mouse, and rat tissues, labeling site-containing segments as positive, and removing redundancy with CD-HIT at <80% sequence similarity before CNN training.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input FASTA is already a deduplicated benchmark matching the Table 3 counts — re-running CD-HIT could discard valid sequences without benefit. The goal is m6A prediction on new sequences rather than benchmark construction — invoke im6A-TS-CNN directly with its -s/-t/-ts options instead. Segments are not 41-nt windows centered on candidate sites, or come from species/tissues outside the human/mouse/rat brain, liver, kidney, heart, and testis scope of the source m6A data.

skills.description: Use when quantifying how isoform-quantification accuracy degrades with sequencing depth: you have simulated Nanopore FASTQ reads with 10x-style cell barcode/UMI, a ground-truth cell-by-isoform matrix, and need depth-response curves of per-cell accuracy.
skills.name: fastq-downsampling-depth-analysis
skills.search_text: fastq-downsampling-depth-analysis Use when quantifying how isoform-quantification accuracy degrades with sequencing depth: you have simulated Nanopore FASTQ reads with 10x-style cell barcode/UMI, a ground-truth cell-by-isoform matrix, and need depth-response curves of per-cell accuracy. Real (non-simulated) Nanopore reads with no ground-truth isoform expression matrix — per-cell correlation to truth cannot be computed The question is the effect of per-base sequencing error quality (low/middle/high transition matrices), which is benchmarked by error regime rather than by downsampling Bulk or spatial analysis goals (e.g., spatial isoform switching with LongcellPre/Longcell Splice objects) rather than method benchmarking http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark long-read single-cell isoform quantification accuracy as a function of sequencing depth by subsampling simulated Nanopore FASTQ reads with seqtk and correlating method outputs against a simulated ground-truth cell-by-isoform matrix. It isolates the effect of read depth from the effects of read quality (error regime). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-60902-2
skills.summary: Benchmark long-read single-cell isoform quantification accuracy as a function of sequencing depth by subsampling simulated Nanopore FASTQ reads with seqtk and correlating method outputs against a simulated ground-truth cell-by-isoform matrix. It isolates the effect of read depth from the effects of read quality (error regime).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Real (non-simulated) Nanopore reads with no ground-truth isoform expression matrix — per-cell correlation to truth cannot be computed The question is the effect of per-base sequencing error quality (low/middle/high transition matrices), which is benchmarked by error regime rather than by downsampling Bulk or spatial analysis goals (e.g., spatial isoform switching with LongcellPre/Longcell Splice objects) rather than method benchmarking

skills.name: fastq-preprocessing-and-downsampling
skills.search_text: fastq-preprocessing-and-downsampling Use when starting from published scRNA-seq resources (e.g. Cell Ranger 1.1.0 BAMs from Chromium, or oversized FASTQs from ICELL8) that must be converted, reduced to chromosome 21, or downsampled to a fixed read count before pipeline benchmarking. Input FASTQs are already size-appropriate for full analysis and no downsampling or platform-specific reference restriction (e.g. Chr21) is intended Data are 5' scRNA-seq technologies other than Chromium, which UniverSC does not support at the time of writing The downstream goal is full-genome analysis rather than the reduced chromosome 21 benchmark, since Chr21 filtering exists only to reduce output data size http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Prepares published single-cell RNA-seq datasets for cross-platform processing by converting 10x Cell Ranger BAM output back to FASTQ with bamtofastq, filtering reads to chromosome 21, and downsampling large FASTQs (e.g. ICELL8) with seqtk, enabling fair UniverSC-vs-native-pipeline benchmarks on the GRCh38 (hg38) Chr21 reference. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-34681-z

skills.search_text: fastq-read-barcode-annotation Use when FASTQ reads must be filtered for reads containing a known sequence/variant (with mismatches tolerated) and then annotated with cell-barcode and UMI assignments in a single command-line pipeline. Only a simple grep-like sequence search is needed with no downstream barcode demultiplexing — a single Flexiplex instance suffices. Barcodes are unknown and only flanking sequences are known — use Flexiplex discovery mode instead of known-sequence chaining. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Chain two piped Flexiplex instances to first perform an error-tolerant (Levenshtein-based) grep-like search of FASTQ reads for a variant of interest, then demultiplex cell barcodes/UMIs from the matched reads using a 10x Chromium v3 preset and a known barcode whitelist. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae102

skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a simple grep-like sequence search is needed with no downstream barcode demultiplexing — a single Flexiplex instance suffices. Barcodes are unknown and only flanking sequences are known — use Flexiplex discovery mode instead of known-sequence chaining.

skills.description: Use when raw paired-end SPLiT-seq FASTQ files need barcode/UMI identification and you must count identified labeled reads and compute identified-read ratios per sample.

skills.search_text: fastq-read-preprocessing-and-counting Use when raw paired-end SPLiT-seq FASTQ files need barcode/UMI identification and you must count identified labeled reads and compute identified-read ratios per sample. Input data is not from SPLiT-seq or a similar combinatorial barcoding platform — fault-tolerant and indel alignment was proposed for SPLiT-seq data; support for other single-cell platforms is only potential, not demonstrated Reads have already been barcode-identified and labeled (e.g., an existing labeled-read FASTQ) — recounting would duplicate the SCSit step You need tolerance beyond one mismatch and one indel without accepting the trade-off — the authors found more tolerance yields only 4–5% more identified reads at 20–40% more runtime http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Preprocess SPLiT-seq paired-end FASTQ reads with SCSit to identify combinatorial barcodes and UMIs, output labeled reads, and quantify identified-read counts and ratios per sample against the original SPLiT-seq method. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.08.021
skills.summary: Preprocess SPLiT-seq paired-end FASTQ reads with SCSit to identify combinatorial barcodes and UMIs, output labeled reads, and quantify identified-read counts and ratios per sample against the original SPLiT-seq method.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data is not from SPLiT-seq or a similar combinatorial barcoding platform — fault-tolerant and indel alignment was proposed for SPLiT-seq data; support for other single-cell platforms is only potential, not demonstrated Reads have already been barcode-identified and labeled (e.g., an existing labeled-read FASTQ) — recounting would duplicate the SCSit step You need tolerance beyond one mismatch and one indel without accepting the trade-off — the authors found more tolerance yields only 4–5% more identified reads at 20–40% more runtime

skills.search_text: fastq-read-region-indexing Use when preprocessing single-cell genomics FASTQs (e.g. dogmaseq-dig RNA/tag/atac/protein splits) and you need the per-tool technology string describing where barcodes, UMIs, and cDNA lie in R1/R2/R3 before kb count or alevin-fry. skills.description: Use when a small RNA-seq FASTQ(.gz) file must be reduced to unique sequences with per-sequence counts before alignment and counting, e.g. producing collapsed.fa as consumed by tiny-count in the tinyRNA pipeline.
skills.name: fastq-read-sequence-collapsing
skills.search_text: fastq-read-sequence-collapsing Use when a small RNA-seq FASTQ(.gz) file must be reduced to unique sequences with per-sequence counts before alignment and counting, e.g. producing collapsed.fa as consumed by tiny-count in the tinyRNA pipeline. The input is already a collapsed FASTA with count-bearing headers — re-collapsing would double-count or corrupt the embedded count fields. Per-read information (individual read identities, per-read alignment positions) must be preserved downstream, since collapsing discards everything but the unique sequence and its total count. The FASTQ file is not demultiplexed — the tinyRNA pipeline requires demultiplexed sequencing data as input. http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 Collapses demultiplexed small RNA-seq FASTQ reads into a collapsed FASTA in which each unique nucleotide sequence appears exactly once with its occurrence count embedded in the identifier (FASTX-Toolkit collapse convention), as done by the tiny-collapse step of the tinyRNA workflow to shrink the input for downstream genomic alignment and feature counting. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad065
skills.summary: Collapses demultiplexed small RNA-seq FASTQ reads into a collapsed FASTA in which each unique nucleotide sequence appears exactly once with its occurrence count embedded in the identifier (FASTX-Toolkit collapse convention), as done by the tiny-collapse step of the tinyRNA workflow to shrink the input for downstream genomic alignment and feature counting.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a collapsed FASTA with count-bearing headers — re-collapsing would double-count or corrupt the embedded count fields. Per-read information (individual read identities, per-read alignment positions) must be preserved downstream, since collapsing discards everything but the unique sequence and its total count. The FASTQ file is not demultiplexed — the tinyRNA pipeline requires demultiplexed sequencing data as input.

skills.search_text: fastq-sample-folder-organization Use when preparing raw 10x-style GEX and ADT (CITE-Seq) FASTQs for the gExcite or scAmpi Snakemake pipelines, which require one sub-directory per sample and SAMPLENAME_S[Number]_L00[Lane]_[ReadType]_001.fastq.gz naming before cellranger count. skills.description: Use when the input is a quality-filtered single-end FASTQ whose reads carry the UMI at the 5' start and you must move it into the read header before alignment and UMI counting.
skills.name: fastq-umi-clipping
skills.search_text: fastq-umi-clipping Use when the input is a quality-filtered single-end FASTQ whose reads carry the UMI at the 5' start and you must move it into the read header before alignment and UMI counting. Input reads do not carry the UMI at the 5' start (e.g. UMI located elsewhere or already stored in a separate index read) The FASTQ has not yet been demultiplexed/quality-filtered and you also need quality-based read selection — run fastq_qual_filter first Library preparation does not use 5' UMI placement, so clip_length would exceed the read length or remove biological sequence http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Removes the UMI from the 5' start of each FASTQ read and stores it in the FASTQ header by replacing the index at the end of header 1, using the C program fastq_umi_clipper from the UMI-analysis pipeline. skills.summary: Removes the UMI from the 5' start of each FASTQ read and stores it in the FASTQ header by replacing the index at the end of header 1, using the C program fastq_umi_clipper from the UMI-analysis pipeline. skills.search_text: feature-selection-method-comparison Use when the goal is to benchmark which gene/feature-selection method (e.g., E-test vs F-test vs M3Drop) yields the highest cell-classification accuracy, holding the classifier and train/test protocol fixed across methods and multiple labeled scRNA-seq datasets. Input data lacks cell-type labels — stratified 70/30 train/test splits and classification accuracy are undefined without annotations The analysis goal is cell-type classification itself (e.g., annotation of new data with SciBet/scmap) rather than comparing which gene-selection method produces the best classifier Only a single small dataset is available — the benchmark's conclusion (E-test consistently highest across 14 datasets) is a cross-dataset comparison, not a per-dataset recommendation http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmarks gene feature-selection methods for single-cell classification (E-test, F-test/one-way ANOVA, M3Drop) by pairing each with an identical classifier and split protocol, so accuracy differences are attributable to gene selection alone. Used to reproduce the Fig. 2a comparison across 14 scRNA-seq benchmarking datasets from the SciBet paper. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-15523-2
skills.summary: Benchmarks gene feature-selection methods for single-cell classification (E-test, F-test/one-way ANOVA, M3Drop) by pairing each with an identical classifier and split protocol, so accuracy differences are attributable to gene selection alone. Used to reproduce the Fig. 2a comparison across 14 scRNA-seq benchmarking datasets from the SciBet paper.

skills.search_text: feature-space-alignment-single-cell Use when running SIMS label-transfer prediction on a query .h5ad dataset whose gene set differs in size or ordering from the genes the reference TabNet model was trained on. The query dataset already contains exactly the same genes in the same order as the model's training features — no intersection/reordering is needed The goal is cross-species label transfer: the article notes 'we have limited our work to samples within the same species', so alignment across species is untested The model needs metadata such as sequencing technology or cell line as features — the article states this is not yet integrated into the SIMS model http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Aligns the gene panel of a query single-cell RNA-seq AnnData object to the feature space of a trained SIMS/TabNet label-transfer model by computing the set intersection of gene-name vectors and reordering the query expression matrix, enabling cross-dataset prediction (e.g., PBMC68K ~20k genes vs Han landscape ~5k genes) without feature-mismatch errors. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.xgen.2024.100581
skills.summary: Aligns the gene panel of a query single-cell RNA-seq AnnData object to the feature space of a trained SIMS/TabNet label-transfer model by computing the set intersection of gene-name vectors and reordering the query expression matrix, enabling cross-dataset prediction (e.g., PBMC68K ~20k genes vs Han landscape ~5k genes) without feature-mismatch errors.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query dataset already contains exactly the same genes in the same order as the model's training features — no intersection/reordering is needed The goal is cross-species label transfer: the article notes 'we have limited our work to samples within the same species', so alignment across species is untested The model needs metadata such as sequencing technology or cell line as features — the article states this is not yet integrated into the SIMS model

skills.description: Use when clustering a large single-cell RNA-seq expression matrix where direct clustering on raw gene expression is computationally prohibitive, and reduced O(n) complexity via subsampling plus Spearman-correlation feature projection is desired.
skills.name: feature-space-clustering
skills.search_text: feature-space-clustering Use when clustering a large single-cell RNA-seq expression matrix where direct clustering on raw gene expression is computationally prohibitive, and reduced O(n) complexity via subsampling plus Spearman-correlation feature projection is desired. The dataset is small enough that clustering directly on raw gene expression (or a plain SCC subsampling pipeline) is already tractable — the feature-projection layer is designed for large-scale data where O(n^2) complexity impedes scaling. The analysis requires clustering in raw gene-expression space rather than a correlation-based feature space, e.g. when per-gene expression structure must be preserved. Cells lack enough expressed genes for stable Spearman rank-correlation estimates (heavy dropout), since the projection relies on correlation as the feature. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Clusters large-scale scRNA-seq data by first projecting cells into a Spearman-correlation feature space and then clustering the subsampled cells there, using classification to assign all unsampled cells — the feature-projection step (Figure 1B Step 3) that SSCC adds on top of the SCC subsampling-clustering-classification strategy. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2018.10.003
skills.summary: Clusters large-scale scRNA-seq data by first projecting cells into a Spearman-correlation feature space and then clustering the subsampled cells there, using classification to assign all unsampled cells — the feature-projection step (Figure 1B Step 3) that SSCC adds on top of the SCC subsampling-clustering-classification strategy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is small enough that clustering directly on raw gene expression (or a plain SCC subsampling pipeline) is already tractable — the feature-projection layer is designed for large-scale data where O(n^2) complexity impedes scaling. The analysis requires clustering in raw gene-expression space rather than a correlation-based feature space, e.g. when per-gene expression structure must be preserved. Cells lack enough expressed genes for stable Spearman rank-correlation estimates (heavy dropout), since the projection relies on correlation as the feature.

skills.search_text: feature-subset-benchmark-comparison Use when an scaLR-trained model on top-K features must be evaluated for DGE sensitivity, specifically when asked whether running dge_pseudobulk/dge_lmem on all samples rather than test samples changes DEG counts. skills.search_text: feature-wise-hypothesis-testing Use when you have a merged feature matrix (e.g. CRIT's MATRIX.txt) plus group labels (e.g. NMF cluster membership separating 90 predicted regulators from 916 other RBPs) and need to identify which features distinguish the two groups. skills.search_text: fgwas-genomic-annotation-modeling Use when genome-wide GWAS summary statistics (P-values per SNP) are available together with a catalog of sQTLs and eQTLs, and the goal is to compare their GWAS enrichment per trait. skills.name: fibrosis-colocalization-analysis
skills.search_text: fibrosis-colocalization-analysis Use when analyzing spatial transcriptomics (e.g., Visium) sections from tissue undergoing fibrosis (e.g., post-myocardial-infarction heart) to determine whether senescence-burden spots colocalize with fibrotic regions and are spatially clustered. Input is single-cell (not spatial) transcriptomics with no spot coordinates — colocalization and Moran's I cannot be computed; use standard SenePy single-cell scoring instead Data are already scaled — score_hub expects normalized-or-raw expression that is not scaled, so scaled AnnData must be reloaded or re-derived Non-mouse spatial data where no matching species hub signatures exist (use the Human hubs or merge_hubs-derived universal signature instead of the mouse heart hubs) http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Scores spatial transcriptomics spots (e.g., 10x Visium post-MI heart sections) for cellular senescence using SenePy's cell-type-specific mouse heart hub signatures, then tests whether senescence-high spots colocalize with fibrotic marker expression (Col1a1) and show spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-57047-7
skills.summary: Scores spatial transcriptomics spots (e.g., 10x Visium post-MI heart sections) for cellular senescence using SenePy's cell-type-specific mouse heart hub signatures, then tests whether senescence-high spots colocalize with fibrotic marker expression (Col1a1) and show spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is single-cell (not spatial) transcriptomics with no spot coordinates — colocalization and Moran's I cannot be computed; use standard SenePy single-cell scoring instead Data are already scaled — score_hub expects normalized-or-raw expression that is not scaled, so scaled AnnData must be reloaded or re-derived Non-mouse spatial data where no matching species hub signatures exist (use the Human hubs or merge_hubs-derived universal signature instead of the mouse heart hubs)

skills.description: Use when reconstructing LncDC feature extraction from H-Train-style mRNA/CDS/lncRNA FASTA inputs, or when needing an alignment-free coding-potential value per transcript to feed a coding/noncoding classifier.
skills.name: fickett-score-coding-potential-scoring
skills.search_text: fickett-score-coding-potential-scoring Use when reconstructing LncDC feature extraction from H-Train-style mRNA/CDS/lncRNA FASTA inputs, or when needing an alignment-free coding-potential value per transcript to feed a coding/noncoding classifier. Input is already a feature matrix or imputer/scaler outputs exist — the Fickett score is a raw per-transcript feature, not a post-processing step on scaled data Only secondary structure features (SSFs) are needed — Fickett scoring belongs to the SIFs and requires only sequence, not RNAfold folding Aligning transcripts to protein databases is the goal (e.g. CPC-style homology search) — LncDC is explicitly an alignment-free approach http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Compute the Fickett coding-potential score for RNA transcripts as one of the sequence intrinsic features (SIFs) in LncDC's 57-column feature matrix used by the XGBoost model to discriminate lncRNAs from mRNAs. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-022-22082-7
skills.summary: Compute the Fickett coding-potential score for RNA transcripts as one of the sequence intrinsic features (SIFs) in LncDC's 57-column feature matrix used by the XGBoost model to discriminate lncRNAs from mRNAs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a feature matrix or imputer/scaler outputs exist — the Fickett score is a raw per-transcript feature, not a post-processing step on scaled data Only secondary structure features (SSFs) are needed — Fickett scoring belongs to the SIFs and requires only sequence, not RNAfold folding Aligning transcripts to protein databases is the goal (e.g. CPC-style homology search) — LncDC is explicitly an alignment-free approach

skills.description: Use when validating a network-based driver gene predictor by quantifying what fraction of its CGC-overlapping predictions are rarely-mutated (<0.05 SNV frequency) versus frequently-mutated across TCGA cancer types.
skills.name: figure-4-fraction-reproduction
skills.search_text: figure-4-fraction-reproduction Use when validating a network-based driver gene predictor by quantifying what fraction of its CGC-overlapping predictions are rarely-mutated (<0.05 SNV frequency) versus frequently-mutated across TCGA cancer types. The goal is to run WMDS.net itself on new expression matrices rather than evaluate its driver predictions against SNV mutation frequency and CGC overlap. Only one cancer type or no CGC reference list is available, so the per-cancer-type low/high fraction split of CGC-overlapping drivers cannot be computed. The mutation data lack non-synonymous SNV annotations (e.g. unannotated VCFs), making the 'fraction of tumor samples carrying non-synonymous somatic mutations' frequency uncomputable. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Reproduces Figure 4 of the WMDS.net paper: per-cancer-type fractions of CGC-overlapping predicted driver genes that are low-frequency (<0.05) versus high-frequency (>0.05) SNV mutations across 14 TCGA cancer types, plus the ERBB3-in-LUAD low-frequency driver case. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad071
skills.summary: Reproduces Figure 4 of the WMDS.net paper: per-cancer-type fractions of CGC-overlapping predicted driver genes that are low-frequency (<0.05) versus high-frequency (>0.05) SNV mutations across 14 TCGA cancer types, plus the ERBB3-in-LUAD low-frequency driver case.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to run WMDS.net itself on new expression matrices rather than evaluate its driver predictions against SNV mutation frequency and CGC overlap. Only one cancer type or no CGC reference list is available, so the per-cancer-type low/high fraction split of CGC-overlapping drivers cannot be computed. The mutation data lack non-synonymous SNV annotations (e.g. unannotated VCFs), making the 'fraction of tumor samples carrying non-synonymous somatic mutations' frequency uncomputable.

skills.description: Use when a published clustering paper claims a hyperparameter (e.g., a penalty ratio rho/lambda) is stable over an interval and you must verify that claim by sweeping the parameter on its original benchmark datasets.
skills.name: figure-reproduction-from-published-curves
skills.search_text: figure-reproduction-from-published-curves Use when a published clustering paper claims a hyperparameter (e.g., a penalty ratio rho/lambda) is stable over an interval and you must verify that claim by sweeping the parameter on its original benchmark datasets. The goal is to compare SSRE against competing clustering methods rather than to verify a specific hyperparameter's stability range — a benchmark comparison workflow is more appropriate The dataset is a large-scale scRNA-seq set where SSRE's known runtime limitation makes a full 15-value sweep prohibitively expensive without parallel computing The target figure does not depend on a continuous numeric hyperparameter (e.g., qualitative t-SNE visualization figures), so a ratio sweep cannot reproduce it http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Reproduces published parameter-sensitivity curves (e.g., SSRE's NMI/ARI stability versus the rho/lambda penalty ratio in Figures 2 and S1) by systematically sweeping the parameter on the paper's original benchmark datasets and comparing against its stated stable range (6–20) and default (rho/lambda = 10). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2020.09.004
skills.summary: Reproduces published parameter-sensitivity curves (e.g., SSRE's NMI/ARI stability versus the rho/lambda penalty ratio in Figures 2 and S1) by systematically sweeping the parameter on the paper's original benchmark datasets and comparing against its stated stable range (6–20) and default (rho/lambda = 10).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to compare SSRE against competing clustering methods rather than to verify a specific hyperparameter's stability range — a benchmark comparison workflow is more appropriate The dataset is a large-scale scRNA-seq set where SSRE's known runtime limitation makes a full 15-value sweep prohibitively expensive without parallel computing The target figure does not depend on a continuous numeric hyperparameter (e.g., qualitative t-SNE visualization figures), so a ratio sweep cannot reproduce it

skills.description: Use when a data matrix plus response vector (e.g., fat datasets like Relathe 1,427×4,322 or SRBCT 63×2,308) needs ranked feature selection and out-of-sample classification performance assessment.
skills.name: filter-based-feature-selection-rank-correlation
skills.search_text: filter-based-feature-selection-rank-correlation Use when a data matrix plus response vector (e.g., fat datasets like Relathe 1,427×4,322 or SRBCT 63×2,308) needs ranked feature selection and out-of-sample classification performance assessment. The task requires wrapper or embedded FS with model interaction (RRCT is a filter algorithm that scores features before any classifier is trained) The data requires mutual-information estimation via proper density estimation on continuous variables — the paper's mRMR_Spearman variant explicitly avoids computationally demanding mutual information computation in favor of Spearman correlation The goal is unsupervised feature selection: the uts function requires a response vector y for relevance quantification http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 A rank-correlation-based filter feature-selection workflow centered on the RRCT algorithm, which trades off relevance, redundancy, and complementarity via information-theoretic transformations of Spearman rank correlations and partial correlations. It is benchmarked by feeding selected feature subsets (1…min(M,30)) into a random forest and recording out-of-sample misclassification percentage. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2022.100471
skills.summary: A rank-correlation-based filter feature-selection workflow centered on the RRCT algorithm, which trades off relevance, redundancy, and complementarity via information-theoretic transformations of Spearman rank correlations and partial correlations. It is benchmarked by feeding selected feature subsets (1…min(M,30)) into a random forest and recording out-of-sample misclassification percentage.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires wrapper or embedded FS with model interaction (RRCT is a filter algorithm that scores features before any classifier is trained) The data requires mutual-information estimation via proper density estimation on continuous variables — the paper's mRMR_Spearman variant explicitly avoids computationally demanding mutual information computation in favor of Spearman correlation The goal is unsupervised feature selection: the uts function requires a response vector y for relevance quantification

skills.description: Use when a fused high-dimensional sequence-encoding feature matrix (e.g., PSP + k-mer + PCPseDNC + PseEIIP for RNA modification data) must be ranked and reduced by filter selection, and when comparing F score vs MRMD vs PCC to pick the subset dimension.
skills.name: filter-feature-ranking-mrmd-pcc-fscore
skills.search_text: filter-feature-ranking-mrmd-pcc-fscore Use when a fused high-dimensional sequence-encoding feature matrix (e.g., PSP + k-mer + PCPseDNC + PseEIIP for RNA modification data) must be ranked and reduced by filter selection, and when comparing F score vs MRMD vs PCC to pick the subset dimension. Input is already a small or low-dimensional feature table where filter ranking offers no dimension-reduction benefit The task requires a wrapper or embedded selection method rather than the three filter algorithms (MRMD, PCC, F score) evaluated here Prediction-time use of the pre-trained Staem5 model via m5C_predict.py — feature selection is part of training/model-building, not inference http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Compares three filter-type feature selection methods — F score, MRMD (maximum-relevance-maximum-distance), and PCC (Pearson correlation coefficient) — on a fused feature matrix (PSP, k-mer k=1–3, PCPseDNC, PseEIIP) for Staem5 m5C site prediction, ranking features and sweeping subset dimensions in steps of 5 to balance accuracy against dimensionality and computing time. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.omtn.2021.10.012
skills.summary: Compares three filter-type feature selection methods — F score, MRMD (maximum-relevance-maximum-distance), and PCC (Pearson correlation coefficient) — on a fused feature matrix (PSP, k-mer k=1–3, PCPseDNC, PseEIIP) for Staem5 m5C site prediction, ranking features and sweeping subset dimensions in steps of 5 to balance accuracy against dimensionality and computing time.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a small or low-dimensional feature table where filter ranking offers no dimension-reduction benefit The task requires a wrapper or embedded selection method rather than the three filter algorithms (MRMD, PCC, F score) evaluated here Prediction-time use of the pre-trained Staem5 model via m5C_predict.py — feature selection is part of training/model-building, not inference

skills.description: Use when benchmarking or auditing MUSIC-style preprocessing on single-cell CRISPR screening data and you need per-dataset QC-filtered and sgRNA-filtered cell proportions comparable to published Fig. 4a statistics.
skills.name: filtered-cell-proportion-quantification
skills.search_text: filtered-cell-proportion-quantification Use when benchmarking or auditing MUSIC-style preprocessing on single-cell CRISPR screening data and you need per-dataset QC-filtered and sgRNA-filtered cell proportions comparable to published Fig. 4a statistics. The goal is downstream perturbation effect prioritization or topic modeling rather than auditing how much data the filtering steps discard Input is not yet in MUSIC's standard format (expression matrix plus named perturbation vector) and would first require Input_preprocess_10X() conversion Working with non-single-cell or bulk CRISPR screening data where per-cell QC thresholds (genes, UMIs, mitochondrial percentage) do not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Quantify the proportion of single-cell CRISPR screening cells removed by MUSIC's quality control and sgRNA-based cell filtering steps, per dataset and averaged across datasets, to assess how much data each filter discards. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-10216-x
skills.summary: Quantify the proportion of single-cell CRISPR screening cells removed by MUSIC's quality control and sgRNA-based cell filtering steps, per dataset and averaged across datasets, to assess how much data each filter discards.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is downstream perturbation effect prioritization or topic modeling rather than auditing how much data the filtering steps discard Input is not yet in MUSIC's standard format (expression matrix plus named perturbation vector) and would first require Input_preprocess_10X() conversion Working with non-single-cell or bulk CRISPR screening data where per-cell QC thresholds (genes, UMIs, mitochondrial percentage) do not apply

skills.description: Use when two or more droplet/background-filtering methods (e.g., DIEM and EmptyDrops) must be compared on the same scRNA-seq or snRNA-seq count matrix to determine which retains dying/debris-contaminated droplets.
skills.name: filtering-method-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: filtering-method-benchmark-comparison Use when two or more droplet/background-filtering methods (e.g., DIEM and EmptyDrops) must be compared on the same scRNA-seq or snRNA-seq count matrix to determine which retains dying/debris-contaminated droplets.
