skills.description: Use when testing whether marginal-correlation feature screening recovers predictive genes in p>>n transcriptomic data (e.g. the aml dataset, 116 observations x 6283 genes) by benchmarking screening FNR against a graphical-lasso-derived pseudo-true β*.
skills.name: graphical-lasso-precision-matrix-estimation
skills.search_text: graphical-lasso-precision-matrix-estimation Use when testing whether marginal-correlation feature screening recovers predictive genes in p>>n transcriptomic data (e.g. the aml dataset, 116 observations x 6283 genes) by benchmarking screening FNR against a graphical-lasso-derived pseudo-true β*. The goal is prediction or classification itself (e.g. fitting SuffPCR on X and y with suffPCR(X, y, d=1:3)) rather than evaluating or reproducing the screening counterexample. The dataset is not p>>n transcriptomic data, so the sample covariance is full-rank and marginal-correlation screening is not the object of study. You need guaranteed feature recovery under conditions where model assumptions hold; the paper's own scope is that 'These methods can fail to select the correct features, predict poorly relative to non-sparse alternatives or ignore any unknown grouping structures for the features.' http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Reproduces the AML counterexample from the SuffPCR paper by estimating a sparse inverse covariance (precision matrix) with Graphical Lasso across sparsity levels, forming the pseudo-true coefficient vector β* = Σ^-1 Φ, and showing marginal-correlation screening has high false negative rates even under highly favorable sparsity assumptions. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac033
skills.summary: Reproduces the AML counterexample from the SuffPCR paper by estimating a sparse inverse covariance (precision matrix) with Graphical Lasso across sparsity levels, forming the pseudo-true coefficient vector β* = Σ^-1 Φ, and showing marginal-correlation screening has high false negative rates even under highly favorable sparsity assumptions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is prediction or classification itself (e.g. fitting SuffPCR on X and y with suffPCR(X, y, d=1:3)) rather than evaluating or reproducing the screening counterexample. The dataset is not p>>n transcriptomic data, so the sample covariance is full-rank and marginal-correlation screening is not the object of study. You need guaranteed feature recovery under conditions where model assumptions hold; the paper's own scope is that 'These methods can fail to select the correct features, predict poorly relative to non-sparse alternatives or ignore any unknown grouping structures for the features.'

skills.description: Use when inferring a sparse gene co-expression network from normalized single-cell expression data and the penalization strength (lda) of a Gaussian graphical model must be selected by BIC.

skills.search_text: graphical-model-regularization-tuning Use when inferring a sparse gene co-expression network from normalized single-cell expression data and the penalization strength (lda) of a Gaussian graphical model must be selected by BIC. When Pearson/Spearman correlations or bulk RNA-seq co-expression methods already suffice — scLink's penalized graphical model is motivated by excessive zero counts in sparse single-cell data When the gene list is very large; the article suggests first dividing genes into major modules based on scLink's correlation and applying scLink separately to each module instead of fitting one network When edge direction or edge type (regulatory vs co-regulatory) is required — scLink edges are undirected and their type cannot be distinguished from expression data alone http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Tunes the penalized Gaussian graphical model of scLink by sweeping the regularization parameter grid (lda) and selecting the value by BIC so each inferred gene co-expression network stays sparse (at most ~5% of possible edges). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2020.11.006

skills.description: Use when you need to retrieve per-cell-type differential expression or marker scores for a gene (e.g. insulin) from ingested H5AD-derived single-cell studies stored in Cellenium's PostgreSQL backend, especially for cross-study comparisons.
skills.name: graphql-database-querying-for-scrnaseq
skills.search_text: graphql-database-querying-for-scrnaseq Use when you need to retrieve per-cell-type differential expression or marker scores for a gene (e.g. insulin) from ingested H5AD-derived single-cell studies stored in Cellenium's PostgreSQL backend, especially for cross-study comparisons. skills.summary: Query Cellenium's PostgreSQL-backed single-cell study database through its Postgraphile GraphQL API to retrieve differential expression values and marker statistics per annotated cell type across imported scRNA-seq studies (e.g. the blood_covid.ipynb example), enabling within- and cross-study marker gene searches such as finding pancreatic beta-cells for insulin.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The study data has not yet been ingested — the database is empty until the data_import notebooks are run and a make ..._studydata_import target completes (before make reset_database, errors about the missing 'postgraphile' user appear). The task is raw H5AD processing, normalization, or DE calculation — that is done in the data_import jupyter notebooks, not via the GraphQL API. skills.description: Use when a minimum-weight one-to-one matching is needed on a large weighted bipartite graph (e.g. many anchor cells across two scRNA-seq batches) and the exact blossom algorithm is too slow; accepts up to 2x suboptimality.
skills.name: greedy-approximate-matching-on-weighted-graphs
skills.search_text: greedy-approximate-matching-on-weighted-graphs Use when a minimum-weight one-to-one matching is needed on a large weighted bipartite graph (e.g. many anchor cells across two scRNA-seq batches) and the exact blossom algorithm is too slow; accepts up to 2x suboptimality. When the exact minimum total weight is required and dataset size permits the blossom-based algorithm — the greedy result can be up to twice the optimal total edge weight When integrating more than two datasets — the current BATMAN implementation only supports two datasets When inputs are not log-count matrices with identified anchor cells (e.g. raw counts or already-integrated embeddings) http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 An approximate alternative to the exact blossom-based minimum-weight matching: edges of a weighted bipartite graph (here, anchor cells across two scRNA-seq datasets, weighted by Euclidean distance in N-dimensional gene space) are matched greedily, guaranteeing a total weight within a factor of 2 of optimal. BATMAN exposes this via the -greedy flag and recommends it for extra-large datasets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2020.101185
skills.summary: An approximate alternative to the exact blossom-based minimum-weight matching: edges of a weighted bipartite graph (here, anchor cells across two scRNA-seq datasets, weighted by Euclidean distance in N-dimensional gene space) are matched greedily, guaranteeing a total weight within a factor of 2 of optimal. BATMAN exposes this via the -greedy flag and recommends it for extra-large datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the exact minimum total weight is required and dataset size permits the blossom-based algorithm — the greedy result can be up to twice the optimal total edge weight When integrating more than two datasets — the current BATMAN implementation only supports two datasets When inputs are not log-count matrices with identified anchor cells (e.g. raw counts or already-integrated embeddings)

skills.description: Use when a set of tumor sub-cluster gene expression profiles (GEPs) must be matched against LINCS L1000 perturbation bulk profiles to build a minimal combination therapy covering as many sub-clusters as possible.
skills.name: greedy-combination-treatment-search
skills.search_text: greedy-combination-treatment-search Use when a set of tumor sub-cluster gene expression profiles (GEPs) must be matched against LINCS L1000 perturbation bulk profiles to build a minimal combination therapy covering as many sub-clusters as possible. When the goal is single-agent IC50/drug-kill prediction per cluster rather than combination therapy — use scDrug's Drug Response Prediction module (CaDRReS-Sc/GDSC or PRISM) instead. When the perturbation bulk data cannot be linked to a LINCS L1000 reference cell line or the scDrug prediction is limited to experimentally screened compounds and a de novo compound is required. When input is raw scRNA-seq data without sub-clusters and GEPs computed yet — run Single-Cell Data Analysis (sub-clustering, --GEP) first. http://edamontology.org/topic_0208 A greedy search over LINCS L1000 perturbation signatures that identifies a minimal drug combination killing the maximum number of tumor sub-clusters, as implemented in scDrug's Premnas-based Treatment Selection module. Sub-clusters are deconvolved from bulk perturbation samples with CIBERSORTx and labeled 'killed' when a compound reduces their proportion by >90%. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.11.055
skills.summary: A greedy search over LINCS L1000 perturbation signatures that identifies a minimal drug combination killing the maximum number of tumor sub-clusters, as implemented in scDrug's Premnas-based Treatment Selection module. Sub-clusters are deconvolved from bulk perturbation samples with CIBERSORTx and labeled 'killed' when a compound reduces their proportion by >90%.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is single-agent IC50/drug-kill prediction per cluster rather than combination therapy — use scDrug's Drug Response Prediction module (CaDRReS-Sc/GDSC or PRISM) instead. When the perturbation bulk data cannot be linked to a LINCS L1000 reference cell line or the scDrug prediction is limited to experimentally screened compounds and a de novo compound is required. skills.name: greedy-feature-ranking-scoring
skills.search_text: greedy-feature-ranking-scoring Use when a data matrix and response vector must be reduced to a small ranked feature subset, and plain mRMR is insufficient because feature interactions (complementarity) should be explicitly scored. Inputs are continuous and a mutual-information toolbox like FEAST is required — FEAST expects discrete inputs and produces unreliable results on continuous values without discretisation The task requires exhaustive or non-greedy subset search rather than a fast heuristic off-the-shelf ranking (RRCT is a greedy heuristic extension of mRMR) The problem is not representable as a data matrix plus response vector, the scope the article sets for a generic FS algorithm http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 Implements the RRCT greedy feature-selection scoring criterion, which combines Spearman rank-correlation-based relevance and redundancy terms with a partial-correlation-based complementarity (conditional relevance) term to rank candidate features at each selection step. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2022.100471
skills.summary: Implements the RRCT greedy feature-selection scoring criterion, which combines Spearman rank-correlation-based relevance and redundancy terms with a partial-correlation-based complementarity (conditional relevance) term to rank candidate features at each selection step.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Inputs are continuous and a mutual-information toolbox like FEAST is required — FEAST expects discrete inputs and produces unreliable results on continuous values without discretisation The task requires exhaustive or non-greedy subset search rather than a fast heuristic off-the-shelf ranking (RRCT is a greedy heuristic extension of mRMR) The problem is not representable as a data matrix plus response vector, the scope the article sets for a generic FS algorithm

skills.description: Use when you need a global, discriminative marker set across many overlapping phenotype pairs (e.g., cell-type/tissue combinations in scRNA-seq data) rather than per-group differentially expressed genes, and can supply a phenotype-pair × feature score matrix.
skills.name: greedy-set-cover-feature-selection
skills.search_text: greedy-set-cover-feature-selection Use when you need a global, discriminative marker set across many overlapping phenotype pairs (e.g., cell-type/tissue combinations in scRNA-seq data) rather than per-group differentially expressed genes, and can supply a phenotype-pair × feature score matrix. When only a small number of distinct groups is present and standard per-group differential expression (top DE genes) suffices — the PC formulation targets many groups with overlapping DE genes When a provably optimal solution to the multicover problem is required — G-PC is a greedy approximation and 'does not provide an optimal solution' When the input is already a feature table rather than raw counts needing preprocessing into the phenotype × feature score matrix M http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Greedy feature selection (G-PC) based on the extended greedy algorithm to set cover, applied to the phenotype cover (PC) marker-selection problem formulated over a phenotype × feature score matrix and shown equivalent to NP-complete multiset multicover. Implemented as GreedyPC in the phenotype-cover Python package, it greedily approximates a small marker set such that every phenotype pair is covered to a chosen coverage level. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2022.100332
skills.summary: Greedy feature selection (G-PC) based on the extended greedy algorithm to set cover, applied to the phenotype cover (PC) marker-selection problem formulated over a phenotype × feature score matrix and shown equivalent to NP-complete multiset multicover. Implemented as GreedyPC in the phenotype-cover Python package, it greedily approximates a small marker set such that every phenotype pair is covered to a chosen coverage level.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only a small number of distinct groups is present and standard per-group differential expression (top DE genes) suffices — the PC formulation targets many groups with overlapping DE genes When a provably optimal solution to the multicover problem is required — G-PC is a greedy approximation and 'does not provide an optimal solution' When the input is already a feature table rather than raw counts needing preprocessing into the phenotype × feature score matrix M

skills.description: Use when you need a compact, globally discriminative marker set from a phenotype × feature score matrix (e.g., scRNA-seq cell-type × gene scores) such that every phenotype pair is covered (distinguished) at least K times.
skills.name: greedy-set-cover-implementation
skills.search_text: greedy-set-cover-implementation Use when you need a compact, globally discriminative marker set from a phenotype × feature score matrix (e.g., scRNA-seq cell-type × gene scores) such that every phenotype pair is covered (distinguished) at least K times. You only need per-group differentially expressed genes for a small number of distinct cell types — the paper notes standard DE approaches work well for few distinct groups but fail with many overlapping groups. You require a provably optimal minimum-size cover — the paper states 'While G-PC worked well for the data analyzed in this paper, it does not provide an optimal solution.' Input is already a compact curated marker list (e.g., HuBMAP ASCT+B markers used as reference) rather than a matrix requiring selection. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Implements G-PC, the extended greedy algorithm for the phenotype cover (PC) problem, which selects a minimal marker set so that every phenotype pair is distinguished at coverage K via a multiset-multicover formulation of the phenotype × feature score matrix M. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2022.100332
skills.summary: Implements G-PC, the extended greedy algorithm for the phenotype cover (PC) problem, which selects a minimal marker set so that every phenotype pair is distinguished at coverage K via a multiset-multicover formulation of the phenotype × feature score matrix M.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need per-group differentially expressed genes for a small number of distinct cell types — the paper notes standard DE approaches work well for few distinct groups but fail with many overlapping groups. You require a provably optimal minimum-size cover — the paper states 'While G-PC worked well for the data analyzed in this paper, it does not provide an optimal solution.' Input is already a compact curated marker list (e.g., HuBMAP ASCT+B markers used as reference) rather than a matrix requiring selection.

skills.description: Use when predicting novel secondary drug combinations for a chemotherapy-resistant cancer, given pharmacogenomics drug-response data (e.g., GDSC1000 IC50) partitioned into resistant/sensitive groups and a standard-of-care primary drug query.
skills.name: greedy-set-cover-optimization
skills.search_text: greedy-set-cover-optimization Use when predicting novel secondary drug combinations for a chemotherapy-resistant cancer, given pharmacogenomics drug-response data (e.g., GDSC1000 IC50) partitioned into resistant/sensitive groups and a standard-of-care primary drug query. The goal is testing combinations of more than two secDrugs — the pipeline is currently limited to two-drug combinations per the article's discussion. Pre-clinical/clinical efficacy validation is required — the pipeline predicts candidates only; novel secDrugs such as KIN001-102 and SB505124 lack xenograft or mouse-model validation. The input is already a ranked combination table with confidence scores rather than raw pharmacogenomics drug-response data. http://edamontology.org/topic_0208 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 The secDrug greedy set cover algorithm selects secondary drug combinations that maximally kill resistant cancer cell lines, outputting ranked candidates with proportion-based confidence scores via an R package. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41408-022-00636-2
skills.summary: The secDrug greedy set cover algorithm selects secondary drug combinations that maximally kill resistant cancer cell lines, outputting ranked candidates with proportion-based confidence scores via an R package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is testing combinations of more than two secDrugs — the pipeline is currently limited to two-drug combinations per the article's discussion. Pre-clinical/clinical efficacy validation is required — the pipeline predicts candidates only; novel secDrugs such as KIN001-102 and SB505124 lack xenograft or mouse-model validation. The input is already a ranked combination table with confidence scores rather than raw pharmacogenomics drug-response data.

skills.description: Use when a large scRNA-seq expression matrix (cells x genes/PCs, e.g. CSV of principal components) must be reduced to a fixed number of representative cells that evenly cover transcriptomic space before downstream clustering or trajectory inference.
skills.name: greedy-set-cover-sphere-center-selection
skills.search_text: greedy-set-cover-sphere-center-selection Use when a large scRNA-seq expression matrix (cells x genes/PCs, e.g. CSV of principal components) must be reduced to a fixed number of representative cells that evenly cover transcriptomic space before downstream clustering or trajectory inference. The dataset is small enough that full-dataset analysis (e.g. SC3 consensus clustering or Monocle 2 on all cells) is already computationally feasible The analysis requires uniform random subsampling or box/geometric (k-means++) sketching rather than sphere-based coverage — Sphetcher specifically improves on geometric box approximations Only a per-cluster random sample is needed and cluster labels exist; clustering-then-sampling (dropClust) may suffice, though it provides unbalanced samples that hamper downstream analyses http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Selects a fixed-size sketch of representative cells from a single-cell expression matrix by binary-searching a covering-sphere radius and using a greedy set-cover step to pick sphere centers, as implemented in the Sphetcher tool. It approximates the transcriptomic space with spheres rather than boxes, preserving rare cell states better than uniform subsampling. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2020.101126
skills.summary: Selects a fixed-size sketch of representative cells from a single-cell expression matrix by binary-searching a covering-sphere radius and using a greedy set-cover step to pick sphere centers, as implemented in the Sphetcher tool. It approximates the transcriptomic space with spheres rather than boxes, preserving rare cell states better than uniform subsampling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is small enough that full-dataset analysis (e.g. SC3 consensus clustering or Monocle 2 on all cells) is already computationally feasible The analysis requires uniform random subsampling or box/geometric (k-means++) sketching rather than sphere-based coverage — Sphetcher specifically improves on geometric box approximations Only a per-cluster random sample is needed and cluster labels exist; clustering-then-sampling (dropClust) may suffice, though it provides unbalanced samples that hamper downstream analyses

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how reproducible the feature sets selected by G-PC or CEM-PC are across repeated runs on randomly sampled scRNA-seq data, e.g. IPF lung, mouse cortex, or Human Cell Atlas matrices.
skills.name: greedy-vs-cross-entropy-marker-solver-benchmarking
skills.search_text: greedy-vs-cross-entropy-marker-solver-benchmarking Use when you need to quantify how reproducible the feature sets selected by G-PC or CEM-PC are across repeated runs on randomly sampled scRNA-seq data, e.g. IPF lung, mouse cortex, or Human Cell Atlas matrices. When the goal is to evaluate discriminative classification accuracy of the marker sets rather than their run-to-run reproducibility When benchmarking deterministic global marker-selection methods (e.g. ReliefF, F values) alone, whose stability behavior the paper reports separately from G-PC and CEM-PC http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmarks the stability of marker sets produced by the phenotype-cover solvers GreedyPC (G-PC) and CEMPC (CEM-PC) by repeatedly re-running each solver on randomly resampled half-datasets and computing pairwise overlap statistics of the selected features. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2022.100332
skills.summary: Benchmarks the stability of marker sets produced by the phenotype-cover solvers GreedyPC (G-PC) and CEMPC (CEM-PC) by repeatedly re-running each solver on randomly resampled half-datasets and computing pairwise overlap statistics of the selected features.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to evaluate discriminative classification accuracy of the marker sets rather than their run-to-run reproducibility When benchmarking deterministic global marker-selection methods (e.g. ReliefF, F values) alone, whose stability behavior the paper reports separately from G-PC and CEM-PC

skills.description: Use when the goal is TWAS Stage I: estimating per-gene eQTL weights from a reference panel, especially when only summary-level eQTL data (e.g., eQTLGen, GTEx V8) are available instead of individual-level genotype/expression data.
skills.name: grex-imputation-weight-training
skills.search_text: grex-imputation-weight-training Use when the goal is TWAS Stage I: estimating per-gene eQTL weights from a reference panel, especially when only summary-level eQTL data (e.g., eQTLGen, GTEx V8) are available instead of individual-level genotype/expression data. The analysis needs trans-eQTL effects or cross-population transferability to non-European reference data — OTTERS currently considers only cis-eQTL effects and available summary references are mainly European The downstream result must report the direction of the gene-phenotype association from the omnibus test — OTTERS cannot provide this; users must refer to per-method TWAS Z-scores Reference eQTL summary statistics for the target tissue are unavailable and no individual-level genotype/expression data exist as an alternative reference http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 Trains GReX/eQTL imputation weights (TWAS Stage I) from reference data, either summary-level eQTL statistics via OTTERS' adaptation of four PRS methods (P+T, lassosum, SDPR, PRS-CS), or individual-level genotypes and expression via FUSION, producing per-gene weight files for downstream TWAS testing. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-36862-w
skills.summary: Trains GReX/eQTL imputation weights (TWAS Stage I) from reference data, either summary-level eQTL statistics via OTTERS' adaptation of four PRS methods (P+T, lassosum, SDPR, PRS-CS), or individual-level genotypes and expression via FUSION, producing per-gene weight files for downstream TWAS testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis needs trans-eQTL effects or cross-population transferability to non-European reference data — OTTERS currently considers only cis-eQTL effects and available summary references are mainly European The downstream result must report the direction of the gene-phenotype association from the omnibus test — OTTERS cannot provide this; users must refer to per-method TWAS Z-scores Reference eQTL summary statistics for the target tissue are unavailable and no individual-level genotype/expression data exist as an alternative reference

skills.description: Use when ranking candidate transcription-factor perturbations from CellOracle GRN simulations: simulated KO/overexpression transitions must be scored against a reference differentiation trajectory on a low-dimensional embedding.
skills.name: grid-based-transition-probability-estimation
skills.search_text: grid-based-transition-probability-estimation Use when ranking candidate transcription-factor perturbations from CellOracle GRN simulations: simulated KO/overexpression transitions must be scored against a reference differentiation trajectory on a low-dimensional embedding. When the goal is static GRN inference or network topology analysis (degree/connectivity of regulators like Mef2a or Klf6) rather than scoring simulated fate-transition outcomes When no reference differentiation trajectory (pseudotime-derived gradient) is available to compare simulated transitions against, since the inner-product score is undefined without both vector fields http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Quantifies in silico TF perturbation effects in CellOracle by converting simulated cell-state transitions and a pseudotime-derived differentiation gradient into 2D grid-based vector fields, then computing the inner product of the two vectors at each grid point to obtain a perturbation score per candidate TF. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.stemcr.2022.11.010
skills.summary: Quantifies in silico TF perturbation effects in CellOracle by converting simulated cell-state transitions and a pseudotime-derived differentiation gradient into 2D grid-based vector fields, then computing the inner product of the two vectors at each grid point to obtain a perturbation score per candidate TF.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is static GRN inference or network topology analysis (degree/connectivity of regulators like Mef2a or Klf6) rather than scoring simulated fate-transition outcomes When no reference differentiation trajectory (pseudotime-derived gradient) is available to compare simulated transitions against, since the inner-product score is undefined without both vector fields

skills.description: Use when you have single-cell data with global x/y spatial coordinates (e.g. seqFISH slides) and need simulated ST spot data with known cell-type ground truth to benchmark or validate single-cell-to-spatial mapping methods.
skills.name: grid-pseudo-spot-coordinate-generation
skills.search_text: grid-pseudo-spot-coordinate-generation Use when you have single-cell data with global x/y spatial coordinates (e.g. seqFISH slides) and need simulated ST spot data with known cell-type ground truth to benchmark or validate single-cell-to-spatial mapping methods. You already have real ST spot data and do not need simulated ground truth — deconvolve or map directly instead of synthesizing pseudo-spots. The single-cell data lacks global spatial coordinates, since grid placement over the slide requires per-cell x/y positions. You need single-cell-resolution ST benchmarks rather than spot-level mixtures; the pseudo-spots discard within-spot single-cell identity except as aggregated cell-type proportions. http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 Synthesizes pseudo-Visium-like spatial transcriptomics spots from single-cell spatial data by placing a grid of spot locations over tissue slide coordinates and summing the gene expression of the single cells covered by each spot. This creates paired SC/ST ground-truth data for benchmarking spatial mapping methods like STEM in semi-simulation experiments. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-023-05640-1
skills.summary: Synthesizes pseudo-Visium-like spatial transcriptomics spots from single-cell spatial data by placing a grid of spot locations over tissue slide coordinates and summing the gene expression of the single cells covered by each spot. This creates paired SC/ST ground-truth data for benchmarking spatial mapping methods like STEM in semi-simulation experiments.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have real ST spot data and do not need simulated ground truth — deconvolve or map directly instead of synthesizing pseudo-spots. The single-cell data lacks global spatial coordinates, since grid placement over the slide requires per-cell x/y positions. You need single-cell-resolution ST benchmarks rather than spot-level mixtures; the pseudo-spots discard within-spot single-cell identity except as aggregated cell-type proportions.

skills.search_text: grid-search-map-confidence-interval-estimation Use when reconstructing exact ecDNA breakpoints from ATAC-Seq junction evidence (discordant read pairs, soft-clipped/supplementary reads) and quantifying breakpoint confidence intervals across read lengths, e.g. down to 35 bp. skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq data and a CellOracle Links/GRN object are available and the goal is to predict, in silico, how knocking out or overexpressing a candidate TF (e.g., Fos) redirects cells among known clusters or attractors before committing to experiments.
skills.name: grn-based-cell-identity-transition-simulation
skills.search_text: grn-based-cell-identity-transition-simulation Use when scRNA-seq data and a CellOracle Links/GRN object are available and the goal is to predict, in silico, how knocking out or overexpressing a candidate TF (e.g., Fos) redirects cells among known clusters or attractors before committing to experiments. The input is raw sequencing data that has not been processed (e.g., no Cell Ranger matrix or no inferred CellOracle Links/GRN object yet) — GRN inference must precede simulation The cell states of interest lack annotated clusters or a reference for identity scoring, so simulated transition probabilities cannot be anchored to real identity labels The question concerns TFs or regulatory edges absent from the inferred base GRN (e.g., base GRN derived from the Mouse sci-ATAC-seq Atlas lacks accessible motifs for the factor), since edge removal/reinforcement requires existing network edges http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Simulates how transcription factor perturbation (KO via edge removal, overexpression via edge reinforcement) shifts cell identity along a CellOracle-inferred gene regulatory network, projecting predicted fate transitions as vector-field and Sankey-style transition maps over a scRNA-seq embedding. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.stemcr.2022.11.010
skills.summary: Simulates how transcription factor perturbation (KO via edge removal, overexpression via edge reinforcement) shifts cell identity along a CellOracle-inferred gene regulatory network, projecting predicted fate transitions as vector-field and Sankey-style transition maps over a scRNA-seq embedding.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw sequencing data that has not been processed (e.g., no Cell Ranger matrix or no inferred CellOracle Links/GRN object yet) — GRN inference must precede simulation The cell states of interest lack annotated clusters or a reference for identity scoring, so simulated transition probabilities cannot be anchored to real identity labels The question concerns TFs or regulatory edges absent from the inferred base GRN (e.g., base GRN derived from the Mouse sci-ATAC-seq Atlas lacks accessible motifs for the factor), since edge removal/reinforcement requires existing network edges

skills.description: Use when a GRN/gene-module method needs a functional benchmark against SCENIC regulons on single-cell lineages, comparing enrichment precision and NMI of clustering.
skills.name: grn-baseline-comparison-against-scenic
skills.search_text: grn-baseline-comparison-against-scenic Use when a GRN/gene-module method needs a functional benchmark against SCENIC regulons on single-cell lineages, comparing enrichment precision and NMI of clustering. Input GRNs or driver regulators have not yet been generated by an upstream CEFCON run (the benchmark assumes precomputed lineage-specific GRNs with edge_threshold_avgDegree=8) The data do not contain a developmental cell lineage trajectory with reference cell-type labels, since NMI cannot be computed without ground-truth labels The goal is GRN edge-level accuracy benchmarking (e.g., against GENELink-style supervised methods) rather than gene module functional quality http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmark regulon-like gene modules (RGMs) from CEFCON against pySCENIC regulons on the hESC, mESC, and mHSC lineage datasets, scoring both by GO_BP/KEGG enrichment precision and NMI of AUCell-based cell clustering to demonstrate CEFCON's superiority in gene module identification (Fig. 5b-d). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-44103-3
skills.summary: Benchmark regulon-like gene modules (RGMs) from CEFCON against pySCENIC regulons on the hESC, mESC, and mHSC lineage datasets, scoring both by GO_BP/KEGG enrichment precision and NMI of AUCell-based cell clustering to demonstrate CEFCON's superiority in gene module identification (Fig. 5b-d).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input GRNs or driver regulators have not yet been generated by an upstream CEFCON run (the benchmark assumes precomputed lineage-specific GRNs with edge_threshold_avgDegree=8) The data do not contain a developmental cell lineage trajectory with reference cell-type labels, since NMI cannot be computed without ground-truth labels The goal is GRN edge-level accuracy benchmarking (e.g., against GENELink-style supervised methods) rather than gene module functional quality

skills.description: Use when a Bayes-Factor-ranked scGATE edge list (from/to/BF_score) must be scored against ground-truth networks such as Cus_KO/Cus_Chip or ChIP-Atlas-derived GRNs using precision-recall/AUPR, or when comparing scGATE against other network-inference tools on single-cell multi-omics data.
skills.name: grn-benchmark-against-ground-truth-networks
skills.search_text: grn-benchmark-against-ground-truth-networks Use when a Bayes-Factor-ranked scGATE edge list (from/to/BF_score) must be scored against ground-truth networks such as Cus_KO/Cus_Chip or ChIP-Atlas-derived GRNs using precision-recall/AUPR, or when comparing scGATE against other network-inference tools on single-cell multi-omics data. The inference target is a large-scale, de novo network: the paper states scGATE 'is currently applicable to a rather small (<200) subset of genes with a refined list of candidate regulatory TFs based on external hints', so benchmarking on unfiltered genome-wide gene sets is out of scope. The goal is inference rather than evaluation, and no external-hint base GRN (scATAC-seq + TF motifs) is available to constrain candidate TF–target pairs. Ground truth comes from large protein complex interactions, which the authors note 'will be missed both in our current model as well as the ground-truth', making such edges unreliable for scoring. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmarks a scGATE-inferred TF–target network against curated gold-standard GRNs (e.g. Cus_KO and Cus_Chip for human haematopoiesis, or ChIP-Atlas-derived ChIP-seq networks) by computing precision–recall/AUPR on the Bayes-Factor-ranked edge list, to reproduce the paper's claim that scGATE outperforms existing GRN-inference tools. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbae180
skills.summary: Benchmarks a scGATE-inferred TF–target network against curated gold-standard GRNs (e.g. Cus_KO and Cus_Chip for human haematopoiesis, or ChIP-Atlas-derived ChIP-seq networks) by computing precision–recall/AUPR on the Bayes-Factor-ranked edge list, to reproduce the paper's claim that scGATE outperforms existing GRN-inference tools.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The inference target is a large-scale, de novo network: the paper states scGATE 'is currently applicable to a rather small (<200) subset of genes with a refined list of candidate regulatory TFs based on external hints', so benchmarking on unfiltered genome-wide gene sets is out of scope. The goal is inference rather than evaluation, and no external-hint base GRN (scATAC-seq + TF motifs) is available to constrain candidate TF–target pairs. Ground truth comes from large protein complex interactions, which the authors note 'will be missed both in our current model as well as the ground-truth', making such edges unreliable for scoring.

skills.description: Use when comparing multiple GRN-inference algorithms on the same scRNA-seq input matrix (e.g., BEELINE GSD 19 genes x 2,000 cells or SERGIO-simulated 100-gene matrices) where ground-truth regulatory edges exist and AUROC/AUPRC/runtime ranking is the goal.
skills.name: grn-benchmark-auroc-auprc-evaluation
skills.search_text: grn-benchmark-auroc-auprc-evaluation Use when comparing multiple GRN-inference algorithms on the same scRNA-seq input matrix (e.g., BEELINE GSD 19 genes x 2,000 cells or SERGIO-simulated 100-gene matrices) where ground-truth regulatory edges exist and AUROC/AUPRC/runtime ranking is the goal. No ground-truth regulatory network is available for the dataset, so AUROC/AUPRC cannot be computed and only relative internal validation is possible The goal is differential-regulation discovery between two conditions rather than comparing GRN-construction algorithms; use the full scTenifoldNet manifold-alignment workflow instead The input is normalized/processed expression rather than a raw counts matrix with genes as rows and cells as columns, breaking comparability with the uniform benchmark pipeline http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Uniformly benchmark single-cell GRN-construction methods (scTenifoldNet PC regression, PIDC, SCC, MI, GENIE3, etc.) by scoring predicted edge rankings against a ground-truth network with AUROC and AUPRC, and recording per-method computation time. In this article's benchmarks, PC regression outperformed the other GRN construction algorithms in specificity, sensitivity, and computational efficiency. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2020.100139
skills.summary: Uniformly benchmark single-cell GRN-construction methods (scTenifoldNet PC regression, PIDC, SCC, MI, GENIE3, etc.) by scoring predicted edge rankings against a ground-truth network with AUROC and AUPRC, and recording per-method computation time. In this article's benchmarks, PC regression outperformed the other GRN construction algorithms in specificity, sensitivity, and computational efficiency.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No ground-truth regulatory network is available for the dataset, so AUROC/AUPRC cannot be computed and only relative internal validation is possible The goal is differential-regulation discovery between two conditions rather than comparing GRN-construction algorithms; use the full scTenifoldNet manifold-alignment workflow instead The input is normalized/processed expression rather than a raw counts matrix with genes as rows and cells as columns, breaking comparability with the uniform benchmark pipeline

skills.description: Use when you have one or more inferred GRNs and Perturb-seq count matrices (e.g., Dixit GSE90063 or Papalexi GSE153056) and need a quantitative, comparable ranking of network accuracy via perturbation-target prediction.
skills.name: grn-benchmark-auroc-tpr-evaluation
skills.search_text: grn-benchmark-auroc-tpr-evaluation Use when you have one or more inferred GRNs and Perturb-seq count matrices (e.g., Dixit GSE90063 or Papalexi GSE153056) and need a quantitative, comparable ranking of network accuracy via perturbation-target prediction. You do not have Perturb-seq data with known perturbation targets — use goodness-of-fit (cosine similarity on held-out train/test splits) or disease subnetwork random-walk validation instead. The GRN was inferred on a subset of genes/cells inconsistent with the perturbation dataset, so downstream genes of the perturbed gene are not represented in the network. http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmark single-cell GRN inference methods (SCING, GRNBOOST2, PIDC, ppcor) by predicting downstream perturbed genes in Perturb-seq datasets, scoring each method with AUROC and TPR at FPR 0.05 to quantify how accurately inferred networks capture real perturbation effects. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2023.107124
skills.summary: Benchmark single-cell GRN inference methods (SCING, GRNBOOST2, PIDC, ppcor) by predicting downstream perturbed genes in Perturb-seq datasets, scoring each method with AUROC and TPR at FPR 0.05 to quantify how accurately inferred networks capture real perturbation effects.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You do not have Perturb-seq data with known perturbation targets — use goodness-of-fit (cosine similarity on held-out train/test splits) or disease subnetwork random-walk validation instead. The GRN was inferred on a subset of genes/cells inconsistent with the perturbation dataset, so downstream genes of the perturbed gene are not represented in the network.

skills.description: Use when an inferred gene regulatory network (e.g., from Augusta on DREAM 4 or time-series RNA-Seq) needs quantitative evaluation against a reference edge set, using sensitivity/specificity/accuracy metrics.
skills.name: grn-benchmark-evaluation-against-gold-standard
skills.search_text: grn-benchmark-evaluation-against-gold-standard Use when an inferred gene regulatory network (e.g., from Augusta on DREAM 4 or time-series RNA-Seq) needs quantitative evaluation against a reference edge set, using sensitivity/specificity/accuracy metrics. The gold standard includes signed or directed edges and you want signed/direction-aware evaluation without the simplification step (dropping interaction types and negatives) used here You need autoregulation assessment — the article notes 'inferring autoregulations remains a significant challenge' The network is a refined Augusta GRN with signed interactions destined for Boolean model construction rather than benchmarking http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_0204 Benchmark a GRN inference pipeline (e.g., Augusta's MI-based initial GRN with MSD edge orientation) against an undirected gold-standard network by computing sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy from a confusion matrix of predicted versus true edges. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2024.01.013
skills.summary: Benchmark a GRN inference pipeline (e.g., Augusta's MI-based initial GRN with MSD edge orientation) against an undirected gold-standard network by computing sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy from a confusion matrix of predicted versus true edges.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The gold standard includes signed or directed edges and you want signed/direction-aware evaluation without the simplification step (dropping interaction types and negatives) used here You need autoregulation assessment — the article notes 'inferring autoregulations remains a significant challenge' The network is a refined Augusta GRN with signed interactions destined for Boolean model construction rather than benchmarking

skills.description: Use when benchmarking cell-specific network inference (CSNI) methods such as pySCENIC, LIONESS, or SSN on simulated single-cell data where the ground-truth cellwise regulatory network is known.
skills.name: grn-benchmark-evaluation-auroc-aupr
skills.search_text: grn-benchmark-evaluation-auroc-aupr Use when benchmarking cell-specific network inference (CSNI) methods such as pySCENIC, LIONESS, or SSN on simulated single-cell data where the ground-truth cellwise regulatory network is known. The data are real single-cell measurements without ground-truth cellwise regulatory networks — quantitative AUROC/AUPR evaluation requires dyngen's known ground truth The method requires motif enrichment information for regulon filtering (e.g. full SCENIC motif step) — dyngen does not generate motif data, so that step must be skipped Evaluating trajectory inference, trajectory alignment, or RNA velocity rather than cell-specific regulatory network inference http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Evaluate cell-specific gene regulatory network (GRN) inference methods by comparing predicted (cell, regulator, target, score) tuples against dyngen's ground-truth cellwise regulatory networks using AUROC and AUPR scores, averaged across cells and datasets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-24152-2
skills.summary: Evaluate cell-specific gene regulatory network (GRN) inference methods by comparing predicted (cell, regulator, target, score) tuples against dyngen's ground-truth cellwise regulatory networks using AUROC and AUPR scores, averaged across cells and datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are real single-cell measurements without ground-truth cellwise regulatory networks — quantitative AUROC/AUPR evaluation requires dyngen's known ground truth The method requires motif enrichment information for regulon filtering (e.g. full SCENIC motif step) — dyngen does not generate motif data, so that step must be skipped Evaluating trajectory inference, trajectory alignment, or RNA velocity rather than cell-specific regulatory network inference

skills.description: Use when comparing inferred gene networks (from scPRINT, GENIE3, scGPT, DeepSEM, Geneformer, etc.) against a binary perturb-seq or literature ground truth and you need comparable AUPRC/EPR scores.
skills.name: grn-benchmark-metric-computation-epr-auprc
skills.search_text: grn-benchmark-metric-computation-epr-auprc Use when comparing inferred gene networks (from scPRINT, GENIE3, scGPT, DeepSEM, Geneformer, etc.) against a binary perturb-seq or literature ground truth and you need comparable AUPRC/EPR scores. The ground truth is not binary or cannot be thresholded into directed gene-by-gene edges (e.g. raw weighted association matrices without a defensible cutoff) Inferred networks cannot be aligned to the ground truth gene set and orientation (regulators as columns, targets as rows), since mismatched dimensions invalidate TP/TN/FP/FN counts http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Scores inferred gene regulatory networks against a binarized ground truth (e.g. the genome-wide perturb-seq K562 network at a 0.05 cutoff on corrected p-values) using AUPRC above the positive-class prevalence floor and EPR, a diagnostic-odds-ratio-based enrichment metric, via the benGRN and GRnnData packages. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-58699-1
skills.summary: Scores inferred gene regulatory networks against a binarized ground truth (e.g. the genome-wide perturb-seq K562 network at a 0.05 cutoff on corrected p-values) using AUPRC above the positive-class prevalence floor and EPR, a diagnostic-odds-ratio-based enrichment metric, via the benGRN and GRnnData packages.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The ground truth is not binary or cannot be thresholded into directed gene-by-gene edges (e.g. raw weighted association matrices without a defensible cutoff) Inferred networks cannot be aligned to the ground truth gene set and orientation (regulators as columns, targets as rows), since mismatched dimensions invalidate TP/TN/FP/FN counts

skills.description: Use when one or more predicted GRNs (e.g., Augusta MI-only, Augusta with TFBM/DB refinement, GENIE3, TDAracne, KBoost) must be quantitatively compared against a gold-standard network with directed-edge ground truth.
skills.name: grn-confusion-matrix-evaluation
skills.search_text: grn-confusion-matrix-evaluation Use when one or more predicted GRNs (e.g., Augusta MI-only, Augusta with TFBM/DB refinement, GENIE3, TDAracne, KBoost) must be quantitatively compared against a gold-standard network with directed-edge ground truth. No gold-standard network is available for the organism/dataset, so no confusion matrix against known edges can be computed Evaluating Augusta Boolean network drafts, which the paper cautions 'should be treated with caution as they rather present first drafts than final BNs' rather than final networks to be scored Gold standard includes edge types/interaction semantics that the predictor explicitly does not model and cannot be simplified away http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Benchmarking protocol for scoring inferred gene regulatory networks (Augusta, GENIE3, TDAracne, KBoost) against gold-standard networks using confusion matrices that yield sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and execution time, as done on the DREAM 4 In Silico Network Challenge and B. subtilis 168 datasets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2024.01.013
skills.summary: Benchmarking protocol for scoring inferred gene regulatory networks (Augusta, GENIE3, TDAracne, KBoost) against gold-standard networks using confusion matrices that yield sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and execution time, as done on the DREAM 4 In Silico Network Challenge and B. subtilis 168 datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No gold-standard network is available for the organism/dataset, so no confusion matrix against known edges can be computed Evaluating Augusta Boolean network drafts, which the paper cautions 'should be treated with caution as they rather present first drafts than final BNs' rather than final networks to be scored Gold standard includes edge types/interaction semantics that the predictor explicitly does not model and cannot be simplified away

skills.description: Use when refining a MI-inferred GRN with curated database interactions and the same regulator-target pair receives contradictory edge types (e.g., activation vs. inhibition) from inference or from multiple databases.
skills.name: grn-edge-conflict-resolution
skills.search_text: grn-edge-conflict-resolution Use when refining a MI-inferred GRN with curated database interactions and the same regulator-target pair receives contradictory edge types (e.g., activation vs. inhibition) from inference or from multiple databases. The organism under study is a non-model organism absent from OmniPath, Signor, SignaLink, and TRRUST — database mining adds no verified edges, and refinement relies only on de novo TFBM prediction You only have a raw RNA-Seq count table and no initial GRN yet — infer the network first with Augusta.RNASeq_to_GRN before conflict resolution is meaningful Your goal is Boolean Network conversion with logical rules — that is handled downstream by the Cell Collective database search in Augusta.GRN_to_BN, not by edge conflict resolution http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Resolves conflicting regulatory edge types that arise when merging manually curated database interactions (OmniPath, Signor, SignaLink, TRRUST) into an initial mutual-information-inferred GRN during Augusta's refinement step, producing a final GRN adjacency matrix. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2024.01.013
skills.summary: Resolves conflicting regulatory edge types that arise when merging manually curated database interactions (OmniPath, Signor, SignaLink, TRRUST) into an initial mutual-information-inferred GRN during Augusta's refinement step, producing a final GRN adjacency matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The organism under study is a non-model organism absent from OmniPath, Signor, SignaLink, and TRRUST — database mining adds no verified edges, and refinement relies only on de novo TFBM prediction You only have a raw RNA-Seq count table and no initial GRN yet — infer the network first with Augusta.RNASeq_to_GRN before conflict resolution is meaningful Your goal is Boolean Network conversion with logical rules — that is handled downstream by the Cell Collective database search in Augusta.GRN_to_BN, not by edge conflict resolution

skills.description: Use when GRouNdGAN has been trained with an imposed GRN (e.g., GRNBoost2- or PPCOR-derived) on PBMC-CTL or a similar reference dataset and you need to test whether knocking out each regulating TF significantly changes its target genes' simulated expression.
skills.name: grn-edge-significance-quantification
skills.search_text: grn-edge-significance-quantification Use when GRouNdGAN has been trained with an imposed GRN (e.g., GRNBoost2- or PPCOR-derived) on PBMC-CTL or a similar reference dataset and you need to test whether knocking out each regulating TF significantly changes its target genes' simulated expression. The model was trained without an imposed bipartite GRN (GRouNdGAN's current version only supports bipartite GRNs, so multi-layer or TF-gene-phenotype graphs cannot be tested) You need to predict TF knockout outcomes in real (not simulated) cells — the paper notes this would require a high-quality GRN plus additional modalities such as (sc)ATAC-seq or TF ChIP-seq Perturbed and control cells come from different simulated batches — the Wilcoxon signed-rank comparison requires matched case-control pairs from the same fixed batch http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Quantifies the fraction of imposed TF-gene edges whose target-gene expression is significantly altered by in silico TF knockout in GRouNdGAN-simulated cells, using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. It validates that the imposed causal GRN is reflected in the interventional (perturbed) simulations. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-48516-6
skills.summary: Quantifies the fraction of imposed TF-gene edges whose target-gene expression is significantly altered by in silico TF knockout in GRouNdGAN-simulated cells, using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. It validates that the imposed causal GRN is reflected in the interventional (perturbed) simulations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The model was trained without an imposed bipartite GRN (GRouNdGAN's current version only supports bipartite GRNs, so multi-layer or TF-gene-phenotype graphs cannot be tested) You need to predict TF knockout outcomes in real (not simulated) cells — the paper notes this would require a high-quality GRN plus additional modalities such as (sc)ATAC-seq or TF ChIP-seq Perturbed and control cells come from different simulated batches — the Wilcoxon signed-rank comparison requires matched case-control pairs from the same fixed batch

skills.description: Use when you need reference-based simulation of scRNA-seq data that retains the regulatory dynamics of a user-provided causal GRN, e.g. for benchmarking GRN inference or pseudo-time preservation studies.
skills.name: grn-guided-gan-training
skills.search_text: grn-guided-gan-training Use when you need reference-based simulation of scRNA-seq data that retains the regulatory dynamics of a user-provided causal GRN, e.g. for benchmarking GRN inference or pseudo-time preservation studies. You need unnormalized count data — GRouNdGAN currently only generates expression values library-size normalized across the considered genes and TFs Your GRN is multi-layer or includes TF-gene-phenotype edges — the current version only supports imposing a bipartite GRN You want to predict outcomes on a new dataset without retraining — GRouNdGAN is generative, not predictive, and must be retrained for a new dataset http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Train GRouNdGAN, a GRN-guided causal implicit GAN, on a preprocessed scRNA-seq reference dataset with a GRNBoost2-inferred causal graph, then generate in-silico single cells (simulated.h5ad) that preserve gene identities, trajectories, and pseudo-time ordering. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-48516-6
skills.summary: Train GRouNdGAN, a GRN-guided causal implicit GAN, on a preprocessed scRNA-seq reference dataset with a GRNBoost2-inferred causal graph, then generate in-silico single cells (simulated.h5ad) that preserve gene identities, trajectories, and pseudo-time ordering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need unnormalized count data — GRouNdGAN currently only generates expression values library-size normalized across the considered genes and TFs Your GRN is multi-layer or includes TF-gene-phenotype edges — the current version only supports imposing a bipartite GRN You want to predict outcomes on a new dataset without retraining — GRouNdGAN is generative, not predictive, and must be retrained for a new dataset

skills.description: Use when a fitted scKINETICS model (GRN matrix A plus per-cell velocities) is available and you need per-cell TF activity scores across all regulators to identify regulators driving a transition, such as acinar-to-ductal metaplasia.
skills.name: grn-in-silico-knockout-analysis
skills.search_text: grn-in-silico-knockout-analysis Use when a fitted scKINETICS model (GRN matrix A plus per-cell velocities) is available and you need per-cell TF activity scores across all regulators to identify regulators driving a transition, such as acinar-to-ductal metaplasia. No fitted scKINETICS model exists yet — the GRN matrix A and original velocities must first be produced by fitting the scKINETICS dynamical model (EM estimation); use the model-fitting skill first. The goal is differential gene expression analysis rather than regulator activity: cosine distance of velocity perturbation measures regulatory influence, not expression level, so it will not summarize expression (e.g. Ptf1a is recovered by activity despite low expression). The perturbation of interest is a multi-gene or pathway-level perturbation rather than removal of a single TF's column in the GRN. http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 In silico transcription factor knockout using scKINETICS: zero out each TF's column in the learned gene regulatory network, recompute per-cell velocities, and score each regulator's activity by the cosine distance between original and perturbed velocity vectors to recover regulators of acinar-to-ductal metaplasia. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad267
skills.summary: In silico transcription factor knockout using scKINETICS: zero out each TF's column in the learned gene regulatory network, recompute per-cell velocities, and score each regulator's activity by the cosine distance between original and perturbed velocity vectors to recover regulators of acinar-to-ductal metaplasia.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No fitted scKINETICS model exists yet — the GRN matrix A and original velocities must first be produced by fitting the scKINETICS dynamical model (EM estimation); use the model-fitting skill first. The goal is differential gene expression analysis rather than regulator activity: cosine distance of velocity perturbation measures regulatory influence, not expression level, so it will not summarize expression (e.g. Ptf1a is recovered by activity despite low expression). The perturbation of interest is a multi-gene or pathway-level perturbation rather than removal of a single TF's column in the GRN.

skills.description: Use when you need to decide how many cells and how many candidate TFs per target are sufficient for reliable scGATE logic-gate inference, or when reproducing runtime/saturation curves like Figure 5C before committing to a full-network run.
skills.name: grn-inference-benchmarking
skills.search_text: grn-inference-benchmarking Use when you need to decide how many cells and how many candidate TFs per target are sufficient for reliable scGATE logic-gate inference, or when reproducing runtime/saturation curves like Figure 5C before committing to a full-network run. When the goal is large-scale de novo GRN inference: scGATE is applicable only to a small (<200) subset of genes with a refined candidate TF list based on external hints When candidate TF sets exceed k=5 regulators per target, since overfitting makes high-order Boolean logic (>5 TFs) unreliable When the scRNA-seq data have far fewer cells than the log10(n) ≈ #TFs heuristic requires for the chosen candidate TF count (inference quality will not have saturated) http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 A sensitivity-analysis skill for scGATE-based gene regulatory network inference that quantifies how inference quality (log10 Bayes Factor, AUROC, EPR) and runtime scale with the number of sampled cells and the number of candidate regulatory TFs per target, establishing sample-size adequacy via the log10(n) ≈ #TFs heuristic. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbae180
skills.summary: A sensitivity-analysis skill for scGATE-based gene regulatory network inference that quantifies how inference quality (log10 Bayes Factor, AUROC, EPR) and runtime scale with the number of sampled cells and the number of candidate regulatory TFs per target, establishing sample-size adequacy via the log10(n) ≈ #TFs heuristic.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is large-scale de novo GRN inference: scGATE is applicable only to a small (<200) subset of genes with a refined candidate TF list based on external hints When candidate TF sets exceed k=5 regulators per target, since overfitting makes high-order Boolean logic (>5 TFs) unreliable When the scRNA-seq data have far fewer cells than the log10(n) ≈ #TFs heuristic requires for the chosen candidate TF count (inference quality will not have saturated)

skills.description: Use when a workflow depends on a GRN inferred from a single-cell gene expression matrix and you need to test whether the downstream results (e.g., cell-type communication matrices) are robust to swapping the GRN inference algorithm.
skills.name: grn-inference-benchmarking-with-genie3-and-grnboost
skills.search_text: grn-inference-benchmarking-with-genie3-and-grnboost Use when a workflow depends on a GRN inferred from a single-cell gene expression matrix and you need to test whether the downstream results (e.g., cell-type communication matrices) are robust to swapping the GRN inference algorithm. The downstream method requires predefined ligand-receptor pairs or signaling pathway knowledge (e.g., CellChat, CellPhoneDB, iTALK workflows) rather than an inferred GRN adjacency matrix You have no cell classification labels or fewer than 10 cells in the input expression data, so MDIC3's cell-to-cell-type communication inference cannot be run The goal is to evaluate GRN inference accuracy against a known gold-standard network directly, rather than assessing robustness of a downstream communication result http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmark a gene regulatory network (GRN) inference step by substituting alternative tools (GENIE3, GRNBoost, in place of GNIPLR) into a downstream pipeline (MDIC3 cell-cell communication inference) and comparing resulting outputs element-wise to test robustness. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100911
skills.summary: Benchmark a gene regulatory network (GRN) inference step by substituting alternative tools (GENIE3, GRNBoost, in place of GNIPLR) into a downstream pipeline (MDIC3 cell-cell communication inference) and comparing resulting outputs element-wise to test robustness.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The downstream method requires predefined ligand-receptor pairs or signaling pathway knowledge (e.g., CellChat, CellPhoneDB, iTALK workflows) rather than an inferred GRN adjacency matrix You have no cell classification labels or fewer than 10 cells in the input expression data, so MDIC3's cell-to-cell-type communication inference cannot be run The goal is to evaluate GRN inference accuracy against a known gold-standard network directly, rather than assessing robustness of a downstream communication result

skills.description: Use when a scRNA-seq expression matrix (genes x cells, .txt, rows = genes, columns = cells) must be converted into a GRN adjacency matrix to serve as the left submatrix R in MDIC3, or when benchmarking GNIPLR against GENIE3/GRNBoost as GRN sources.
skills.name: grn-inference-gniplr
skills.search_text: grn-inference-gniplr Use when a scRNA-seq expression matrix (genes x cells, .txt, rows = genes, columns = cells) must be converted into a GRN adjacency matrix to serve as the left submatrix R in MDIC3, or when benchmarking GNIPLR against GENIE3/GRNBoost as GRN sources. The downstream method requires predefined ligand-receptor interactions or a species-specific L-R database (e.g., CellChatDB) — GRN-based inference like GNIPLR/MDIC3 is chosen precisely to avoid L-R dependence, and vice versa L-R tools are the wrong choice for species lacking L-R annotations The expression data is a time-series where Equation 2-style direct inference is applicable and time ordering is available — GNIPLR constructs pseudo-time via projection rather than using real time-series data The input is not a raw gene x cell expression matrix (e.g., it is already a GRN, a communication matrix, or a feature table) — the GRN inference step would be redundant or invalid http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Infer a gene regulatory network (GRN) adjacency matrix from single-cell gene expression data using GNIPLR (gene networks inference based on projection and lagged regression), as used by MDIC3 to supply the left submatrix R of its matrix decomposition. This skill also covers substituting alternative GRN tools (GENIE3, GRNBoost) at the same interface to test robustness of downstream communication inference. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100911
skills.summary: Infer a gene regulatory network (GRN) adjacency matrix from single-cell gene expression data using GNIPLR (gene networks inference based on projection and lagged regression), as used by MDIC3 to supply the left submatrix R of its matrix decomposition. This skill also covers substituting alternative GRN tools (GENIE3, GRNBoost) at the same interface to test robustness of downstream communication inference.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The downstream method requires predefined ligand-receptor interactions or a species-specific L-R database (e.g., CellChatDB) — GRN-based inference like GNIPLR/MDIC3 is chosen precisely to avoid L-R dependence, and vice versa L-R tools are the wrong choice for species lacking L-R annotations The expression data is a time-series where Equation 2-style direct inference is applicable and time ordering is available — GNIPLR constructs pseudo-time via projection rather than using real time-series data The input is not a raw gene x cell expression matrix (e.g., it is already a GRN, a communication matrix, or a feature table) — the GRN inference step would be redundant or invalid

skills.description: Use when a co-expression module (e.g. a WGCNA module correlated with a trait or cell type) must be converted into a directed TF–target regulatory network to identify the transcription factors controlling it.
skills.name: grn-inference-with-gradient-boosting
skills.search_text: grn-inference-with-gradient-boosting Use when a co-expression module (e.g. a WGCNA module correlated with a trait or cell type) must be converted into a directed TF–target regulatory network to identify the transcription factors controlling it. When the goal is a pure co-expression (undirected) GCN without TF attribution — SCANet's WGCNA-based module inference is the appropriate upstream step, not GRNBoost2 When no transcription factor genes are present in the selected module — GRNBoost2 requires TFs to propose TF–TG edges When downstream drug-repurposing needs only gene–drug interactions on the GCN rather than regulatory directionality http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Infer a directed gene regulatory network (GRN) for a selected co-expression module by first proposing candidate TF–target edges with gradient-boosting (GRNBoost2) and then retaining only edges whose TF-binding motif is significantly enriched at the target's cis-regulatory region (RcisTarget), as applied in SCANet to the M4 lipid-metabolism GRN of intestinal stem cells in HFHSD obese mice. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad644
skills.summary: Infer a directed gene regulatory network (GRN) for a selected co-expression module by first proposing candidate TF–target edges with gradient-boosting (GRNBoost2) and then retaining only edges whose TF-binding motif is significantly enriched at the target's cis-regulatory region (RcisTarget), as applied in SCANet to the M4 lipid-metabolism GRN of intestinal stem cells in HFHSD obese mice.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is a pure co-expression (undirected) GCN without TF attribution — SCANet's WGCNA-based module inference is the appropriate upstream step, not GRNBoost2 When no transcription factor genes are present in the selected module — GRNBoost2 requires TFs to propose TF–TG edges When downstream drug-repurposing needs only gene–drug interactions on the GCN rather than regulatory directionality

skills.description: Use when preparing a GRN-guided causal GAN run: you have a preprocessed single-cell expression matrix (e.g., 1000 highly variable genes, library-size normalized to 20,000) and need a causal graph of TF-gene edges to impose during GRouNdGAN training.
skills.name: grn-inference-with-grnboost2
skills.search_text: grn-inference-with-grnboost2 Use when preparing a GRN-guided causal GAN run: you have a preprocessed single-cell expression matrix (e.g., 1000 highly variable genes, library-size normalized to 20,000) and need a causal graph of TF-gene edges to impose during GRouNdGAN training. You already have a trusted, user-provided GRN to impose on GRouNdGAN — in that case skip --create_grn and use the imposing-custom-GRNs route. You need a multi-layer or TF-gene-phenotype causal graph — the current GRouNdGAN version only supports imposing bipartite GRNs. You are simulating unnormalized count data — the model generates expression values library-size normalized across the considered genes and TFs. http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Infers a gene regulatory network (GRN) from preprocessed scRNA-seq training data using GRNBoost2 via GRouNdGAN's --create_grn command, keeping the k=15 top TFs per gene and formatting the result as the pickled causal graph that guides GRouNdGAN's causal GAN. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-48516-6
skills.summary: Infers a gene regulatory network (GRN) from preprocessed scRNA-seq training data using GRNBoost2 via GRouNdGAN's --create_grn command, keeping the k=15 top TFs per gene and formatting the result as the pickled causal graph that guides GRouNdGAN's causal GAN.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already have a trusted, user-provided GRN to impose on GRouNdGAN — in that case skip --create_grn and use the imposing-custom-GRNs route. You need a multi-layer or TF-gene-phenotype causal graph — the current GRouNdGAN version only supports imposing bipartite GRNs. You are simulating unnormalized count data — the model generates expression values library-size normalized across the considered genes and TFs.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking multiple GRN inference methods on single-cell (snRNAseq/scRNAseq) expression matrices and you need quantified edge reproducibility, scale-free topology fit, network characteristic metrics, and runtime per method.
skills.name: grn-reproducibility-overlap-assessment
skills.search_text: grn-reproducibility-overlap-assessment Use when benchmarking multiple GRN inference methods on single-cell (snRNAseq/scRNAseq) expression matrices and you need quantified edge reproducibility, scale-free topology fit, network characteristic metrics, and runtime per method. skills.search_text: ground-truth-deg-label-derivation Use when benchmarking DEG prediction accuracy on artificial Splatter datasets: simulated count matrices exist but lack reference labels, and each gene's simulated DEFac value is available to define the DEG ground truth. Working with real scRNA-seq datasets (e.g., MOCA, Tabula Muris thymus) where no simulated DEFac ground truth exists and labels cannot be derived Simulations not generated by Splatter or that lack per-gene differential expression factor annotations, since the DEFac != 1 criterion is undefined Evaluating methods that need continuous (non-binary) expression-level ground truth; the derived labels only encode detection-style differential expression status http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Derives binary differentially expressed gene (DEG) ground-truth label files from Splatter-simulated scRNA-seq datasets by flagging genes whose differential expression factor (DEFac) differs from 1, enabling quantitative accuracy benchmarking of DEG prediction methods such as singleCellHaystack against clustering-based approaches. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-17900-3
skills.summary: Derives binary differentially expressed gene (DEG) ground-truth label files from Splatter-simulated scRNA-seq datasets by flagging genes whose differential expression factor (DEFac) differs from 1, enabling quantitative accuracy benchmarking of DEG prediction methods such as singleCellHaystack against clustering-based approaches.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Working with real scRNA-seq datasets (e.g., MOCA, Tabula Muris thymus) where no simulated DEFac ground truth exists and labels cannot be derived Simulations not generated by Splatter or that lack per-gene differential expression factor annotations, since the DEFac != 1 criterion is undefined Evaluating methods that need continuous (non-binary) expression-level ground truth; the derived labels only encode detection-style differential expression status

skills.description: Decision support for ranking gene regulatory network inference methods when synthetic single-cell data with an imposed causal ground-truth GRN is available, or when reproducing BEELINE-style benchmark comparisons.
skills.name: ground-truth-grn-validation
skills.search_text: ground-truth-grn-validation Decision support for ranking gene regulatory network inference methods when synthetic single-cell data with an imposed causal ground-truth GRN is available, or when reproducing BEELINE-style benchmark comparisons. Evaluating GRN inference on real experimental scRNA-seq data without a reliable imposed ground truth, since curated databases are not ideal benchmarks due to context specificity of gene regulation Benchmarking on multi-cell-type datasets such as PBMC-All, where the article states results are not conclusive and follow-up studies are required Evaluating a cell-type-specific method like CeSpGRN in isolation, since no comprehensive evaluation of this method class from different perspectives has been performed http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Validates GRN inference methods against an imposed ground-truth GRN using GRouNdGAN's benchmarking command, computing per-gene precision-at-k (k = 15, matching the top-15 GRNBoost2-derived regulators per gene) and a global precision-recall curve with AUPRC against a random-predictor baseline, then ranks methods (e.g., PIDC > GENIE3 > GRNBoost2) for comparison with BEELINE's curated-benchmark ordering. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-48516-6
skills.summary: Validates GRN inference methods against an imposed ground-truth GRN using GRouNdGAN's benchmarking command, computing per-gene precision-at-k (k = 15, matching the top-15 GRNBoost2-derived regulators per gene) and a global precision-recall curve with AUPRC against a random-predictor baseline, then ranks methods (e.g., PIDC > GENIE3 > GRNBoost2) for comparison with BEELINE's curated-benchmark ordering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating GRN inference on real experimental scRNA-seq data without a reliable imposed ground truth, since curated databases are not ideal benchmarks due to context specificity of gene regulation Benchmarking on multi-cell-type datasets such as PBMC-All, where the article states results are not conclusive and follow-up studies are required Evaluating a cell-type-specific method like CeSpGRN in isolation, since no comprehensive evaluation of this method class from different perspectives has been performed

skills.description: Use when generating synthetic benchmark data (e.g. two-condition, two-batch scRNA-seq simulations) that require known injected signal — DS genes at specified proportions (5%/10%) and logFC ranges — to be written alongside the counts as label annotations.
