skills.search_text: high-dimensional-gene-expression-feature-selection Use when the task is selecting a small, sparse set of predictive genes from high-dimensional, correlated omics/expression data (p >> n) for regression or classification, and unknown feature groupings (e.g. ribosomal or MHCII genes) should be respected. The input is already a small feature table or the features are not high-dimensional/correlated — sparse PCA offers no benefit and other linear models suffice The prediction task is not linear regression or classification on a continuous/binary response — suffPCR implements row-sparse PCA followed by OLS or logistic regression only A previously selected gene signature already exists and the goal is validation rather than de novo feature discovery http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Feature selection for high-dimensional transcriptomic regression/classification via SuffPCR: row-sparse PCA followed by OLS or logistic regression on the recovered sparse subspace, so predictions depend on only a small subset of genes (e.g. 87 features / 32 genes / 2 ESTs selected from DLBCL expression data). transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac033

skills.search_text: high-dimensional-genomic-covariate-regression Use when fitting Cox or logistic regression with thousands of gene-expression/mutation covariates (e.g., TCGA mRNA Z-scores) and you need penalized variable selection, optional FDR screening, and cross-validated AUC/C-index. skills.description: Use when a high-dimensional regression or classification task on correlated omics/microarray feature data needs a quantitative benchmark of sparse linear methods — e.g. reproducing the paper's Table 2 test-MSE and feature-count comparison across the five public microarray datasets.
skills.name: high-dimensional-microarray-regression-benchmarking
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-microarray-regression-benchmarking Use when a high-dimensional regression or classification task on correlated omics/microarray feature data needs a quantitative benchmark of sparse linear methods — e.g. reproducing the paper's Table 2 test-MSE and feature-count comparison across the five public microarray datasets. The goal is prediction from an already-fitted model or a low-dimensional (small p) feature table where sparse PCA offers no advantage over ordinary regression A single train/test evaluation is sufficient — the skill's ranking pattern is defined over 10 repeated 40/30/30 splits, so a one-split comparison cannot reproduce the paper's benchmark http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmark SuffPCR against feature-selecting sparse regression alternatives (SPC, Lasso, Elastic Net, SPCA, DSPCA) on the five suffpcr microarray datasets (aml, dlbcl, miller, nsclc, vantveer), comparing average test-set prediction MSE and number of selected features under a shared 40/30/30 train/validation/test splitting and lambda-selection protocol. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac033
skills.summary: Benchmark SuffPCR against feature-selecting sparse regression alternatives (SPC, Lasso, Elastic Net, SPCA, DSPCA) on the five suffpcr microarray datasets (aml, dlbcl, miller, nsclc, vantveer), comparing average test-set prediction MSE and number of selected features under a shared 40/30/30 train/validation/test splitting and lambda-selection protocol.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is prediction from an already-fitted model or a low-dimensional (small p) feature table where sparse PCA offers no advantage over ordinary regression A single train/test evaluation is sufficient — the skill's ranking pattern is defined over 10 repeated 40/30/30 splits, so a one-split comparison cannot reproduce the paper's benchmark

skills.description: Use when comparing prediction methods (e.g. SuffPCR vs sparse linear models vs non-sparse PCR) on high-dimensional omics data where both out-of-sample MSE and correct feature selection must be evaluated.
skills.name: high-dimensional-mse-benchmarking
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-mse-benchmarking Use when comparing prediction methods (e.g. SuffPCR vs sparse linear models vs non-sparse PCR) on high-dimensional omics data where both out-of-sample MSE and correct feature selection must be evaluated. When the response is real rather than semi-synthetic and no ground-truth sparse signal direction exists, feature-selection overlap cannot be computed and only MSE is meaningful. When the goal is low-dimensional regression with few, weakly correlated features — the method targets high-dimensional omics with correlated features. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmark SuffPCR against sparse linear models and non-sparse principal component regression on high-dimensional transcriptomic data by comparing out-of-sample MSE and feature-selection overlap (the paper's Figure 3 semi-synthetic NSCLC evaluation). transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac033
skills.summary: Benchmark SuffPCR against sparse linear models and non-sparse principal component regression on high-dimensional transcriptomic data by comparing out-of-sample MSE and feature-selection overlap (the paper's Figure 3 semi-synthetic NSCLC evaluation).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the response is real rather than semi-synthetic and no ground-truth sparse signal direction exists, feature-selection overlap cannot be computed and only MSE is meaningful. When the goal is low-dimensional regression with few, weakly correlated features — the method targets high-dimensional omics with correlated features.

skills.description: Use when a dataset has far more predictors than samples (P >> n, e.g. RNA-seq with >16,000 genes in n=68 samples) and you need hyperparameter tuning plus an unbiased estimate of model accuracy or AUC.
skills.name: high-dimensional-nested-cross-validation
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-nested-cross-validation Use when a dataset has far more predictors than samples (P >> n, e.g. RNA-seq with >16,000 genes in n=68 samples) and you need hyperparameter tuning plus an unbiased estimate of model accuracy or AUC. A held-out external test set already exists, so unbiased performance can be measured directly without nested CV Predictor count is modest relative to sample size (P not >> n), making a conventional 2/3-1/3 split or simple CV sufficient You plan to filter or select predictors on the whole dataset before CV — the article notes this 'creates a bias when determining accuracy of models' http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Fully nested k × l-fold cross-validation (default 10 × 10) for lasso/elastic-net models via nestcv.glmnet, in which inner folds tune hyperparameters (alpha, lambda) and outer-fold test predictions yield an unbiased performance estimate for P ≫ n transcriptomic data. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad048
skills.summary: Fully nested k × l-fold cross-validation (default 10 × 10) for lasso/elastic-net models via nestcv.glmnet, in which inner folds tune hyperparameters (alpha, lambda) and outer-fold test predictions yield an unbiased performance estimate for P ≫ n transcriptomic data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: A held-out external test set already exists, so unbiased performance can be measured directly without nested CV Predictor count is modest relative to sample size (P not >> n), making a conventional 2/3-1/3 split or simple CV sufficient You plan to filter or select predictors on the whole dataset before CV — the article notes this 'creates a bias when determining accuracy of models'

skills.description: Use when validating a cross-validation workflow for leakage bias: you need a null dataset (no true signal, P >> n) where any AUC above ~0.5 from filtered models demonstrates information leakage.
skills.name: high-dimensional-noise-data-simulation
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-noise-data-simulation Use when validating a cross-validation workflow for leakage bias: you need a null dataset (no true signal, P >> n) where any AUC above ~0.5 from filtered models demonstrates information leakage. Your goal is to fit a final predictive model on real data rather than to benchmark CV design for leakage bias — the noise simulation exists only as a null control Your data are low-dimensional (P << n) where whole-dataset filtering bias is not the concern and a conventional train/test split suffices Your dataset already contains real signal structure — any elevated AUC then reflects signal, not leakage, defeating the null-dataset rationale http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Generates pure gaussian-noise predictor matrices with P >> n and random balanced binary outcomes to benchmark whether whole-dataset feature filtering inflates apparent ROC AUC versus fully nested CV with filters embedded in the outer loop. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad048
skills.summary: Generates pure gaussian-noise predictor matrices with P >> n and random balanced binary outcomes to benchmark whether whole-dataset feature filtering inflates apparent ROC AUC versus fully nested CV with filters embedded in the outer loop.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is to fit a final predictive model on real data rather than to benchmark CV design for leakage bias — the noise simulation exists only as a null control Your data are low-dimensional (P << n) where whole-dataset filtering bias is not the concern and a conventional train/test split suffices Your dataset already contains real signal structure — any elevated AUC then reflects signal, not leakage, defeating the null-dataset rationale

skills.description: Use when fitting regression models with survival (or binary) outcomes against ~thousands to hundred-thousands of genomic covariates (e.g., 9,548 TCGA ovarian mRNA entries) and a robust, intersection-based candidate gene list with concordance estimates is needed.
skills.name: high-dimensional-omics-cross-model-gene-intersection
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-omics-cross-model-gene-intersection Use when fitting regression models with survival (or binary) outcomes against ~thousands to hundred-thousands of genomic covariates (e.g., 9,548 TCGA ovarian mRNA entries) and a robust, intersection-based candidate gene list with concordance estimates is needed. The covariate dimension is low (tens of variables); penalized regression with first-step FDR screening is designed for high-dimensional genomic data. The data are already pre-reduced to a small feature table without a multiple-testing problem, making FDR screening unnecessary. The goal is differential expression per gene rather than selecting genes predictive of a survival (Cox) or binary (logistic) outcome. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 A penalized-regression workflow, implemented in HDMAC (R/Shiny), that first screens high-dimensional mRNA covariates by Benjamini-Hochberg FDR via univariate Cox regression, then fits Ridge, Lasso, and adaptive Lasso Cox models and intersects their selected genes to yield a robust candidate survival-gene list for TCGA ovarian cancer data. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-60791-z
skills.summary: A penalized-regression workflow, implemented in HDMAC (R/Shiny), that first screens high-dimensional mRNA covariates by Benjamini-Hochberg FDR via univariate Cox regression, then fits Ridge, Lasso, and adaptive Lasso Cox models and intersects their selected genes to yield a robust candidate survival-gene list for TCGA ovarian cancer data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The covariate dimension is low (tens of variables); penalized regression with first-step FDR screening is designed for high-dimensional genomic data. The data are already pre-reduced to a small feature table without a multiple-testing problem, making FDR screening unnecessary. The goal is differential expression per gene rather than selecting genes predictive of a survival (Cox) or binary (logistic) outcome.

skills.description: Use when input is a high-dimensional protein x condition omics matrix (TSV/CSV, AnnData-compatible) with sparseness and redundancy, and a dense low-dimensional per-protein embedding is needed before network inference.
skills.name: high-dimensional-omics-latent-embedding-generation
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-omics-latent-embedding-generation Use when input is a high-dimensional protein x condition omics matrix (TSV/CSV, AnnData-compatible) with sparseness and redundancy, and a dense low-dimensional per-protein embedding is needed before network inference. The data are already a low-dimensional or dense embedding — FAVA exists to compress high-dimensional, sparse, redundant data The goal is direct co-expression correlation on the raw high-dimensional matrix; the article states this approach works poorly due to sparseness and redundancy Input rows are conditions/cells rather than proteins, since the embedding is one latent vector per input protein http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Compress high-dimensional scRNA-seq/proteomics protein-condition matrices into a dense, regularized Gaussian latent space using FAVA's VAE (single hidden layer, ReLU encoder, sigmoid decoder, 0.9 reconstruction / 0.1 KL-to-N(1, 0.1) weighting, Adam at lr 1e-3). The latent embeddings are the basis from which downstream correlation-based functional association networks are inferred. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae010
skills.summary: Compress high-dimensional scRNA-seq/proteomics protein-condition matrices into a dense, regularized Gaussian latent space using FAVA's VAE (single hidden layer, ReLU encoder, sigmoid decoder, 0.9 reconstruction / 0.1 KL-to-N(1, 0.1) weighting, Adam at lr 1e-3). The latent embeddings are the basis from which downstream correlation-based functional association networks are inferred.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are already a low-dimensional or dense embedding — FAVA exists to compress high-dimensional, sparse, redundant data The goal is direct co-expression correlation on the raw high-dimensional matrix; the article states this approach works poorly due to sparseness and redundancy Input rows are conditions/cells rather than proteins, since the embedding is one latent vector per input protein

skills.description: Use when a numeric predictor matrix x has far more columns than rows (transcriptomics-style P >> n) and you must rank/select predictors by univariate tests (t-test, Wilcoxon, ANOVA, correlation) before model fitting inside nested cross-validation.
skills.name: high-dimensional-predictor-ranking
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-predictor-ranking Use when a numeric predictor matrix x has far more columns than rows (transcriptomics-style P >> n) and you must rank/select predictors by univariate tests (t-test, Wilcoxon, ANOVA, correlation) before model fitting inside nested cross-validation. When filtering on the whole dataset outside CV loops — this biases outer-fold accuracy because left-out hold-out rows are touched during feature selection When predictors are fewer than samples and full-model selection (e.g. glmnet alone without an embedded filter) suffices When the outcome is multinomial and a strictly binary two-sample t-test contract is required without switching to anova_filter or stat_filter http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Ranks high-dimensional predictors (P >> n) by univariate association with the outcome using nestedcv's filter functions such as ttest_filter, which returns the indices of predictors in x to retain, with contract options force_vars, nfilter, p_cutoff and rsq_cutoff. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad048
skills.summary: Ranks high-dimensional predictors (P >> n) by univariate association with the outcome using nestedcv's filter functions such as ttest_filter, which returns the indices of predictors in x to retain, with contract options force_vars, nfilter, p_cutoff and rsq_cutoff.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When filtering on the whole dataset outside CV loops — this biases outer-fold accuracy because left-out hold-out rows are touched during feature selection When predictors are fewer than samples and full-model selection (e.g. glmnet alone without an embedded filter) suffices When the outcome is multinomial and a strictly binary two-sample t-test contract is required without switching to anova_filter or stat_filter

skills.description: Use when the dataset has far more predictors than samples (P >> n, e.g. RNA-Seq like E-MTAB-11611), an unbiased estimate of model accuracy is required, and feature selection must be nested within CV to avoid leakage bias.
skills.name: high-dimensional-rnaseq-predictive-modeling
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-rnaseq-predictive-modeling Use when the dataset has far more predictors than samples (P >> n, e.g. RNA-Seq like E-MTAB-11611), an unbiased estimate of model accuracy is required, and feature selection must be nested within CV to avoid leakage bias. When predictors are fewer than or comparable to samples and a conventional 2/3-1/3 train/test split gives an adequately sized test set When feature selection has already been performed on the whole dataset and you only need to evaluate a fixed model — nested re-filtering is unnecessary, and prior whole-dataset filtering would still bias results When the target model is not available through glmnet or caret's prediction methods http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Build predictive models on high-dimensional transcriptomic data (P >> n) using the nestedcv R package, which performs fully nested k x l-fold cross-validation (default 10 x 10 folds) with feature-selection filters embedded inside the outer loop and inner-loop hyperparameter tuning via glmnet or caret. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad048
skills.summary: Build predictive models on high-dimensional transcriptomic data (P >> n) using the nestedcv R package, which performs fully nested k x l-fold cross-validation (default 10 x 10 folds) with feature-selection filters embedded inside the outer loop and inner-loop hyperparameter tuning via glmnet or caret.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When predictors are fewer than or comparable to samples and a conventional 2/3-1/3 train/test split gives an adequately sized test set When feature selection has already been performed on the whole dataset and you only need to evaluate a fixed model — nested re-filtering is unnecessary, and prior whole-dataset filtering would still bias results When the target model is not available through glmnet or caret's prediction methods

skills.description: Use when you need to demonstrate or benchmark that marginal-correlation screening fails to recover predictive genes in a high-dimensional transcriptomic setting where p >> n (e.g., AML: 116 samples, 6283 genes).
skills.name: high-dimensional-screening-benchmark-reproduction
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-screening-benchmark-reproduction Use when you need to demonstrate or benchmark that marginal-correlation screening fails to recover predictive genes in a high-dimensional transcriptomic setting where p >> n (e.g., AML: 116 samples, 6283 genes). Your goal is to build a predictive model on the data rather than to evaluate/benchmark a screening rule — SuffPCR itself (row-sparse PCA plus OLS or logistic regression) is the fitting method, this skill is the counterexample benchmark The feature dimension is not substantially larger than n, so the sample covariance is not rank-deficient and the top-n-entries covariance truncation of Φ is not required You already have ground-truth coefficients from a known simulation design, so the pseudo-true β* via precision-matrix estimation is unnecessary http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Reproduces the AML counterexample from the suffPCR paper, quantifying the false negative rate of marginal-correlation (SPC-style) gene screening against a pseudo-true coefficient vector β* = Σ^-1 Φ under increasingly sparse Graphical Lasso estimates of the precision matrix. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac033
skills.summary: Reproduces the AML counterexample from the suffPCR paper, quantifying the false negative rate of marginal-correlation (SPC-style) gene screening against a pseudo-true coefficient vector β* = Σ^-1 Φ under increasingly sparse Graphical Lasso estimates of the precision matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is to build a predictive model on the data rather than to evaluate/benchmark a screening rule — SuffPCR itself (row-sparse PCA plus OLS or logistic regression) is the fitting method, this skill is the counterexample benchmark The feature dimension is not substantially larger than n, so the sample covariance is not rank-deficient and the top-n-entries covariance truncation of Φ is not required You already have ground-truth coefficients from a known simulation design, so the pseudo-true β* via precision-matrix estimation is unnecessary

skills.description: Use when base-level RNA-seq pileup matrices must be compared per sample against a gene mean shape reference, e.g. to derive per-gene on/off statistics or exclude genes with many off samples before shape-change analysis.
skills.name: high-dimensional-shape-similarity-measurement
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-shape-similarity-measurement Use when base-level RNA-seq pileup matrices must be compared per sample against a gene mean shape reference, e.g. to derive per-gene on/off statistics or exclude genes with many off samples before shape-change analysis. Input data are gene-level summarized expression (e.g., normalized RSEM values) rather than base-level pileup coverage — shape angles require the uncompressed base-resolution representation SCISSOR builds from pileup files The goal is junction-spanning or known-transcript isoform analysis better served by methods such as DEXSeq, SpliceTrap, MISO, or rMATS rather than shape-change screening The cohort is too small for unsupervised shape analysis — the authors note ~30 samples is the smallest cohort considered successfully http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Quantifies per-sample RNA coverage shape similarity to a gene-level mean vector by computing high-dimensional angles (SCISSOR's angle.hy), which underpins the on/off classification used to flag genes with many non-expressed samples in the 522-sample TCGA HNSC cohort. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-20593-3
skills.summary: Quantifies per-sample RNA coverage shape similarity to a gene-level mean vector by computing high-dimensional angles (SCISSOR's angle.hy), which underpins the on/off classification used to flag genes with many non-expressed samples in the 522-sample TCGA HNSC cohort.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data are gene-level summarized expression (e.g., normalized RSEM values) rather than base-level pileup coverage — shape angles require the uncompressed base-resolution representation SCISSOR builds from pileup files The goal is junction-spanning or known-transcript isoform analysis better served by methods such as DEXSeq, SpliceTrap, MISO, or rMATS rather than shape-change screening The cohort is too small for unsupervised shape analysis — the authors note ~30 samples is the smallest cohort considered successfully

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether a sparse supervised dimension-reduction method still predicts well and recovers features when the marginal-correlation screening assumption is deliberately violated (zero-marginal-correlation, non-zero-coefficient features).
skills.name: high-dimensional-simulation-design
skills.search_text: high-dimensional-simulation-design Use when evaluating whether a sparse supervised dimension-reduction method still predicts well and recovers features when the marginal-correlation screening assumption is deliberately violated (zero-marginal-correlation, non-zero-coefficient features). The data are real experimental transcriptomic data (use the suffpcr aml/dlbcl/miller/nsclc/vantveer data applications instead of the synthetic benchmark). The goal is to benchmark screening methods under their favorable assumption, i.e., features with strong marginal correlation to the response — this construction is designed to violate marginal-correlation screening. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Design and run an adversarial high-dimensional synthetic benchmark (n=100, p=1000, rank-1 latent factor structure) in which features have zero marginal correlation but non-zero coefficients, then compare SuffPCR against penalized and sparse-PCA competitors on test MSE, feature selection precision/recall, and regularization-path ROC curves. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac033
skills.summary: Design and run an adversarial high-dimensional synthetic benchmark (n=100, p=1000, rank-1 latent factor structure) in which features have zero marginal correlation but non-zero coefficients, then compare SuffPCR against penalized and sparse-PCA competitors on test MSE, feature selection precision/recall, and regularization-path ROC curves.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are real experimental transcriptomic data (use the suffpcr aml/dlbcl/miller/nsclc/vantveer data applications instead of the synthetic benchmark). The goal is to benchmark screening methods under their favorable assumption, i.e., features with strong marginal correlation to the response — this construction is designed to violate marginal-correlation screening.

skills.search_text: high-order-gene-interaction-term-expansion Use when building a cell-to-cell affinity matrix from raw scRNAseq counts where the analysis goal is full-dimensionality similarity — capturing high-order gene interactions without feature selection, PCA, or marker-gene filtering. skills.search_text: high-throughput-read-query-evaluation Use when you need to characterize how partitioning a large IBF index (e.g., 8 GiB) into x parts affects wall-clock build time, query time, peak memory, and specificity, before choosing a partition count for large-scale read search. skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to compare Raptor against competitor tools (Mantis, COBS) on real RefSeq data rather than to characterize the internal x-PIBF partitioning trade-off. skills.description: Use when benchmarking supervised cell-annotation methods on scRNA-seq data containing closely correlated cell types, or when constructing difficult vs easy prediction tasks from real PBMC data to stress-test hierarchical vs flat classifiers.
skills.name: highly-correlated-t-cell-subset-simulation
skills.search_text: highly-correlated-t-cell-subset-simulation Use when benchmarking supervised cell-annotation methods on scRNA-seq data containing closely correlated cell types, or when constructing difficult vs easy prediction tasks from real PBMC data to stress-test hierarchical vs flat classifiers. The research question involves identifying novel or unknown cell types — NeuCA assumes all cell types in the new sample already exist in the training/reference data The data contain no closely correlated cell types and a simple feed-forward classifier would suffice (NeuCA's own correlation check would select the flat network, so the difficult-subset design adds no signal) Training data with known labels are unavailable — supervised methods like NeuCA outperform unsupervised ones only when training data exist http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 A benchmark simulation design that constructs a difficult cell-annotation task by restricting real 10X Genomics PBMC data to the five highly correlated T-cell types, and an easy counterpart by merging them into a single 'T cells' class, to quantify how high inter-type correlation degrades annotation accuracy and ARI across methods. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-04473-4
skills.summary: A benchmark simulation design that constructs a difficult cell-annotation task by restricting real 10X Genomics PBMC data to the five highly correlated T-cell types, and an easy counterpart by merging them into a single 'T cells' class, to quantify how high inter-type correlation degrades annotation accuracy and ARI across methods.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The research question involves identifying novel or unknown cell types — NeuCA assumes all cell types in the new sample already exist in the training/reference data The data contain no closely correlated cell types and a simple feed-forward classifier would suffice (NeuCA's own correlation check would select the flat network, so the difficult-subset design adds no signal) Training data with known labels are unavailable — supervised methods like NeuCA outperform unsupervised ones only when training data exist

skills.description: Use when constructing a cell-type-specific GRN with scRank and candidate genes must be narrowed to highly variable genes, transcription factors, and the drug-target gene before network inference.
skills.name: highly-variable-gene-and-transcription-factor-feature-selection
skills.search_text: highly-variable-gene-and-transcription-factor-feature-selection Use when constructing a cell-type-specific GRN with scRank and candidate genes must be narrowed to highly variable genes, transcription factors, and the drug-target gene before network inference. The goal is downstream perturbation scoring (rank_celltype), not network construction — this skill only covers the feature-selection/GRN-reconstruction stage. The drug has multiple targets, since scRank's multi-target extension is only preliminary and requires specifically tailored methodologies not yet developed. The input is treated/paired disease-control data or bulk expression rather than untreated single-cell transcriptomic data, which is scRank's design scope. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3307 Feature-selection step of scRank's Constr_net stage: cells are subsampled within each cell-type cluster and candidate network nodes are restricted to highly variable genes, transcription factors, and the drug-target gene, so that principal-component regression can infer a tractable cell-type-specific gene-gene adjacency (GRN). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.xcrm.2024.101568
skills.summary: Feature-selection step of scRank's Constr_net stage: cells are subsampled within each cell-type cluster and candidate network nodes are restricted to highly variable genes, transcription factors, and the drug-target gene, so that principal-component regression can infer a tractable cell-type-specific gene-gene adjacency (GRN).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is downstream perturbation scoring (rank_celltype), not network construction — this skill only covers the feature-selection/GRN-reconstruction stage. The drug has multiple targets, since scRank's multi-target extension is only preliminary and requires specifically tailored methodologies not yet developed. The input is treated/paired disease-control data or bulk expression rather than untreated single-cell transcriptomic data, which is scRank's design scope.

skills.description: Use when a normalized scRNA-seq matrix (e.g., PBMC3k UMI counts after QC filtering and log-normalization) needs a reduced set of informative features before PCA, clustering, or downstream SCALA/Seurat analyses.
skills.name: highly-variable-gene-detection-vst
skills.search_text: highly-variable-gene-detection-vst Use when a normalized scRNA-seq matrix (e.g., PBMC3k UMI counts after QC filtering and log-normalization) needs a reduced set of informative features before PCA, clustering, or downstream SCALA/Seurat analyses. Non-human or non-mouse datasets: SCALA currently supports 'the analysis of only human and mouse datasets' for scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq. Datasets > 2 GB on the online SCALA server, where dataset size is restricted and no more than 2 CPU threads are allocated per session; some steps cannot complete for > 50,000 cells online. Input is already a reduced feature set or the variable-feature table exists — rerunning VST detection would be redundant. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Detects highly variable genes in scRNA-seq data as implemented in SCALA's scRNA-seq pipeline, which relies on the mean-variance-plot (MVP) method of the Seurat package backed by Variance Stabilizing Transformation (VST), identifying 1535 variable genes on the PBMC3k dataset. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.10.032
skills.summary: Detects highly variable genes in scRNA-seq data as implemented in SCALA's scRNA-seq pipeline, which relies on the mean-variance-plot (MVP) method of the Seurat package backed by Variance Stabilizing Transformation (VST), identifying 1535 variable genes on the PBMC3k dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Non-human or non-mouse datasets: SCALA currently supports 'the analysis of only human and mouse datasets' for scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq. Datasets > 2 GB on the online SCALA server, where dataset size is restricted and no more than 2 CPU threads are allocated per session; some steps cannot complete for > 50,000 cells online. Input is already a reduced feature set or the variable-feature table exists — rerunning VST detection would be redundant.

skills.description: Use when preparing normalized single-cell expression matrices (e.g., log-transformed TISCH tumor microenvironment data) as model inputs, and a compact, informative gene feature set is needed before training a classifier.
skills.name: highly-variable-gene-feature-selection
skills.search_text: highly-variable-gene-feature-selection Use when preparing normalized single-cell expression matrices (e.g., log-transformed TISCH tumor microenvironment data) as model inputs, and a compact, informative gene feature set is needed before training a classifier. Input data has not yet been log-normalized — variance ranking on raw counts is dominated by sequencing depth and total-count differences The goal is spatial transcriptomics spot annotation with a spatially trained Cancer-Finder model, where the training set and feature space differ from the 4572-gene scRNA-seq feature set Hematologic tumor data, for which the article explicitly does not recommend Cancer-Finder, making feature selection for it moot http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Ranks genes by variance across all cells of the normalized training matrix and retains the most variable ones as the input feature vector for Cancer-Finder (4572 features for scRNA-seq), reducing input dimensionality while preserving genes with informative expression variability. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-46413-6
skills.summary: Ranks genes by variance across all cells of the normalized training matrix and retains the most variable ones as the input feature vector for Cancer-Finder (4572 features for scRNA-seq), reducing input dimensionality while preserving genes with informative expression variability.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data has not yet been log-normalized — variance ranking on raw counts is dominated by sequencing depth and total-count differences The goal is spatial transcriptomics spot annotation with a spatially trained Cancer-Finder model, where the training set and feature space differ from the 4572-gene scRNA-seq feature set Hematologic tumor data, for which the article explicitly does not recommend Cancer-Finder, making feature selection for it moot

skills.name: highly-variable-gene-filtering
skills.search_text: highly-variable-gene-filtering Use when preparing single-cell count matrices (e.g. scEU-seq rpeLabeling.h5ad or .jld2) for RNAForecaster neural-ODE training, when high gene sparsity or dimensionality would destabilize gradient descent. The matrices are already sparsity-filtered and restricted to highly variable genes (re-filtering would discard informative genes) The downstream analysis needs the full gene universe, e.g. unbiased marker discovery or pathway-level quantification rather than neural ODE forecasting The data are not single-cell counts but bulk or already-normalized low-dimensional embeddings, where the 98% zero cutoff and top-quartile variance rule do not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Preprocessing skill from the RNAForecaster neural-ODE paper: remove genes with extreme sparsity (>98% zero counts) and restrict to the top-quartile variance genes before training neural ODEs on scRNA-seq data, because spurious zeroes destabilize gradient descent. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100793
skills.summary: Preprocessing skill from the RNAForecaster neural-ODE paper: remove genes with extreme sparsity (>98% zero counts) and restrict to the top-quartile variance genes before training neural ODEs on scRNA-seq data, because spurious zeroes destabilize gradient descent.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The matrices are already sparsity-filtered and restricted to highly variable genes (re-filtering would discard informative genes) The downstream analysis needs the full gene universe, e.g. unbiased marker discovery or pathway-level quantification rather than neural ODE forecasting The data are not single-cell counts but bulk or already-normalized low-dimensional embeddings, where the 98% zero cutoff and top-quartile variance rule do not apply

skills.description: Use when preparing raw multi-batch single-cell RNA-seq count matrices (e.g., the two-batch Zilionis mouse lung data with B-cell and T-cell clusters) as input to batch-correction/integration methods that require a reduced gene set.
skills.name: highly-variable-gene-preprocessing
skills.search_text: highly-variable-gene-preprocessing Use when preparing raw multi-batch single-cell RNA-seq count matrices (e.g., the two-batch Zilionis mouse lung data with B-cell and T-cell clusters) as input to batch-correction/integration methods that require a reduced gene set. The input is already a reduced/normalized feature matrix from a prior HVG selection step — re-filtering would discard signal needed for batch-correction benchmarks The dataset is small enough that JIVE's original bulk implementation runs feasibly without gene filtering, and full-gene-resolution results are desired The analysis goal does not involve batch effects or multi-source integration (scJIVE is designed to extract shared biological patterns while adjusting for batch effect) http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Selects the top highly variable genes from multi-batch scRNA-seq data to produce a compact expression matrix (e.g., 2000 genes x 2533 cells in the Zilionis mouse lung benchmark) with batch labels and cell-type annotations retained, so that batch-correction methods like scJIVE, Seurat v5, and Harmony can run efficiently and comparably. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbae134
skills.summary: Selects the top highly variable genes from multi-batch scRNA-seq data to produce a compact expression matrix (e.g., 2000 genes x 2533 cells in the Zilionis mouse lung benchmark) with batch labels and cell-type annotations retained, so that batch-correction methods like scJIVE, Seurat v5, and Harmony can run efficiently and comparably.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a reduced/normalized feature matrix from a prior HVG selection step — re-filtering would discard signal needed for batch-correction benchmarks The dataset is small enough that JIVE's original bulk implementation runs feasibly without gene filtering, and full-gene-resolution results are desired The analysis goal does not involve batch effects or multi-source integration (scJIVE is designed to extract shared biological patterns while adjusting for batch effect)

skills.search_text: highly-variable-gene-selection Use when preparing raw per-individual UMI count matrices (e.g., human PBMC, mouse lung, human skin droplet-based datasets) for clustering with BAMM-SC or competitors, and a reduced gene feature space must be defined before clustering. The goal is rare cell type identification — the article warns that filtering genes with excessive zeros 'may be problematic for rare cell type identification' The input is already a normalized or reduced feature matrix rather than raw droplet-based UMI counts, so re-filtering by zero fraction would double-filter The data are bulk RNA-seq or sequencing-depth-downsampled Cell Ranger aggregates, since downsampling in the aggregation step causes substantial information loss for individuals with higher sequencing depth http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Preprocess droplet-based scRNA-seq UMI count matrices by filtering out genes with excessive zeros (detected in fewer than 1% of cells) and retaining the top 1000 highly variable genes, defining a compact feature space consumed by BAMM-SC and competing clustering methods. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-09639-3
skills.summary: Preprocess droplet-based scRNA-seq UMI count matrices by filtering out genes with excessive zeros (detected in fewer than 1% of cells) and retaining the top 1000 highly variable genes, defining a compact feature space consumed by BAMM-SC and competing clustering methods.

skills.description: Use when preparing scRNA-seq expression matrices from multiple time points as features for supervised cross-timepoint cell-annotation, and you must reduce thousands of genes to a manageable, informative subset before neural-network training.
skills.name: highly-variable-gene-selection
skills.search_text: highly-variable-gene-selection Use when preparing scRNA-seq expression matrices from multiple time points as features for supervised cross-timepoint cell-annotation, and you must reduce thousands of genes to a manageable, informative subset before neural-network training. Input is not a gene-by-cell expression matrix (e.g., already a reduced feature table or bulk RNA-seq data), so variability-based gene filtering does not apply. The initial timepoint's data is dramatically different from later timepoints' data — the article warns the neural network 'would fail to borrow useful information and could not be very well trained', so HVG features learned from t0 would not transfer. Cell populations differ across conditions and pooling matters — the article notes CASi's annotation step 'pools the data from all the samples together for training and applying the neural network', which may be inappropriate; a condition-aware feature selection would be needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Feature-reduction step for CASi's cross-timepoint cell annotation: restrict single-cell gene expression matrices to the top 2000 highly variable genes (nfeature default) and min-max normalize them, so the Keras neural network classifier trains on a compact, discriminative feature set instead of the full transcriptome. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-024-58566-x
skills.summary: Feature-reduction step for CASi's cross-timepoint cell annotation: restrict single-cell gene expression matrices to the top 2000 highly variable genes (nfeature default) and min-max normalize them, so the Keras neural network classifier trains on a compact, discriminative feature set instead of the full transcriptome.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not a gene-by-cell expression matrix (e.g., already a reduced feature table or bulk RNA-seq data), so variability-based gene filtering does not apply. The initial timepoint's data is dramatically different from later timepoints' data — the article warns the neural network 'would fail to borrow useful information and could not be very well trained', so HVG features learned from t0 would not transfer. Cell populations differ across conditions and pooling matters — the article notes CASi's annotation step 'pools the data from all the samples together for training and applying the neural network', which may be inappropriate; a condition-aware feature selection would be needed.
