skills.description: Use when evaluating cell-specific network inference (CSNI) methods on dyngen simulations: datasets carry transcriptomics plus per-cell ground-truth GRNs, and no motif data is available, so LIONESS must run with Pearson correlation rather than PANDA.
skills.name: lioness-sample-perturbation-network-inference
skills.search_text: lioness-sample-perturbation-network-inference Use when evaluating cell-specific network inference (CSNI) methods on dyngen simulations: datasets carry transcriptomics plus per-cell ground-truth GRNs, and no motif data is available, so LIONESS must run with Pearson correlation rather than PANDA. Motif data is available for the dataset and a PANDA-based LIONESS run is intended — dyngen benchmarking here is specifically the Pearson-only fallback because dyngen provides no motif data The evaluation target is RNA velocity accuracy or trajectory alignment (ABWAP), the other dyngen use cases, rather than cell-specific GRN inference You need method performance on real biological data: this skill's ground truth exists only because dyngen's synthetic data provides completely known cellwise regulatory networks Benchmark LIONESS, a sample (cell)-specific network inference method, on dyngen's 42 simulated single-cell datasets against their cell-specific ground-truth regulatory networks, scoring each cell with AUROC and AUPR and averaging per dataset. It exists because dyngen provides the cellwise regulatory ground truth that real single-cell data lacks for CSNI evaluation. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-24152-2
skills.summary: Benchmark LIONESS, a sample (cell)-specific network inference method, on dyngen's 42 simulated single-cell datasets against their cell-specific ground-truth regulatory networks, scoring each cell with AUROC and AUPR and averaging per dataset. It exists because dyngen provides the cellwise regulatory ground truth that real single-cell data lacks for CSNI evaluation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Motif data is available for the dataset and a PANDA-based LIONESS run is intended — dyngen benchmarking here is specifically the Pearson-only fallback because dyngen provides no motif data The evaluation target is RNA velocity accuracy or trajectory alignment (ABWAP), the other dyngen use cases, rather than cell-specific GRN inference You need method performance on real biological data: this skill's ground truth exists only because dyngen's synthetic data provides completely known cellwise regulatory networks

skills.description: Use when a query single-cell RNA-seq dataset carries explicit batch or technology-of-origin labels (e.g., three 10x protocols 3'v1/3'v2/5') and you need a numeric measure of how well batches mix before vs. after projecting cells into a reference atlas embedding.
skills.name: lisi-batch-mixing-quantification
skills.search_text: lisi-batch-mixing-quantification Use when a query single-cell RNA-seq dataset carries explicit batch or technology-of-origin labels (e.g., three 10x protocols 3'v1/3'v2/5') and you need a numeric measure of how well batches mix before vs. after projecting cells into a reference atlas embedding. The query contains no batch/technology covariate to quantify mixing over (LISI needs a categorical label such as protocol, donor, or batch) The query cells contain novel cell states absent from the reference atlas — fixed-model projections may be misleading, so the LISI-on-mapped-embedding comparison would not be interpretable You are evaluating batch integration rather than reference mapping and have no pre-built model/reference embedding to project into http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Quantifies batch/protocol mixing in a single-cell embedding using the Local Inverse Simpson's Index (LISI), comparing uncorrected vs. reference-mapped embeddings (e.g., ProjectSVR-projected ref.umap) to demonstrate that platform-driven clustering (10x 3'v1/3'v2/5') is corrected in favor of biological identity. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbaf586
skills.summary: Quantifies batch/protocol mixing in a single-cell embedding using the Local Inverse Simpson's Index (LISI), comparing uncorrected vs. reference-mapped embeddings (e.g., ProjectSVR-projected ref.umap) to demonstrate that platform-driven clustering (10x 3'v1/3'v2/5') is corrected in favor of biological identity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query contains no batch/technology covariate to quantify mixing over (LISI needs a categorical label such as protocol, donor, or batch) The query cells contain novel cell states absent from the reference atlas — fixed-model projections may be misleading, so the LISI-on-mapped-embedding comparison would not be interpretable You are evaluating batch integration rather than reference mapping and have no pre-built model/reference embedding to project into

skills.description: Use when evaluating scRNA-seq integration quality on datasets with batch origin and cell type annotations, especially when cell type imbalance across batches makes standard cell type-agnostic iLISI mis.
skills.name: lisi-entropy-score-computation
skills.search_text: lisi-entropy-score-computation Use when evaluating scRNA-seq integration quality on datasets with batch origin and cell type annotations, especially when cell type imbalance across batches makes standard cell type-agnostic iLISI mis. Datasets lack cell type annotations — CiLISI and similar metrics require cell type labels A cell type is present in only one dataset — CiLISI cannot be calculated for it and the type must be dropped Datasets have highly unequal numbers of cells — LISI/CiLISI remains suboptimal there http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Computes batch-mixing scores based on the LISI (Local Inverse Simpson Index) family, including the cell type-aware CiLISI implemented in the scIntegrationMetrics R package, to quantify how well batches are mixed in integrated scRNA-seq data while accounting for cell type composition. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-45240-z
skills.summary: Computes batch-mixing scores based on the LISI (Local Inverse Simpson Index) family, including the cell type-aware CiLISI implemented in the scIntegrationMetrics R package, to quantify how well batches are mixed in integrated scRNA-seq data while accounting for cell type composition.

skills.description: Use when comparing single-cell batch integration methods on multi-sample, multi-condition data (e.g. pancreas + lung mixtures) and you need quantitative evidence of batch removal (iLISI) without over-correction (cLISI, condition separation, condition-specific DE genes).
skills.name: lisi-integration-metric-computation
skills.search_text: lisi-integration-metric-computation Use when comparing single-cell batch integration methods on multi-sample, multi-condition data (e.g. pancreas + lung mixtures) and you need quantitative evidence of batch removal (iLISI) without over-correction (cLISI, condition separation, condition-specific DE genes). Single-sample, single-condition datasets with no batch_label variable — iLISI measures batch mixing and has no technical confound to quantify When the goal is gene-level interpretability of what drives integration — the article notes 'such metrics do not provide insight into the genes or features driving integration and clustering' http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Computes iLISI/cLISI-style integration scores plus ARI/NMI cluster-label agreement to quantify whether a batch-integration method (JOINTLY, Harmony, fastMNN, scVI, LIGER, Scanorama) removes within-tissue batch effects while retaining across-tissue biological variability, i.e. resists over-correction. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-44279-8
skills.summary: Computes iLISI/cLISI-style integration scores plus ARI/NMI cluster-label agreement to quantify whether a batch-integration method (JOINTLY, Harmony, fastMNN, scVI, LIGER, Scanorama) removes within-tissue batch effects while retaining across-tissue biological variability, i.e. resists over-correction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Single-sample, single-condition datasets with no batch_label variable — iLISI measures batch mixing and has no technical confound to quantify When the goal is gene-level interpretability of what drives integration — the article notes 'such metrics do not provide insight into the genes or features driving integration and clustering'

skills.description: Use when quantifying batch effects in scRNA-seq data via local batch-label diversity: you have an embedding (BEENE or PCA), per-cell batch labels across multiple batches/platforms, and need per-sample iLISI values for downstream kBET/iLISI comparison tables.
skills.name: lisi-metric-computation-on-embeddings
skills.search_text: lisi-metric-computation-on-embeddings Use when quantifying batch effects in scRNA-seq data via local batch-label diversity: you have an embedding (BEENE or PCA), per-cell batch labels across multiple batches/platforms, and need per-sample iLISI values for downstream kBET/iLISI comparison tables. The goal is batch effect removal/correction (e.g., integration with Harmony) rather than detection and estimation of the extent of batch effects The downstream metric is kBET and you want a pure-Python path: kBET has no Python implementation and must run in R, so rpy2 transfer is mandatory You expect iLISI to be bounded by [1, 5] on a dataset with fewer (or more) than five batch categories — the iLISI upper bound equals the number of batches, so range checks must match the batch count http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Computes the Local Inverse Simpson's Index (iLISI) batch-mixing metric on BEENE nonlinear embeddings instead of PCA space, quantifying how well cells from different batches (e.g., inDrop, Fluidigm C1, Smart-Seq2, CEL-seq, CEL-seq2) are locally mixed. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad479
skills.summary: Computes the Local Inverse Simpson's Index (iLISI) batch-mixing metric on BEENE nonlinear embeddings instead of PCA space, quantifying how well cells from different batches (e.g., inDrop, Fluidigm C1, Smart-Seq2, CEL-seq, CEL-seq2) are locally mixed.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is batch effect removal/correction (e.g., integration with Harmony) rather than detection and estimation of the extent of batch effects The downstream metric is kBET and you want a pure-Python path: kBET has no Python implementation and must run in R, so rpy2 transfer is mandatory You expect iLISI to be bounded by [1, 5] on a dataset with fewer (or more) than five batch categories — the iLISI upper bound equals the number of batches, so range checks must match the batch count

skills.search_text: lisi-neighborhood-continuity-scoring Use when benchmarking spatially aware color assignments or spatial proximity metrics on 2D single-cell/cluster point data, and you need a neighborhood-mixing score that separates mixed/interlaced pairs from isolated ones. skills.search_text: literature-support-verification Use when building or validating a curated ligand-receptor interaction database where each pair must carry primary literature support, or when auditing merged resources for pairs whose cited PMID does not actually back the interaction. You need computationally predicted interactions or downstream signalling consequences rather than literature-supported direct pairs (the authors point to NicheNet/SoptSC for signalling consequences and note NATMI does not model heteromeric complexes) The input is already a verified, deduplicated curated database and no PMID audit or merging of resources is required You need ligand-receptor pairs that include heteromeric complexes, which were deliberately excluded during extraction from CellPhoneDB http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_3068 A curation skill for assembling or auditing literature-supported ligand-receptor databases (e.g., connectomeDB2020) by merging pair lists from prior resources (CellPhoneDB, RNA-Magnet, SingleCellSignalR, ICELLNET) and verifying that each cited PubMedID actually supports the claimed interaction, dropping unsupported entries (e.g., HPRD-derived pairs). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-18873-z
skills.summary: A curation skill for assembling or auditing literature-supported ligand-receptor databases (e.g., connectomeDB2020) by merging pair lists from prior resources (CellPhoneDB, RNA-Magnet, SingleCellSignalR, ICELLNET) and verifying that each cited PubMedID actually supports the claimed interaction, dropping unsupported entries (e.g., HPRD-derived pairs).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need computationally predicted interactions or downstream signalling consequences rather than literature-supported direct pairs (the authors point to NicheNet/SoptSC for signalling consequences and note NATMI does not model heteromeric complexes) The input is already a verified, deduplicated curated database and no PMID audit or merging of resources is required You need ligand-receptor pairs that include heteromeric complexes, which were deliberately excluded during extraction from CellPhoneDB

skills.description: Use when a processed Seurat object of human liver scRNA-seq data (e.g. transplanted liver samples, cold perfusion/portal reperfusion stages) has PCA/UMAP clusters but no cell-type labels and needs annotation compatible with scCrossTalk's sc_celltype input.
skills.name: liver-cell-type-annotation
skills.search_text: liver-cell-type-annotation Use when a processed Seurat object of human liver scRNA-seq data (e.g. transplanted liver samples, cold perfusion/portal reperfusion stages) has PCA/UMAP clusters but no cell-type labels and needs annotation compatible with scCrossTalk's sc_celltype input. Input data are not human liver scRNA-seq counts — the reference populations (MAIT cells, S100A12+ neutrophils, etc.) are liver-transplant-specific and will not map to other tissues Cells are already labeled with cell types — re-annotation only adds noise before scCrossTalk communication inference Only raw unnormalized counts are available without any clustering/dimensional reduction performed — cluster-level annotation requires the Seurat UMAP/graph step first http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Annotate clusters from an integrated human liver transplant single-cell dataset (12 samples, 75,231 cells) into hepatic parenchymal and non-parenchymal populations (hepatocytes, endothelial cells, MAIT cells, GZMB+ GZMK+ NK cells, S100A12+ neutrophils) so the labels can feed downstream scCrossTalk cell-cell communication inference. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.eng.2023.12.004
skills.summary: Annotate clusters from an integrated human liver transplant single-cell dataset (12 samples, 75,231 cells) into hepatic parenchymal and non-parenchymal populations (hepatocytes, endothelial cells, MAIT cells, GZMB+ GZMK+ NK cells, S100A12+ neutrophils) so the labels can feed downstream scCrossTalk cell-cell communication inference.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data are not human liver scRNA-seq counts — the reference populations (MAIT cells, S100A12+ neutrophils, etc.) are liver-transplant-specific and will not map to other tissues Cells are already labeled with cell types — re-annotation only adds noise before scCrossTalk communication inference Only raw unnormalized counts are available without any clustering/dimensional reduction performed — cluster-level annotation requires the Seurat UMAP/graph step first

skills.description: Use when preparing a single-cell dataset for tree-shaped trajectory inference (e.g., Totem CLARA k-medoids clustering) and a fast low-dimensional embedding is needed instead of PCA or full MDS on large datasets.
skills.name: lmds-dimensionality-reduction-for-trajectory-input
skills.search_text: lmds-dimensionality-reduction-for-trajectory-input Use when preparing a single-cell dataset for tree-shaped trajectory inference (e.g., Totem CLARA k-medoids clustering) and a fast low-dimensional embedding is needed instead of PCA or full MDS on large datasets. The dataset must be visualized in an embedding with 3 or more dimensions — the article notes 3-dimensional embeddings are not supported for plotting at the moment The downstream analysis involves trajectories with cycles or disconnected components, which Totem (operating on this embedding) cannot generate The dataset has extremely rare and extremely prevalent cell types simultaneously — k-medoids on this embedding may fail and require manual cluster merging Generate a low-dimensional embedding of single-cell data with landmark Multi-Dimensional Scaling (LMDS) from the dyndimred package (5 dimensions) so that downstream trajectory inference tools such as Totem, Slingshot, and TinGa all consume a common, fast-to-compute input space. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad515
skills.summary: Generate a low-dimensional embedding of single-cell data with landmark Multi-Dimensional Scaling (LMDS) from the dyndimred package (5 dimensions) so that downstream trajectory inference tools such as Totem, Slingshot, and TinGa all consume a common, fast-to-compute input space.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset must be visualized in an embedding with 3 or more dimensions — the article notes 3-dimensional embeddings are not supported for plotting at the moment The downstream analysis involves trajectories with cycles or disconnected components, which Totem (operating on this embedding) cannot generate The dataset has extremely rare and extremely prevalent cell types simultaneously — k-medoids on this embedding may fail and require manual cluster merging

skills.description: Use when you have LncCat/CatBoost prediction scores for transcripts labeled lncRNA or PCT and need to reproduce or benchmark MCC/F1 classification results against the paper's fixed 0.5-cutoff baseline.
skills.name: lncrna-classification-evaluation
skills.search_text: lncrna-classification-evaluation Use when you have LncCat/CatBoost prediction scores for transcripts labeled lncRNA or PCT and need to reproduce or benchmark MCC/F1 classification results against the paper's fixed 0.5-cutoff baseline. Input is raw transcript FASTA sequences rather than model prediction scores — use the full LncCat feature-extraction and classification pipeline first (Orfipy ORF extraction, BERT peptide encoding, CatBoost), not just the evaluation step You need to distinguish lncRNAs from other ncRNA classes (rRNA, tRNA, etc.) — LncCat only classifies lncRNA versus protein-coding transcripts (PCTs) http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 Evaluate a CatBoost-based lncRNA-vs-PCT classifier (LncCat) by thresholding prediction scores at a fixed cutoff of 0.5 and computing MCC and F1 on held-out test sets from human, mouse, zebrafish, wheat, and chicken, with a cutoff sweep (0.1–0.9) to confirm optima fall between 0.4 and 0.6. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.02.012
skills.summary: Evaluate a CatBoost-based lncRNA-vs-PCT classifier (LncCat) by thresholding prediction scores at a fixed cutoff of 0.5 and computing MCC and F1 on held-out test sets from human, mouse, zebrafish, wheat, and chicken, with a cutoff sweep (0.1–0.9) to confirm optima fall between 0.4 and 0.6.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw transcript FASTA sequences rather than model prediction scores — use the full LncCat feature-extraction and classification pipeline first (Orfipy ORF extraction, BERT peptide encoding, CatBoost), not just the evaluation step You need to distinguish lncRNAs from other ncRNA classes (rRNA, tRNA, etc.) — LncCat only classifies lncRNA versus protein-coding transcripts (PCTs)

skills.description: Use when you need to distinguish lncRNAs from PCTs in FASTA transcript sequences across species (human, mouse, zebrafish, wheat, chicken), especially for transcripts containing sORFs where existing coding-potential tools perform poorly.
skills.name: lncrna-coding-potential-classification
skills.search_text: lncrna-coding-potential-classification Use when you need to distinguish lncRNAs from PCTs in FASTA transcript sequences across species (human, mouse, zebrafish, wheat, chicken), especially for transcripts containing sORFs where existing coding-potential tools perform poorly. Input transcripts lack species annotations and the target species has no suitable training data, making model construction infeasible (the article notes 'Species may lack annotations, and it is impossible to build models for all species.') You need sORF-translated peptide functional annotation, which is out of scope of this method (future work per the discussion) A feature table is already provided and only model scoring is needed rather than the full five-type feature extraction pipeline http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Classify transcripts as lncRNA vs. protein-coding transcripts (PCTs) using CatBoost-based ensemble learning with fused codon-related, GC-related, sequence-related, peptide-related, and ORF-attention features, following the LncCat method. Particularly effective for lncRNAs with small ORFs (sORFs) where CPAT, CNCI, PLEK, CPC2, LncFinder, CPPred, mRNN, and RNAsamba underperform. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.02.012
skills.summary: Classify transcripts as lncRNA vs. protein-coding transcripts (PCTs) using CatBoost-based ensemble learning with fused codon-related, GC-related, sequence-related, peptide-related, and ORF-attention features, following the LncCat method. Particularly effective for lncRNAs with small ORFs (sORFs) where CPAT, CNCI, PLEK, CPC2, LncFinder, CPPred, mRNN, and RNAsamba underperform.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input transcripts lack species annotations and the target species has no suitable training data, making model construction infeasible (the article notes 'Species may lack annotations, and it is impossible to build models for all species.') You need sORF-translated peptide functional annotation, which is out of scope of this method (future work per the discussion) A feature table is already provided and only model scoring is needed rather than the full five-type feature extraction pipeline

skills.description: Use when building a coding-potential classifier for RNA transcripts and you must design the feature space (SIFs, SSFs, PFs, ORF-type features) or trim it down with recursive feature elimination while preserving accuracy.
skills.name: lncrna-coding-potential-feature-engineering
skills.search_text: lncrna-coding-potential-feature-engineering Use when building a coding-potential classifier for RNA transcripts and you must design the feature space (SIFs, SSFs, PFs, ORF-type features) or trim it down with recursive feature elimination while preserving accuracy. Prediction-only runs where a prebuilt/self-trained model already exists (python lncDC.py with -m model.pkl) — feature engineering and RFECV are training-time activities, not needed per prediction Input is a single expression matrix or a feature table that is already numeric and complete — skip re-engineering of SIFs/SSFs/PFs from raw FASTA Transcripts cannot be aligned to training data or lack CDS annotations for the mRNA class (cds.fa must match mrna.fa in order and number for lncDC-train.py) http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Engineering and reducing the numeric feature matrix that an XGBoost-based lncRNA/mRNA classifier consumes: sequence intrinsic features (SIFs), secondary structure features (SSFs), and protein features (PFs) are extracted from RNA transcripts, then a compact subset is selected by RFECV on the SMOTE-balanced H-Train matrix. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-022-22082-7
skills.summary: Engineering and reducing the numeric feature matrix that an XGBoost-based lncRNA/mRNA classifier consumes: sequence intrinsic features (SIFs), secondary structure features (SSFs), and protein features (PFs) are extracted from RNA transcripts, then a compact subset is selected by RFECV on the SMOTE-balanced H-Train matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Prediction-only runs where a prebuilt/self-trained model already exists (python lncDC.py with -m model.pkl) — feature engineering and RFECV are training-time activities, not needed per prediction Input is a single expression matrix or a feature table that is already numeric and complete — skip re-engineering of SIFs/SSFs/PFs from raw FASTA Transcripts cannot be aligned to training data or lack CDS annotations for the mRNA class (cds.fa must match mrna.fa in order and number for lncDC-train.py)

skills.description: Use when you need to visually demonstrate that a fused feature representation (e.g. ORF-attention features from BERT-encoded ORF peptides) discriminates lncRNAs from PCTs in feature space, via per-species UMAP scatter plots colored by class.
skills.name: lncrna-pct-class-separation-visualization
skills.search_text: lncrna-pct-class-separation-visualization Use when you need to visually demonstrate that a fused feature representation (e.g. ORF-attention features from BERT-encoded ORF peptides) discriminates lncRNAs from PCTs in feature space, via per-species UMAP scatter plots colored by class. Input is already a 2D embedding or a rendered figure — this skill requires raw per-transcript feature vectors as input The goal is quantitative classification performance (MCC/F1) rather than qualitative class-separation visualization — use the LncCat CatBoost prediction workflow instead Transcripts are shorter than 200 nt or the dataset is not redundancy-reduced, since the paper's filtering (200 nt minimum, CD-HIT 80%) defines the data regime being visualized http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Reproduce the LncCat paper's UMAP comparison showing that ORF-attention feature vectors separate lncRNAs from protein-coding transcripts (PCTs) into distinct 2D clusters, whereas base features lacking ORF-attention do not, across five species datasets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.02.012
skills.summary: Reproduce the LncCat paper's UMAP comparison showing that ORF-attention feature vectors separate lncRNAs from protein-coding transcripts (PCTs) into distinct 2D clusters, whereas base features lacking ORF-attention do not, across five species datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a 2D embedding or a rendered figure — this skill requires raw per-transcript feature vectors as input The goal is quantitative classification performance (MCC/F1) rather than qualitative class-separation visualization — use the LncCat CatBoost prediction workflow instead Transcripts are shorter than 200 nt or the dataset is not redundancy-reduced, since the paper's filtering (200 nt minimum, CD-HIT 80%) defines the data regime being visualized

skills.description: Use when you have raw transcript FASTA files (mRNA sequences, their matching CDS sequences, and lncRNA sequences) and need to build a labeled feature matrix for training or reproducing an lncRNA/mRNA classification model such as LncDC's.
skills.name: lncrna-transcript-feature-extraction
skills.search_text: lncrna-transcript-feature-extraction Use when you have raw transcript FASTA files (mRNA sequences, their matching CDS sequences, and lncRNA sequences) and need to build a labeled feature matrix for training or reproducing an lncRNA/mRNA classification model such as LncDC's. You only need to classify unknown transcripts with an existing model — use lncDC.py prediction instead of re-extracting a training feature matrix You lack matched mRNA/CDS/lncRNA training FASTAs for the organism and cannot obtain well-annotated lncRNAs from an evolutionarily close model organism You need alignment- or homology-based lncRNA identification (e.g. CPC/CPAT-style coding-potential searches against protein databases) rather than alignment-free feature-based classification Extracts an alignment-free machine learning feature matrix from transcript FASTA sequences (mRNA, CDS, lncRNA) using the LncDC pipeline, combining sequence intrinsic features (SIFs), flexible ORF features, protein features (PFs), and optional sequence-and-secondary-structure (SASS) k-mer features. It is the preprocessing step that produces the training matrices and support files (hexamer table, imputer, scaler, SS k-mer tables) consumed by LncDC's XGBoost model. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-022-22082-7
skills.summary: Extracts an alignment-free machine learning feature matrix from transcript FASTA sequences (mRNA, CDS, lncRNA) using the LncDC pipeline, combining sequence intrinsic features (SIFs), flexible ORF features, protein features (PFs), and optional sequence-and-secondary-structure (SASS) k-mer features. It is the preprocessing step that produces the training matrices and support files (hexamer table, imputer, scaler, SS k-mer tables) consumed by LncDC's XGBoost model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need to classify unknown transcripts with an existing model — use lncDC.py prediction instead of re-extracting a training feature matrix You lack matched mRNA/CDS/lncRNA training FASTAs for the organism and cannot obtain well-annotated lncRNAs from an evolutionarily close model organism You need alignment- or homology-based lncRNA identification (e.g. CPC/CPAT-style coding-potential searches against protein databases) rather than alignment-free feature-based classification

skills.description: Use when you have tRF-5::tRNA interface sequences (tRF-5s of 15-19 nt) extracted from tncRNA Toolkit output and need to score their local alignments to detect a conserved cleavage motif across plant species.
skills.name: local-alignment-scoring-with-pairwise2
skills.search_text: local-alignment-scoring-with-pairwise2 Use when you have tRF-5::tRNA interface sequences (tRF-5s of 15-19 nt) extracted from tncRNA Toolkit output and need to score their local alignments to detect a conserved cleavage motif across plant species. Input is raw sRNA FASTQ rather than a classified tncRNA catalog - reads must first be classified by tncRNA Toolkit as mapping exclusively to the artificial tRNA+50nt chromosomes The sequences are not tRNA-derived fragments (e.g., miRNA or siRNA analysis); this scoring was applied specifically to tRF-5::tRNA cleavage interfaces You need to detect tncRNAs or modified nucleosides de novo (HAMR step) rather than score already-extracted interface sequences - use the upstream toolkit pipeline steps instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Scores tRF-5::tRNA cleavage-interface sequences from plant tncRNA catalogs using Biopython pairwise2 local alignment with the scoring scheme match +1, mismatch -1, gap-open -1, gap-extend -0.5, to recover the conserved AG::TGG cleavage motif across angiosperms. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.09.021
skills.summary: Scores tRF-5::tRNA cleavage-interface sequences from plant tncRNA catalogs using Biopython pairwise2 local alignment with the scoring scheme match +1, mismatch -1, gap-open -1, gap-extend -0.5, to recover the conserved AG::TGG cleavage motif across angiosperms.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sRNA FASTQ rather than a classified tncRNA catalog - reads must first be classified by tncRNA Toolkit as mapping exclusively to the artificial tRNA+50nt chromosomes The sequences are not tRNA-derived fragments (e.g., miRNA or siRNA analysis); this scoring was applied specifically to tRF-5::tRNA cleavage interfaces You need to detect tncRNAs or modified nucleosides de novo (HAMR step) rather than score already-extracted interface sequences - use the upstream toolkit pipeline steps instead

skills.description: Use when you need to visually assess whether condition labels (e.g., treatment vs. control) are locally imbalanced across a low-dimensional cell embedding, as the first diagnostic step before differential topology testing with condiments.
skills.name: local-score-smoothing-cubic-splines
skills.search_text: local-score-smoothing-cubic-splines Use when you need to visually assess whether condition labels (e.g., treatment vs. control) are locally imbalanced across a low-dimensional cell embedding, as the first diagnostic step before differential topology testing with condiments. When you need to test differential topology, differential progression, or differential fate selection — use topologyTest, progressionTest, or fateSelectionTest instead, as imbalance_score is a diagnostic, not a statistical test When cells come from a steady-state system where clustering and per-cluster differential abundance is the reasonable approach, and trajectory continuity is not at issue When the input is raw count data rather than a reduced-dimensional representation — the score must be computed on embedded coordinates (e.g., Dim1/Dim2), not expression matrices http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 This skill reconstructs condiments' imbalance_score diagnostic, which quantifies per-cell imbalance between the local and global distributions of condition labels over a k-nearest-neighbor graph on a reduced-dimensional representation (X), then locally scales raw scores with cubic-spline smoothing to produce the visual diagnostic for condition imbalance. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-44823-0
skills.summary: This skill reconstructs condiments' imbalance_score diagnostic, which quantifies per-cell imbalance between the local and global distributions of condition labels over a k-nearest-neighbor graph on a reduced-dimensional representation (X), then locally scales raw scores with cubic-spline smoothing to produce the visual diagnostic for condition imbalance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When you need to test differential topology, differential progression, or differential fate selection — use topologyTest, progressionTest, or fateSelectionTest instead, as imbalance_score is a diagnostic, not a statistical test When cells come from a steady-state system where clustering and per-cluster differential abundance is the reasonable approach, and trajectory continuity is not at issue When the input is raw count data rather than a reduced-dimensional representation — the score must be computed on embedded coordinates (e.g., Dim1/Dim2), not expression matrices

skills.description: Use when integrating two scRNA-seq datasets (e.g., Seurat V3.0 log-count matrices) where batch correction should move query cells toward matched reference anchors using per-anchor local shifting vectors rather than global or MNN-based correction.
skills.name: local-shifting-vector-batch-correction
skills.search_text: local-shifting-vector-batch-correction Use when integrating two scRNA-seq datasets (e.g., Seurat V3.0 log-count matrices) where batch correction should move query cells toward matched reference anchors using per-anchor local shifting vectors rather than global or MNN-based correction. Integrating more than two datasets — 'The current implementation of BATMAN works only with two datasets.' Input data are raw counts or already normalized by another pipeline — BATMAN expects Seurat V3.0-style log-counts pre-processing. The analysis goal requires methods with different structural assumptions (e.g., MNN-based tools) — the paper shows MNN-based methods fail to both correct batch effects and maintain local structure, but BATMAN's one-to-one anchor matching may be too sparse if fine-grained per-cell correction is needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 BATMAN's batch-correction step: for every matched anchor pair found by minimum-weight matching on the weighted bipartite anchor graph, determine a local shifting vector from the query cell to its matched reference cell in N-dimensional gene space, then apply these vectors to the query dataset to produce the integrated expression matrix. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2020.101185
skills.summary: BATMAN's batch-correction step: for every matched anchor pair found by minimum-weight matching on the weighted bipartite anchor graph, determine a local shifting vector from the query cell to its matched reference cell in N-dimensional gene space, then apply these vectors to the query dataset to produce the integrated expression matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Integrating more than two datasets — 'The current implementation of BATMAN works only with two datasets.' Input data are raw counts or already normalized by another pipeline — BATMAN expects Seurat V3.0-style log-counts pre-processing. The analysis goal requires methods with different structural assumptions (e.g., MNN-based tools) — the paper shows MNN-based methods fail to both correct batch effects and maintain local structure, but BATMAN's one-to-one anchor matching may be too sparse if fine-grained per-cell correction is needed.

skills.description: Reference for judging integration quality when a method must both mix batches (iLISI) and retain local neighborhood structure (50-RNN), e.g. benchmarking BATMAN, Seurat V3.0, MNNcorrect, or Scanorama.
skills.name: local-structure-preservation-rnn-evaluation
skills.search_text: local-structure-preservation-rnn-evaluation Reference for judging integration quality when a method must both mix batches (iLISI) and retain local neighborhood structure (50-RNN), e.g. benchmarking BATMAN, Seurat V3.0, MNNcorrect, or Scanorama. When the integration pipeline only has more than two datasets to correct — BATMAN's current implementation supports only two datasets, so the metrics still apply but the BATMAN method being evaluated does not. When the goal is only mixing without regard to local structure (iLISI alone) — this skill exists specifically to catch over-correction that destroys cell-to-cell relationships, as seen with Scanorama's 50-RNN of 0.14. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Evaluates whether a single-cell RNA-seq batch-integration method preserves cell-to-cell (local) relationships while correcting batch effects, using the mean 50-RNN (retain-nearest-neighbor) metric reported alongside mean iLISI in the BATMAN benchmark. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2020.101185
skills.summary: Evaluates whether a single-cell RNA-seq batch-integration method preserves cell-to-cell (local) relationships while correcting batch effects, using the mean 50-RNN (retain-nearest-neighbor) metric reported alongside mean iLISI in the BATMAN benchmark.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the integration pipeline only has more than two datasets to correct — BATMAN's current implementation supports only two datasets, so the metrics still apply but the BATMAN method being evaluated does not. When the goal is only mixing without regard to local structure (iLISI alone) — this skill exists specifically to catch over-correction that destroys cell-to-cell relationships, as seen with Scanorama's 50-RNN of 0.14.

skills.description: Use when a monolithic, clustering-free estimate of per-cell rareness/density is needed on ultra-large scRNA-seq data (tens of thousands of profiles) where pairwise-clustering methods like RaceID or GiniClust scale too slowly.
skills.name: locality-sensitive-hashing-density-estimation
skills.search_text: locality-sensitive-hashing-density-estimation Use when a monolithic, clustering-free estimate of per-cell rareness/density is needed on ultra-large scRNA-seq data (tens of thousands of profiles) where pairwise-clustering methods like RaceID or GiniClust scale too slowly. The goal is doublet detection — doublet rate varies between 1% and 30%, which does not necessarily comply with the notion of cell rareness The task requires distinguishing true outliers from cells of minor cell types — FiRE does not discriminate between an outlier and cells representing minor cell types The input is a small dataset where slower but more interpretable clustering-based methods (RaceID, GiniClust) suffice http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Sketches each cell's expression profile into an M=50-bit hash code using L=100 locality-sensitive hash estimators, and uses bucket populousness as a local density proxy so that rare cells receive high FiRE rareness scores (consensus score -2*sum_l log(p_il)). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-07234-6
skills.summary: Sketches each cell's expression profile into an M=50-bit hash code using L=100 locality-sensitive hash estimators, and uses bucket populousness as a local density proxy so that rare cells receive high FiRE rareness scores (consensus score -2*sum_l log(p_il)).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is doublet detection — doublet rate varies between 1% and 30%, which does not necessarily comply with the notion of cell rareness The task requires distinguishing true outliers from cells of minor cell types — FiRE does not discriminate between an outlier and cells representing minor cell types The input is a small dataset where slower but more interpretable clustering-based methods (RaceID, GiniClust) suffice

skills.description: Use when raw scRNA-seq reads must be transformed into reference-free cell features without genome alignment, and k-mers with similar abundance profiles need to be grouped via simhash fingerprints.
skills.name: locality-sensitive-hashing-fingerprinting
skills.search_text: locality-sensitive-hashing-fingerprinting Use when raw scRNA-seq reads must be transformed into reference-free cell features without genome alignment, and k-mers with similar abundance profiles need to be grouped via simhash fingerprints. Input is already a cell-level feature or gene expression table rather than a k-mer abundance matrix — the cell matrix generation module, not simhash, transforms k-mer abundance to CKG expression A complete, well-annotated reference genome exists and standard alignment-based gene expression features are sufficient, since CKG derivation is motivated by incomplete or insufficient reference genomes The k-mer matrix generation step has not been run — simhash requires the sparse k-mer matrix as its direct input http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Applies simhash locality-sensitive hashing to compress informative k-mer abundance vectors from scRNA-seq reads into fixed-size fingerprints, grouping k-mers with similar abundance profiles into compressed k-mer groups (CKGs) that serve as reference-free cell features. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2021.102855
skills.summary: Applies simhash locality-sensitive hashing to compress informative k-mer abundance vectors from scRNA-seq reads into fixed-size fingerprints, grouping k-mers with similar abundance profiles into compressed k-mer groups (CKGs) that serve as reference-free cell features.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a cell-level feature or gene expression table rather than a k-mer abundance matrix — the cell matrix generation module, not simhash, transforms k-mer abundance to CKG expression A complete, well-annotated reference genome exists and standard alignment-based gene expression features are sufficient, since CKG derivation is motivated by incomplete or insufficient reference genomes The k-mer matrix generation step has not been run — simhash requires the sparse k-mer matrix as its direct input

skills.description: Use when a locus-level TE quantification matrix (e.g., MATES output with loci named chr|start|end) must be annotated with coordinates and flanking genes to interpret cell-type-specific TE markers such as RLTR44B in macrophages.
skills.name: locus-level-annotation-extraction-with-flanking-genes
skills.search_text: locus-level-annotation-extraction-with-flanking-genes Use when a locus-level TE quantification matrix (e.g., MATES output with loci named chr|start|end) must be annotated with coordinates and flanking genes to interpret cell-type-specific TE markers such as RLTR44B in macrophages. Working from subfamily-level TE counts (e.g., scTE-style subfamily matrices), which lack the locus identifiers and coordinates needed for flanking-gene extraction Long autonomously expressed TEs such as L1HS spanning several thousand bases, where the 2001 bp flanking window and multi-mapping rate estimates are unreliable TE copies with high sequence similarity and no uniquely mappable flanking regions (e.g., HERVK isoforms), where locus-specific annotation cannot be distinguished http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 Extract specific transposable element loci from MATES locus-level quantification together with their genomic coordinates and flanking genes, providing locus-level annotation (e.g., chr13|89384655|89385083 adjacent to Edil3/Hapln1) that links cell-type-specific TE activity to nearby regulatory context. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-53114-7
skills.summary: Extract specific transposable element loci from MATES locus-level quantification together with their genomic coordinates and flanking genes, providing locus-level annotation (e.g., chr13|89384655|89385083 adjacent to Edil3/Hapln1) that links cell-type-specific TE activity to nearby regulatory context.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Working from subfamily-level TE counts (e.g., scTE-style subfamily matrices), which lack the locus identifiers and coordinates needed for flanking-gene extraction Long autonomously expressed TEs such as L1HS spanning several thousand bases, where the 2001 bp flanking window and multi-mapping rate estimates are unreliable TE copies with high sequence similarity and no uniquely mappable flanking regions (e.g., HERVK isoforms), where locus-specific annotation cannot be distinguished

skills.description: Use when building a custom BIRD prediction model from training RNA-seq expression and DNase-seq DH data, or when cluster-level model performance is uncertain and the locus-level model must be used via BIRD_predict -l.
skills.name: locus-level-linear-regression-model-fitting
skills.search_text: locus-level-linear-regression-model-fitting Use when building a custom BIRD prediction model from training RNA-seq expression and DNase-seq DH data, or when cluster-level model performance is uncertain and the locus-level model must be used via BIRD_predict -l. You only need to apply an existing prebuilt model (e.g., human_hg38_model.bin) to new expression data — use standard BIRD_predict without retraining The full/cluster-level model already performs well; the README notes -l is mainly useful when 'you are not sure if the cluster-level model works or not' Goal is discovering new DHS locations in a new sample — BIRD will not discover new DHS locations beyond its training loci http://edamontology.org/topic_3169 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Fits BIRD's locus-level model BIR(X-bar, Y), which compresses co-expressed genes into k-means gene-cluster predictors (X-bar), selects the most informative cluster predictors per DHS locus, and fits a per-locus linear regression predicting DNase I hypersensitivity (DH) from genome-wide gene expression. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-017-01188-x
skills.summary: Fits BIRD's locus-level model BIR(X-bar, Y), which compresses co-expressed genes into k-means gene-cluster predictors (X-bar), selects the most informative cluster predictors per DHS locus, and fits a per-locus linear regression predicting DNase I hypersensitivity (DH) from genome-wide gene expression.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need to apply an existing prebuilt model (e.g., human_hg38_model.bin) to new expression data — use standard BIRD_predict without retraining The full/cluster-level model already performs well; the README notes -l is mainly useful when 'you are not sure if the cluster-level model works or not' Goal is discovering new DHS locations in a new sample — BIRD will not discover new DHS locations beyond its training loci

skills.description: Use when evaluating a locus-specific TE quantification method (e.g., MATES, scTE, SoloTE) against simulated single-cell data with known ground-truth locus abundances, or when reproducing the controlled-simulation validation reported in a TE quantification paper.
skills.name: locus-level-te-count-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: locus-level-te-count-correlation-analysis Use when evaluating a locus-specific TE quantification method (e.g., MATES, scTE, SoloTE) against simulated single-cell data with known ground-truth locus abundances, or when reproducing the controlled-simulation validation reported in a TE quantification paper. Input is real sequencing data without a simulated ground truth — R2 against ground truth cannot be computed; use orthogonal validation (e.g., long-read read-back) instead The TE of interest is a long autonomously expressed element (e.g., L1HS spanning several thousand bases) — MATES' 2001-bp coverage vector limits quantification accuracy The goal is subfamily-level rather than locus-specific TE quantification, where simpler counting methods suffice http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Benchmark locus-specific transposable element (TE) quantification by comparing method-estimated per-locus counts against simulated Polyester ground truth using locus-level R2 correlation and percent of simulated reads recaptured, as done for MATES vs scTE/SoloTE. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-53114-7
skills.summary: Benchmark locus-specific transposable element (TE) quantification by comparing method-estimated per-locus counts against simulated Polyester ground truth using locus-level R2 correlation and percent of simulated reads recaptured, as done for MATES vs scTE/SoloTE.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real sequencing data without a simulated ground truth — R2 against ground truth cannot be computed; use orthogonal validation (e.g., long-read read-back) instead The TE of interest is a long autonomously expressed element (e.g., L1HS spanning several thousand bases) — MATES' 2001-bp coverage vector limits quantification accuracy The goal is subfamily-level rather than locus-specific TE quantification, where simpler counting methods suffice

skills.description: Use when processing single-cell RNA-Seq BAM files (CellRanger or STAR output) to detect locus-specific transposable element activity that standard pipelines discard, and to merge TE counts into a gene+TE expression matrix for downstream tools like Seurat.
skills.name: locus-specific-te-expression-summarization
skills.search_text: locus-specific-te-expression-summarization Use when processing single-cell RNA-Seq BAM files (CellRanger or STAR output) to detect locus-specific transposable element activity that standard pipelines discard, and to merge TE counts into a gene+TE expression matrix for downstream tools like Seurat. Input is already a processed expression/feature table rather than an unprocessed CellRanger/STAR BAM file The goal is family-level TE metagene summarization only (e.g. scTE-style analysis) without locus resolution Reads assigned to genes should also be counted against overlapping TEs and the 'dual' behavior is not desired as the default discard rule http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Summarize transposable element (TE) expression at individual genomic loci in scRNA-Seq data using SoloTE, which overlaps unassigned reads from CellRanger/STAR BAMs against a TE BED annotation and emits a combined gene+TE expression matrix compatible with Seurat. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-022-04020-5
skills.summary: Summarize transposable element (TE) expression at individual genomic loci in scRNA-Seq data using SoloTE, which overlaps unassigned reads from CellRanger/STAR BAMs against a TE BED annotation and emits a combined gene+TE expression matrix compatible with Seurat.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed expression/feature table rather than an unprocessed CellRanger/STAR BAM file The goal is family-level TE metagene summarization only (e.g. scTE-style analysis) without locus resolution Reads assigned to genes should also be counted against overlapping TEs and the 'dual' behavior is not desired as the default discard rule

skills.description: Use when differentially expressed uTAR coverage tracks need smoothing and peak-coordinate extraction (FWHM) to define the nucleotide sequence that will be BLASTn-annotated.
skills.name: loess-coverage-smoothing-genomic-tracks
skills.search_text: loess-coverage-smoothing-genomic-tracks Use when differentially expressed uTAR coverage tracks need smoothing and peak-coordinate extraction (FWHM) to define the nucleotide sequence that will be BLASTn-annotated. Coverage tracks that are already peak-called or the uTAR coordinates themselves are the intended BLAST query and peak refinement is unnecessary Annotating aTARs that already overlap a known genome annotation — homology-based labeling is aimed at unannotated TARs (uTARs) Read-level variant or splice analysis; LOESS smoothing destroys base-level resolution by design http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Smooth per-uTAR read coverage from SAMtools depth with locally weighted (LOESS) regression (span = 0.25) and locate the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) coordinates of the largest coverage peak, so a compact nucleotide sequence can be extracted for BLASTn homology annotation of differentially expressed uTARs. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-22496-3
skills.summary: Smooth per-uTAR read coverage from SAMtools depth with locally weighted (LOESS) regression (span = 0.25) and locate the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) coordinates of the largest coverage peak, so a compact nucleotide sequence can be extracted for BLASTn homology annotation of differentially expressed uTARs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Coverage tracks that are already peak-called or the uTAR coordinates themselves are the intended BLAST query and peak refinement is unnecessary Annotating aTARs that already overlap a known genome annotation — homology-based labeling is aimed at unannotated TARs (uTARs) Read-level variant or splice analysis; LOESS smoothing destroys base-level resolution by design

skills.description: Use when computing per-gene entropy-reduction statistics (ds) from a gene-by-cell scRNA-seq count matrix to feed the ROGUE cluster-purity calculation, or when modeling the expected mean-expression vs. sample-entropy relationship.
skills.name: loess-regression-residual-computation
skills.search_text: loess-regression-residual-computation Use when computing per-gene entropy-reduction statistics (ds) from a gene-by-cell scRNA-seq count matrix to feed the ROGUE cluster-purity calculation, or when modeling the expected mean-expression vs. sample-entropy relationship. When the goal is clustering or rare-cell-type detection rather than purity assessment — tools like GiniClust, GiniClust2 or RaceID3 are designed for that; ROGUE quantifies homogeneity of an already-defined cluster. When assessing purity of cell populations integrated across different protocols/platforms — the paper states current ROGUE does not yet handle integrated populations (proposed future work). Input is not raw count data (e.g., log-transformed expression): GiniClust's README explicitly warns log2-transformed RNA-seq data may not work for related count-based models; the S–E entropy model likewise expects counts under the Poisson-Gamma framework. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Fit a LOESS regression of ln E(X) against average expression within the S–E entropy model and take per-gene residuals as the entropy-reduction statistic (ds), which feeds the ROGUE purity score. This is the core inferential step of the ROGUE (Ratio of Global Unshifted Entropy) method for quantifying single-cell cluster purity. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-16904-3
skills.summary: Fit a LOESS regression of ln E(X) against average expression within the S–E entropy model and take per-gene residuals as the entropy-reduction statistic (ds), which feeds the ROGUE purity score. This is the core inferential step of the ROGUE (Ratio of Global Unshifted Entropy) method for quantifying single-cell cluster purity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is clustering or rare-cell-type detection rather than purity assessment — tools like GiniClust, GiniClust2 or RaceID3 are designed for that; ROGUE quantifies homogeneity of an already-defined cluster. When assessing purity of cell populations integrated across different protocols/platforms — the paper states current ROGUE does not yet handle integrated populations (proposed future work). Input is not raw count data (e.g., log-transformed expression): GiniClust's README explicitly warns log2-transformed RNA-seq data may not work for related count-based models; the S–E entropy model likewise expects counts under the Poisson-Gamma framework.

skills.description: Use when a gene-by-cell relative expression matrix (counts minus a normal-cell baseline) must be denoised before copy number segmentation while preserving piecewise-constant discontinuities (breakpoints) along genomic coordinates.
skills.name: log-cosh-edge-preserving-regularization
skills.search_text: log-cosh-edge-preserving-regularization Use when a gene-by-cell relative expression matrix (counts minus a normal-cell baseline) must be denoised before copy number segmentation while preserving piecewise-constant discontinuities (breakpoints) along genomic coordinates. The sample has no aneuploidy signal (tumors with minimal genomic alterations such as leukemias, pediatric cancers, or Ependymomas), where the copy-number-based smoothing-segmentation framework is not suited No relative expression matrix exists yet — the baseline subtraction step must precede smoothing The goal is segmentation itself rather than pre-segmentation denoising; use the Mumford-Shah greedy segmentation skill instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 Applies an edge-preserving total-variation (TV) smoothing with the phi(x)=logcosh(x) prior to the relative expression matrix, denoising the per-cell expression signal while retaining copy number breakpoints before segmentation, as implemented inside SCEVAN::classifyTumorCells. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-36790-9
skills.summary: Applies an edge-preserving total-variation (TV) smoothing with the phi(x)=logcosh(x) prior to the relative expression matrix, denoising the per-cell expression signal while retaining copy number breakpoints before segmentation, as implemented inside SCEVAN::classifyTumorCells.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample has no aneuploidy signal (tumors with minimal genomic alterations such as leukemias, pediatric cancers, or Ependymomas), where the copy-number-based smoothing-segmentation framework is not suited No relative expression matrix exists yet — the baseline subtraction step must precede smoothing The goal is segmentation itself rather than pre-segmentation denoising; use the Mumford-Shah greedy segmentation skill instead

skills.description: Use when you have a CSV data frame of significantly changed genes with expression values / log-fold-change values and need per-gene LFC scores to drive OmicInt's GMM clustering or gene-network exploration.
skills.name: log-fold-change-gene-scoring
skills.search_text: log-fold-change-gene-scoring Use when you have a CSV data frame of significantly changed genes with expression values / log-fold-change values and need per-gene LFC scores to drive OmicInt's GMM clustering or gene-network exploration. Input data is not a CSV data frame containing significantly changed genes and their expression/log-fold-change values — the user must ensure data is in the right format before scoring Goal is integrated scRNA-seq/proteomics expression profiles rather than per-gene LFC scoring — use the OmicInt integration pipeline instead Gene identifiers are not aligned across omics layers, making per-gene LFC computation ambiguous http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Computes the OmicInt LFC-based gene score — a novel scoring function capturing expression and pathology associations — over significantly changed genes supplied as a CSV data frame. The score is the key analytical parameter of OmicInt's Gaussian mixture modelling pipeline for exploring gene networks and interactome complexity. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.ailsci.2021.100025
skills.summary: Computes the OmicInt LFC-based gene score — a novel scoring function capturing expression and pathology associations — over significantly changed genes supplied as a CSV data frame. The score is the key analytical parameter of OmicInt's Gaussian mixture modelling pipeline for exploring gene networks and interactome complexity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data is not a CSV data frame containing significantly changed genes and their expression/log-fold-change values — the user must ensure data is in the right format before scoring Goal is integrated scRNA-seq/proteomics expression profiles rather than per-gene LFC scoring — use the OmicInt integration pipeline instead Gene identifiers are not aligned across omics layers, making per-gene LFC computation ambiguous

skills.description: Use when a quantile-normalized microarray intensity matrix contains a mixed background/signal distribution and a log2-scale histogram inflection must be identified to set a background cutoff (e.g. 6.1 in the PIMENTo pipeline).
skills.name: log-intensity-distribution-analysis
skills.search_text: log-intensity-distribution-analysis Use when a quantile-normalized microarray intensity matrix contains a mixed background/signal distribution and a log2-scale histogram inflection must be identified to set a background cutoff (e.g. 6.1 in the PIMENTo pipeline). The matrix is already background-subtracted or contains only signal-range intensities (no background mixture to resolve). The data are not microarray intensity distributions (e.g. RNA-seq count tables), where PIMENTo's histogram-based background cutoff does not apply. The zoomed [5,7] log-intensity histogram shows no resolvable valley, so the cutoff cannot be defensibly read from an inflection. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Analysis of the log2-scale intensity distribution of quantile-normalized microarray data to locate the valley separating background from signal, yielding a background cutoff (e.g. 6.1) used to strip unexpressed genes from the data matrix before downstream testing. transcriptomics/v2 10.1007/978-1-4939-9004-7_11
skills.summary: Analysis of the log2-scale intensity distribution of quantile-normalized microarray data to locate the valley separating background from signal, yielding a background cutoff (e.g. 6.1) used to strip unexpressed genes from the data matrix before downstream testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The matrix is already background-subtracted or contains only signal-range intensities (no background mixture to resolve). The data are not microarray intensity distributions (e.g. RNA-seq count tables), where PIMENTo's histogram-based background cutoff does not apply. The zoomed [5,7] log-intensity histogram shows no resolvable valley, so the cutoff cannot be defensibly read from an inflection.

skills.description: Use when raw scRNA-seq count matrices (UMI or read count, e.g. CSV with cells x genes) must be normalized before PCA/RMT-based signal detection and you need to prevent log normalization from creating false variability from TGC bias.
skills.name: log-l2-normalization-preprocessing
skills.search_text: log-l2-normalization-preprocessing Use when raw scRNA-seq count matrices (UMI or read count, e.g. CSV with cells x genes) must be normalized before PCA/RMT-based signal detection and you need to prevent log normalization from creating false variability from TGC bias. When the goal is to impute zeros rather than detect signals — the article notes imputation approaches 'risk biasing data, leading to false signal' When the analysis explicitly requires feature selection of highly variable genes, since selection based on high variance 'potentially compromise[s] the local structure contained in low variance genes' When data are already normalized and L2-scaled (e.g. prior scLENS output saved as AnnData .h5ad or PCA CSV); re-running would double-normalize the cell vectors http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A scRNA-seq preprocessing scheme in which log normalization (scaling factor L=1) followed by per-gene scaling and L2 normalization of cell vector lengths removes the artificial signals (TGC-bias-driven distortion) that log normalization alone introduces before dimensionality reduction. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-47884-3
skills.summary: A scRNA-seq preprocessing scheme in which log normalization (scaling factor L=1) followed by per-gene scaling and L2 normalization of cell vector lengths removes the artificial signals (TGC-bias-driven distortion) that log normalization alone introduces before dimensionality reduction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to impute zeros rather than detect signals — the article notes imputation approaches 'risk biasing data, leading to false signal' When the analysis explicitly requires feature selection of highly variable genes, since selection based on high variance 'potentially compromise[s] the local structure contained in low variance genes' When data are already normalized and L2-scaled (e.g. prior scLENS output saved as AnnData .h5ad or PCA CSV); re-running would double-normalize the cell vectors

skills.description: Use when you have an adjacency network (e.g., a differential gene co-expression network) and must verify its degree distribution follows an approximate scale-free topology before downstream node-control analysis.
skills.name: log-log-distribution-visualization
skills.search_text: log-log-distribution-visualization Use when you have an adjacency network (e.g., a differential gene co-expression network) and must verify its degree distribution follows an approximate scale-free topology before downstream node-control analysis. The input network was not constructed from the paper's differential co-expression workflow (e.g., it is an unvalidated random graph or a directed interaction network such as the DawnRank-derived Gene_Net hub network), so the scale-free assumption does not apply You need to test a different topology hypothesis (e.g., small-world or power-law via maximum-likelihood fitting) rather than the paper's log2-log2 linear-regression R-square criterion http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Assesses whether a differential co-expression network approximates a scale-free topology by fitting log2(degree frequency) versus log2(degree) with linear regression and checking the R-square, as done for the 14 TCGA cancer-type networks in the WMDS.net framework. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad071
skills.summary: Assesses whether a differential co-expression network approximates a scale-free topology by fitting log2(degree frequency) versus log2(degree) with linear regression and checking the R-square, as done for the 14 TCGA cancer-type networks in the WMDS.net framework.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input network was not constructed from the paper's differential co-expression workflow (e.g., it is an unvalidated random graph or a directed interaction network such as the DawnRank-derived Gene_Net hub network), so the scale-free assumption does not apply You need to test a different topology hypothesis (e.g., small-world or power-law via maximum-likelihood fitting) rather than the paper's log2-log2 linear-regression R-square criterion

skills.description: Use when benchmarking computational scalability of a method: you have one large input dataset, need runtime as a function of size (e.g. number of cells), and want a fitted scaling exponent comparable across methods.
skills.name: log-log-scaling-slope-fitting
skills.search_text: log-log-scaling-slope-fitting Use when benchmarking computational scalability of a method: you have one large input dataset, need runtime as a function of size (e.g. number of cells), and want a fitted scaling exponent comparable across methods. You need quality or accuracy benchmarking (denoising performance), not runtime scalability — use task-level quality metrics instead The tool cannot run on the downsampled sizes at all (e.g. SAVER/scImpute on 100,000 cells took hours) — partial timing curves would not support a fair slope comparison The input is not a size-scalable single dataset; timing across heterogeneous datasets conflates size with dataset difficulty http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Empirically characterizes how a tool's runtime scales with input size by timing the tool on progressively downsampled datasets and fitting a linear regression in log10-log10 space to extract the scaling slope. In the DCA paper this established that DCA's runtime scales near-linearly with cell count (slope 0.66 on the 1.3M cell dataset), unlike MAGIC, SAVER and scImpute. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-07931-2
skills.summary: Empirically characterizes how a tool's runtime scales with input size by timing the tool on progressively downsampled datasets and fitting a linear regression in log10-log10 space to extract the scaling slope. In the DCA paper this established that DCA's runtime scales near-linearly with cell count (slope 0.66 on the 1.3M cell dataset), unlike MAGIC, SAVER and scImpute.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need quality or accuracy benchmarking (denoising performance), not runtime scalability — use task-level quality metrics instead The tool cannot run on the downsampled sizes at all (e.g. SAVER/scImpute on 100,000 cells took hours) — partial timing curves would not support a fair slope comparison The input is not a size-scalable single dataset; timing across heterogeneous datasets conflates size with dataset difficulty

skills.description: Use when building synthetic multi-sample multi-condition scRNA-seq benchmark data: condition-permuted counts must be given sample-level technical variation (batch structure) before ground-truth DS genes are injected.
skills.name: log-normal-batch-effect-injection
skills.search_text: log-normal-batch-effect-injection Use when building synthetic multi-sample multi-condition scRNA-seq benchmark data: condition-permuted counts must be given sample-level technical variation (batch structure) before ground-truth DS genes are injected. The task is to remove or correct batch variability from real data — that is scMerge2 integration, not simulation of batch effects The analysis must preserve genuine condition effects (e.g., real disease-vs-control contrasts); this pipeline first permutes condition labels to construct a null dataset The input already contains real batch artifacts (platform/chemistry effects) — adding synthetic log-normal batch effects would confound them http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 A simulation step that adds log-normal, sample-level batch effects to condition-permuted single-cell counts, producing a controlled two-condition, two-batch null onto which ground-truth DS genes (logFC 1.1–2 at 5%/10%) are injected to benchmark DS detection and integration methods such as scMerge2. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-39923-2
skills.summary: A simulation step that adds log-normal, sample-level batch effects to condition-permuted single-cell counts, producing a controlled two-condition, two-batch null onto which ground-truth DS genes (logFC 1.1–2 at 5%/10%) are injected to benchmark DS detection and integration methods such as scMerge2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is to remove or correct batch variability from real data — that is scMerge2 integration, not simulation of batch effects The analysis must preserve genuine condition effects (e.g., real disease-vs-control contrasts); this pipeline first permutes condition labels to construct a null dataset The input already contains real batch artifacts (platform/chemistry effects) — adding synthetic log-normal batch effects would confound them

skills.description: Use when a known-truth negative-control dataset is needed to test whether an scRNA-seq method (e.g., Normalisr) falsely detects co-expression or nonlinear library-size confounders when none exist.
skills.name: log-normal-biological-variation-modeling
skills.search_text: log-normal-biological-variation-modeling Use when a known-truth negative-control dataset is needed to test whether an scRNA-seq method (e.g., Normalisr) falsely detects co-expression or nonlinear library-size confounders when none exist. The simulated matrix should not be treated as real biological data — by construction it contains no co-expression and represents a homogeneous gRNA-free K562-like cell null Normalisr (and this null-model validation scheme) was only evaluated on UMI-based datasets; full-length platforms may need revalidation of the nonlinear cellular summary covariates Not suitable for hypothesis testing of arbitrary nonlinear associations, for which Normalisr is explicitly not designed http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Constructs a synthetic null scRNA-seq read-count matrix of homogeneous gRNA-free K562-like cells by applying log-normal biological variation to empirically sampled gene expression proportions and multinomial read sampling with sampled library sizes, yielding a co-expression-free null with ground-truth log expression proportions. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-26682-1
skills.summary: Constructs a synthetic null scRNA-seq read-count matrix of homogeneous gRNA-free K562-like cells by applying log-normal biological variation to empirically sampled gene expression proportions and multinomial read sampling with sampled library sizes, yielding a co-expression-free null with ground-truth log expression proportions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The simulated matrix should not be treated as real biological data — by construction it contains no co-expression and represents a homogeneous gRNA-free K562-like cell null Normalisr (and this null-model validation scheme) was only evaluated on UMI-based datasets; full-length platforms may need revalidation of the nonlinear cellular summary covariates Not suitable for hypothesis testing of arbitrary nonlinear associations, for which Normalisr is explicitly not designed

skills.description: Use when UMI-based scRNA-seq counts must be log-normalized (scale factor 10000) after SAVER-X denoising, or CITE-seq/REAP-seq ADT protein counts must be converted to relative-abundance log-ratios before cTP-net protein imputation.
skills.name: log-normalize-count-transformation
skills.search_text: log-normalize-count-transformation Use when UMI-based scRNA-seq counts must be log-normalized (scale factor 10000) after SAVER-X denoising, or CITE-seq/REAP-seq ADT protein counts must be converted to relative-abundance log-ratios before cTP-net protein imputation. Expression data are TPM or RPKM rather than UMI-based counts — cTP-net can only apply to count-based (UMI) input and TPM/RPKM accuracy is untested Goal is imputing proteins without paired multi-omic training data — LogNormalize alone does not predict protein abundance Input is already normalized/denoised — re-applying LogNormalize to non-count values invalidates the per-cell total m_j in X_ij = log(Λ_ij × 10000 / m_j) http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Seurat-default LogNormalize of SAVER-X-denoised UMI counts (X_ij = log(Λ_ij × 10000 / m_j)) paired with the Stoeckius et al. relative-abundance log-ratio transform of surface-protein ADT counts, producing the paired training input and response vectors for cTP-net. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-14391-0

skills.when_to_use_negative: Expression data are TPM or RPKM rather than UMI-based counts — cTP-net can only apply to count-based (UMI) input and TPM/RPKM accuracy is untested Goal is imputing proteins without paired multi-omic training data — LogNormalize alone does not predict protein abundance Input is already normalized/denoised — re-applying LogNormalize to non-count values invalidates the per-cell total m_j in X_ij = log(Λ_ij × 10000 / m_j)

skills.description: Use when two patient subtype calls (e.g., basal-like vs classical from signature scoring of 150 TCGA PAAD tumors) must be validated against overall survival with KM curves, a log-rank P value, and a hazard ratio.

skills.search_text: log-space-expression-cap-enforcement Use when performing recursive (multi-step) neural ODE expression forecasting with RNAForecaster, e.g. predicting scEU-seq RPE cell-cycle gene expression over 72 hourly steps, to prevent extreme predictions. Standard scRNA-seq protocols without paired time-point measurements of the same cell — RNAForecaster training requires dynamic (e.g. metabolic labeling) data, so there are no recursive predictions to cap. Single one-step predictions that stay within the training expression distribution and do not feed outputs back into the network inputs — no extreme-prediction control loop is needed. You need a learned prior on expression outside the observed range — the cap is enforced post hoc, not learned, so it is the wrong mechanism for probabilistic extrapolation. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Enforces a realistic prior on expression bounds during RNAForecaster's recursive predictions by capping predicted expression at the allowed maximum (default two times the maximum observed in the training data, in log space) and clamping negative predictions to zero, preventing runaway growth over multi-step forecasts. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100793
skills.summary: Enforces a realistic prior on expression bounds during RNAForecaster's recursive predictions by capping predicted expression at the allowed maximum (default two times the maximum observed in the training data, in log space) and clamping negative predictions to zero, preventing runaway growth over multi-step forecasts.
