skills.name: matthews-correlation-coefficient-computation
skills.search_text: matthews-correlation-coefficient-computation Use when benchmarking a binary transcript classifier (lncRNA vs. protein-coding transcript, lncRNA as positive class) on imbalanced five-species datasets and you need a single balanced metric, or when quantifying cross-species model transfer. When the task requires threshold-free metrics such as ROC-AUC or PR-AUC — MCC here depends on the fixed 0.5 prediction-score cutoff (>= 0.5 = lncRNA, < 0.5 = PCT). When input is already an aggregate performance table or published matrix rather than per-transcript predictions — no confusion matrix can be recomputed. For multi-class or regression outputs; LncCat's task is binary lncRNA vs. PCT classification. http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Compute the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) to evaluate binary lncRNA vs. PCT classification performance in LncCat, both on same-species test sets and to fill a 5x5 cross-species transfer matrix where predictions use a 0.5 score cutoff (score >= 0.5 labeled lncRNA, < 0.5 labeled PCT). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.02.012
skills.summary: Compute the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) to evaluate binary lncRNA vs. PCT classification performance in LncCat, both on same-species test sets and to fill a 5x5 cross-species transfer matrix where predictions use a 0.5 score cutoff (score >= 0.5 labeled lncRNA, < 0.5 labeled PCT).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the task requires threshold-free metrics such as ROC-AUC or PR-AUC — MCC here depends on the fixed 0.5 prediction-score cutoff (>= 0.5 = lncRNA, < 0.5 = PCT). When input is already an aggregate performance table or published matrix rather than per-transcript predictions — no confusion matrix can be recomputed. For multi-class or regression outputs; LncCat's task is binary lncRNA vs. PCT classification.

skills.description: Use when you have RgnTX permutation test results (e.g., m6A sites vs stop codon regions via permTestTxIA_customPick) and need to verify that the association peak sits exactly at the original ROI positions rather than reflecting generic 3'UTR enrichment.
skills.name: mature-mrna-region-shifting
skills.search_text: mature-mrna-region-shifting Use when you have RgnTX permutation test results (e.g., m6A sites vs stop codon regions via permTestTxIA_customPick) and need to verify that the association peak sits exactly at the original ROI positions rather than reflecting generic 3'UTR enrichment. Input regions already have a clear transcript/isoform association and you only need a single permutation p-value, not a positional-shift profile You are performing genome-based colocalization (e.g., GREAT, LOLA, GenomeRunner-style tests) rather than transcriptome/mRNA-space analysis The question is whether two region sets overlap at all, not whether the association is tied to exact ROI positions http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Applies RgnTX's shifted z-score machinery (shiftedZScoreTx, shiftExonTx) to slide regions of interest over mature mRNA space (exons) and profile how a permutation-test colocalization signal changes when ROI positions are shifted, distinguishing true positional association from background enrichment. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.08.021
skills.summary: Applies RgnTX's shifted z-score machinery (shiftedZScoreTx, shiftExonTx) to slide regions of interest over mature mRNA space (exons) and profile how a permutation-test colocalization signal changes when ROI positions are shifted, distinguishing true positional association from background enrichment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input regions already have a clear transcript/isoform association and you only need a single permutation p-value, not a positional-shift profile You are performing genome-based colocalization (e.g., GREAT, LOLA, GenomeRunner-style tests) rather than transcriptome/mRNA-space analysis The question is whether two region sets overlap at all, not whether the association is tied to exact ROI positions

skills.description: Use when gene-by-cell scRNA-seq expression matrices and a redPATH pseudotime ordering are available and you need to rank genes by non-linear association with developmental/cancer trajectory, e.g. recovering CSF1R or Foxm1/Tubb5/Nek2.
skills.name: maximal-information-coefficient-scoring
skills.search_text: maximal-information-coefficient-scoring Use when gene-by-cell scRNA-seq expression matrices and a redPATH pseudotime ordering are available and you need to rank genes by non-linear association with developmental/cancer trajectory, e.g. recovering CSF1R or Foxm1/Tubb5/Nek2. When pseudotime results perform poorly — the article notes this gene-discovery approach may fail when the pseudotime results perform poorly When you only need linear associations and already have dCor scores sufficient for selection — MIC adds non-linear detection but at higher computational cost When the goal is cell cycle state assignment rather than gene discovery along pseudotime — use the reCAT-based G0-like cell detection or HMM segmentation functions instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Computes Maximal Information Coefficient (MIC) scores between each gene's expression profile and the redPATH-inferred pseudotime using calc_correlation(type='mic'), to discover genes whose non-linear dependence on developmental ordering is significant in single-cell RNA-seq datasets such as MGH45, MGH107, and the NSC-Llorens neural stem cell data. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2020.06.014
skills.summary: Computes Maximal Information Coefficient (MIC) scores between each gene's expression profile and the redPATH-inferred pseudotime using calc_correlation(type='mic'), to discover genes whose non-linear dependence on developmental ordering is significant in single-cell RNA-seq datasets such as MGH45, MGH107, and the NSC-Llorens neural stem cell data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When pseudotime results perform poorly — the article notes this gene-discovery approach may fail when the pseudotime results perform poorly When you only need linear associations and already have dCor scores sufficient for selection — MIC adds non-linear detection but at higher computational cost When the goal is cell cycle state assignment rather than gene discovery along pseudotime — use the reCAT-based G0-like cell detection or HMM segmentation functions instead

skills.description: Use when inferring RNA velocity and latent time jointly from spliced/unspliced count matrices (AnnData) with a top-down dynamic model, especially when unified transcriptome-wide latent time or gene-specific time modes are needed.
skills.name: maximum-likelihood-em-optimization
skills.search_text: maximum-likelihood-em-optimization Use when inferring RNA velocity and latent time jointly from spliced/unspliced count matrices (AnnData) with a top-down dynamic model, especially when unified transcriptome-wide latent time or gene-specific time modes are needed. When downstream analysis requires unsupervised selection of dynamically informed genes — the paper states this remains an open challenge in UniTVelo When Bayesian propagation of latent time uncertainty is required — the article notes Bayesian treatment of latent time uncertainty is anticipated but not implemented When spliced/unspliced count data is unavailable (e.g. only spliced reads were sequenced), since the model relies on both layers An EM-style maximum-likelihood inference loop from UniTVelo that alternately estimates per-gene kinetic parameters and cell latent times via TensorFlow 2 automatic differentiation and a gradient-based Adam optimizer, computing RNA velocity as the time derivative (ds/dt) of a radial basis function (RBF) modeled spliced-RNA profile rather than from deviation to a steady-state equilibrium. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-34188-7
skills.summary: An EM-style maximum-likelihood inference loop from UniTVelo that alternately estimates per-gene kinetic parameters and cell latent times via TensorFlow 2 automatic differentiation and a gradient-based Adam optimizer, computing RNA velocity as the time derivative (ds/dt) of a radial basis function (RBF) modeled spliced-RNA profile rather than from deviation to a steady-state equilibrium.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When downstream analysis requires unsupervised selection of dynamically informed genes — the paper states this remains an open challenge in UniTVelo When Bayesian propagation of latent time uncertainty is required — the article notes Bayesian treatment of latent time uncertainty is anticipated but not implemented When spliced/unspliced count data is unavailable (e.g. only spliced reads were sequenced), since the model relies on both layers

skills.description: Use when GWAS summary statistics for a trait are available together with binary functional annotations (e.g. sQTL vs expression-only variants) and you need to test whether associations are enriched in one annotation class via fgwas.
skills.name: maximum-likelihood-enrichment-estimation
skills.search_text: maximum-likelihood-enrichment-estimation Use when GWAS summary statistics for a trait are available together with binary functional annotations (e.g. sQTL vs expression-only variants) and you need to test whether associations are enriched in one annotation class via fgwas. Your GWAS has few independent loci — fgwas works best with at least ~20 independent loci with p-values less than 5e-8 You lack a binary functional annotation distinguishing variant classes (e.g. no sQTL/eQTL classification), making the annotation-contrast model unidentifiable You need causal fine-mapping or co-localization rather than annotation enrichment — the article notes available co-localization/fine-mapping methods are not directly applicable within their multivariate framework, and enrichment estimates alone cannot distinguish whether paired sQTL/eQTL effects come from the same variant or two variants in LD http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Fit fgwas genomic annotation enrichment models by maximum likelihood to estimate whether GWAS associations are enriched in functional annotations (here, sQTL versus expression-only variants), extracting effect-size estimates and 95% CIs per trait. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-20578-2
skills.summary: Fit fgwas genomic annotation enrichment models by maximum likelihood to estimate whether GWAS associations are enriched in functional annotations (here, sQTL versus expression-only variants), extracting effect-size estimates and 95% CIs per trait.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your GWAS has few independent loci — fgwas works best with at least ~20 independent loci with p-values less than 5e-8 You lack a binary functional annotation distinguishing variant classes (e.g. no sQTL/eQTL classification), making the annotation-contrast model unidentifiable You need causal fine-mapping or co-localization rather than annotation enrichment — the article notes available co-localization/fine-mapping methods are not directly applicable within their multivariate framework, and enrichment estimates alone cannot distinguish whether paired sQTL/eQTL effects come from the same variant or two variants in LD

skills.description: Use when per-dose toxicity (or other monotone dose-response) proportions violate the increasing order constraint and you need monotonicity-constrained MLEs, e.g. isotonic DLT rate estimates for TSNP dose escalation decisions.
skills.name: maximum-likelihood-under-order-constraints
skills.search_text: maximum-likelihood-under-order-constraints Use when per-dose toxicity (or other monotone dose-response) proportions violate the increasing order constraint and you need monotonicity-constrained MLEs, e.g. isotonic DLT rate estimates for TSNP dose escalation decisions. When the raw per-dose proportions already satisfy the monotonic increasing constraint — no pooling is needed and raw proportions are the constrained MLEs. When dose-response need not be monotone (the constraint p1 ≤ p2 ≤ ... ≤ pJ is a design assumption of TSNP; violating it structurally invalidates isotonic fitting). http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Computes order-constrained maximum likelihood estimates of per-dose DLT rates in the TSNP phase I/II design by applying the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm (PAVA) to raw toxicity proportions, yielding isotonic estimates p̂_j that satisfy p1 ≤ p2 ≤ ... ≤ pJ. transcriptomics/v2 10.1002/pst.2075
skills.summary: Computes order-constrained maximum likelihood estimates of per-dose DLT rates in the TSNP phase I/II design by applying the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm (PAVA) to raw toxicity proportions, yielding isotonic estimates p̂_j that satisfy p1 ≤ p2 ≤ ... ≤ pJ.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the raw per-dose proportions already satisfy the monotonic increasing constraint — no pooling is needed and raw proportions are the constrained MLEs. When dose-response need not be monotone (the constraint p1 ≤ p2 ≤ ... ≤ pJ is a design assumption of TSNP; violating it structurally invalidates isotonic fitting).

skills.description: Use when benchmarking synthetic or simulated scRNA-seq data (e.g. from scGAN, Splatter, SUGAR) against a real reference dataset such as Fresh 68k PBMCs (Donor A) to quantify how close the generated distribution is to the real one.
skills.name: maximum-mean-discrepancy-computation
skills.search_text: maximum-mean-discrepancy-computation Use when benchmarking synthetic or simulated scRNA-seq data (e.g. from scGAN, Splatter, SUGAR) against a real reference dataset such as Fresh 68k PBMCs (Donor A) to quantify how close the generated distribution is to the real one. The real-vs-generated comparison targets realism of t-SNE embeddings or trajectory structure rather than distributional fidelity metrics Only scGAN/cscGAN training or generation is needed without any benchmarking against Splatter or SUGAR baselines http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Computes the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between real scRNA-seq cells and cells generated by simulation methods (scGAN, Splatter, SUGAR) to benchmark distributional fidelity, complemented by random-forest discrimination AUC (RF-AUC) as a realism check. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-14018-z
skills.summary: Computes the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between real scRNA-seq cells and cells generated by simulation methods (scGAN, Splatter, SUGAR) to benchmark distributional fidelity, complemented by random-forest discrimination AUC (RF-AUC) as a realism check.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The real-vs-generated comparison targets realism of t-SNE embeddings or trajectory structure rather than distributional fidelity metrics Only scGAN/cscGAN training or generation is needed without any benchmarking against Splatter or SUGAR baselines

skills.description: Use when comparing groups of cells as whole transcriptomic distributions (e.g., rexels from MERFISH spatial scRNAseq parcellization) so that spatial regions can be clustered or segmented on distributional rather than per-cell distance.
skills.name: maximum-mean-discrepancy-estimation
skills.search_text: maximum-mean-discrepancy-estimation Use when comparing groups of cells as whole transcriptomic distributions (e.g., rexels from MERFISH spatial scRNAseq parcellization) so that spatial regions can be clustered or segmented on distributional rather than per-cell distance. When comparing individual cells rather than distributions of cells — the kernel between all cell pairs, not set-wise MMD, is the appropriate operation When the spatial modality has low per-region cell counts such that within-set kernel averages are unreliable (the paper's rexels justify k=16 neighborhood size only for the smaller rexel-rexel comparisons) http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Compute pairwise maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) distances between sets of cells (rexels) using a q-diffused kernel, treating each spatial region as a transcriptomic distribution rather than individual cells, as used in the local distributional segmentation (LDS) approach for spatial scRNAseq. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s42003-024-06104-w
skills.summary: Compute pairwise maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) distances between sets of cells (rexels) using a q-diffused kernel, treating each spatial region as a transcriptomic distribution rather than individual cells, as used in the local distributional segmentation (LDS) approach for spatial scRNAseq.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When comparing individual cells rather than distributions of cells — the kernel between all cell pairs, not set-wise MMD, is the appropriate operation When the spatial modality has low per-region cell counts such that within-set kernel averages are unreliable (the paper's rexels justify k=16 neighborhood size only for the smaller rexel-rexel comparisons)

skills.description: Use when a set of uncontrolled free-text cell type annotations (synonyms, misspellings, abbreviations) must be converted one-to-one into Cell Ontology terms, and per-label nearest-neighbor retrieval alone may yield inconsistent or duplicated assignments.
skills.name: maximum-weight-bipartite-matching
skills.search_text: maximum-weight-bipartite-matching Use when a set of uncontrolled free-text cell type annotations (synonyms, misspellings, abbreviations) must be converted one-to-one into Cell Ontology terms, and per-label nearest-neighbor retrieval alone may yield inconsistent or duplicated assignments. Cell labels are already controlled Cell Ontology term IDs — no NLP mapping or matching refinement is needed Cell types are absent from the Cell Ontology entirely (the Cell Ontology 'likely misses cell types and cell states'), since no valid CL target term exists for matching The analysis goal is classifying cells by expression (BuildModel/Train on single-cell transcriptomes) rather than harmonizing label terminology http://edamontology.org/topic_3307 Global assignment step used inside OnClass's NLP terminology-mapping stage: after computing text-embedding similarities between user free-text cell type labels and Cell Ontology term definitions, maximum-weight bipartite matching pairs each free-text label to its best overall controlled-vocabulary CL term. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-25725-x
skills.summary: Global assignment step used inside OnClass's NLP terminology-mapping stage: after computing text-embedding similarities between user free-text cell type labels and Cell Ontology term definitions, maximum-weight bipartite matching pairs each free-text label to its best overall controlled-vocabulary CL term.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Cell labels are already controlled Cell Ontology term IDs — no NLP mapping or matching refinement is needed Cell types are absent from the Cell Ontology entirely (the Cell Ontology 'likely misses cell types and cell states'), since no valid CL target term exists for matching The analysis goal is classifying cells by expression (BuildModel/Train on single-cell transcriptomes) rather than harmonizing label terminology

skills.description: Use when two single-cell modalities (scRNA-seq expression and scDNA-seq copy number) must be matched cell-to-cell or cell-to-clone with no ground-truth correspondence, i.e., the cell association problem.
skills.name: maximum-weighted-bipartite-matching
skills.search_text: maximum-weighted-bipartite-matching Use when two single-cell modalities (scRNA-seq expression and scDNA-seq copy number) must be matched cell-to-cell or cell-to-clone with no ground-truth correspondence, i.e., the cell association problem. The sample is biologically homogeneous (e.g., healthy/NDBE BE biopsies), where the article shows matching cells is distinctively challenging and assignments show lower stability and definiteness Probabilistic confidence measures are required, since unlike clonealign, MaCroDNA does not provide them Ground-truth RNA–DNA correspondence already exists, making optimization unnecessary http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 Maximum weighted bipartite matching of per-gene read counts is the core optimization used by MaCroDNA to associate scRNA-seq cells with scDNA-seq cells or clones. Edge weights are per-gene Pearson correlation coefficients, and the assignment is solved as a binary integer program with Gurobi. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-44014-3
skills.summary: Maximum weighted bipartite matching of per-gene read counts is the core optimization used by MaCroDNA to associate scRNA-seq cells with scDNA-seq cells or clones. Edge weights are per-gene Pearson correlation coefficients, and the assignment is solved as a binary integer program with Gurobi.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample is biologically homogeneous (e.g., healthy/NDBE BE biopsies), where the article shows matching cells is distinctively challenging and assignments show lower stability and definiteness Probabilistic confidence measures are required, since unlike clonealign, MaCroDNA does not provide them Ground-truth RNA–DNA correspondence already exists, making optimization unnecessary

skills.description: Use when fitting iSC.MEB to multi-sample SRT data and the number of spatial clusters K is unknown — e.g. grid-searching K=16:19 on six seqFISH embryo sections and picking the MBIC-minimizing K with c_penalty=0.2.
skills.name: mbic-cluster-number-selection
skills.search_text: mbic-cluster-number-selection Use when fitting iSC.MEB to multi-sample SRT data and the number of spatial clusters K is unknown — e.g. grid-searching K=16:19 on six seqFISH embryo sections and picking the MBIC-minimizing K with c_penalty=0.2. K is already known or fixed by design (e.g. a benchmark calling iSCMEB(K=7) on DLPFC layers) — fit a single model rather than grid-selecting Input is the raw Seurat list without iSC.MEB prerequisites (CreateNeighbors adjacency plus runPCA embeddings); SelectModel cannot run on raw counts Single-sample or non-spatial analysis where iSC.MEB's multi-sample batch-effect integration is not needed http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 Selects the optimal number of spatial clusters K for iSC.MEB by fitting the hidden Markov random field with empirical Bayes over a candidate K grid (e.g. K=16:19 for the six seqFISH mouse embryo sections) and choosing the MBIC-minimizing K with a tuned c_penalty (0.2 in the seqFISH vignette). transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad019
skills.summary: Selects the optimal number of spatial clusters K for iSC.MEB by fitting the hidden Markov random field with empirical Bayes over a candidate K grid (e.g. K=16:19 for the six seqFISH mouse embryo sections) and choosing the MBIC-minimizing K with a tuned c_penalty (0.2 in the seqFISH vignette).
skills.when_to_use_negative: K is already known or fixed by design (e.g. a benchmark calling iSCMEB(K=7) on DLPFC layers) — fit a single model rather than grid-selecting Input is the raw Seurat list without iSC.MEB prerequisites (CreateNeighbors adjacency plus runPCA embeddings); SelectModel cannot run on raw counts Single-sample or non-spatial analysis where iSC.MEB's multi-sample batch-effect integration is not needed

skills.description: Use when a binary sequence classifier (e.g. lncRNA vs protein-coding transcript) produces probability scores on a test set and you must compute MCC and companion metrics against published benchmark values.
skills.name: mcc-based-confusion-matrix-evaluation
skills.search_text: mcc-based-confusion-matrix-evaluation Use when a binary sequence classifier (e.g. lncRNA vs protein-coding transcript) produces probability scores on a test set and you must compute MCC and companion metrics against published benchmark values. Input is raw multi-class or regression output rather than binary lncRNA/PCT predictions with scores comparable to a 0.5 cutoff Predictions come from a model not trained on the same CD-HIT-80%-filtered, >=200 nt, 70/10/20-split data, so direct MCC comparison against the published table is invalid You only need ranking quality (AUC) and class prevalence prevents interpreting fixed-cutoff confusion-matrix metrics meaningfully http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Evaluate lncRNA/PCT classifier predictions on held-out test sets by binarizing predicted scores at a fixed 0.5 cutoff and computing a confusion-matrix-derived panel of seven metrics (ACC, SEN, SPE, F1, PRE, MCC, AUC), with MCC as the headline score for cross-method and cross-species benchmark comparison. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.02.012
skills.summary: Evaluate lncRNA/PCT classifier predictions on held-out test sets by binarizing predicted scores at a fixed 0.5 cutoff and computing a confusion-matrix-derived panel of seven metrics (ACC, SEN, SPE, F1, PRE, MCC, AUC), with MCC as the headline score for cross-method and cross-species benchmark comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw multi-class or regression output rather than binary lncRNA/PCT predictions with scores comparable to a 0.5 cutoff Predictions come from a model not trained on the same CD-HIT-80%-filtered, >=200 nt, 70/10/20-split data, so direct MCC comparison against the published table is invalid You only need ranking quality (AUC) and class prevalence prevents interpreting fixed-cutoff confusion-matrix metrics meaningfully

skills.description: Use when benchmarking lncRNA identification methods (or any binary sequence classifiers) on the human/mouse/zebrafish sORF test datasets and you need MCC/F1 values to compare against a published reference table (e.g. Tables 8–9, S12–S14 of LncCat).
skills.name: mcc-f1-metric-computation
skills.search_text: mcc-f1-metric-computation Use when benchmarking lncRNA identification methods (or any binary sequence classifiers) on the human/mouse/zebrafish sORF test datasets and you need MCC/F1 values to compare against a published reference table (e.g. Tables 8–9, S12–S14 of LncCat). Data are unlabeled transcripts with no lncRNA/PCT ground truth — confusion-matrix-based metrics (MCC, F1, SEN, SPE) cannot be computed Multi-class or regression prediction tasks — MCC/F1 as applied here assume a binary lncRNA-vs-PCT classification with a specified positive class http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 Compute PRE, SEN, SPE, ACC, F1, MCC, and AUC for binary lncRNA/PCT classifiers on sORF test datasets, treating lncRNAs as the positive class, to quantify performance gaps between LncCat (CatBoost + ORF-attention features) and eight competing methods (CPAT, CNCI, PLEK, CPC2, LncFinder, CPPred, mRNN, RNAsamba). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.02.012
skills.summary: Compute PRE, SEN, SPE, ACC, F1, MCC, and AUC for binary lncRNA/PCT classifiers on sORF test datasets, treating lncRNAs as the positive class, to quantify performance gaps between LncCat (CatBoost + ORF-attention features) and eight competing methods (CPAT, CNCI, PLEK, CPC2, LncFinder, CPPred, mRNN, RNAsamba).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are unlabeled transcripts with no lncRNA/PCT ground truth — confusion-matrix-based metrics (MCC, F1, SEN, SPE) cannot be computed Multi-class or regression prediction tasks — MCC/F1 as applied here assume a binary lncRNA-vs-PCT classification with a specified positive class

skills.description: Use when you have an edge list of protein-protein functional associations (interactions given in both directions) and need to detect functional modules/communities for subsequent enrichment analysis in Cytoscape stringApp.
skills.name: mcl-graph-clustering-of-protein-networks
skills.search_text: mcl-graph-clustering-of-protein-networks Use when you have an edge list of protein-protein functional associations (interactions given in both directions) and need to detect functional modules/communities for subsequent enrichment analysis in Cytoscape stringApp. The input is raw high-dimensional omics data (scRNA-seq/proteomics matrix) — run favapy first to infer the association network before clustering You need literature-curated physical PPIs rather than inferred functional associations; FAVA networks are meant to be free of literature bias and complement existing networks The network is tiny or the goal is single-pair interaction prediction rather than modular structure detection http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 Partitions a dense protein functional-association network (e.g. the FAVA network inferred from scRNA-seq and proteomics data) into functional modules using the Markov Cluster Algorithm (MCL), then validates cluster count and size distribution against reported values for downstream enrichment analysis. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae010
skills.summary: Partitions a dense protein functional-association network (e.g. the FAVA network inferred from scRNA-seq and proteomics data) into functional modules using the Markov Cluster Algorithm (MCL), then validates cluster count and size distribution against reported values for downstream enrichment analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw high-dimensional omics data (scRNA-seq/proteomics matrix) — run favapy first to infer the association network before clustering You need literature-curated physical PPIs rather than inferred functional associations; FAVA networks are meant to be free of literature bias and complement existing networks The network is tiny or the goal is single-pair interaction prediction rather than modular structure detection

skills.description: Use when a comparative-genomics pipeline needs proteins grouped into similar-function gene clusters to build an absence/presence matrix, and the Markov clustering inflation value must be selected and justified.
skills.name: mcl-inflation-parameter-tuning
skills.search_text: mcl-inflation-parameter-tuning Use when a comparative-genomics pipeline needs proteins grouped into similar-function gene clusters to build an absence/presence matrix, and the Markov clustering inflation value must be selected and justified. When orthologous (one-to-one) gene families rather than similar-function clusters are required — OrthoFinder was used as the comparison baseline, not the production method When input proteins have not been redundancy-reduced or quality-filtered — the linclust pre-clustering at >90% identity/80% coverage and CheckM filtering presuppose those upstream steps When the goal is nucleotide-level genome comparison rather than protein-function clustering http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Skill for building functional gene clusters from pooled protein FASTA via MMseqs2 linclust pre-clustering, diamond all-vs-all bitscore networks, and Markov clustering with an inflation parameter tuned against EC-number consistency and benchmarked against OrthoFinder defaults. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-46302-y
skills.summary: Skill for building functional gene clusters from pooled protein FASTA via MMseqs2 linclust pre-clustering, diamond all-vs-all bitscore networks, and Markov clustering with an inflation parameter tuned against EC-number consistency and benchmarked against OrthoFinder defaults.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When orthologous (one-to-one) gene families rather than similar-function clusters are required — OrthoFinder was used as the comparison baseline, not the production method When input proteins have not been redundancy-reduced or quality-filtered — the linclust pre-clustering at >90% identity/80% coverage and CheckM filtering presuppose those upstream steps When the goal is nucleotide-level genome comparison rather than protein-function clustering

skills.description: Use when a SingleCellGGM GGM network (e.g., MCA_GGM with 127,229 gene pairs or MouseBrain_GGM with 73,786 pairs) must be clustered into gene co-expression modules (GEPs) for enrichment analysis or cell-type annotation.
skills.name: mcl-network-module-clustering
skills.search_text: mcl-network-module-clustering Use when a SingleCellGGM GGM network (e.g., MCA_GGM with 127,229 gene pairs or MouseBrain_GGM with 73,786 pairs) must be clustered into gene co-expression modules (GEPs) for enrichment analysis or cell-type annotation. The input is a raw single-cell count matrix rather than a constructed gene co-expression network — run SingleCellGGM first to compute partial correlations Modules smaller than 10 genes are needed — the retained GEPs are filtered to >= 10 genes The goal is cell-level clustering rather than gene-level co-expression module detection — MCL here clusters gene-pair networks, not cells http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Partitions a SingleCellGGM gene co-expression network (GGM GCN edge list) into gene co-expression modules using the MCL graph-clustering algorithm, retaining modules of >=10 genes as gene expression programs (GEPs) for downstream GO/MP enrichment and cell annotation. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2024.100813
skills.summary: Partitions a SingleCellGGM gene co-expression network (GGM GCN edge list) into gene co-expression modules using the MCL graph-clustering algorithm, retaining modules of >=10 genes as gene expression programs (GEPs) for downstream GO/MP enrichment and cell annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a raw single-cell count matrix rather than a constructed gene co-expression network — run SingleCellGGM first to compute partial correlations Modules smaller than 10 genes are needed — the retained GEPs are filtered to >= 10 genes The goal is cell-level clustering rather than gene-level co-expression module detection — MCL here clusters gene-pair networks, not cells

skills.description: Use when running the ScribbleDom pipeline without expert-drawn manual_scribble.csv input, or when reproducing AutoScribbleDom baselines (e.g., melanoma ARI 0.74, breast cancer bcdc_ffpe ARI 0.83) on Visium or ST data.
skills.name: mclust-automated-scribble-generation
skills.search_text: mclust-automated-scribble-generation Use when running the ScribbleDom pipeline without expert-drawn manual_scribble.csv input, or when reproducing AutoScribbleDom baselines (e.g., melanoma ARI 0.74, breast cancer bcdc_ffpe ARI 0.83) on Visium or ST data. A human expert has already produced manual_scribble.csv via Loupe browser and you want the ScribbleDom (expert-scribble) result rather than the unsupervised AutoScribbleDom result. The data are not Visium or ST spatial transcriptomics samples processed through the ScribbleDom preprocessing scripts (e.g., already-clustered label tables with no raw counts). Generates an automated scribble (mclust_backbone.csv) by running R's Mclust model-based clustering on the principal components of the top 2000 highly variable genes from a spatial transcriptomics sample, enabling ScribbleDom to run in fully unsupervised AutoScribbleDom mode when no expert scribbles exist. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad594
skills.summary: Generates an automated scribble (mclust_backbone.csv) by running R's Mclust model-based clustering on the principal components of the top 2000 highly variable genes from a spatial transcriptomics sample, enabling ScribbleDom to run in fully unsupervised AutoScribbleDom mode when no expert scribbles exist.
skills.when_to_use_negative: A human expert has already produced manual_scribble.csv via Loupe browser and you want the ScribbleDom (expert-scribble) result rather than the unsupervised AutoScribbleDom result. The data are not Visium or ST spatial transcriptomics samples processed through the ScribbleDom preprocessing scripts (e.g., already-clustered label tables with no raw counts).

skills.description: Use when you need to model the distribution of dsb step-I ambient-corrected ADT values within each single cell as a Gaussian mixture and pick the number of components (k) per cell via BIC.
skills.name: mclust-em-algorithm-parameterization
skills.search_text: mclust-em-algorithm-parameterization Use when you need to model the distribution of dsb step-I ambient-corrected ADT values within each single cell as a Gaussian mixture and pick the number of components (k) per cell via BIC. Input is raw ADT UMI counts that have not been dsb step-I corrected (log + background standardization) — mixture components will reflect unnormalized noise The goal is general clustering of cells rather than modeling the within-cell protein-level background/positive bimodality Fit per-cell Gaussian mixture models with the R package mclust via the EM algorithm, selecting the optimal number of mixture components (k) by the mclust BIC convention (higher is better). In the dsb workflow this determines the fitted background protein subpopulation mean (µ1) and shows k=2 best fits the majority of single cells. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-29356-8
skills.summary: Fit per-cell Gaussian mixture models with the R package mclust via the EM algorithm, selecting the optimal number of mixture components (k) by the mclust BIC convention (higher is better). In the dsb workflow this determines the fitted background protein subpopulation mean (µ1) and shows k=2 best fits the majority of single cells.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw ADT UMI counts that have not been dsb step-I corrected (log + background standardization) — mixture components will reflect unnormalized noise The goal is general clustering of cells rather than modeling the within-cell protein-level background/positive bimodality

skills.description: Use when clustering raw UMI count matrices from multiple individuals (each a genes x cells matrix in a list) where individual-level heterogeneity/batch effects exist, or when a trained model must predict cluster labels for held-out cells via a training-proportion split.
skills.name: mcmc-based-bayesian-mixture-modeling
skills.search_text: mcmc-based-bayesian-mixture-modeling Use when clustering raw UMI count matrices from multiple individuals (each a genes x cells matrix in a list) where individual-level heterogeneity/batch effects exist, or when a trained model must predict cluster labels for held-out cells via a training-proportion split. Data consist of normalized, batch-corrected expression matrices rather than raw UMI counts — BAMM-SC explicitly takes raw count data and models library/depth variation itself Single-cell data are plate-based/Smart-seq2 rather than droplet-based (10x Chromium) scRNA-seq from population studies Identifying rare cell clusters is critical — the authors note the supervised strategy 'may potentially miss some rare clusters', and genes with excessive zeros are filtered out, which is problematic for rare cell type identification http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 BAMM-SC clusters droplet-based scRNA-seq UMI count data from multiple individuals simultaneously using a Bayesian hierarchical Dirichlet multinomial mixture model fitted by MCMC, explicitly modeling gene, cell-type, and individual-level variability to handle batch effects such as unbalanced sequencing depths. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-09639-3
skills.summary: BAMM-SC clusters droplet-based scRNA-seq UMI count data from multiple individuals simultaneously using a Bayesian hierarchical Dirichlet multinomial mixture model fitted by MCMC, explicitly modeling gene, cell-type, and individual-level variability to handle batch effects such as unbalanced sequencing depths.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data consist of normalized, batch-corrected expression matrices rather than raw UMI counts — BAMM-SC explicitly takes raw count data and models library/depth variation itself Single-cell data are plate-based/Smart-seq2 rather than droplet-based (10x Chromium) scRNA-seq from population studies Identifying rare cell clusters is critical — the authors note the supervised strategy 'may potentially miss some rare clusters', and genes with excessive zeros are filtered out, which is problematic for rare cell type identification

skills.description: Use when Canopy2 requires the 1 x M alpha and beta hyperparameter vectors and single-cell expression counts are available for the mutation-host genes (e.g., the featurecounts.qc slot of GBM10_preproc).
skills.name: mcmc-based-hyperparameter-inference
skills.search_text: mcmc-based-hyperparameter-inference Use when Canopy2 requires the 1 x M alpha and beta hyperparameter vectors and single-cell expression counts are available for the mutation-host genes (e.g., the featurecounts.qc slot of GBM10_preproc). The goal is to estimate bursting kinetics from the SNV read-count matrices themselves — alpha/beta are derived from gene expression and are independent of mutational read counts, hence decoupled from SNV carrier status The host gene's expression cannot be aligned to the SNV row via biomaRt (no estimable kinetics) — the row should be excluded via id.g subsetting rather than forced through BPSC Only bulk DNA WES read counts (Rb/Xb) are available with no scRNA-seq expression matrix — BPSC/SCALE require single-cell expression counts http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Estimates mutation-specific gene activation (alpha) and deactivation (beta) rates for Canopy2's beta-Poisson bursting model, using BPSC's MCMC sampling (get_burstiness_bpsc) or SCALE's moment estimators (get_burstiness_scale) on single-cell gene expression, decoupled from SNV read counts. transcriptomics/v2 10.1007/s12561-024-09466-1
skills.summary: Estimates mutation-specific gene activation (alpha) and deactivation (beta) rates for Canopy2's beta-Poisson bursting model, using BPSC's MCMC sampling (get_burstiness_bpsc) or SCALE's moment estimators (get_burstiness_scale) on single-cell gene expression, decoupled from SNV read counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to estimate bursting kinetics from the SNV read-count matrices themselves — alpha/beta are derived from gene expression and are independent of mutational read counts, hence decoupled from SNV carrier status The host gene's expression cannot be aligned to the SNV row via biomaRt (no estimable kinetics) — the row should be excluded via id.g subsetting rather than forced through BPSC Only bulk DNA WES read counts (Rb/Xb) are available with no scRNA-seq expression matrix — BPSC/SCALE require single-cell expression counts

skills.description: Use when comparing computational efficiency of spatial transcriptomics clustering methods (e.g. iSC.MEB vs MCMC-based BASS/BayesSpace) across multiple tissue sections and a sequence of K cluster numbers.
skills.name: mcmc-based-spatial-clustering-benchmarking
skills.search_text: mcmc-based-spatial-clustering-benchmarking Use when comparing computational efficiency of spatial transcriptomics clustering methods (e.g. iSC.MEB vs MCMC-based BASS/BayesSpace) across multiple tissue sections and a sequence of K cluster numbers. The goal is accuracy (e.g. ARI) rather than computational efficiency benchmarking — use the clustering-evaluation workflow instead Data are not multi-sample SRT sections (e.g. single-cell non-spatial data), where spatial adjacency and HMRF methods do not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 Benchmark the wall-clock runtime of spatial clustering methods (iSC.MEB, SC.MEB vs MCMC-based BASS and BayesSpace) across a grid of cluster numbers K on the 12-section DLPFC Visium dataset, to demonstrate the computational advantage of empirical-Bayes HMRF fitting over MCMC sampling. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad019
skills.summary: Benchmark the wall-clock runtime of spatial clustering methods (iSC.MEB, SC.MEB vs MCMC-based BASS and BayesSpace) across a grid of cluster numbers K on the 12-section DLPFC Visium dataset, to demonstrate the computational advantage of empirical-Bayes HMRF fitting over MCMC sampling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is accuracy (e.g. ARI) rather than computational efficiency benchmarking — use the clustering-evaluation workflow instead Data are not multi-sample SRT sections (e.g. single-cell non-spatial data), where spatial adjacency and HMRF methods do not apply

skills.description: Use when running get_trees() MCMC sampling in Canopy2 across a Klist of subclone counts and you must verify chain mixing and convergence before get__tree() selects the minimum-BIC configuration.
skills.name: mcmc-convergence-diagnostics
skills.search_text: mcmc-convergence-diagnostics Use when running get_trees() MCMC sampling in Canopy2 across a Klist of subclone counts and you must verify chain mixing and convergence before get__tree() selects the minimum-BIC configuration. No MCMC sampling has been run yet — diagnostics require trees and posteriors from get_trees() and cannot be applied to raw Rs, Xs, Rb, Xb read count matrices The underlying inference method is not Metropolis-within-Gibbs MCMC (e.g., comparator tools Canopy or Cardelino), where these ACF/density/trace criteria and pburn/thin parameters do not apply Assess Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence for Canopy2 tumor phylogeny inference using get_diagnostics() on trees and posteriors from get_trees(), checking lag ACF, posterior density alignment, and trace plots before selecting a tree by BIC. transcriptomics/v2 10.1007/s12561-024-09466-1
skills.summary: Assess Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence for Canopy2 tumor phylogeny inference using get_diagnostics() on trees and posteriors from get_trees(), checking lag ACF, posterior density alignment, and trace plots before selecting a tree by BIC.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No MCMC sampling has been run yet — diagnostics require trees and posteriors from get_trees() and cannot be applied to raw Rs, Xs, Rb, Xb read count matrices The underlying inference method is not Metropolis-within-Gibbs MCMC (e.g., comparator tools Canopy or Cardelino), where these ACF/density/trace criteria and pburn/thin parameters do not apply

skills.description: Use when you need per-gene or per-cluster kinetic parameter distributions (kon, koff, s) estimated from real scRNA-seq count data to parameterize a two-state transcription bursting model, e.g. for SymSim simulation inputs.
skills.name: mcmc-gibbs-sampling-inference
skills.search_text: mcmc-gibbs-sampling-inference Use when you need per-gene or per-cluster kinetic parameter distributions (kon, koff, s) estimated from real scRNA-seq count data to parameterize a two-state transcription bursting model, e.g. for SymSim simulation inputs. Raw (non-imputed) counts are used for fitting — the paper explicitly uses imputed read counts rather than raw read counts The cell population is heterogeneous and cannot be partitioned into clusters sharing the same kinetic parameters The dataset is small non-UMI data where scVI is inapplicable — restrict imputation to MAGIC in that case http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 Fits the two-state transcription kinetic model (kon, koff, s) to single-cell RNA-seq counts via MCMC with the Gibbs sampler implemented in RJAGS, using imputed counts from cell clusters to obtain posterior parameter distributions for SymSim simulations. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-10500-w
skills.summary: Fits the two-state transcription kinetic model (kon, koff, s) to single-cell RNA-seq counts via MCMC with the Gibbs sampler implemented in RJAGS, using imputed counts from cell clusters to obtain posterior parameter distributions for SymSim simulations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Raw (non-imputed) counts are used for fitting — the paper explicitly uses imputed read counts rather than raw read counts The cell population is heterogeneous and cannot be partitioned into clusters sharing the same kinetic parameters The dataset is small non-UMI data where scVI is inapplicable — restrict imputation to MAGIC in that case

skills.description: Use when running Bfimpute on scRNA-seq count matrices and you must set or tune the MCMC factorization settings (D, totalepoch, burnin, threshold, sn_init/sn_max, priors) to reproduce published benchmarks or trade accuracy vs. compute time.
skills.name: mcmc-hyperparameter-configuration
skills.search_text: mcmc-hyperparameter-configuration Use when running Bfimpute on scRNA-seq count matrices and you must set or tune the MCMC factorization settings (D, totalepoch, burnin, threshold, sn_init/sn_max, priors) to reproduce published benchmarks or trade accuracy vs. compute time. If you need a universally best imputation setting — the article's discussion states no consensus exists about the best imputation method and it is premature to conclude Bfimpute wins across all datasets If the count matrix is already CPM-normalized and log-transformed — set normalized=TRUE instead of relying on the default transform path, otherwise the chain receives double-transformed input When the goal is a fast exploratory imputation where accuracy can be traded for time — do not keep accuracy-oriented defaults (D=32, totalepoch=300, burnin=200) uncritically, per the README's accuracy/runtime trade-off note http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Configure the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) hyperparameters of Bfimpute's full Bayesian factorization imputation for scRNA-seq dropouts — latent dimension D, totalepoch, burnin, dropout-probability threshold, and Normal-Inverse-Wishart priors — balancing imputation accuracy against runtime. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2021.100133
skills.summary: Configure the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) hyperparameters of Bfimpute's full Bayesian factorization imputation for scRNA-seq dropouts — latent dimension D, totalepoch, burnin, dropout-probability threshold, and Normal-Inverse-Wishart priors — balancing imputation accuracy against runtime.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If you need a universally best imputation setting — the article's discussion states no consensus exists about the best imputation method and it is premature to conclude Bfimpute wins across all datasets If the count matrix is already CPM-normalized and log-transformed — set normalized=TRUE instead of relying on the default transform path, otherwise the chain receives double-transformed input When the goal is a fast exploratory imputation where accuracy can be traded for time — do not keep accuracy-oriented defaults (D=32, totalepoch=300, burnin=200) uncritically, per the README's accuracy/runtime trade-off note

skills.description: Use when you need to reproduce or unit-test VIA's pseudotime computation and forward-biased MCMC lineage refinement on a PARC cluster graph (e.g. mESC CyTOF cell-cycle data) with explicit x_lazy/alpha_teleport settings.
skills.name: mcmc-lineage-refinement
skills.search_text: mcmc-lineage-refinement Use when you need to reproduce or unit-test VIA's pseudotime computation and forward-biased MCMC lineage refinement on a PARC cluster graph (e.g. mESC CyTOF cell-cycle data) with explicit x_lazy/alpha_teleport settings. You need atlas-scale visualization with metadata integration, higher-order random walks with memory, or Atlas View — those are StaVia (Via 2.0) features, not this Via 1.0 hitting-time + MCMC stage The input is raw single-cell data without a PARC cluster graph or a defined root cell — the expected hitting time computation requires a rooted cluster graph You need only pseudotime ranking with no lineage/branch-probability output — the 500-simulation-per-terminal-state MCMC stage is then unnecessary overhead Reconstructs VIA's two-stage lazy-teleporting pseudotime and lineage-inference stage on the PARC cluster graph: expected hitting times (Eqs. 1-8) give initial pseudotime/directionality, then lazy-teleporting MCMC simulations on the forward-biased graph refine branch probabilities and terminal states. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-25773-3
skills.summary: Reconstructs VIA's two-stage lazy-teleporting pseudotime and lineage-inference stage on the PARC cluster graph: expected hitting times (Eqs. 1-8) give initial pseudotime/directionality, then lazy-teleporting MCMC simulations on the forward-biased graph refine branch probabilities and terminal states.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need atlas-scale visualization with metadata integration, higher-order random walks with memory, or Atlas View — those are StaVia (Via 2.0) features, not this Via 1.0 hitting-time + MCMC stage The input is raw single-cell data without a PARC cluster graph or a defined root cell — the expected hitting time computation requires a rooted cluster graph You need only pseudotime ranking with no lineage/branch-probability output — the 500-simulation-per-terminal-state MCMC stage is then unnecessary overhead

skills.description: Use when analyzing allele-specific expression (ASE) from scRNA-Seq allele counts (e.g., CAST×B6 F1 embryo data) and you need population-informed priors to overcome low per-cell coverage before assigning P/B/M expression states per gene per cell.
skills.name: mcmc-prior-estimation-single-cell
skills.search_text: mcmc-prior-estimation-single-cell Use when analyzing allele-specific expression (ASE) from scRNA-Seq allele counts (e.g., CAST×B6 F1 embryo data) and you need population-informed priors to overcome low per-cell coverage before assigning P/B/M expression states per gene per cell. Data are bulk RNA-Seq or already-aggregated allelic proportions — the hierarchical pooling across cells is designed for single-cell sparsity Reads cannot be assigned to a phase-known diploid genome (no strain SNP/indel reconstruction), so maternal/paternal counts are unreliable The goal is transcriptional burst kinetics inference (burst frequency/size), for which txburst-style ML/PL methods on UMI counts are the appropriate choice, not ASE state classification http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 Estimates state-specific priors (concentration/hyperparameters of the beta-binomial) by running the MCMC stage of scBASE's hierarchical mixture model on allele-specific read counts pooled across all cells, then fixes those priors for downstream EM classification of each cell's genes into paternal monoallelic, bi-allelic, or maternal monoallelic states. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-13099-0
skills.summary: Estimates state-specific priors (concentration/hyperparameters of the beta-binomial) by running the MCMC stage of scBASE's hierarchical mixture model on allele-specific read counts pooled across all cells, then fixes those priors for downstream EM classification of each cell's genes into paternal monoallelic, bi-allelic, or maternal monoallelic states.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are bulk RNA-Seq or already-aggregated allelic proportions — the hierarchical pooling across cells is designed for single-cell sparsity Reads cannot be assigned to a phase-known diploid genome (no strain SNP/indel reconstruction), so maternal/paternal counts are unreliable The goal is transcriptional burst kinetics inference (burst frequency/size), for which txburst-style ML/PL methods on UMI counts are the appropriate choice, not ASE state classification

skills.description: Use when two classifiers predict the same labeled sample set (e.g., DeepCC CMS labels vs RF/SVM/GBM/MLR on 13 independent CRC validation sets) and you need a paired significance test on error counts.
skills.name: mcnemar-significance-testing
skills.search_text: mcnemar-significance-testing Use when two classifiers predict the same labeled sample set (e.g., DeepCC CMS labels vs RF/SVM/GBM/MLR on 13 independent CRC validation sets) and you need a paired significance test on error counts. The classifiers were evaluated on different sample sets, so errors are not paired and a two-sample test is required instead of McNemar's test The goal is unsupervised grouping of patients — DeepCC is specifically developed for classification, not clustering of cancer patients http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Applies McNemar's test on paired per-sample classification errors to test whether the DeepCC ANN classifier's error rate on CRC validation sets is significantly lower than signature gene-based baselines (RF, SVM, GBM, multinomial logistic regression), yielding P-values for the Fig. 2 / Table S2 performance comparison. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41389-019-0157-8
skills.summary: Applies McNemar's test on paired per-sample classification errors to test whether the DeepCC ANN classifier's error rate on CRC validation sets is significantly lower than signature gene-based baselines (RF, SVM, GBM, multinomial logistic regression), yielding P-values for the Fig. 2 / Table S2 performance comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The classifiers were evaluated on different sample sets, so errors are not paired and a two-sample test is required instead of McNemar's test The goal is unsupervised grouping of patients — DeepCC is specifically developed for classification, not clustering of cancer patients

skills.summary: The robustSingleCell get.variable.genes step identifies highly variable genes by binning genes by mean expression and computing dispersion-scaled statistics within each bin, correcting for the mean-dispersion relationship (heteroscedasticity) before selecting genes for downstream PCA and clustering.

skills.search_text: mean-expression-binned-background-gene-sampling Use when scoring single-cell transcriptomes (AnnData) against a gene signature and you need an expression-matched background control instead of naive whole-transcriptome averaging, e.g. re-implementing or validating SenePy score_hub. You want default scanpy.score_genes behavior without expression-matched binning — then call score_hub with binarize=False and importance=False on normalized, log1p-transformed data instead. You need signatures that account for genes downregulated in senescent cells — the method accounts only for positively enriched (no negative) markers. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Background-gene control strategy underlying SenePy's score_hub: measured genes are binned by mean expression level, and expression-matched non-signature control genes are sampled within each bin so per-cell senescence scores reflect signature expression above expression-matched background expectations (Methods Eq. 11-15). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-57047-7

skills.search_text: mean-variance-fit-assessment Use when single-cell counts have been simulated from a real scRNA-seq dataset (e.g., the Cuomo et al. Simulated data are bulk or pseudobulk aggregates rather than single-cell level counts — the per-gene zero-fraction criterion is specific to sparse single-cell count matrices. The real reference has not been quality-controlled and normalized, or lacks cell-level metadata (cell, individual, cell type), so there is no trustworthy baseline for the distributional comparison. In the CTMM paper this gate was applied before simulations were used to assess robustness to sequencing depth and number of cells. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-49242-9

skills.description: Use when snapshot single-cell data have been ordered in pseudotime (e.g. by Wanderlust or DPT) and marker trajectories must be interpreted on a real time or spatial scale for which a true-scale cell density distribution is available.
skills.name: measure-preserving-pseudotime-to-real-scale-transformation
skills.search_text: measure-preserving-pseudotime-to-real-scale-transformation Use when snapshot single-cell data have been ordered in pseudotime (e.g. by Wanderlust or DPT) and marker trajectories must be interpreted on a real time or spatial scale for which a true-scale cell density distribution is available. When no prior knowledge of the true-scale cell density distribution exists — constructing a target distribution for processes like stem cell differentiation can be challenging and may require measured cell death and division rates at every stage. When the cell ordering from the trajectory inference algorithm itself is unreliable — MAPiT is reliant on the correctness of the provided cell order and does not fix a wrong ordering. When sources and sinks along the process (cell death or cell division) are unknown, since they are critical for obtaining the correct real-time distribution. http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 MAPiT is a measure-preserving nonlinear transformation that maps pseudotime-scale joint densities of markers onto a real temporal or spatial scale, using prior knowledge of the true-scale cell density distribution. It conserves the area under the density curve so conditional marker profiles p(y|x) are recovered on the real scale. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-60400-z
skills.summary: MAPiT is a measure-preserving nonlinear transformation that maps pseudotime-scale joint densities of markers onto a real temporal or spatial scale, using prior knowledge of the true-scale cell density distribution. It conserves the area under the density curve so conditional marker profiles p(y|x) are recovered on the real scale.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When no prior knowledge of the true-scale cell density distribution exists — constructing a target distribution for processes like stem cell differentiation can be challenging and may require measured cell death and division rates at every stage. When the cell ordering from the trajectory inference algorithm itself is unreliable — MAPiT is reliant on the correctness of the provided cell order and does not fix a wrong ordering. When sources and sinks along the process (cell death or cell division) are unknown, since they are critical for obtaining the correct real-time distribution.

skills.name: measure-preserving-transformation-calibration
skills.search_text: measure-preserving-transformation-calibration Use when you have an nx1 vector of pseudotime values (from Wanderlust, Monocle or Diffusion Pseudotime) plus single-cell marker signals, and a theoretically or empirically known cell-density distribution on a true real-time or spatial scale that the pseudotime ordering must be mapped onto. skills.search_text: measurement-noise-variance-estimation Use when preparing droplet scRNA-seq counts for CTMM: individual-level or individual-by-cell-type measurement-noise variances must be quantified before fitting op.free_REML or ctp.free_REML models. Cells per individual-cell type pair are <= 10 or individuals have <= 100 cells — CTMM requires > 10 cells per pair and is not reliable for sample sizes below ~50 individuals Genes are lowly expressed such that the Gaussian approximation of pseudobulk noise is invalid, requiring more cells per pair than the ctnu-based model assumes Data are not single-cell-derived pseudobulk (e.g., bulk RNA-seq without per-cell noise estimates) — no cell-level noise variance can be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Computes the variance of measurement noise for each individual (nu) or each individual-cell type pair (ctnu) from single-cell counts, a required input for fitting CTMM linear mixed models on Overall Pseudobulk (OP) and Cell Type-specific Pseudobulk (CTP) gene expression data. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-49242-9
skills.summary: Computes the variance of measurement noise for each individual (nu) or each individual-cell type pair (ctnu) from single-cell counts, a required input for fitting CTMM linear mixed models on Overall Pseudobulk (OP) and Cell Type-specific Pseudobulk (CTP) gene expression data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Cells per individual-cell type pair are <= 10 or individuals have <= 100 cells — CTMM requires > 10 cells per pair and is not reliable for sample sizes below ~50 individuals Genes are lowly expressed such that the Gaussian approximation of pseudobulk noise is invalid, requiring more cells per pair than the ctnu-based model assumes Data are not single-cell-derived pseudobulk (e.g., bulk RNA-seq without per-cell noise estimates) — no cell-level noise variance can be computed

skills.search_text: median-auc-benchmark-comparison Use when you have ClonoCluster cluster assignments across a range of α values plus a count matrix and need to verify that hybrid clustering did not degrade top-marker sensitivity/specificity (AUC) relative to transcriptome-only clustering. Input is not hybrid cluster assignments spanning α levels — e.g. a single transcriptome-only Seurat/scanpy clustering with no clone-weighted variants to compare No barcode/clone information exists for the cells, so there is no α > 0 clustering to benchmark against the α = 0 baseline The goal is functional validation of cluster homogeneity rather than marker fidelity — the paper notes further testing of homogeneity of functional properties is still required to determine which clustering methods match biological distinctions http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Benchmarks whether hybrid clusters produced by ClonoCluster at each α level retain marker fidelity by computing ROC AUC of each cluster's top marker (Find_Markers_ROC/ROCR) and comparing the per-α median top-marker AUC to the transcriptome-only (α = 0) baseline across datasets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.xgen.2022.100247
skills.summary: Benchmarks whether hybrid clusters produced by ClonoCluster at each α level retain marker fidelity by computing ROC AUC of each cluster's top marker (Find_Markers_ROC/ROCR) and comparing the per-α median top-marker AUC to the transcriptome-only (α = 0) baseline across datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not hybrid cluster assignments spanning α levels — e.g. a single transcriptome-only Seurat/scanpy clustering with no clone-weighted variants to compare No barcode/clone information exists for the cells, so there is no α > 0 clustering to benchmark against the α = 0 baseline The goal is functional validation of cluster homogeneity rather than marker fidelity — the paper notes further testing of homogeneity of functional properties is still required to determine which clustering methods match biological distinctions

skills.description: Use when OTTERS Stage II output (testing.py) has produced per-gene TWAS Z-scores from multiple eQTL weight training methods that must be calibrated per method before ACAT-O aggregation, e.g. UKBB cardiovascular disease GWAS with eQTLGen-derived weights.
skills.name: median-pvalue-inflation-calibration
skills.search_text: median-pvalue-inflation-calibration Use when OTTERS Stage II output (testing.py) has produced per-gene TWAS Z-scores from multiple eQTL weight training methods that must be calibrated per method before ACAT-O aggregation, e.g. UKBB cardiovascular disease GWAS with eQTLGen-derived weights. The p values are already the ACAT-O omnibus output — genomic control must be applied per training method BEFORE aggregation, not to the combined omnibus p value. The goal is to obtain the direction of the gene–phenotype association: OTTERS cannot provide direction, and users must refer to the sign of the per-method TWAS Z-score rather than the calibrated p value. Only a small subset of genes is available per method, making the median-of-squared-Z inflation estimate unstable or unrepresentative. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Per-method genomic control of TWAS test statistics in the OTTERS pipeline: within each of the five Stage II training models (P0.001, P0.05, lassosum, SDPR, PRS-CS), gene-level Z-scores are rescaled so the median two-sided p value equals 0.5 before the per-gene, per-method p values are aggregated by the ACAT-O omnibus test. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-36862-w
skills.summary: Per-method genomic control of TWAS test statistics in the OTTERS pipeline: within each of the five Stage II training models (P0.001, P0.05, lassosum, SDPR, PRS-CS), gene-level Z-scores are rescaled so the median two-sided p value equals 0.5 before the per-gene, per-method p values are aggregated by the ACAT-O omnibus test.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The p values are already the ACAT-O omnibus output — genomic control must be applied per training method BEFORE aggregation, not to the combined omnibus p value. The goal is to obtain the direction of the gene–phenotype association: OTTERS cannot provide direction, and users must refer to the sign of the per-method TWAS Z-score rather than the calibrated p value. Only a small subset of genes is available per method, making the median-of-squared-Z inflation estimate unstable or unrepresentative.

skills.description: Use when stress-testing a trajectory-level differential test against trajectory-inference errors — you have a simulated reference with true pseudotimes/lineage labels and want sensitivity to pseudotime noise and lineage misassignment.
skills.name: median-robustness-curve-visualization
skills.search_text: median-robustness-curve-visualization Use when stress-testing a trajectory-level differential test against trajectory-inference errors — you have a simulated reference with true pseudotimes/lineage labels and want sensitivity to pseudotime noise and lineage misassignment. The trajectory topology itself differs between conditions — differential topology should be assessed first with topologyTest, not progressionTest robustness curves Input is real data without ground-truth pseudotimes and lineage assignments — perturbation-based robustness quantification requires known truth http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Reproduces the condiments progressionTest noise-robustness simulation (Fig. S4): perturb known pseudotimes with Gaussian noise and randomly misassign cells to lineages, then aggregate progressionTest p-values across replicates into median-p-value curves plotted with ggplot2. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-44823-0
skills.summary: Reproduces the condiments progressionTest noise-robustness simulation (Fig. S4): perturb known pseudotimes with Gaussian noise and randomly misassign cells to lineages, then aggregate progressionTest p-values across replicates into median-p-value curves plotted with ggplot2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The trajectory topology itself differs between conditions — differential topology should be assessed first with topologyTest, not progressionTest robustness curves Input is real data without ground-truth pseudotimes and lineage assignments — perturbation-based robustness quantification requires known truth

skills.name: median-split-patient-stratification
skills.search_text: median-split-patient-stratification Use when bulk RNA-seq expression matrices with clinical metadata (survival time/status, radiologic response) are available and a single-cell-derived gene signature (e.g., NK-2 from scDist) must be validated for association with outcome. When the aim is to detect which cell types are perturbed between conditions from single-cell data — that is scDist's differential state analysis, not the downstream bulk-cohort stratification When patient-level survival or response metadata are unavailable, since median-split strata cannot be linked to outcomes When the cohort is too small for a meaningful median split — the article's validation relies on 789 patients across 7 cohorts http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Dichotomizes bulk-RNA-seq patients at the cohort-median of a single-cell-derived signature score (here the NK-2 signature from FCER1G+ NK cells found by scDist) and tests high- vs low-score strata with Kaplan-Meier/log-rank survival analysis and responder-vs-non-responder contrasts, reproducing the paper's validation across 7 cohorts and 789 immunotherapy patients. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-51649-3
skills.summary: Dichotomizes bulk-RNA-seq patients at the cohort-median of a single-cell-derived signature score (here the NK-2 signature from FCER1G+ NK cells found by scDist) and tests high- vs low-score strata with Kaplan-Meier/log-rank survival analysis and responder-vs-non-responder contrasts, reproducing the paper's validation across 7 cohorts and 789 immunotherapy patients.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the aim is to detect which cell types are perturbed between conditions from single-cell data — that is scDist's differential state analysis, not the downstream bulk-cohort stratification When patient-level survival or response metadata are unavailable, since median-split strata cannot be linked to outcomes When the cohort is too small for a meaningful median split — the article's validation relies on 789 patients across 7 cohorts

skills.search_text: median-summary-statistics-by-subgroup Use when drug response (e.g., 5-FU IC50) is available per sample and samples carry subgroup labels (CMS1-CMS4 from CMScaller), and you need per-group median summaries plus a CMS4-vs-CMS1/2/3 comparison.
