skills.search_text: omics-gene-cluster-interactor-analysis Use when you have a list of key interactor genes/proteins produced by an interactome assessment and need to summarise their functional classes and typical cellular compartments. The goal is clustering or scoring of gene expression patterns (e.g. Gaussian mixture modelling of LFC values) rather than annotating an existing interactor list The input is raw single cell RNA-seq or proteomics data that has not yet been reduced to a key interactor list via the interactome assessment The input data is not a CSV data frame in the format OmicInt expects http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 An OmicInt (R) workflow that classifies key interactor proteins from an interactome assessment by assigning each a protein type label and a cellular compartment/location label based on UniProt-based annotations. It turns a bare gene/protein hit list into an interpretable annotation table. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.ailsci.2021.100025
skills.summary: An OmicInt (R) workflow that classifies key interactor proteins from an interactome assessment by assigning each a protein type label and a cellular compartment/location label based on UniProt-based annotations. It turns a bare gene/protein hit list into an interpretable annotation table.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is clustering or scoring of gene expression patterns (e.g. Gaussian mixture modelling of LFC values) rather than annotating an existing interactor list The input is raw single cell RNA-seq or proteomics data that has not yet been reduced to a key interactor list via the interactome assessment The input data is not a CSV data frame in the format OmicInt expects

skills.description: Use when you have gene sets stratified by a regulatory metric (e.g., CAFEH top-component sharing across tissues) and want to test overrepresentation of curated disease genes from OMIM, separately for dominant and recessive inheritance modes.
skills.name: omim-disease-gene-fisher-enrichment
skills.search_text: omim-disease-gene-fisher-enrichment Use when you have gene sets stratified by a regulatory metric (e.g., CAFEH top-component sharing across tissues) and want to test overrepresentation of curated disease genes from OMIM, separately for dominant and recessive inheritance modes. When the regulatory stratification itself is unreliable — CAFEH relies on a single LD matrix, so large LD differences between studies (e.g., ancestry differences) could invalidate the gene set definitions feeding the enrichment test When the question concerns coding-variant-mediated loci: loci whose effects are mediated via coding variants may not show eQTL effects and cannot be explored with CAFEH, so they would be absent from the gene sets When colocalization is being interpreted as mediation — colocalizing signals may arise without a linking causal pathway due to horizontal pleiotropic effects, so disease-gene enrichment does not prove causal mediation http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3517 Tests whether gene sets defined by CAFEH eQTL colocalization sharing (highly vs poorly colocalizing vs background) are overrepresented for OMIM dominant and recessive disease genes using hypergeometric-style Fisher exact tests. This connects tissue specificity of genetic regulation to human disease relevance. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.ajhg.2022.01.002
skills.summary: Tests whether gene sets defined by CAFEH eQTL colocalization sharing (highly vs poorly colocalizing vs background) are overrepresented for OMIM dominant and recessive disease genes using hypergeometric-style Fisher exact tests. This connects tissue specificity of genetic regulation to human disease relevance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the regulatory stratification itself is unreliable — CAFEH relies on a single LD matrix, so large LD differences between studies (e.g., ancestry differences) could invalidate the gene set definitions feeding the enrichment test When the question concerns coding-variant-mediated loci: loci whose effects are mediated via coding variants may not show eQTL effects and cannot be explored with CAFEH, so they would be absent from the gene sets When colocalization is being interpreted as mediation — colocalizing signals may arise without a linking causal pathway due to horizontal pleiotropic effects, so disease-gene enrichment does not prove causal mediation

skills.description: Use when a .h5ad single-cell dataset is too large for memory (e.g., 4.4M-cell atlas in backed mode) and needs a persistent, queryable SQL database for downstream runtime benchmarking or repeated SQL queries.
skills.name: on-disk-sql-database-construction
skills.search_text: on-disk-sql-database-construction Use when a .h5ad single-cell dataset is too large for memory (e.g., 4.4M-cell atlas in backed mode) and needs a persistent, queryable SQL database for downstream runtime benchmarking or repeated SQL queries. Dataset fits comfortably in memory and only a few ad-hoc queries are needed — the in-memory AnnSQL(adata=adata) path is simpler and avoids build overhead You need a performance-optimized relational schema — the paper states the table structure mirrors AnnData 'rather than being optimized for performance' The AnnData object has more than ~30k genes — the paper notes a known unresolved DuckDB memory leak on such databases http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Constructs a persistent on-disk AnnSQL (.asql) DuckDB database from an AnnData object using the MakeDb class, enabling SQL queries on single-cell datasets that exceed available memory (e.g., the 4.4-million-cell Macosko Mouse Atlas loaded in backed mode). transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbaf105
skills.summary: Constructs a persistent on-disk AnnSQL (.asql) DuckDB database from an AnnData object using the MakeDb class, enabling SQL queries on single-cell datasets that exceed available memory (e.g., the 4.4-million-cell Macosko Mouse Atlas loaded in backed mode).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Dataset fits comfortably in memory and only a few ad-hoc queries are needed — the in-memory AnnSQL(adata=adata) path is simpler and avoids build overhead You need a performance-optimized relational schema — the paper states the table structure mirrors AnnData 'rather than being optimized for performance' The AnnData object has more than ~30k genes — the paper notes a known unresolved DuckDB memory leak on such databases

skills.description: Use when you have a set of ecDNA or focal-amplification gene calls and need to test whether known oncogenes are significantly enriched for amplification, expression, or functional effects.
skills.name: oncogene-copy-number-enrichment-testing
skills.search_text: oncogene-copy-number-enrichment-testing Use when you have a set of ecDNA or focal-amplification gene calls and need to test whether known oncogenes are significantly enriched for amplification, expression, or functional effects. Input is raw sequencing data and ecDNA calls have not yet been produced — run the circlehunter Snakemake pipeline first The gene set comes from whole-genome sequencing ecDNA callers (e.g. AmpliconArchitect, JaBbA, LINX) requiring WGS copy-number input rather than ATAC-Seq-based circlehunter calls No known-oncogene annotation or external CCLE/DepMap/PCAWG tables are available, so enrichment tests cannot be grounded http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Quantify and test enrichment of oncogenes among ecDNA-amplified genes identified by circlehunter, joining amplified-gene sets with CCLE/DepMap copy-number, expression, and CRISPR gene-effect tables plus PCAWG copy-number gains to obtain copy-number, expression, gene-effect, coincidence, and mutation-enrichment P values. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41389-023-00476-0
skills.summary: Quantify and test enrichment of oncogenes among ecDNA-amplified genes identified by circlehunter, joining amplified-gene sets with CCLE/DepMap copy-number, expression, and CRISPR gene-effect tables plus PCAWG copy-number gains to obtain copy-number, expression, gene-effect, coincidence, and mutation-enrichment P values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing data and ecDNA calls have not yet been produced — run the circlehunter Snakemake pipeline first The gene set comes from whole-genome sequencing ecDNA callers (e.g. AmpliconArchitect, JaBbA, LINX) requiring WGS copy-number input rather than ATAC-Seq-based circlehunter calls No known-oncogene annotation or external CCLE/DepMap/PCAWG tables are available, so enrichment tests cannot be grounded

skills.description: Use when a gene fusion (e.g., IgH-WHSC1) has been detected per cell in scRNA-seq data and you must test whether the fusion partner oncogene is overexpressed in fusion-bearing cells.
skills.name: oncogene-expression-quantification
skills.search_text: oncogene-expression-quantification Use when a gene fusion (e.g., IgH-WHSC1) has been detected per cell in scRNA-seq data and you must test whether the fusion partner oncogene is overexpressed in fusion-bearing cells. No fusion calls exist yet — scFusion (STAR, samtools, bedtools, statistical/deep-learning filters) must first produce per-cell fusion calls before expression stratification is meaningful The data are not from a Smart-Seq single-cell protocol or the fusion is not expressed in the sequenced cells The candidate oncogene lies far from the fusion breakpoint so coverage and expression cannot be linked to the fusion event http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Quantifies expression of an oncogene (e.g., WHSC1) in fusion-positive versus fusion-negative single cells, and profiles per-base sequencing coverage across the fusion breakpoint, to test whether a detected fusion drives oncogene overexpression as in scFusion's multiple myeloma IgH-WHSC1 analysis (Fig 7d-e). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-28661-6
skills.summary: Quantifies expression of an oncogene (e.g., WHSC1) in fusion-positive versus fusion-negative single cells, and profiles per-base sequencing coverage across the fusion breakpoint, to test whether a detected fusion drives oncogene overexpression as in scFusion's multiple myeloma IgH-WHSC1 analysis (Fig 7d-e).
skills.when_to_use_negative: No fusion calls exist yet — scFusion (STAR, samtools, bedtools, statistical/deep-learning filters) must first produce per-cell fusion calls before expression stratification is meaningful The data are not from a Smart-Seq single-cell protocol or the fusion is not expressed in the sequenced cells The candidate oncogene lies far from the fusion breakpoint so coverage and expression cannot be linked to the fusion event

skills.description: Use when a uniform-format list of annotated plus newly predicted miRNA precursors (output of miRNATranslate) must be filtered into promising candidates using the one-class SVM classifier of iwa-miRNA's miRNASelection step with default parameters.
skills.name: one-class-svm-mirna-classification
skills.search_text: one-class-svm-mirna-classification Use when a uniform-format list of annotated plus newly predicted miRNA precursors (output of miRNATranslate) must be filtered into promising candidates using the one-class SVM classifier of iwa-miRNA's miRNASelection step with default parameters. Input sRNA-Seq data come from a species without a reference genome — iwa-miRNA cannot handle sRNA-Seq data from species without genome sequences. You only need candidate prediction, not filtering — use miRNAPredict; the one-class SVM belongs to the downstream miRNASelection step. Candidates require functional validation for investigation — the SVM label is computational; wet experiments are still required before functional investigation. Within the iwa-miRNA MiRNA Selection module, a one-class SVM classifier trained on sequence-, structure-, and expression-based features labels miRNA precursor candidates (e.g., Ara-Set2, maize-Set2, wheat-Set2) as true positives, run in parallel with high-throughput (HT) criteria filtering to reduce false positives in the aggregated candidate list. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2021.02.010
skills.summary: Within the iwa-miRNA MiRNA Selection module, a one-class SVM classifier trained on sequence-, structure-, and expression-based features labels miRNA precursor candidates (e.g., Ara-Set2, maize-Set2, wheat-Set2) as true positives, run in parallel with high-throughput (HT) criteria filtering to reduce false positives in the aggregated candidate list.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sRNA-Seq data come from a species without a reference genome — iwa-miRNA cannot handle sRNA-Seq data from species without genome sequences. You only need candidate prediction, not filtering — use miRNAPredict; the one-class SVM belongs to the downstream miRNASelection step. Candidates require functional validation for investigation — the SVM label is computational; wet experiments are still required before functional investigation.

skills.description: Use when constructing a scHPL hierarchical classification tree on annotated single-cell data where novel/unseen cell populations must be detected (rejection), or when reference batches may lack populations present in other batches.
skills.name: one-class-svm-novel-population-rejection
skills.search_text: one-class-svm-novel-population-rejection Use when constructing a scHPL hierarchical classification tree on annotated single-cell data where novel/unseen cell populations must be detected (rejection), or when reference batches may lack populations present in other batches. Datasets are not aligned/harmonized first — scHPL is not a batch correction tool, so population matching (and hence one-class rejection) will be confounded by batch effects Maximum classification accuracy on fully known populations is the goal — the linear SVM matched or exceeded the one-class SVM on all datasets, and its performance drop on small populations was less severe http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A classifier choice in scHPL's hierarchical tree where a one-class SVM is trained per tree node instead of a linear SVM, enabling explicit rejection of cells as unseen (sub)populations and more stable tree construction when batch populations are missing. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-23196-8
skills.summary: A classifier choice in scHPL's hierarchical tree where a one-class SVM is trained per tree node instead of a linear SVM, enabling explicit rejection of cells as unseen (sub)populations and more stable tree construction when batch populations are missing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Datasets are not aligned/harmonized first — scHPL is not a batch correction tool, so population matching (and hence one-class rejection) will be confounded by batch effects Maximum classification accuracy on fully known populations is the goal — the linear SVM matched or exceeded the one-class SVM on all datasets, and its performance drop on small populations was less severe

skills.description: Use when a hierarchical single-cell classifier must flag cells from cell populations that were excluded from training (novelty/unseen-population detection), e.g. testing whether held-out 'Group 3' AMB nodes are rejected.
skills.name: one-class-svm-novelty-detection
skills.search_text: one-class-svm-novelty-detection Use when a hierarchical single-cell classifier must flag cells from cell populations that were excluded from training (novelty/unseen-population detection), e.g. testing whether held-out 'Group 3' AMB nodes are rejected. scHPL is not a batch correction tool — if datasets from different batches are not yet aligned (e.g. with scVI or scArches), align them first rather than feeding raw combined data The goal is accurate classification of known populations rather than rejection of unseen ones — the linear SVM matches or exceeds one-class SVM accuracy on known classes, and the one-class SVM degrades more on small populations No labeled population annotations exist to build the hierarchical tree in the first place http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Use scHPL's one-class SVM at each node of a hierarchical classification tree to reject cells from unseen cell populations that were held out from training, complementing the linear SVM used for classifying known populations. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-23196-8
skills.summary: Use scHPL's one-class SVM at each node of a hierarchical classification tree to reject cells from unseen cell populations that were held out from training, complementing the linear SVM used for classifying known populations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: scHPL is not a batch correction tool — if datasets from different batches are not yet aligned (e.g. with scVI or scArches), align them first rather than feeding raw combined data The goal is accurate classification of known populations rather than rejection of unseen ones — the linear SVM matches or exceeds one-class SVM accuracy on known classes, and the one-class SVM degrades more on small populations No labeled population annotations exist to build the hierarchical tree in the first place

skills.description: Use when a sequence-based classifier (e.g., the InPACT CNN sequence module) requires fixed-length genomic windows converted to binary one-hot nucleotide tensors, and you need reproducible positive/negative training and held-out test sets for polyA site prediction.
skills.name: one-hot-genomic-sequence-encoding
skills.search_text: one-hot-genomic-sequence-encoding Use when a sequence-based classifier (e.g., the InPACT CNN sequence module) requires fixed-length genomic windows converted to binary one-hot nucleotide tensors, and you need reproducible positive/negative training and held-out test sets for polyA site prediction. The candidate polyA site annotation file (InPACT_polyAsites.hg38.saf) is already provided — InPACT's site-identification and read modules can consume it directly without retraining the sequence module The goal is transcript abundance quantification or IPA usage estimation, which is handled by gffread/Salmon and InPACT_quantify, not by sequence encoding Held-out test sites overlap the RefSeq training data — evaluation would be contaminated and AUROCs inflated http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Encodes fixed-length genomic windows as binary nucleotide feature tensors (A=[1,0,0,0], T=[0,1,0,0], G=[0,0,1,0], C=[0,0,0,1]) so they can be fed into the InPACT CNN sequence module for polyA site prediction, benchmarked by AUROC on held-out GENCODE, PolyA_DB 3, and PolyASite 2.0 test sets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-46875-8
skills.summary: Encodes fixed-length genomic windows as binary nucleotide feature tensors (A=[1,0,0,0], T=[0,1,0,0], G=[0,0,1,0], C=[0,0,0,1]) so they can be fed into the InPACT CNN sequence module for polyA site prediction, benchmarked by AUROC on held-out GENCODE, PolyA_DB 3, and PolyASite 2.0 test sets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The candidate polyA site annotation file (InPACT_polyAsites.hg38.saf) is already provided — InPACT's site-identification and read modules can consume it directly without retraining the sequence module The goal is transcript abundance quantification or IPA usage estimation, which is handled by gffread/Salmon and InPACT_quantify, not by sequence encoding Held-out test sites overlap the RefSeq training data — evaluation would be contaminated and AUROCs inflated

skills.description: Use when raw nucleotide sequences (e.g., 41-nt RNA segments centered on a candidate m6A site) must be converted to fixed-dimensional numeric feature vectors before feeding a CNN classifier such as im6A-TS-CNN.
skills.name: one-hot-nucleotide-sequence-encoding
skills.search_text: one-hot-nucleotide-sequence-encoding Use when raw nucleotide sequences (e.g., 41-nt RNA segments centered on a candidate m6A site) must be converted to fixed-dimensional numeric feature vectors before feeding a CNN classifier such as im6A-TS-CNN. Input is already a numeric feature matrix or embedding (e.g., Gene2Vec-style features) rather than raw nucleotide sequences The downstream model expects sequence-based encodings other than plain one-hot (e.g., learned embeddings or k-mer features), since im6A-TS-CNN was designed and benchmarked specifically on one-hot encoding Sequences are not the canonical 41-nt m6A segments and contain ambiguity codes not covered by the A/U/C/G one-hot scheme http://edamontology.org/topic_3524 http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 Encode 41-nt RNA segments as fixed-length one-hot vectors so they can serve as numerical input to the im6A-TS-CNN tissue-specific m6A classifiers, with A=(1,0,0,0), U=(0,1,0,0), C=(0,0,1,0), G=(0,0,0,1). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.omtn.2020.07.034
skills.summary: Encode 41-nt RNA segments as fixed-length one-hot vectors so they can serve as numerical input to the im6A-TS-CNN tissue-specific m6A classifiers, with A=(1,0,0,0), U=(0,1,0,0), C=(0,0,1,0), G=(0,0,0,1).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a numeric feature matrix or embedding (e.g., Gene2Vec-style features) rather than raw nucleotide sequences The downstream model expects sequence-based encodings other than plain one-hot (e.g., learned embeddings or k-mer features), since im6A-TS-CNN was designed and benchmarked specifically on one-hot encoding Sequences are not the canonical 41-nt m6A segments and contain ambiguity codes not covered by the A/U/C/G one-hot scheme

skills.description: Use when preparing Ψ-site candidate fragments (uridine-centered, 25 nt flanks each side) as fixed-length categorical matrices for a dual-branch 1D-CNN classifier that reads both sequence and secondary-structure context.
skills.name: one-of-k-encoding-of-rna-sequence-and-structure
skills.search_text: one-of-k-encoding-of-rna-sequence-and-structure Use when preparing Ψ-site candidate fragments (uridine-centered, 25 nt flanks each side) as fixed-length categorical matrices for a dual-branch 1D-CNN classifier that reads both sequence and secondary-structure context. The downstream model accepts a single sequence-modality input only (e.g., a sequence-only CNN baseline) — the structure matrix is unnecessary and cannot be consumed Input fragments are not length-fixed at 51 nt or are not uridine-centered, so the matrices would be incommensurable with the trained MU-PseUDeep architecture The task involves protein sequences or other alphabets, for which the 4-channel nucleotide and 6-channel dot-bracket encodings do not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 Encodes RNA sequences and their RNAshapes-derived secondary-structure contexts as fixed-size one-of-K binary matrices (51×4 for sequence, 51×6 for structure dot-bracket classes) so that two parallel 1D-CNN branches of MU-PseUDeep can consume them. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2020.07.010
skills.summary: Encodes RNA sequences and their RNAshapes-derived secondary-structure contexts as fixed-size one-of-K binary matrices (51×4 for sequence, 51×6 for structure dot-bracket classes) so that two parallel 1D-CNN branches of MU-PseUDeep can consume them.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The downstream model accepts a single sequence-modality input only (e.g., a sequence-only CNN baseline) — the structure matrix is unnecessary and cannot be consumed Input fragments are not length-fixed at 51 nt or are not uridine-centered, so the matrices would be incommensurable with the trained MU-PseUDeep architecture The task involves protein sequences or other alphabets, for which the 4-channel nucleotide and 6-channel dot-bracket encodings do not apply

skills.description: Use when two quantification methods have been benchmarked against a common ground truth (e.g., long-read TE counts) and you must show one method's residuals are significantly smaller, not just descriptively better.
skills.name: one-sided-f-test-variance-comparison
skills.search_text: one-sided-f-test-variance-comparison Use when two quantification methods have been benchmarked against a common ground truth (e.g., long-read TE counts) and you must show one method's residuals are significantly smaller, not just descriptively better. When the comparison is two-directional (no prior hypothesis that MATES outperforms the baseline) — a two-sided variance test is then the appropriate choice When only locus-level rather than subfamily-level TE counts are being validated, since the reported reference values (e.g., 0.7531 vs 0.6499 vs 0.6841) are subfamily-level When no common ground truth exists to define residual variances for both methods http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Applies a one-sided F-test on residual variances to attach statistical significance (p < 0.05) to differences in short-read TE quantification accuracy between methods (MATES vs scTE and SoloTE), complementing R2 comparison against long-read ground truth. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-53114-7
skills.summary: Applies a one-sided F-test on residual variances to attach statistical significance (p < 0.05) to differences in short-read TE quantification accuracy between methods (MATES vs scTE and SoloTE), complementing R2 comparison against long-read ground truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the comparison is two-directional (no prior hypothesis that MATES outperforms the baseline) — a two-sided variance test is then the appropriate choice When only locus-level rather than subfamily-level TE counts are being validated, since the reported reference values (e.g., 0.7531 vs 0.6499 vs 0.6841) are subfamily-level When no common ground truth exists to define residual variances for both methods

skills.description: Use when two or more quantification/clustering methods have been run on the same datasets and per-seed metric distributions (e.g., ARI/NMI over 10 random seeds) are available, and the goal is to test whether the proposed method is significantly better, not just different.
skills.name: one-sided-t-test-method-comparison
skills.search_text: one-sided-t-test-method-comparison Use when two or more quantification/clustering methods have been run on the same datasets and per-seed metric distributions (e.g., ARI/NMI over 10 random seeds) are available, and the goal is to test whether the proposed method is significantly better, not just different. You have only a single metric value per method (no seed-level distribution) — a t-test on singleton observations is undefined/meaningless The comparison hypothesis is non-directional (any difference matters) — use a two-sided test instead of a one-sided one Clustering metrics are not computed against the same ground-truth labels for both methods, making the paired distributions incomparable http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Statistical validation pattern for benchmarking a new method (here, MATES) against existing tools (scTE, SoloTE) by comparing performance-metric distributions (ARI/NMI over N=10 random seeds) with one-sided Student's t-tests, establishing directional superiority rather than mere difference. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-53114-7
skills.summary: Statistical validation pattern for benchmarking a new method (here, MATES) against existing tools (scTE, SoloTE) by comparing performance-metric distributions (ARI/NMI over N=10 random seeds) with one-sided Student's t-tests, establishing directional superiority rather than mere difference.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have only a single metric value per method (no seed-level distribution) — a t-test on singleton observations is undefined/meaningless The comparison hypothesis is non-directional (any difference matters) — use a two-sided test instead of a one-sided one Clustering metrics are not computed against the same ground-truth labels for both methods, making the paired distributions incomparable

skills.description: Use when validating whether cells predicted as primed for a lineage (e.g. GP/MEMP MPPs or HS/IRS TACs) show significantly higher fate probability, TF motif activity, or chromatin accessibility than unprimed or opposite-primed cells.
skills.name: one-sided-wilcoxon-rank-sum-testing
skills.search_text: one-sided-wilcoxon-rank-sum-testing Use when validating whether cells predicted as primed for a lineage (e.g. GP/MEMP MPPs or HS/IRS TACs) show significantly higher fate probability, TF motif activity, or chromatin accessibility than unprimed or opposite-primed cells. When comparing more than two ordered groups or needing effect-size estimates beyond rank ordering — the one-sided rank-sum test only asserts directional elevation of one group. When the lineage TF lacks a DNA-binding motif (e.g. UHRF1), TF-activity tests cannot be applied and only accessibility-based comparisons are valid. When cells cannot be uniquely assigned to one lineage (overlapping primed assignments), since the test requires mutually exclusive groups — exclude overlaps via intersect/setdiff first. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Apply one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (alternative='greater') to compare primed versus unprimed cell groups in the DICE framework, both to derive marker genes of primed cells from scRNA-Seq data and to statistically validate priming in matched scATAC-Seq readouts (Palantir fate probability, chromVAR TF activity, gene-level accessibility). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2022.105709
skills.summary: Apply one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (alternative='greater') to compare primed versus unprimed cell groups in the DICE framework, both to derive marker genes of primed cells from scRNA-Seq data and to statistically validate priming in matched scATAC-Seq readouts (Palantir fate probability, chromVAR TF activity, gene-level accessibility).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When comparing more than two ordered groups or needing effect-size estimates beyond rank ordering — the one-sided rank-sum test only asserts directional elevation of one group. When the lineage TF lacks a DNA-binding motif (e.g. UHRF1), TF-activity tests cannot be applied and only accessibility-based comparisons are valid. When cells cannot be uniquely assigned to one lineage (overlapping primed assignments), since the test requires mutually exclusive groups — exclude overlaps via intersect/setdiff first.

skills.description: Use when you have paired per-gene scores (e.g., marker-gene specificity with vs. without constraints) averaged over repeated clusterings and need a one-sided test of whether the constrained condition improves scores.
skills.name: one-sided-wilcoxon-signed-rank-testing
skills.search_text: one-sided-wilcoxon-signed-rank-testing Use when you have paired per-gene scores (e.g., marker-gene specificity with vs. without constraints) averaged over repeated clusterings and need a one-sided test of whether the constrained condition improves scores. When the two conditions being compared are unpaired (e.g., independent genes or independent runs rather than paired per-gene score pairs) When scores are not averaged across the same number of repeats (ten scDCC runs) for both conditions, breaking the pairing assumption When the goal is unsupervised clustering performance rather than testing whether constraints improve marker-gene cluster specificity http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 A paired non-parametric significance test used in the scDCC study to verify that adding soft pairwise constraints to scDCC clustering increases DESeq2-based cluster-specificity scores for 55 uniquely assigned marker genes in the human liver dataset (reported p-value = 0.00024). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-22008-3
skills.summary: A paired non-parametric significance test used in the scDCC study to verify that adding soft pairwise constraints to scDCC clustering increases DESeq2-based cluster-specificity scores for 55 uniquely assigned marker genes in the human liver dataset (reported p-value = 0.00024).
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the two conditions being compared are unpaired (e.g., independent genes or independent runs rather than paired per-gene score pairs) When scores are not averaged across the same number of repeats (ten scDCC runs) for both conditions, breaking the pairing assumption When the goal is unsupervised clustering performance rather than testing whether constraints improve marker-gene cluster specificity

skills.description: Use when benchmarking marker gene panels for cell type discrimination on labeled scRNA-seq data (e.g. Zeisel GSE60361) or synthetic multimodal simulations and you need the per-gene one-vs-all baseline to quantify scGeneFit's joint-selection gain.
skills.name: one-vs-all-marker-baseline-comparison
skills.search_text: one-vs-all-marker-baseline-comparison Use when benchmarking marker gene panels for cell type discrimination on labeled scRNA-seq data (e.g. Zeisel GSE60361) or synthetic multimodal simulations and you need the per-gene one-vs-all baseline to quantify scGeneFit's joint-selection gain. The labeling is continuous or manifold-valued (e.g. placing unlabeled cells along trajectories or in spatial assays) — the paper limits both scGeneFit and one-vs-all to categorical labels Cell type classes are not linearly separable in the intended low-dimensional projection — both methods rely on linear separability, which the authors note is only reasonable in high dimensions You need nonlinear dimension reduction for marker selection — the article reports none is implemented in scGeneFit and defers this to future work http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Establishes the one-vs-all marker selection baseline — scoring each gene separately for each label against all remaining labels and retaining the top k markers — so that scGeneFit's label-aware joint selection can be benchmarked against it on the same scRNA-seq or synthetic expression matrices. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-21453-4
skills.summary: Establishes the one-vs-all marker selection baseline — scoring each gene separately for each label against all remaining labels and retaining the top k markers — so that scGeneFit's label-aware joint selection can be benchmarked against it on the same scRNA-seq or synthetic expression matrices.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The labeling is continuous or manifold-valued (e.g. placing unlabeled cells along trajectories or in spatial assays) — the paper limits both scGeneFit and one-vs-all to categorical labels Cell type classes are not linearly separable in the intended low-dimensional projection — both methods rely on linear separability, which the authors note is only reasonable in high dimensions You need nonlinear dimension reduction for marker selection — the article reports none is implemented in scGeneFit and defers this to future work

skills.description: Use when newly arriving (streaming) data points must be assigned to existing clusters or evaluated for novel cluster emergence, without refitting the clustering model on the full combined dataset.
skills.name: online-inductive-label-inference
skills.search_text: online-inductive-label-inference Use when newly arriving (streaming) data points must be assigned to existing clusters or evaluated for novel cluster emergence, without refitting the clustering model on the full combined dataset. Data has only one cluster — Monte Carlo internal validation cannot accurately estimate uncertainty since every point receives a single label type Data must be analyzed in very high dimensions without nonlinear dimensionality reduction — the method mimics a low-dimensional fire propagation process and suffers from the curse of dimensionality http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Extends Forest Fire Clustering labels to newly arriving (out-of-sample) data via low-dimensional projection, mutual nearest neighbor batch correction, and joint-affinity-based label propagation, enabling robust online-learning inference of new clusters. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-31107-8
skills.summary: Extends Forest Fire Clustering labels to newly arriving (out-of-sample) data via low-dimensional projection, mutual nearest neighbor batch correction, and joint-affinity-based label propagation, enabling robust online-learning inference of new clusters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data has only one cluster — Monte Carlo internal validation cannot accurately estimate uncertainty since every point receives a single label type Data must be analyzed in very high dimensions without nonlinear dimensionality reduction — the method mimics a low-dimensional fire propagation process and suffers from the curse of dimensionality

skills.description: Use when annotating scRNA-seq cells against a controlled vocabulary (Cell Ontology) and the test set contains cell types absent from training data, or when benchmarking classifiers on unseen-term annotation.
skills.name: ontology-aware-cell-type-classification
skills.search_text: ontology-aware-cell-type-classification Use when annotating scRNA-seq cells against a controlled vocabulary (Cell Ontology) and the test set contains cell types absent from training data, or when benchmarking classifiers on unseen-term annotation. Labels are free text rather than controlled-vocabulary Cell Ontology IDs — the NLP mapping path (nlp_mapping=True) is required, but the article notes improving NLP models remains future work Distinguishing topologically identical unseen cell types (siblings sharing the same parents in the Cell Ontology graph) is required — OnClass explicitly cannot do this The task is batch correction with many unseen cell types present — the article states such methods are not yet developed http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0621 Classify single cells into Cell Ontology terms — including unseen terms with no annotated training cells — by projecting scRNA-seq transcriptomes and the ontology graph into a shared low-dimensional space with OnClass, and benchmark against baselines like ACTINN, SVM, and LR using AUROC and Accuracy@k. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-25725-x
skills.summary: Classify single cells into Cell Ontology terms — including unseen terms with no annotated training cells — by projecting scRNA-seq transcriptomes and the ontology graph into a shared low-dimensional space with OnClass, and benchmark against baselines like ACTINN, SVM, and LR using AUROC and Accuracy@k.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Labels are free text rather than controlled-vocabulary Cell Ontology IDs — the NLP mapping path (nlp_mapping=True) is required, but the article notes improving NLP models remains future work Distinguishing topologically identical unseen cell types (siblings sharing the same parents in the Cell Ontology graph) is required — OnClass explicitly cannot do this The task is batch correction with many unseen cell types present — the article states such methods are not yet developed

skills.description: Use when evaluating cell type classifiers on CELLxGENE-style annotations where predictions of a more specific Cell Ontology subtype should count as correct against a parent true label.
skills.name: ontology-aware-prediction-scoring
skills.search_text: ontology-aware-prediction-scoring Use when evaluating cell type classifiers on CELLxGENE-style annotations where predictions of a more specific Cell Ontology subtype should count as correct against a parent true label. The label space has no ontology structure or you need strict exact-match accuracy — the ontology-aware rule deliberately credits subtype predictions, inflating scores relative to plain accuracy. Evaluating on cell types not mappable to Cell Ontology terms (e.g., rare or coarsely annotated labels) — the article notes not all cell types can be matched to an ontology term. You need metrics reflecting tissue/protocol imbalance — the article warns plain macro F1 may not properly reflect the complexity of unbalanced datasets. http://edamontology.org/topic_0621 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Scores cell type classifier predictions using the Cell Ontology child-node lookup so a prediction is counted correct if it matches the annotator label exactly or predicts a subtype of it. This is the evaluation rule used across all scTab benchmark tasks (macro F1 and test loss) to credit biologically consistent subtype predictions. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-51059-5
skills.summary: Scores cell type classifier predictions using the Cell Ontology child-node lookup so a prediction is counted correct if it matches the annotator label exactly or predicts a subtype of it. This is the evaluation rule used across all scTab benchmark tasks (macro F1 and test loss) to credit biologically consistent subtype predictions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The label space has no ontology structure or you need strict exact-match accuracy — the ontology-aware rule deliberately credits subtype predictions, inflating scores relative to plain accuracy. Evaluating on cell types not mappable to Cell Ontology terms (e.g., rare or coarsely annotated labels) — the article notes not all cell types can be matched to an ontology term. You need metrics reflecting tissue/protocol imbalance — the article warns plain macro F1 may not properly reflect the complexity of unbalanced datasets.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking cell type annotation tools (e.g. Cell Marker Accordion vs ScType, SCINA, clustifyR, scCATCH, scSorter) and you need a Cell Ontology-aware similarity metric instead of exact label matching.
skills.name: ontology-based-cell-type-similarity-scoring
skills.search_text: ontology-based-cell-type-similarity-scoring Use when benchmarking cell type annotation tools (e.g. Cell Marker Accordion vs ScType, SCINA, clustifyR, scCATCH, scSorter) and you need a Cell Ontology-aware similarity metric instead of exact label matching. Comparing annotations across cell types that cannot be mapped to the Cell Ontology (no shared ontology terms), since similarity would be undefined or misleading Evaluating non-marker-based annotation approaches — the article explicitly notes no direct comparison was conducted with tools that do not rely on marker genes Scoring datasets lacking reliable ground truth, which the discussion identifies as constraining benchmark expansion http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Scores cell type annotation accuracy by computing the semantic similarity between predicted and ground-truth cell type labels over the Cell Ontology tree (release 2024-08-16) using the ontologySimilarity R package, producing a finite 0-100 percentage similarity per cluster/dataset. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-025-60900-4
skills.summary: Scores cell type annotation accuracy by computing the semantic similarity between predicted and ground-truth cell type labels over the Cell Ontology tree (release 2024-08-16) using the ontologySimilarity R package, producing a finite 0-100 percentage similarity per cluster/dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Comparing annotations across cell types that cannot be mapped to the Cell Ontology (no shared ontology terms), since similarity would be undefined or misleading Evaluating non-marker-based annotation approaches — the article explicitly notes no direct comparison was conducted with tools that do not rely on marker genes Scoring datasets lacking reliable ground truth, which the discussion identifies as constraining benchmark expansion

skills.description: Use when you need to measure logical inconsistency of independent binary classifiers against a hierarchy — e.g. comparing one-vs-rest vs hierarchical CellO outputs, or validating a probability matrix against ontology DAG constraints.
skills.name: ontology-edge-consistency-analysis
skills.search_text: ontology-edge-consistency-analysis Use when you need to measure logical inconsistency of independent binary classifiers against a hierarchy — e.g. comparing one-vs-rest vs hierarchical CellO outputs, or validating a probability matrix against ontology DAG constraints. You are annotating new single-cell RNA-seq data with CellO itself (use cello_predict classification instead — this skill is a diagnostic on training-set classifier outputs) Your ontology lacks 'is a' parent-child edges or you have only a flat label set with no DAG structure to check You are working with non-human data (e.g. mouse), since no comprehensive curated mouse training set from the SRA exists yet http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 A diagnostic skill that quantifies how frequently independently trained one-vs-rest CellO classifiers (the 'IR' isotonic-regression algorithm) produce probabilities that logically violate Cell Ontology 'is a' parent-child edges, justifying hierarchical classification. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2020.101913
skills.summary: A diagnostic skill that quantifies how frequently independently trained one-vs-rest CellO classifiers (the 'IR' isotonic-regression algorithm) produce probabilities that logically violate Cell Ontology 'is a' parent-child edges, justifying hierarchical classification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are annotating new single-cell RNA-seq data with CellO itself (use cello_predict classification instead — this skill is a diagnostic on training-set classifier outputs) Your ontology lacks 'is a' parent-child edges or you have only a flat label set with no DAG structure to check You are working with non-human data (e.g. mouse), since no comprehensive curated mouse training set from the SRA exists yet

skills.description: Use when you must annotate scRNA-seq cells to Cell Ontology terms that lack annotated training cells (unseen terms), leveraging the ontology graph rather than per-term supervised training alone.
skills.name: ontology-embedding-usage
skills.search_text: ontology-embedding-usage Use when you must annotate scRNA-seq cells to Cell Ontology terms that lack annotated training cells (unseen terms), leveraging the ontology graph rather than per-term supervised training alone. When every Cell Ontology term of interest already has annotated cells in the training set, so a purely supervised classifier suffices When the target cell types are topologically identical siblings in the Cell Ontology graph — OnClass cannot distinguish them, and the ontology-based propagation will not resolve the ambiguity When the vocabulary is uncontrolled free text and no mapping to Cell Ontology terms is available Embed Cell Ontology terms into a low-dimensional space and use the ontology graph structure (e.g., random walk with restart score propagation) to extend per-cell confidence scores from seen cell types to unseen Cell Ontology terms. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-25725-x
skills.summary: Embed Cell Ontology terms into a low-dimensional space and use the ontology graph structure (e.g., random walk with restart score propagation) to extend per-cell confidence scores from seen cell types to unseen Cell Ontology terms.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When every Cell Ontology term of interest already has annotated cells in the training set, so a purely supervised classifier suffices When the target cell types are topologically identical siblings in the Cell Ontology graph — OnClass cannot distinguish them, and the ontology-based propagation will not resolve the ambiguity When the vocabulary is uncontrolled free text and no mapping to Cell Ontology terms is available

skills.description: Use when annotating human scRNA-seq or bulk RNA-seq cells against the Cell Ontology hierarchy, or when benchmarking hierarchical classifiers (IR, CLR) against flat baselines such as a Pearson-correlation 1NN.
skills.name: ontology-graph-classifier-training
skills.search_text: ontology-graph-classifier-training Use when annotating human scRNA-seq or bulk RNA-seq cells against the Cell Ontology hierarchy, or when benchmarking hierarchical classifiers (IR, CLR) against flat baselines such as a Pearson-correlation 1NN. Input RNA-seq data is from non-human species (e.g., mouse) — CellO's pre-trained models were trained only on human primary samples from the SRA The input gene set does not match the classifier's training genes and retraining on a single small dataset would be unreliable The task requires lineage-based or evolutionary relationships between cell types that the Cell Ontology does not encode http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Train per-term binary linear classifiers (isotonic regression 'IR' or cascaded logistic regression 'CLR') against the graph-structured Cell Ontology, using bulk RNA-seq training data, to hierarchically annotate single-cell RNA-seq data. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2020.101913
skills.summary: Train per-term binary linear classifiers (isotonic regression 'IR' or cascaded logistic regression 'CLR') against the graph-structured Cell Ontology, using bulk RNA-seq training data, to hierarchically annotate single-cell RNA-seq data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input RNA-seq data is from non-human species (e.g., mouse) — CellO's pre-trained models were trained only on human primary samples from the SRA The input gene set does not match the classifier's training genes and retraining on a single small dataset would be unreliable The task requires lineage-based or evolutionary relationships between cell types that the Cell Ontology does not encode

skills.description: Use when a scRNA-seq classifier must reason over a controlled vocabulary of cell type terms — e.g. to score unseen Cell Ontology terms or compute marker genes for all ontology categories — and raw obo/network files are available.
skills.name: ontology-graph-construction
skills.search_text: ontology-graph-construction Use when a scRNA-seq classifier must reason over a controlled vocabulary of cell type terms — e.g. to score unseen Cell Ontology terms or compute marker genes for all ontology categories — and raw obo/network files are available. The task only needs classifying into a fixed, flat label set with no ontology vocabulary — a standard classifier (e.g. ACTINN) suffices and graph embedding adds overhead Cell types of interest are topologically identical siblings (same parents in the Cell Ontology graph) that must be distinguished — OnClass cannot separate these The Cell Ontology lacks terms for the cell states being studied, since it was not developed specifically for scRNA-seq and likely misses cell types and cell states http://edamontology.org/topic_0089 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Constructs an undirected cell type similarity graph from the Cell Ontology 'is_a' hierarchy and embeds its terms into a low-dimensional space (random walk with restart followed by SVD, OnClass 1.2/TensorFlow 2.0), so that single-cell transcriptomes can be projected into the same shared embedding space. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-25725-x
skills.summary: Constructs an undirected cell type similarity graph from the Cell Ontology 'is_a' hierarchy and embeds its terms into a low-dimensional space (random walk with restart followed by SVD, OnClass 1.2/TensorFlow 2.0), so that single-cell transcriptomes can be projected into the same shared embedding space.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task only needs classifying into a fixed, flat label set with no ontology vocabulary — a standard classifier (e.g. ACTINN) suffices and graph embedding adds overhead Cell types of interest are topologically identical siblings (same parents in the Cell Ontology graph) that must be distinguished — OnClass cannot separate these The Cell Ontology lacks terms for the cell states being studied, since it was not developed specifically for scRNA-seq and likely misses cell types and cell states

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how similar cell types are according to ontology structure (direct-neighbor vs multi-hop graph distance) and test whether ontology similarity tracks expression similarity.
skills.name: ontology-graph-distance-traversal
skills.search_text: ontology-graph-distance-traversal Use when you need to quantify how similar cell types are according to ontology structure (direct-neighbor vs multi-hop graph distance) and test whether ontology similarity tracks expression similarity. When the goal is annotating/query cells with a trained OnClass model rather than characterizing ontology structure itself (use OnClass prediction workflow instead) When the cell type vocabulary has no formal ontology (e.g., free-text labels only) — traversal requires the cl.obo graph structure Computes cell-type similarity matrices by traversing the Cell Ontology hierarchical graph (treating edges as undirected similarities with uniform weights) and validates them against text-embedding and gene-expression similarity, as done for OnClass on Tabula Muris Senis lung and pancreas data. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-25725-x
skills.summary: Computes cell-type similarity matrices by traversing the Cell Ontology hierarchical graph (treating edges as undirected similarities with uniform weights) and validates them against text-embedding and gene-expression similarity, as done for OnClass on Tabula Muris Senis lung and pancreas data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is annotating/query cells with a trained OnClass model rather than characterizing ontology structure itself (use OnClass prediction workflow instead) When the cell type vocabulary has no formal ontology (e.g., free-text labels only) — traversal requires the cl.obo graph structure

skills.description: Use when DCNet abundance predictions must be restricted to or interpreted for specific terminal cell types (e.g. FGC, somatic cells) in a Cell Ontology hierarchy, rather than the full 434-type landscape.
skills.name: ontology-leaf-node-cell-type-mapping
skills.search_text: ontology-leaf-node-cell-type-mapping Use when DCNet abundance predictions must be restricted to or interpreted for specific terminal cell types (e.g. FGC, somatic cells) in a Cell Ontology hierarchy, rather than the full 434-type landscape. When the goal is the full 434-cell-type landscape rather than specific Cell Ontology leaf nodes — DCNet already outputs all embedded cell types directly. When the cell type of interest is not among the 434 cell types embedded in the DCNet network (e.g. cell types whose marker genes were not detected and were discarded during filtering). http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Maps the 434 cell-type neurons embedded in DCNet's network structure to their leaf-node positions in the Cell Ontology hierarchy (e.g. fetal germ cells and somatic cells), so predicted abundances can be extracted and validated against ground-truth single-cell-derived abundances. transcriptomics/v2 10.1080/2162402x.2022.2043662
skills.summary: Maps the 434 cell-type neurons embedded in DCNet's network structure to their leaf-node positions in the Cell Ontology hierarchy (e.g. fetal germ cells and somatic cells), so predicted abundances can be extracted and validated against ground-truth single-cell-derived abundances.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is the full 434-cell-type landscape rather than specific Cell Ontology leaf nodes — DCNet already outputs all embedded cell types directly. When the cell type of interest is not among the 434 cell types embedded in the DCNet network (e.g. cell types whose marker genes were not detected and were discarded during filtering).

skills.description: Use when you have a fitted topic model's gene association vector (Ntopics x Ngenes beta matrix) and an ontology/cell-type gene membership list, and need to test if a topic's top genes capture a known cell identity program.
skills.name: ontology-membership-contingency-analysis
skills.search_text: ontology-membership-contingency-analysis Use when you have a fitted topic model's gene association vector (Ntopics x Ngenes beta matrix) and an ontology/cell-type gene membership list, and need to test if a topic's top genes capture a known cell identity program. When the gene set of interest is not ranked by model association weights (e.g., it is an arbitrary feature table or a differential-expression list with no topic beta scores) — a simple ORA is sufficient and the topic-LFC correlation is not defined. When testing enrichment for pathways rather than a cell-type identity program validated by LFC correlation — the correlation-to-LFC check (Fig. 3f, g trend) is the paper's identity confirmation and would not apply. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Tests whether a gene set ranked by a topic model's association weights (e.g., CODAL/MIRA Topic 14 beta weights) is enriched for members of a cell-type ontology (e.g., HuBMAP CD16+ monocyte genes) via a one-sided Fisher's exact test on a 2x2 contingency table, and correlates topic scores with cell-type log-fold changes to confirm the identity program. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-39494-2
skills.summary: Tests whether a gene set ranked by a topic model's association weights (e.g., CODAL/MIRA Topic 14 beta weights) is enriched for members of a cell-type ontology (e.g., HuBMAP CD16+ monocyte genes) via a one-sided Fisher's exact test on a 2x2 contingency table, and correlates topic scores with cell-type log-fold changes to confirm the identity program.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the gene set of interest is not ranked by model association weights (e.g., it is an arbitrary feature table or a differential-expression list with no topic beta scores) — a simple ORA is sufficient and the topic-LFC correlation is not defined. When testing enrichment for pathways rather than a cell-type identity program validated by LFC correlation — the correlation-to-LFC check (Fig. 3f, g trend) is the paper's identity confirmation and would not apply.

skills.search_text: ontology-metadata-mapping-ncbi-mesh-ncit Use when preparing .h5ad study files for import into Cellenium (e.g. via the blood_covid.ipynb or heart_failure_reichart2022 notebooks) and study-level metadata must be mapped to NCBI taxonomy, MeSH, and NCIT ontologies. skills.description: Use when a phase I/II dose-finding design needs quantitative performance evaluation across dose-toxicity-efficacy scenarios, e.g. reproducing OBD selection or null-case early-termination rates from simulated trials.
