skills.summary: A calibration-check skill that aggregates gene-set p-values from null simulations, computes the genomic-control inflation factor lambda_gc, and plots observed vs expected p-value quantiles to verify whether a GSE method (iDEA, fGSEA, PAGE, GSEA, CAMERA) produces well-calibrated p-values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The p-values come from simulations with embedded DE signal or gene-set enrichment (non-null tau1) — QQ calibration plots only assess null behavior, not power The goal is FDR control assessment across overlapping gene sets, where the permuted-null pipeline (iDEA.fit.null + iDEA.FDR) is the appropriate mechanism instead Input is per-gene DE p-value calibration rather than aggregated gene-set p-values; the QQ stratification here is built around gene-set-level tests at defined coverage rates

skills.description: Use when raw microarray intensity data must be normalized and there is no a priori reason to prefer quantile or LOESS; compare both, inspect MA plots for linearity, and check the dendrogram for batch effects.
skills.name: quantile-vs-loess-normalization-comparison
skills.search_text: quantile-vs-loess-normalization-comparison Use when raw microarray intensity data must be normalized and there is no a priori reason to prefer quantile or LOESS; compare both, inspect MA plots for linearity, and check the dendrogram for batch effects. Input is already normalized or is a processed feature/count table rather than raw per-sample microarray intensity columns Data are RNA-seq read counts rather than microarray intensities — PIMENTo's quantile/LOESS comparison targets microarray data such as Illumina Bead arrays and Affymetrix GeneChips Only one normalization method is mandated by the platform's standard preprocessing protocol, making a side-by-side comparison unnecessary http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 A PIMENTo-based workflow that applies both shipped normalization methods (quantile via limma, LOESS via affy) to a raw microarray intensity table, then judges which is better by inspecting MA plots for linearity on the MA scale and a Ward-clustered dendrogram for batch effects. transcriptomics/v2 10.1007/978-1-4939-9004-7_11
skills.summary: A PIMENTo-based workflow that applies both shipped normalization methods (quantile via limma, LOESS via affy) to a raw microarray intensity table, then judges which is better by inspecting MA plots for linearity on the MA scale and a Ward-clustered dendrogram for batch effects.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already normalized or is a processed feature/count table rather than raw per-sample microarray intensity columns Data are RNA-seq read counts rather than microarray intensities — PIMENTo's quantile/LOESS comparison targets microarray data such as Illumina Bead arrays and Affymetrix GeneChips Only one normalization method is mandated by the platform's standard preprocessing protocol, making a side-by-side comparison unnecessary

skills.description: Use when you have a continuous per-cell FiRE rareness score vector and need a binary rare-cell label per cell (0/1) via a distribution-based, parameter-free cutoff on scRNA-seq data.
skills.name: quartile-based-statistical-filtering
skills.search_text: quartile-based-statistical-filtering Use when you have a continuous per-cell FiRE rareness score vector and need a binary rare-cell label per cell (0/1) via a distribution-based, parameter-free cutoff on scRNA-seq data. FiRE has not yet been run: no continuous score vector exists, so there is nothing to threshold (this filter consumes scores, not raw expression data) You need to distinguish true minor cell types from technical outliers — the paper notes FiRE 'does not discriminate between an outlier and cells representing minor cell types', so downstream clustering (e.g., dropClust) is still required A rare fraction with a known expected proportion is targeted and a fixed quantile cut (e.g., top 1%) is preferable — the 1.5*IQR fence yields a data-driven count that may not match a prespecified rare-cell rate http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3516 Converts FiRE's continuous per-cell rareness scores into binary rare/not-rare calls by thresholding at the Tukey upper fence q3 + 1.5*IQR of the score distribution, mirroring the IQR-based criterion used in the FiRE paper and its reference Python demo. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-07234-6
skills.summary: Converts FiRE's continuous per-cell rareness scores into binary rare/not-rare calls by thresholding at the Tukey upper fence q3 + 1.5*IQR of the score distribution, mirroring the IQR-based criterion used in the FiRE paper and its reference Python demo.
skills.when_to_use_negative: FiRE has not yet been run: no continuous score vector exists, so there is nothing to threshold (this filter consumes scores, not raw expression data) You need to distinguish true minor cell types from technical outliers — the paper notes FiRE 'does not discriminate between an outlier and cells representing minor cell types', so downstream clustering (e.g., dropClust) is still required A rare fraction with a known expected proportion is targeted and a fixed quantile cut (e.g., top 1%) is preferable — the 1.5*IQR fence yields a data-driven count that may not match a prespecified rare-cell rate

skills.description: Use when building a quantitative low-dimensional representation of single-cell RNA-seq cells by clustering genes whose expression-rank vectors show akin (not identical) trends into landmark consensus vectors.
skills.name: quasi-trend-preserved-gene-grouping
skills.search_text: quasi-trend-preserved-gene-grouping Use when building a quantitative low-dimensional representation of single-cell RNA-seq cells by clustering genes whose expression-rank vectors show akin (not identical) trends into landmark consensus vectors. You need a binary/qualitative cell representation — that is the LC1 module, which binarizes the matrix and clusters genes with qualitative quasi-trend-preserved patterns instead You want final cell cluster labels directly — clustering cells from Q1/Q2 requires the downstream Cluster Constructor (CC) and label propagation modules The dataset has not been filtered/HVG-selected and normalized to [0,1]; raw sparse counts violate the binning assumption of LC2 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Implements scQA's quantitative landmark constructor (LC2): discretize normalized gene expression into k bins, group genes by bin usage, and cluster quasi-trend-preserved genes within each group into landmark consensus vectors that form the quantitative low-dimensional cell representation (LM2/Q2 matrix). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.12.021
skills.summary: Implements scQA's quantitative landmark constructor (LC2): discretize normalized gene expression into k bins, group genes by bin usage, and cluster quasi-trend-preserved genes within each group into landmark consensus vectors that form the quantitative low-dimensional cell representation (LM2/Q2 matrix).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a binary/qualitative cell representation — that is the LC1 module, which binarizes the matrix and clusters genes with qualitative quasi-trend-preserved patterns instead You want final cell cluster labels directly — clustering cells from Q1/Q2 requires the downstream Cluster Constructor (CC) and label propagation modules The dataset has not been filtered/HVG-selected and normalized to [0,1]; raw sparse counts violate the binning assumption of LC2

skills.description: Use when planning scCODA case-control scRNA-seq experiments: compositional count data with known ground-truth changes have been simulated per (baseline abundance × fold-change × sample size), and per-setting detection rates are available.
skills.name: quasibinomial-power-curve-fitting
skills.search_text: quasibinomial-power-curve-fitting Use when planning scCODA case-control scRNA-seq experiments: compositional count data with known ground-truth changes have been simulated per (baseline abundance × fold-change × sample size), and per-setting detection rates are available. The input is a real experimental dataset without replicated, ground-truth compositional changes — power estimation requires simulated data with known effects (scCODA reproducibility benchmarks supply such data via zenodo). The goal is differential abundance testing of an actual dataset rather than experimental design/sample-size planning — use CompositionalAnalysis with credible_effects directly instead. Sample-level response heterogeneity matters — scCODA does not model response variability within a condition, so power curves from it will not capture donor variability. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Fits a quasibinomial generalized linear model of true positive rate on sample size to scCODA detection results over synthetic case-control grids, then inverts the fit to estimate the sample size needed for power 0.8 at a given effect size and FDR level. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-27150-6
skills.summary: Fits a quasibinomial generalized linear model of true positive rate on sample size to scCODA detection results over synthetic case-control grids, then inverts the fit to estimate the sample size needed for power 0.8 at a given effect size and FDR level.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a real experimental dataset without replicated, ground-truth compositional changes — power estimation requires simulated data with known effects (scCODA reproducibility benchmarks supply such data via zenodo). The goal is differential abundance testing of an actual dataset rather than experimental design/sample-size planning — use CompositionalAnalysis with credible_effects directly instead. Sample-level response heterogeneity matters — scCODA does not model response variability within a condition, so power curves from it will not capture donor variability.

skills.description: Use when new scRNA-seq data (h5ad/AnnData) needs cell type labels or continuous fate annotations transferred from a curated reference dataset, especially across batches or species, or when screening for putative novel cell types rejected by the query.
skills.name: query-based-cell-annotation-transfer
skills.search_text: query-based-cell-annotation-transfer Use when new scRNA-seq data (h5ad/AnnData) needs cell type labels or continuous fate annotations transferred from a curated reference dataset, especially across batches or species, or when screening for putative novel cell types rejected by the query. Reference datasets with fewer than ~1000 cells, since the over-parameterized DIRECTi model may suffer under-training (3000 cells is generally sufficient) Mega-scale dataset integration with highly skewed cell-type composition, where adversarial batch alignment may over-correct batches Queries against data lacking unified, curated annotations, since no suitable reference exists for label transfer http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Annotate unlabeled single-cell RNA-seq query cells by searching a curated reference with Cell BLAST, which fits a DIRECTi deep generative model on the reference and transfers reference annotations (cell type or continuous fate probabilities) to query cells via a posterior-distribution-based cell-to-cell similarity metric. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-17281-7
skills.summary: Annotate unlabeled single-cell RNA-seq query cells by searching a curated reference with Cell BLAST, which fits a DIRECTi deep generative model on the reference and transfers reference annotations (cell type or continuous fate probabilities) to query cells via a posterior-distribution-based cell-to-cell similarity metric.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reference datasets with fewer than ~1000 cells, since the over-parameterized DIRECTi model may suffer under-training (3000 cells is generally sufficient) Mega-scale dataset integration with highly skewed cell-type composition, where adversarial batch alignment may over-correct batches Queries against data lacking unified, curated annotations, since no suitable reference exists for label transfer

skills.description: Use when a normalized query dataset (e.g., log(CP10k+1)) must be placed into an existing integrated reference embedding — e.g., a 10x 5' PBMC query against 3'v1/3'v2 donors, or annotation/trajectory localization against a saved Symphony reference.
skills.name: query-cell-projection-onto-reference-embedding
skills.search_text: query-cell-projection-onto-reference-embedding Use when a normalized query dataset (e.g., log(CP10k+1)) must be placed into an existing integrated reference embedding — e.g., a 10x 5' PBMC query against 3'v1/3'v2 donors, or annotation/trajectory localization against a saved Symphony reference. The goal is novel cell-type discovery — Symphony does not replace de novo analyses of the query alone, and its metrics are uninformative for novel populations similar to existing reference types The reference does not comprehensively cover the query's cell types (Condition I), so query cells may map spuriously Reference and query were analyzed with different peak sets (scATAC-seq), where the optimal feature selection for mapping is undefined http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Project query single-cell expression data into a precomputed Symphony reference embedding by scaling query genes with stored reference means/standard deviations, projecting through stored PCA loadings, softly assigning cells to harmonized soft-cluster centroids, and applying mixture-model batch correction — enabling annotation transfer in seconds without re-running integration. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-25957-x
skills.summary: Project query single-cell expression data into a precomputed Symphony reference embedding by scaling query genes with stored reference means/standard deviations, projecting through stored PCA loadings, softly assigning cells to harmonized soft-cluster centroids, and applying mixture-model batch correction — enabling annotation transfer in seconds without re-running integration.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is novel cell-type discovery — Symphony does not replace de novo analyses of the query alone, and its metrics are uninformative for novel populations similar to existing reference types The reference does not comprehensively cover the query's cell types (Condition I), so query cells may map spuriously Reference and query were analyzed with different peak sets (scATAC-seq), where the optimal feature selection for mapping is undefined

skills.description: Use when a new scRNA-seq dataset (e.g. the Lafleur Ptpn2-KO/WT P14 or Yao Tox-KO query matrices) must be loaded as a query object before Run.ProjecTILs projection onto a reference map.
skills.name: query-expression-matrix-loading
skills.search_text: query-expression-matrix-loading Use when a new scRNA-seq dataset (e.g. the Lafleur Ptpn2-KO/WT P14 or Yao Tox-KO query matrices) must be loaded as a query object before Run.ProjecTILs projection onto a reference map. Input is already a projected Seurat object with a dimensionality reduction — re-loading via read.sc.query could discard it; use ProjecTILs.classifier or Run.ProjecTILs directly The goal is to integrate datasets into an atlas itself (multi-study reference construction) — that is a STACAS/make.reference task, not query loading http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Loads a scRNA-seq query expression matrix (e.g. 10x/hdf5 raw or log counts, or a Seurat object) into ProjecTILs via read.sc.query so it can be projected onto a reference atlas. Correct handling of the counts layer and normalization here is a prerequisite for accurate cell state label transfer. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-23324-4
skills.summary: Loads a scRNA-seq query expression matrix (e.g. 10x/hdf5 raw or log counts, or a Seurat object) into ProjecTILs via read.sc.query so it can be projected onto a reference atlas. Correct handling of the counts layer and normalization here is a prerequisite for accurate cell state label transfer.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a projected Seurat object with a dimensionality reduction — re-loading via read.sc.query could discard it; use ProjecTILs.classifier or Run.ProjecTILs directly The goal is to integrate datasets into an atlas itself (multi-study reference construction) — that is a STACAS/make.reference task, not query loading

skills.description: Use when comparing the querying-time scalability of cell-querying tools across increasing reference sizes, e.g. validating that a method scales to 1,000,000-cell references before deployment on large scRNA-seq databases.
skills.name: query-latency-curve-visualization
skills.search_text: query-latency-curve-visualization Use when comparing the querying-time scalability of cell-querying tools across increasing reference sizes, e.g. validating that a method scales to 1,000,000-cell references before deployment on large scRNA-seq databases. The goal is accuracy or cell-type annotation quality rather than querying-time scalability benchmarking Reference datasets contain fewer than ~1,000 cells, where neural network-based models like DIRECTi may be under-trained and timings are not meaningful for scalability testing The comparison targets batch correction or integration quality instead of computational efficiency http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Benchmarks and visualizes how cell-querying wall-clock times (Cell BLAST, scmap, CellFishing.jl) scale as the reference dataset grows from 1,000 to 1,000,000 cells subsampled from the 1.3M mouse brain scRNA-seq dataset, reproducing the Fig. 2d scalability comparison. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-17281-7
skills.summary: Benchmarks and visualizes how cell-querying wall-clock times (Cell BLAST, scmap, CellFishing.jl) scale as the reference dataset grows from 1,000 to 1,000,000 cells subsampled from the 1.3M mouse brain scRNA-seq dataset, reproducing the Fig. 2d scalability comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is accuracy or cell-type annotation quality rather than querying-time scalability benchmarking Reference datasets contain fewer than ~1,000 cells, where neural network-based models like DIRECTi may be under-trained and timings are not meaningful for scalability testing The comparison targets batch correction or integration quality instead of computational efficiency

skills.description: Use when preparing a query scRNA-seq AnnData for TOSICA.pre() prediction after training on a ref_adata, and the query's var_names (genes) may differ from or be ordered differently than the reference genes.
skills.name: query-reference-gene-alignment
skills.search_text: query-reference-gene-alignment Use when preparing a query scRNA-seq AnnData for TOSICA.pre() prediction after training on a ref_adata, and the query's var_names (genes) may differ from or be ordered differently than the reference genes. Query and reference AnnData already have identical var_names in the same order — no alignment is needed Input is raw count matrices or a feature table not stored as an AnnData object with var_names You intend to train a new model rather than predict with an existing trained project folder http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Subset and reorder the query AnnData so its var_names exactly match the reference training AnnData's gene list before running TOSICA prediction, since the trained Transformer model expects inputs in the reference gene order. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-35923-4
skills.summary: Subset and reorder the query AnnData so its var_names exactly match the reference training AnnData's gene list before running TOSICA prediction, since the trained Transformer model expects inputs in the reference gene order.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Query and reference AnnData already have identical var_names in the same order — no alignment is needed Input is raw count matrices or a feature table not stored as an AnnData object with var_names You intend to train a new model rather than predict with an existing trained project folder

skills.description: Use when a single-cell expression or annotation query (e.g. SELECT ... FROM X/obs with LIMIT or WHERE clauses) has been executed against an on-disk or in-memory AnnSQL DuckDB database and the result must be persisted as a Parquet file for reuse.
skills.name: query-result-parquet-export
skills.search_text: query-result-parquet-export Use when a single-cell expression or annotation query (e.g. SELECT ... FROM X/obs with LIMIT or WHERE clauses) has been executed against an on-disk or in-memory AnnSQL DuckDB database and the result must be persisted as a Parquet file for reuse. You need an interactive in-memory result for immediate further AnnSQL/Scanpy operations — the default pandas DataFrame return is more appropriate than writing Parquet The data is not stored as AnnData layers converted to a relational DuckDB database (AnnSQL only queries AnnData-derived databases) The database has more than 30k genes, where a known unresolved DuckDB memory leak is flagged in the article http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Run SQL against an instantiated AnnSQL database via the query method and capture results as a Parquet file (pandas DataFrame is the default return format; AnnData is also supported), persisting query output for downstream tools. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbaf105
skills.summary: Run SQL against an instantiated AnnSQL database via the query method and capture results as a Parquet file (pandas DataFrame is the default return format; AnnData is also supported), persisting query output for downstream tools.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need an interactive in-memory result for immediate further AnnSQL/Scanpy operations — the default pandas DataFrame return is more appropriate than writing Parquet The data is not stored as AnnData layers converted to a relational DuckDB database (AnnSQL only queries AnnData-derived databases) The database has more than 30k genes, where a known unresolved DuckDB memory leak is flagged in the article

skills.description: Use when measuring how query time or throughput on a PAC index changes with index configuration (plain Bloom matrix vs. 1 or 2 aggregated Bloom filters) across batches that are similar, dissimilar, or random relative to the indexed genomes.
skills.name: query-throughput-analysis
skills.search_text: query-throughput-analysis Use when measuring how query time or throughput on a PAC index changes with index configuration (plain Bloom matrix vs. 1 or 2 aggregated Bloom filters) across batches that are similar, dissimilar, or random relative to the indexed genomes. The query batch is highly similar to the indexed genomes (e.g. same-species S. enterica batch), where the single Aggregated Bloom filter hardly improves query time and the benchmark adds little signal The goal is exact sequence search or alignment (BLAST-like) rather than approximate membership queries listing datasets that may contain a sequence http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmarks PAC query throughput (elapsed time and per-query shared kmer counts) on a partitioned aggregated Bloom comb tree index across sequence batches of varying similarity, comparing index configurations with zero, one, or two Aggregated Bloom Comb trees. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad225
skills.summary: Benchmarks PAC query throughput (elapsed time and per-query shared kmer counts) on a partitioned aggregated Bloom comb tree index across sequence batches of varying similarity, comparing index configurations with zero, one, or two Aggregated Bloom Comb trees.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query batch is highly similar to the indexed genomes (e.g. same-species S. enterica batch), where the single Aggregated Bloom filter hardly improves query time and the benchmark adds little signal The goal is exact sequence search or alignment (BLAST-like) rather than approximate membership queries listing datasets that may contain a sequence

skills.description: Use when inferring a sparse gene co-expression network from normalized single-cell expression data for a fixed gene set, after computing scLink's robust correlation matrix, and needing to select lambda by BIC.
skills.name: quic-convex-optimization
skills.search_text: quic-convex-optimization Use when inferring a sparse gene co-expression network from normalized single-cell expression data for a fixed gene set, after computing scLink's robust correlation matrix, and needing to select lambda by BIC. The goal is directed or regulatory edges — scLink edges are undirected statistical dependencies and expression data alone cannot distinguish regulatory from co-regulatory edges Genes have not been filtered/normalized first (sclink_norm with library size 10^6, gene filtering by detection rate or mean expression) — the penalized likelihood assumes the preprocessed matrix A simple co-expression strength measure suffices — use sclink_cor correlations rather than the penalized network step http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Solves scLink's data-adaptive penalized-likelihood estimation of the Gaussian graphical model concentration matrix using the QUIC solver, with penalty weights (1 - |r_j1j2|) derived from robust correlations and a positive semidefinite covariance correction S_p = S + |min{0,tau}|I. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2020.11.006
skills.summary: Solves scLink's data-adaptive penalized-likelihood estimation of the Gaussian graphical model concentration matrix using the QUIC solver, with penalty weights (1 - |r_j1j2|) derived from robust correlations and a positive semidefinite covariance correction S_p = S + |min{0,tau}|I.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is directed or regulatory edges — scLink edges are undirected statistical dependencies and expression data alone cannot distinguish regulatory from co-regulatory edges Genes have not been filtered/normalized first (sclink_norm with library size 10^6, gene filtering by detection rate or mean expression) — the penalized likelihood assumes the preprocessed matrix A simple co-expression strength measure suffices — use sclink_cor correlations rather than the penalized network step

skills.description: Use when single-cell 2D/3D dimension-reduction embeddings (UMAP/tSNE) with cell-type or cluster annotations are available and you need an area-based, quantitative measure of population overlap between cell types or clusters.
skills.name: quickhull-computational-geometry
skills.search_text: quickhull-computational-geometry Use when single-cell 2D/3D dimension-reduction embeddings (UMAP/tSNE) with cell-type or cluster annotations are available and you need an area-based, quantitative measure of population overlap between cell types or clusters. Input is raw single-cell expression data without precomputed dimension-reduction coordinates — run UMAP/tSNE first The goal is a Shannon-index (entropy) overlap measure rather than area-based convex hull overlap — use the entropy_2dvs3d code instead Cell populations are highly non-convex or multipolar, where a single convex hull per population poorly represents its footprint Quantifies pairwise overlap between cell-type/cluster populations in dimension-reduction plots by computing Quickhull convex hulls on 2D and 3D UMAP/tSNE projections and comparing hull-overlap areas, as used in the CellexalVR 2D-vs-3D analysis. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2021.103251
skills.summary: Quantifies pairwise overlap between cell-type/cluster populations in dimension-reduction plots by computing Quickhull convex hulls on 2D and 3D UMAP/tSNE projections and comparing hull-overlap areas, as used in the CellexalVR 2D-vs-3D analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw single-cell expression data without precomputed dimension-reduction coordinates — run UMAP/tSNE first The goal is a Shannon-index (entropy) overlap measure rather than area-based convex hull overlap — use the entropy_2dvs3d code instead Cell populations are highly non-convex or multipolar, where a single convex hull per population poorly represents its footprint

skills.description: Use when a supervised 2D embedding must reveal differentiation pathways across a prior cell-type clustering by linking each instance to denser, differently-labeled neighbors (e.g. scRNA-seq data with cluster assignments).
skills.name: quickshift-density-gradient-edge-computation
skills.search_text: quickshift-density-gradient-edge-computation Use when a supervised 2D embedding must reveal differentiation pathways across a prior cell-type clustering by linking each instance to denser, differently-labeled neighbors (e.g. scRNA-seq data with cluster assignments). All instances share the same class label — no denser different-label neighbors exist, so no k-shift edges can be formed The goal is pure cluster-membership visualization without differentiation-trajectory structure — the 'knn' same-label edges alone suffice Class assignments are unreliable placeholders rather than prior cluster knowledge, since edge direction and deletion depend on label differences http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Computes the 'k_shift' edges of the GraphDDP/GraphEmbed graph: each instance is linked to its d nearest neighbors that are denser (density = sum of pairwise cosine similarities) and carry a different class label. These quick-shift-style density-gradient edges encode candidate differentiation trajectories that the force-based (Kamada-Kawai) 2D layout renders in blue. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-05988-7
skills.summary: Computes the 'k_shift' edges of the GraphDDP/GraphEmbed graph: each instance is linked to its d nearest neighbors that are denser (density = sum of pairwise cosine similarities) and carry a different class label. These quick-shift-style density-gradient edges encode candidate differentiation trajectories that the force-based (Kamada-Kawai) 2D layout renders in blue.
skills.when_to_use_negative: All instances share the same class label — no denser different-label neighbors exist, so no k-shift edges can be formed The goal is pure cluster-membership visualization without differentiation-trajectory structure — the 'knn' same-label edges alone suffice Class assignments are unreliable placeholders rather than prior cluster knowledge, since edge direction and deletion depend on label differences

skills.description: Use when comparing expression distributions of pathway gene sets across conditions (e.g. COVID vs healthy, 0/12/24 h T cell activation) and you need to rank which pathways are most perturbed.
skills.name: qval-based-pathway-ranking
skills.search_text: qval-based-pathway-ranking Use when comparing expression distributions of pathway gene sets across conditions (e.g. COVID vs healthy, 0/12/24 h T cell activation) and you need to rank which pathways are most perturbed. When the question is only gene-set over-representation of a fixed gene list (e.g. ORA of DE genes) rather than comparing pathway expression distributions across cell populations When input is bulk expression or an already-summarized enrichment table with no per-cell data — SCPA requires single-cell expression matrices or Seurat/SCE objects When fold change direction alone is sufficient and distributional shape change is not of interest http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 Rank single-cell pathway perturbations by the SCPA qval statistic — a distribution-free measure of change in a pathway's multivariate expression distribution — treating fold change/enrichment only as secondary information. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.celrep.2022.111697
skills.summary: Rank single-cell pathway perturbations by the SCPA qval statistic — a distribution-free measure of change in a pathway's multivariate expression distribution — treating fold change/enrichment only as secondary information.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the question is only gene-set over-representation of a fixed gene list (e.g. ORA of DE genes) rather than comparing pathway expression distributions across cell populations When input is bulk expression or an already-summarized enrichment table with no per-cell data — SCPA requires single-cell expression matrices or Seurat/SCE objects When fold change direction alone is sufficient and distributional shape change is not of interest

skills.description: Use when an Mpath landmark graph (landmark coordinates, edges, and cell-to-landmark transition assignments) exists and cells must be assigned a pseudo-temporal ordering along each edge between adjacent landmarks.
skills.name: r-based-cell-ordering-implementation
skills.search_text: r-based-cell-ordering-implementation Use when an Mpath landmark graph (landmark coordinates, edges, and cell-to-landmark transition assignments) exists and cells must be assigned a pseudo-temporal ordering along each edge between adjacent landmarks. No ground-truth clone labels exist (e.g. the BE dataset, where the article notes the absence of ground truth about cell correspondence) — resampling/stability analyses are used instead The task is cell-to-cell assignment confidence rather than clonal prevalence comparison, since MaCroDNA, unlike clonealign, does not provide probabilistic confidence measures for its assignments http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Constructs a random cell-to-clone assignment baseline and plots true-vs-predicted clonal prevalences per method (MaCroDNA, clonealign, Seurat) against the diagonal, to judge whether an integration method beats chance on the CRC scTrio-seq benchmark. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-44014-3
skills.summary: Constructs a random cell-to-clone assignment baseline and plots true-vs-predicted clonal prevalences per method (MaCroDNA, clonealign, Seurat) against the diagonal, to judge whether an integration method beats chance on the CRC scTrio-seq benchmark.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No ground-truth clone labels exist (e.g. the BE dataset, where the article notes the absence of ground truth about cell correspondence) — resampling/stability analyses are used instead The task is cell-to-cell assignment confidence rather than clonal prevalence comparison, since MaCroDNA, unlike clonealign, does not provide probabilistic confidence measures for its assignments

skills.description: Use when validating lineage-inference or gene-expression-memory claims by comparing transcriptome similarity of barcode-defined related cell pairs against an equal-sized set of randomly sampled unrelated pairs from the same scRNA-seq dataset.
skills.name: random-cell-pair-sampling
skills.search_text: random-cell-pair-sampling Use when validating lineage-inference or gene-expression-memory claims by comparing transcriptome similarity of barcode-defined related cell pairs against an equal-sized set of randomly sampled unrelated pairs from the same scRNA-seq dataset. The population contains only distantly related cells, where GEMLI and memory-based similarity signals are known to perform less robustly The goal is de novo lineage prediction rather than validating a lineage-similarity signal; use the GEMLI predict_lineages / test_lineage_prediction workflow instead Expression values are raw counts rather than normalized, quality-controlled data, making whole-transcriptome Pearson correlations incomparable across cells http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Samples unrelated cell pairs (cells with different barcode IDs) from a normalized scRNA-seq expression matrix and computes their Pearson correlation distances as a negative-control distribution for testing whether lineage-related cells show gene expression memory. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-47158-y
skills.summary: Samples unrelated cell pairs (cells with different barcode IDs) from a normalized scRNA-seq expression matrix and computes their Pearson correlation distances as a negative-control distribution for testing whether lineage-related cells show gene expression memory.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The population contains only distantly related cells, where GEMLI and memory-based similarity signals are known to perform less robustly The goal is de novo lineage prediction rather than validating a lineage-similarity signal; use the GEMLI predict_lineages / test_lineage_prediction workflow instead Expression values are raw counts rather than normalized, quality-controlled data, making whole-transcriptome Pearson correlations incomparable across cells

skills.description: Use when clustering large-scale scRNA-seq count matrices (e.g., tens of thousands of cells such as the 68,578-cell human blood dataset) where running a base clustering algorithm on all pairwise cell relationships is computationally infeasible.
skills.name: random-cell-subsampling
skills.search_text: random-cell-subsampling Use when clustering large-scale scRNA-seq count matrices (e.g., tens of thousands of cells such as the 68,578-cell human blood dataset) where running a base clustering algorithm on all pairwise cell relationships is computationally infeasible. The dataset is small enough to cluster all cells directly without the O(n^2) memory/time burden (sscClust's ssc.run supports subsampling=F) Clustering accuracy on known labels is paramount and no feature-construction step will be added — the SCC strategy alone 'suffers from biases introduced by subsampling which may greatly decrease the clustering accuracy and robustness' Input is not a cell-level expression matrix (e.g., already aggregated pseudobulk or a feature table) http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A clustering strategy for large-scale scRNA-seq in which cells are randomly subsampled, the subset is clustered, and remaining cells are classified into those clusters, reducing computational complexity from O(n^2) to O(n). As implemented in the SSCC framework (sscClust), it is combined with Spearman-correlation feature construction to mitigate subsampling bias. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2018.10.003
skills.summary: A clustering strategy for large-scale scRNA-seq in which cells are randomly subsampled, the subset is clustered, and remaining cells are classified into those clusters, reducing computational complexity from O(n^2) to O(n). As implemented in the SSCC framework (sscClust), it is combined with Spearman-correlation feature construction to mitigate subsampling bias.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is small enough to cluster all cells directly without the O(n^2) memory/time burden (sscClust's ssc.run supports subsampling=F) Clustering accuracy on known labels is paramount and no feature-construction step will be added — the SCC strategy alone 'suffers from biases introduced by subsampling which may greatly decrease the clustering accuracy and robustness' Input is not a cell-level expression matrix (e.g., already aggregated pseudobulk or a feature table)

skills.description: Use when benchmarking or comparing runtime scaling of scRNA-seq pipelines across dataset sizes, and you need controlled random cell subsets drawn from a large public count matrix.
skills.name: random-cell-subsampling-from-scrna-seq-count-matrices
skills.search_text: random-cell-subsampling-from-scrna-seq-count-matrices Use when benchmarking or comparing runtime scaling of scRNA-seq pipelines across dataset sizes, and you need controlled random cell subsets drawn from a large public count matrix. The goal is a definitive biological result rather than a performance benchmark — subsampled cells may not preserve population structure or rare cell types The pipeline under test does not accept .csv or .parquet inputs and format conversion would confound the timing measurement The dataset is already small enough that runtime scaling differences cannot be distinguished from noise http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Draws random cell subsets of increasing size (e.g., 2,000–10,000 cells from the 68K PBMC dataset, Zheng et al. 2017, 10x Genomics) to generate benchmark inputs for measuring how an scRNA-seq pipeline's runtime scales with cell count under different compute configurations. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-025-12897-5
skills.summary: Draws random cell subsets of increasing size (e.g., 2,000–10,000 cells from the 68K PBMC dataset, Zheng et al. 2017, 10x Genomics) to generate benchmark inputs for measuring how an scRNA-seq pipeline's runtime scales with cell count under different compute configurations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a definitive biological result rather than a performance benchmark — subsampled cells may not preserve population structure or rare cell types The pipeline under test does not accept .csv or .parquet inputs and format conversion would confound the timing measurement The dataset is already small enough that runtime scaling differences cannot be distinguished from noise

skills.description: Use when you must quantify how stable an unsupervised cell clustering (e.g., SCASL spectral clustering on AS probabilities) is to sparsity, forced dropout, or cell sub-sampling, with a comparator clustering on gene expression.
skills.name: random-cell-subsampling-stability-analysis
skills.search_text: random-cell-subsampling-stability-analysis Use when you must quantify how stable an unsupervised cell clustering (e.g., SCASL spectral clustering on AS probabilities) is to sparsity, forced dropout, or cell sub-sampling, with a comparator clustering on gene expression. The goal is discovering new clusters rather than benchmarking stability of an existing clustering — run SCASL normally on the full unperturbed matrix instead The clustering input is already a complete, dense feature table without missing values — dropout robustness testing adds little information Only one perturbation level is feasible and no comparator method (e.g., gene-expression clustering) can be run — the skill's core output is the SCASL-vs-expression entropy comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Stress-tests cell cluster definitions by forcing 50% AS-value dropout and randomly retaining 100%, 75%, and 50% of cells, then comparing normalized entropy of re-clustered labels against the reference clustering. Applied to demonstrate that SCASL clusters from single-cell AS profiles are more robust and stable than Seurat-style gene-expression clusters. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-46480-9
skills.summary: Stress-tests cell cluster definitions by forcing 50% AS-value dropout and randomly retaining 100%, 75%, and 50% of cells, then comparing normalized entropy of re-clustered labels against the reference clustering. Applied to demonstrate that SCASL clusters from single-cell AS profiles are more robust and stable than Seurat-style gene-expression clusters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is discovering new clusters rather than benchmarking stability of an existing clustering — run SCASL normally on the full unperturbed matrix instead The clustering input is already a complete, dense feature table without missing values — dropout robustness testing adds little information Only one perturbation level is feasible and no comparator method (e.g., gene-expression clustering) can be run — the skill's core output is the SCASL-vs-expression entropy comparison

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether subtype-calling references built from randomly sampled cohort subsets (e.g., ten 60/40 ER+/ER− TCGA splits) change PAM50 labels, stability, or concordance with published calls.
skills.name: random-cohort-subset-sampling
skills.search_text: random-cohort-subset-sampling Use when evaluating whether subtype-calling references built from randomly sampled cohort subsets (e.g., ten 60/40 ER+/ER− TCGA splits) change PAM50 labels, stability, or concordance with published calls. The goal is single-sample classification of a new patient profile — use the pretrained AWCA-PAM50 or mLR single-sample callers instead of resampling the cohort. Comparing non-PAM50 classifiers such as AIMS or mLR feature-selected signatures, where reference-cohort resampling is not the mechanism being evaluated. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Draws repeated random 60/40 ER+/ER− stratified training/test splits of a TCGA RNA-seq cohort, builds an AWCA-based PAM50 reference from each 60% training subset, and quantifies how much the resulting classifications vary in concordance and stability versus standard median-based references. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-70832-2
skills.summary: Draws repeated random 60/40 ER+/ER− stratified training/test splits of a TCGA RNA-seq cohort, builds an AWCA-based PAM50 reference from each 60% training subset, and quantifies how much the resulting classifications vary in concordance and stability versus standard median-based references.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is single-sample classification of a new patient profile — use the pretrained AWCA-PAM50 or mLR single-sample callers instead of resampling the cohort. Comparing non-PAM50 classifiers such as AIMS or mLR feature-selected signatures, where reference-cohort resampling is not the mechanism being evaluated.

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how much of the scRNA-seq SNV recovery rate is due to read depth vs. caller bias, by simulating known variants in aligned reads.
skills.name: random-exonic-snv-simulation
skills.search_text: random-exonic-snv-simulation Use when you need to quantify how much of the scRNA-seq SNV recovery rate is due to read depth vs. caller bias, by simulating known variants in aligned reads. You need realistic somatic mutation spectra rather than uniform random exonic variants — random placement does not model mutation hotspots or allele-specific coverage Your data are bulk DNA-seq or whole-exome with deep, near-complete coverage; the depth-stratified TPR benchmark targets sparse single-cell transcriptome data You only need eeSNV ranking/feature selection — that is handled downstream by SSrGE's LASSO model, not by the simulation http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3569 Benchmark a GATK-based SNV calling pipeline for scRNA-seq by seeding each single-cell BAM with 50,000 randomly placed exonic SNVs as ground-truth variants, then computing true/false positive rates as a function of read depth. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-07170-5
skills.summary: Benchmark a GATK-based SNV calling pipeline for scRNA-seq by seeding each single-cell BAM with 50,000 randomly placed exonic SNVs as ground-truth variants, then computing true/false positive rates as a function of read depth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need realistic somatic mutation spectra rather than uniform random exonic variants — random placement does not model mutation hotspots or allele-specific coverage Your data are bulk DNA-seq or whole-exome with deep, near-complete coverage; the depth-stratified TPR benchmark targets sparse single-cell transcriptome data You only need eeSNV ranking/feature selection — that is handled downstream by SSrGE's LASSO model, not by the simulation

skills.description: Use when comparing imputation or normalization methods on labeled single-cell RNA-seq expression matrices and you need a classifier-based metric (out-of-bag error) of cell-type separation before vs after imputation.
skills.name: random-forest-cell-type-classification
skills.search_text: random-forest-cell-type-classification Use when comparing imputation or normalization methods on labeled single-cell RNA-seq expression matrices and you need a classifier-based metric (out-of-bag error) of cell-type separation before vs after imputation. Cell-identity labels are unavailable or unreliable, since the classifier requires supervised labels to produce OOB error The matrix is not in cells-as-rows, genes-as-columns orientation (ALRA/normalize_data expects this layout, and mixing it up silently corrupts the classification) The goal is clustering of unlabeled cells rather than quantifying class separability with a supervised metric http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Trains a ranger random forest with default settings to predict cell class from normalized (raw or imputed) scRNA-seq expression matrices and uses the out-of-bag classification error as a quantitative benchmark for whether imputation (e.g. ALRA vs MAGIC, SAVER, DCA, scImpute) improves cell-type separability. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-27729-z
skills.summary: Trains a ranger random forest with default settings to predict cell class from normalized (raw or imputed) scRNA-seq expression matrices and uses the out-of-bag classification error as a quantitative benchmark for whether imputation (e.g. ALRA vs MAGIC, SAVER, DCA, scImpute) improves cell-type separability.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Cell-identity labels are unavailable or unreliable, since the classifier requires supervised labels to produce OOB error The matrix is not in cells-as-rows, genes-as-columns orientation (ALRA/normalize_data expects this layout, and mixing it up silently corrupts the classification) The goal is clustering of unlabeled cells rather than quantifying class separability with a supervised metric

skills.name: random-forest-cell-type-classification-on-embeddings
skills.search_text: random-forest-cell-type-classification-on-embeddings Use when labeled single-cell data (e.g. BMMC cells with 14 manually gated populations) has been embedded with ivis and you need a quantitative accuracy readout of the embedding, especially for held-out cells mapped with the parametric transform. Cells are unlabeled or labels are too coarse/noisy to serve as ground truth for supervised evaluation The goal is the embedding itself (structure preservation, Mantel-test distance correlation) rather than a downstream classification-accuracy metric You plan to retrain a new dimensionality-reduction model on the held-out cells — this skill specifically evaluates the parametric out-of-sample transform without retraining http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Trains a random forest classifier on low-dimensional ivis embeddings to score cell-type label recovery, including for out-of-sample cells projected via ivis's parametric transform. Used to quantify how embedding quality (e.g. on BMMC subsamples) translates into classification accuracy. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-019-45301-0
skills.summary: Trains a random forest classifier on low-dimensional ivis embeddings to score cell-type label recovery, including for out-of-sample cells projected via ivis's parametric transform. Used to quantify how embedding quality (e.g. on BMMC subsamples) translates into classification accuracy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Cells are unlabeled or labels are too coarse/noisy to serve as ground truth for supervised evaluation The goal is the embedding itself (structure preservation, Mantel-test distance correlation) rather than a downstream classification-accuracy metric You plan to retrain a new dimensionality-reduction model on the held-out cells — this skill specifically evaluates the parametric out-of-sample transform without retraining

skills.search_text: random-forest-classification-evaluation Use when comparing filter FS algorithms on tabular data (data matrix + response): each algorithm's ranked feature list must be translated into downstream RF out-of-sample misclassification percentages to judge which selections generalize. skills.summary: Evaluate filter feature-selection algorithms by feeding their ranked feature subsets (1 to min(M,30) features) into a random forest (RF) classifier and recording the out-of-sample misclassification percentage, as done in the RRCT benchmark against 19 baseline FS algorithms across eight real-world datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to compare selections against known true features on synthetic data only — use the paper's false discovery rate (FDR) evaluation at the number of true features instead of RF misclassification When the dataset has no response variable — the RF evaluation is supervised and requires a data matrix plus response When more than 30 features need to be evaluated without truncation — the protocol caps evaluated subset size at min(M,30), so it will not characterize performance beyond the top 30 features

skills.description: Use when gene-expression data from CRC pre-clinical models (cell lines, organoids, PDXs) needs CMS1-CMS4 subtype calls, and you must quantify how the original primary-CRC classifier's stromal/immune signal dependency leaves samples (notably CMS4) unclassified.

Samples whose human stromal component differs from primary CRCs, e.g. metastatic CRC biopsies — CMScaller is not recommended there Datasets with fewer than approximately forty samples — centering/scaling inescapably introduces prediction uncertainty Single-cell RNA-seq data — it is exceedingly noisy and CMScaller is not optimized for it http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmark a tumor microenvironment-dependent CMS classifier (classifyCMS.RF) against the cancer cell-intrinsic CMScaller R package to reproduce its failure mode (219 unclassified, only 3 CMS4 of 551) and demonstrate recovery of all four CMS groups across CRC cell lines, organoids and PDXs. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-017-16747-x
skills.summary: Benchmark a tumor microenvironment-dependent CMS classifier (classifyCMS.RF) against the cancer cell-intrinsic CMScaller R package to reproduce its failure mode (219 unclassified, only 3 CMS4 of 551) and demonstrate recovery of all four CMS groups across CRC cell lines, organoids and PDXs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Samples whose human stromal component differs from primary CRCs, e.g. metastatic CRC biopsies — CMScaller is not recommended there Datasets with fewer than approximately forty samples — centering/scaling inescapably introduces prediction uncertainty Single-cell RNA-seq data — it is exceedingly noisy and CMScaller is not optimized for it

skills.search_text: random-forest-discrimination-auc Decision support for quantifying how realistic synthetic scRNA-seq cells are: train a random forest on real-vs-generated labels and use the resulting AUC, where values near 0.5 (positive control ~0.52) indicate generated cells are indistinguishable from real PBMC cells. The goal is comparing distributional fidelity (MMD) rather than classifier-based realism — use an MMD-based comparison instead Generated cells were produced from a different training set than the real cells, since the discriminator must compare matched real and synthetic data The synthetic data is not single-cell RNA-seq count data from this scGAN/Splatter/SUGAR workflow http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Train a random forest classifier to discriminate real scRNA-seq cells from GAN-generated cells and record the cross-validated AUC (RF-AUC) as a realism metric for synthetic data, benchmarked against Splatter and SUGAR on the Fresh 68k PBMCs (Donor A) dataset. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-019-14018-z
skills.summary: Train a random forest classifier to discriminate real scRNA-seq cells from GAN-generated cells and record the cross-validated AUC (RF-AUC) as a realism metric for synthetic data, benchmarked against Splatter and SUGAR on the Fresh 68k PBMCs (Donor A) dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is comparing distributional fidelity (MMD) rather than classifier-based realism — use an MMD-based comparison instead Generated cells were produced from a different training set than the real cells, since the discriminator must compare matched real and synthetic data The synthetic data is not single-cell RNA-seq count data from this scGAN/Splatter/SUGAR workflow

skills.description: Use when classifying unlabelled cancer genes into TSGs/OGs from somatic mutation feature matrices (37 ratio-metric/entropy features), e.g. pan-cancer or tissue-specific driver gene prediction with CGC training labels.
skills.name: random-forest-driver-gene-classification
skills.search_text: random-forest-driver-gene-classification Use when classifying unlabelled cancer genes into TSGs/OGs from somatic mutation feature matrices (37 ratio-metric/entropy features), e.g. pan-cancer or tissue-specific driver gene prediction with CGC training labels. Input genes already have TSG/OG labels or the goal is only to re-validate training-set genes rather than classify unlabelled genes Somatic mutation data contains samples with ≥2000 mutations or lacks COSMIC mutation-type annotations needed to compute the 37 ratio-metric/entropy features A background-mutation-rate method is required instead — cTaG deliberately avoids background mutation rate modelling and is not biased towards highly mutated genes, so it should not be used when such bias is desired http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Train and apply the cTaG random-forest model that classifies genes as tumour suppressor genes (TSGs) or oncogenes (OGs) using 37 ratio-metric and entropy mutation-type features from COSMIC somatic mutation data, with stable hyper-parameters estimated via fivefold cross-validation plus multiple random iterations to avoid overfitting. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-04015-y
skills.summary: Train and apply the cTaG random-forest model that classifies genes as tumour suppressor genes (TSGs) or oncogenes (OGs) using 37 ratio-metric and entropy mutation-type features from COSMIC somatic mutation data, with stable hyper-parameters estimated via fivefold cross-validation plus multiple random iterations to avoid overfitting.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input genes already have TSG/OG labels or the goal is only to re-validate training-set genes rather than classify unlabelled genes Somatic mutation data contains samples with ≥2000 mutations or lacks COSMIC mutation-type annotations needed to compute the 37 ratio-metric/entropy features A background-mutation-rate method is required instead — cTaG deliberately avoids background mutation rate modelling and is not biased towards highly mutated genes, so it should not be used when such bias is desired

skills.description: Use when a small labelled gene set (e.g. 136 TSGs and 76 OGs from CGC) must be extended to unlabelled genes using somatic mutation-derived features, and consensus across ensemble fold models is needed to reduce overfitting.
skills.name: random-forest-ensemble-inference
skills.search_text: random-forest-ensemble-inference Use when a small labelled gene set (e.g. 136 TSGs and 76 OGs from CGC) must be extended to unlabelled genes using somatic mutation-derived features, and consensus across ensemble fold models is needed to reduce overfitting. Input is already a classified driver-gene list or you only need mutation rates — MutSigCV-style rate estimation is the appropriate comparison tool, not ensemble re-classification Somatic mutation samples exceed the 2000-mutation filter used to build the feature matrix, or the goal is tissue-specific prediction from subsets with fewer than 1000 samples Labelled training genes are not available from CGC — the random forest requires TSG/OG labels to train per-fold models http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Apply a random-forest ensemble (cTaG pan-cancer model) to classify unlabelled genes as tumour suppressor genes (TSGs) or oncogenes (OGs) using 37 ratio-metric and entropy mutation features, then consolidate per-fold model predictions into a consensus set of candidate new driver genes. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-04015-y
skills.summary: Apply a random-forest ensemble (cTaG pan-cancer model) to classify unlabelled genes as tumour suppressor genes (TSGs) or oncogenes (OGs) using 37 ratio-metric and entropy mutation features, then consolidate per-fold model predictions into a consensus set of candidate new driver genes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a classified driver-gene list or you only need mutation rates — MutSigCV-style rate estimation is the appropriate comparison tool, not ensemble re-classification Somatic mutation samples exceed the 2000-mutation filter used to build the feature matrix, or the goal is tissue-specific prediction from subsets with fewer than 1000 samples Labelled training genes are not available from CGC — the random forest requires TSG/OG labels to train per-fold models

skills.description: Use when a small, class-imbalanced labelled gene set (e.g. 136 TSGs vs 76 OGs) must be ranked by which mutation-type features (entropy, frequency, ratio-metric) drive random forest classification, avoiding single-model importance instability.
skills.name: random-forest-feature-importance-ranking
skills.search_text: random-forest-feature-importance-ranking Use when a small, class-imbalanced labelled gene set (e.g. 136 TSGs vs 76 OGs) must be ranked by which mutation-type features (entropy, frequency, ratio-metric) drive random forest classification, avoiding single-model importance instability. The goal is predicting new driver genes on unlabelled genes rather than interpreting which features drive classification — use the consensus prediction pipeline (consolidateModelPredictions.py) instead. The input data lacks the entropy/frequency features (e.g. Tokheim et al. data where missense and frameshift entropy and frequency could not be calculated), so the 37-feature ranking cannot be reproduced. A background-mutation-rate-based driver prediction (e.g. MutSigCV) is intended; this skill addresses feature-based classification, which is explicitly not biased towards high mutation-rate genes. http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains a random forest classifier per fivefold cross-validation fold on a 37-feature gene-by-feature matrix (136 TSGs, 76 OGs), extracts per-fold feature importances, converts them to ranks, and averages ranks across folds to obtain a consensus importance ranking of mutation-type features for TSG vs OG classification. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-04015-y
skills.summary: Trains a random forest classifier per fivefold cross-validation fold on a 37-feature gene-by-feature matrix (136 TSGs, 76 OGs), extracts per-fold feature importances, converts them to ranks, and averages ranks across folds to obtain a consensus importance ranking of mutation-type features for TSG vs OG classification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is predicting new driver genes on unlabelled genes rather than interpreting which features drive classification — use the consensus prediction pipeline (consolidateModelPredictions.py) instead. The input data lacks the entropy/frequency features (e.g. Tokheim et al. data where missense and frameshift entropy and frequency could not be calculated), so the 37-feature ranking cannot be reproduced. A background-mutation-rate-based driver prediction (e.g. MutSigCV) is intended; this skill addresses feature-based classification, which is explicitly not biased towards high mutation-rate genes.

skills.description: Use when a log-normalized scRNA-seq expression matrix with initial cluster labels needs a supervised, label-aware gene ranking (HIG) to complement unsupervised HVG selection before rare cell type detection.
skills.name: random-forest-gene-importance-ranking
skills.search_text: random-forest-gene-importance-ranking Use when a log-normalized scRNA-seq expression matrix with initial cluster labels needs a supervised, label-aware gene ranking (HIG) to complement unsupervised HVG selection before rare cell type detection. Input is raw counts without initial cluster labels — the random forest requires supervised cluster assignments and cannot rank genes without them The analysis goal is purely unsupervised gene dispersion filtering — use Seurat-style mean vs dispersion HVG selection instead The dataset has few or degenerate clusters (e.g. no rare populations at all), making Gini importance dominated by abundant-type marker genes http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Rank genes by supervised importance using a random forest classifier trained on initial Louvain cluster labels, retaining the top 2000 highly important genes (HIG). In scCAD these HIG are merged with the top 2000 mean-dispersion HVG to build the gene set used for downstream rare cell type identification. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-51891-9
skills.summary: Rank genes by supervised importance using a random forest classifier trained on initial Louvain cluster labels, retaining the top 2000 highly important genes (HIG). In scCAD these HIG are merged with the top 2000 mean-dispersion HVG to build the gene set used for downstream rare cell type identification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw counts without initial cluster labels — the random forest requires supervised cluster assignments and cannot rank genes without them The analysis goal is purely unsupervised gene dispersion filtering — use Seurat-style mean vs dispersion HVG selection instead The dataset has few or degenerate clusters (e.g. no rare populations at all), making Gini importance dominated by abundant-type marker genes

skills.description: Use when classifying single-cell RNA-seq cells from CKG or gene expression feature matrices with supervised tree-based models, or when RF/GBM feature_importances_ rankings are needed to compare feature representations.
skills.name: random-forest-gradient-boosting-classification
skills.search_text: random-forest-gradient-boosting-classification Use when classifying single-cell RNA-seq cells from CKG or gene expression feature matrices with supervised tree-based models, or when RF/GBM feature_importances_ rankings are needed to compare feature representations. Input is raw reads or jellyfish k-mer files (BAM/FASTA) — the k-mer matrix, CKG generation, and cell matrix generation modules must run upstream before classification. The goal is CKG generation or k-mer compression itself (simhash fingerprinting); this skill starts from existing CKG/GE feature matrices with labels. No cell type labels are available — RF and GBM here are supervised classifiers that require the provided cell labels as targets. http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Trains scikit-learn random forest (RF) and gradient boosting (GBM) classifiers on single-cell feature representations — CKG compressed k-mer group cell matrices and gene expression (GE) matrices — to classify cell types, then ranks features via feature_importances_ to test whether CKG features capture signal comparable to gene expression features. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2021.102855
skills.summary: Trains scikit-learn random forest (RF) and gradient boosting (GBM) classifiers on single-cell feature representations — CKG compressed k-mer group cell matrices and gene expression (GE) matrices — to classify cell types, then ranks features via feature_importances_ to test whether CKG features capture signal comparable to gene expression features.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw reads or jellyfish k-mer files (BAM/FASTA) — the k-mer matrix, CKG generation, and cell matrix generation modules must run upstream before classification. The goal is CKG generation or k-mer compression itself (simhash fingerprinting); this skill starts from existing CKG/GE feature matrices with labels. No cell type labels are available — RF and GBM here are supervised classifiers that require the provided cell labels as targets.

skills.summary: Reproduces the cTaG random-forest classification of tumour suppressor genes (TSGs) and oncogenes (OGs) by performing fivefold cross-validation with iterative hyper-parameter estimation on a 37-feature pan-cancer mutation feature matrix, yielding stable per-class accuracy, precision, recall and F1 metrics despite a small training set of 136 TSGs and 76-77 OGs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a background mutation rate model is desired instead — cTaG is deliberately not biased towards genes with high mutation frequency, so it is the wrong tool if mutation-rate-based ranking (e.g. MutSigCV) is the goal When the goal is a three-way driver/TSG/OG classification on a single cancer type — the pan-cancer model uses binary TSG-vs-OG classification on COSMIC pan-cancer data, and tissue-specific models require feature matrices from tissues with greater than 1000 samples When input is a raw COSMIC mutation file — this skill starts from the already-built 37-feature matrix (FeatureMat.tsv); building features from mutation data is a separate step (identifyTSGOG.py)

skills.search_text: random-forest-vs-logistic-regression-benchmarking Use when benchmarking which classifier (random forest vs logistic regression) better drives active learning cell selection from single-cell expression data when the initial training set is randomly chosen and may not contain all cell types.
