skills.search_text: read-length-filtering-of-ribosome-footprints Use when preprocessing Ribo-seq FastQ files and only footprints within a defined nucleotide-length window (e.g. 25–35 nt, or a user-fixed range such as 20–22 nt) should be retained for analysis. skills.search_text: read-pair-segment-concatenation-parsing Use when input FASTQ libraries follow sequencing protocols whose cell-barcode/UMI layout is variable-length, floating-position, or split across multiple segments — i.e., not expressible as a single fixed-position barcode+UMI geometry a mapper like piscem natively supports. skills.summary: A tokenizer/parser for read-pair geometry strings (e.g., 10x Chromium v3 '1{b[16]u[12]x:}2{r:}', 10xv2 '1{b[16]u[10]x:}2{r:}', concatenated-barcode '1{b[16]u[12]b[4]x:}') that converts complex fragment layouts into fixed-position extraction records so simple-geometry mappers can process them unchanged.

skills.search_text: read-set-overlap-consistency-analysis Use when validating a new SPLiT-seq barcode/UMI identification tool against the original baseline by computing the overlap fraction of identified reads per sample on paired-end FASTQ data. Input data is not SPLiT-seq combinatorial-barcoded paired-end FASTQ (SCSit's fault-tolerant and indel alignment was proposed for SPLiT-seq data; other platforms are only potential future use) Goal is already-mapped read quantification rather than barcode/UMI identification consistency (downstream mapping with STAR to mm10-hg19 or mm10 is a separate step) Only one sample is available and a per-sample cross-method consistency range across five samples is required http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Reproduce the 96~97% per-sample consistency between reads identified by SCSit and reads identified by the original SPLiT-seq filtering method, by intersecting per-sample sets of (read ID, barcode combination, UMI) over five SPLiT-seq datasets. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.08.021
skills.summary: Reproduce the 96~97% per-sample consistency between reads identified by SCSit and reads identified by the original SPLiT-seq filtering method, by intersecting per-sample sets of (read ID, barcode combination, UMI) over five SPLiT-seq datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data is not SPLiT-seq combinatorial-barcoded paired-end FASTQ (SCSit's fault-tolerant and indel alignment was proposed for SPLiT-seq data; other platforms are only potential future use) Goal is already-mapped read quantification rather than barcode/UMI identification consistency (downstream mapping with STAR to mm10-hg19 or mm10 is a separate step) Only one sample is available and a per-sample cross-method consistency range across five samples is required

skills.description: Use when comparing multiple DNA storage pipeline designs (e.g., with/without MSA, with/without an inner code like HEDGES) on measured read density and write density outputs from fault-injection simulations, and you need the Pareto-optimal set.
skills.name: read-write-density-frontier-analysis
skills.search_text: read-write-density-frontier-analysis Use when comparing multiple DNA storage pipeline designs (e.g., with/without MSA, with/without an inner code like HEDGES) on measured read density and write density outputs from fault-injection simulations, and you need the Pareto-optimal set. You have only a single pipeline or error model — the frontier requires Pareto comparison across multiple pipelines' configurations. You lack fault-injection (simulated sequencing) outputs and only have analytical or theoretical density estimates not tied to an error model. Your metric of interest is not read/write density (e.g., you are studying decoding success rate alone). Computes the cross-pipeline Pareto frontier of read density vs. write density for DNA-based data storage designs under a fault-injection test bed (e.g., FrameD driven by the DNArSim nanopore channel model), and identifies which pipeline configurations compose the frontier. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad572
skills.summary: Computes the cross-pipeline Pareto frontier of read density vs. write density for DNA-based data storage designs under a fault-injection test bed (e.g., FrameD driven by the DNArSim nanopore channel model), and identifies which pipeline configurations compose the frontier.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have only a single pipeline or error model — the frontier requires Pareto comparison across multiple pipelines' configurations. You lack fault-injection (simulated sequencing) outputs and only have analytical or theoretical density estimates not tied to an error model. Your metric of interest is not read/write density (e.g., you are studying decoding success rate alone).

skills.description: Decision support for choosing a DNA storage encoding pipeline (RS vs HEDGES vs HEDGES-MSA) when fault-injection simulation outputs are available and trade-offs between read density (reads required for recovery) and write density must be compared across error rates.
skills.name: read-write-density-pareto-front-computation
skills.search_text: read-write-density-pareto-front-computation Decision support for choosing a DNA storage encoding pipeline (RS vs HEDGES vs HEDGES-MSA) when fault-injection simulation outputs are available and trade-offs between read density (reads required for recovery) and write density must be compared across error rates. When no fault-injection simulation results exist yet — this skill consumes FrameD 'fi.stats' outputs, it does not run the encoding/decoding fault injection itself When comparing pipelines under an error model not supported by the configured FrameD/DNArSim setup (e.g., custom error channels without a valid configuration JSON) http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 Computes read/write density Pareto fronts for DNA storage pipelines (e.g., RS, HEDGES, HEDGES-MSA) from FrameD fault-injection simulation results, to determine which pipeline configuration is optimal at a given error rate and error model. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad572
skills.summary: Computes read/write density Pareto fronts for DNA storage pipelines (e.g., RS, HEDGES, HEDGES-MSA) from FrameD fault-injection simulation results, to determine which pipeline configuration is optimal at a given error rate and error model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When no fault-injection simulation results exist yet — this skill consumes FrameD 'fi.stats' outputs, it does not run the encoding/decoding fault injection itself When comparing pipelines under an error model not supported by the configured FrameD/DNArSim setup (e.g., custom error channels without a valid configuration JSON)

skills.description: Use when inferring the spatial distance of a signaling pathway from scRNA-seq data with a SpaOTsc-derived cell–cell distance matrix, and known ligand, receptor, and downstream target gene lists are available (e.g. Wg/fz in the Drosophila embryo).
skills.name: receptor-weighted-sample-fitting
skills.search_text: receptor-weighted-sample-fitting Use when inferring the spatial distance of a signaling pathway from scRNA-seq data with a SpaOTsc-derived cell–cell distance matrix, and known ligand, receptor, and downstream target gene lists are available (e.g. Wg/fz in the Drosophila embryo). The signaling system's ligand, receptor, and downstream genes are unknown — the article notes that cell–cell communication inference relies on known genes involved in specific signaling No spatial cell–cell distance matrix exists yet — this skill requires the upstream SpaOTsc transport_plan/cell_cell_distance steps to have been run first Dataset is excessively large — the article warns the optimal-transport-based computation 'can become intractable when the dataset is excessively large' Fits random-forest regression models that predict downstream target gene expression from spatially aggregated ligand features, weighting each cell by its receptor expression so that the fit emphasizes cells capable of receiving the signal; used by SpaOTsc's infer_signal_range_ml to estimate spatial signaling ranges. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-15968-5
skills.summary: Fits random-forest regression models that predict downstream target gene expression from spatially aggregated ligand features, weighting each cell by its receptor expression so that the fit emphasizes cells capable of receiving the signal; used by SpaOTsc's infer_signal_range_ml to estimate spatial signaling ranges.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The signaling system's ligand, receptor, and downstream genes are unknown — the article notes that cell–cell communication inference relies on known genes involved in specific signaling No spatial cell–cell distance matrix exists yet — this skill requires the upstream SpaOTsc transport_plan/cell_cell_distance steps to have been run first Dataset is excessively large — the article warns the optimal-transport-based computation 'can become intractable when the dataset is excessively large'

skills.description: Use when a Scanpy AnnData object (scanpyobj.h5ad) from Single-Cell Data Analysis is available and you need cluster-wise IC50 and cell death percentage (drug kill efficacy) predictions for GDSC drugs.
skills.name: recommender-system-pharmacogenomic-inference
skills.search_text: recommender-system-pharmacogenomic-inference Use when a Scanpy AnnData object (scanpyobj.h5ad) from Single-Cell Data Analysis is available and you need cluster-wise IC50 and cell death percentage (drug kill efficacy) predictions for GDSC drugs. The input is raw 10x mtx or CSV scRNA-seq data that has not yet been clustered into a scanpyobj.h5ad by Single-Cell Data Analysis. The goal is PRISM drug sensitivity AUC prediction (--model PRISM, output AUC_prediction.csv) rather than GDSC IC50/kill-efficiency reporting. The drug of interest was not experimentally screened in the GDSC training data; scDrug's response prediction is limited to screened compounds. http://edamontology.org/topic_0202 Predicts drug response of single-cell-defined tumor clusters by estimating IC50 with the CaDRReS-Sc recommender system (GDSC pre-trained model) and converting predictions to cell death percentages reported as drug kill efficacy. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.11.055
skills.summary: Predicts drug response of single-cell-defined tumor clusters by estimating IC50 with the CaDRReS-Sc recommender system (GDSC pre-trained model) and converting predictions to cell death percentages reported as drug kill efficacy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw 10x mtx or CSV scRNA-seq data that has not yet been clustered into a scanpyobj.h5ad by Single-Cell Data Analysis. The goal is PRISM drug sensitivity AUC prediction (--model PRISM, output AUC_prediction.csv) rather than GDSC IC50/kill-efficiency reporting. The drug of interest was not experimentally screened in the GDSC training data; scDrug's response prediction is limited to screened compounds.

skills.description: Use when you have paired single-cell count matrices (genes as rows, cells as columns) from two consecutive time points and need to predict future expression states beyond that interval, e.g., forecasting 50-100 recursive steps or anticipating lineage bifurcations.
skills.name: recursive-multi-step-expression-forecasting
skills.search_text: recursive-multi-step-expression-forecasting Use when you have paired single-cell count matrices (genes as rows, cells as columns) from two consecutive time points and need to predict future expression states beyond that interval, e.g., forecasting 50-100 recursive steps or anticipating lineage bifurcations. Only a single static scRNA-seq snapshot is available with no paired time points — standard protocols destroy the cell, so the required t0/t1 pairing does not exist The goal is ordering cells along a trajectory rather than forecasting future expression values forward in time (trajectory inference methods address the former) Long-horizon forecasting is required well beyond the trained interval, e.g., training before a bifurcation and expecting fate prediction across it — accuracy holds only over a limited prediction horizon http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains a neural ODE (RNAForecaster, Tsit5 solver) on paired t0/t1 single-cell expression matrices and then feeds each prediction back into the input layer to forecast expression over many future time points (e.g., 50-200 recursive steps). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100793
skills.summary: Trains a neural ODE (RNAForecaster, Tsit5 solver) on paired t0/t1 single-cell expression matrices and then feeds each prediction back into the input layer to forecast expression over many future time points (e.g., 50-200 recursive steps).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single static scRNA-seq snapshot is available with no paired time points — standard protocols destroy the cell, so the required t0/t1 pairing does not exist The goal is ordering cells along a trajectory rather than forecasting future expression values forward in time (trajectory inference methods address the former) Long-horizon forecasting is required well beyond the trained interval, e.g., training before a bifurcation and expecting fate prediction across it — accuracy holds only over a limited prediction horizon

skills.description: Use when you have paired single-cell expression measurements of the same cells at two time points (e.g., metabolic labeling scEU-seq) and need to predict future expression states several steps beyond the observed horizon.
skills.name: recursive-transcriptomic-forecasting
skills.search_text: recursive-transcriptomic-forecasting Use when you have paired single-cell expression measurements of the same cells at two time points (e.g., metabolic labeling scEU-seq) and need to predict future expression states several steps beyond the observed horizon. The skill was validated on scEU-seq metabolic labeling data by scoring 72-hour forecasts against tricycle cell-cycle ordering. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100793
skills.summary: Train a neural ODE ensemble (RNAForecaster) on paired earlier/later single-cell expression matrices, then recursively feed predictions back through the network to forecast transcriptomic states multiple time steps ahead. The skill was validated on scEU-seq metabolic labeling data by scoring 72-hour forecasts against tricycle cell-cycle ordering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is standard scRNA-seq without metabolic labeling, since paired earlier/later measurements of the same cell are required but not available from destructive protocols The goal is cell ordering or pseudotime trajectory inference alone, not forward modeling of gene expression values over time Predictions are needed for rare events such as cell-cycle checkpoints, which the training population may not contain (the scEU-seq training set had only 405 cells)

The data are raw per-cell expression profiles rather than aggregated per-sample cell-type proportions — scCODA requires cell-type definitions from prior clustering The scientific question concerns within-condition response variability or donor-level heterogeneity, which scCODA explicitly does not model The expected effect is non-log-linear in covariates, since scCODA assumes a log-linear relationship between covariates and cell abundance http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Selecting the reference cell type for scCODA's Dirichlet-multinomial compositional model, either pre-specified (e.g., CD16+ monocytes in the supercentenarian PBMC analysis) or via scCODA's automatic reference selection (e.g., the UC colon lamina propria/epithelium analyses), so that credible spike-and-slab effects are interpretable relative to an abundant, stable baseline cell type. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-27150-6
skills.summary: Selecting the reference cell type for scCODA's Dirichlet-multinomial compositional model, either pre-specified (e.g., CD16+ monocytes in the supercentenarian PBMC analysis) or via scCODA's automatic reference selection (e.g., the UC colon lamina propria/epithelium analyses), so that credible spike-and-slab effects are interpretable relative to an abundant, stable baseline cell type.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are raw per-cell expression profiles rather than aggregated per-sample cell-type proportions — scCODA requires cell-type definitions from prior clustering The scientific question concerns within-condition response variability or donor-level heterogeneity, which scCODA explicitly does not model The expected effect is non-log-linear in covariates, since scCODA assumes a log-linear relationship between covariates and cell abundance

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether annotation accuracy of a cell-based method (e.g., SingleR) is reference-database dependent, or when testing whether substituting a curated tissue-specific reference such as CellMatch improves cluster annotation consistency.
skills.name: reference-database-substitution-analysis
skills.search_text: reference-database-substitution-analysis Use when evaluating whether annotation accuracy of a cell-based method (e.g., SingleR) is reference-database dependent, or when testing whether substituting a curated tissue-specific reference such as CellMatch improves cluster annotation consistency. The goal is to evaluate scCATCH itself rather than reference-database sensitivity of an existing annotation tool — use the full scCATCH comparison workflow (findmarkergene/findcelltype) instead The scRNA-seq dataset has no trusted benchmark or ground-truth labels, so annotation consistency cannot be computed The species or tissue of interest is not represented in CellMatch (human/mouse references across 184 tissue types), since the article notes a limited reference database can lead to incorrect annotation http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 A benchmarking skill that swaps the reference database underlying a cell-annotation tool (SingleR's default ImmGen/HPCA/Encode/Blueprint references) with an alternative (scCATCH's CellMatch: 353 cell types, 686 subtypes, 184 tissues, 2,096 human/mouse references) and quantifies the impact on annotation consistency against benchmark labels. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2020.100882
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill that swaps the reference database underlying a cell-annotation tool (SingleR's default ImmGen/HPCA/Encode/Blueprint references) with an alternative (scCATCH's CellMatch: 353 cell types, 686 subtypes, 184 tissues, 2,096 human/mouse references) and quantifies the impact on annotation consistency against benchmark labels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to evaluate scCATCH itself rather than reference-database sensitivity of an existing annotation tool — use the full scCATCH comparison workflow (findmarkergene/findcelltype) instead The scRNA-seq dataset has no trusted benchmark or ground-truth labels, so annotation consistency cannot be computed The species or tissue of interest is not represented in CellMatch (human/mouse references across 184 tissue types), since the article notes a limited reference database can lead to incorrect annotation

skills.description: Use when a clustered Scanpy AnnData object (scanpyobj.h5ad) needs cell type labels per Louvain cluster, or when single-cell clusters must be matched against a curated reference GEP dataset like FANTOM5.
skills.name: reference-dataset-matching-scmatch
skills.search_text: reference-dataset-matching-scmatch Use when a clustered Scanpy AnnData object (scanpyobj.h5ad) needs cell type labels per Louvain cluster, or when single-cell clusters must be matched against a curated reference GEP dataset like FANTOM5. Cells have not yet been clustered — scMatch within scDrug annotates cluster-wise average GEPs, not individual raw cells No suitable reference dataset is available for the tissue/cell types of interest (FANTOM5 and SingleR-merged references cover specific curated cell types) The goal is drug response prediction (use Drug Response Prediction with CaDRReS-Sc / PRISM models), not cell type identification http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Cluster-wise cell type annotation for scRNA-seq data using scMatch, which scores each cluster's average gene expression profile against reference datasets such as the truncated FANTOM5 database (916 cell types) to assign a known cell type label. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.11.055
skills.summary: Cluster-wise cell type annotation for scRNA-seq data using scMatch, which scores each cluster's average gene expression profile against reference datasets such as the truncated FANTOM5 database (916 cell types) to assign a known cell type label.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Cells have not yet been clustered — scMatch within scDrug annotates cluster-wise average GEPs, not individual raw cells No suitable reference dataset is available for the tissue/cell types of interest (FANTOM5 and SingleR-merged references cover specific curated cell types) The goal is drug response prediction (use Drug Response Prediction with CaDRReS-Sc / PRISM models), not cell type identification

skills.description: Use when analyzing multi-cellular pixel-resolution ST data (e.g., Spatial Transcriptomics, 10X Visium, DBiT-seq) and no appropriate scRNA-seq reference exists, or when the goal is to recover cell-type-specific gene-expression changes from mixed pixel measurements.
skills.name: reference-free-cell-type-deconvolution
skills.search_text: reference-free-cell-type-deconvolution Use when analyzing multi-cellular pixel-resolution ST data (e.g., Spatial Transcriptomics, 10X Visium, DBiT-seq) and no appropriate scRNA-seq reference exists, or when the goal is to recover cell-type-specific gene-expression changes from mixed pixel measurements. Input is sub-cellular pixel-resolution ST data; the authors state STdeconvolve may not be best suited for that resolution and new methods will be needed Genes lack variability across pixels due to homogeneous/uniform cell-type proportions across pixels, or the data are too sparse with high stochastic drop-out rates Tissue covers only a few pixels (e.g., tissue slivers or thin structures), which presents challenges for deconvolution http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 STdeconvolve applies latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) to multi-cellular pixel-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) data to recover cell-type transcriptional profiles (beta) and their pixel-level proportions (theta) without any single-cell RNA-seq reference. It is an unsupervised alternative to reference-based methods (SPOTlight, RCTD, spatialDWLS) when no suitable scRNA-seq reference exists. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-30033-z
skills.summary: STdeconvolve applies latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) to multi-cellular pixel-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) data to recover cell-type transcriptional profiles (beta) and their pixel-level proportions (theta) without any single-cell RNA-seq reference. It is an unsupervised alternative to reference-based methods (SPOTlight, RCTD, spatialDWLS) when no suitable scRNA-seq reference exists.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is sub-cellular pixel-resolution ST data; the authors state STdeconvolve may not be best suited for that resolution and new methods will be needed Genes lack variability across pixels due to homogeneous/uniform cell-type proportions across pixels, or the data are too sparse with high stochastic drop-out rates Tissue covers only a few pixels (e.g., tissue slivers or thin structures), which presents challenges for deconvolution

skills.description: Use when the input is a multi-cellular pixel-resolution ST count matrix (e.g. Spatial Transcriptomics, 10X Visium, DBiT-seq pixels) and no suitable matched scRNA-seq reference exists for supervised deconvolution.
skills.name: reference-free-cell-type-proportion-inference
skills.search_text: reference-free-cell-type-proportion-inference Use when the input is a multi-cellular pixel-resolution ST count matrix (e.g. Spatial Transcriptomics, 10X Visium, DBiT-seq pixels) and no suitable matched scRNA-seq reference exists for supervised deconvolution. Sub-cellular pixel-resolution ST data, where new methods specific to that resolution are anticipated to be needed Datasets where cell-type proportions are homogeneous/uniform across pixels so genes lack variability, or where ST profiles thin tissue structures covering only a few pixels Very sparse ST data with high stochastic drop-out rates, where the LDA model may struggle to identify distinct groups of co-expressed genes Reference-free (unsupervised) deconvolution of multi-cellular pixel-resolution spatial transcriptomics data using latent Dirichlet allocation (STdeconvolve), which recovers per-pixel cell-type proportions (theta) and cell-type transcriptional profiles (beta) without a single-cell reference. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-30033-z
skills.summary: Reference-free (unsupervised) deconvolution of multi-cellular pixel-resolution spatial transcriptomics data using latent Dirichlet allocation (STdeconvolve), which recovers per-pixel cell-type proportions (theta) and cell-type transcriptional profiles (beta) without a single-cell reference.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Sub-cellular pixel-resolution ST data, where new methods specific to that resolution are anticipated to be needed Datasets where cell-type proportions are homogeneous/uniform across pixels so genes lack variability, or where ST profiles thin tissue structures covering only a few pixels Very sparse ST data with high stochastic drop-out rates, where the LDA model may struggle to identify distinct groups of co-expressed genes

skills.description: Use when you have raw CT qPCR array data with many candidate reference genes/miRNAs and need to select and benchmark the most stable weighted combination (virtual reference gene) across candidate weighting schemes.
skills.name: reference-gene-combination-benchmarking
skills.search_text: reference-gene-combination-benchmarking Use when you have raw CT qPCR array data with many candidate reference genes/miRNAs and need to select and benchmark the most stable weighted combination (virtual reference gene) across candidate weighting schemes. You only have 2-3 preselected internal controls and no combinatorial search is needed — use calcWeight directly instead of run_experiment Aggregating more than 5 reference genes — geom(sd) does not have expected benefits compared to the regular geometric mean in that regime Input data are already normalized expression values without raw CT values and sample size does not support weight optimization on normalized data http://edamontology.org/topic_3519 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmarks weighted aggregation methods (geom(sd), geom(cv), arith(sd), arith(cv), plus the unweighted geometric mean) for combining qPCR reference genes into a stable virtual reference, using the InterOpt R package on qPCR array datasets with SD, CV, GeNorm, and NormFinder stability measures. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2023.107945
skills.summary: Benchmarks weighted aggregation methods (geom(sd), geom(cv), arith(sd), arith(cv), plus the unweighted geometric mean) for combining qPCR reference genes into a stable virtual reference, using the InterOpt R package on qPCR array datasets with SD, CV, GeNorm, and NormFinder stability measures.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have 2-3 preselected internal controls and no combinatorial search is needed — use calcWeight directly instead of run_experiment Aggregating more than 5 reference genes — geom(sd) does not have expected benefits compared to the regular geometric mean in that regime Input data are already normalized expression values without raw CT values and sample size does not support weight optimization on normalized data

skills.description: Use when you have a gene expression DataFrame (e.g. GEO microarray data like GSE125792 or GSE4786, probe-level or gene-level) and need to identify stable endogenous reference genes for qPCR/microarray normalization in Python.
skills.name: reference-gene-screening
skills.search_text: reference-gene-screening Use when you have a gene expression DataFrame (e.g. GEO microarray data like GSE125792 or GSE4786, probe-level or gene-level) and need to identify stable endogenous reference genes for qPCR/microarray normalization in Python. Your toolchain is R or Excel — the article notes geNorm (qbase+/Excel) and Normfinder (R/Excel) exist there; ERgene fills the absence of a Python screening package You intend to normalize with a single reference gene without evidence of invariable expression — MIQE guidelines make this unacceptable unless clearly demonstrated The dataset is too large with computational depth set too large — efficiency declines at depth 3+ and there may be no result http://edamontology.org/topic_3512 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Screen candidate endogenous reference genes from a gene expression matrix using ERgene's FindERG function, which applies the inverse process of the internal reference method with robust matrix block operation (1000-gene blocks) and returns the top 20 genes ranked by smallest variance of relative factor change. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-75586-5
skills.summary: Screen candidate endogenous reference genes from a gene expression matrix using ERgene's FindERG function, which applies the inverse process of the internal reference method with robust matrix block operation (1000-gene blocks) and returns the top 20 genes ranked by smallest variance of relative factor change.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your toolchain is R or Excel — the article notes geNorm (qbase+/Excel) and Normfinder (R/Excel) exist there; ERgene fills the absence of a Python screening package You intend to normalize with a single reference gene without evidence of invariable expression — MIQE guidelines make this unacceptable unless clearly demonstrated The dataset is too large with computational depth set too large — efficiency declines at depth 3+ and there may be no result

skills.description: Use when a raw gene expression matrix (tab-delimited GSE-style file or Pandas DataFrame) must be screened for stable endogenous reference genes by ranking ΔF variance, or when reproducing/validating ERgene's FindERG top-20 output.
skills.name: reference-gene-stability-variance-ranking
skills.search_text: reference-gene-stability-variance-ranking Use when a raw gene expression matrix (tab-delimited GSE-style file or Pandas DataFrame) must be screened for stable endogenous reference genes by ranking ΔF variance, or when reproducing/validating ERgene's FindERG top-20 output. The goal is normalization of expression data by already-selected reference genes — use ERgene.normalizationdata / Ergene.Normalizationdata instead of FindERG screening The investigator intends to normalize with a single reference gene without evidence of invariable expression — MIQE guidelines deem this unacceptable, so a stability screen (or multi-gene set) is required instead The computational depth is set very large, where efficiency declines and the program may return no result http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Implements ERgene's inverse internal-reference algorithm: build per-sample relative correction factor matrices (F1, F2), compute their difference ΔF, rank genes by the variance of ΔF across samples, and return the top 20 most stable candidate endogenous reference genes. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-75586-5
skills.summary: Implements ERgene's inverse internal-reference algorithm: build per-sample relative correction factor matrices (F1, F2), compute their difference ΔF, rank genes by the variance of ΔF across samples, and return the top 20 most stable candidate endogenous reference genes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is normalization of expression data by already-selected reference genes — use ERgene.normalizationdata / Ergene.Normalizationdata instead of FindERG screening The investigator intends to normalize with a single reference gene without evidence of invariable expression — MIQE guidelines deem this unacceptable, so a stability screen (or multi-gene set) is required instead The computational depth is set very large, where efficiency declines and the program may return no result

skills.description: Use when raw CT values (or a compatible normalized high-throughput dataset) are available for 2 or more internal controls and a weighted mean must replace the unweighted geometric mean for ΔΔCT normalization.
skills.name: reference-gene-weight-optimization
skills.search_text: reference-gene-weight-optimization Use when raw CT values (or a compatible normalized high-throughput dataset) are available for 2 or more internal controls and a weighted mean must replace the unweighted geometric mean for ΔΔCT normalization. When aggregating more than ~5 reference genes — geom(sd) does not have expected benefits over the regular geometric mean in that regime When only a very small qPCR sample set (e.g. ~20 samples) is available and no biologically compatible external dataset exists for weight optimization When a single reference gene suffices or the experiment design does not permit computing CT values for multiple internal controls http://edamontology.org/topic_3519 http://edamontology.org/topic_0204 Computes optimal aggregation weights for combining multiple qPCR reference genes (internal controls) into a single virtual reference gene via weighted mean, using the InterOpt weighting methods (geom(sd), geom(cv), arith(sd), arith(cv)), with geom(sd) as the best-performing candidate. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2023.107945
skills.summary: Computes optimal aggregation weights for combining multiple qPCR reference genes (internal controls) into a single virtual reference gene via weighted mean, using the InterOpt weighting methods (geom(sd), geom(cv), arith(sd), arith(cv)), with geom(sd) as the best-performing candidate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When aggregating more than ~5 reference genes — geom(sd) does not have expected benefits over the regular geometric mean in that regime When only a very small qPCR sample set (e.g. ~20 samples) is available and no biologically compatible external dataset exists for weight optimization When a single reference gene suffices or the experiment design does not permit computing CT values for multiple internal controls

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a sequence-search pre-filter or distributed read mapper against reference collections that must be partitioned into bins, or when reproducing the Raptor Table 7 DREAM-Yara experiments on clustered NCBI RefSeq data.
skills.name: reference-genome-binning-dataset-preparation
skills.search_text: reference-genome-binning-dataset-preparation Use when benchmarking a sequence-search pre-filter or distributed read mapper against reference collections that must be partitioned into bins, or when reproducing the Raptor Table 7 DREAM-Yara experiments on clustered NCBI RefSeq data. The task requires genome assembly or single-genome annotation rather than partitioning many reference genomes into search bins. Benchmarks must use real, uneven clinical/metagenomic samples — the paper notes the main limiting factor of the method is its susceptibility to uneven bin sizes and a high number of bins. Only a small collection of genomes is involved, where a plain FM-index mapper without binning is sufficient. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Prepare taxonomically clustered reference-genome bin sets (e.g., Clustered NCBI RefSeq with 64 or 1,024 bins) and matching artificial query read sets, using TaxSBP hierarchical bin packing over the NCBI Taxonomy, so that pre-filter/mapping benchmarks like the Raptor DREAM-Yara case study can be reproduced. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2021.102782
skills.summary: Prepare taxonomically clustered reference-genome bin sets (e.g., Clustered NCBI RefSeq with 64 or 1,024 bins) and matching artificial query read sets, using TaxSBP hierarchical bin packing over the NCBI Taxonomy, so that pre-filter/mapping benchmarks like the Raptor DREAM-Yara case study can be reproduced.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires genome assembly or single-genome annotation rather than partitioning many reference genomes into search bins. Benchmarks must use real, uneven clinical/metagenomic samples — the paper notes the main limiting factor of the method is its susceptibility to uneven bin sizes and a high number of bins. Only a small collection of genomes is involved, where a plain FM-index mapper without binning is sufficient.

skills.description: Use when preparing a reference for alevin-fry/simpleaf single-cell RNA-seq quantification: you have a genome FASTA plus GTF/GFF3 annotation and need a spliced+intronic (splici) or spliced+unspliced (spliceu) expanded reference with a piscem index.
skills.name: reference-genome-expanded-reference-construction
skills.search_text: reference-genome-expanded-reference-construction Use when preparing a reference for alevin-fry/simpleaf single-cell RNA-seq quantification: you have a genome FASTA plus GTF/GFF3 annotation and need a spliced+intronic (splici) or spliced+unspliced (spliceu) expanded reference with a piscem index. The reference is already indexed or the analysis consumes a pre-built piscem/alevin-fry index rather than raw genome FASTA + GTF Bulk RNA-seq or scATAC mapping, where piscem map-bulk/map-sc-atac use non-spliced or genome-mode references and splici transcriptome expansion is inappropriate Quantification against a probe set without a genome FASTA+GTF pair, unless you intend the probe-set CSV to FASTA conversion path rather than splici construction Builds an expanded (splici/spliceu) reference from a genome FASTA and GTF using roers via the simpleaf index command, then indexes it with piscem build, yielding the ref FASTA, 3-column transcript-to-gene map, and piscem index needed for alevin-fry single-cell quantification. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad614
skills.summary: Builds an expanded (splici/spliceu) reference from a genome FASTA and GTF using roers via the simpleaf index command, then indexes it with piscem build, yielding the ref FASTA, 3-column transcript-to-gene map, and piscem index needed for alevin-fry single-cell quantification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reference is already indexed or the analysis consumes a pre-built piscem/alevin-fry index rather than raw genome FASTA + GTF Bulk RNA-seq or scATAC mapping, where piscem map-bulk/map-sc-atac use non-spliced or genome-mode references and splici transcriptome expansion is inappropriate Quantification against a probe set without a genome FASTA+GTF pair, unless you intend the probe-set CSV to FASTA conversion path rather than splici construction

skills.description: Use when preparing an RNA-seq alignment reference: a genome FASTA plus Ensembl GTF must be compiled into a STAR index, or the reference must be re-built after masking known variant positions with Bedtools to reduce reference-allele bias.
skills.name: reference-genome-indexing
skills.search_text: reference-genome-indexing Use when preparing an RNA-seq alignment reference: a genome FASTA plus Ensembl GTF must be compiled into a STAR index, or the reference must be re-built after masking known variant positions with Bedtools to reduce reference-allele bias. Input is already an aligned BAM produced with a consistent genome build and GTF — indexing is unnecessary and would not change results Genome and GTF come from mismatched builds/annotations (e.g., Gallus_gallus_6.0 GTF with Gallus_gallus_5.0 FASTA) — rebuild with a coherent pair instead Short-read DNA variant calling against GRCh38/other non-chicken references — the index specifics here are Gallus gallus and RNA-seq oriented http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Builds a STAR splice-aware genome index from a Gallus gallus reference genome build plus matching Ensembl GTF annotation (and, when needed, a Bedtools-masked variant-corrected genome) so that two-pass STAR RNA-seq alignment can run correctly. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-83459-8
skills.summary: Builds a STAR splice-aware genome index from a Gallus gallus reference genome build plus matching Ensembl GTF annotation (and, when needed, a Bedtools-masked variant-corrected genome) so that two-pass STAR RNA-seq alignment can run correctly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an aligned BAM produced with a consistent genome build and GTF — indexing is unnecessary and would not change results Genome and GTF come from mismatched builds/annotations (e.g., Gallus_gallus_6.0 GTF with Gallus_gallus_5.0 FASTA) — rebuild with a coherent pair instead Short-read DNA variant calling against GRCh38/other non-chicken references — the index specifics here are Gallus gallus and RNA-seq oriented

skills.description: Use when RNA-seq-based ASE or allele-count analyses show inflated reference allele ratios (e.g., >51%) and you need to quantify or mitigate mapping bias before calling ASE from biallelic SNP allele depths.
skills.name: reference-genome-masking-with-variants
skills.search_text: reference-genome-masking-with-variants Use when RNA-seq-based ASE or allele-count analyses show inflated reference allele ratios (e.g., >51%) and you need to quantify or mitigate mapping bias before calling ASE from biallelic SNP allele depths. Input is whole-genome DNA-seq or already reference-unbiased data where no reference allele inflation is observed No variant call set is available to build a global VCF for masking, so variant positions cannot be defined The analysis targets non-biallelic or multi-allelic variants that VADT filtering would remove anyway http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Reduces reference-allele mapping bias in allele-specific expression (ASE) analyses by masking the reference genome (Gallus_gallus_5.0) at variant positions using Bedtools and re-aligning RNA-seq reads with STAR two-pass, shifting per-tissue reference allele ratios toward the expected 50%. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-83459-8
skills.summary: Reduces reference-allele mapping bias in allele-specific expression (ASE) analyses by masking the reference genome (Gallus_gallus_5.0) at variant positions using Bedtools and re-aligning RNA-seq reads with STAR two-pass, shifting per-tissue reference allele ratios toward the expected 50%.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is whole-genome DNA-seq or already reference-unbiased data where no reference allele inflation is observed No variant call set is available to build a global VCF for masking, so variant positions cannot be defined The analysis targets non-biallelic or multi-allelic variants that VADT filtering would remove anyway

skills.description: Use when a clustering/statistical flagging step yields a candidate cell or feature set and a published reference set (count or labeled IDs) exists for the same dataset to verify against.
skills.name: reference-label-overlap-comparison
skills.search_text: reference-label-overlap-comparison Use when a clustering/statistical flagging step yields a candidate cell or feature set and a published reference set (count or labeled IDs) exists for the same dataset to verify against. No published reference set or labeled ground truth exists for the dataset — there is nothing to compare the flagged set against The goal is pseudotime trajectory reconstruction itself (use the redpath cHMT pipeline) rather than validating a flagged cell set Input data lacks cell-cycle scores (e.g. no reCAT output), so no G0-like flagging can be produced for comparison Validates a newly derived cell set (e.g. redPATH's G0-like cells flagged via k-means on reCAT mean cell-cycle scores and pairwise ANOVA at P < 0.001) by computing its overlap against a published reference count or label list (e.g. the 89 G0-like cells removed from the 145-cell Llorens-Bobadilla neural stem cell dataset). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2020.06.014

skills.when_to_use_negative: No published reference set or labeled ground truth exists for the dataset — there is nothing to compare the flagged set against The goal is pseudotime trajectory reconstruction itself (use the redpath cHMT pipeline) rather than validating a flagged cell set Input data lacks cell-cycle scores (e.g. no reCAT output), so no G0-like flagging can be produced for comparison

skills.name: reference-label-transfer-evaluation
skills.search_text: reference-label-transfer-evaluation Use when prior reference-annotations (e.g., Azimuth label transfer, Seurat label transfer, cellHarmony) must be reconciled with Leiden clusters from one or more modalities, or when benchmarking clustering solutions against a reference atlas with Homogeneity/Completeness/V-Measure. skills.description: Use when scRNA-seq query data (raw counts, 10x/h5 or Seurat objects) must be mapped onto a pre-built reference atlas — e.g. the LCMV viral CD8+ T cell atlas — to quantify how a perturbation (KO, infection condition) shifts cell subtype frequencies.
skills.name: reference-map-projection-of-query-cells
skills.search_text: reference-map-projection-of-query-cells Use when scRNA-seq query data (raw counts, 10x/h5 or Seurat objects) must be mapped onto a pre-built reference atlas — e.g. the LCMV viral CD8+ T cell atlas — to quantify how a perturbation (KO, infection condition) shifts cell subtype frequencies. Only cell state labels are needed and query dimensionality reductions must be preserved — use the classifier mode (ProjecTILs.classifier) rather than full reference embedding The cell types of interest (e.g. CD4+ TIL subtypes, gamma-delta T cells) are under-represented or absent from the available reference atlases The goal is de novo discovery of transcriptomic states without an annotated reference — unsupervised clustering may be preferable, though ProjecTILs can flag cells that deviate from reference subtypes http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 Project new single-cell RNA-seq query data (e.g. Ptpn2-KO/WT or Tox-KO P14 T cells) onto a curated reference T cell atlas with ProjecTILs, embedding queries in the reference PCA/UMAP space and assigning cell state labels by nearest-neighbor prediction, without altering the reference structure. This enables direct comparison of cell subtype composition across perturbation conditions in a stable system of coordinates. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-23324-4
skills.summary: Project new single-cell RNA-seq query data (e.g. Ptpn2-KO/WT or Tox-KO P14 T cells) onto a curated reference T cell atlas with ProjecTILs, embedding queries in the reference PCA/UMAP space and assigning cell state labels by nearest-neighbor prediction, without altering the reference structure. This enables direct comparison of cell subtype composition across perturbation conditions in a stable system of coordinates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only cell state labels are needed and query dimensionality reductions must be preserved — use the classifier mode (ProjecTILs.classifier) rather than full reference embedding The cell types of interest (e.g. CD4+ TIL subtypes, gamma-delta T cells) are under-represented or absent from the available reference atlases The goal is de novo discovery of transcriptomic states without an annotated reference — unsupervised clustering may be preferable, though ProjecTILs can flag cells that deviate from reference subtypes

skills.description: Use when choosing a reference-mapping tool for scRNA-seq data and you need quantitative evidence on projection fidelity and cell-state classification accuracy rather than qualitative UMAP comparisons.
skills.name: reference-mapping-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: reference-mapping-benchmark-comparison Use when choosing a reference-mapping tool for scRNA-seq data and you need quantitative evidence on projection fidelity and cell-state classification accuracy rather than qualitative UMAP comparisons. You have no labeled reference atlas or no ground-truth cell state annotations, so cross-validated accuracy cannot be scored You want to project genuinely novel query data rather than benchmark mapping methods — use Run.ProjecTILs directly instead of splitting the reference Your goal is atlas integration/batch correction rather than projecting new data into a fixed reference space (STACAS, Harmony or Seurat integration is the wrong comparator here) http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 A cross-validation benchmarking protocol that quantifies how accurately ProjecTILs projects and classifies held-out scRNA-seq data onto a reference T cell atlas, and compares it head-to-head against alternative reference-mapping methods (Azimuth/Seurat 4, scmap) using shared projection- and label-accuracy metrics. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-23324-4
skills.summary: A cross-validation benchmarking protocol that quantifies how accurately ProjecTILs projects and classifies held-out scRNA-seq data onto a reference T cell atlas, and compares it head-to-head against alternative reference-mapping methods (Azimuth/Seurat 4, scmap) using shared projection- and label-accuracy metrics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have no labeled reference atlas or no ground-truth cell state annotations, so cross-validated accuracy cannot be scored You want to project genuinely novel query data rather than benchmark mapping methods — use Run.ProjecTILs directly instead of splitting the reference Your goal is atlas integration/batch correction rather than projecting new data into a fixed reference space (STACAS, Harmony or Seurat integration is the wrong comparator here)

skills.description: Use when a trained cell-annotation model has produced ranked per-class feature/biomarker lists and you need to quantify how many of the top-K markers are literature-validated, or compare marker recall across tools.
skills.name: reference-marker-database-mapping
skills.search_text: reference-marker-database-mapping Use when a trained cell-annotation model has produced ranked per-class feature/biomarker lists and you need to quantify how many of the top-K markers are literature-validated, or compare marker recall across tools. No reference marker set exists for the target classes — the README notes gene recall curve was skipped for COVID-19/normal conditions because 'there are many possibilities of genes in the case of normal conditions'. A comparison tool does not expose per-class feature importances (scBalance, scvi, devCellPy, CellPLM cannot produce ranked top features), making recall comparison impossible. Goal is differential gene expression (DGE) rather than validated marker recall — use DgePseudoBulk/DgeLMEM instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Maps ranked cell-type biomarkers predicted by a trained model (e.g. scaLR) onto a curated reference marker database such as CellMarker2.0, computing per-cell-type overlap (recall) counts and gene recall curves to validate biomarker discovery. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbaf243
skills.summary: Maps ranked cell-type biomarkers predicted by a trained model (e.g. scaLR) onto a curated reference marker database such as CellMarker2.0, computing per-cell-type overlap (recall) counts and gene recall curves to validate biomarker discovery.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No reference marker set exists for the target classes — the README notes gene recall curve was skipped for COVID-19/normal conditions because 'there are many possibilities of genes in the case of normal conditions'. A comparison tool does not expose per-class feature importances (scBalance, scvi, devCellPy, CellPLM cannot produce ranked top features), making recall comparison impossible. Goal is differential gene expression (DGE) rather than validated marker recall — use DgePseudoBulk/DgeLMEM instead.

skills.description: Use when annotating single-cell clusters or bulk RNA-seq samples (e.g. iPSC-derived NPC/neuron profiles) against deCS built-in reference panels and you must choose and load the correct reference before running deCS.correlation().
skills.name: reference-panel-selection-and-loading
skills.search_text: reference-panel-selection-and-loading Use when annotating single-cell clusters or bulk RNA-seq samples (e.g. iPSC-derived NPC/neuron profiles) against deCS built-in reference panels and you must choose and load the correct reference before running deCS.correlation(). The query cells are novel cell types with no reference counterpart — deCS is a mapping-based toolkit that fails to characterize novel cell types The query is a cancer/malignant cell sample where expression profiles differ strongly from the healthy reference panels The query input is a plain marker gene list rather than an expression profile — use the deCS.fisher() enrichment route instead of deCS.correlation() http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2640 Load deCS's pre-calculated cell type specificity score reference panels (BlueprintEncode, DICE, MonacoImmune, HCL, HCAF) via data() and select the panel appropriate to the query tissue or developmental stage, then feed the scaled markers_expression matrix into deCS.correlation() to obtain query-to-cell-type annotations. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2022.04.001
skills.summary: Load deCS's pre-calculated cell type specificity score reference panels (BlueprintEncode, DICE, MonacoImmune, HCL, HCAF) via data() and select the panel appropriate to the query tissue or developmental stage, then feed the scaled markers_expression matrix into deCS.correlation() to obtain query-to-cell-type annotations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query cells are novel cell types with no reference counterpart — deCS is a mapping-based toolkit that fails to characterize novel cell types The query is a cancer/malignant cell sample where expression profiles differ strongly from the healthy reference panels The query input is a plain marker gene list rather than an expression profile — use the deCS.fisher() enrichment route instead of deCS.correlation()

skills.description: Use when annotating single-cell clusters or gene lists against a human cell type reference panel and you must choose which built-in deCS panel (main vs fine) and CTgene cutoff (e.g. ref_panel_markers_ratio = 0.05) to apply.
skills.name: reference-panel-selection-for-cell-annotation
skills.search_text: reference-panel-selection-for-cell-annotation Use when annotating single-cell clusters or gene lists against a human cell type reference panel and you must choose which built-in deCS panel (main vs fine) and CTgene cutoff (e.g. ref_panel_markers_ratio = 0.05) to apply. The query is a cancer or malignant-cell dataset: deCS is a mapping-based toolkit that may be challenging for cancer cells due to expression profile differences between healthy and malignant cells The cell type of interest is likely novel/uncharacterized: deCS fails to characterize novel cell types because it maps to fixed reference panels The query data is already a finished cell type label file or a non-human species expression matrix outside the collected human reference panels http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Selecting and parameterizing human cell type reference panels (BlueprintEncode, DICE, MonacoImmune, HCL, HCAF) inside deCS to define cell type-specific genes (CTgenes) from t-score/z-score specificity scores, which drives accurate cluster-level scRNA-seq annotation. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.gpb.2022.04.001
skills.summary: Selecting and parameterizing human cell type reference panels (BlueprintEncode, DICE, MonacoImmune, HCL, HCAF) inside deCS to define cell type-specific genes (CTgenes) from t-score/z-score specificity scores, which drives accurate cluster-level scRNA-seq annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The query is a cancer or malignant-cell dataset: deCS is a mapping-based toolkit that may be challenging for cancer cells due to expression profile differences between healthy and malignant cells The cell type of interest is likely novel/uncharacterized: deCS fails to characterize novel cell types because it maps to fixed reference panels The query data is already a finished cell type label file or a non-human species expression matrix outside the collected human reference panels

skills.description: Use when a query scRNA-seq dataset needs cell type labels consistent with an annotated reference, and gene-order-matched AnnData objects (ref_adata, query_adata) are available for label transfer.
skills.name: reference-query-label-transfer
skills.search_text: reference-query-label-transfer Use when a query scRNA-seq dataset needs cell type labels consistent with an annotated reference, and gene-order-matched AnnData objects (ref_adata, query_adata) are available for label transfer. Query and reference AnnData objects cannot be made to share identical var_names in the same order — the README warns predictions require this and the workflow fails otherwise The task is unsupervised discovery of novel cell types rather than label transfer from an existing annotated reference; TOSICA predicts only labels present in label_dictionary.csv Interpretability at the pathway-token level is not needed and a simpler classifier with lower overhead would suffice http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Transfer cell type labels from a labeled reference scRNA-seq dataset (AnnData) to a new query dataset using TOSICA, a Transformer-based multi-head self-attention annotator whose tokens are masked by pathway gene sets (e.g. GO_bp.gmt, reactome.gmt), yielding predictions, probabilities, and interpretable attention weights. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-35923-4
skills.summary: Transfer cell type labels from a labeled reference scRNA-seq dataset (AnnData) to a new query dataset using TOSICA, a Transformer-based multi-head self-attention annotator whose tokens are masked by pathway gene sets (e.g. GO_bp.gmt, reactome.gmt), yielding predictions, probabilities, and interpretable attention weights.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Query and reference AnnData objects cannot be made to share identical var_names in the same order — the README warns predictions require this and the workflow fails otherwise The task is unsupervised discovery of novel cell types rather than label transfer from an existing annotated reference; TOSICA predicts only labels present in label_dictionary.csv Interpretability at the pathway-token level is not needed and a simpler classifier with lower overhead would suffice

skills.description: Use when subtyping TCGA RNA-seq breast cancer samples with PAM50 and you need to test whether reference-construction strategy (AWCA vs median centroids) affects concordance and reproducibility of subtype calls.
skills.name: reference-stability-assessment
skills.search_text: reference-stability-assessment Use when subtyping TCGA RNA-seq breast cancer samples with PAM50 and you need to test whether reference-construction strategy (AWCA vs median centroids) affects concordance and reproducibility of subtype calls. The input is already a feature/signature score table rather than a raw gene expression matrix needing subtype assignment The goal is single-sample classification without reference construction (e.g. the paper's mLR or AIMS approaches, which classify without a reference sample) The expression data are not RNA-seq PAM50-panel profiles (e.g. Affymetrix microarrays such as GSE4922/GSE1456 require log2-transformed variants of the AWCA pipeline) http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Quantifies how stable a nearest-centroid PAM50 reference is to the cohort used to build it, by reconstructing references with the AWCA (average of within-class averages) strategy from repeated random ER+/ER− splits and measuring concordance with published subtype calls and among replicate classifications. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-70832-2
skills.summary: Quantifies how stable a nearest-centroid PAM50 reference is to the cohort used to build it, by reconstructing references with the AWCA (average of within-class averages) strategy from repeated random ER+/ER− splits and measuring concordance with published subtype calls and among replicate classifications.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a feature/signature score table rather than a raw gene expression matrix needing subtype assignment The goal is single-sample classification without reference construction (e.g. the paper's mLR or AIMS approaches, which classify without a reference sample) The expression data are not RNA-seq PAM50-panel profiles (e.g. Affymetrix microarrays such as GSE4922/GSE1456 require log2-transformed variants of the AWCA pipeline)

skills.description: Use when you have recomputed clustering/integration metrics (ARI, kBET, ASW, ASW-beta) for a batch-effect benchmark and need to verify them against the paper's published reference table before trusting the reproduction.
skills.name: reference-table-metric-comparison
skills.search_text: reference-table-metric-comparison Use when you have recomputed clustering/integration metrics (ARI, kBET, ASW, ASW-beta) for a batch-effect benchmark and need to verify them against the paper's published reference table before trusting the reproduction. The input is a raw count matrix or cell embeddings with no recomputed ARI/kBET/ASW/ASW-beta values yet — run the evaluate workflow first. The benchmark uses a different dataset or cell-removal design than the Human Pancreas beta-cell-removal variant (Supplementary Table 4), making the Supplementary Table 5 reference values inapplicable. Only one metric is available (e.g. ARI alone); the comparison relies on the joint pattern across ARI, kBET, ASW, and ASW-beta to detect overcorrection. http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Validates a reproduced single-cell integration benchmark by comparing freshly computed metrics (ARI, kBET, ASW, ASW-beta) against the published reference values from Supplementary Table 5 of the scETM paper, exposing deviations that indicate pipeline drift. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-021-25534-2
skills.summary: Validates a reproduced single-cell integration benchmark by comparing freshly computed metrics (ARI, kBET, ASW, ASW-beta) against the published reference values from Supplementary Table 5 of the scETM paper, exposing deviations that indicate pipeline drift.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a raw count matrix or cell embeddings with no recomputed ARI/kBET/ASW/ASW-beta values yet — run the evaluate workflow first. The benchmark uses a different dataset or cell-removal design than the Human Pancreas beta-cell-removal variant (Supplementary Table 4), making the Supplementary Table 5 reference values inapplicable. Only one metric is available (e.g. ARI alone); the comparison relies on the joint pattern across ARI, kBET, ASW, and ASW-beta to detect overcorrection.

skills.description: Use when reproducing or validating published gene-marker panels derived from COMET on an SCA latent-space frequency matrix, where a reference table of expected panels and COMETsc/TP/TN statistics is available for comparison.
skills.name: reference-table-result-reproduction
skills.search_text: reference-table-result-reproduction Use when reproducing or validating published gene-marker panels derived from COMET on an SCA latent-space frequency matrix, where a reference table of expected panels and COMETsc/TP/TN statistics is available for comparison. Input is a raw UMI counts table or FASTQ rather than an SCA-derived latent-space frequency matrix — run the SCA encoding and clustering first The goal is de novo marker discovery without a published reference table to validate against — this skill is specifically a reference-result reproduction Clusters other than those in the reference table, or combinations restricted to more than 4 genes, since the reference panels and statistics were defined under the ≤4-gene constraint http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Reproduces a published marker-panel result by re-running COMET (rCASC cometsc) on the TF-based SCA latent-space frequency matrix for setA clusters 1 and 2 and validating the top panels and statistics against the paper's Table 1 reference values (COMETsc 1.45E-49 / 1.19E-46, TP 0.589, TN 0.997). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41540-020-00162-6
skills.summary: Reproduces a published marker-panel result by re-running COMET (rCASC cometsc) on the TF-based SCA latent-space frequency matrix for setA clusters 1 and 2 and validating the top panels and statistics against the paper's Table 1 reference values (COMETsc 1.45E-49 / 1.19E-46, TP 0.589, TN 0.997).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw UMI counts table or FASTQ rather than an SCA-derived latent-space frequency matrix — run the SCA encoding and clustering first The goal is de novo marker discovery without a published reference table to validate against — this skill is specifically a reference-result reproduction Clusters other than those in the reference table, or combinations restricted to more than 4 genes, since the reference panels and statistics were defined under the ≤4-gene constraint

skills.description: Use when a paper's reported numeric table values (e.g., effective text ratios r(k) per binning and k-mer size) must be independently recomputed and validated from a downloadable dataset with the authors' tool.
skills.name: reference-table-value-reproduction
skills.search_text: reference-table-value-reproduction Use when a paper's reported numeric table values (e.g., effective text ratios r(k) per binning and k-mer size) must be independently recomputed and validated from a downloadable dataset with the authors' tool. The goal is approximate sequence search or binning-directory querying (Raptor's actual use case), not recomputing publication statistics The reference table depends on real data (e.g., Clustered NCBI RefSeq 64/1,024-bin partitions on Zenodo) rather than the artificial dataset, so values will not match Table 8 Uneven bin sizes or a very high number of bins are involved, since the paper notes the method's main limiting factor is 'its susceptibility to uneven bin sizes as well as a high number of bins' Reproduces published table values (e.g., Table 8 of the Raptor paper) by recomputing the effective text ratios r(k) of winnowing-minimizer representative k-mers on the artificial 64-bin and 1,024-bin datasets for k=12..20 using Raptor, and validating the recomputed numbers against the reported values. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.isci.2021.102782
skills.summary: Reproduces published table values (e.g., Table 8 of the Raptor paper) by recomputing the effective text ratios r(k) of winnowing-minimizer representative k-mers on the artificial 64-bin and 1,024-bin datasets for k=12..20 using Raptor, and validating the recomputed numbers against the reported values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is approximate sequence search or binning-directory querying (Raptor's actual use case), not recomputing publication statistics The reference table depends on real data (e.g., Clustered NCBI RefSeq 64/1,024-bin partitions on Zenodo) rather than the artificial dataset, so values will not match Table 8 Uneven bin sizes or a very high number of bins are involved, since the paper notes the method's main limiting factor is 'its susceptibility to uneven bin sizes as well as a high number of bins'

skills.description: Use when a PAM50-style centroid reference must be rebuilt from subtype-labeled RNA-seq cohorts so that classification no longer depends on cohort composition, or when an existing reference table (e.g., Supplementary Table S3 format) must be structurally verified before downstream classification.
skills.name: reference-vector-validation
skills.search_text: reference-vector-validation Use when a PAM50-style centroid reference must be rebuilt from subtype-labeled RNA-seq cohorts so that classification no longer depends on cohort composition, or when an existing reference table (e.g., Supplementary Table S3 format) must be structurally verified before downstream classification. The goal is single-sample classification without reference construction — in that case the regularized multiclass Logistic Regression (mLR) approach reaches 90% concordance with PAM50-based calls without needing a reference sample. Input is already a validated precomputed external reference (e.g., Supplementary Material Table S3); rebuilding it from scratch is unnecessary. Builds and validates a subtype-balanced AWCA reference table for PAM50-based breast cancer intrinsic subtyping by averaging within-class expression means per gene across training cohorts, removing the dependence of subtype calls on the arbitrary composition of the cohort used to build the reference. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-70832-2
skills.summary: Builds and validates a subtype-balanced AWCA reference table for PAM50-based breast cancer intrinsic subtyping by averaging within-class expression means per gene across training cohorts, removing the dependence of subtype calls on the arbitrary composition of the cohort used to build the reference.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is single-sample classification without reference construction — in that case the regularized multiclass Logistic Regression (mLR) approach reaches 90% concordance with PAM50-based calls without needing a reference sample. Input is already a validated precomputed external reference (e.g., Supplementary Material Table S3); rebuilding it from scratch is unnecessary.

skills.description: Use when building a gene-level TF affinity matrix from region-level TRAP affinities: to pick gene-window (default 50 kb around 5' TSS) vs ABC-based (5 Mb, i.e. ±2.5 Mb) mapping, or to decide scaling of promoter-proximal vs distant regions.
skills.name: region-gene-window-mapping
skills.search_text: region-gene-window-mapping Use when building a gene-level TF affinity matrix from region-level TRAP affinities: to pick gene-window (default 50 kb around 5' TSS) vs ABC-based (5 Mb, i.e. ±2.5 Mb) mapping, or to decide scaling of promoter-proximal vs distant regions. You only need enhancer-gene interaction scores and not gene-level TF affinities — STARE exposes the ABC-scoring part independently. Regions are already assigned to genes (e.g. precomputed enhancer-gene links); re-windowing would duplicate regions across genes and change the summation. No Gencode-style GTF gene annotation is available, so 5' TSS coordinates for the window cannot be defined. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 The STARE region-gene mapping step that assigns open-chromatin candidate regions to genes within a window centred at the 5' TSS, defining which TRAP TF affinities (from 818 non-redundant PSEMs) are summed into the per-gene per-TF affinity matrix. The mapping choice (gene-window vs ABC-based) also determines the per-region scaling applied before summation. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad062
skills.summary: The STARE region-gene mapping step that assigns open-chromatin candidate regions to genes within a window centred at the 5' TSS, defining which TRAP TF affinities (from 818 non-redundant PSEMs) are summed into the per-gene per-TF affinity matrix. The mapping choice (gene-window vs ABC-based) also determines the per-region scaling applied before summation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need enhancer-gene interaction scores and not gene-level TF affinities — STARE exposes the ABC-scoring part independently. Regions are already assigned to genes (e.g. precomputed enhancer-gene links); re-windowing would duplicate regions across genes and change the summation. No Gencode-style GTF gene annotation is available, so 5' TSS coordinates for the window cannot be defined.

skills.search_text: region-merging-pyramidal-segmentation Use when a smoothed, gene-order-sorted expression matrix must be converted into a copy number segmentation with shared breakpoints across cells, as in SCEVAN's joint segmentation step. The input is a raw, unsmoothed count matrix — edge-preserving TV smoothing (logcosh prior) must be applied first Genes are not sorted by genomic coordinates, since merging assumes adjacent regions along the genome The goal is malignant vs non-malignant classification only, without clonal structure (SUBCLONES = FALSE) http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 http://edamontology.org/topic_2229 A greedy piecewise-constant Mumford–Shah minimization, ported from Computer Vision, that jointly segments the smoothed scRNA-seq expression matrix into a copy number matrix by iteratively merging adjacent genomic regions along a pyramid with a dynamic regularization weight lambda. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-36790-9
skills.summary: A greedy piecewise-constant Mumford–Shah minimization, ported from Computer Vision, that jointly segments the smoothed scRNA-seq expression matrix into a copy number matrix by iteratively merging adjacent genomic regions along a pyramid with a dynamic regularization weight lambda.
