skills.search_text: repeated-run-stability-boxplot-visualization Use when a stochastic deep model's dimension reduction varies across runs (e.g. VASC with variational/Gumbel-softmax optimization) and you must show whether an added component, such as the ZI dropout layer, improves median clustering scores and tightens their spread. skills.summary: Fits negative binomial regressions (MASS::glm.nb) of cell-type counts (e.g. naive vs mature Cd4+ T-cells) on a biological variable such as age, using biological replicates (e.g. mouse) as the replicate structure, to produce Wald and likelihood-ratio test statistics for differential abundance in ELVAR.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When each condition lacks genuine biological replicates (e.g. only one mouse per age-group) — the negative binomial regression replicate structure in DoDA requires replicate-level variance estimation When communities have not been tested for attribute enrichment via ProcessEVA first — running DoDA on arbitrary Louvain clusters loses the ELVAR sensitivity advantage over the Louvain benchmark When the analysis goal is differential expression rather than differential abundance of cell-type/community counts

Datasets have not yet been individually clustered — the method requires precomputed per-dataset clusters and marker fold-change statistics as input The goal is de novo joint clustering on a single pooled matrix rather than matching independently derived clusters across pre-clustered datasets Only one dataset (no replicate or cross-condition comparison) is available, leaving no second set of clusters to correlate against http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 A cross-dataset cluster similarity analysis from robustSingleCell (Magen et al. 2019) that matches cell subpopulations identified independently in two or more scRNAseq datasets (e.g., tumor-infiltrating CD4+ TILs vs draining lymph node vs acute LCMV CD44+ T cells) by correlating fold-change (FC) vectors of cluster markers and retaining statistically robust cluster-pair matches. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.celrep.2019.10.131
skills.summary: A cross-dataset cluster similarity analysis from robustSingleCell (Magen et al. 2019) that matches cell subpopulations identified independently in two or more scRNAseq datasets (e.g., tumor-infiltrating CD4+ TILs vs draining lymph node vs acute LCMV CD44+ T cells) by correlating fold-change (FC) vectors of cluster markers and retaining statistically robust cluster-pair matches.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Datasets have not yet been individually clustered — the method requires precomputed per-dataset clusters and marker fold-change statistics as input The goal is de novo joint clustering on a single pooled matrix rather than matching independently derived clusters across pre-clustered datasets Only one dataset (no replicate or cross-condition comparison) is available, leaving no second set of clusters to correlate against

Only one replicate is available, so no cross-replicate agreement can be estimated Scores are not perturbation simulation outputs (e.g. raw gene expression matrices), where aggregation of negative perturbation scores across Monocle states is not meaningful The comparison goal is differential expression between conditions rather than reproducibility of a ranked TF perturbation list http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Quantify reproducibility of CellOracle in silico TF knockout perturbation rankings across independent biological replicates of MEF-to-iEP reprogramming by computing Pearson correlation between replicate-level summed KO scores, plotted as a replicate-agreement scatter (Figure 3D). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.stemcr.2022.11.010
skills.summary: Quantify reproducibility of CellOracle in silico TF knockout perturbation rankings across independent biological replicates of MEF-to-iEP reprogramming by computing Pearson correlation between replicate-level summed KO scores, plotted as a replicate-agreement scatter (Figure 3D).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only one replicate is available, so no cross-replicate agreement can be estimated Scores are not perturbation simulation outputs (e.g. raw gene expression matrices), where aggregation of negative perturbation scores across Monocle states is not meaningful The comparison goal is differential expression between conditions rather than reproducibility of a ranked TF perturbation list

skills.search_text: replicate-pearson-correlation-analysis Use when a normalized barcode counts table (e.g. counts/all_counts_combined.tsv) contains biological replicates per treatment (e.g. DMSO, IBET-151) and replicate concordance must be quantified before downstream clonal analyses. The input is raw, unnormalized barcode counts with differing library sizes — normalize first, otherwise correlation is driven by sequencing depth rather than clonal composition Samples lack biological replicates per condition (e.g. single AraC IC90 samples) — pairwise replicate correlation cannot be computed The goal is barcode read pre-processing quality control (quality, UMI, chimerism filtering) — that is handled upstream in the BARtab pipeline, not by replicate correlation http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Quantifies concordance of biological replicates in a cellular barcoding experiment by computing pairwise Pearson correlations between replicate samples over log-normalized barcode counts, validating that replicate clonal composition is highly similar (correlations > 0.95). transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.crmeth.2024.100763
skills.summary: Quantifies concordance of biological replicates in a cellular barcoding experiment by computing pairwise Pearson correlations between replicate samples over log-normalized barcode counts, validating that replicate clonal composition is highly similar (correlations > 0.95).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw, unnormalized barcode counts with differing library sizes — normalize first, otherwise correlation is driven by sequencing depth rather than clonal composition Samples lack biological replicates per condition (e.g. single AraC IC90 samples) — pairwise replicate correlation cannot be computed The goal is barcode read pre-processing quality control (quality, UMI, chimerism filtering) — that is handled upstream in the BARtab pipeline, not by replicate correlation

skills.summary: A statistical validation step in RiboDoc that assesses whether ribosome profiling replicates are reproducible enough for downstream differential-expression analysis, using pairwise Spearman correlation coefficients and a PCA of per-sample count vectors.

skills.summary: Assesses whether InPACT-identified novel IPA isoforms show reproducible expression between biological RNA-seq replicates by independently detecting IPA sites, assembling isoforms, quantifying transcripts with Salmon, and computing the Pearson correlation of novel isoform expression between replicates.

skills.description: Use when a published numeric result (e.g., a network statistic like a network density score reported in Fig. 1C of Kahraman et al., Scientific Reports 2020) must be independently reproduced from raw network data to validate a pipeline or database-derived value.
skills.name: reported-value-benchmark-verification
skills.search_text: reported-value-benchmark-verification Use when a published numeric result (e.g., a network statistic like a network density score reported in Fig. 1C of Kahraman et al., Scientific Reports 2020) must be independently reproduced from raw network data to validate a pipeline or database-derived value. The analysis goal is predicting or browsing the pathogenic impact of isoform switching events across the 31 disease types in CanIsoNet, rather than verifying a published numeric benchmark. The quantity of interest depends on sample-level isoform switching calls (e.g., per-sample expression values or dMDTs) rather than a static whole-network interaction statistic. The protein is absent from the human STRING network, so a normalized network density score cannot be defined. http://edamontology.org/topic_0128 A benchmarking skill that independently recomputes a published quantitative statistic — here, the HSPH1 network density score of 78% from Fig. 1C of Kahraman et al., Scientific Reports 2020 — from raw source data (the human STRING interaction network) and checks the recomputed value against the reported one within a defined tolerance. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbad050
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill that independently recomputes a published quantitative statistic — here, the HSPH1 network density score of 78% from Fig. 1C of Kahraman et al., Scientific Reports 2020 — from raw source data (the human STRING interaction network) and checks the recomputed value against the reported one within a defined tolerance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is predicting or browsing the pathogenic impact of isoform switching events across the 31 disease types in CanIsoNet, rather than verifying a published numeric benchmark. The quantity of interest depends on sample-level isoform switching calls (e.g., per-sample expression values or dMDTs) rather than a static whole-network interaction statistic. The protein is absent from the human STRING network, so a normalized network density score cannot be defined.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking biclustering algorithms on synthetic data with known ground truth — e.g. implanting trend-preserving, shift-scale, or constant biclusters into random N(0,1) matrices with fixed seeds for reproducibility.

skills.search_text: reproducible-random-data-generation Use when benchmarking biclustering algorithms on synthetic data with known ground truth — e.g. implanting trend-preserving, shift-scale, or constant biclusters into random N(0,1) matrices with fixed seeds for reproducibility. When the goal is biclustering real gene expression data (e.g. BicatYeast, airway, GDS589) rather than benchmarking on controlled synthetic ground truth When the downstream algorithm targets non-trend-preserving structures (e.g. additive/multiplicative models) not representable by the Type I-VI implant patterns http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Generate reproducible synthetic benchmark matrices by drawing N(0,1) backgrounds in R with fixed seeds and implanting ground-truth trend-preserving biclusters (Types I-VI), enabling controlled evaluation of biclustering algorithms such as UniBic. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/srep23466
skills.summary: Generate reproducible synthetic benchmark matrices by drawing N(0,1) backgrounds in R with fixed seeds and implanting ground-truth trend-preserving biclusters (Types I-VI), enabling controlled evaluation of biclustering algorithms such as UniBic.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is biclustering real gene expression data (e.g. BicatYeast, airway, GDS589) rather than benchmarking on controlled synthetic ground truth When the downstream algorithm targets non-trend-preserving structures (e.g. additive/multiplicative models) not representable by the Type I-VI implant patterns

skills.search_text: reproducible-random-seed-sampling Use when a trajectory-inference or ensemble-clustering step requires many randomly initialized clusterings on a low-dimensional embedding and results must be bit-reproducible across runs via seeded RNG. Dataset with extremely rare and extremely prevalent cell types at the same time, where k-medoids may not work properly and manual cluster merging is needed Embedding is a high-dimensional PCA (e.g. 30 principal components), where k-medoids is unstable and produces 1–2 cell clusters rather than meaningful partitions Data contain a trajectory with cycles or disconnected components, which Totem cannot model regardless of the clustering ensemble Generate a large ensemble of random clusterings by running CLARA k-medoids many times (default 10,000) over a sampled range of k with RNG seeds enabled, so the stochastic sampling underlying Totem's cell-connectivity MST search is reproducible. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad515
skills.summary: Generate a large ensemble of random clusterings by running CLARA k-medoids many times (default 10,000) over a sampled range of k with RNG seeds enabled, so the stochastic sampling underlying Totem's cell-connectivity MST search is reproducible.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Dataset with extremely rare and extremely prevalent cell types at the same time, where k-medoids may not work properly and manual cluster merging is needed Embedding is a high-dimensional PCA (e.g. 30 principal components), where k-medoids is unstable and produces 1–2 cell clusters rather than meaningful partitions Data contain a trajectory with cycles or disconnected components, which Totem cannot model regardless of the clustering ensemble

skills.description: Use when two count matrices from different platforms (scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics .csv files) must be brought into a comparable feature space before joint downstream analysis such as pseudo-space projection.
skills.name: reproducing-kernel-hilbert-space-embedding
skills.search_text: reproducing-kernel-hilbert-space-embedding Use when two count matrices from different platforms (scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics .csv files) must be brought into a comparable feature space before joint downstream analysis such as pseudo-space projection. The two datasets are already in a shared low-dimensional feature space or the downstream analysis does not require cross-domain integration of scRNA-seq and ST data. The spatial reference tissue has low spatial coherence or differs architecturally from the scRNA-seq tissue (the paper advises caution, e.g. SCC Patients 5 and 9, dACC lacking cortical layer 4), so batch correction alone would not make the integration meaningful. The goal is spatial domain identification of ST data rather than spatial analysis of scRNA-seq data, which scSpace explicitly does not target. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Kernel embedding step within scSpace's transfer component analysis (TCA): single-cell scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics count matrices are mapped into a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space so that a shared low-dimensional latent feature can be learned that eliminates the batch effect between the two domains. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-023-38121-4
skills.summary: Kernel embedding step within scSpace's transfer component analysis (TCA): single-cell scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics count matrices are mapped into a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space so that a shared low-dimensional latent feature can be learned that eliminates the batch effect between the two domains.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The two datasets are already in a shared low-dimensional feature space or the downstream analysis does not require cross-domain integration of scRNA-seq and ST data. The spatial reference tissue has low spatial coherence or differs architecturally from the scRNA-seq tissue (the paper advises caution, e.g. SCC Patients 5 and 9, dACC lacking cortical layer 4), so batch correction alone would not make the integration meaningful. The goal is spatial domain identification of ST data rather than spatial analysis of scRNA-seq data, which scSpace explicitly does not target.

Trajectory structure must be inferred de novo without pre-annotated source and target subpopulations — CellRouter's reprogramming scoring is subpopulation-aware and requires defined start and end states Data types other than single-cell transcriptomics (e.g., single-cell chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, mass cytometry) — the article only envisions these as future applications, not demonstrated ones The goal is functional validation of engraftable HSC-like cells — the article explicitly defers thorough characterization of each identified gene beyond the scope of the computational ranking http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Rank overexpression and knockdown candidate transcriptional regulators for cell reprogramming by scoring genes along CellRouter flow-network trajectories between source and target subpopulations, integrating the reconstructed gene regulatory network with transition-specific expression dynamics. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-018-03214-y

When you only need to infer GRN edges from single-cell transcriptome and epigenome data (use CellOracle GRN inference instead) rather than compare topology across already-inferred cluster networks When the goal is in silico TF perturbation simulation (KO/overexpression) of gene expression changes rather than graph-theoretic network comparison When clusters do not form an ordered trajectory — centrality trajectory and early-vs-late comparisons require cluster ordering along reprogramming progress http://edamontology.org/topic_0602 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Compares cluster-specific gene regulatory networks (GRNs) along a fibroblast-to-iEP reprogramming trajectory using CellOracle's igraph-based network analysis, computing Hnf4α-Foxa1 edge-strength scores, degree/eigenvector centrality trajectories, and network cartography to identify connector-hub configurations and candidate TFs such as Fos, Eno1, Hes1, Foxq1, Zfp57, Klf2, and Egr1. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.stemcr.2022.11.010

skills.search_text: resampling-based-clustering-evaluation Use when a clustering dataset is too large for full hierarchical clustering (e.g. mass cytometry datasets with 86,864–265,627 cells) and you need repeatable resample-based clustering with performance metrics (accuracy, NMI, ARI) aggregated over resamples. When the goal is to validate or re-detect known RMBase Ψ sites rather than discover novel ones — masking would remove exactly the positive signal When working with a species or modification type not covered by RMBase v2.0 annotations, since no reliable mask intervals can be constructed http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 Masks known RMBase v2.0 pseudouridine (Ψ) sites plus 25 bases of flanking sequence on each side using BEDTools, so that a downstream transcriptome-wide scan (e.g., with MU-PseUDeep) targets only novel candidate Ψ sites. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2020.07.010
skills.summary: Masks known RMBase v2.0 pseudouridine (Ψ) sites plus 25 bases of flanking sequence on each side using BEDTools, so that a downstream transcriptome-wide scan (e.g., with MU-PseUDeep) targets only novel candidate Ψ sites.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to validate or re-detect known RMBase Ψ sites rather than discover novel ones — masking would remove exactly the positive signal When working with a species or modification type not covered by RMBase v2.0 annotations, since no reliable mask intervals can be constructed

skills.description: Use when you need to validate that a fitted fragment length distribution model generalizes across scRNA-seq datasets, i.e., when fitting Forseti's spline model and quantifying held-out prediction accuracy via RMSE.
skills.name: rmse-benchmark-evaluation
skills.search_text: rmse-benchmark-evaluation Use when you need to validate that a fitted fragment length distribution model generalizes across scRNA-seq datasets, i.e., when fitting Forseti's spline model and quantifying held-out prediction accuracy via RMSE. You only have a single scRNA-seq dataset with no held-out test data, so cross-dataset generalization RMSE cannot be computed You are evaluating Forseti's MLP binding affinity component rather than the fragment length distribution (that component is assessed via AUC, not fragment-length RMSE) Input fragment length data does not come from paired-end scRNA-seq libraries (e.g., bulk RNA-seq or short-read single-end data), since the spline models the scRNA-seq cDNA fragment length distribution http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Reproduce and benchmark Forseti's cubic-spline cDNA fragment length distribution model by fitting it to paired-end fragment lengths from the eight training datasets, then computing held-out RMSE and 5-fold cross-validation variation to verify cross-dataset generalizability. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae207
skills.summary: Reproduce and benchmark Forseti's cubic-spline cDNA fragment length distribution model by fitting it to paired-end fragment lengths from the eight training datasets, then computing held-out RMSE and 5-fold cross-validation variation to verify cross-dataset generalizability.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have a single scRNA-seq dataset with no held-out test data, so cross-dataset generalization RMSE cannot be computed You are evaluating Forseti's MLP binding affinity component rather than the fragment length distribution (that component is assessed via AUC, not fragment-length RMSE) Input fragment length data does not come from paired-end scRNA-seq libraries (e.g., bulk RNA-seq or short-read single-end data), since the spline models the scRNA-seq cDNA fragment length distribution

skills.description: Use when comparing competing marker gene sets (e.g., COT-derived via obtain_subtype_markers(), one-vs-rest t-test, a priori lists) for deconvolving bulk expression mixtures where true cell-type proportions are known, and a head-to-head accuracy table is needed.
skills.name: rmse-correlation-performance-evaluation
skills.search_text: rmse-correlation-performance-evaluation Use when comparing competing marker gene sets (e.g., COT-derived via obtain_subtype_markers(), one-vs-rest t-test, a priori lists) for deconvolving bulk expression mixtures where true cell-type proportions are known, and a head-to-head accuracy table is needed. Ground-truth cell-type proportions are unknown (e.g., real bulk tissue samples), so RMSE against true proportions cannot be computed You only need to detect marker genes themselves (that is COT's obtain_subtype_markers() task), not to evaluate how well they support deconvolution Input is a single bulk sample rather than a panel of mixtures with known composition — sample-wise correlation over 100 mixtures is the design's core signal http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark skill for quantifying marker-gene-guided deconvolution accuracy: cell-type proportions estimated by marker-gene-restricted linear regression on simulated bulk mixtures are scored by RMSE against true proportions and by sample-wise Pearson correlation, as done for COT-MG versus OVR t-test and a priori marker sets (Supplementary Table S2 on GSE28490). transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioadv/vbac037
skills.summary: Benchmark skill for quantifying marker-gene-guided deconvolution accuracy: cell-type proportions estimated by marker-gene-restricted linear regression on simulated bulk mixtures are scored by RMSE against true proportions and by sample-wise Pearson correlation, as done for COT-MG versus OVR t-test and a priori marker sets (Supplementary Table S2 on GSE28490).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Ground-truth cell-type proportions are unknown (e.g., real bulk tissue samples), so RMSE against true proportions cannot be computed You only need to detect marker genes themselves (that is COT's obtain_subtype_markers() task), not to evaluate how well they support deconvolution Input is a single bulk sample rather than a panel of mixtures with known composition — sample-wise correlation over 100 mixtures is the design's core signal

skills.description: Use when benchmarking deconvolution methods (STdeconvolve, SPOTlight, RCTD, spatialDWLS) on simulated multi-cellular pixel-resolution ST data with known ground-truth cell-type proportions and a significance test for RMSE differences is required.
skills.name: rmse-evaluation-against-simulated-ground-truth
skills.search_text: rmse-evaluation-against-simulated-ground-truth Use when benchmarking deconvolution methods (STdeconvolve, SPOTlight, RCTD, spatialDWLS) on simulated multi-cellular pixel-resolution ST data with known ground-truth cell-type proportions and a significance test for RMSE differences is required. Real ST datasets with no simulated ground-truth proportions — RMSE against truth cannot be computed; use qualitative agreement or annotation-based validation instead. Sub-cellular pixel-resolution ST data — the article states STdeconvolve 'may not be best suited for analysis of such sub-cellular resolution ST data', so this simulated-pixel benchmark does not transfer. Datasets where cell-type proportions are homogeneous across pixels or extremely sparse with high stochastic drop-outs — LDA-based STdeconvolve may fail, invalidating the RMSE comparison baseline. http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmark cell-type deconvolution of multi-cellular pixel-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) data by comparing estimated pixel-level cell-type proportions against simulated ground-truth proportions using RMSE, supplemented with one-sided Diebold-Mariano tests to establish significance (as in the STdeconvolve paper, DOI 10.1038/s41467-022-30033-z). transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-30033-z
skills.summary: Benchmark cell-type deconvolution of multi-cellular pixel-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) data by comparing estimated pixel-level cell-type proportions against simulated ground-truth proportions using RMSE, supplemented with one-sided Diebold-Mariano tests to establish significance (as in the STdeconvolve paper, DOI 10.1038/s41467-022-30033-z).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Real ST datasets with no simulated ground-truth proportions — RMSE against truth cannot be computed; use qualitative agreement or annotation-based validation instead. Sub-cellular pixel-resolution ST data — the article states STdeconvolve 'may not be best suited for analysis of such sub-cellular resolution ST data', so this simulated-pixel benchmark does not transfer. Datasets where cell-type proportions are homogeneous across pixels or extremely sparse with high stochastic drop-outs — LDA-based STdeconvolve may fail, invalidating the RMSE comparison baseline.

skills.description: Use when multiple trained deep learning variants (e.g. autoencoders of different widths or dropout settings) must be compared by reconstruction RMSE on held-out and independent datasets to pick the deployment model.
skills.name: rmse-model-comparison-benchmarking
skills.search_text: rmse-model-comparison-benchmarking Use when multiple trained deep learning variants (e.g. autoencoders of different widths or dropout settings) must be compared by reconstruction RMSE on held-out and independent datasets to pick the deployment model. The goal is cell-type abundance inference from bulk RNA-seq rather than model selection — use DCNet directly with the recommended dropout-0.1 setting instead of re-benchmarking variants Input data lacks the neuron-gene index or gene-cell relation matrix, so DCNet variants cannot be reconstructed for RMSE comparison The dataset is not a gene-expression matrix with human gene symbols as rows (e.g. methylation or mutation data), making reconstruction RMSE over the marker-gene layer meaningless http://edamontology.org/topic_3577 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Benchmark trained network variants (AE64–AE4096 autoencoders, Full-DCNet, and dropout-augmented DCNet-D0–D50) by computing RMSE on a held-out TCGA test split and an independent CRC single-cell dataset (GSE81861), then tabulate results to select the best model (AE2048 for autoencoders, dropout 0.1 for DCNet). transcriptomics/v2 10.1080/2162402x.2022.2043662
skills.summary: Benchmark trained network variants (AE64–AE4096 autoencoders, Full-DCNet, and dropout-augmented DCNet-D0–D50) by computing RMSE on a held-out TCGA test split and an independent CRC single-cell dataset (GSE81861), then tabulate results to select the best model (AE2048 for autoencoders, dropout 0.1 for DCNet).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is cell-type abundance inference from bulk RNA-seq rather than model selection — use DCNet directly with the recommended dropout-0.1 setting instead of re-benchmarking variants Input data lacks the neuron-gene index or gene-cell relation matrix, so DCNet variants cannot be reconstructed for RMSE comparison The dataset is not a gene-expression matrix with human gene symbols as rows (e.g. methylation or mutation data), making reconstruction RMSE over the marker-gene layer meaningless

skills.description: Use when comparing cell-type proportion estimation methods on simulated spatial transcriptomics data with known ground-truth pixel-level proportions, and per-pixel RMSE plus pairwise statistical accuracy tests are needed.
skills.name: rmse-performance-evaluation
skills.search_text: rmse-performance-evaluation Use when comparing cell-type proportion estimation methods on simulated spatial transcriptomics data with known ground-truth pixel-level proportions, and per-pixel RMSE plus pairwise statistical accuracy tests are needed. Input is real ST data without simulated ground-truth cell-type proportions — per-pixel RMSE against truth cannot be computed Comparing single-cell-resolution or sub-cellular ST data, where multi-cellular pixel deconvolution benchmarks do not apply Evaluating only one method with no competitor — the Diebold-Mariano test is defined for pairwise accuracy comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Benchmark deconvolution accuracy by computing per-pixel RMSE between estimated and ground-truth cell-type proportions on simulated multi-cellular pixel-resolution ST data, and compare methods (STdeconvolve vs. transcriptional clustering and BayesSpace resolution-enhanced clustering) with Diebold-Mariano tests. This is the quantitative framework behind Fig. 3h/3l of the STdeconvolve paper. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-022-30033-z
skills.summary: Benchmark deconvolution accuracy by computing per-pixel RMSE between estimated and ground-truth cell-type proportions on simulated multi-cellular pixel-resolution ST data, and compare methods (STdeconvolve vs. transcriptional clustering and BayesSpace resolution-enhanced clustering) with Diebold-Mariano tests. This is the quantitative framework behind Fig. 3h/3l of the STdeconvolve paper.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real ST data without simulated ground-truth cell-type proportions — per-pixel RMSE against truth cannot be computed Comparing single-cell-resolution or sub-cellular ST data, where multi-cellular pixel deconvolution benchmarks do not apply Evaluating only one method with no competitor — the Diebold-Mariano test is defined for pairwise accuracy comparison

skills.description: Use when preprocessing scRNA-seq count data (e.g., ZhengMix PBMC) and you need a data-driven, non-manual threshold to separate signal dimensions from noise before dimensionality reduction or UMAP embedding.
skills.name: rmt-eigenvalue-noise-filtering
skills.search_text: rmt-eigenvalue-noise-filtering Use when preprocessing scRNA-seq count data (e.g., ZhengMix PBMC) and you need a data-driven, non-manual threshold to separate signal dimensions from noise before dimensionality reduction or UMAP embedding. When the input is already a low-dimensional feature embedding or a feature table of highly variable genes — RMT filtering operates on the full gene-by-cell count matrix, and selecting highly variable genes first can compromise local structure in low-variance genes When the dataset is too large for available hardware — the approach requires computing all eigenvalues of the large cell-to-cell similarity matrix, demanding significant memory resources and a computer with high specifications When the user needs an interactive, subjective dimension cutoff — this skill is designed to replace manual threshold decisions, so do not apply it expecting user-tunable signal counts http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Random matrix theory (RMT)-based noise filtering, as implemented in scLENS, builds the cell-to-cell similarity matrix G=XX^T/N, computes all eigenvalues, fits the Marchenko-Pastur distribution, and counts eigenvalues exceeding the Tracy-Widom threshold (p=0.05) to provide a data-driven signal/noise cutoff for scRNA-seq data. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-024-47884-3
skills.summary: Random matrix theory (RMT)-based noise filtering, as implemented in scLENS, builds the cell-to-cell similarity matrix G=XX^T/N, computes all eigenvalues, fits the Marchenko-Pastur distribution, and counts eigenvalues exceeding the Tracy-Widom threshold (p=0.05) to provide a data-driven signal/noise cutoff for scRNA-seq data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a low-dimensional feature embedding or a feature table of highly variable genes — RMT filtering operates on the full gene-by-cell count matrix, and selecting highly variable genes first can compromise local structure in low-variance genes When the dataset is too large for available hardware — the approach requires computing all eigenvalues of the large cell-to-cell similarity matrix, demanding significant memory resources and a computer with high specifications When the user needs an interactive, subjective dimension cutoff — this skill is designed to replace manual threshold decisions, so do not apply it expecting user-tunable signal counts

skills.description: Use when a highly sparse single-cell expression matrix (~95% sparse, e.g. 6,573 PBMC or 3,005 mouse cortex cells) must be denoised and signal-like genes selected before clustering or latent-space embedding.
skills.name: rmt-eigenvector-based-feature-selection
skills.search_text: rmt-eigenvector-based-feature-selection Use when a highly sparse single-cell expression matrix (~95% sparse, e.g. 6,573 PBMC or 3,005 mouse cortex cells) must be denoised and signal-like genes selected before clustering or latent-space embedding. The input is not a highly sparse single-cell expression matrix — the RMT noise model assumes the ~95%-sparse regime where universality holds and sparsity dominates the spectrum. Genes are already pre-selected to a small curated panel, leaving too few features for eigenvalue/eigenvector statistics to be meaningful. The task requires supervised phenotype prediction with labels rather than unsupervised feature selection and denoising. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A feature selection method that denoises sparse single-cell expression matrices using random matrix theory (RMT): genes responsible for eigenvector localization in a randomized (sparsity-only) version of the data are discarded, leaving a low-rank biological signal. It is the core of the Randomly library from Aparicio et al., Patterns 2020. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2020.100035
skills.summary: A feature selection method that denoises sparse single-cell expression matrices using random matrix theory (RMT): genes responsible for eigenvector localization in a randomized (sparsity-only) version of the data are discarded, leaving a low-rank biological signal. It is the core of the Randomly library from Aparicio et al., Patterns 2020.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not a highly sparse single-cell expression matrix — the RMT noise model assumes the ~95%-sparse regime where universality holds and sparsity dominates the spectrum. Genes are already pre-selected to a small curated panel, leaving too few features for eigenvalue/eigenvector statistics to be meaningful. The task requires supervised phenotype prediction with labels rather than unsupervised feature selection and denoising.

skills.description: Use when eigenvectors from an eigendecomposition of a single-cell covariance matrix must be classified as signal candidates or noise, especially when eigenvalues lie outside the Marchenko-Pastur bulk yet may still be sparsity-driven, delocalized noise.
skills.name: rmt-marchenko-pastur-bulk-screening
skills.search_text: rmt-marchenko-pastur-bulk-screening Use when eigenvectors from an eigendecomposition of a single-cell covariance matrix must be classified as signal candidates or noise, especially when eigenvalues lie outside the Marchenko-Pastur bulk yet may still be sparsity-driven, delocalized noise. The input is a raw gene-expression count matrix or per-gene feature table rather than an eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix The goal is imputation of zero-inflated values (e.g., MAGIC, scImpute, ZIFA) rather than RMT-based classification of eigenvectors The analysis requires i.i.d. expression-distribution assumptions, which the paper explicitly avoids A Random Matrix Theory (RMT) screening skill for classifying eigenvectors of the single-cell covariance matrix as informative (localized) or non-informative (delocalized), combining Marchenko-Pastur bulk membership with Shapiro-Wilk normality testing so that Gaussian-profile eigenvectors are discarded even when their eigenvalues fall outside the MP bulk. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.patter.2020.100035
skills.summary: A Random Matrix Theory (RMT) screening skill for classifying eigenvectors of the single-cell covariance matrix as informative (localized) or non-informative (delocalized), combining Marchenko-Pastur bulk membership with Shapiro-Wilk normality testing so that Gaussian-profile eigenvectors are discarded even when their eigenvalues fall outside the MP bulk.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a raw gene-expression count matrix or per-gene feature table rather than an eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix The goal is imputation of zero-inflated values (e.g., MAGIC, scImpute, ZIFA) rather than RMT-based classification of eigenvectors The analysis requires i.i.d. expression-distribution assumptions, which the paper explicitly avoids

skills.description: Use when raw RNA sequences of length 41 (5hmC benchmark Dataset.csv) must be transformed into position-specific gapped/ungapped k-mer descriptors, or when the stability of position-specific discriminative k-mer patterns must be verified across cross-validation partitions.
skills.name: rna-5hmc-position-specific-gapped-kmer-feature-generation
skills.search_text: rna-5hmc-position-specific-gapped-kmer-feature-generation Use when raw RNA sequences of length 41 (5hmC benchmark Dataset.csv) must be transformed into position-specific gapped/ungapped k-mer descriptors, or when the stability of position-specific discriminative k-mer patterns must be verified across cross-validation partitions. Input is already a precomputed feature table (e.g., All_Features_Dataset.csv exists) and only model training/evaluation via Model.ipynb is needed Sequences are not 41-nt RNA fragments, since position-specific descriptors assume a fixed coordinate frame relative to the 41-nt sequence The goal is combining frequency-based k-mer features with position-specific features in a single model — the paper reports these do not work well together and defers such combination to a future feature-subspace ensemble approach http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Generates Position-Specific Gapped k-mer (PSG k-mer) and Position-Specific k-mer features from 41-nt RNA sequences via the Feature Generation pipeline of iRNA5hmC-PS, then validates the resulting features by intersecting RF-selected feature sets across 5-times 5-fold cross-validation partitions to recover the consistently discriminative position-specific patterns. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2020.10.032
skills.summary: Generates Position-Specific Gapped k-mer (PSG k-mer) and Position-Specific k-mer features from 41-nt RNA sequences via the Feature Generation pipeline of iRNA5hmC-PS, then validates the resulting features by intersecting RF-selected feature sets across 5-times 5-fold cross-validation partitions to recover the consistently discriminative position-specific patterns.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a precomputed feature table (e.g., All_Features_Dataset.csv exists) and only model training/evaluation via Model.ipynb is needed Sequences are not 41-nt RNA fragments, since position-specific descriptors assume a fixed coordinate frame relative to the 41-nt sequence The goal is combining frequency-based k-mer features with position-specific features in a single model — the paper reports these do not work well together and defers such combination to a future feature-subspace ensemble approach

skills.description: Use when RNA sequences of length 41 need to be classified as 5hmC site vs non-site using position-specific sequence descriptors, or when reproducing the iRNA5hmC-PS benchmark (78.3% accuracy, 0.56 MCC) on Dataset.csv.
skills.name: rna-5hmc-site-classification
skills.search_text: rna-5hmc-site-classification Use when RNA sequences of length 41 need to be classified as 5hmC site vs non-site using position-specific sequence descriptors, or when reproducing the iRNA5hmC-PS benchmark (78.3% accuracy, 0.56 MCC) on Dataset.csv. The goal is combining these position-specific features with frequency-based k-mer features in a single model — the authors report this does not work well and defer it to a future feature subspace ensemble approach Sequences are not 41 nt long or not in FASTA format — the webserver and pipeline assume 41-nt RNA sequences Input is already an engineered feature table from a different descriptor family; the group-wise feature selection strategy is tailored to the paper's PSG k-mer feature groups http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 Reproduce iRNA5hmC-PS: classify RNA 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) sites using position-specific k-mer and position-specific gapped k-mer (PSG k-mer) features with group-wise feature selection and a Logistic Regression classifier, evaluated by repeated 5-fold cross-validation and an independent test set. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2020.10.032
skills.summary: Reproduce iRNA5hmC-PS: classify RNA 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) sites using position-specific k-mer and position-specific gapped k-mer (PSG k-mer) features with group-wise feature selection and a Logistic Regression classifier, evaluated by repeated 5-fold cross-validation and an independent test set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is combining these position-specific features with frequency-based k-mer features in a single model — the authors report this does not work well and defer it to a future feature subspace ensemble approach Sequences are not 41 nt long or not in FASTA format — the webserver and pipeline assume 41-nt RNA sequences Input is already an engineered feature table from a different descriptor family; the group-wise feature selection strategy is tailored to the paper's PSG k-mer feature groups

skills.description: Use when multiple small RNA-seq samples have been annotated by COMPSRA and per-sample tab-delimited RNA count files must be merged into one RNA-by-sample count matrix before downstream normalization or differential expression.
skills.name: rna-count-matrix-aggregation
skills.search_text: rna-count-matrix-aggregation Use when multiple small RNA-seq samples have been annotated by COMPSRA and per-sample tab-delimited RNA count files must be merged into one RNA-by-sample count matrix before downstream normalization or differential expression. Case/control differential expression statistics are needed — use the -fd mode with -fdcase/-fdctrl, -fdnorm cpm and -fdtest mwu instead of merge-only -fm/-fms Input is raw FASTQ or unmapped reads — samples must first pass QC, Alignment (STAR) and Annotation modules before counts exist to merge Only a single sample is available — there is nothing to aggregate across sample columns http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0099 Aggregate per-sample small RNA read-count files output by the COMPSRA Annotation module into a single tab-delimited matrix with RNA molecules as rows and samples as columns, using the COMPSRA Function module's -fm/-fms merge mode. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-61495-0
skills.summary: Aggregate per-sample small RNA read-count files output by the COMPSRA Annotation module into a single tab-delimited matrix with RNA molecules as rows and samples as columns, using the COMPSRA Function module's -fm/-fms merge mode.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Case/control differential expression statistics are needed — use the -fd mode with -fdcase/-fdctrl, -fdnorm cpm and -fdtest mwu instead of merge-only -fm/-fms Input is raw FASTQ or unmapped reads — samples must first pass QC, Alignment (STAR) and Annotation modules before counts exist to merge Only a single sample is available — there is nothing to aggregate across sample columns

skills.description: Use when preparing base-level RNA-seq pileup matrices (e.g., TCGA cohort) for SCISSOR shape-change detection and genes with many non-expressed samples must be identified and excluded.
skills.name: rna-coverage-angle-based-on-off-classification
skills.search_text: rna-coverage-angle-based-on-off-classification Use when preparing base-level RNA-seq pileup matrices (e.g., TCGA cohort) for SCISSOR shape-change detection and genes with many non-expressed samples must be identified and excluded. Genes have already been filtered by expression-level thresholds (e.g., percentile cutoffs on median and MAD of normalized RSEM values), so on/off shape classification would be redundant The cohort is too small or too heterogeneous in library preparation for a gene mean vector to be a meaningful shape reference (SCISSOR has been used successfully down to ~30 samples) http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A SCISSOR-based on/off gene classification step that measures, per gene, the high-dimensional angle between each sample's base-level coverage vector and the gene mean vector, then flags genes with many 'off' samples (>20%) for exclusion before genome-wide shape-change analysis. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41467-020-20593-3
skills.summary: A SCISSOR-based on/off gene classification step that measures, per gene, the high-dimensional angle between each sample's base-level coverage vector and the gene mean vector, then flags genes with many 'off' samples (>20%) for exclusion before genome-wide shape-change analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Genes have already been filtered by expression-level thresholds (e.g., percentile cutoffs on median and MAD of normalized RSEM values), so on/off shape classification would be redundant The cohort is too small or too heterogeneous in library preparation for a gene mean vector to be a meaningful shape reference (SCISSOR has been used successfully down to ~30 samples)

skills.description: Use when REDInet inference needs tabix-indexed REDItools outTables from coordinate-sorted RNAseq BAMs, or when benchmarking REDItools v1 vs v3 pileup runtime on very deep HEK293T libraries.

skills.search_text: rna-editing-pileup-generation Use when REDInet inference needs tabix-indexed REDItools outTables from coordinate-sorted RNAseq BAMs, or when benchmarking REDItools v1 vs v3 pileup runtime on very deep HEK293T libraries. Input is already a tabix-indexed REDItools outTable — go directly to REDInet_Inference.py / REDInet_Inference_light_ver.py instead of re-running pileup The goal is classifying candidate A-to-G substitutions as RNA editing or artifacts — that is REDInet (TCN classifier) inference, not pileup generation The analysis requires WGS/WES-coupled empirical filtering or ML comparison via RED-ML/RDDpred guidelines rather than plain RNAseq pileup profiles http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Generate complete genome-wide RNAseq pileup profiles (REDItools outTables) from coordinate-sorted RNAseq BAMs using REDItools v1 (REDItoolDnaRna.py) or the re-implemented REDItools3, choosing v3 when wall-clock time matters on deep libraries (~277M reads/sample). transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bib/bbaf107
skills.summary: Generate complete genome-wide RNAseq pileup profiles (REDItools outTables) from coordinate-sorted RNAseq BAMs using REDItools v1 (REDItoolDnaRna.py) or the re-implemented REDItools3, choosing v3 when wall-clock time matters on deep libraries (~277M reads/sample).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a tabix-indexed REDItools outTable — go directly to REDInet_Inference.py / REDInet_Inference_light_ver.py instead of re-running pileup The goal is classifying candidate A-to-G substitutions as RNA editing or artifacts — that is REDInet (TCN classifier) inference, not pileup generation The analysis requires WGS/WES-coupled empirical filtering or ML comparison via RED-ML/RDDpred guidelines rather than plain RNAseq pileup profiles

skills.description: Use when you have tabix-indexed REDItools outTables of candidate A-to-G substitutions from RNAseq BAMs and need to distinguish genuine ADAR-mediated editing sites from SNPs or artifacts, especially when matched DNAseq data is unavailable.
skills.name: rna-editing-site-deep-learning-inference
skills.search_text: rna-editing-site-deep-learning-inference Use when you have tabix-indexed REDItools outTables of candidate A-to-G substitutions from RNAseq BAMs and need to distinguish genuine ADAR-mediated editing sites from SNPs or artifacts, especially when matched DNAseq data is unavailable. When a high-quality reference transcriptome exists and genome-guided alignment or barcode-aware reconstruction (cloudrnaSPAdes) is available — standard short-read assemblers left most simulated isoforms undetected When input is large-genome whole-genome sequencing data rather than transcriptomic reads — SPAdes was designed for small genomes and offers separate pipelines (metaSPAdes, plasmidSPAdes) for those cases http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Assemble full-length transcript isoforms de novo from RNA-seq (including bulk barcoded linked-read) data using SPAdes-family assemblers — specifically rnaSPAdes via rnaspades.py and cloudrnaSPAdes — and benchmark the resulting contigs against barcode-aware pipelines. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad781
skills.summary: Assemble full-length transcript isoforms de novo from RNA-seq (including bulk barcoded linked-read) data using SPAdes-family assemblers — specifically rnaSPAdes via rnaspades.py and cloudrnaSPAdes — and benchmark the resulting contigs against barcode-aware pipelines.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a high-quality reference transcriptome exists and genome-guided alignment or barcode-aware reconstruction (cloudrnaSPAdes) is available — standard short-read assemblers left most simulated isoforms undetected When input is large-genome whole-genome sequencing data rather than transcriptomic reads — SPAdes was designed for small genomes and offers separate pipelines (metaSPAdes, plasmidSPAdes) for those cases

skills.description: Use when modeling RNA-seq gene counts from paired/related sample designs where a genetic kinship matrix is available, and you need per-gene DEG calls plus AIC-based comparison of models with and without the kinship covariance random effect.
skills.name: rna-seq-differential-expression-analysis
skills.search_text: rna-seq-differential-expression-analysis Use when modeling RNA-seq gene counts from paired/related sample designs where a genetic kinship matrix is available, and you need per-gene DEG calls plus AIC-based comparison of models with and without the kinship covariance random effect. Samples are unrelated — without a meaningful kinship matrix, run only the lm/lme forms; the paper's kinship comparison requires a related cohort where kinship impacts model fit You need a model form not supported by kimma (it targets covariates, weights, random effects, covariance matrices, and fit metrics for RNA-seq, not arbitrary non-linear or single-cell modeling) Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ) — kimma starts from a gene count matrix, not from alignment or quantification http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Fit per-gene linear models and linear mixed effects models to RNA-seq gene counts using the kimma R package, including a kinship-covariance model variant executed through lme4qtl::relmatLmer, then compare model fit (delta AIC) and differential expression calls (FDR) between kinship and non-kinship forms. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad279
skills.summary: Fit per-gene linear models and linear mixed effects models to RNA-seq gene counts using the kimma R package, including a kinship-covariance model variant executed through lme4qtl::relmatLmer, then compare model fit (delta AIC) and differential expression calls (FDR) between kinship and non-kinship forms.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Samples are unrelated — without a meaningful kinship matrix, run only the lm/lme forms; the paper's kinship comparison requires a related cohort where kinship impacts model fit You need a model form not supported by kimma (it targets covariates, weights, random effects, covariance matrices, and fit metrics for RNA-seq, not arbitrary non-linear or single-cell modeling) Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ) — kimma starts from a gene count matrix, not from alignment or quantification

skills.description: Use when a normalized RNA-seq expression matrix with two-group labels (e.g., 46 critical vs 23 non-critical COVID-19 cases from SEMdata) must be turned into per-gene DEG P-values to seed network analyses.
skills.name: rna-seq-differential-expression-analysis
skills.search_text: rna-seq-differential-expression-analysis Use when a normalized RNA-seq expression matrix with two-group labels (e.g., 46 critical vs 23 non-critical COVID-19 cases from SEMdata) must be turned into per-gene DEG P-values to seed network analyses. The expression data are raw counts requiring normalization first — limma linear modeling here assumes normalized RNA-seq data as input. The goal is already perturbation analysis (SEMrun node/edge models) on an existing graph rather than deriving the DEG P-values that seed it. The dataset is not the two-group benchmark (e.g., single-group or time-series designs) since the design matrix here encodes the critical-vs-non-critical contrast. http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Computes gene-level differential expression P-values on the GSE172114 COVID-19 RNA-seq benchmark (46 critical cases vs 23 non-critical controls) using limma's empirical Bayes linear modeling with Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment, producing the seed/P-value table consumed by downstream SEMtree and active subnetwork analyses. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad377
skills.summary: Computes gene-level differential expression P-values on the GSE172114 COVID-19 RNA-seq benchmark (46 critical cases vs 23 non-critical controls) using limma's empirical Bayes linear modeling with Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment, producing the seed/P-value table consumed by downstream SEMtree and active subnetwork analyses.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The expression data are raw counts requiring normalization first — limma linear modeling here assumes normalized RNA-seq data as input. The goal is already perturbation analysis (SEMrun node/edge models) on an existing graph rather than deriving the DEG P-values that seed it. The dataset is not the two-group benchmark (e.g., single-group or time-series designs) since the design matrix here encodes the critical-vs-non-critical contrast.

skills.description: Use when a raw RNA-seq counts matrix (.csv, Ensembl ID rows, sample ID columns) must be tested for differentially expressed genes between sample groups, or when edgeR/limma/DESeq2 runtimes must be benchmarked on identical input.
skills.name: rna-seq-differential-expression-analysis
skills.search_text: rna-seq-differential-expression-analysis Use when a raw RNA-seq counts matrix (.csv, Ensembl ID rows, sample ID columns) must be tested for differentially expressed genes between sample groups, or when edgeR/limma/DESeq2 runtimes must be benchmarked on identical input. Input is already a TPM matrix or GSVA score matrix — ARMT normalizes counts to log2(TPM+1) for GSVA, but DEG analysis needs the raw counts matrix Differential analysis of GSVA scores or gene mutation (.maf) data — ARMT routes these through separate workflows, not the counts-based DEG path A single quick DEG call is needed and runtime on a large TCGA cohort is critical — DESeq2 is significantly slower than edgeR and limma on the same input http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Differential expression analysis of RNA-seq count matrices (Ensembl gene IDs x samples, e.g. TCGA LUAD raw counts) using the R packages edgeR, limma and DESeq2 that the ARMT paper integrates, including side-by-side runtime comparison of the three tools on an identical counts matrix. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.csbj.2021.08.009
skills.summary: Differential expression analysis of RNA-seq count matrices (Ensembl gene IDs x samples, e.g. TCGA LUAD raw counts) using the R packages edgeR, limma and DESeq2 that the ARMT paper integrates, including side-by-side runtime comparison of the three tools on an identical counts matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a TPM matrix or GSVA score matrix — ARMT normalizes counts to log2(TPM+1) for GSVA, but DEG analysis needs the raw counts matrix Differential analysis of GSVA scores or gene mutation (.maf) data — ARMT routes these through separate workflows, not the counts-based DEG path A single quick DEG call is needed and runtime on a large TCGA cohort is critical — DESeq2 is significantly slower than edgeR and limma on the same input

skills.description: Use when you have a raw RNA-seq count matrix plus sample metadata with a defined experimental design and need robust DEG calls that are not biased by one method's assumptions.
skills.name: rna-seq-differential-expression-analysis
skills.search_text: rna-seq-differential-expression-analysis Use when you have a raw RNA-seq count matrix plus sample metadata with a defined experimental design and need robust DEG calls that are not biased by one method's assumptions. Input is already a DEG call set or consensus table rather than raw counts — no DE detection step is needed. The goal is downstream interpretation only (co-expression module detection or functional enrichment on existing DEGs) rather than DEG detection itself. The data are not RNA-seq counts (e.g. single-cell or proteomics data) for which DESeq2/edgeR/limma count-model assumptions do not apply. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Detect differentially expressed genes from an RNA-seq count table by running multiple DE methods (DESeq2, edgeR/limma, NOISeq) through the DEgenes Hunter pipeline of ExpHunter Suite and combining their calls via a minimum vote threshold, because single-method results vary by dataset properties. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-021-94343-w
skills.summary: Detect differentially expressed genes from an RNA-seq count table by running multiple DE methods (DESeq2, edgeR/limma, NOISeq) through the DEgenes Hunter pipeline of ExpHunter Suite and combining their calls via a minimum vote threshold, because single-method results vary by dataset properties.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a DEG call set or consensus table rather than raw counts — no DE detection step is needed. The goal is downstream interpretation only (co-expression module detection or functional enrichment on existing DEGs) rather than DEG detection itself. The data are not RNA-seq counts (e.g. single-cell or proteomics data) for which DESeq2/edgeR/limma count-model assumptions do not apply.

skills.description: Use when you have a gene-by-cell RNA-seq expression matrix (thousands of genes) with batch labels and need a lower-dimensional embedding that preserves batch-specific variation for batch effect detection/quantification.
skills.name: rna-seq-dimensionality-reduction
skills.search_text: rna-seq-dimensionality-reduction Use when you have a gene-by-cell RNA-seq expression matrix (thousands of genes) with batch labels and need a lower-dimensional embedding that preserves batch-specific variation for batch effect detection/quantification. Input features have already been reduced to a few hundreds by another dimensionality reduction technique — use the λ1=λ3=1, λ2=2 hyperparameter regime rather than the high-dimensional settings, and PCA may suffice The goal is batch effect removal/correction of the expression data rather than detection/quantification of batch effects via an embedding Only linear batch effects need assessment on local cell distributions in PC space — simpler PCA-based batch estimation may be adequate http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Generate a low-dimensional nonlinear BEENE embedding from RNA-seq data using a deep auto-encoder that simultaneously learns batch and biological variables, suitable for detecting both linear and nonlinear batch effects where PCA-based embeddings fail. transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad479
skills.summary: Generate a low-dimensional nonlinear BEENE embedding from RNA-seq data using a deep auto-encoder that simultaneously learns batch and biological variables, suitable for detecting both linear and nonlinear batch effects where PCA-based embeddings fail.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input features have already been reduced to a few hundreds by another dimensionality reduction technique — use the λ1=λ3=1, λ2=2 hyperparameter regime rather than the high-dimensional settings, and PCA may suffice The goal is batch effect removal/correction of the expression data rather than detection/quantification of batch effects via an embedding Only linear batch effects need assessment on local cell distributions in PC space — simpler PCA-based batch estimation may be adequate

skills.description: Use when benchmarking an alternative-splicing or ASAS detection method against competitors and you need simulated paired allelic count data with controlled variance and replicate number instead of real RNA-seq reads.
skills.name: rna-seq-exon-count-simulation-from-population-parameters
skills.search_text: rna-seq-exon-count-simulation-from-population-parameters Use when benchmarking an alternative-splicing or ASAS detection method against competitors and you need simulated paired allelic count data with controlled variance and replicate number instead of real RNA-seq reads. You need ASAS detection on real RNA-seq data (e.g. GM12878 or Geuvadis samples) rather than a controlled power comparison — use the full PAIRADISE pipeline with fastq inputs instead Your differential-splicing comparison uses unpaired (single-condition) RNA-seq replicates, where the paired-model framing of PAIRADISE vs the rMATS paired model does not apply You only have raw fastq/vcf data and no population psi/effective-length distribution to sample simulation parameters from Simulates exon-skipping inclusion/skipping count data (IJC/SJC with incLen/skpLen effective lengths, mirroring the PAIRADISE output table schema) by sampling psi and effective-length parameters from the Geuvadis CEU population distribution, to benchmark ASAS detection methods by ROC AUC and TPR at 5% FPR. transcriptomics/v2 10.1016/j.ajhg.2020.07.005
skills.summary: Simulates exon-skipping inclusion/skipping count data (IJC/SJC with incLen/skpLen effective lengths, mirroring the PAIRADISE output table schema) by sampling psi and effective-length parameters from the Geuvadis CEU population distribution, to benchmark ASAS detection methods by ROC AUC and TPR at 5% FPR.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need ASAS detection on real RNA-seq data (e.g. GM12878 or Geuvadis samples) rather than a controlled power comparison — use the full PAIRADISE pipeline with fastq inputs instead Your differential-splicing comparison uses unpaired (single-condition) RNA-seq replicates, where the paired-model framing of PAIRADISE vs the rMATS paired model does not apply You only have raw fastq/vcf data and no population psi/effective-length distribution to sample simulation parameters from

skills.description: Use when you need to evaluate whether genes from extracted active subnetworks discriminate between two patient groups (case/control) and to compare classifier performance (accuracy, predictor gene set size) across subnetwork detection methods.
skills.name: rna-seq-expression-classification
skills.search_text: rna-seq-expression-classification Use when you need to evaluate whether genes from extracted active subnetworks discriminate between two patient groups (case/control) and to compare classifier performance (accuracy, predictor gene set size) across subnetwork detection methods. Input data are raw counts without the nonparanormal transform applied — normality assumptions needed for SEM/LDA-based classification are violated; run SEMgraph::transformData first. The task is subnetwork extraction itself rather than classification benchmarking — use the upstream SEMtree/Steiner-tree skill instead. Only one sample group is available (no binary case/control label vector) — the penalized discriminant classifier requires the group vector to train. http://edamontology.org/topic_3518 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Classifies patients (e.g., critical vs non-critical COVID-19 cases from GSE172114) by fitting a PenalizedLDA penalized Fisher's discriminant classifier on genes extracted from SEMtree-derived active subnetworks, benchmarking classifier accuracy and parsimony per subnetwork detection method (mirroring Table 3 of the SEMtree paper). transcriptomics/v2 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad377
skills.summary: Classifies patients (e.g., critical vs non-critical COVID-19 cases from GSE172114) by fitting a PenalizedLDA penalized Fisher's discriminant classifier on genes extracted from SEMtree-derived active subnetworks, benchmarking classifier accuracy and parsimony per subnetwork detection method (mirroring Table 3 of the SEMtree paper).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data are raw counts without the nonparanormal transform applied — normality assumptions needed for SEM/LDA-based classification are violated; run SEMgraph::transformData first. The task is subnetwork extraction itself rather than classification benchmarking — use the upstream SEMtree/Steiner-tree skill instead. Only one sample group is available (no binary case/control label vector) — the penalized discriminant classifier requires the group vector to train.

skills.description: Use when raw TCGA RNA-Seq gene expression matrices must be filtered and normalized before computing gene co-expression networks, and only protein-coding/lncRNA genes with sufficient expression (mean zFPKM > -3.0) should be kept.
skills.name: rna-seq-expression-data-preprocessing
skills.search_text: rna-seq-expression-data-preprocessing Use when raw TCGA RNA-Seq gene expression matrices must be filtered and normalized before computing gene co-expression networks, and only protein-coding/lncRNA genes with sufficient expression (mean zFPKM > -3.0) should be kept. Input data is already a filtered expression matrix or a precomputed co-expression network rather than raw TCGA RNA-Seq expression data The target gene set includes miRNAs or non-coding RNAs other than protein-coding and long non-coding RNA genes, which are excluded by this preprocessing filter http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Pre-processes TCGA RNA-Seq gene expression data using GMQL/PyGMQL, retaining protein-coding and long non-coding RNA genes whose mean zFPKM exceeds -3.0 in both normal and cancer conditions, as the first step of building fused co-expression networks for KIRC, LIHC and PRAD. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41540-021-00175-9
skills.summary: Pre-processes TCGA RNA-Seq gene expression data using GMQL/PyGMQL, retaining protein-coding and long non-coding RNA genes whose mean zFPKM exceeds -3.0 in both normal and cancer conditions, as the first step of building fused co-expression networks for KIRC, LIHC and PRAD.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data is already a filtered expression matrix or a precomputed co-expression network rather than raw TCGA RNA-Seq expression data The target gene set includes miRNAs or non-coding RNAs other than protein-coding and long non-coding RNA genes, which are excluded by this preprocessing filter

skills.description: Use when a TCGA-style RNA-seq expression matrix with five intrinsic subtype labels (Luminal A/B, Basal, Her2-enriched, Normal-like) must be turned into a classifier feature space for supervised single-sample subtyping.
skills.name: rna-seq-expression-feature-representation
skills.search_text: rna-seq-expression-feature-representation Use when a TCGA-style RNA-seq expression matrix with five intrinsic subtype labels (Luminal A/B, Basal, Her2-enriched, Normal-like) must be turned into a classifier feature space for supervised single-sample subtyping. The task requires reference-based centroid classification (standard PAM50) rather than a trained single-sample caller, and a matched reference cohort is genuinely available No subtype labels exist for the expression data, since this representation depends on supervised training with the five intrinsic subtype classes Input is restricted to a small predefined gene panel (e.g. PAM50-only genes) when the goal is global-transcriptome feature selection with Lasso/Ridge regularization http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Build a supervised-learning feature representation for breast cancer intrinsic subtyping from the global TCGA RNA-seq transcriptome (19,737 genes), where ad-hoc gene selection plus Lasso/Ridge-regularized multiclass logistic regression (mLR) outperformed Decision Forest, Decision Jungle, FFNN and SVM learners. It replaces reference-cohort-dependent PAM50 centroid correlation with single-sample classification on the full gene expression matrix. transcriptomics/v2 10.1038/s41598-020-70832-2
skills.summary: Build a supervised-learning feature representation for breast cancer intrinsic subtyping from the global TCGA RNA-seq transcriptome (19,737 genes), where ad-hoc gene selection plus Lasso/Ridge-regularized multiclass logistic regression (mLR) outperformed Decision Forest, Decision Jungle, FFNN and SVM learners. It replaces reference-cohort-dependent PAM50 centroid correlation with single-sample classification on the full gene expression matrix.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires reference-based centroid classification (standard PAM50) rather than a trained single-sample caller, and a matched reference cohort is genuinely available No subtype labels exist for the expression data, since this representation depends on supervised training with the five intrinsic subtype classes Input is restricted to a small predefined gene panel (e.g. PAM50-only genes) when the goal is global-transcriptome feature selection with Lasso/Ridge regularization

skills.search_text: rna-seq-fastq-download-from-geo-ena Use when raw RNA-seq reads for a published study must be fetched from public archives — GSE accessions via GEO/SRA or a BioProject via direct ENA run downloads — before transcript-level quantification. skills.summary: Retrieves raw paired-end RNA-seq FASTQ files for published disease datasets (OIH, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Behcet's) from GEO/SRA accessions (GSE203206, GSE128177, GSE205867) and via direct ENA run downloads for BioProject PRJNA433105, as the entry step of the CanIsoNet transcript-abundance pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The transcript abundance matrix (e.g. tpm_abundance_matrix.tsv) already exists and quantification is complete — downloading FASTQ again is redundant. The target data are the 27 cancer types from the PCAWG project, which CanIsoNet covers through PCAWG rather than these four RNA-seq dataset downloads.
